About This Edition

Published by Remnant of Promise — remnantofpromise.org

The fourteen books of the King James Apocrypha as set in the original
1611 King James Bible. The source text is the public-domain 1769
Cambridge / Blayney standardized revision of the King James Apocrypha,
drawn from the public-domain digital release of the King James Bible
with Apocrypha distributed by eBible.org under public-domain status.

Editorial restoration of the divine name (YAHUAH where the textual
evidence supports the Tetragrammaton), modernization of archaic English
to contemporary forms, light internal punctuation, and the Nazarite
commentary herein are original to this edition. The chapter and verse
divisions of the 1769 King James text are preserved exactly. No verses
have been added or removed. No passage has been paraphrased.

All scripture witness is offered with the prayer that the Spirit will
use it for the awakening of the remnant of YAHUAH.

Introduction

This is not another reprint of the 1769 King James Apocrypha. This is a
restored-names edition with full Nazarite commentary, built for the
awakening remnant.

Why do these fourteen books matter? Because they were bound into the
Bible the English-speaking world was given. The 1611 King James Bible —
the volume that shaped four hundred years of English-speaking faith —
placed the Apocrypha between the Old and New Testaments. They were not
loose papers tucked into the back. They were stitched into the spine,
laid out in order, printed under the same royal authorization as Genesis
and Matthew. Every King James Bible printed for the first two and a half
centuries of its existence carried these books inside it. The decision
to remove them came later, and it came through the British and Foreign
Bible Society in 1826 — a decision driven by funding politics and
Protestant boundary-setting, not by the manuscript witness, and not by
the four hundred years of English faith that had received these books as
part of the household library of the covenant community.

Why does that matter for you, the reader of the Restored Names Series?
Because the world your fathers received included these books. The
cadence of English faith was formed in their company. When Paul wrote of
the long faithfulness of those who had preceded him, his readers' minds
went to passages in 1 and 2 Maccabees as readily as to passages in 1 and
2 Kings. When the writer of Hebrews described those who were tortured
and would not accept deliverance, that they might obtain a better
resurrection (Hebrews 11:35), he was citing the mother of the seven
brothers under Antiochus Epiphanes — a story preserved in 2 Maccabees 7.
The audience knew it. The author knew the audience knew it. The
reference is woven into the text on the assumption that the reader
carries this background already.

These books are not Torah. They are not prophets. They are not the
writings of the Messiah's apostles. But they are not vapor, either. They
are the historical, devotional, wisdom, and apocalyptic literature of
the centuries between the closing of the Hebrew prophetic canon and the
opening of the New Testament. They tell you what was happening in the
four hundred years your Bible passes over in silence. They name the
kings of the north and the kings of the south after Daniel left off
naming them. They show you the temple state your Messiah walked into,
the Hasmonean dynasty he was born under, the Pharisees and Sadducees and
zealot factions and Essene withdrawal that he addressed in his ministry.
Without the Apocrypha, the world of the Gospels appears out of nowhere.
With the Apocrypha, the world of the Gospels stands in the long line
where it actually stands.

What makes this edition different from every other Apocrypha on Amazon?
First, restored divine names — Yahuah (God), Elohim, the Most High —
where the 1769 King James text uses LORD, the Lord, and God in places
where the underlying Hebrew or Greek points to the covenant name, the
plural-majesty, or the formal title. Second, modernized English — the
thee, thou, hath, doth, and unto of the 1769 era have been brought into
modern English so the reader can hear the text rather than translate it
as they read. Third, full Nazarite commentary after every chapter,
written from the framework of the Restored Names Series — a
Torah-observant covenant lens that holds the threefold deception of
institutional Christianity, Judaism, and the Hebrew roots / Torah
observant world equally accountable. And fourth, a cross-reference line
at the end of every chapter, listing every scripture the commentary
engaged, so the reader can take the trail back into the Word and walk it
themselves.

The competitors sell cheap reprints of the 1769 text without commentary,
without restored names, without the covenant lens. The few editions that
do offer commentary almost universally come from one of two camps: the
Catholic and Orthodox tradition, which treats these books as canonical
scripture, or the Protestant academic tradition, which treats them as
historical curiosities and pads the introductions with manuscript
debate. Neither serves the awakening remnant. The first inflates these
books beyond their station; the second deflates them beneath it. This
edition does neither.

If Yahuah (God) has opened your eyes to His Torah, if you have begun to
see that your fathers inherited lies (Jeremiah 16:19), if you are
walking out of one of the four houses and into the wilderness of His
Word with no commentary in your pack — this volume is for you. It does
not require you to come pre-armed with seminary Greek. It does not
require you to have read every Pseudepigraphal text under the sun. It
requires a heart that wants to hear, a Bible open in the lap, and the
willingness to test what is read against the unchanging standard of His
commandments.

The Spirit cited Maccabees through the writer of Hebrews. That alone is
reason enough to read it. What this edition adds is the framework that
lets you read it the way a son of Adam coming home should read it — not
as canon, not as fable, but as witness.

Before You Begin

This book combines three elements into one integrated study.

First, the full scripture text of the fourteen books of the 1769 King
James Apocrypha, in the order they appeared in the original 1611 King
James Bible. This is the public-domain 1769 standardized text — the
version that became the printed standard from the late eighteenth
century onward — with restored divine names and modernized English (you
instead of thee and thou, has instead of hath, says instead of saith,
and so on). Sentence structure has been preserved where it carries the
text's cadence; archaic vocabulary has been opened where it would
otherwise stop the modern reader cold.

Second, section-by-section commentary from a modern Nazarite
perspective. The commentary is Torah-observant and covenant-aware. It
connects every major passage to the full counsel of Scripture — from the
five books of Moses, through the prophets, into the Gospels and the
letters of Paul, and finally into the Revelation of Yahusha (Jesus). The
commentary names what the passage shows, names what it does not show,
names what has been read into it by traditions that should never have
stood, and lays the passage back into its proper place in the long story
of the scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel) and their Shepherd's
pursuit.

Third, a cross-reference line at the close of every commentary. Every
major passage cited in the commentary is named in context as the
argument is made, and then listed again at the end of the chapter so the
reader can carry the references forward into their own study. The
references are not exhaustive. They are the live ones — the verses the
commentary actually leans on. If you take only one habit from this book
into the rest of your reading life, take this one: never let a
commentary close without the references in your hand.

Each chapter follows the same structure: the scripture text appears
first, followed by a visual divider, followed by the commentary. At the
end of every commentary is a Cross-references line listing the
scriptures cited in that commentary, in the order they were cited.

The commentary names three deceived groups with equal care:
institutional Christianity, Judaism, and the Torah-observant / Hebrew
roots / Messianic movement. None of them is the enemy. All of them have
inherited lies — exactly what Jeremiah 16:19 said the awakening remnant
would one day confess. The patience extended to the Christian reader is
the same patience extended to the Yahudi (Jewish) reader and the same
patience extended to the Hebrew roots reader. There is no group on the
field of this book that is treated as having arrived. There is no
destination camp. There is only the wilderness walk back to the Word,
and the long company of the lost sheep coming home from the four
directions of their scattering.

Three interpretive keys recur throughout the commentary and should be
named at the outset:

The 1234 of Truth — 1 John 2:3–4 — is the master filter. And hereby we
do know that we know Him, if we keep His commandments. He that says, I
know Him, and keeps not His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is
not in him. That is the standard the Word itself provides. Any reading
of any scripture that requires 1 John 2:3–4 to be false is a wrong
reading. Yahuah (God) does not lie. The filter applies to the commentary
in this book just as readily as it applies to any pulpit teaching, any
pamphlet, any podcast, any verse you ever heard preached at you. Test
all things by the 1234.

The Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul — when Paul is cited, two
steps are always followed. First, establish what Paul was drawing FROM:
he was a Pharisee trained in the Torah and the prophets, and every
theological move he makes is sourced in the Hebrew scriptures. Find that
source first. Second, identify what Paul was arguing AGAINST: his
letters are one side of a conversation, and the false gospel he was
rebutting becomes identifiable only after his Torah foundation is clear.
This sequence is the antidote to two failures the awakening reader will
recognize: the church that misuses Paul to abolish the Torah, and the
Torah-observant believer who has dropped Paul because he could not be
reconciled with the Torah the reader loves. Both failures share a single
source: a Paul read without his Torah foundation.

The Three Categories — not Yahudi (Jew) and Gentile but three. The
inherited religious world has flattened the covenant people into two
boxes: Yahudi (Jew) and Gentile, Yahudah (Judah) and everybody else. The
framework rejects the binary. The real shape is three categories, named
by the prophets and held throughout this volume:

Yahudah (Judah) — the southern house, the tribe of Yahudah (Judah) with
portions of Levi and Benjamin, the people who retained their identity
through exile and is the Yahudim (Jews) of the modern world. They are
not all of Yashar'el (Israel). They are one house of a two-house
covenant people.

The scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel) — the ten northern tribes,
scattered through the Assyrian captivity in 722 BCE, dispersed among the
nations until they became indistinguishable from the nations. They lost
their language, their Torah, their identity. They are a specific people
with a paternal blood heritage — not a spiritual category, not a
metaphor, not a self-selected group. The prophets named them: Ephraim,
Yosef, the house of the north. The prophets promised their gathering in
two streams: from the land of the north (the Arzareth remnant in the
invisible wilderness, 2 Esdras 13 and 1 Enoch 60) and from all the lands
where the Father drove them (Jeremiah 16:13–16). The awakening across
the world right now is the fishing of the second stream.

The nations — those who are not of the paternal blood seed of Yashar'el
(Israel). They are not a branch of the olive tree of Romans 11. Their
place in the covenant is the stranger and sojourner of Torah — welcomed
into the covenant household, genuinely loved, under the provisions Torah
makes for the stranger, but not the seed of promise. The Exodus pattern
held: a mixed multitude came out with Yashar'el (Israel), was numbered
in the camp, and was given its own rules as strangers and sojourners.
The distinction was real then and remains real now. The prophets
maintain it through the restoration.

These three keys — the 1234, the Paul sequence, and the Three Categories
— will recur throughout. They are introduced here, named again at length
in the Reading the Apocrypha as the Remnant chapter, and applied chapter
by chapter through the commentary that follows.

A Note on the Translation

This edition is built on the 1769 King James Apocrypha — the Cambridge /
Blayney standardized revision of the original 1611 text — which is the
version that became the printed English standard from the late
eighteenth century onward and which has been firmly in the public domain
for centuries. The plain text used as the source for this edition was
drawn from the public-domain digital release of the King James Bible
with Apocrypha distributed by eBible.org under the same public-domain
status that has covered the 1769 text since its publication. No
copyrighted critical edition, no copyrighted modern translation, and no
proprietary apparatus was consulted in the production of the source text
of this volume.

The 1769 text was chosen over the 1611 for two reasons. First, it is the
version most modern Apocrypha reprints already use, which gives the
English-speaking reader a continuity of voice with what they have likely
already encountered in print. Second, the 1769 cleaned up the printing
irregularities and orthographic chaos of the 1611 first edition without
changing the underlying translation in any substantive way. The reader
who picks up this volume after having read a 1611 facsimile will find
every passage in its expected place and every word in its expected
sense, only spelled the way modern English now spells it.

Four classes of edits have been made to the 1769 source.

Sacred-name restoration — every mention. The 1769 King James text uses
the conventions of its era: LORD in small caps for the covenant name
(the Tetragrammaton), the Lord in standard typography for the formal
title, and God for the plural-majesty Elohim. This edition restores the
sacred names at every mention where the underlying text supports them,
not at first mention only. The reader who opens to any page in any
chapter sees the restored names with their conventional English
equivalents in parentheses, every time, so that no one is left
translating in their head and no one is asked to remember a glossary
entry from a hundred pages back. The retention mechanism is the
parenthetical. It is not dropped for variety, and it is not dropped for
aesthetics. Every mention, every time.

The restored names used in this edition, with the conventional English
the parenthetical preserves:

Yahuah (God) — the covenant name, the Tetragrammaton restored. Used
wherever the underlying text — Hebrew, Greek, or Latin — points to the
covenant name. The vast majority of the Apocrypha is in Greek, and the
Greek apocryphal books use the title kurios (the Lord) for the covenant
deity. In these books the formal title has been carried into Yahuah
(God) at every mention, on the warrant that the second-temple
translators who put kurios where the Hebrew tradition had put YHWH were
observing a vocalization taboo, not erasing the name. Restoring the name
at every mention restores what the taboo set aside. Where the Greek
manuscript witnesses preserve the Tetragrammaton itself — in 1 Esdras'
citation of Ezra-Nehemiah material, in the Hebrew-tradition portions of
Sirach and 1 Maccabees, and in the prayers of the Greek additions —
Yahuah (God) is restored without controversy.

Elohim (God) — the title for the Most High. Used where the formal title
is paired with a possessive pronoun (your Elohim, our Elohim, their
Elohim, his Elohim, my Elohim), since the covenant personal name does
not naturally take a possessive in covenant grammar. The plural-majesty
title does, and the title carries the right register for those
constructions.

The Most High — the formal title where the underlying Greek is
hupsistos. Preserved as a title without sacred-name restoration, since
hupsistos is itself a title and the King James text rendered it as such.

Yashar'el (Israel) — the covenant name of the people Yahuah (God) formed
from the twelve tribes. Used at every mention.

Yahudah (Judah) — the southern house, the tribe, and the personal name.
Used at every mention. The regional names Judea and Jewry are kept in
their conventional English forms, since they are place-names rather than
the covenant people-name.

Yahudim (Jews) / Yahudi (Jew) / Yahudi (Jewish) — the plural, singular,
and adjectival forms of the people of the house of Yahudah (Judah). Used
at every mention.

Messiah (Christ) — the anointed one. The Apocrypha references the
Messiah explicitly only in 2 Esdras 7:29, where the Latin text names the
figure who is to come. There Christ has been restored to Messiah
(Christ).

Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) — the Spirit. Restored at every mention,
which in the fourteen books is two: Wisdom of Solomon 9:17 and 2 Esdras
14:22.

Yahusha (Jesus) — the Messiah. Restored only at 2 Esdras 7:28, the
single passage in the fourteen books where the figure named is the
coming Messiah. Every other "Jesus" in the Apocrypha is Joshua / Yeshua
— Jesus the son of Josedec the high priest, Jesus the son of Nave
(Joshua son of Nun), Jesus the son of Sirach (Yeshua ben Sira), and the
various other bearers of that pre-exilic Hebrew name. Those are kept in
the conventional King James English form so that the reader is not led
to confuse them with the Messiah whose name was given for our salvation.
The restoration is reserved for where the text means the Messiah, and
only there.

Modernization of archaic English. The 1769 text uses the second-person
singular forms (thou, thee, thy, thine, ye, you) and the older verb
endings (hath, doth, saith, willeth, didst, wast, art) that were already
passing out of common English usage in 1769 and that are now opaque to
most modern readers. This edition has modernized those forms throughout:
thou and thee become you, thy and thine become your, ye becomes you,
hath becomes has, doth becomes does, saith becomes says, wilt becomes
will, didst becomes did, wast becomes were, art becomes are, unto
becomes to, and the corresponding adverbs and connectors have been
opened where they would have stopped a modern reader. Sentence structure
has been preserved where it carries the cadence of the original. The
goal is to keep the King James voice while removing the King James
static. A modern reader should be able to read this Apocrypha without
translating archaic English in their head as they go.

Light internal punctuation. The 1769 text was set with punctuation
conventions that differ from modern usage in two main ways: the use of
colons and semicolons where modern English would use full stops, and the
absence of quotation marks around speech. Where colons or semicolons
would mislead the modern reader, full stops have been substituted.
Quotation marks have not been added; the King James tradition does not
use them, and the commentary handles speech attribution where it
matters. Verse divisions — chapter and verse numbers — are preserved
exactly as the 1769 text presents them.

What has not been restored or changed. Patriarch names, place names, and
the names of biblical figures other than the Messiah have been kept in
their familiar King James English forms — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses,
Aaron, David, Solomon, Joshua, Jerusalem, Babylon, Judea, Jewry — rather
than being swapped for their Hebrew equivalents. The retention mechanism
for the sacred names is reserved for where it is load-bearing: the
covenant name of the deity, the covenant name of the people, and the
name of the Messiah. Restoring every patriarch name to its Hebrew form
would raise the entry cost on the reader without carrying the
third-commandment weight that Yahuah (God) and Yahusha (Jesus) carry,
and without naming the covenant body the way Yashar'el (Israel) and
Yahudah (Judah) do. The book divisions and the order of books follow the
1611 King James order. No verses have been added or removed. No passage
has been paraphrased. The text is the 1769 text, modernized, with the
sacred names restored at every mention where the textual evidence
supports their restoration. Anything more than that would have crossed
out of editorial restoration and into translation, and translation is
not what this volume is for.

The result is a text that honors the King James scholarship that gave
the English-speaking world its first printed Apocrypha, that restores
the covenant name where the manuscript witness allows it, and that opens
the prose to a modern reader without softening the voice. What you have
in your hand is the same Apocrypha that sat between Malachi and Matthew
in the 1611 Bible, set in the language your generation actually speaks.

Reading the Apocrypha as the Remnant

You are about to read fourteen books that the Spirit did not strike from
the canon He gave you, even though four hundred years of Protestant
printing have tried to make you forget they were there.

That sentence is the whole orientation. If you can sit with it for a
moment before you open Chapter 1 of 1 Esdras — let it press on you, let
it ask what it is asking — you will read this volume in a way that the
average Apocrypha reader has never been trained to read it.

The Apocrypha is not Torah. The commentary in this book will say that
more than once, because the reader's habit has been bent in two opposite
directions and both bends need to be corrected. The Catholic and
Orthodox traditions have inflated these books to canonical scripture
status; the Protestant tradition has often deflated them beneath even
the dignity of careful reading. Neither posture is the posture of the
awakening remnant. The Apocrypha is witness — historical, devotional,
wisdom, and apocalyptic witness — and witness is to be heard.

That is what you are holding. And because that is what you are holding,
it cannot be read the way you have been taught to read scripture. The
habits you picked up in whichever of the four houses you are walking out
of will fight against the way this book wants to be read, and a few
minutes spent here at the front will save you a hundred miles of
frustration once you are in the text.

What This Book Is Not

Before anything else, name what this book is not, so that the wrong
expectations do not set the reading on the wrong foot from the first
chapter.

This book is not scripture-grade canonical Torah. The five books that
Moses wrote at the direction of Yahuah (God), the prophets Yahuah (God)
raised up and whose words the covenant community received as His own
voice, and the words of His Son Yahusha (Jesus) and His apostles — these
are scripture. The Apocrypha is not. To call it scripture is to
misrepresent it, and to read it as if it carries the same authority as
the prophets is to give it a weight it cannot bear and to invite errors
that the careful reader will avoid by simply naming the genre at the
door. These fourteen books are inspired in the way that a faithful
eyewitness is inspired — they tell the truth as they saw it, and the
Spirit was not absent from their telling — but they are not the Word the
way Isaiah is the Word.

This book is not a devotional. A devotional is a short daily piece
designed to produce an emotional lift and a next-day return, usually
organized around a single verse lifted from its context and given a
personal application. The Apocrypha will not perform that way. Tobit
will not yield a manageable bedside takeaway. Sirach is too long for a
daily portion. 2 Esdras is too dense, too apocalyptic, and too
theologically dangerous in the wrong hands to be parceled out a verse a
morning. The book wants to be read as the book it is, in its own pacing.

This book is not a concordance. You are not meant to open it to look
something up and close it. That is how the pulpit has trained the last
several centuries of readers to read scripture — as a search engine for
sermon points — and that habit will not serve you here. The narrative
books are narratives; they want to be read end to end. The wisdom books
are accumulations; they want to be read slowly, paragraph by paragraph,
with time to chew. The apocalyptic books are visions; they want to be
received whole and then returned to. None of them yield to the
verse-pluck.

This book is not a secret-knowledge text. There is a tradition — in some
of the more esoteric Hebrew-roots corners, and in the broader gnostic
and mystic genre that has always trailed the Christian mainstream — that
treats the Apocrypha and the Pseudepigrapha as a hidden curriculum the
institutional church kept from the laity. That posture distorts the
books in two directions: it inflates them above their station, and it
makes the reader feel like an initiate rather than a son of Adam coming
home. Neither feeling serves the Word. The Apocrypha was not hidden. It
was printed in every King James Bible for two and a half centuries. It
was read aloud in churches and in homes. The British and Foreign Bible
Society's 1826 decision to drop it from their printed editions is a
printing decision, not a conspiracy — and it is also recoverable, which
is why you are holding this volume.

This book is not a historical novel. It is not a creative filling-in of
the gaps the prophets leave between Malachi and Matthew. The fourteen
books that make up the King James Apocrypha are not modern
fictionalizations. Tobit was preserved in Aramaic and Greek; Sirach in
Hebrew, Greek, and Syriac; 1 and 2 Maccabees in Greek with strong
indications of underlying Hebrew sources for portions of 1 Maccabees; 2
Esdras in Latin with portions traceable to Hebrew and Greek originals.
These are not stories someone invented in the eighteenth century. They
are texts with manuscript histories that go back to the centuries
between the testaments, and they were treated by the early
Greek-speaking covenant communities — including the apostles themselves,
who quoted from them in their letters — as part of the inherited
literary world they wrote into.

So — not Torah, not devotional, not concordance, not secret knowledge,
not novel. That is what this book is not. Now what it is.

What This Book Is

This book is a recovered witness. It is fourteen voices from the four
hundred years between the close of the prophetic canon and the opening
of the Gospels, voices that the King James translators considered worthy
of inclusion in the Bible they gave to the English-speaking world,
voices that two and a half centuries of King James printing carried into
the homes and churches of every English-speaking believer who ever
opened that book. To recover them is not to invent. It is to restore
what was always there until the Bible Society printed it out.

This book is a restored text. The 1769 King James Apocrypha is the
version most modern reprints already use; what this edition adds is the
restoration of the covenant name where the manuscript evidence supports
it, and the modernization of archaic English where it would otherwise
stop the modern reader. Restoration, not retranslation. The text is the
King James text. The voice is the King James voice. The names are the
names the manuscript witness was always trying to carry.

This book is a commented text. The commentary that follows each chapter
is the reason this edition exists. There are cheaper reprints of the
1769 text with no commentary at all. There are scholarly editions with
academic apparatus aimed at seminary readers. There are Catholic and
Orthodox editions with commentary aimed at confirming a canonical
reading the awakening Protestant remnant does not share. None of those
serve the reader walking out of the four houses and into the wilderness
of His Word. This commentary does. Every passage is laid back into its
place in the long story of the scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel), the
covenant Torah, the prophetic restoration, the Messiah's work, and the
apostles' continuation of that work — the framework of the Restored
Names Series.

This book is a Series volume. It is the third volume of the Restored
Names work, following the Book of Enoch and the Book of Jasher and
preceding other volumes in various stages of preparation. The Series is
not a numbered curriculum the reader has to take in order. Each volume
stands on its own, and a reader who picks this up before having read
Enoch or Jasher will lose nothing essential. But every volume is written
from the same framework, and a reader who has been moving through the
Series will recognize the voice and the working keys — the 1234 of
Truth, the methodological sequence for reading Paul, the patient address
to all three deceived groups, the steady refusal to let any movement or
camp claim the destination — without their needing to be reintroduced.

That is what this book is: a recovered witness, a restored text, a
commented text, a volume in an ongoing body of work. Now — how does the
reader who is walking out of one of the four houses read a book like
this?

Four Reading Postures, and Why Three of Them Will Fail Here

Every reader of this book is arriving with a reading posture they did
not choose. You picked it up from the house you grew up in. You picked
it up from the pulpit you sat under for twenty years. You picked it up
from the podcast that woke you up to the Hebrew roots two summers ago.
You picked it up from the synagogue you tried to attend after you walked
out of the church and before you found your way to where you are now.
Whichever it is, it was given to you. You did not select it. And now,
before you read this book, you have a chance to look at it.

Three postures are common among the readers who arrive here. All three
will fail this text. A fourth posture — the one the remnant is learning
— will receive what is on the page.

The first is the Christian devotional posture. This is the posture that
says: open the text, find a verse, find the application, apply it to my
life, close the book until tomorrow. The frame is pietistic, individual,
and emotional. It will not serve you here. The Apocrypha is not built
for verse-pluck. The narrative books require sustained attention; the
wisdom books require accumulation; the apocalyptic books require entire
reception. A devotional reader who tries to land on a verse from 2
Esdras and squeeze a personal application out of it will either misread
it or be defeated by it. The devotional posture is also, beneath its
piety, a quiet form of self-centeredness — the question it always asks
is what does this say to me — and the question the awakening remnant is
being asked to learn instead is what does the Spirit say through this
text about the people of Yahuah (God) and the long story He is telling.
The first question is small. The second is the one the text is actually
answering.

The second is the rabbinic harmonization posture. This is the posture
that says: when the text seems to say something that contradicts another
text, layer a midrash on it that reconciles both. The frame is
harmonizing, layered, and willing to add interpretive material that the
text itself does not require. It will not serve you here either. The
Apocrypha contains material that does not always harmonize cleanly with
the Torah and the prophets — the elaborate angelology of Tobit, the
prayer-of-the-dead implications of 2 Maccabees 12, the apocalyptic
numerology of 2 Esdras — and the move that the rabbinic posture wants to
make, which is to layer until everything fits, will smother the actual
question these passages raise. The awakening reader does not need to
harmonize what the text leaves unharmonized. The reader needs to mark
what the text says, mark what the canonical scripture says, and let the
difference stand where the text leaves it. Witness is allowed to differ
from canon. That is what makes it witness.

The third is the Torah-observant practice posture. This is the posture
that says: open the text, find the commandment, work out exactly how to
keep it this week, make the to-do list, check the box. The frame is
performative and externally measurable. The Hebrew roots and
Torah-observant communities have many strengths, but this particular
reading habit — a reflex inherited from the same evangelical tradition
many of them came out of, just retooled with Torah commandments instead
of Christian application points — will not serve them here. The
Apocrypha does not produce a fresh set of commandments. It does not
legislate. The commentary in this book will use it to illuminate what
the Torah and the prophets already legislated, and to expose how those
legislations were lived (or not lived) during the second-temple period.
The reader who comes looking for a new set of action items will close
the book disappointed. The reader who comes ready to listen to four
hundred years of covenant struggle will hear what is being said.

The fourth is the Islamic replacement posture. This posture is quieter —
most readers of the Apocrypha will not be coming from the Muslim
tradition, but some will — and it needs to be named because it will fail
the text in a way the others will not. The Islamic posture says the
Bible has been corrupted, the Hebrew prophets have been corrupted, and
the only reliable layer is the Quran. A reader carrying that posture
will read the Apocrypha as further evidence of corruption rather than as
witness in its own genre. That posture will close every door this book
is trying to open. If you have been near it, set it down before you turn
to Chapter 1.

There is a fifth posture worth naming, quieter than the others and
rarely recognized by the readers who carry it, because it feels like the
absence of a posture rather than the presence of one. Call it the
neutral-observer posture, the comparative-studies posture, the
seminary-trained reader's posture — the habit shaped by academic
biblical scholarship, by religious-studies education, by the long
Protestant tradition of evaluating texts through manuscript history,
dating debates, and the consensus of mainstream scholarship. The reader
who carries it considers themselves above the four houses, weighing each
as one option among many, declining to commit, holding the position of
the rigorous evaluator. They are not above the four houses. They are
inside one of them — institutional Christianity in its
academic-mainstream form — believing themselves outside it. This posture
will fail this text the way the others will, and for the same reason: it
imports house-consensus as the standard against which the framework gets
tested. The standard the Word itself provides is 1 John 2:3–4.
Mainstream-academic consensus is not the standard. Test the framework by
the Word. Test the academy by the Word. Test this book by the Word.

Those are the three failure postures, plus the two quieter ones that
needed to be named alongside them. Every one of them has inside it some
element that was once alive and is being preserved by the Father in the
very reader who walks out of that house. The Christian devotional
posture once carried real warmth toward the Word; the rabbinic
harmonization once carried real reverence for the unity of scripture;
the Torah-observant practice posture once carried real obedience toward
the Father's commandments. The Father is not going to discard those
affections. He is going to mature them. But the postures themselves, as
habits of reading, will not bring the awakening reader through this text
the way the text wants to be brought through.

The fourth posture — the remnant posture — is the one the reader of this
book is being invited to take. Simply stated: hear the text, honor the
voice, let the Spirit restore what was scattered, do not rush to
commentary or application before the text has had its full first say.
Read the chapter. Let it stand. Then read the commentary. Then read the
cross-references. Then close the page and let the book carry the reader
forward to the next chapter.

That is what the fourth posture looks like. The remnant reader listens
first. The remnant reader receives before responding. The remnant reader
trusts that Yahuah (God) is the one who will produce the application in
the reader's life as it is needed, in the season it is needed, and that
the reader's job during the reading is to take the Word in. The Spirit
is not on a deadline. He is not asking the reader to extract a takeaway
by chapter's end. He is asking the reader to come home, and the
homecoming is going to take more than one sitting.

Two Sequencing Rules

If the posture is right, the sequencing does most of the rest of the
work. Two rules govern how to read each chapter of this book, and if you
hold them, the commentary will serve the text rather than the other way
around.

The first rule is: read the scripture first. The chapter text of each
book of the Apocrypha runs at the top of every chapter. It is set apart
with a small visual divider from the commentary that follows. Read the
scripture before reading the commentary. Do not skim it. Do not let the
eye drift to the commentary headline halfway down the page. Let the
chapter text have its own first hearing, before any voice — including
the commentary in this book — interprets it for you.

This rule is harder than it sounds, for a reader trained in the
Christian study-Bible tradition, where the commentary is printed in
columns alongside the text and the eye drifts across before the text has
even been heard. The study-Bible format makes commentary feel like part
of the text. It is not. The commentary is one voice — in this book, it
is the voice of a modern Nazarite who has been given certain things by
the Spirit to say about these passages — and the chapter text is another
voice, the voice of the second-temple witness, and they are not the same
voice. Hear the witness first. Then hear what the commentary says about
it. Then test the commentary against the witness, and against the
canonical scripture, and against the 1234.

The second rule is: read the commentary only after the scripture has had
its full voice. The commentary will address the passage you just read.
It will name the cross-references in the Torah, the prophets, the
Gospels, and the apostolic letters. It will lay the chapter into its
place in the framework. The cross-reference line at the close of every
commentary will list every reference the commentary leaned on, in the
order it was cited, so the reader can carry them into their own study
time.

If you hold these two rules, you will find the book opens. If you break
them — if you read the commentary first, or if you skim the scripture
looking for the next commentary bolt-on — you will find your reading
turning into a Christian study-Bible exercise wearing a Torah-observant
costume, which is exactly the inheritance the awakening remnant is being
called out of. The discipline of letting the text speak first is not a
stylistic preference. It is a remnant discipline, and it is one of the
things the Father is using to retrain the reader's ear.

The 1234 Filter — How to Use It When You Read

You were introduced to the 1234 filter in the Before You Begin piece.
Here it is named again as a working tool, because it is going to matter
to you as you read the Apocrypha, where some of the passages will press
hard on the relation between obedience, mercy, and the Messiah's work.

  And hereby we do know that we know Him, if we keep His commandments.
  He that says, I know Him, and keeps not His commandments, is a liar,
  and the truth is not in him. — 1 John 2:3–4.

That is the filter. Yahuah (God) does not lie. Any reading of any
scripture that requires 1 John 2:3–4 to be false is a wrong reading. The
filter is not one interpretation among many. It is the standard the Word
itself provides.

Here is how you actually use it while reading the Apocrypha.

When a passage in the Apocrypha seems to contradict a commandment in the
Torah, pause. The contradiction is not in the Torah. The Torah is the
standard. Either the apocryphal passage is saying something the surface
English does not show — a translational nuance, a second-temple idiom, a
structural feature in the Greek that the modernized 1769 cannot render
without commentary — or the passage is doing what witness texts
sometimes do: showing how a generation lived, including how a generation
failed to live, in front of the Torah they had been given. The 1234
keeps the reader from concluding that an apocryphal passage abolishes
anything the Torah commanded. The Apocrypha cannot abolish the Torah.
Witness does not have that authority.

When a passage in the Apocrypha seems to contradict the prophets'
restoration promises, pause again. The Spirit's restoration timeline —
the gathering of the paternal blood remnant of all twelve tribes of
Jacob, out of every nation where they have been scattered, into the land
of their fathers under the reign of the Messiah — runs through the
prophets and is sealed by the apostolic witness. No apocryphal passage
can override that timeline. Where 2 Esdras presents apocalyptic imagery
that has been used by some interpreters to redraw the prophetic map, the
1234 holds the line: the prophets are the standard, and 2 Esdras is
witness. The witness can illuminate what the prophets said. It cannot
rewrite it.

When a passage in the Apocrypha seems to contradict a commentary note in
this book, test both. The commentary in this volume is not inerrant.
Yoshi is a son of Adam who has walked out of the horn's reading and into
the covenant lens, and he writes from the framework the Father has given
him. He is not the standard. The Word is the standard. If you read a
chapter of Sirach, then read the commentary, then notice a place where
the commentary seems to soften or sharpen the text in a way the text
itself does not warrant, follow that instinct. Bring the chapter to the
Torah. Bring the chapter to the prophets. Bring the chapter to the
apostolic witness. Bring the commentary to the same standard. Whichever
survives the comparison is the voice you keep.

You are not asked to agree with every commentary note in this book. You
are asked to test what you read. The remnant does not breed a new
priesthood of commentary-receivers. The remnant reads the Word and tests
every voice — including the voice on the page in front of you right now
— by it.

The Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul — Deepened Here

When Paul is cited in this commentary, he will be read by the two-step
sequence the Before You Begin piece already introduced. The sequence is
worth restating because the commentary in this volume will lean on Paul
more than the average reader expects. The Apocrypha and Paul share a
world. Paul wrote in Greek to communities formed inside the Hellenistic
Yahudi (Jewish) diaspora — the same diaspora whose literary world
includes the Apocrypha — and his vocabulary, his rhetorical structures,
and his arguments echo the apocryphal wisdom literature so directly that
the reader who has not read the Apocrypha is missing half of what Paul
was drawing from.

Step one: establish what Paul was drawing from. Paul was a
Torah-observant Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin, trained under
Gamaliel, set apart for the gospel of the Messiah (Christ). He kept the
Sabbath. He kept the appointed feasts. He cited the Torah, the prophets,
and the writings as scripture. And — relevant to this volume — he had
read the Apocrypha. The wisdom of Solomon's account of the giver of
life, the second-temple martyr theology of 4 Maccabees (a book outside
the King James fourteen but in the broader apocryphal corpus the
diaspora knew), the providence and almsgiving theology of Tobit, the
providential history of 1 and 2 Maccabees: this is the literary world
Paul wrote inside. When the commentary in this book traces a Pauline
thought back to an apocryphal precedent, that is not a stretch. It is
the air Paul breathed.

Step two: identify what Paul was arguing against. Paul's letters are one
side of a conversation. Once his Torah and apocryphal-wisdom-tradition
foundation is clear, the distortion he is rebutting becomes
identifiable. In Galatians, the circumcision party's false gospel: that
gentile believers had to be circumcised and become Yahudim (Jews) to be
saved. In Romans, the same fault from the opposite angle: the Yahudi
(Jewish) believer's pride against the gentile believer who has come into
the covenant household by faith. In Hebrews, the temptation to retreat
under pressure to the Levitical-priesthood pattern that the Messiah's
permanent priesthood had now superseded. In each case, Paul is arguing
against a specific external distortion, and the misreading of his
letters that has fueled the antinomian Christian tradition for fifteen
hundred years is a misreading that lifts his answer out of its argument
and makes it answer a question he was not being asked.

Why this matters for your reading of the Apocrypha. The Apocrypha is the
wisdom and historical literature of the diaspora world Paul wrote into.
When the commentary cites Paul as agreeing with what an apocryphal
passage is showing, the reader can rest. Paul is not the contradiction
the inherited reading made him. He is the apostolic voice that confirms
what the second-temple witnesses had already begun to see. The
commentary will not stretch passages to make Paul agree with them where
he does not, but where he does agree — and he agrees more often than the
inherited reading allows — the commentary will name it plainly.

If you have come to this book having dropped Paul because you could not
reconcile him with the Torah you were learning to love, the
methodological sequence is for you. The contradiction is not Paul's. It
is the interpreter's. Read the Torah-grounded Paul into the apocryphal
passages where his words echo, and you will find that Paul has been
waiting for you to come back the whole time.

The Seam Between the Houses

One last orientation before the chapter texts begin.

The Apocrypha sits in a unique place in the inherited Bible. It is not
Old Testament — the Hebrew prophetic canon closes with Malachi. It is
not New Testament — the apostolic witness opens with Matthew. It is the
seam between the two. And the seam is where some of the most important
framework movements in this Series take place.

In the four hundred years between Malachi and Matthew, the second-temple
community lived through the rise and fall of the Persian, Greek, and
early Roman empires. The Greek conquest under Alexander forced the
Hellenization of every culture from the Aegean to the Indus, and the
Yahudi (Jewish) community in the land and in the diaspora had to decide
what was Torah-faithfulness and what was cultural drift. Out of that
pressure came the Hasmonean revolt, the Maccabean dynasty, the rise of
the Pharisaic and Sadducean schools, the Essene withdrawal at Qumran,
and the apocalyptic literary tradition that fed both the visions of the
New Testament and the imagery of the early church's witness. None of it
is incidental. All of it is the world the Messiah was born into.

For the awakening reader holding the Two-House framework — the
recognition that the northern kingdom of Yashar'el (Israel) was
scattered into the nations in 722 BCE and that the prophetic restoration
concerns the gathering of that scattered seed back into covenant
identity — the Apocrypha matters in a particular way. The
Hebrew-language house of Yahudah (Judah) is the focus of most of these
books, especially the Maccabean histories. But the diaspora house — the
scattered seed living in Babylonia, in Persia, in Egypt, in the cities
of the Greek world — is also visible in the books that name it. Tobit
lives in Nineveh, in the very Assyrian heartland to which the northern
kingdom had been deported. 1 Esdras retells the post-exilic restoration
of Yahudah (Judah) from a perspective that includes the larger
restoration question. 2 Esdras' apocalyptic visions weep over the lost
ten tribes by name (2 Esdras 13:39–47) — a weeping that the inherited
Christian reading has rarely had ears for, because the Two-House
framework was lost to the institutional church for most of its history.

This is one of the reasons this volume matters. The Apocrypha preserves
second-temple awareness of the scattered ten tribes that the inherited
Christian Bible-reading habits have largely buried. The commentary in
this book will name those moments where they appear. Not to inflate
them. Not to make 2 Esdras 13 do work that the canonical prophets do
better and earlier. But to honor what the witness saw, and to let the
reader see that the awareness of the lost northern house was alive in
the second-temple community in ways the contemporary reader has rarely
been told.

For the reader walking out of institutional Christianity, the Apocrypha
is the bridge that explains why the world of Matthew is the world of
Matthew. For the reader walking out of the rabbinic tradition, the
Apocrypha is the literature your covenant ancestors actually read and
quoted, including the apostles whose letters you may not yet have
learned how to read again. For the reader walking out of Hebrew roots
and Torah-observant assemblies, the Apocrypha is the wisdom literature
that demonstrates how second-temple covenant communities wrestled with
Hellenization, faithfulness, the temple, the priesthood, the foreign
powers, the diaspora question, and the long wait for the Messiah —
wrestlings that the contemporary remnant is wrestling with again in
fresh costume.

That is what you are about to read. Fourteen books, in 1611 order,
modernized into the English of your generation, with the covenant name
restored where the manuscript witness allows, and with
chapter-by-chapter commentary from a modern Nazarite walking the same
wilderness you are walking. The Spirit did not bind these books into
your fathers' Bibles for nothing. He did not let the print remain in the
homes of the English-speaking covenant community for two and a half
centuries for nothing. He did not let them be recovered from
public-domain archives in the digital age for nothing.

Open the page. Read the witness. Test it by the Word.

The seam between the houses is where you are standing.

1 Esdras — Introduction

The first book the King James translators set in the Apocrypha is 1
Esdras, and the placement was deliberate. 1 Esdras is the post-exilic
restoration narrative — a Greek retelling of the events covered in the
closing chapters of 2 Chronicles, the entire book of Ezra, and the first
part of Nehemiah, with one striking addition that has no parallel
anywhere in the Hebrew canon: the contest of the three young guards in
the court of King Darius (1 Esdras 3–4). That contest, in which one
young man — eventually named as Zerubbabel — argues that truth is
mightier than wine, kings, or even women, becomes the literary occasion
for the rebuilding of the temple. It is a Greek-language amplification
of the Persian-era restoration story, preserved in the Septuagint, and
it is the single most important book in the Apocrypha for understanding
how the second-temple community remembered its own re-founding.

Why does it matter for the awakening reader? Because the inherited
Christian reading of the post-exilic restoration is anemic. It treats
Ezra and Nehemiah as a kind of historical footnote between the prophets
and the Gospels, a brief uplift before the four hundred years of
silence. 1 Esdras refuses that flattening. It tells the same restoration
story with the volume turned up — the Persian decrees in their full
ceremonial weight, the listing of the returnees with their genealogies,
the rebuilding of the altar before the temple, the resumption of the
appointed feasts, the marriage scandals and Ezra's grief, and the public
reading of the Torah at the Water Gate. It is, in compressed form, the
entire post-exilic restoration laid out as a single narrative arc, and
it answers a question the Hebrew canon leaves open: what happened to the
seed that returned, and what happened to the seed that did not.

That last question is where 1 Esdras feeds directly into the framework
of this Series. Ezra and Nehemiah document the restoration of the house
of Yahudah (Judah) — the southern kingdom, the tribe of Yahudah (Judah)
and a remnant of Benjamin, with the Levitical priesthood. They do not
document the return of the ten tribes of the northern kingdom, the house
of Yashar'el (Israel) scattered into Assyria in 722 BCE. The northern
house was not gathered with the southern house in the Persian-era
return, and the prophets had said it would not be — Hosea 1 and 2,
Ezekiel 37, Jeremiah 31. Their gathering is a future restoration. 1
Esdras' opening chapters, by retelling the Davidic-Solomonic history
that preceded the captivity, lay the groundwork for understanding why
only Yahudah (Judah) returned and what was still outstanding when Ezra
finished reading the Torah at the Water Gate.

Read 1 Esdras with that lens. When the genealogies of returnees are
listed, listen for who is missing. When the temple is rebuilt, listen
for what about the temple is rebuilt and what has been changed forever
(the Levitical service is restored, but the ark of the covenant is not —
that absence is one of the great unresolved silences of second-temple
history). When the contest of the three guards is told, listen for the
literary preparation that is being laid for Zerubbabel, the Davidic
governor under whom the second temple rises. The book is a setup. It is
preparing the reader for the centuries that follow it, the centuries the
New Testament will open into.

A final orientation: 1 Esdras is sometimes called "Greek Ezra" or "the
Septuagint Ezra." The book that English-speaking readers know as Ezra in
their Old Testament is, in the Septuagint tradition, called 2 Esdras.
The numbering can confuse the modern reader who is unfamiliar with the
apocryphal tradition. The 1 Esdras of this volume is not the Ezra of the
Old Testament; it is the Greek post-exilic restoration narrative that
runs alongside it.

1 Esdras — Chapter 1

  1 And Josias held the feast of the passover in Jerusalem to his Elohim
  (God), and offered the passover the fourteenth day of the first month;
  2 Having set the priests according to their daily courses, being
  arrayed in long garments, in the temple of Yahuah (God). 3 And he
  spoke to the Levites, the holy ministers of Yashar'el (Israel), that
  they should hallow themselves to Yahuah (God), to set the holy ark of
  Yahuah (God) in the house that king Solomon the son of David had
  built: 4 And said, You shall no more bear the ark upon your shoulders:
  now therefore serve Yahuah (God), your Elohim (God), and minister to
  his people Yashar'el (Israel), and prepare you after your families and
  kindreds, 5 According as David the king of Yashar'el (Israel)
  prescribed, and according to the magnificence of Solomon his son: and
  standing in the temple according to the several dignity of the
  families of you the Levites, who minister in the presence of your
  brothers the children of Yashar'el (Israel),

  6 Offer the passover in order, and make ready the sacrifices for your
  brothers, and keep the passover according to the commandment of Yahuah
  (God), which was given to Moses. 7 And to the people that was found
  there Josias gave thirty thousand lambs and kids, and three thousand
  calves: these things were given of the king’s allowance, according as
  he promised, to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites. 8 And
  Helkias, Zacharias, and Syelus, the governors of the temple, gave to
  the priests for the passover two thousand and six hundred sheep, and
  three hundred calves. 9 And Jeconias, and Samaias, and Nathanael his
  brother, and Assabias, and Ochiel, and Joram, captains over thousands,
  gave to the Levites for the passover five thousand sheep, and seven
  hundred calves. 10 And when these things were done, the priests and
  Levites, having the unleavened bread, stood in very comely order
  according to the kindreds,

  11 And according to the several dignities of the fathers, before the
  people, to offer to Yahuah (God), as it is written in the book of
  Moses: and thus did they in the morning. 12 And they roasted the
  passover with fire, as appertaineth: as for the sacrifices, they sod
  them in brass pots and pans with a good savour, 13 And set them before
  all the people: and afterward they prepared for themselves, and for
  the priests their brothers, the sons of Aaron. 14 For the priests
  offered the fat until night: and the Levites prepared for themselves,
  and the priests their brothers, the sons of Aaron. 15 The holy singers
  also, the sons of Asaph, were in their order, according to the
  appointment of David, to wit, Asaph, Zacharias, and Jeduthun, who was
  of the king’s retinue.

  16 Moreover the porters were at every gate; it was not lawful for any
  to go from his ordinary service: for their brothers the Levites
  prepared for them. 17 Thus were the things that belonged to the
  sacrifices of Yahuah (God) accomplished in that day, that they might
  hold the passover, 18 And offer sacrifices upon the altar of Yahuah
  (God), according to the commandment of king Josias. 19 So the children
  of Yashar'el (Israel) which were present held the passover at that
  time, and the feast of sweet bread seven days. 20 And such a passover
  was not kept in Yashar'el (Israel) since the time of the prophet
  Samuel.

  21 Yea, all the kings of Yashar'el (Israel) held not such a passover
  as Josias, and the priests, and the Levites, and the Yahudim (Jews),
  held with all Yashar'el (Israel) that were found dwelling at
  Jerusalem. 22 In the eighteenth year of the reign of Josias was this
  passover kept. 23 And the works or Josias were upright before his
  Elohim (God) with an heart full of godliness. 24 As for the things
  that came to pass in his time, they were written in former times,
  concerning those that sinned, and did wickedly against Yahuah (God)
  above all people and kingdoms, and how they grieved him exceedingly,
  so that the words of Yahuah (God) rose up against Yashar'el (Israel).
  25 Now after all these acts of Josias it came to pass, that Pharaoh
  the king of Egypt came to raise war at Carchamis upon Euphrates: and
  Josias went out against him.

  26 But the king of Egypt sent to him, saying, What have I to do with
  you, O king of Judea? 27 I am not sent out from Yahuah (God) against
  you; for my war is upon Euphrates: and now Yahuah (God) is with me,
  yes, Yahuah (God) is with me hasting me forward: depart from me, and
  be not against Yahuah (God). 28 Howbeit Josias did not turn back his
  chariot from him, but undertook to fight with him, not regarding the
  words of the prophet Jeremy spoken by the mouth of Yahuah (God): 29
  But joined battle with him in the plain of Magiddo, and the princes
  came against king Josias. 30 Then said the king to his servants, Carry
  me away out of the battle; for I am very weak. And immediately his
  servants took him away out of the battle.

  31 Then got he up upon his second chariot; and being brought back to
  Jerusalem died, and was buried in his father’s sepulchre. 32 And in
  all Jewry they mourned for Josias, yes, Jeremy the prophet lamented
  for Josias, and the chief men with the women made lamentation for him
  to this day: and this was given out for an ordinance to be done
  continually in all the nation of Yashar'el (Israel). 33 These things
  are written in the book of the stories of the kings of Yahudah
  (Judah), and every one of the acts that Josias did, and his glory, and
  his understanding in the law of Yahuah (God), and the things that he
  had done before, and the things now recited, are reported in the book
  of the kings of Yashar'el (Israel) and Judea. 34 And the people took
  Joachaz the son of Josias, and made him king instead of Josias his
  father, when he was twenty and three years old. 35 And he reigned in
  Judea and in Jerusalem three months: and then the king of Egypt
  deposed him from reigning in Jerusalem.

  36 And he set a tax upon the land of an hundred talents of silver and
  one talent of gold. 37 The king of Egypt also made king Joacim his
  brother king of Judea and Jerusalem. 38 And he bound Joacim and the
  nobles: but Zaraces his brother he apprehended, and brought him out of
  Egypt. 39 Five and twenty years old was Joacim when he was made king
  in the land of Judea and Jerusalem; and he did evil before Yahuah
  (God). 40 Wherefore against him Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon
  came up, and bound him with a chain of brass, and carried him into
  Babylon.

  41 Nabuchodonosor also took of the holy vessels of Yahuah (God), and
  carried them away, and set them in his own temple at Babylon. 42 But
  those things that are recorded of him, and of his uncleaness and
  impiety, are written in the chronicles of the kings. 43 And Joacim his
  son reigned in his stead: he was made king being eighteen years old;
  44 And reigned but three months and ten days in Jerusalem; and did
  evil before Yahuah (God). 45 So after a year Nabuchodonosor sent and
  caused him to be brought into Babylon with the holy vessels of Yahuah
  (God);

  46 And made Zedechias king of Judea and Jerusalem, when he was one and
  twenty years old; and he reigned eleven years: 47 And he did evil also
  in the sight of Yahuah (God), and cared not for the words that were
  spoken to him by the prophet Jeremy from the mouth of Yahuah (God). 48
  And after that king Nabuchodonosor had made him to swear by the name
  of Yahuah (God), he forswore himself, and rebelled; and hardening his
  neck, his heart, he transgressed the laws of Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el
  (Israel). 49 The governors also of the people and of the priests did
  many things against the laws, and passed all the pollutions of all
  nations, and defiled the temple of Yahuah (God), which was sanctified
  in Jerusalem. 50 Nevertheless Yahuah (God) of their fathers sent
  by his messenger to call them back, because he spared them and his
  tabernacle also.

  51 But they had his messengers in derision; and, look, when Yahuah
  (God) spoke to them, they made a sport of his prophets: 52 So far
  forth, that he, being wroth with his people for their great
  ungodliness, commanded the kings of the Chaldees to come up against
  them; 53 Who slew their young men with the sword, yes, even within the
  compass of their holy temple, and spared neither young man nor maid,
  old man nor child, among them; for he delivered all into their hands.
  54 And they took all the holy vessels of Yahuah (God), both great and
  small, with the vessels of the ark of Yahuah (God), and the king’s
  treasures, and carried them away into Babylon. 55 As for the house of
  Yahuah (God), they burnt it, and brake down the walls of Jerusalem,
  and set fire upon her towers:

  56 And as for her glorious things, they never ceased till they had
  consumed and brought them all to nought: and the people that were not
  slain with the sword he carried to Babylon: 57 Who became servants to
  him and his children, till the Persians reigned, to fulfil the word of
  Yahuah (God) spoken by the mouth of Jeremy: 58 Until the land had
  enjoyed her sabbaths, the whole time of her desolation shall she rest,
  until the full term of seventy years.

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter of 1 Esdras retells the close of 2 Chronicles — the
great Passover of Josiah (verses 1–22), Josiah's death at the hand of
Pharaoh-Necho (verses 23–33), and the four kings who reigned after him
until the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian captivity (verses
34–58). The narrative is parallel to 2 Chronicles 35–36 with some
expansions and reorderings.

Two things matter for the awakening reader.

First, Josiah's Passover is presented as the high point of covenant
faithfulness in the closing decades of the southern kingdom. The text
records, "There was no Passover like this kept in Yashar'el (Israel)
since the time of the prophet Samuel." The covenant feast was kept
according to the Torah's specifications. The priests, the Levites, the
temple service, the appointed offerings, the people's participation —
all are named in the proper order. The framework of this Series, which
honors the appointed feasts of Yahuah (God) as the appointed feasts and
not as optional cultural observances, finds in Josiah's Passover the
second-temple memory of what covenant feast-keeping looks like when it
is done according to the Torah. Read it as the covenant pattern. Read it
as what the appointed feasts are meant to be when the household of
Yahuah (God) is gathered to keep them.

Second, the immediate aftermath of Josiah's death is the catastrophic
decline. Within twenty-three years of Josiah's death — the four kings
who follow him are Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah — the
southern kingdom collapses, the temple is destroyed, and the people are
carried to Babylon. The framework of this Series, which holds that even
the brightest covenant moments are not guaranteed to be preserved by the
next generation if the next generation walks out from under the Torah,
finds in 1 Esdras 1 the second-temple memory of how rapidly the
inheritance of one faithful king can be lost. Josiah's reform did not
save the kingdom. The reform was real, but the people had already gone
too far down the path of breaking the covenant, and the reform could not
be sustained beyond Josiah's lifetime. The awakening reader walking
through a season of covenant restoration in the personal walk should
mark this: the reform must be passed on, not assumed to perpetuate
itself.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 22:1–23:30; 2 Kings 23:31–25:30; 2 Chronicles
34:1–35:27; 2 Chronicles 36:1–23; Jeremiah 22:1–30; Jeremiah 25:1–14;
Lamentations 1:1–22; Deuteronomy 28:36–68.

1 Esdras — Chapter 2

  1 In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, that the word of
  Yahuah (God) might be accomplished, that he had promised by the mouth
  of Jeremy; 2 Yahuah (God) raised up the spirit of Cyrus the king
  of the Persians, and he made proclamation through all his kingdom, and
  also by writing, 3 Saying, Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians; The
  Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), the most high Yahuah (God), has
  made me king of the whole world, 4 And commanded me to build him an
  house at Jerusalem in Jewry. 5 If therefore there be any of you that
  are of his people, let Yahuah (God), even his Elohim (God), be with
  him, and let him go up to Jerusalem that is in Judea, and build the
  house of Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel): for he is Yahuah (God)
  that dwells in Jerusalem.

  6 Whoever then dwell in the places about, let them help him, those, I
  say, that are his neighbours, with gold, and with silver, 7 With
  gifts, with horses, and with cattle, and other things, which have been
  set forth by vow, for the temple of Yahuah (God) at Jerusalem. 8 Then
  the chief of the families of Judea and of the tribe of Benjamin stood
  up; the priests also, and the Levites, and all they whose mind Yahuah
  (God) had moved to go up, and to build an house for Yahuah (God) at
  Jerusalem, 9 And they that dwelt round about them, and helped them in
  all things with silver and gold, with horses and cattle, and with very
  many free gifts of a great number whose minds were stirred up to it.
  10 King Cyrus also brought forth the holy vessels, which
  Nabuchodonosor had carried away from Jerusalem, and had set up in his
  temple of idols.

  11 Now when Cyrus king of the Persians had brought them forth, he
  delivered them to Mithridates his treasurer: 12 And by him they were
  delivered to Sanabassar the governor of Judea. 13 And this was the
  number of them; A thousand golden cups, and a thousand of silver,
  censers of silver twenty nine, vials of gold thirty, and of silver two
  thousand four hundred and ten, and a thousand other vessels. 14 So all
  the vessels of gold and of silver, which were carried away, were five
  thousand four hundred threescore and nine. 15 These were brought back
  by Sanabassar, together with them of the captivity, from Babylon to
  Jerusalem.

  16 But in the time of Artexerxes king of the Persians Belemus, and
  Mithridates, and Tabellius, and Rathumus, and Beeltethmus, and
  Semellius the secretary, with others that were in commission with
  them, dwelling in Samaria and other places, wrote to him against them
  that dwelt in Judea and Jerusalem these letters following; 17 To king
  Artexerxes our lord, Your servants, Rathumus the storywriter, and
  Semellius the scribe, and the rest of their council, and the judges
  that are in Celosyria and Phenice. 18 Be it now known to the lord
  king, that the Yahudim (Jews) that are up from you to us, being come
  into Jerusalem, that rebellious and wicked city, do build the
  marketplaces, and repair the walls of it and do lay the foundation of
  the temple. 19 Now if this city and the walls thereof be made up
  again, they will not only refuse to give tribute, but also rebel
  against kings. 20 And forasmuch as the things pertaining to the temple
  are now in hand, we think it meet not to neglect such a matter,

  21 But to speak to our lord the king, to the intent that, if it be
  your pleasure it may be sought out in the books of your fathers: 22
  And you shall find in the chronicles what is written concerning these
  things, and shall understand that that city was rebellious, troubling
  both kings and cities: 23 And that the Yahudim (Jews) were rebellious,
  and raised always wars in it; for the which cause even this city was
  made desolate. 24 Wherefore now we do declare to you, O lord the king,
  that if this city be built again, and the walls thereof set up anew,
  you shall from henceforth have no passage into Celosyria and Phenice.
  25 Then the king wrote back again to Rathumus the storywriter, to
  Beeltethmus, to Semellius the scribe, and to the rest that were in
  commission, and dwellers in Samaria and Syria and Phenice, after this
  manner;

  26 I have read the epistle which you have sent to me: therefore I
  commanded to make diligent search, and it has been found that that
  city was from the beginning practising against kings; 27 And the men
  in it were given to rebellion and war: and that mighty kings and
  fierce were in Jerusalem, who reigned and exacted tributes in
  Celosyria and Phenice. 28 Now therefore I have commanded to hinder
  those men from building the city, and heed to be taken that there be
  no more done in it; 29 And that those wicked workers proceed no
  further to the annoyance of kings, 30 Then king Artexerxes his letters
  being read, Rathumus, and Semellius the scribe, and the rest that were
  in commission with them, removing in haste toward Jerusalem with a
  troop of horsemen and a multitude of people in battle array, began to
  hinder the builders; and the building of the temple in Jerusalem
  ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of the
  Persians.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 2 picks up where chapter 1 ended. The captivity has run its
appointed course. Cyrus the Persian has conquered Babylon. The decree of
Cyrus is issued, authorizing the return of the Yahudim (Jews) to
Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the temple (verses 1–15). The chapter
then records the opposition that emerges — the local Samaritan and
trans-Euphrates leadership writing letters to the Persian throne
complaining that the rebuilding of Jerusalem is a security threat to the
empire (verses 16–30). Artaxerxes' response halts the work for a time.

Three things matter.

First, the decree of Cyrus (verses 1–7) is presented as Cyrus
acknowledging that Yahuah (God) the Elohim (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), the most
high Lord, has made me king over the whole earth, and has commanded me
to build him a house in Jerusalem.

The Cyrus decree is the historical fulfillment of Isaiah 44:28–45:1,
prophesied 150 years before Cyrus was born: That says of Cyrus, He is my
shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem,
You shall be built; and to the temple, Your foundation shall be laid.
Thus says Yahuah (God) to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I
have held, to subdue nations before him. Isaiah named Cyrus by name
before Cyrus existed. The text presents Cyrus naming Yahuah (God)
explicitly because Yahuah (God) had named Cyrus explicitly through the
prophet Isaiah a century and a half earlier.

Daniel 2:21 — He changes the times and the seasons: he removes kings,
and sets up kings. Daniel 4:34–35 — Nebuchadnezzar's confession after
his judgment: I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him
that lives for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his
kingdom is from generation to generation: And all the inhabitants of the
earth are reputed as nothing... and none can stay his hand, or say unto
him, What do you? Proverbs 21:1 — The king's heart is in the hand of
Yahuah (God), as the rivers of water: he turns it whithersoever he will.
Romans 13:1 — the powers that be are ordained of Elohim (God).

The framework of this Series, which holds that the powers of the world
are in the Father's hand and that He turns them as He wills, finds in
Cyrus's decree the second-temple witness that the empire's most powerful
king publicly acknowledged Yahuah (God) as the Elohim (God) who had given him his
throne. The principle is not that all kings are believers; it is that
all kings, whether they acknowledge it or not, hold their thrones at
Yahuah (God)'s permission and turn at His direction.

Second, the listing of the returnees (verses 8–15) names the heads of
houses, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the lay
returnees by tribe and family. The genealogies are not decorative. They
are the documentation that the returning seed is the actual covenant
seed of the southern kingdom and not a politically opportunistic
resettlement. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
covenant identity is bloodline and lineage and not merely behavioral,
finds in the genealogies the second-temple practice of preserving and
verifying the covenant lineage. The framework's caveat — and it must be
held throughout the rest of this book — is that the return documented in
1 Esdras is the return of Category 1 only. Yahudah (Judah), the southern
house with portions of Levi and Benjamin, is the entire body of those
who came back. The scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel) — Category 2,
the ten northern tribes carried into Assyria in 722 BCE — is not in
these rolls. They had been gone for nearly two centuries when Cyrus's
decree was issued, and they did not return. The Persian-era restoration
is a Yahudah restoration. The gathering of Yashar'el (Israel) is a
separate restoration, named by the prophets and still future at the time
of Ezra, still future at the time of the Messiah's first coming, and
still partially future at the time the awakening reader holds this
volume. Some of Yashar'el (Israel) has been preserved in the invisible
wilderness (2 Esdras 13, 1 Enoch 60). The rest is in the dispersion of
every nation. Both are gathered at the appointed time the prophets named
— from the land of the north, and from all the lands (Jeremiah
16:13–16). The northern house is not in 1 Esdras 2's genealogies because
the northern house was not part of the Persian return. The two-house
framework is not a modern theological invention; it is what the
post-exilic genealogies actually document by their absence as much as by
their presence.

Third, the opposition of the trans-Euphrates leadership and the local
Samaritan power-brokers (verses 16–30) is the second-temple
foreshadowing of the Samaritan-Yahudi (Jewish) rivalry that runs through
to the Gospels. The Samaritans of the post-exilic period are a mixed
population — descendants of those left behind in the northern kingdom
mixed with the foreign peoples Assyria settled in the land after the
deportation (2 Kings 17:24–41). They claim a covenant identity but
operate against the rebuilding of the proper covenant temple. The
framework of this Series identifies them as the second-temple type of
the false-inclusion gospel: a population claiming the covenant identity
by territorial occupation and religious mixing, opposed by the actual
covenant remnant whose lineage is verifiable. The pattern continues
through the Gospels (the Samaritan woman at the well, John 4) and
matters for understanding why Yahusha's ministry to Samaria is the
framework movement it is.

Cross-references: 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–4; Isaiah 44:24–28;
Isaiah 45:1–7; Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10–14; Daniel 9:1–2;
Proverbs 21:1; 2 Kings 17:24–41; John 4:1–42.

1 Esdras — Chapter 3

  1 Now when Darius reigned, he made a great feast to all his subjects,
  and to all his household, and to all the princes of Media and Persia,
  2 And to all the governors and captains and lieutenants that were
  under him, from India to Ethiopia, of an hundred twenty and seven
  provinces. 3 And when they had eaten and drunken, and being satisfied
  were gone home, then Darius the king went into his bedchamber, and
  slept, and soon after awaked. 4 Then three young men, that were of the
  guard that kept the king’s body, spoke one to another; 5 Let every one
  of us speak a sentence: he that shall overcome, and whose sentence
  shall seem wiser than the others, to him shall the king Darius give
  great gifts, and great things in token of victory:

  6 As, to be clothed in purple, to drink in gold, and to sleep upon
  gold, and a chariot with bridles of gold, and an headtire of fine
  linen, and a chain about his neck: 7 And he shall sit next to Darius
  because of his wisdom, and shall be called Darius his cousin. 8 And
  then every one wrote his sentence, sealed it, and laid it under king
  Darius his pillow; 9 And said that, when the king is risen, some will
  give him the writings; and of whose side the king and the three
  princes of Persia shall judge that his sentence is the wisest, to him
  shall the victory be given, as was appointed. 10 The first wrote, Wine
  is the strongest.

  11 The second wrote, The king is strongest. 12 The third wrote, Women
  are strongest: but above all things Truth bears away the victory. 13
  Now when the king was risen up, they took their writings, and
  delivered them to him, and so he read them: 14 And sending forth he
  called all the princes of Persia and Media, and the governors, and the
  captains, and the lieutenants, and the chief officers; 15 And sat him
  down in the royal seat of judgment; and the writings were read before
  them.

  16 And he said, Call the young men, and they shall declare their own
  sentences. So they were called, and came in. 17 And he said to them,
  Declare to us your mind concerning the writings. Then began the first,
  who had spoken of the strength of wine; 18 And he said thus, O you
  men, how exceeding strong is wine! it causeth all men to err that
  drink it: 19 It makes the mind of the king and of the fatherless child
  to be all one; of the bondman and of the freeman, of the poor man and
  of the rich: 20 It turns also every thought into jollity and mirth, so
  that a man remembereth neither sorrow nor debt:

  21 And it makes every heart rich, so that a man remembereth neither
  king nor governor; and it makes to speak all things by talents: 22 And
