  when they are in their cups, they forget their love both to friends
  and brothers, and a little after draw out swords: 23 But when they are
  from the wine, they remember not what they have done. 24 O you men, is
  not wine the strongest, that enforceth to do thus? And when he had so
  spoken, he held his peace.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 3 introduces the most distinctive material in 1 Esdras —
material with no parallel in the canonical Old Testament. King Darius
the Persian holds a great banquet for all the nobility of his empire.
After the banquet, the king sleeps. Three young men of his bodyguard —
including, as the text will reveal, Zerubbabel — agree to compose
answers to the question of what is the strongest thing in the world.
They write their answers and place them under the king's pillow. When
the king wakes, he reads the answers and convenes his court to hear the
three young men defend their respective claims.

The first young man argues that wine is strongest. The second argues
that the king is strongest. The third — Zerubbabel — argues that women
are strongest, but truth bears away the victory.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the literary device of the contest of strengths is a
Hellenistic-period genre, not a Hebrew narrative form. The genre is
similar to the disputation literature of Greek and Persian wisdom
traditions. The framework of this Series does not require the awakening
reader to defend the historical exactitude of the contest. The contest
is a literary occasion — a vehicle for the second-temple wisdom
tradition to set up the moment when truth is named as the highest
strength and Zerubbabel is the one who names it. The witness of the
chapter is what the chapter does, not whether the contest happened
literally.

Second, the structure of the answers builds toward the climax. Wine is
strong because it overwhelms the strong and weakens the wise. The king
is strong because his commands move armies and shape kingdoms. Women are
strong because they bring forth kings, sustain men, and draw the heart
of the most powerful. But truth bears away the victory because all the
things that have been named — wine, kings, women — are bounded, finite,
and pass away, while truth endures forever. The argument structurally
elevates each strength only to surpass them all with the unbounded
strength of truth.

Third, the chapter is preparing the literary occasion for Zerubbabel's
restoration of the temple. The text will reveal in chapter 4 that
Zerubbabel is the third young man, that he has named truth as the
highest strength, and that the king will reward him by authorizing him
to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple. The framework of this Series, which
holds that truth is the basis of restoration and that the awakening of
the remnant proceeds by the recovery of truth from inherited lies, finds
in 1 Esdras 3 the second-temple literary occasion for that recovery
being placed at the foundation of the temple's rebuilding. The temple is
rebuilt by the man who named truth.

Cross-references: Esther 1:1–22; Daniel 5:1–31; Proverbs 23:29–35;
Proverbs 31:1–9; John 8:31–32; John 14:6; John 18:37–38.

1 Esdras — Chapter 4

  1 Then the second, that had spoken of the strength of the king, began
  to say, 2 O you men, do not men excel in strength that bear rule over
  sea and land and all things in them? 3 But yet the king is more
  mighty: for he is lord of all these things, and has dominion over
  them; and whatsoever he commands them they do. 4 If he bid them make
  war the one against the other, they do it: if he send them out against
  the enemies, they go, and break down mountains walls and towers. 5
  They slay and are slain, and transgress not the king’s commandment: if
  they get the victory, they bring all to the king, as well the spoil,
  as all things else.

  6 Likewise for those that are no soldiers, and have not to do with
  wars, but use husbundry, when they have reaped again that which they
  had sown, they bring it to the king, and compel one another to pay
  tribute to the king. 7 And yet he is but one man: if he command to
  kill, they kill; if he command to spare, they spare; 8 If he command
  to smite, they smite; if he command to make desolate, they make
  desolate; if he command to build, they build; 9 If he command to cut
  down, they cut down; if he command to plant, they plant. 10 So all his
  people and his armies obey him: furthermore he lieth down, he eats and
  drinks, and takes his rest:

  11 And these keep watch round about him, neither may any one depart,
  and do his own business, neither disobey they him in any thing. 12 O
  you men, how should not the king be mightiest, when in such sort he is
  obeyed? And he held his tongue. 13 Then the third, who had spoken of
  women, and of the truth, (this was Zorobabel) began to speak. 14 O you
  men, it is not the great king, nor the multitude of men, neither is it
  wine, that excelleth; who is it then that ruleth them, or has the
  lordship over them? are they not women? 15 Women have borne the king
  and all the people that bear rule by sea and land.

  16 Even of them came they: and they nourished them up that planted the
  vineyards, from whence the wine comes. 17 These also make garments for
  men; these bring glory to men; and without women cannot men be. 18
  Yea, and if men have gathered together gold and silver, or any other
  goodly thing, do they not love a woman which is comely in favour and
  beauty? 19 And letting all those things go, do they not gape, and even
  with open mouth fix their eyes fast on her; and have not all men more
  desire to her than to silver or gold, or any goodly thing whatsoever?
  20 A man leaveth his own father that brought him up, and his own
  country, and cleaveth to his wife.

  21 He sticketh not to spend his life with his wife. and remembereth
  neither father, nor mother, nor country. 22 By this also you must know
  that women have dominion over you: do you not labour and toil, and
  give and bring all to the woman? 23 Yea, a man takes his sword, and
  goes his way to rob and to steal, to sail upon the sea and upon
  rivers; 24 And looketh upon a lion, and goes in the darkness; and when
  he has stolen, spoiled, and robbed, he brings it to his love. 25
  Wherefore a man loves his wife better than father or mother.

  26 Yea, many there be that have run out of their wits for women, and
  become servants for their sakes. 27 Many also have perished, have
  erred, and sinned, for women. 28 And now do you not believe me? is not
  the king great in his power? do not all regions fear to touch him? 29
  Yet did I see him and Apame the king’s concubine, the daughter of the
  admirable Bartacus, sitting at the right hand of the king, 30 And
  taking the crown from the king’s head, and setting it upon her own
  head; she also struck the king with her left hand.

  31 And yet for all this the king gaped and gazed upon her with open
  mouth: if she laughed upon him, he laughed also: but if she took any
  displeasure at him, the king was fain to flatter, that she might be
  reconciled to him again. 32 O you men, how can it be but women should
  be strong, seeing they do thus? 33 Then the king and the princes
  looked one upon another: so he began to speak of the truth. 34 O you
  men, are not women strong? great is the earth, high is the heaven,
  swift is the sun in his course, for he compasseth the heavens round
  about, and fetcheth his course again to his own place in one day. 35
  Is he not great that makes these things? therefore great is the truth,
  and stronger than all things.

  36 All the earth cries upon the truth, and the heaven blesses it: all
  works shake and tremble at it, and with it is no unrighteous thing. 37
  Wine is wicked, the king is wicked, women are wicked, all the children
  of men are wicked, and such are all their wicked works; and there is
  no truth in them; in their unrighteousness also they shall perish. 38
  As for the truth, it endureth, and is always strong; it lives and
  conquereth for evermore. 39 With her there is no accepting of persons
  or rewards; but she doeth the things that are just, and refraineth
  from all unjust and wicked things; and all men do well like of her
  works. 40 Neither in her judgment is any unrighteousness; and she is
  the strength, kingdom, power, and majesty, of all ages. Blessed be the
  Yahuah (God) of truth.

  41 And with that he held his peace. And all the people then shouted,
  and said, Great is Truth, and mighty above all things. 42 Then said
  the king to him, Ask what you will more than is appointed in the
  writing, and we will give it you, because you are found wisest; and
  you shall sit next me, and shall be called my cousin. 43 Then said he
  to the king, Remember your vow, which you have vowed to build
  Jerusalem, in the day when you camest to your kingdom, 44 And to send
  away all the vessels that were taken away out of Jerusalem, which
  Cyrus set apart, when he vowed to destroy Babylon, and to send them
  again thither. 45 You also have vowed to build up the temple, which
  the Edomites burned when Judea was made desolate by the Chaldees.

  46 And now, O lord the king, this is that which I require, and which I
  desire of you, and this is the princely liberality proceeding from
  thyself: I desire therefore that you make good the vow, the
  performance of which with your own mouth you have vowed to the King of
  heaven. 47 Then Darius the king stood up, and kissed him, and wrote
  letters for him to all the treasurers and lieutenants and captains and
  governors, that they should safely convey on their way both him, and
  all those that go up with him to build Jerusalem. 48 He wrote letters
  also to the lieutenants that were in Celosyria and Phenice, and to
  them in Libanus, that they should bring cedar wood from Libanus to
  Jerusalem, and that they should build the city with him. 49 Moreover
  he wrote for all the Yahudim (Jews) that went out of his realm up into
  Jewry, concerning their freedom, that no officer, no ruler, no
  lieutenant, nor treasurer, should forcibly enter into their doors; 50
  And that all the country which they hold should be free without
  tribute; and that the Edomites should give over the villages of the
  Yahudim (Jews) which then they held:

  51 Yea, that there should be yearly given twenty talents to the
  building of the temple, until the time that it were built; 52 And
  other ten talents yearly, to maintain the burnt offerings upon the
  altar every day, as they had a commandment to offer seventeen: 53 And
  that all they that went from Babylon to build the city should have
  free liberty, as well they as their posterity, and all the priests
  that went away. 54 He wrote also concerning. the charges, and the
  priests’ vestments in which they minister; 55 And likewise for the
  charges of the Levites, to be given them until the day that the house
  were finished, and Jerusalem builded up.

  56 And he commanded to give to all that kept the city pensions and
  wages. 57 He sent away also all the vessels from Babylon, that Cyrus
  had set apart; and all that Cyrus had given in commandment, the same
  charged he also to be done, and sent to Jerusalem. 58 Now when this
  young man was gone forth, he lifted up his face to heaven toward
  Jerusalem, and praised the King of heaven, 59 And said, From you comes
  victory, from you comes wisdom, and yours is the glory, and I am your
  servant. 60 Blessed art you, who have given me wisdom: for to you I
  give thanks, O Yahuah (God) of our fathers.

  61 And so he took the letters, and went out, and came to Babylon, and
  told it all his brothers. 62 And they praised Yahuah (God) of
  their fathers, because he had given them freedom and liberty 63 To go
  up, and to build Jerusalem, and the temple which is called by his
  name: and they feasted with instruments of musick and gladness seven
  days.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 4 develops the answers in detail. Verses 1–32 are the speeches
on women and on truth — Zerubbabel's argument occupying most of the
chapter. The argument moves from women's power over kings and over the
strong to the higher claim that truth is supreme. "All the earth calls
upon truth, and the heaven blesses it: all works shake and tremble at
it, and with it is no unrighteous thing... With her there is no
accepting of persons or rewards; but she does the things that are just,
and refrains from all unjust and wicked things; and all men do well like
of her works. Neither in her judgment is any unrighteousness; and she is
the strength, kingdom, power, and majesty of all ages. Blessed is the
Elohim (God) of truth."

The court erupts. Zerubbabel is awarded the prize. He is offered any
request, and he names two: that Darius fulfill the vow Cyrus had made to
rebuild Jerusalem, and that the holy vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried
away from the temple be returned. Darius grants both requests in formal
decree (verses 47–63), and the chapter closes with the rejoicing of the
people upon hearing of the decree.

Three things matter.

First, the speech of Zerubbabel on truth is one of the great wisdom
passages in the apocryphal corpus. Wine is wicked, the king is wicked,
women are wicked, all the children of men are wicked, and such are all
their wicked works; and there is no truth in them; in their
unrighteousness also they shall perish. As for the truth, it endures,
and is always strong; it lives and conquers for evermore... Blessed be
the Elohim (God) of truth. The framework of this Series, which holds that truth
is the standard against which every inherited lie must be tested, and
that the awakening reader's confession is our fathers have inherited
lies (Jeremiah 16:19), finds in Zerubbabel's speech the second-temple
voice already articulating the supremacy of truth as the framework of
the covenant restoration.

The truth-language of Zerubbabel's speech runs into the canonical
witness in a continuous line. Psalm 117:2 — the truth of Yahuah (God)
endures forever. Psalm 119:142 — Your righteousness is an everlasting
righteousness, and your law is the truth. Psalm 119:151 — all your
commandments are truth. Psalm 119:160 — Your word is true from the
beginning: and every one of your righteous judgments endures forever.
Proverbs 12:19 — the lip of truth shall be established forever. Isaiah
65:16 — he who blesses himself in the earth shall bless himself in the
Elohim (God) of truth; and he who swears in the earth shall swear by the Elohim (God) of
truth. Jeremiah 10:10 — Yahuah (God) is the true Elohim (God), he is the living
Elohim (God), and an everlasting King. The covenant scriptures consistently name
truth as Yahuah (God)'s own attribute, the Torah as truth, and the
believer's witness as walking in truth.

Yahusha (Jesus) brings this entire tradition to its concentrated
apostolic statement. John 14:6: I am the way, the truth, and the life.
John 17:17: Sanctify them through your truth: your word is truth. John
8:31–32: If you continue in my word, then are you my disciples indeed;
and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. John
18:37: To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world,
that I should bear witness to the truth. Every one that is of the truth
hears my voice. Zerubbabel said truth conquers and lives forever;
Yahusha said I am the truth. The second-temple wisdom-tradition's
prediction was vindicated when the Word came in the flesh as the
embodied truth.

The apostolic letters complete the line. 1 John 5:6: the Spirit is
truth. 2 Corinthians 13:8: we can do nothing against the truth, but for
the truth. 3 John 1:4: I have no greater joy than to hear that my
children walk in truth. The covenant pattern is one continuous line:
Yahuah (God) is the Elohim (God) of truth, the Torah is truth, the prophets bore
witness to truth, the Messiah came as truth in the flesh, the Spirit is
truth, and the awakening reader walks in truth as the proper response to
all of it. Zerubbabel's speech in 1 Esdras 4 is one of the second-temple
voices that named the line as the line. The temple is rebuilt by the man
who knew that truth was the foundation — and the temple stands until the
imperial powers of Rome destroy it, after which the Messiah-temple of
the resurrected body (John 2:19–22) becomes the appointed dwelling-place
toward which all subsequent restoration is moving.

Second, Zerubbabel's request is selfless. He does not ask for personal
wealth, position, or political power. He asks for the rebuilding of
Jerusalem and the return of the temple vessels. The framework of this
Series, which honors the awakening leader who seeks the restoration of
the covenant community rather than personal advancement, finds in
Zerubbabel a model. The reward of the wise is not to be given more for
himself; the reward of the wise is to be given the resources to do the
work the Father has appointed.

Third, the decree of Darius (verses 47–57) is comprehensive. Darius
commands the trans-Euphrates leaders to give Zerubbabel safe conduct, to
provide the materials for rebuilding the temple, to return the holy
vessels, to authorize the offering of sacrifices, to exempt the priests
and Levites from tribute, to forbid future interference. The decree is
the formal political reversal of the opposition Artaxerxes had granted
in chapter 2. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
political setbacks of the awakening community are temporary and that the
Father turns the empire as He wills toward the restoration of His own,
finds in the decree of Darius the second-temple memory of one such
turning. The setbacks are real. The setbacks are not the final word.
Yahuah (God) turns the empire when His appointed time comes.

Cross-references: Ezra 6:1–15; Daniel 2:21; Daniel 4:34–37; Proverbs
21:1; Isaiah 41:8–10; Romans 13:1–7; John 8:31–32; John 17:17.

1 Esdras — Chapter 5

  1 After this were the principal men of the families chosen according
  to their tribes, to go up with their wives and sons and daughters,
  with their menservants and maidservants, and their cattle. 2 And
  Darius sent with them a thousand horsemen, till they had brought them
  back to Jerusalem safely, and with musical instruments tabrets and
  flutes. 3 And all their brothers played, and he made them go up
  together with them. 4 And these are the names of the men which went
  up, according to their families among their tribes, after their
  several heads. 5 The priests, the sons of Phinees the son of Aaron:
  Jesus the son of Josedec, the son of Saraias, and Joacim the son of
  Zorobabel, the son of Salathiel, of the house of David, out of the
  kindred of Phares, of the tribe of Yahudah (Judah);

  6 Who spoke wise sentences before Darius the king of Persia in the
  second year of his reign, in the month Nisan, which is the first
  month. 7 And these are they of Jewry that came up from the captivity,
  where they dwelt as strangers, whom Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon
  had carried away to Babylon. 8 And they returned to Jerusalem, and to
  the other parts of Jewry, every man to his own city, who came with
  Zorobabel, with Jesus, Nehemias, and Zacharias, and Reesaias, Enenius,
  Mardocheus. Beelsarus, Aspharasus, Reelius, Roimus, and Baana, their
  guides. 9 The number of them of the nation, and their governors, sons
  of Phoros, two thousand an hundred seventy and two; the sons of
  Saphat, four hundred seventy and two: 10 The sons of Ares, seven
  hundred fifty and six:

  11 The sons of Phaath Moab, two thousand eight hundred and twelve: 12
  The sons of Elam, a thousand two hundred fifty and four: the sons of
  Zathul, nine hundred forty and five: the sons of Corbe, seven hundred
  and five: the sons of Bani, six hundred forty and eight: 13 The sons
  of Bebai, six hundred twenty and three: the sons of Sadas, three

  Aterezias, ninety and two: the sons of Ceilan and Azetas threescore

  16 The sons of Ananias, an hundred and one: the sons of Arom, thirty

  18 They of Netophah, fifty and five: they of Anathoth, an hundred

  Chadias and Ammidoi, four hundred twenty and two: they of Cirama and
  Gabdes, six hundred twenty and one:

  21 They of Macalon, an hundred twenty and two: they of Betolius, fifty
  and two: the sons of Nephis, an hundred fifty and six: 22 The sons of

  26 The Levites: the sons of Jessue, and Cadmiel, and Banuas, and

  36 These came up from Thermeleth and Thelersas, Charaathalar leading

  priests that usurped the office of the priesthood, and were not found:
  the sons of Obdia, the sons of Accoz, the sons of Addus, who married

  41 So of Yashar'el (Israel), from them of twelve years old and upward,
  they were all in number forty thousand, beside menservants and
  womenservants two thousand three hundred and sixty. 42 Their
  menservants and handmaids were seven thousand three hundred forty and
  seven: the singing men and singing women, two hundred forty and five:
  43 Four hundred thirty and five camels, seven thousand thirty and six
  horses, two hundred forty and five mules, five thousand five hundred
  twenty and five beasts used to the yoke. 44 And certain of the chief
  of their families, when they came to the temple of Yahuah (God) that
  is in Jerusalem, vowed to set up the house again in his own place
  according to their ability, 45 And to give into the holy treasury of
  the works a thousand pounds of gold, five thousand of silver, and an
  hundred priestly vestments.

  46 And so dwelt the priests and the Levites and the people in
  Jerusalem, and in the country, the singers also and the porters; and
  all Yashar'el (Israel) in their villages. 47 But when the seventh
  month was at hand, and when the children of Yashar'el (Israel) were
  every man in his own place, they came all together with one consent
  into the open place of the first gate which is toward the east. 48
  Then stood up Jesus the son of Josedec, and his brothers the priests
  and Zorobabel the son of Salathiel, and his brothers, and made ready
  the altar of Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), 49 To offer burnt
  sacrifices upon it, according as it is expressly commanded in the book
  of Moses the man of Yahuah (God). 50 And there were gathered to them
  out of the other nations of the land, and they erected the altar upon
  his own place, because all the nations of the land were at enmity with
  them, and oppressed them; and they offered sacrifices according to the
  time, and burnt offerings to Yahuah (God) both morning and evening.

  51 Also they held the feast of tabernacles, as it is commanded in the
  law, and offered sacrifices daily, as was meet: 52 And after that, the
  continual oblations, and the sacrifice of the sabbaths, and of the new
  moons, and of all holy feasts. 53 And all they that had made any vow
  to Yahuah (God) began to offer sacrifices to Yahuah (God) from the
  first day of the seventh month, although the temple of Yahuah (God)
  was not yet built. 54 And they gave to the masons and carpenters
  money, meat, and drink, with cheerfulness. 55 To them of Zidon also
  and Tyre they gave carrs, that they should bring cedar trees from
  Libanus, which should be brought by floats to the haven of Joppa,
  according as it was commanded them by Cyrus king of the Persians.

  56 And in the second year and second month after his coming to the
  temple of Yahuah (God) at Jerusalem began Zorobabel the son of
  Salathiel, and Jesus the son of Josedec, and their brothers, and the
  priests, and the Levites, and all they that were come to Jerusalem out
  of the captivity: 57 And they laid the foundation of the house of
  Yahuah (God) in the first day of the second month, in the second year
  after they were come to Jewry and Jerusalem. 58 And they appointed the
  Levites from twenty years old over the works of Yahuah (God). Then
  stood up Jesus, and his sons and brothers, and Cadmiel his brother,
  and the sons of Madiabun, with the sons of Joda the son of Eliadun,
  with their sons and brothers, all Levites, with one accord setters
  forward of the business, labouring to advance the works in the house
  of Yahuah (God). So the workmen built the temple of Yahuah (God). 59
  And the priests stood arrayed in their vestments with musical
  instruments and trumpets; and the Levites the sons of Asaph had
  cymbals, 60 Singing songs of thanksgiving, and praising Yahuah (God),
  according as David the king of Yashar'el (Israel) had ordained.

  61 And they sung with loud voices songs to the praise of Yahuah (God),
  because his mercy and glory is for ever in all Yashar'el (Israel). 62
  And all the people sounded trumpets, and shouted with a loud voice,
  singing songs of thanksgiving to Yahuah (God) for the rearing up of
  the house of Yahuah (God). 63 Also of the priests and Levites, and of
  the chief of their families, the ancients who had seen the former
  house came to the building of this with weeping and great crying. 64
  But many with trumpets and joy shouted with loud voice, 65 Insomuch
  that the trumpets might not be heard for the weeping of the people:
  yet the multitude sounded marvellously, so that it was heard afar off.

  66 Wherefore when the enemies of the tribe of Yahudah (Judah) and
  Benjamin heard it, they came to know what that noise of trumpets
  should mean. 67 And they perceived that they that were of the
  captivity did build the temple to Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel).
  68 So they went to Zorobabel and Jesus, and to the chief of the
  families, and said to them, We will build together with you. 69 For we
  likewise, as you, do obey your Elohim (God), and do sacrifice to him
  from the days of Azbazareth the king of the Assyrians, who brought us
  hither. 70 Then Zorobabel and Jesus and the chief of the families of
  Yashar'el (Israel) said to them, It is not for us and you to build
  together an house to Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God).

  71 We ourselves alone will build to Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el
  (Israel), according as Cyrus the king of the Persians has commanded
  us. 72 But the heathen of the land lying heavy upon the inhabitants of
  Judea, and holding them strait, hindered their building; 73 And by
  their secret plots, and popular persuasions and commotions, they
  hindered the finishing of the building all the time that king Cyrus
  lived: so they were hindered from building for the space of two years,
  until the reign of Darius.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 5 records the second wave of return under Zerubbabel and Joshua
the high priest, with extensive lists of the returnees by family and by
function (verses 1–46), and the laying of the foundation of the second
temple (verses 47–73). The narrative parallels Ezra 2 and Ezra 3
closely.

Three things matter.

First, the lists of returnees are not decorative. They are the
documented covenant lineage of the household of Yashar'el (Israel)
returning to the land of their inheritance. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the covenant identity is the actual paternal
lineage of the seed of promise, finds in the lists the second-temple
practice of preserving and verifying that lineage. The principle: the
covenant is preserved through documented lineage, and the seed is
preserved across the dispersion by the keeping of the documentation. The
contemporary awakening reader, whose own covenant lineage may be
uncertain after centuries of dispersion among the nations, can take from
the second-temple practice the principle that lineage matters even when
the records are incomplete; the Father knows His own.

Second, the foundation of the temple is laid with a specific liturgy
(verses 56–60). The priests in their vestments stand with trumpets. The
Levites stand with cymbals to praise Yahuah (God) according to the order
of David. The people sing antiphonally: He is good, and his mercy
endures for ever toward Yashar'el (Israel). The framework of this
Series, which honors the appointed worship of Yahuah (God) as the
covenant community's right response to His mercy, finds in 1 Esdras 5
the second-temple practice of that worship at the foundation of the
rebuilt temple.

The "according to the order of David" phrase is significant. The Davidic
order of temple music is established in 1 Chronicles 23–26: David
appointed the Levites by their courses for the temple service, including
the appointed singers (1 Chronicles 25) and the appointed gatekeepers (1
Chronicles 26). David did not invent worship; he organized it. The
post-exilic community returning to rebuild the temple did not invent a
new liturgy; they recovered David's appointed pattern. The framework's
principle: the covenant worship of Yahuah (God) is by the appointed
order, preserved across centuries of dispersion, recovered when the
community returns to the appointed pattern. Hebrews 4:7 names David as
the speaker of an again, today call to enter Yahuah (God)'s rest; the
Davidic order of worship and the Davidic call to rest run continuously
into the apostolic period.

The antiphonal refrain — He is good, and his mercy endures forever
toward Yashar'el (Israel) — is the canonical refrain of Psalm 136 (where
the phrase repeats twenty-six times) and of Psalm 118:1, 29 and Psalm
107:1. The post-exilic community is singing the canonical Psalter at the
foundation. They are not innovating a praise; they are joining the
praise Yahuah (God) had given the covenant community through the
inspired psalmists. 2 Chronicles 5:13 records the same refrain at
Solomon's dedication of the first temple. Ezra 3:11 confirms the same at
the foundation of the second temple. The mercy of Yahuah (God) endures
forever toward Yashar'el (Israel) — and the covenant community sings the
same refrain at every appointed dedication.

Third, the chapter records the curious mixed response of the people
(verses 61–65). The young men shout for joy at the laying of the
foundation, while the old men — those who had seen the first temple in
Solomon's day — weep with a loud voice because the foundation of the
second temple is so far below the glory of the first. The two voices are
mixed together so that the noise was heard far off, and the people could
not distinguish the shouting of joy from the noise of weeping. The
framework of this Series, which honors the awakening of the remnant as
the work of the Father even when the awakening is partial and the
restoration is below the glory of what was lost, finds in the mixed
response of 1 Esdras 5 the proper second-temple posture: rejoice in what
has been restored, weep for what has been lost, and let both responses
be heard at the same time. The restoration is real. The loss is real.
Both are true. The awakening reader walking out of the four houses can
hold both at once.

Cross-references: Ezra 2:1–70; Ezra 3:1–13; 1 Chronicles 9:1–34; 2
Chronicles 5:1–14; Psalm 118:1–29; Psalm 136:1–26; Haggai 2:1–9;
Zechariah 4:6–10.

1 Esdras — Chapter 6

  1 Now in the second year of the reign of Darius Aggeus and Zacharias
  the son of Addo, the prophets, prophesied to the Yahudim (Jews) in
  Jewry and Jerusalem in the name of Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel),
  which was upon them. 2 Then stood up Zorobabel the son of Salatiel,
  and Jesus the son of Josedec, and began to build the house of Yahuah
  (God) at Jerusalem, the prophets of Yahuah (God) being with them, and
  helping them. 3 At the same time came to them Sisinnes the governor of
  Syria and Phenice, with Sathrabuzanes and his companions, and said to
  them, 4 By whose appointment do you build this house and this roof,
  and perform all the other things? and who are the workmen that perform
  these things? 5 Nevertheless the elders of the Yahudim (Jews) obtained
  favour, because Yahuah (God) had visited the captivity;

  6 And they were not hindered from building, until such time as
  signification was given to Darius concerning them, and an answer
  received. 7 The copy of the letters which Sisinnes, governor of Syria
  and Phenice, and Sathrabuzanes, with their companions, rulers in Syria
  and Phenice, wrote and sent to Darius; To king Darius, greeting: 8 Let
  all things be known to our lord the king, that being come into the
  country of Judea, and entered into the city of Jerusalem we found in
  the city of Jerusalem the ancients of the Yahudim (Jews) that were of
  the captivity 9 Building an house to Yahuah (God), great and new, of
  hewn and costly stones, and the timber already laid upon the walls. 10
  And those works are done with great speed, and the work goes on
  prosperously in their hands, and with all glory and diligence is it
  made.

  11 Then asked we these elders, saying, By whose commandment build you
  this house, and lay the foundations of these works? 12 Therefore to
  the intent that we might give knowledge to you by writing, we demanded
  of them who were the chief doers, and we required of them the names in
  writing of their principal men. 13 So they gave us this answer, We are
  the servants of Yahuah (God) which made heaven and earth. 14 And as
  for this house, it was builded many years ago by a king of Yashar'el
  (Israel) great and strong, and was finished. 15 But when our fathers
  provoked Yahuah (God) to wrath, and sinned against Yahuah (God) of
  Yashar'el (Israel) which is in heaven, he gave them over into the
  power of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, of the Chaldees;

  16 Who pulled down the house, and burned it, and carried away the
  people captives to Babylon. 17 But in the first year that king Cyrus
  reigned over the country of Babylon Cyrus the king wrote to build up
  this house. 18 And the holy vessels of gold and of silver, that
  Nabuchodonosor had carried away out of the house at Jerusalem, and had
  set them in his own temple those Cyrus the king brought forth again
  out of the temple at Babylon, and they were delivered to Zorobabel and
  to Sanabassarus the ruler, 19 With commandment that he should carry
  away the same vessels, and put them in the temple at Jerusalem; and
  that the temple of Yahuah (God) should be built in his place. 20 Then
  the same Sanabassarus, being come hither, laid the foundations of the
  house of Yahuah (God) at Jerusalem; and from that time to this being
  still a building, it is not yet fully ended.

  21 Now therefore, if it seem good to the king, let search be made
  among the records of king Cyrus: 22 And if it be found that the
  building of the house of Yahuah (God) at Jerusalem has been done with
  the consent of king Cyrus, and if our lord the king be so minded, let
  him signify to us thereof. 23 Then commanded king Darius to seek among
  the records at Babylon: and so at Ecbatane the palace, which is in the
  country of Media, there was found a roll in which these things were
  recorded. 24 In the first year of the reign of Cyrus king Cyrus
  commanded that the house of Yahuah (God) at Jerusalem should be built
  again, where they do sacrifice with continual fire: 25 Whose height
  shall be sixty cubits and the breadth sixty cubits, with three rows of
  hewn stones, and one row of new wood of that country; and the expences
  thereof to be given out of the house of king Cyrus:

  26 And that the holy vessels of the house of Yahuah (God), both of
  gold and silver, that Nabuchodonosor took out of the house at
  Jerusalem, and brought to Babylon, should be restored to the house at
  Jerusalem, and be set in the place where they were before. 27 And also
  he commanded that Sisinnes the governor of Syria and Phenice, and
  Sathrabuzanes, and their companions, and those which were appointed
  rulers in Syria and Phenice, should be careful not to meddle with the
  place, but suffer Zorobabel, the servant of Yahuah (God), and governor
  of Judea, and the elders of the Yahudim (Jews), to build the house of
  Yahuah (God) in that place. 28 I have commanded also to have it built
  up whole again; and that they look diligently to help those that be of
  the captivity of the Yahudim (Jews), till the house of Yahuah (God) be
  finished: 29 And out of the tribute of Celosyria and Phenice a portion
  carefully to be given these men for the sacrifices of Yahuah (God),
  that is, to Zorobabel the governor, for bullocks, and rams, and lambs;
  30 And also corn, salt, wine, and oil, and that continually every year
  without further question, according as the priests that be in
  Jerusalem shall signify to be daily spent:

  31 That offerings may be made to the most high Yahuah (God) for the
  king and for his children, and that they may pray for their lives. 32
  And he commanded that whoever should transgress, yes, or make light of
  any thing afore spoken or written, out of his own house should a tree
  be taken, and he on it be hanged, and all his goods seized for the
  king. 33 Yahuah (God) therefore, whose name is there called upon,
  utterly destroy every king and nation, that stretcheth out his hand to
  hinder or endamage that house of Yahuah (God) in Jerusalem. 34 I
  Darius the king have ordained that according to these things it be
  done with diligence.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 6 records the renewed opposition to the rebuilding (verses
1–22), the prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraging the work (verses
1–2), the search of the Persian archives that finds the original decree
of Cyrus (verses 23–34), and Darius's confirmatory decree authorizing
the completion of the temple (verses 23–34). The narrative parallels
Ezra 5 and Ezra 6.

Two things matter.

First, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah are named (verse 1). The
framework of this Series, which honors the prophets as the standard
against which apocryphal witness is measured, marks the moment. Haggai
and Zechariah are the prophetic voices that called the post-exilic
community back to the work of the temple. Their oracles are preserved in
the Hebrew canon. 1 Esdras names them but does not preserve their
oracles. The reader who wants to hear the prophetic word that drove the
rebuilding has it in the Hebrew canon, not in 1 Esdras. The awakening
reader who has been retrained on the framework of this Series will know
to read Haggai and Zechariah for the prophetic substance, and 1 Esdras
for the historical chronicle that surrounds them.

Second, the discovery of the Cyrus decree in the Persian archives
(verses 23–24) is presented as a remarkable moment. The opposition had
assumed that the Cyrus decree was lost, forgotten, or never genuinely
issued. The search of the archives at Ecbatane turns up the original
document. The decree is reaffirmed. The opposition is overturned. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the truth has been preserved
across centuries of inherited deception and that the awakening reader's
task is to recover what has been buried in the archives of forgotten
texts, finds in 1 Esdras 6 a small but meaningful illustration. The
decree was real. The decree had not been revoked. The decree had only
been buried in the archives. The opposition had lied about its having
been lost. The truth was recoverable, and the recovery turned the
political situation. The principle: the truth has not been lost; it has
been buried, and the awakening proceeds by digging it back up.

Cross-references: Ezra 5:1–17; Ezra 6:1–22; Haggai 1:1–2:23; Zechariah
1:1–8:23; Jeremiah 16:19; Daniel 9:1–19; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy
3:16–17.

1 Esdras — Chapter 7

  1 Then Sisinnes the governor of Celosyria and Phenice, and
  Sathrabuzanes, with their companions following the commandments of
  king Darius, 2 Did very carefully oversee the holy works, assisting
  the ancients of the Yahudim (Jews) and governors of the temple. 3 And
  so the holy works prospered, when Aggeus and Zacharias the prophets
  prophesied. 4 And they finished these things by the commandment of
  Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), and with the consent of Cyrus,
  Darius, and Artexerxes, kings of Persia. 5 And thus was the holy house
  finished in the three and twentieth day of the month Adar, in the
  sixth year of Darius king of the Persians

  6 And the children of Yashar'el (Israel), the priests, and the
  Levites, and others that were of the captivity, that were added to
  them, did according to the things written in the book of Moses. 7 And
  to the dedication of the temple of Yahuah (God) they offered an
  hundred bullocks two hundred rams, four hundred lambs; 8 And twelve
  goats for the sin of all Yashar'el (Israel), according to the number
  of the chief of the tribes of Yashar'el (Israel). 9 The priests also
  and the Levites stood arrayed in their vestments, according to their
  kindreds, in the service of Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel),
  according to the book of Moses: and the porters at every gate. 10 And
  the children of Yashar'el (Israel) that were of the captivity held the
  passover the fourteenth day of the first month, after that the priests
  and the Levites were sanctified.

  11 They that were of the captivity were not all sanctified together:
  but the Levites were all sanctified together. 12 And so they offered
  the passover for all them of the captivity, and for their brothers the
  priests, and for themselves. 13 And the children of Yashar'el (Israel)
  that came out of the captivity did eat, even all they that had
  separated themselves from the abominations of the people of the land,
  and sought Yahuah (God). 14 And they kept the feast of unleavened
  bread seven days, making merry before Yahuah (God), 15 For that he had
  turned the counsel of the king of Assyria toward them, to strengthen
  their hands in the works of Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel).

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 7 records the completion of the second temple in the sixth year
of Darius (verses 1–9), the dedication celebration (verses 10–15), and
the keeping of Passover by the returned community (verses 16–25). The
chapter parallels Ezra 6:14–22.

Three things matter.

First, the temple is completed. The framework of this Series, which
honors the appointed dwelling-place of Yahuah (God) as the covenant
community's gathering-point under the appointed worship, finds in the
completion of the second temple a real restoration — though not the
final one. The first temple had been built by Solomon at the height of
the united kingdom; the second temple was built by the returnees at the
lowest point of the covenant community's political fortunes. The second
temple is below the first in glory, as Haggai 2 had named. The third
temple — the temple of the gathered remnant under the reign of the
Messiah, which Ezekiel 40–48 describes — has not yet been built. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the appointed worship at the
temple is one of the destinations of the long restoration, marks the
second temple as a stage in that restoration, not as the destination.
Read the completion of the second temple with that lens.

Second, the dedication celebration includes specific offerings: a
hundred bullocks, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, twelve goats —
one for each tribe of Yashar'el (Israel) — for the sin of all Yashar'el
(Israel) (verse 8). The twelve goats matter. The text presents the
post-exilic covenant community offering twelve goats, one for each
tribe, for the sin of all Yashar'el (Israel) — including the ten tribes
that had not returned, the scattered northern house. The framework of
this Series, which holds that the gathering of all twelve tribes is the
destination of the long restoration and that the second-temple community
knew it was praying for the gathering of the houses that had not yet
returned, finds in the twelve goats a small but explicit illustration.
The post-exilic community did not consider the ten tribes lost. They
offered for them. They prayed for them. They held the place open at the
offering.

Third, the keeping of Passover (verses 16–25) is the proper close. The
Torah's appointed feast is kept according to the Torah's specifications.

The Torah commanded Passover as the foundational covenant memorial.
Exodus 12:14 — And this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and you
shall keep it a feast to Yahuah (God) throughout your generations; you
shall keep it a feast by an ordinance for ever. Exodus 12:26–27 — And it
shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you, What mean you
by this service? That you shall say, It is the sacrifice of Yahuah
(God)'s passover, who passed over the houses of the children of
Yashar'el (Israel) in Egypt. Leviticus 23:5 — In the fourteenth day of
the first month at even is Yahuah (God)'s passover. The post-exilic
community keeping Passover is the covenant pattern recovering. 1
Corinthians 5:7 names the Messianic fulfillment of the Passover: Messiah
(Christ) our passover is sacrificed for us.

The framework of this Series, which honors the appointed feasts as the
appointed feasts and which sees in the post-exilic community's
restoration of feast-keeping the proper covenant pattern, finds in 1
Esdras 7 the model the awakening reader can carry into his or her own
walk.

Cross-references: Ezra 6:14–22; Haggai 2:1–9; Zechariah 4:1–14; Ezekiel
40:1–48:35; Numbers 7:1–89; Numbers 28:1–29:40; Leviticus 23:1–44.

1 Esdras — Chapter 8

  1 And after these things, when Artexerxes the king of the Persians
  reigned came Esdras the son of Saraias, the son of Ezerias, the son of
  Helchiah, the son of Salum, 2 The son of Sadduc, the son of Achitob,
  the son of Amarias, the son of Ezias, the son of Meremoth, the son of
  Zaraias, the son of Savias, the son of Boccas, the son of Abisum, the
  son of Phinees, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest.
  3 This Esdras went up from Babylon, as a scribe, being very ready in
  the law of Moses, that was given by Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el
  (Israel). 4 And the king did him honour: for he found grace in his
  sight in all his requests. 5 There went up with him also certain of
  the children of Yashar'el (Israel), of the priest of the Levites, of
  the holy singers, porters, and ministers of the temple, to Jerusalem,

  6 In the seventh year of the reign of Artexerxes, in the fifth month,
  this was the king’s seventh year; for they went from Babylon in the
  first day of the first month, and came to Jerusalem, according to the
  prosperous journey which Yahuah (God) gave them. 7 For Esdras had very
  great skill, so that he omitted nothing of the law and commandments of
  Yahuah (God), but taught all Yashar'el (Israel) the ordinances and
  judgments. 8 Now the copy of the commission, which was written from
  Artexerxes the king, and came to Esdras the priest and reader of the

  Esdras the priest and reader of the law of Yahuah (God) sends

  that such of the nation of the Yahudim (Jews), and of the priests and
  Levites being within our realm, as are willing and desirous should go
  with you to Jerusalem.

  11 As many therefore as have a mind to it, let them depart with you,
  as it has seemed good both to me and my seven friends the counsellors;
  12 That they may look to the affairs of Judea and Jerusalem, agreeably
  to that which is in the law of Yahuah (God); 13 And carry the gifts to
  Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel) to Jerusalem, which I and my
  friends have vowed, and all the gold and silver that in the country of
  Babylon can be found, to Yahuah (God) in Jerusalem, 14 With that also
  which is given of the people for the temple of Yahuah (God), their
  Elohim (God) at Jerusalem: and that silver and gold may be collected
  for bullocks, rams, and lambs, and things to it appertaining; 15 To
  the end that they may offer sacrifices to Yahuah (God) upon the altar
  of Yahuah (God), their Elohim (God), which is in Jerusalem.

  16 And whatsoever you and your brothers will do with the silver and
  gold, that do, according to the will of your Elohim (God). 17 And the
  holy vessels of Yahuah (God), which are given you for the use of the
  temple of your Elohim (God), which is in Jerusalem, you shall set
  before your Elohim (God) in Jerusalem. 18 And whatsoever thing else
  you shall remember for the use of the temple of your Elohim (God), you
  shall give it out of the king’s treasury. 19 And I king Artexerxes
  have also commanded the keepers of the treasures in Syria and Phenice,
  that whatsoever Esdras the priest and the reader of the law of the
  most high Yahuah (God) shall send for, they should give it him with
  speed, 20 To the sum of an hundred talents of silver, likewise also of
  wheat even to an hundred cors, and an hundred pieces of wine, and
  other things in abundance.

  21 Let all things be performed after the law of Yahuah (God)
  diligently to the most high Yahuah (God), that wrath come not upon the
  kingdom of the king and his sons. 22 I command you also, that you
  require no tax, nor any other imposition, of any of the priests, or
  Levites, or holy singers, or porters, or ministers of the temple, or
  of any that have doings in this temple, and that no man have authority
  to impose any thing upon them. 23 And you, Esdras, according to the
  wisdom of Yahuah (God) ordain judges and justices, that they may judge
  in all Syria and Phenice all those that know the law of your Elohim
  (God); and those that know it not you shall teach. 24 And whoever
  shall transgress the law of your Elohim (God), and of the king, shall
  be punished diligently, whether it be by death, or other punishment,
  by penalty of money, or by imprisonment. 25 Then said Esdras the
  scribe, Blessed be the only Yahuah (God) of my fathers, who has put
  these things into the heart of the king, to glorify his house that is
  in Jerusalem:

  26 And has honoured me in the sight of the king, and his counsellors,
  and all his friends and nobles. 27 Therefore was I encouraged by the
  help of Yahuah (God), my Elohim (God), and gathered together men of
  Yashar'el (Israel) to go up with me. 28 And these are the chief

  Phinees, Gerson: of the sons of Ithamar, Gamael: of the sons of David,

  31 Of the sons of Pahath Moab, Eliaonias, the son of Zaraias, and with

  Bebai, and with him twenty and eight men: 38 Of the sons of Astath,

  41 And these I gathered together to the river called Theras, where we

  Eleazar, and Iduel, and Masman, 44 And Alnathan, and Mamaias, and

  46 And commanded them that they should speak to Daddeus, and to his

  journey both for us and them that were with us, for our children, and

  51 For I was ashamed to ask the king footmen, and horsemen, and

  besought our Elohim (God) as touching these things, and found him

  priests, Esebrias, and Assanias, and ten men of their brothers with

  (God) of our fathers. 59 Watch you, and keep them till you deliver

  of the house of our Elohim (God). 60 So the priests and the Levites,

  the son of Phinees, and with them were Josabad the son of Jesu and

  Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), even twelve bullocks for all
  Yashar'el (Israel), fourscore and sixteen rams,

  66 Threescore and twelve lambs, goats for a peace offering, twelve;
  all of them a sacrifice to Yahuah (God). 67 And they delivered the
  king’s commandments to the king’s stewards’ and to the governors of

  Yahuah (God). 68 Now when these things were done, the rulers came to
  me, and said, 69 The nation of Yashar'el (Israel), the princes, the
  priests and Levites, have not put away from them the strange people of

  and the holy garment rent, and bowing my knees, and stretching forth
  my hands to Yahuah (God), 74 I said, O Yahuah (God), I am confounded
  and ashamed before your face; 75 For our sins are multiplied above our
  heads, and our ignorances have reached up to heaven.

  76 For ever since the time of our fathers we have been and are in
  great sin, even to this day. 77 And for our sins and our fathers’ we
  with our brothers and our kings and our priests were given up to the
  kings of the earth, to the sword, and to captivity, and for a prey
  with shame, to this day. 78 And now in some measure has mercy been
  shewed to us from you, O Yahuah (God), that there should be left us a
  root and a name in the place of your sanctuary; 79 And to discover to

  before the kings of Persia, so that they gave us food;

  81 Yea, and honoured the temple of our Elohim (God), and raised up the
  desolate Sion, that they have given us a sure abiding in Jewry and

  things? for we have transgressed your commandments, which you gavest
  by the hand of your servants the prophets, saying, 83 That the land,
  which you enter into to possess as an heritage, is a land polluted
  with the pollutions of the strangers of the land, and they have filled
  it with their uncleanness. 84 Therefore now shall you not join your
  daughters to their sons, neither shall you take their daughters to
  your sons. 85 Moreover you shall never seek to have peace with them,
  that you may be strong, and eat the good things of the land, and that
  you may leave the inheritance of the land to your children for
  evermore.

  86 And all that is befallen is done to us for our wicked works and
  great sins; for you, O Yahuah (God), did make our sins light, 87 And
  did give to us such a root: but we have turned back again to
  transgress your law, and to mingle ourselves with the uncleanness of

  91 And as Esdras in his prayer made his confession, weeping, and lying

  Jerusalem a very great multitude of men and women and children: for

  of Jeelus, one of the sons of Yashar'el (Israel), called out, and
  said, O Esdras, we have sinned against Yahuah (God), we have married
  strange women of the nations of the land, and now is all Yashar'el
  (Israel) aloft. 93 Let us make an oath to Yahuah (God), that we will
  put away all our wives, which we have taken of the heathen, with their
  children, 94 Like as you have decreed, and as many as do obey the law
  of Yahuah (God). 95 Arise and put in execution: for to you does this
  matter appertain, and we will be with you: do valiantly.

  96 So Esdras arose, and took an oath of the chief of the priests and
  Levites of all Yashar'el (Israel) to do after these things; and so
  they sware.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 8 records the coming of Ezra to Jerusalem (verses 1–67), Ezra's
grief upon learning that many of the returnees have married foreign
women in defiance of the Torah (verses 68–96), and the assembly of the
people to address the crisis. The chapter parallels Ezra 7 and Ezra 9.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, Ezra's lineage is named in detail (verses 1–2). He is "Ezra the
son of Saraias, the son of Ezerias, the son of Helkias, the son of
Sallumus, the son of Sadduk, the son of Achitob, the son of Amarias, the
son of Eziras, the son of Marimoth, the son of Phinehas, the son of
Eleazar, the son of Aaron the high priest." The lineage runs sixteen
generations back to Aaron. The framework of this Series, which holds
that the priestly line is the actual paternal lineage of Aaron and not a
behavioral category, finds in Ezra's documented lineage the
second-temple practice of preserving the priestly line. Ezra is
qualified to do what he is about to do because he is, in fact, of the
priestly seed.

Second, the mixed-marriage crisis (verses 68–96) is sharper than the
inherited Christian reading has often allowed. The text records that the
returnees — including priests, Levites, and laypeople — had married
women from the surrounding peoples, including the very nations the Torah
had named in Deuteronomy 7 as forbidden marriage partners for the
covenant community.

Ezra's prayer of confession in 1 Esdras 8:73–90 (paralleling Ezra
9:6–15) is one of the great corporate-confession prayers of the
post-exilic period. Read it against Daniel 9, Nehemiah 9, and Solomon's
temple-dedication prayer in 1 Kings 8 — the canonical confession-prayer
line. Ezra 9:6: O my Elohim (God), I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to
you, my Elohim (God): for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our
trespass is grown up to the heavens. Daniel 9:5: We have sinned, and
have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even
by departing from your precepts and from your judgments. Nehemiah 9:33:
Howbeit you are just in all that is brought upon us; for you have done
right, but we have done wickedly. 1 Kings 8:46–50, Solomon's prayer: If
they sin against you, (for there is no man that sins not,) and you be
angry with them, and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them
away captives unto the land of the enemy... yet if they shall bethink
themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent,
and make supplication unto you... and so return unto you with all their
heart, and with all their soul... then hear you their prayer. Ezra is
praying inside this canonical line.

Ezra's response is not measured. He tears his garments, plucks the hair
from his head and beard, sits in stunned grief, prays a prayer of
corporate confession (verses 73–90), and assembles the people to address
the crisis. The Torah's standard is being applied to a community that
had walked out from under it.

The framework of this Series, on the question of mixed marriage, must be
held precisely. The Torah's prohibition on marrying women from the
surrounding pagan nations (Deuteronomy 7:1–4) is grounded in the danger
of being turned away to other gods.

Read Deuteronomy 7:3–4 carefully: Neither shall you make marriages with
them; your daughter you shall not give to his son, nor his daughter
shall you take to your son. For they will turn away your son from
following me, that they may serve other gods: so will the anger of
Yahuah (God) be kindled against you, and destroy you suddenly. The
reason is named: the marriage will turn the covenant son's heart away to
other gods. 1 Kings 11:1–4 records the historical fulfillment of the
warning in Solomon's case: King Solomon loved many strange women,
together with the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites,
Edomites, Zidonians, and Hittites... For it came to pass, when Solomon
was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods.
Solomon's marriages produced exactly what Deuteronomy 7 had warned
against. Sirach 47:21 names the same: Solomon polluted your seed by his
marriages.

The framework's caveat: the Torah is not against marriage to foreigners
as such; the Torah is against marriage that draws the covenant community
into the worship of other gods. The principle is preservation of
covenant worship, not racial purity. Boaz married Ruth the Moabitess;
Ruth had renounced the gods of Moab (Ruth 1:16: your people shall be my
people, and your Elohim (God) my God). Rahab married into Yashar'el (Israel)
(Matthew 1:5 names her in the Messiah's genealogy); Rahab had renounced
the gods of Canaan (Joshua 2:11: Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God), he is Elohim (God) in
heaven above, and in earth beneath). The principle is: the covenant
person does not marry a worshiper of other gods, because the marriage
will draw the covenant person away. 2 Corinthians 6:14 articulates the
same in apostolic vocabulary: Be not unequally yoked together with
unbelievers: for what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness?
and what communion has light with darkness? The principle is the
covenant. The principle is the Torah. The framework holds the canonical
witness as the standard.

Third, Ezra's response is to apply the Torah, not to soften it. The
dissolution of the mixed marriages that follows in chapter 9 is the most
painful pastoral application in the post-exilic period. The framework of
this Series does not require the awakening reader to legislate
contemporary marriage dissolution from Ezra's case. The awakening
reader's principle is the principle the Torah teaches: marry within the
covenant; do not marry someone whose worship will draw you away;
preserve the covenant lineage where possible. The application of the
principle to specific contemporary marriages is pastoral and personal,
not legislative.

Cross-references: Ezra 7:1–10:44; Nehemiah 8:1–9:38; Deuteronomy 7:1–11;
Numbers 25:1–18; Genesis 24:1–67; Genesis 28:1–9; Joshua 23:11–13; 1
Kings 11:1–13; Ezekiel 16:1–63; 2 Corinthians 6:14–18.

1 Esdras — Chapter 9

  1 Then Esdras rising from the court of the temple went to the chamber
  of Joanan the son of Eliasib, 2 And remained there, and did eat no
  meat nor drink water, mourning for the great iniquities of the
  multitude. 3 And there was a proclamation in all Jewry and Jerusalem
  to all them that were of the captivity, that they should be gathered
  together at Jerusalem: 4 And that whoever met not there within two or
  three days according as the elders that bare rule appointed, their
  cattle should be seized to the use of the temple, and himself cast out
  from them that were of the captivity. 5 And in three days were all
  they of the tribe of Yahudah (Judah) and Benjamin gathered together at
  Jerusalem the twentieth day of the ninth month.

  6 And all the multitude sat trembling in the broad court of the temple
  because of the present foul weather. 7 So Esdras arose up, and said to
  them, You have transgressed the law in marrying strange wives, thereby
  to increase the sins of Yashar'el (Israel). 8 And now by confessing
  give glory to Yahuah (God) of our fathers, 9 And do his will, and
  separate yourselves from the heathen of the land, and from the strange
  women. 10 Then cried the whole multitude, and said with a loud voice,
  Like as you have spoken, so will we do.

  11 But forasmuch as the people are many, and it is foul weather, so
  that we cannot stand without, and this is not a work of a day or two,
  seeing our sin in these things is spread far: 12 Therefore let the

  Levites published all things to the people, saying, This day is holy

  words in which they were instructed, and for the which they had been
  assembled.

⸻

Commentary

The closing chapter records the dissolution of the mixed marriages
(verses 1–36) and the public reading of the Torah at the Water Gate by
Ezra (verses 37–55). The chapter parallels Ezra 10 and Nehemiah 8.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the dissolution of the mixed marriages is conducted under the
assembly's deliberation, not by individual ad-hoc action. The text
records the assembly's careful process: the heads of houses are
convened, the cases are heard, the dissolutions proceed orderly. The
framework of this Series, which honors orderly covenant-community action
under the Torah rather than individual zealotry, finds in 1 Esdras 9 the
proper covenant-community process. The Torah is the standard. The
community applies it. The application is documented. The applications
proceed by case.

Second, the public reading of the Torah at the Water Gate (verses 37–55)
is one of the great moments in the second-temple history. Ezra stands on
a wooden pulpit. The Levites assist in reading and explaining the text.
The people stand for the reading and weep at the hearing of the words.
Ezra and the Levites comfort the people: Mourn not, nor weep; for all
the people wept, when they heard the law. Go then, and eat the fat, and
drink the sweet, and send part to them that have nothing; for this day
is holy to Yahuah (God): be not sorrowful. The framework of this Series,
which holds that the public reading and explanation of the Torah is the
foundational practice of the awakening community, finds in 1 Esdras 9
the second-temple model.

The canonical anchor is Nehemiah 8:1–8: And all the people gathered
themselves together as one man into the street that was before the water
gate; and they spake unto Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law
of Moses, which Yahuah (God) had commanded to Yashar'el (Israel). And
Ezra the priest brought the law before the congregation both of men and
women, and all that could hear with understanding... And he read therein
before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until
midday, before the men and the women, and those that could understand;
and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the
law... So they read in the book in the law of Elohim (God) distinctly, and gave
the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. The 1 Esdras and
Nehemiah accounts are the same event preserved in two textual
traditions. Both name the Water Gate. Both name Ezra. Both name the
Levites assisting. Both name the standing of the people. Both name the
reading from morning until midday. Both name the Levites giving the
sense — that is, translating from the Hebrew of the Torah scroll into
the Aramaic the post-exilic community could understand.

The Levitical giving of the sense is the foundational pattern for what
the framework of this Series is doing in the commentary chapters of this
volume itself. The Torah text is read; the explanation is offered; the
people are caused to understand. This is the proper covenant order of
teaching: scripture first, explanation that names what scripture says
(without adding to it or subtracting from it), the people gathered to
receive both. Deuteronomy 31:10–13 commanded this very practice: At the
end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in
the feast of tabernacles, when all Yashar'el (Israel) is come to appear
before Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God) in the place which he shall choose, you
shall read this law before all Yashar'el (Israel) in their hearing.
Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and the
stranger that is within your gates, that they may hear, and that they
may learn, and fear Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God), and observe to do all the
words of this law. The Water-Gate reading was the first appointed
Tabernacles-reading after the return; the post-exilic community was
recovering what the Torah had commanded.

The weeping of the people upon hearing the Torah read is the response of
those who recognize, mid-reading, how far they have walked out from
under it. 2 Kings 22:11 records the same response in Josiah when the
book of the law was found: And it came to pass, when the king had heard
the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes. The covenant
pattern is consistent: when the Torah is read freshly to a generation
that has been distant from it, the response is grief — not because the
Torah is harsh, but because the distance between what it commands and
how the people have been living has now been seen plainly. Ezra and the
Levites do not soften the grief; they redirect it: the joy of Yahuah
(God) is your strength (Nehemiah 8:10). The Torah-grief turns to
feast-joy when the people respond by walking back into the appointed
pattern.

Third, the closing of 1 Esdras is unfinished. The text breaks off
mid-sentence: "And they came together..." The fragmentation is one of
the textual peculiarities of 1 Esdras and is preserved in this volume as
it stands in the manuscript tradition. The framework of this Series does
not require the awakening reader to speculate about what would have
followed. The book is what is preserved. The post-exilic community had
begun to gather. The Torah had been read. The covenant had been
re-established. The work that follows — the rebuilding of the walls
under Nehemiah, the centuries of second-temple life, the rise of the
schools and parties, the long wait for the Messiah — is the rest of the
second-temple story. 1 Esdras has done what it set out to do: it has
shown the covenant community of the southern kingdom returning to the
land, rebuilding the temple, dissolving the mixed marriages, and
gathering to hear the Torah read. The framework of this Series, which
sees in the second-temple restoration a partial fulfillment of the
prophetic gathering and a foreshadowing of the final gathering of all
twelve tribes, finds in 1 Esdras the second-temple opening movement of
that long restoration.

Cross-references: Ezra 10:1–44; Nehemiah 8:1–18; Nehemiah 9:1–38;
Deuteronomy 31:9–13; Joshua 8:30–35; 2 Kings 23:1–3; Acts 15:21; Luke
4:16–21; 1 Timothy 4:13.

2 Esdras — Introduction

2 Esdras is the apocalypse. Of all fourteen books in the King James
Apocrypha, this is the one most likely to disorient a reader who has
only ever encountered the gentle wisdom of Tobit or the historical
chronicle of 1 Maccabees. 2 Esdras is visions. Seven of them, given to
the seer Ezra (or Salathiel, in some manuscript traditions), addressing
the most weighted theological questions of the second-temple period: why
did Yahuah (God) allow His people to fall to Babylon? Why are the wicked
among the nations prospering while the righteous remnant suffers? When
will the Messiah come? How will the resurrection of the dead unfold?
What will the world to come look like? And most painfully — what about
the lost ten tribes?

The book is composite. The middle five visions (chapters 3–14) are the
original Hebrew or Aramaic core, dated by most scholars to the late
first century CE — that is, they were composed by an unknown Yahudi
(Jewish) seer in the immediate aftermath of the destruction of the
second temple by Rome in 70 CE, and they are written in the voice of
Ezra weeping over the destruction of the first temple by Babylon five
centuries earlier. The opening two chapters and the closing two chapters
(1–2 and 15–16) are later Christian additions, surviving only in Latin
and largely absent from the Greek and Syriac manuscript traditions. The
King James translators included the entire sixteen-chapter form, and so
this volume includes it — but the awakening reader should know that the
central five visions are the substantial witness, and the bracketing
chapters are early Christian framings.

Three things matter for the reader of this Series.

First, 2 Esdras 13:39–47 contains one of the most direct second-temple
references to the lost ten tribes anywhere in the apocryphal corpus.
Ezra sees a man rising from the sea — a Messianic figure — and gathering
to himself another multitude that was peaceable. The seer asks who this
multitude is. The answer is given: these are the ten tribes who were
carried away in the days of King Hoshea, who took counsel among
themselves to leave the heathen and depart into a further country called
Arzareth (likely another land in Hebrew), where they have lived in their
own counsel and kept their statutes which they did not keep in their own
land. The framework's reading lands here precisely: the Arzareth
multitude is a remnant of the ten tribes, not the whole. A portion took
counsel and went further into a hidden country; the rest remained
scattered through the nations under the broken covenant. Both groups are
the seed. The Arzareth remnant is preserved in the invisible wilderness
1 Enoch 60 names — the desert east of the garden where Behemoth dwells,
hidden from common sight, kept across the centuries for the appointed
gathering. The wider scattered seed is in all the lands where Yahuah
(God) drove them (Jeremiah 16:13–16). The gathering at the end is a
two-stream gathering — from the land of the north, and from all the
lands — converging into one homecoming. The river dries up to make the
way (Revelation 16:12, Isaiah 11:15–16, 2 Esdras 13:47). The wilderness
of the people receives the gathering (Ezekiel 20:34–38), and there the
rod passes over the seed and the rebels are purged before the refined
enter the land. The passage is not a footnote. It is the explicit
second-temple memory that the ten tribes did not vanish — and the
framework alignment with Enoch, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and
Revelation lands the picture whole. The inherited Christian reading has
treated this passage as folklore, because the framework of scattered
Yashar'el (Israel) was lost to institutional Christianity. The Spirit
has restored that framework to the awakening remnant, and 2 Esdras 13 is
one of the witnesses that the restoration was always there in the texts
of the second temple, waiting for ears to hear it.

Second, 2 Esdras' apocalyptic vocabulary illuminates the imagery of the
New Testament Revelation. The eagle vision of chapter 11–12, the
Messiah's appearing on Mount Zion, the gathering of the elect, the
tribulation of the righteous — these are the imagery and the syntax that
fed the first-century church's reception of the Revelation given to
John. The two books are not the same. 2 Esdras was not written by an
apostle and was not received as scripture. But it is the literary world
inside which the apostolic apocalypses were composed, and reading it
equips the reader to see what the New Testament writers were drawing
from when they used the apocalyptic vocabulary they used.

Third, 2 Esdras presses the question of theodicy harder than any other
apocryphal book. The seer is not a comfortable believer. He weeps. He
argues with the angel Uriel. He demands answers. He is told that the
answers are too high for him and that he must wait for the appointed
time. The book is honest about the cost of being a remnant in a world
that does not understand the covenant, and that honesty is one of the
things this book has to offer the reader walking out of the four houses,
who will recognize the ache of the seer because he or she has been
carrying it too.

Read 2 Esdras slowly. It does not yield to fast reading. The cyclical
revelations of Yahusha (Jesus) — particularly the Revelation given to
John — are governed in this Series by a specific interpretive framework
that names Revelation as cyclical rather than linear (see the framework
note in the volume on Revelation if available). Where 2 Esdras'
apocalyptic imagery overlaps with the New Testament Revelation, the same
cyclical reading applies. Witness is not chronology. Witness is showing
the same end-arc from a different angle, in a different vocabulary, for
a different audience, by a different seer.

2 Esdras — Chapter 1

  1 The second book of the prophet Esdras, the son of Saraias, the son
  of Azarias, the son of Helchias, the son of Sadamias, the son of
  Sadoc, the son of Achitob, 2 The son of Achias, the son of Phinees,
  the son of Heli, the son of Amarias, the son of Aziei, the son of
  Marimoth, the son of Arna, the son of Ozias, the son of Borith, the
  son of Abisei, the son of Phinees, the son of Eleazar, 3 The son of
  Aaron, of the tribe of Levi; which was captive in the land of the
  Medes, in the reign of Artexerxes king of the Persians. 4 And the word
  of Yahuah (God) came to me, saying, 5 Go your way, and shew my people
  their sinful deeds, and their children their wickedness which they
  have done against me; that they may tell their children’s children:

  6 Because the sins of their fathers are increased in them: for they
  have forgotten me, and have offered to strange gods. 7 Am not I even
  he that brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the house of
  bondage? but they have provoked me to wrath, and despised my counsels.
  8 Pull you off then the hair of your head, and cast all evil upon
  them, for they have not been obedient to my law, but it is a
  rebellious people. 9 How long shall I forbear them, into whom I have
  done so much good? 10 Many kings have I destroyed for their sakes;
  Pharaoh with his servants and all his power have I struck down.

  11 All the nations have I destroyed before them, and in the east I
  have scattered the people of two provinces, even of Tyrus and Sidon,
  and have slain all their enemies. 12 Speak you therefore to them,
  saying, Thus says Yahuah (God), 13 I led you through the sea and in
  the beginning gave you a large and safe passage; I gave you Moses for
  a leader, and Aaron for a priest. 14 I gave you light in a pillar of
  fire, and great wonders have I done among you; yet have you forgotten
  me, says Yahuah (God). 15 Thus says the Almighty Yahuah (God), The
  quails were as a token to you; I gave you tents for your safeguard:
  nevertheless you murmured there,

  16 And triumphed not in my name for the destruction of your enemies,
  but ever to this day do you yet murmur. 17 Where are the benefits that
  I have done for you? when you were hungry and thirsty in the
  wilderness, did you not cry to me, 18 Saying, Why have you brought us
  into this wilderness to kill us? it had been better for us to have
  served the Egyptians, than to die in this wilderness. 19 Then had I
  pity upon your mournings, and gave you manna to eat; so you did eat
  angels’ bread. 20 When you were thirsty, did I not cleave the rock,
  and waters flowed out to your fill? for the heat I covered you with
  the leaves of the trees.

  21 I divided among you a fruitful land, I cast out the Canaanites, the
  Pherezites, and the Philistines, before you: what shall I yet do more
  for you? says Yahuah (God). 22 Thus says the Almighty Yahuah (God),
  When you were in the wilderness, in the river of the Amorites, being
  athirst, and blaspheming my name, 23 I gave you not fire for your
  blasphemies, but cast a tree in the water, and made the river sweet.
  24 What shall I do to you, O Jacob? you, Juda, wouldest not obey me: I
  will turn me to other nations, and to those will I give my name, that
  they may keep my statutes. 25 Seeing you have forsaken me, I will
  forsake you also; when you desire me to be gracious to you, I shall
  have no mercy upon you.

  26 Whenever you shall call upon me, I will not hear you: for you have
  defiled your hands with blood, and your feet are swift to commit
  manslaughter. 27 You have not as it were forsaken me, but your own
  selves, says Yahuah (God). 28 Thus says the Almighty Yahuah (God),
  Have I not prayed you as a father his sons, as a mother her daughters,
  and a nurse her young babes, 29 That you would be my people, and I
  should be your Elohim (God); that you would be my children, and I
  should be your father? 30 I gathered you together, as a hen gathers
  her chickens under her wings: but now, what shall I do to you? I will
  cast you out from my face.

  31 When you offer to me, I will turn my face from you: for your solemn
  feastdays, your new moons, and your circumcisions, have I forsaken. 32
  I sent to you my servants the prophets, whom you have taken and slain,
  and torn their bodies in pieces, whose blood I will require of your
  hands, says Yahuah (God). 33 Thus says the Almighty Yahuah (God), Your
  house is desolate, I will cast you out as the wind does stubble. 34
  And your children shall not be fruitful; for they have despised my
  commandment, and done the thing that is an evil before me. 35 Your
  houses will I give to a people that shall come; which not having heard
  of me yet shall believe me; to whom I have shewed no signs, yet they
  shall do that I have commanded them.

  36 They have seen no prophets, yet they shall call their sins to
  remembrance, and acknowledge them. 37 I take to witness the grace of
  the people to come, whose little ones rejoice in gladness: and though
  they have not seen me with bodily eyes, yet in spirit they believe the
  thing that I say. 38 And now, brother, behold what glory; and see the
  people that come from the east: 39 To whom I will give for leaders,
  Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Oseas, Amos, and Micheas, Joel, Abdias, and
  Jonas, 40 Nahum, and Abacuc, Sophonias, Aggeus, Zachary, and Malachy,
  which is called also an angel of Yahuah (God).

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter of 2 Esdras is one of the four chapters (1, 2, 15,
16) that are Christian additions to the original Yahudi (Jewish)
apocalypse. They survive only in Latin and are absent from the Greek and
Syriac manuscript traditions of the central five visions. The awakening
reader should read them as early Christian framings, not as original
second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) material. This does not strip them of
their value; it simply names what they are.

The chapter is Yahuah (God) speaking through Esdras (the Latinization of
