invisible wilderness. The location is a real place set apart from common
sight, preserved across the centuries for the gathering of the seed and
for the Father's face-to-face dealing with His own. The reader who has
worked through The Book of Enoch — Restored Names Edition will recognize
the framework alignment: Enoch names the place; 2 Esdras 13 shows who is
there; Ezekiel 20 names what happens there when the rest of the seed is
brought to it.

Fifth, the river dries up to make the way. The seer in 2 Esdras 13:47 is
told that the Most High shall stay the springs of the stream again, that
they may go through. This stilling of the waters at the gathering is the
same image Revelation 16:12 names: And the sixth angel poured out his
vial upon the great river Euphrates; and the water thereof was dried up,
that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared. The Euphrates
that the ten tribes crossed at their original deportation, that the
Arzareth remnant crossed at their further departure, is the same river
that dries up for their return. The kings of the east of Revelation 16
are the gathered seed coming home through the dried path. The
framework's cyclical Revelation reading lands here cleanly: the same
gathering-waters-stilled image appears in Isaiah 11:15–16 — Yahuah (God)
shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his
mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river... And there shall be
an highway for the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from
Assyria — in 2 Esdras 13, and in Revelation 16. Three witnesses, one
image, one gathering.

Sixth — and this is the verse that ends the spiritual-Yashar'el (Israel)
argument. The seer is not speaking of a behavioral category. He is not
speaking of anyone who comes into faith and Torah-keeping. He is
speaking of the named, numbered, scattered tribes — Reuben, Simeon,
Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Ephraim, Manasseh — the
actual paternal lineage that was carried into Assyria in 722 BCE under
Shalmaneser. He says they took counsel to depart further, to keep the
statutes they had failed to keep in their own land. He says they crossed
the Euphrates by miracle. He says they dwelt in Arzareth until the
latter time. He says they will come back when the Most High stays the
springs of the stream again. This is not metaphor. This is not a parable
about behavior. This is the second-temple seer telling the awakened
reader what the framework has been telling the awakened reader: the
scattered seed is real, it is preserved, and it is being gathered home
in two streams at the appointed time.

The Christian reading of this passage has been almost universally to
spiritualize it — to say that the ten tribes represents the spiritual
fullness of the Gentiles being grafted in, that Arzareth is a poetic
image for the wilderness of the world, that the gathering is the
church's mission to the nations. The framework rejects this. The seer
does not invite the spiritualization. He gives names — Salmanasar,
Hoshea, Euphrates — and a chronology — 722 BCE, the latter time, the
appointed gathering. He gives geography — a journey of a year and a
half, a region called Arzareth. The plain reading is a plain reading.
The seer is reporting what was shown.

The Hebrew roots reading has often gone the other direction — to claim
the ten tribes as the spiritual ancestry of the contemporary Hebrew
roots / Torah observant community, regardless of bloodline. The
framework rejects this just as firmly. The ten tribes were a paternal
seed. The bloodline is not transferable. A behavioral choice to keep the
Torah does not make a person a descendant of Naphtali. The seed is the
seed. Many of the contemporary Hebrew roots community are, in fact, of
the seed — the scattered seed under judgment for centuries, now waking
up in the appointed time, the very recognition the prophets named in
Jeremiah 16:19. But many is not anyone who shows up. The framework holds
the bloodline specification. The Three Categories hold: Yahudah (Judah)
preserved their identity through exile and is the Yahudim (Jews) of the
modern world; the scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel) lost their
identity in dispersion and is the awakening remnant being gathered now;
the nations sojourn alongside in the covenant household, welcomed and
loved, but not the seed of promise.

Seventh, Romans 11 reads at this passage and reads cleanly. Paul's olive
tree is Yashar'el (Israel). The natural branches are the covenant house
that retained identity. The wild olive branches are the scattered seed
of Yashar'el (Israel) that grew wild among the nations in exile — still
olive, always olive, never anything else — being grafted back into their
own natural root. Paul, of the tribe of Benjamin, was writing to
scattered seed who had forgotten who they were; he calls his hearers
wild olive because they grew wild in foreign soil, not because they are
non-Yashar'el (Israel). The Christian reading of Romans 11 — that
non-Yashar'el (Israel) heathen are spliced onto the olive tree as a new
branch by faith — is the Christian inclusion gospel in covenant clothing
and is the same lie 2 Esdras 13 dismantles when the seer names the ten
tribes as a specific paternal lineage. Romans 11 and 2 Esdras 13 are the
same gathering, articulated by two witnesses, of the same scattered seed
coming home to its own root. The Arzareth remnant is one stream of that
gathering. The wider scattered seed coming out of the nations is the
other.

Eighth, the prophetic anchors converge here. Five prophets, five
witnesses, one promise. Hosea 1:10–11: Yet the number of the children of
Yashar'el (Israel) shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be
measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place
where it was said unto them, You are not my people, there it shall be
said unto them, You are the sons of the living Elohim (God). Then shall the
children of Yahudah (Judah) and the children of Yashar'el (Israel) be
gathered together, and appoint themselves one head, and they shall come
up out of the land. Ezekiel 37:21–22: Behold, I will take the children
of Yashar'el (Israel) from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and
will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land: and
I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Yashar'el
(Israel); and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no
more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any
more at all. Isaiah 11:11–12: And it shall come to pass in that day,
that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the
remnant of his people... He shall set up an ensign for the nations, and
shall assemble the outcasts of Yashar'el (Israel), and gather together
the dispersed of Yahudah (Judah) from the four corners of the earth.
Jeremiah 31:8: I will bring them from the north country, and gather them
from the coasts of the earth. Amos 9:14: And I will bring again the
captivity of my people of Yashar'el (Israel), and they shall build the
waste cities, and inhabit them.

Five prophetic witnesses naming the same gathering. 2 Esdras 13 is
praying inside this prophetic line. The seer is not innovating; he is
confirming. The framework finds in 2 Esdras 13 the most explicit
second-temple confirmation of the prophetic gathering: the ten tribes
did not vanish into the genetic pool of the nations. A remnant was
preserved in Arzareth. The rest were preserved in the dispersion. Both
are coming home — through the dried river, into the invisible
wilderness, under the rod that purges out the rebels, into the bond of
the covenant restored, and from there into the land where the Messiah
reigns.

Ninth, the imagery of the Most High holding still the flood for the ten
tribes to pass over (verse 44) is the reverse-Exodus imagery. The same
kind of miracle that brought Yashar'el (Israel) out of Egypt is being
recounted as having preserved the Arzareth remnant in their further
dispersion. The framework's principle: the Father did not lose track of
His seed when Assyria deported them. He held the river still for the
remnant to cross over into preservation. He will hold it still again for
the gathering to cross back at the appointed time. The same Hand. The
same purpose. The same covenant.

Tenth, the closing detail of the passage matters. The peaceful multitude
that the Man from the sea gathers is the end-state. Not a battle. Not a
campaign. Peace. The destruction by fire from his mouth has already
happened to the assembled nations. The refined remnant —
Arzareth-preserved and nations-gathered, sifted in the wilderness,
brought into the bond of the covenant — comes home into a kingdom
already cleansed. The framework's reading of the appointed reign on the
earth, with the Torah going forth from Tsion (Zion), the appointed
feasts kept, the land restored, finds in this final detail the closing
image: the seed comes home, the city is restored, the war is over, the
reign begins.

The contemporary reader who has been told that the Two-House framework
is a recent fringe development needs 2 Esdras 13 read aloud to him. The
second-temple seer, writing to and for the wise of his own people, was
prophesying the future gathering of the lost ten tribes. He did not have
to be taught the framework by a modern movement. He had been taught it
by the prophets — Hosea 1, Hosea 2, Ezekiel 37, Isaiah 11, Jeremiah 16,
Jeremiah 31, Ezekiel 20, Amos 9. The two houses of Yashar'el (Israel)
and Yahudah (Judah), scattered and gathered, separated and reunited
under the reign of the Messiah, are the prophetic framework of the
entire Hebrew canon. The framework that names this is not a modern
innovation. The reading that flattens it into a single-house spiritual
category is the modern innovation.

The awakening reader who has carried doubts about whether the
framework's reading of the long restoration is real should sit with this
chapter. Read the source text first. Then read this commentary. Then go
back to the text. The framework is not in the commentary. The framework
is in the chapter. The commentary names what the chapter has been
holding for nearly two millennia, waiting for the wise of the people to
read it again.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 17:1–6; 2 Kings 17:18–23; Hosea 1:9–11; Hosea
2:23; Ezekiel 20:34–38; Ezekiel 37:15–22; Isaiah 11:11–16; Isaiah
27:12–13; Jeremiah 16:13–16; Jeremiah 31:1–14; Romans 11:1–32; 1 Enoch
60:7–10; Matthew 15:24; James 1:1; Revelation 7:4–8; Revelation 16:12;
Revelation 19:11–21; Deuteronomy 30:1–10.

2 Esdras — Chapter 14

  1 And it came to pass upon the third day, I sat under an oak, and,
  behold, there came a voice out of a bush over against me, and said,
  Esdras, Esdras. 2 And I said, Here am I, Yahuah (God) And I stood up
  upon my feet. 3 Then said he to me, In the bush I did manifestly
  reveal myself to Moses, and talked with him, when my people served in
  Egypt: 4 And I sent him and led my people out of Egypt, and brought
  him up to the mount of where I held him by me a long season, 5 And
  told him many wondrous things, and shewed him the secrets of the
  times, and the end; and commanded him, saying,

  6 These words shall you declare, and these shall you hide. 7 And now I
  say to you, 8 That you lay up in your heart the signs that I have
  shewed, and the dreams that you have seen, and the interpretations
  which you have heard: 9 For you shall be taken away from all, and from
  henceforth you shall remain with my Son, and with such as be like you,
  until the times be ended. 10 For the world has lost his youth, and the
  times begin to wax old.

  11 For the world is divided into twelve parts, and the ten parts of it
  are gone already, and half of a tenth part: 12 And there remains that
  which is after the half of the tenth part. 13 Now therefore set yours
  house in order, and reprove your people, comfort such of them as be in
  trouble, and now renounce corruption, 14 Let go from you mortal
  thoughts, cast away the burdens of man, put off now the weak nature,
  15 And set aside the thoughts that are most heavy to you, and haste
  you to flee from these times.

  16 For yet greater evils than those which you have seen happen shall
  be done hereafter. 17 For look how much the world shall be weaker
  through age, so much the more shall evils increase upon them that
  dwell in it. 18 For the time is fled far away, and leasing is hard at
  hand: for now hasteth the vision to come, which you have seen. 19 Then
  answered I before you, and said, 20 Behold, Yahuah (God), I will go,
  as you have commanded me, and reprove the people which are present:
  but they that shall be born afterward, who shall admonish them? thus
  the world is set in darkness, and they that dwell in it are without
  light.

  21 For your law is burnt, therefore no man knoweth the things that are
  done of you, or the work that shall begin. 22 But if I have found
  grace before you, send the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) into me, and I
  shall write all that has been done in the world since the beginning,
  which were written in your law, that men may find your path, and that
  they which will live in the latter days may live. 23 And he answered
  me, saying, Go your way, gather the people together, and say to them,
  that they seek you not for forty days. 24 But look you prepare you
  many box trees, and take with you Sarea, Dabria, Selemia, Ecanus, and
  Asiel, these five which are ready to write swiftly; 25 And come
  hither, and I shall light a candle of understanding in yours heart,
  which shall not be put out, till the things be performed which you
  shall begin to write.

  26 And when you have done, some things shall you publish, and some
  things shall you shew secretly to the wise: to morrow this hour shall
  you begin to write. 27 Then went I forth, as he commanded, and
  gathered all the people together, and said, 28 Hear these words, O
  Yashar'el (Israel). 29 Our fathers at the beginning were strangers in
  Egypt, from whence they were delivered: 30 And received the law of
  life, which they kept not, which you also have transgressed after
  them.

  31 Then was the land, even the land of Sion, parted among you by lot:
  but your fathers, and you yourselves, have done unrighteousness, and
  have not kept the ways which the Highest commanded you. 32 And
  forasmuch as he is a righteous judge, he took from you in time the
  thing that he had given you. 33 And now are you here, and your
  brothers among you. 34 Therefore if so be that you will subdue your
  own understanding, and reform your hearts, you shall be kept alive and
  after death you shall obtain mercy. 35 For after death shall the
  judgment come, when we shall live again: and then shall the names of
  the righteous be manifest, and the works of the ungodly shall be
  declared.

  36 Let no man therefore come to me now, nor seek after me these forty
  days. 37 So I took the five men, as he commanded me, and we went into
  the field, and remained there. 38 And the next day, behold, a voice
  called me, saying, Esdras, open your mouth, and drink that I give you
  to drink. 39 Then opened I my mouth, and, behold, he reached me a full
  cup, which was full as it were with water, but the colour of it was
  like fire. 40 And I took it, and drank: and when I had drunk of it, my
  heart uttered understanding, and wisdom grew in my breast, for my
  spirit strengthened my memory:

  41 And my mouth was opened, and shut no more. 42 The Highest gave
  understanding to the five men, and they wrote the wonderful visions of
  the night that were told, which they knew not: and they sat forty
  days, and they wrote in the day, and at night they ate bread. 43 As
  for me. I spoke in the day, and I held not my tongue by night. 44 In
  forty days they wrote two hundred and four books. 45 And it came to
  pass, when the forty days were filled, that the Highest spoke, saying,
  The first that you have written publish openly, that the worthy and
  unworthy may read it:

  46 But keep the seventy last, that you may deliver them only to such
  as be wise among the people: 47 For in them is the spring of
  understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the stream of knowledge. 48
  And I did so.

⸻

Commentary

The seer is told that he will be taken up from among men in forty days,
and that before he is taken up he should write down what has been
revealed to him — that he should restore the books that were burned in
the destruction of the temple. He is given five scribes, and dictated
for forty days. By the end he produces ninety-four books — twenty-four
to be made public (the canonical Hebrew books) and seventy to be kept
hidden for the wise.

Three things matter.

First, the restoration of the burned books is the second-temple legend
explaining how the Hebrew canon was preserved after the destruction of
the first temple. The legend treats Ezra (the seer) as the restorer of
the canonical scriptures. The framework of this Series does not require
the awakening reader to defend the literal historicity of the legend;
the canonical Hebrew books were preserved through manuscript copies that
survived the destruction, not through dictation under prophetic
inspiration after the fact. The legend is second-temple. The historical
preservation was through more ordinary means.

Second, the distinction between the twenty-four public books and the
seventy hidden books is the second-temple framework for understanding
the relationship between the canonical Hebrew scriptures and the
apocryphal-pseudepigraphal corpus. The twenty-four are public,
accessible, the standard. The seventy are reserved for the wise. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the apocryphal books are
witness to be heard but not Torah to be legislated from, finds in 2
Esdras 14 the second-temple articulation of the same distinction. The
Apocrypha is not equal to the Torah and the prophets. The Apocrypha is
the seventy hidden books — preserved for the wise, useful in their
place, but not the standard.

This is the verse that gives the awakened reader the genre-anchor for
everything else in this volume. The reader who has been taught by the
Catholic and Orthodox traditions to treat the Apocrypha as canonical
scripture has inflated the seventy to the level of the twenty-four. The
reader who has been taught by the modern Protestant tradition to treat
the Apocrypha as worthless has deflated the seventy below the threshold
of useful witness. 2 Esdras 14 holds the middle and names the genre. The
seventy are real. The seventy are valuable. The seventy are not the
twenty-four. Read this volume of the Apocrypha as the second-temple seer
says to read it — as the books reserved for the wise of the people,
useful for understanding the world the canonical scriptures were written
into and the world the Messiah was born into, but not the standard
against which the canonical scriptures themselves are measured. The
standard runs the other way.

Third, the seer's dictation for forty days (verses 40–48) parallels the
forty days Moses was on Sinai receiving the Torah. The literary parallel
is intentional: the seer is being shown as a Moses-figure restoring what
had been lost. The framework of this Series, which honors Moses as the
unique receiver of the Torah on Sinai, finds in 2 Esdras 14's parallel a
literary device, not a claim of equal authority.

Cross-references: Exodus 24:18; Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9; Ezra
7:6–10; Ezra 7:25–26; Nehemiah 8:1–18; 2 Kings 22:8–13; 2 Timothy
3:14–17; Revelation 22:18–19.

2 Esdras — Chapter 15

  1 Behold, speak you in the ears of my people the words of prophecy,
  which I will put in your mouth, says Yahuah (God): 2 And cause them to
  be written in paper: for they are faithful and true. 3 Fear not the
  imaginations against you, let not the incredulity of them trouble you,
  that speak against you. 4 For all the unfaithful shall die in their
  unfaithfulness. 5 Behold, says Yahuah (God), I will bring plagues upon
  the world; the sword, famine, death, and destruction.

  6 For wickedness has exceedingly polluted the whole earth, and their
  hurtful works are fulfilled. 7 Therefore says Yahuah (God), 8 I will
  hold my tongue no more as touching their wickedness, which they
  profanely commit, neither will I suffer them in those things, in which
  they wickedly exercise themselves: behold, the innocent and righteous
  blood cries to me, and the souls of the just complain continually. 9
  And therefore, says Yahuah (God), I will surely avenge them, and
  receive to me all the innocent blood from among them. 10 Behold, my
  people is led as a flock to the slaughter: I will not suffer them now
  to dwell in the land of Egypt:

  11 But I will bring them with a mighty hand and a stretched out arm,
  and smite Egypt with plagues, as before, and will destroy all the land
  thereof. 12 Egypt shall mourn, and the foundation of it shall be
  struck with the plague and punishment that Yahuah (God) shall bring
  upon it. 13 They that till the ground shall mourn: for their seeds
  shall fail through the blasting and hail, and with a fearful
  constellation. 14 Woe to the world and them that dwell in it! 15 For
  the sword and their destruction draws nigh, and one people shall stand
  up and fight against another, and swords in their hands.

  16 For there shall be sedition among men, and invading one another;
  they shall not regard their kings nor princes, and the course of their
  actions shall stand in their power. 17 A man shall desire to go into a
  city, and shall not be able. 18 For because of their pride the cities
  shall be troubled, the houses shall be destroyed, and men shall be
  afraid. 19 A man shall have no pity upon his neighbour, but shall
  destroy their houses with the sword, and spoil their goods, because of
  the lack of bread, and for great tribulation. 20 Behold, says Yahuah
  (God), I will call together all the kings of the earth to reverence
  me, which are from the rising of the sun, from the south, from the
  east, and Libanus; to turn themselves one against another, and repay
  the things that they have done to them.

  21 Like as they do yet this day to my chosen, so will I do also, and
  recompense in their bosom. Thus says Yahuah (God); 22 My right hand
  shall not spare the sinners, and my sword shall not cease over them
  that shed innocent blood upon the earth. 23 The fire is gone forth
  from his wrath, and has consumed the foundations of the earth, and the
  sinners, like the straw that is kindled. 24 Woe to them that sin, and
  keep not my commandments! says Yahuah (God). 25 I will not spare them:
  go your way, you children, from the power, defile not my sanctuary.

  26 For Yahuah (God) knoweth all them that sin against him, and
  therefore delivers he them to death and destruction. 27 For now are
  the plagues come upon the whole earth and you shall remain in them:
  for Yahuah (God) shall not deliver you, because you have sinned
  against him. 28 Behold an horrible vision, and the appearance thereof
  from the east: 29 Where the nations of the dragons of Arabia shall
  come out with many chariots, and the multitude of them shall be
  carried as the wind upon earth, that all they which hear them may fear
  and tremble. 30 Also the Carmanians raging in wrath shall go forth as
  the wild boars of the wood, and with great power shall they come, and
  join battle with them, and shall waste a portion of the land of the
  Assyrians.

  31 And then shall the dragons have the upper hand, remembering their
  nature; and if they shall turn themselves, conspiring together in
  great power to persecute them, 32 Then these shall be troubled bled,
  and keep silence through their power, and shall flee. 33 And from the
  land of the Assyrians shall the enemy besiege them, and consume some
  of them, and in their host shall be fear and dread, and strife among
  their kings. 34 Behold clouds from the east and from the north to the
  south, and they are very horrible to look upon, full of wrath and
  storm. 35 They shall smite one upon another, and they shall smite down
  a great multitude of stars upon the earth, even their own star; and
  blood shall be from the sword to the belly,

  36 And dung of men to the camel’s hough. 37 And there shall be great
  fearfulness and trembling upon earth: and they that see the wrath
  shall be afraid, and trembling shall come upon them. 38 And then shall
  there come great storms from the south, and from the north, and
  another part from the west. 39 And strong winds shall arise from the
  east, and shall open it; and the cloud which he raised up in wrath,
  and the star stirred to cause fear toward the east and west wind,
  shall be destroyed. 40 The great and mighty clouds shall be puffed up
  full of wrath, and the star, that they may make all the earth afraid,
  and them that dwell in it; and they shall pour out over every high and
  eminent place an horrible star,

  41 Fire, and hail, and flying swords, and many waters, that all fields
  may be full, and all rivers, with the abundance of great waters. 42
  And they shall break down the cities and walls, mountains and hills,
  trees of the wood, and grass of the meadows, and their corn. 43 And
  they shall go stedfastly to Babylon, and make her afraid. 44 They
  shall come to her, and besiege her, the star and all wrath shall they
  pour out upon her: then shall the dust and smoke go up to the heaven,
  and all they that be about her shall bewail her. 45 And they that
  remain under her shall do service to them that have put her in fear.

  46 And you, Asia, that are partaker of the hope of Babylon, and art
  the glory of her person: 47 Woe be to you, you wretch, because you
  have made thyself like to her; and have decked your daughters in
  whoredom, that they might please and glory in your lovers, which have
  always desired to commit whoredom with you. 48 You have followed her
  that is hated in all her works and inventions: therefore says Yahuah
  (God), 49 I will send plagues upon you; widowhood, poverty, famine,
  sword, and pestilence, to waste your houses with destruction and
  death. 50 And the glory of your Power shall be dried up as a flower,
  the heat shall arise that is sent over you.

  51 You shall be weakened as a poor woman with stripes, and as one
  chastised with wounds, so that the mighty and lovers shall not be able
  to receive you. 52 Would I with jealousy have so proceeded against
  you, says Yahuah (God), 53 If you had not always slain my chosen,
  exalting the stroke of yours hands, and saying over their dead, when
  you were drunken, 54 Set forth the beauty of your countenance? 55 The
  reward of your whoredom shall be in your bosom, therefore shall you
  receive recompence.

  56 Like as you have done to my chosen, says Yahuah (God), even so
  shall Yahuah (God) do to you, and shall deliver you into mischief 57
  Your children shall die of hunger, and you shall fall through the
  sword: your cities shall be broken down, and all yours shall perish
  with the sword in the field. 58 They that be in the mountains shall
  die of hunger, and eat their own flesh, and drink their own blood, for
  very hunger of bread, and thirst of water. 59 You as unhappy shall
  come through the sea, and receive plagues again. 60 And in the passage
  they shall rush on the idle city, and shall destroy some portion of
  your land, and consume part of your glory, and shall return to Babylon
  that was destroyed.

  61 And you shall be cast down by them as stubble, and they shall be to
  you as fire; 62 And shall consume you, and your cities, your land, and
  your mountains; all your woods and your fruitful trees shall they burn
  up with fire. 63 Your children shall they carry away captive, and,
  look, what you have, they shall spoil it, and mar the beauty of your
  face.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 15 is one of the late Christian additions (chapters 15–16 were
added to the Latin tradition and are absent from the Greek and Syriac).
The chapter pronounces judgment on the nations — Egypt, Assyria,
Babylon, and others — and announces the coming of judgment with a sword.

The framework finds two things.

First, the chapter contains imagery that parallels the prophets' oracles
against the nations and Revelation's bowl judgments. The vocabulary is
consistent with the apocalyptic tradition. The Christian addition has
framed the older Yahudi (Jewish) apocalyptic vocabulary inside a
specifically early-Christian eschatological frame.

Second, the chapter's pronouncement of judgment on the nations does not
require special framework attention. The pattern is the prophetic
pattern: Yahuah (God) judges the powers that have oppressed His people.
The framework of this Series finds nothing controversial in the
substance, only that it should be recognized as a Christian-addition
development of the older Yahudi (Jewish) apocalyptic tradition.

The framework's note for the awakening reader: the
judgment-on-the-nations imagery in the apocalyptic literature is
sometimes read by the awakened reader as a license for triumphalism — as
if the awakened community now stands on the right side of the appointed
judgment and can look down on those still under the empire. The
framework's correction is firm. The awakened community is not the
judging party. The Messiah is. The awakened community is the gathered
seed, drawn out of the very same nations that are being judged, called
to come out of Babylon (Revelation 18:4) before the verdict falls. The
right posture toward the imperial-pattern is to come out of it; not to
gloat over those who are still inside it; not to imagine that one's own
awakening makes one the executor of the judgment. Read the addition with
the right posture. The judgment is His. The walk is yours.

Cross-references: Isaiah 13:1–14:23; Isaiah 19:1–25; Jeremiah
46:1–51:64; Ezekiel 25:1–32:32; Revelation 16:1–21; Revelation 18:1–24;
Revelation 18:4.

2 Esdras — Chapter 16

  1 Woe be to you, Babylon, and Asia! woe be to you, Egypt and Syria! 2
  Gird up yourselves with cloths of sack and hair, bewail your children,
  and be sorry; for your destruction is at hand. 3 A sword is sent upon
  you, and who may turn it back? 4 A fire is sent among you, and who may
  quench it? 5 Plagues are sent to you, and what is he that may drive
  them away?

  6 May any man drive away an hungry lion in the wood? or may any one
  quench the fire in stubble, when it has begun to burn? 7 May one turn
  again the arrow that is shot of a strong archer? 8 The mighty Yahuah
  (God) sends the plagues and who is he that can drive them away? 9 A
  fire shall go forth from his wrath, and who is he that may quench it?
  10 He shall cast lightnings, and who shall not fear? he shall thunder,
  and who shall not be afraid?

  11 Yahuah (God) shall threaten, and who shall not be utterly
  beaten to powder at his presence? 12 The earth quakes, and the

  the world. 14 Behold, the plagues are sent, and shall not return

  shall not be put out, till it consume the foundation of the earth.

  16 Like as an arrow which is shot of a mighty archer returns not
  backward: even so the plagues that shall be sent upon earth shall not
  return again. 17 Woe is me! woe is me! who will deliver me in those
  days? 18 The beginning of sorrows and great mournings; the beginning
  of famine and great death; the beginning of wars, and the powers shall
  stand in fear; the beginning of evils! what shall I do when these
  evils shall come? 19 Behold, famine and plague, tribulation and
  anguish, are sent as scourges for amendment. 20 But for all these
  things they shall not turn from their wickedness, nor be always
  mindful of the scourges.

  21 Behold, victuals shall be so good cheap upon earth, that they shall
  think themselves to be in good case, and even then shall evils grow

  cast out as dung, and there shall be no man to comfort them: for the
  earth shall be wasted, and the cities shall be cast down. 24 There
  shall be no man left to till the earth, and to sow it 25 The trees
  shall give fruit, and who shall gather them?

  26 The grapes shall ripen, and who shall tread them? for all places
  shall be desolate of men: 27 So that one man shall desire to see

  diligently seek through the vineyard:

  31 Even so in those days there shall be three or four left by them
  that search their houses with the sword. 32 And the earth shall be
  laid waste, and the fields thereof shall wax old, and her ways and all
  her paths shall grow full of thorns, because no man shall travel
  therethrough. 33 The virgins shall mourn, having no bridegrooms; the
  women shall mourn, having no husbands; their daughters shall mourn,
  having no helpers. 34 In the wars shall their bridegrooms be
  destroyed, and their husbands shall perish of famine. 35 Hear now

  36 Behold, the word of Yahuah (God), receive it: believe not the gods

  forth her son, with two or three hours of her birth great pains

  battle, and in those evils be even as pilgrims upon the earth.

  41 He that selleth, let him be as he that fleeth away: and he that
  buyeth, as one that will lose: 42 He that occupieth merchandise, as he
  that has no profit by it: and he that buildeth, as he that shall not
  dwell in it: 43 He that sows, as if he should not reap: so also he
  that planteth the vineyard, as he that shall not gather the grapes: 44
  They that marry, as they that shall get no children; and they that
  marry not, as the widowers. 45 And therefore they that labour labour
  in vain:

  46 For strangers shall reap their fruits, and spoil their goods,

  whore envies a right honest and virtuous woman: 50 So shall

  imaginations, their thoughts, and their hearts: 55 Which spoke but the

  56 In his word were the stars made, and he knoweth the number of them.

  guide,

  76 And the guide of them who keep my commandments and precepts, says
  Yahuah (God): let not your sins weigh you down, and let not your
  iniquities lift up themselves. 77 Woe be to them that are bound with
  their sins, and covered with their iniquities like as a field is
  covered over with bushes, and the path thereof covered with thorns,
  that no man may travel through! 78 It is left undressed, and is cast
  into the fire to be consumed with it.

⸻

Commentary

The closing chapter (also a Christian addition) continues the
judgment-and-consolation pattern. Disasters are pronounced on the
nations. The remnant is consoled. The chapter ends with an exhortation
to keep the faith.

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's pattern of disasters-on-the-nations and
consolation-of-the-remnant is consistent with the prophetic and
apocalyptic tradition. The framework of this Series finds nothing
controversial in the substance.

Second, the closing exhortations (verses 65–78) — that the people should
not provoke Yahuah (God) to anger, that they should keep his
commandments, that they should not depart from his way — are consistent
with the 1234 of Truth. The Christian addition's eschatological frame
does not erase the standard of commandment-keeping; the standard
remains. The framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening of
the remnant is the working out of the keeping of the commandments by the
Spirit, finds in the closing of 2 Esdras the same standard the original
five visions affirmed.

The book ends with the Christian addition's call to faithfulness. The
original Yahudi (Jewish) core (chapters 3–14) is the substantial work;
the Christian additions provide opening and closing frames. The
framework's reading of 2 Esdras: the original five visions are the
second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) apocalyptic substance, of which 2 Esdras
13 is the most important framework moment for this Series. Read those
visions. Recognize the additions for what they are. Hold the framework's
reading of the lost ten tribes — preserved, awaited, returning at the
appointed time — as the second-temple confirmation of the long
restoration the prophets named. And then go back to Jeremiah 31, Ezekiel
37, Hosea 1–2, Isaiah 11 — the prophetic anchors that 2 Esdras 13 was
rehearsing — and read them again with the seer's voice in your ear. The
framework is not the commentary's invention. The framework is the
prophetic-and-apocalyptic witness reading itself across the centuries.
The awakening reader is hearing it because the Father has opened ears to
hear, in the appointed time, what the seventy hidden books have been
saying to the wise of the people the whole time.

Cross-references: Isaiah 24:1–23; Joel 2:1–11; Zephaniah 1:1–18; Matthew
24:1–51; 2 Peter 3:1–13; Revelation 6:12–17; Revelation 16:1–21; 1 John
2:3–4; Jeremiah 31:1–14; Ezekiel 37:15–22.

Tobit — Introduction

Tobit is the small jewel of the Apocrypha. A short narrative in fourteen
chapters, set in the Assyrian exile after the fall of the northern
kingdom, it tells the story of a Naphtali Israelite living in Nineveh —
the very heartland of the empire that scattered his people — who keeps
the Torah in his exile, suffers loss, prays, and is delivered through an
unlikely chain of providence involving his son Tobias, the bride Sarah,
the angel Raphael in disguise, and a fish whose gall heals blindness and
whose smoke drives out a demon. It is one of the few apocryphal books
with a recognizable plot, recognizable characters, and a satisfying
narrative arc. It is the book most often read aloud to families in the
traditions that have kept it.

For the awakening reader, Tobit matters in a way that the inherited
Christian reading rarely names. Tobit is a Naphtali Israelite — Category
2 in the framework's three categories. He is not Yahudah (Judah), the
southern house that retained identity through exile. He is the scattered
seed of Yashar'el (Israel), the ten northern tribes carried into Assyria
in 722 BCE under Shalmaneser, dispersed through the centuries until they
became indistinguishable from the nations. Tobit is the narrative window
onto that house. The book opens with him explicitly noting that he kept
going to Jerusalem at the feasts even when his tribe had stopped going,
that he kept the tithes when his tribe had stopped tithing, that he kept
the Torah in exile when his exile was the consequence of his tribe's
having abandoned it. Tobit is, in narrative form, the remnant of
Naphtali — a single faithful seed of the northern kingdom, preserved in
the very Assyrian capital where his people were dispersed.

That framing makes Tobit unique among the apocryphal narratives. 1
Maccabees and 2 Maccabees are stories about the southern kingdom —
Yahudah (Judah), the tribes that returned from Babylon. Judith is a
story about the southern kingdom under Persian-era pressure. Susanna is
set in the Babylonian Yahudi (Jewish) community of the southern exile.
But Tobit is set in the Assyrian community of the northern exile, the
scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel) in their first century of
dispersion, and the book preserves a memory of faithfulness inside that
exile that the inherited Christian reading has treated as folklore but
that the awakening reader will recognize as the witness of one of his
own kin — Category 2, the scattered seed, kept faith with his Father in
a foreign land.

A second thing matters. Tobit is the most explicitly Torah-observant
book in the Apocrypha. Tobit tithes. Tobit gives almsgiving (charity to
the poor, a Torah commandment in Deuteronomy 15). Tobit buries the dead,
even at risk to his own life under hostile authority. Tobit prays the
appointed prayers. He is married within his tribe. He sends his son
Tobias to be married within the family. He keeps the food laws even when
his fellow exiles are not keeping them. The book is a portrait of
Torah-observant exile, and the framework of this Series — which honors
Torah observance as the proper response to Yahuah (God)'s instruction —
finds in Tobit a witness that the Torah was being kept in the diaspora
long before the Hebrew roots movement in the modern Western world named
the question again. The Torah was alive in Nineveh in the eighth century
BCE. Tobit shows you what that life looked like.

A third thing matters, and this one requires care. Tobit's narrative
includes prominent angelology. Raphael is named as one of the seven
angels who present the prayers of the saints before the throne (Tobit
12:15) — a verse that has been used in some Catholic and Orthodox
traditions to develop a doctrine of intercessory angels that the
awakening Protestant reader will rightly hesitate over. The 1234 filter
applies here. The Torah, the prophets, and the apostolic witness do not
develop a doctrine of named angelic intercessors as part of the public
worship of Yahuah (God). Where the apocryphal text shows what the
second-temple imagination believed about angels, the awakening reader
should mark that as second-temple belief, not as instruction to be
implemented. The angel Raphael appears in this book. The angel is real
in the sense that the book reports him. The angel is not a member of a
cultic system the reader is being asked to develop. Tobit shows. It does
not legislate. The legislation is in the Torah, and the Torah does not
include angelic intercession in the appointed worship.

Read Tobit as the family story it is. Read it for the joy of seeing a
Naphtali Israelite keep faith in Nineveh. Read it for the foreshadowing
of the gathering — the marriage of Tobias to Sarah is, on the
second-temple imagination, a small picture of the larger gathering of
the scattered seed back to their own kindred. Read it as the witness of
a tribe the prophets said would be gathered, a tribe whose faithfulness
in exile was preserved and remembered by his own.

Tobit — Chapter 1

  1 The book of the words of Tobit, son of Tobiel, the son of Ananiel,
  the son of Aduel, the son of Gabael, of the seed of Asael, of the
  tribe of Nephthali; 2 Who in the time of Enemessar king of the
  Assyrians was led captive out of Thisbe, which is at the right hand of
  that city, which is called properly Nephthali in Galilee above Aser. 3
  I Tobit have walked all the days of my life in the ways of truth and
  justice, and I did many almsdeeds to my brothers, and my nation, who
  came with me to Nineve, into the land of the Assyrians. 4 And when I
  was in my own country, in the land of Yashar'el (Israel) being but
  young, all the tribe of Nephthali my father fell from the house of
  Jerusalem, which was chosen out of all the tribes of Yashar'el
  (Israel), that all the tribes should sacrifice there, where the temple
  of the habitation of the Most High was consecrated and built for all
  ages. 5 Now all the tribes which together revolted, and the house of
  my father Nephthali, sacrificed to the heifer Baal.

  6 But I alone went often to Jerusalem at the feasts, as it was
  ordained to all the people of Yashar'el (Israel) by an everlasting
  decree, having the firstfruits and tenths of increase, with that which
  was first shorn; and them gave I at the altar to the priests the
  children of Aaron. 7 The first tenth part of all increase I gave to
  the sons of Aaron, who ministered at Jerusalem: another tenth part I
  sold away, and went, and spent it every year at Jerusalem: 8 And the
  third I gave to them to whom it was meet, as Debora my father’s mother
  had commanded me, because I was left an orphan by my father. 9
  Furthermore, when I was come to the age of a man, I married Anna of my
  own kindred, and of her I begat Tobias. 10 And when we were carried
  away captives to Nineve, all my brothers and those that were of my
  kindred did eat of the bread of the Gentiles.

  11 But I kept myself from eating; 12 Because I remembered Yahuah (God)
  with all my heart. 13 And the Most High gave me grace and favour
  before Enemessar, so that I was his purveyor. 14 And I went into
  Media, and left in trust with Gabael, the brother of Gabrias, at Rages
  a city of Media ten talents of silver. 15 Now when Enemessar was dead,
  Sennacherib his son reigned in his stead; whose estate was troubled,
  that I could not go into Media.

  16 And in the time of Enemessar I gave many alms to my brothers, and
  gave my bread to the hungry, 17 And my clothes to the naked: and if I
  saw any of my nation dead, or cast about the walls of Nineve, I buried
  him. 18 And if the king Sennacherib had slain any, when he was come,
  and fled from Judea, I buried them privily; for in his wrath he killed
  many; but the bodies were not found, when they were sought for of the
  king. 19 And when one of the Ninevites went and complained of me to
  the king, that I buried them, and hid myself; understanding that I was
  sought for to be put to death, I withdrew myself for fear. 20 Then all
  my goods were forcibly taken away, neither was there any thing left
  me, beside my wife Anna and my son Tobias.

  21 And there passed not five and fifty days, before two of his sons
  killed him, and they fled into the mountains of Ararath; and
  Sarchedonus his son reigned in his stead; who appointed over his
  father’s accounts, and over all his affairs, Achiacharus my brother
  Anael’s son. 22 And Achiacharus intreating for me, I returned to
  Nineve. Now Achiacharus was cupbearer, and keeper of the signet, and
  steward, and overseer of the accounts: and Sarchedonus appointed him
  next to him: and he was my brother’s son.

⸻

Commentary

The opening of Tobit names the genealogy with care. Tobit is "of the
seed of Asael, of the tribe of Nephthali" — the second of the northern
tribes named in Deuteronomy 33, settled in upper Galilee, and one of the
tribes that was carried away in the Assyrian deportation of 722 BCE. The
book's setting is the Assyrian exile of the northern kingdom — the very
deportation Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah had warned of, and the deportation
that scattered the ten tribes into the nations from which the prophets
promised they would one day be regathered. The framework of this Series
— that the seed of Yashar'el (Israel) was scattered into the nations
under judgment, that the Father has been pursuing them in their
dispersion, and that the gathering is the long restoration the prophets
named — finds in the opening of Tobit the witness of one Naphtali
Israelite who kept the covenant in the Assyrian heartland of his exile.

The chapter records what Tobit kept while the rest of his tribe walked
out from under the covenant. He went often to Jerusalem at the appointed
feasts. He brought firstfruits and tenths to the priests of the sons of
Aaron. He gave a second tenth to be spent at Jerusalem, and a third to
those in need — the threefold tithing pattern the second-temple
community read out of Deuteronomy 14 and 26. He refused to eat of the
bread of the Gentiles in his exile. He buried the dead of his nation
when they were left exposed by Assyrian decree, even at risk to his own
life and property. The list is the working portrait of a Torah-observant
Israelite under foreign occupation.

Each of these practices is anchored in specific Torah commandment.
Deuteronomy 16:16, on appointed-feast pilgrimage: Three times in a year
shall all your males appear before Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God) in the place
which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the
feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles. Numbers 18:11–13, on
firstfruits: the firstfruits... I have given them to you. Deuteronomy
14:22–29, on tithes including the third-year tithe for the poor: At the
end of three years you shall bring forth all the tithe of your increase
the same year, and shall lay it up within your gates: And the Levite...
and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow... shall come, and
shall eat and be satisfied. Deuteronomy 21:22–23, on burial: His body
shall not remain all night upon the tree, but you shall in any wise bury
him that day. Tobit walks each command. The awakening reader who has
been retrained to honor the Torah will recognize the items in the list.
The reader walking out of institutional Christianity will hear the
second-temple witness that the Torah was not a burden to be escaped but
a way to be kept, even at cost.

Verse 5 contains a phrase that should not be missed: all the tribes
which together revolted, and the house of my father Nephthali,
sacrificed to the heifer Baal. The text identifies the northern
kingdom's apostasy specifically — the sacrifice to the Baal heifer at
the Bethel and Dan altars Jeroboam had set up after the kingdom split.

The canonical historical record is concrete. 1 Kings 12:28–30, Jeroboam
after the kingdom split: Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two
calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to
Jerusalem: behold your gods, O Yashar'el (Israel), which brought you up
out of the land of Egypt. And he set the one in Bethel, and the other
put he in Dan. And this thing became a sin: for the people went to
worship before the one, even unto Dan. 1 Kings 14:15–16 names the
consequence: For Yahuah (God) shall smite Yashar'el (Israel), as a reed
is shaken in the water, and he shall root up Yashar'el (Israel) out of
this good land, which he gave to their fathers, and shall scatter them
beyond the river, because they have made their groves, provoking Yahuah
(God) to anger. And he shall give Yashar'el (Israel) up because of the
sins of Jeroboam, who did sin, and who made Yashar'el (Israel) to sin. 2
Kings 17:7–8 closes the case at the Assyrian deportation: For so it was,
that the children of Yashar'el (Israel) had sinned against Yahuah (God)
their Elohim (God), which had brought them up out of the land of Egypt... and
they walked in the statutes of the heathen, whom Yahuah (God) cast out
from before the children of Yashar'el (Israel). Hosea 8:5–6, the
prophetic indictment: Your calf, O Samaria, has cast you off; my anger
is kindled against them: how long will it be ere they attain to
innocency? For from Yashar'el (Israel) was it also: the workman made it;
therefore it is not Elohim (God): but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in
pieces.

Tobit names what his tribe had done. He does not pretend the apostasy
was not real. The apostasy was real. The exile was the consequence. The
framework of this Series — that the curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell
because the people walked out from under the covenant — finds in Tobit's
confession the second-temple memory of why the northern house was
scattered. The exile was not unjust. It was the covenant working as the
covenant said it would work.

Cross-references: Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Deuteronomy 26:12–15;
Deuteronomy 28:36–37; Deuteronomy 28:64–65; Deuteronomy 33:23; 1 Kings
12:25–33; 2 Kings 17:5–23; Hosea 4:1–6; Amos 5:1–17; Isaiah 28:1–4;
Jeremiah 16:14–15; 2 Esdras 13:39–47; Ezekiel 37:15–22.

Tobit — Chapter 2

  1 Now when I was come home again, and my wife Anna was restored to me,
  with my son Tobias, in the feast of Pentecost, which is the holy feast
  of the seven weeks, there was a good dinner prepared me, in the which
  I sat down to eat. 2 And when I saw abundance of meat, I said to my
  son, Go and bring what poor man soever you shall find out of our
  brothers, who is mindful of Yahuah (God); and, lo, I tarry for you. 3
  But he came again, and said, Father, one of our nation is strangled,
  and is cast out in the marketplace. 4 Then before I had tasted of any
  meat, I started up, and took him up into a room until the going down
  of the sun. 5 Then I returned, and washed myself, and ate my meat in
  heaviness,

  6 Remembering that prophecy of Amos, as he said, Your feasts shall be
  turned into mourning, and all your mirth into lamentation. 7 Therefore
  I wept: and after the going down of the sun I went and made a grave,
  and buried him. 8 But my neighbours mocked me, and said, This man is
  not yet afraid to be put to death for this matter: who fled away; and
  yet, lo, he burieth the dead again. 9 The same night also I returned
  from the burial, and slept by the wall of my courtyard, being polluted
  and my face was uncovered: 10 And I knew not that there were sparrows
  in the wall, and my eyes being open, the sparrows muted warm dung into
  my eyes, and a whiteness came in my eyes: and I went to the
  physicians, but they helped me not: moreover Achiacharus did nourish
  me, until I went into Elymais.

  11 And my wife Anna did take women’s works to do. 12 And when she had
  sent them home to the owners, they paid her wages, and gave her also
  besides a kid. 13 And when it was in my house, and began to cry, I
  said to her, From whence is this kid? is it not stolen? render it to
  the owners; for it is not lawful to eat any thing that is stolen. 14
  But she replied upon me, It was given for a gift more than the wages.
  Howbeit I did not believe her, but told her render it to the owners:
  and I was abashed at her. But she replied upon me, Where are your alms
  and your righteous deeds? behold, you and all your works are known.

⸻

Commentary

Tobit's faithfulness in burying the dead becomes the occasion of the
calamity that drives the rest of the narrative. Coming home from a
burial during the Feast of Pentecost, he lies down to sleep against the
wall of his courtyard, and sparrows above him drop droppings into his
open eyes. He is blinded.

The narrative is not a parable about karma. The text does not say Tobit
was being punished. The text records what happened, and the text records
the ridicule that follows: his neighbors mock him, his wife Anna takes
work weaving for hire to support the household, and a goat she earns is
given to her by her employer. Tobit, blind and dependent, accuses his
wife of having stolen the goat. She rebukes him. The chapter ends with
Tobit sitting in the failure of his own household, unable to see, unable
to support his family, distrustful of the wife who has been carrying
him.

The 1234 of Truth (1 John 2:3–4) applies to the chapter in an indirect
way. The standard is keeping the commandments. Tobit had kept the
commandments — the burying of the dead is one of the great commandments
of the Torah's social order — and the keeping had not protected him from
accident, misfortune, financial collapse, or the damage to his marriage.
The framework of this Series does not promise the awakening reader
exemption from the consequences of living in a fallen world.
Faithfulness does not produce comfort. Faithfulness produces what it
produces: the keeping of the covenant, regardless of outcome. Tobit's
faithfulness has made him blind, poor, and ashamed in his own house. He
does not stop being faithful. His prayer in the next chapter will show
this.

Cross-references: Genesis 23:1–20; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Tobit 1:16–18;
Job 1:1–22; Job 2:7–10; Habakkuk 3:17–19; Ecclesiastes 8:14; Romans
8:18; 2 Corinthians 4:16–18.

Tobit — Chapter 3

  1 Then I being grieved did weep, and in my sorrow prayed, saying, 2 O
  Yahuah (God), you are just, and all your works and all your ways are
  mercy and truth, and you judgest truly and justly for ever. 3 Remember
  me, and look on me, punish me not for my sins and ignorances, and the
  sins of my fathers, who have sinned before you: 4 For they obeyed not
  your commandments: wherefore you have delivered us for a spoil, and to
  captivity, and to death, and for a proverb of reproach to all the
  nations among whom we are dispersed. 5 And now your judgments are many
  and true: deal with me according to my sins and my fathers’: because
  we have not kept your commandments, neither have walked in truth
  before you.

  6 Now therefore deal with me as seemeth best to you, and command my
  spirit to be taken from me, that I may be dissolved, and become earth:
  for it is profitable for me to die rather than to live, because I have
  heard false reproaches, and have much sorrow: command therefore that I
  may now be delivered out of this distress, and go into the everlasting
  place: turn not your face away from me. 7 It came to pass the same
  day, that in Ecbatane a city of Media Sara the daughter of Raguel was
  also reproached by her father’s maids; 8 Because that she had been
  married to seven husbands, whom Asmodeus the evil spirit had killed,
  before they had lain with her. Do you not know, said they, that you
  have strangled yours husbands? you have had already seven husbands,
  neither were you named after any of them. 9 Wherefore do you beat us
  for them? if they be dead, go your ways after them, let us never see
  of you either son or daughter. 10 Whe she heard these things, she was
  very sorrowful, so that she thought to have strangled herself; and she
  said, I am the only daughter of my father, and if I do this, it shall
  be a reproach to him, and I shall bring his old age with sorrow to the
  grave.

  11 Then she prayed toward the window, and said, Blessed art you, O
  Yahuah (God), my Elohim (God), and yours holy and glorious name is
  blessed and honourable for ever: let all your works praise you for
  ever. 12 And now, O Yahuah (God), I set my eyes and my face toward
  you, 13 And say, Take me out of the earth, that I may hear no more the
  reproach. 14 You know, Yahuah (God), that I am pure from all sin with
  man, 15 And that I never polluted my name, nor the name of my father,
  in the land of my captivity: I am the only daughter of my father,
  neither has he any child to be his heir, neither any near kinsman, nor
  any son of his alive, to whom I may keep myself for a wife: my seven
  husbands are already dead; and why should I live? but if it please not
  you that I should die, command some regard to be had of me, and pity
  taken of me, that I hear no more reproach.

  16 So the prayers of them both were heard before the majesty of the
  great Yahuah (God). 17 And Raphael was sent to heal them both, that
  is, to scale away the whiteness of Tobit’s eyes, and to give Sara the
  daughter of Raguel for a wife to Tobias the son of Tobit; and to bind
  Asmodeus the evil spirit; because she belonged to Tobias by right of
  inheritance. The selfsame time came Tobit home, and entered into his
  house, and Sara the daughter of Raguel came down from her upper
  chamber.

⸻

Commentary

Tobit prays that he may die. Sarah, the daughter of Raguel in Ecbatane
in the country of the Medes, prays the same thing. The two prayers are
offered on the same day in different cities, and the narrative records
that both prayers are heard by Yahuah (God) and that the angel Raphael
is sent to address both situations.

Tobit's prayer (verses 1–6) is a prayer of resignation grounded in the
covenant. He confesses that the calamities of the people are the
consequence of their having walked out from under the Torah, and he asks
that his soul be received because he cannot bear to live as he is. The
prayer is not faithlessness. It is the prayer of a faithful man whose
body and household have collapsed under burdens he cannot lift. The text
does not condemn the prayer.

Sarah's prayer (verses 11–15) follows. She has been married to seven
husbands, each of whom has been killed on his wedding night by the demon
Asmodeus. The seventh death has just happened. The maids in her father's
household are mocking her. She withdraws to the upper chamber of her
father's house, contemplates suicide, but refuses for her father's sake
— to spare him the disgrace and grief of a daughter's hanging — and
prays instead that she be received in death by Yahuah (God)'s hand
rather than by her own.

The chapter raises three things the awakening reader should mark.

First, the demonology of Tobit is real second-temple demonology.
Asmodeus is named. The pattern of demonic interference in the marriages
of the daughters of the covenant community is a pattern attested in
second-temple literature, including some Pseudepigraphal texts. The
framework of this Series does not require the awakening reader to
develop a full demonology around Asmodeus. The text shows a demonic
affliction; the text shows Yahuah (God)'s deliverance from it through
the angel Raphael; the text does not legislate ongoing practices of
exorcism or demon-naming as part of covenant worship. The Torah does not
develop such practices. The apostolic witness mentions the casting out
of demons as part of the Messiah's authority and the apostles'
commission, but does not legislate liturgical demon-management. Hold the
witness as witness. Do not let the witness become the source of
practices the Torah and the apostles did not establish.

Second, both prayers are heard. The chapter explicitly names this: And
the prayers of them both were heard before the majesty of the great
Yahuah (God).

The canonical anchor is direct. Psalm 34:15 — The eyes of Yahuah (God)
are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry. Psalm 65:2
— O you that hears prayer, unto you shall all flesh come. Psalm
145:18–19 — Yahuah (God) is near unto all them that call upon him, to
all that call upon him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of them that
fear him: he also will hear their cry, and will save them. 1 John
5:14–15 in apostolic vocabulary — And this is the confidence that we
have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he hears
us: And if we know that he hears us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we
have the petitions that we desired of him. Matthew 7:7–11 — Ask, and it
shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be
opened unto you.

The framework of this Series — that Yahuah (God) hears the cries of His
own, that He responds, that He does not abandon the faithful in their
distress even when His response is not immediate — is the framework
Tobit and Sarah are praying inside. They do not know each other. They do
not know that their prayers will be answered through the marriage of
their children. The Father has been arranging the deliverance from
before either of them knew to ask.

Third, the angel Raphael is sent. The framework of this Series, on the
question of named angelic intercessors, is conservative: the Torah does
not develop angelic intercession as part of covenant worship; the
apostolic witness names angels as ministering spirits but does not
address them in prayer. The Apocrypha shows what the second-temple
imagination believed about the angels. Mark what the text shows. Do not
legislate from the witness. The angel arrives to do what the angel of
Yahuah (God) does in the canonical scriptures: to bring the deliverance
the Father has appointed.

Cross-references: Daniel 9:1–19; Jonah 4:1–11; 1 Kings 19:1–18;
Lamentations 5:15–22; Job 7:1–21; Hebrews 1:14; James 5:13–18.

Tobit — Chapter 4

  1 In that day Tobit remembered the money which he had committed to
  Gabael in Rages of Media, 2 And said with himself, I have wished for
  death; wherefore do I not call for my son Tobias that I may signify to
  him of the money before I die? 3 And when he had called him, he said,
  My son, when I am dead, bury me; and despise not your mother, but
  honour her all the days of your life, and do that which shall please
  her, and grieve her not. 4 Remember, my son, that she saw many dangers
  for you, when you were in her womb: and when she is dead, bury her by
  me in one grave. 5 My son, be mindful of Yahuah (God), our Elohim
  (God) all your days, and let not your will be set to sin, or to
  transgress his commandments: do uprightly all your life long, and
  follow not the ways of unrighteousness.

  6 For if you deal truly, your doings shall prosperously succeed to
  you, and to all them that live justly. 7 Give alms of your substance;
  and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your
  face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned
  away from you. 8 If you have abundance give alms accordingly: if you
  have but a little, be not afraid to give according to that little: 9
  For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of
  necessity. 10 Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not
  to come into darkness.

  11 For alms is a good gift to all that give it in the sight of the
  Most High. 12 Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife
  of the seed of your fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife,
  which is not of your father’s tribe: for we are the children of the
  prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our
  fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their
  own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall
  inherit the land. 13 Now therefore, my son, love your brothers, and
  despise not in your heart your brothers, the sons and daughters of
  your people, in not taking a wife of them: for in pride is destruction
  and much trouble, and in lewdness is decay and great want: for
  lewdness is the mother of famine. 14 Let not the wages of any man,
  which has wrought for you, tarry with you, but give him it out of
  hand: for if you serve Yahuah (God), he will also repay you: be
  circumspect my son, in all things you do, and be wise in all your
  conversation. 15 Do that to no man which you hatest: drink not wine to
  make you drunken: neither let drunkenness go with you in your journey.

  16 Give of your bread to the hungry, and of your garments to them that
  are naked; and according to your abundance give alms: and let not your
  eye be envious, when you give alms. 17 Pour out your bread on the
  burial of the just, but give nothing to the wicked. 18 Ask counsel of
  all that are wise, and despise not any counsel that is profitable. 19
  Bless Yahuah (God), your Elohim (God) alway, and desire of him that
  your ways may be directed, and that all your paths and counsels may
  prosper: for every nation has not counsel; but Yahuah (God) himself
  gives all good things, and he humbleth whom he will, as he will; now
  therefore, my son, remember my commandments, neither let them be put
  out of your mind. 20 And now I signify this to they that I committed
  ten talents to Gabael the son of Gabrias at Rages in Media.

  21 And fear not, my son, that we are made poor: for you have much
  wealth, if you fear Yahuah (God), and depart from all sin, and do that
  which is pleasing in his sight.

⸻

Commentary

Tobit, believing he is near death, calls his son Tobias and gives him a
long charge. The chapter is one of the great wisdom-instruction passages
in the apocryphal corpus, in the same tradition as Proverbs 1–9 and the
deathbed instructions of patriarchs in the Pseudepigrapha. Read it for
what it is: a Naphtali father in the Assyrian exile teaching his son the
Torah he has lived.

The instruction includes: keep the Torah and the commandments; be
merciful to your brothers; bury the dead with care; give alms in
proportion to your goods; do not turn your face from the poor; marry
within your own kindred and not from a strange tribe; honor your mother
all the days of her life; remember that what you do not want done to
yourself, do not do to anyone else; do not let pride bear rule in your
speech or in your heart; ask counsel of every wise man; bless Yahuah
(God) at all times. The Torah is the substance. The wisdom tradition is
the form. The result is one of the most concentrated portraits of
Torah-observant fatherhood in any second-temple text.

Compare Tobit's instruction to the canonical fathers' instructions and
the architecture is consistent. Deuteronomy 6:6–9, Moses' instruction to
Yashar'el (Israel): And these words, which I command you this day, shall
be in your heart: and you shall teach them diligently to your children,
and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by
the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up. Proverbs 3:1–7,
Solomon's father-instruction: My son, forget not my law; but let your
heart keep my commandments... Trust in Yahuah (God) with all your heart;
and lean not unto your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge
him, and he shall direct your paths. Proverbs 4:1–4: Hear, you children,
the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding... For I
was my father's son, tender and only beloved in the sight of my mother.
He taught me also, and said unto me, Let your heart retain my words:
keep my commandments, and live. 1 Kings 2:1–4, David's deathbed charge
to Solomon: I go the way of all the earth: be you strong therefore, and
show yourself a man; and keep the charge of Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God), to
walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his
judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses,
that you may prosper in all that you do, and whithersoever you turn
yourself.

Tobit 4 is the second-temple Naphtali version of what Moses, Solomon,
and David had each given. The fathers transmit the covenant by
instruction. The architecture is consistent across Genesis through Tobit
through Sirach and into the apostolic letters (Ephesians 6:4 — fathers,
provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and
admonition of the Lord). The framework of this Series, which holds that
the covenant is preserved through faithful father-to-son transmission,
finds in Tobit 4 the second-temple form of that transmission in the
Assyrian exile.

Verse 15 contains the negative formulation of the Golden Rule: Do that
to no man which you hate. The form precedes the positive formulation in
Yahusha's Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:12) by approximately three
centuries. The reader who has been trained by inherited Christianity to
think of the Golden Rule as a Christian innovation will be quietly
corrected. The principle is in the second-temple wisdom tradition. The
Messiah did not invent it. He brought it to its highest form, but the
form had been growing in the covenant tradition for generations before
he came in the flesh. Hillel the Elder, a Pharisaic rabbi roughly
contemporary with Yahusha, also articulated the negative form: that
which is hateful to you, do not to your neighbor; this is the whole
Torah; the rest is commentary; go and study. The principle is the same
principle. Yahusha's positive formulation is the most concentrated form,
but the principle was alive in the covenant community before he
articulated it.

The closing of the chapter (verses 20–21) introduces the financial
errand that will set the rest of the plot in motion: Tobit reminds
Tobias that he had once left ten talents of silver in trust with Gabael
in Rages of Media, and instructs Tobias to go and recover the silver.
The errand is the occasion. The Father's purpose in arranging the
marriage to Sarah and the healing of Tobit's blindness is the actual
journey beneath the surface errand. The framework of this Series — that
the Father weaves His purposes through the daily errands of His people —
is the framework Tobit is operating inside without yet knowing it.

Cross-references: Deuteronomy 6:4–9; Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Proverbs
1:1–7; Proverbs 3:1–12; Proverbs 22:6; Ecclesiasticus 7:27–28;
Ecclesiasticus 30:1–13; Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31; Ephesians 6:1–4;
Colossians 3:20–21.

Tobit — Chapter 5

  1 Tobias then answered and said, Father, I will do all things which
  you have commanded me: 2 But how can I receive the money, seeing I
  know him not? 3 Then he gave him the handwriting, and said to him,
  Seek you a man which may go with you, whiles I yet live, and I will
  give him wages: and go and receive the money. 4 Therefore when he went
  to seek a man, he found Raphael that was an angel. 5 But he knew not;
  and he said to him, Can you go with me to Rages? and knowest you those
  places well?

  6 To whom the angel said, I will go with you, and I know the way well:
  for I have lodged with our brother Gabael. 7 Then Tobias said to him,
  Tarry for me, till I tell my father. 8 Then he said to him, Go and
  tarry not. So he went in and said to his father, Behold, I have found
  one which will go with me. Then he said, Call him to me, that I may
  know of what tribe he is, and whether he be a trusty man to go with
  you. 9 So he called him, and he came in, and they saluted one another.
  10 Then Tobit said to him, Brother, shew me of what tribe and family
  you are.

  11 To whom he said, Do you seek for a tribe or family, or an hired man
  to go with your son? Then Tobit said to him, I would know, brother,
  your kindred and name. 12 Then he said, I am Azarias, the son of
  Ananias the great, and of your brothers. 13 Then Tobit said, You are
  welcome, brother; be not now angry with me, because I have enquired to
  know your tribe and your family; for you are my brother, of an honest
  and good stock: for I know Ananias and Jonathas, sons of that great
  Samaias, as we went together to Jerusalem to worship, and offered the
  firstborn, and the tenths of the fruits; and they were not seduced
  with the error of our brothers: my brother, you are of a good stock.
  14 But tell me, what wages shall I give you? will you a drachm a day,
  and things necessary, as to my own son? 15 Yea, moreover, if you
  return safe, I will add something to your wages.

  16 So they were well pleased. Then said he to Tobias, Prepare thyself
  for the journey, and Yahuah (God) send you a good journey. And when
  his son had prepared all things for the journey, his father said, Go
  you with this man, and Yahuah (God), which dwells in heaven, prosper
  your journey, and the angel of Yahuah (God) keep you company. So they
  went forth both, and the young man’s dog with them. 17 But Anna his
  mother wept, and said to Tobit, Why have you sent away our son? is he
  not the staff of our hand, in going in and out before us? 18 Be not
  greedy to add money to money: but let it be as refuse in respect of
  our child. 19 For that which Yahuah (God) has given us to live with
  does suffice us. 20 Then said Tobit to her, Take no care, my sister;
  he shall return in safety, and your eyes shall see him.

  21 For the good angel will keep him company, and his journey shall be
  prosperous, and he shall return safe. 22 Then she made an end of
  weeping.

⸻

Commentary

Tobias goes out to find a guide for the journey to Media. He finds the
angel Raphael standing in the road, in the form of a young Israelite man
named Azarias (a name meaning "Yahuah (God) helps"). Raphael identifies
himself in disguise as a kinsman from a nearby tribe. Tobit, blind,
hears him and asks who his father and family are. Raphael answers in the
form of a kinsman.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the angel takes the form of a man. The pattern is not unique to
Tobit.

The canonical witnesses are concrete. Genesis 18:1–2 — And Yahuah (God)
appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre: and he sat in the tent door in
the heat of the day; and he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three
men stood by him. Genesis 32:24 — And Jacob was left alone; and there
wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. Verse 30 names
the wrestler: I have seen Elohim (God) face to face. Genesis 19:1 — And there
came two angels to Sodom at even. Verse 5 records the men of Sodom
calling them men. Joshua 5:13–15 — Joshua lifted up his eyes and looked,
and, behold, there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in
his hand. Verse 14 names him captain of the host of Yahuah (God); verse
15 has him receiving worship. Judges 6:11–22 — the angel of Yahuah (God)
appeared to Gideon as a man under the oak; verse 22 closes with Gideon's
recognition: Alas, O Lord Yahuah (God)! for because I have seen an angel
of Yahuah (God) face to face. Judges 13:3, 9–22 — the angel of Yahuah
(God) appeared to Manoah's wife and then to Manoah himself; verse 22 —
We shall surely die, because we have seen Elohim (God). Hebrews 13:2 brings the
pattern into apostolic warning: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers:
for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.

The pattern of angelic appearance in human form is consistent across the
Hebrew scriptures. Tobit 5 stands inside that pattern.

Second, Raphael's name in disguise is Azarias — "Yahuah (God) helps."
The text is showing the awakening reader the joke. The angel sent to
help has named himself by what he is doing. The Father is not absent in
the journey Tobias is about to take. He is sending the help in disguise.
The reader who has walked through seasons in which Yahuah (God)'s help
came in unexpected forms will recognize the pattern: the help is there,
named by the very thing it is, hidden in plain sight.

Third, Tobit's response is the response of a faithful father in the
Torah-observant covenant community: he asks who Raphael's family is,
what tribe he is from, who his father is. The marriage and travel
arrangements of the second-temple covenant community were within the
kindred. Tobit is checking. The answer Raphael gives — that he is a
kinsman — is enough for Tobit to send Tobias. The covenant was within
the family. The family was the framework of trust. The awakening reader
who has been retrained to honor the covenant household structure will
recognize what Tobit was doing in his blindness.

Cross-references: Genesis 18:1–8; Genesis 19:1–3; Genesis 32:24–30;
Joshua 5:13–15; Judges 6:11–24; Judges 13:2–25; Tobit 12:11–22; Hebrews
13:2.

Tobit — Chapter 6

  1 And as they went on their journey, they came in the evening to the
  river Tigris, and they lodged there. 2 And when the young man went
  down to wash himself, a fish leaped out of the river, and would have
  devoured him. 3 Then the angel said to him, Take the fish. And the
  young man laid hold of the fish, and drew it to land. 4 To whom the
  angel said, Open the fish, and take the heart and the liver and the
  gall, and put them up safely. 5 So the young man did as the angel
  commanded him; and when they had roasted the fish, they did eat it:
  then they both went on their way, till they drew near to Ecbatane.

  6 Then the young man said to the angel, Brother Azarias, to what use
  is the heart and the liver and the gal of the fish? 7 And he said to
  him, Touching the heart and the liver, if a devil or an evil spirit
  trouble any, we must make a smoke thereof before the man or the woman,
  and the party shall be no more vexed. 8 As for the gall, it is good to
  anoint a man that has whiteness in his eyes, and he shall be healed. 9
  And when they were come near to Rages, 10 The angel said to the young
  man, Brother, to day we shall lodge with Raguel, who is your cousin;
  he also has one only daughter, named Sara; I will speak for her, that
  she may be given you for a wife.

  11 For to you does the right of her appertain, seeing you only art of
  her kindred. 12 And the maid is fair and wise: now therefore hear me,
  and I will speak to her father; and when we return from Rages we will
  celebrate the marriage: for I know that Raguel cannot marry her to
  another according to the law of Moses, but he shall be guilty of
  death, because the right of inheritance does rather appertain to you
  than to any other. 13 Then the young man answered the angel, I have
  heard, brother Azarias that this maid has been given to seven men, who
  all died in the marriage chamber. 14 And now I am the only son of my
  father, and I am afraid, lest if I go in to her, I die, as the other
  before: for a wicked spirit loves her, which hurteth no body, but
  those which come to her; wherefore I also fear lest I die, and bring
  my father’s and my mother’s life because of me to the grave with
  sorrow: for they have no other son to bury them. 15 Then the angel
  said to him, Do you not remember the precepts which your father gave
  you, that you should marry a wife of your own kindred? wherefore hear
  me, O my brother; for she shall be given you to wife; and make you no
