  reckoning of the evil spirit; for this same night shall she be given
  you in marriage.

  16 And when you shall come into the marriage chamber, you shall take
  the ashes of perfume, and shall lay upon them some of the heart and
  liver of the fish, and shall make a smoke with it: 17 And the devil
  shall smell it, and flee away, and never come again any more: but when
  you shall come to her, rise up both of you, and pray to Yahuah (God)
  which is merciful, who will have pity on you, and save you: fear not,
  for she is appointed to you from the beginning; and you shall preserve
  her, and she shall go with you. Moreover I suppose that she shall bear
  you children. Now when Tobias had heard these things, he loved her,
  and his heart was effectually joined to her.

⸻

Commentary

The journey to Media. Tobias washes himself in the river Tigris and a
great fish comes up to swallow him. Raphael instructs him to take the
fish, draw out the heart, liver, and gall, and keep them — the heart and
liver for driving away demons by smoke, the gall for restoring sight to
the blind. Tobias does so. They continue toward Ecbatane.

Two notes for the awakening reader.

First, the medicinal use of fish parts is second-temple folk-medical
lore preserved in the narrative. The text presents the practice as
effective — the smoke of the heart and liver will drive Asmodeus from
Sarah's chamber, and the gall will heal Tobit's eyes. The framework of
this Series does not require the awakening reader to develop a
contemporary practice of fish-organ medicine. The witness shows what the
second-temple imagination believed about natural means of deliverance.
The means are not the deliverance. The Father is the deliverance,
working through means He chooses, including means that the modern reader
may find unfamiliar. The miracles in Tobit are not grounded in the
substances. They are grounded in Yahuah (God)'s purpose for the
household.

Second, the conversation between Raphael and Tobias on the road (verses
10–18) reveals that Sarah is Tobias's appointed wife. Raphael tells
Tobias that Sarah is his kinswoman, that the inheritance of her father's
house belongs by Torah right to him as her closest male relative within
marriageable degree, and that the appointed marriage is what the Father
has prepared. Tobias, who knows about the seven previous husbands and
the demon, is afraid. Raphael instructs him: pray, fast, and trust
Yahuah (God); the demon will flee at the smoke of the fish-organs; the
marriage will stand; the appointed providence will hold.

The marriage-by-kindred pattern in Tobit is one of the most important
framework illustrations in the apocryphal corpus. The covenant marriage
was within the kindred. The Torah commanded marriages within the tribes
(Numbers 36) for the preservation of inheritance.

Read this with Genesis 24, the great kindred-marriage narrative of the
patriarchs. Genesis 24:3–4: I will make you swear by Yahuah (God), the
Elohim (God) of heaven, and the Elohim (God) of the earth, that you shall not take a wife
to my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell: but
you shall go to my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife to my son
Isaac. Genesis 24:67: And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's
tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her: and
Isaac was comforted after his mother's death. The Tobit narrative is
composed within the Genesis 24 architecture. Abraham sent Eliezer to
find Isaac a wife from the kindred at the household of Bethuel. Tobit
sends Tobias (with the angel-guide Raphael) to find a wife from the
kindred at the household of Raguel. The names parallel: Bethuel / Raguel
as the bride's father; Rebekah / Sarah as the bride; Eliezer / Raphael
as the guide; Isaac / Tobias as the bridegroom. The covenant pattern is
preserved in literary echo across two thousand years.

Genesis 28:1–2 reinforces the pattern. Isaac to Jacob: You shall not
take a wife of the daughters of Canaan. Arise, go to Padan-aram, to the
house of Bethuel your mother's father; and take you a wife from there of
the daughters of Laban your mother's brother. Three generations of
patriarchs — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob — three kindred-marriages — Sarah's
lineage, Rebekah, Leah-and-Rachel — each preserving the covenant lineage
by marrying within the kindred. Tobit's instruction to Tobias in chapter
4 to marry within the kindred is now being fulfilled by the providence
of Yahuah (God) through Raphael's guidance. Sarah is the kinswoman. The
marriage is the proper marriage. The deliverance from the demon is the
deliverance from what had been preventing the proper marriage from
standing. The framework of this Series — which honors the covenant
lineage as the basis of identity — finds in Tobit 6 an illustration of
how the Father weaves the marriages of the covenant community to
preserve the inheritance He gave.

The post-exilic crisis in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13:23–27 names what
happens when the kindred-marriage pattern is abandoned. Ezra 9:1–2: The
people of Yashar'el (Israel), and the priests, and the Levites, have not
separated themselves from the people of the lands... For they have taken
of their daughters for themselves, and for their sons: so that the holy
seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands. The phrase
holy seed names the bloodline-specific covenant: the seed of Jacob is
holy seed, set apart for the covenant inheritance, and the mixing with
the surrounding peoples is named as a violation of the covenant order.
The framework reads this as one of the canonical anchors for the
bloodline-remnant claim. The seed is named as seed. The seed is named as
holy. The seed is to be preserved through kindred-marriage where
possible. Tobit 6 is the second-temple narrative form of what Ezra 9
articulates as covenant principle.

Cross-references: Numbers 36:1–13; Deuteronomy 7:1–4; Genesis 24:1–67;
Genesis 28:1–9; Tobit 1:9; Tobit 4:12–13; Ezra 9:1–4; Nehemiah 13:23–27;
Malachi 2:10–16.

Tobit — Chapter 7

  1 And when they were come to Ecbatane, they came to the house of
  Raguel, and Sara met them: and after they had saluted one another, she
  brought them into the house. 2 Then said Raguel to Edna his wife, How
  like is this young man to Tobit my cousin! 3 And Raguel asked them,
  From whence are you, brothers? To whom they said, We are of the sons
  of Nephthalim, which are captives in Nineve. 4 Then he said to them,
  Do you know Tobit our kinsman? And they said, We know him. Then said
  he, Is he in good health? 5 And they said, He is both alive, and in
  good health: and Tobias said, He is my father.

  6 Then Raguel leaped up, and kissed him, and wept, 7 And blessed him,
  and said to him, You are the son of an honest and good man. But when
  he had heard that Tobit was blind, he was sorrowful, and wept. 8 And
  likewise Edna his wife and Sara his daughter wept. Moreover they
  entertained them cheerfully; and after that they had killed a ram of
  the flock, they set store of meat on the table. Then said Tobias to
  Raphael, Brother Azarias, speak of those things of which you did talk
  in the way, and let this business be dispatched. 9 So he communicated
  the matter with Raguel: and Raguel said to Tobias, Eat and drink, and
  make merry: 10 For it is meet that you should marry my daughter:
  nevertheless I will declare to you the truth.

  11 I have given my daughter in marriage to seven men, who died that
  night they came in to her: nevertheless for the present be merry. But
  Tobias said, I will eat nothing here, till we agree and swear one to
  another. 12 Raguel said, Then take her from henceforth according to
  the manner, for you are her cousin, and she is yours, and the merciful
  Yahuah (God) give you good success in all things. 13 Then he called
  his daughter Sara, and she came to her father, and he took her by the
  hand, and gave her to be wife to Tobias, saying, Behold, take her
  after the law of Moses, and lead her away to your father. And he
  blessed them; 14 And called Edna his wife, and took paper, and did
  write an instrument of covenants, and sealed it. 15 Then they began to
  eat.

  16 After Raguel called his wife Edna, and said to her, Sister, prepare
  another chamber, and bring her in thither. 17 Which when she had done
  as he had bidden her, she brought her thither: and she wept, and she
  received the tears of her daughter, and said to her, 18 Be of good
  comfort, my daughter; Yahuah (God) of heaven and earth give you joy
  for this your sorrow: be of good comfort, my daughter.

⸻

Commentary

Tobias arrives at the house of Raguel and Edna in Ecbatane. The
reception scene is one of the warmest hospitality scenes in
second-temple narrative. Raguel sees Tobias and weeps because Tobias
resembles Tobit, his cousin. Edna and Sarah welcome them. The marriage
covenant is drawn up the same evening, written on a tablet, and sealed.

Three things matter.

First, the marriage covenant is documented in writing. The framework of
this Series, which holds that the covenant is the basis of identity,
finds in Tobit 7 the Torah-observant practice of formal
covenant-document marriage. The marriage is not an emotional
understanding between two young people. It is a covenant between two
households, recorded in writing, witnessed, and sealed. The awakening
reader walking out of contemporary Christian marriage culture, in which
the covenant has often been reduced to ceremony without legal-covenantal
substance, will recognize what is being preserved here. The marriage is
a covenant. Covenant requires documentation. The household elders are
the witnesses.

Second, the marriage is between kinsmen. Tobias is a Naphtali Israelite
from the diaspora in Nineveh; Sarah is from Raguel's household in
Ecbatane. They are within the covenant kindred. The marriage preserves
the inheritance lines the Torah was structured to preserve. The same
principle is operative in the marriages of the patriarchs (Isaac to
Rebekah, Jacob to Leah and Rachel) and is one of the patterns the
prophets keep returning to as a marker of covenant faithfulness.

Third, the welcoming of the kinsman and the immediate movement to
marriage covenant illustrates how the second-temple Torah-observant
community handled the long-distance scattering of the seed. The covenant
family did not lose track of itself across the dispersion. Tobit, in
Nineveh, knew that his kinsman Raguel was in Ecbatane. The lineage was
remembered. The covenant identity was preserved across geographical
distance. The framework of this Series — that the scattered seed has
been preserved across the dispersion, that the covenant identity has
been remembered, that the gathering is the bringing back of those who
never lost their identity in the eyes of the Father — finds in Tobit 7 a
small but real illustration of how the preservation worked across the
second-temple diaspora.

Cross-references: Genesis 24:1–67; Genesis 29:1–30; Ruth 4:1–13; Tobit
4:12–13; Malachi 2:14–16; Hebrews 13:4.

Tobit — Chapter 8

  1 And when they had supped, they brought Tobias in to her. 2 And as he
  went, he remembered the words of Raphael, and took the ashes of the
  perfumes, and put the heart and the liver of the fish thereupon, and
  made a smoke with it. 3 The which smell when the evil spirit had
  smelled, he fled into the utmost parts of Egypt, and the angel bound
  him. 4 And after that they were both shut in together, Tobias rose out
  of the bed, and said, Sister, arise, and let us pray that Yahuah (God)
  would have pity on us. 5 Then began Tobias to say, Blessed art you, O
  Yahuah (God) of our fathers, and blessed is your holy and glorious
  name for ever; let the heavens bless you, and all your creatures.

  6 You madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay:
  of them came mankind: you have said, It is not good that man should be
  alone; let us make to him an aid like to himself. 7 And now, O Yahuah
  (God), I take not this my sister for lust but uprightly: therefore
  mercifully ordain that we may become aged together. 8 And she said
  with him, Amen. 9 So they slept both that night. And Raguel arose, and
  went and made a grave, 10 Saying, I fear lest he also be dead.

  11 But when Raguel was come into his house, 12 He said to his wife
  Edna. Send one of the maids, and let her see whether he be alive: if
  he be not, that we may bury him, and no man know it. 13 So the maid
  opened the door, and went in, and found them both asleep, 14 And came
  forth, and told them that he was alive. 15 Then Raguel praised Yahuah
  (God), and said, O Yahuah (God), you are worthy to be praised with all
  pure and holy praise; therefore let your saints praise you with all
  your creatures; and let all your angels and your elect praise you for
  ever.

  16 You are to be praised, for you have made me joyful; and that is not
  come to me which I suspected; but you have dealt with us according to
  your great mercy. 17 You are to be praised because you have had mercy
  of two that were the only begotten children of their fathers: grant
  them mercy, O Yahuah (God), and finish their life in health with joy
  and mercy. 18 Then Raguel told his servants to fill the grave. 19 And
  he kept the wedding feast fourteen days. 20 For before the days of the
  marriage were finished, Raguel had said to him by an oath, that he
  should not depart till the fourteen days of the marriage were expired;

  21 And then he should take the half of his goods, and go in safety to
  his father; and should have the rest when I and my wife be dead.

⸻

Commentary

The marriage chamber. Tobias remembers Raphael's instruction. He takes
the heart and liver of the fish, lays them on the burning incense, and
the smoke drives Asmodeus into Egypt where Raphael binds him. Tobias and
Sarah pray before they consummate the marriage — a prayer that the
framework of this Series should mark.

Tobias's prayer (verses 5–8) is one of the great marriage prayers of the
second-temple corpus. He blesses Yahuah (God), the Elohim (God) of the fathers.
He recalls that Yahuah (God) made Adam and gave him Eve. He acknowledges
that he is taking Sarah not for any unclean reason but in truth, and
asks for mercy, that they may grow old together. Sarah joins the prayer
with her amen. The chamber is sanctified. The marriage is consummated
under blessing. The morning comes. Tobias is alive — the first of
Sarah's husbands to live through the wedding night. The household
rejoices.

Two notes for the awakening reader.

First, the prayer of Tobias before consummating the marriage is a model.
The framework of this Series, which honors the marriage as a covenant
under Yahuah (God) and not merely a personal arrangement, finds in this
prayer the appropriate posture.

Read the canonical anchor for marriage as covenant. Genesis 2:24:
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave
unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh. Malachi 2:14: Yet you say,
Wherefore? Because Yahuah (God) has been witness between you and the
wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously: yet is
she your companion, and the wife of your covenant. Proverbs 2:17 names
the wife of one's youth as bound by the covenant of her Elohim (God). Yahusha
cites Genesis 2 in Matthew 19:4–6: Have you not read, that he which made
them at the beginning made them male and female, and said, For this
cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife:
and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but
one flesh. What therefore Elohim (God) has joined together, let not man put
asunder. Ephesians 5:31–32 brings the marriage covenant into apostolic
frame as a picture of the Messiah and his people: For this cause shall a
man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and
they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak
concerning Messiah (Christ) and the church.

The marriage is offered to the Father before it is consummated. The
Adamic precedent is named — Adam and Eve, the original pattern of the
covenant marriage. The mercy of Yahuah (God) is asked for the keeping of
the marriage. The witness of the second-temple Torah-observant household
is a witness the awakening reader can carry into his or her own
marriage. Tobit 8 is the second-temple narrative form of what Genesis 2,
Malachi 2, Proverbs 2, Matthew 19, and Ephesians 5 articulate as
covenant doctrine: marriage is a covenant before Yahuah (God), witnessed
by Him, sustained by His mercy, and joined as one flesh by His act.

Second, the binding of Asmodeus by Raphael in Egypt is a small detail
with framework significance. Egypt in the prophetic imagination is the
land from which the covenant people were delivered, and to which evil is
sometimes consigned. The text does not develop a doctrine of demonic
geography from the detail. The detail shows what the second-temple
imagination believed about how the deliverance from demonic affliction
proceeded. The principle behind the detail is the principle that holds:
Yahuah (God) delivers His own from the principalities and powers that
have afflicted them, and the deliverance is real even when the means He
uses are unfamiliar to the modern reader.

Cross-references: Genesis 1:27–28; Genesis 2:18–25; Tobit 6:7–9; Mark
10:6–9; Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 7:1–7; Hebrews 13:4.

Tobit — Chapter 9

  1 Then Tobias called Raphael, and said to him, 2 Brother Azarias, take
  with you a servant, and two camels, and go to Rages of Media to
  Gabael, and bring me the money, and bring him to the wedding. 3 For
  Raguel has sworn that I shall not depart. 4 But my father counteth the
  days; and if I tarry long, he will be very sorry. 5 So Raphael went
  out, and lodged with Gabael, and gave him the handwriting: who brought
  forth bags which were sealed up, and gave them to him.

  6 And early in the morning they went forth both together, and came to
  the wedding: and Tobias blessed his wife.

⸻

Commentary

Raphael, while Tobias and Sarah are celebrating in Ecbatane, travels to
Rages of Media to recover the silver Tobit had left in trust with
Gabael. The errand that began the journey — the recovery of the ten
talents — is now being completed in the background while the marriage
and feast are in the foreground.

Two notes.

First, the chapter is short and structurally important. It shows how the
providence of Yahuah (God) covers more than one need at a time. Tobit's
blindness, Sarah's affliction, Tobias's marriage, the recovery of the
ten talents, the eventual healing of the household — all of it is being
woven into a single arc. The errand that Tobit thought was the journey
turns out to be only one piece of what the Father was actually doing.
The framework of this Series — that the Father is weaving more than the
awakening reader can yet see — is the framework that runs underneath
Tobit's narrative.

Second, Raphael's identity is still concealed. He has been doing the
work of Yahuah (God) the whole time without Tobias yet knowing who he
is. The framework of this Series — that the Spirit's restoration of the
awakening remnant has been proceeding without the remnant yet knowing
the full picture — has its small parallel here. The work was happening
before the workers knew. The deliverance was being arranged before the
delivered knew to ask.

Cross-references: Tobit 1:14; Tobit 4:1–2; Tobit 4:20; Tobit 5:3; Romans
8:28; Ephesians 1:3–14.

Tobit — Chapter 10

  1 Now Tobit his father counted every day: and when the days of the
  journey were expired, and they came not, 2 Then Tobit said, Are they
  detained? or is Gabael dead, and there is no man to give him the
  money? 3 Therefore he was very sorry. 4 Then his wife said to him, My
  son is dead, seeing he stayeth long; and she began to wail him, and
  said, 5 Now I care for nothing, my son, since I have let you go, the
  light of my eyes.

  6 To whom Tobit said, Hold your peace, take no care, for he is safe. 7
  But she said, Hold your peace, and deceive me not; my son is dead. And
  she went out every day into the way which they went, and did eat no
  meat on the daytime, and ceased not whole nights to bewail her son
  Tobias, until the fourteen days of the wedding were expired, which
  Raguel had sworn that he should spend there. Then Tobias said to
  Raguel, Let me go, for my father and my mother look no more to see me.
  8 But his father in law said to him, Tarry with me, and I will send to
  your father, and they shall declare to him how things go with you. 9
  But Tobias said, No; but let me go to my father. 10 Then Raguel arose,
  and gave him Sara his wife, and half his goods, servants, and cattle,
  and money:

  11 And he blessed them, and sent them away, saying, Yahuah (God)
  of heaven give you a prosperous journey, my children. 12 And he said
  to his daughter, Honour your father and your mother in law, which are
  now your parents, that I may hear good report of you. And he kissed
  her. Edna also said to Tobias, Yahuah (God) of heaven restore you,
  my dear brother, and grant that I may see your children of my daughter
  Sara before I die, that I may rejoice before Yahuah (God): behold, I
  commit my daughter to you of special trust; where are do not entreat
  her evil.

⸻

Commentary

In Nineveh, Tobit and Anna are increasingly anxious about their son's
delay. Anna especially weeps day after day, fearing that her son has
died. The narrative pacing shifts to the worry of the parents, while the
marriage feast in Ecbatane is being celebrated. Tobias and Sarah finally
set out for home, with half of Raguel's substance given as a wedding
gift.

The chapter shows what the awakening reader will recognize: that those
who wait are often more strained than those who travel. The journeying
son does not see what the praying parents see. The praying parents do
not see what the journeying son sees. The Father sees both. The
framework of this Series — that the Father holds the household together
across the distance and the silence — is the framework Tobit and Anna
are praying inside even when they do not feel it.

The blessing Raguel gives at the parting (verses 12–13) is a
wedding-blessing of the second-temple covenant community: that Yahuah
(God) would prosper the marriage, that the children would be many, that
Sarah would honor her father-in-law and mother-in-law as her own, that
Tobias would be a faithful husband. The framework of this Series, which
honors the covenant marriage as the household-building unit of the
covenant community, finds in Raguel's blessing the proper shape of the
parental blessing on a marriage that is leaving home.

Cross-references: Genesis 24:60; Ruth 4:11–12; Tobit 7:11–14; Proverbs
31:10–31; Ephesians 6:1–4.

Tobit — Chapter 11

  1 After these things Tobias went his way, praising Yahuah (God) that
  he had given him a prosperous journey, and blessed Raguel and Edna his
  wife, and went on his way till they drew near to Nineve. 2 Then
  Raphael said to Tobias, You know, brother, how you did leave your
  father: 3 Let us haste before your wife, and prepare the house. 4 And
  take in yours hand the gall of the fish. So they went their way, and
  the dog went after them. 5 Now Anna sat looking about toward the way
  for her son.

  6 And when she espied him coming, she said to his father, Behold, your
  son comes, and the man that went with him. 7 Then said Raphael, I
  know, Tobias, that your father will open his eyes. 8 Therefore anoint
  you his eyes with the gall, and being pricked with it, he shall rub,
  and the whiteness shall fall away, and he shall see you. 9 Then Anna
  ran forth, and fell upon the neck of her son, and said to him, Seeing
  I have seen you, my son, from henceforth I am content to die. And they
  wept both. 10 Tobit also went forth toward the door, and stumbled: but
  his son ran to him,

  11 And took hold of his father: and he strake of the gall on his
  fathers’ eyes, saying, Be of good hope, my father. 12 And when his
  eyes began to smart, he rubbed them; 13 And the whiteness pilled away
  from the corners of his eyes: and when he saw his son, he fell upon
  his neck. 14 And he wept, and said, Blessed art you, O Yahuah (God),
  and blessed is your name for ever; and blessed are all yours holy
  angels: 15 For you have scourged, and have taken pity on me: for,
  behold, I see my son Tobias. And his son went in rejoicing, and told
  his father the great things that had happened to him in Media.

  16 Then Tobit went out to meet his daughter in law at the gate of
  Nineve, rejoicing and praising Yahuah (God): and they which saw him go
  marvelled, because he had received his sight. 17 But Tobias gave
  thanks before them, because Yahuah (God) had mercy on him. And when he
  came near to Sara his daughter in law, he blessed her, saying, You are
  welcome, daughter: Yahuah (God) be blessed, which has brought you to
  us, and blessed be your father and your mother. And there was joy
  among all his brothers which were at Nineve. 18 And Achiacharus, and
  Nasbas his brother’s son, came: 19 And Tobias’ wedding was kept seven
  days with great joy.

⸻

Commentary

The return to Nineveh. Tobit and Anna see Tobias from a distance, weep,
and run to embrace him. Tobias, instructed by Raphael, takes the gall of
the fish, anoints his father's eyes, and the white film of cataract is
peeled away. Tobit's sight is restored. The household rejoices. The
neighbors witness the healing. Tobit blesses Yahuah (God) publicly.

Three things matter.

First, the healing is public. The neighbors who had mocked Tobit in
chapter 2 now witness the healing in chapter 11. The text does not name
them by name, but the framework of the apocryphal narrative is
consistent: the household is restored before the witnesses who had seen
its collapse. The framework of this Series — that the awakening of the
remnant produces a witness those who saw the household's fall will
eventually see — is the framework the chapter is operating inside. The
Father restores publicly what was lost publicly.

Second, the means of healing — the fish gall — has been waiting in
Tobias's bag for chapters. Raphael gave the instruction at the beginning
of the journey. The instruction has been kept. The healing comes through
the keeping of the instruction. The framework of this Series, which
honors patient obedience to the instruction the Spirit has given, finds
in Tobias a small illustration: the means Yahuah (God) provides for
deliverance are means He gave before the moment of deliverance arrived,
and the deliverance comes through the keeping of those means.

Third, Tobit's blessing of Yahuah (God) on his sight being restored
(verse 14) is the proper response: not pride in his own deliverance, not
ascription of the healing to his son's skill or to a fortunate accident,
but the open acknowledgment that Yahuah (God) has done what only Yahuah
(God) can do. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
awakening of any believer is the work of the Father and not of the
believer, finds in Tobit's blessing the right shape: the deliverance is
named, named to Yahuah (God), and named publicly so that everyone in the
household sees who has done the work.

Cross-references: Tobit 2:9–10; Tobit 6:8; Mark 8:22–25; John 9:1–7;
Acts 9:17–19; James 5:14–16.

Tobit — Chapter 12

  1 Then Tobit called his son Tobias, and said to him, My son, see that
  the man have his wages, which went with you, and you must give him
  more. 2 And Tobias said to him, O father, it is no harm to me to give
  him half of those things which I have brought: 3 For he has brought me
  again to you in safety, and made whole my wife, and brought me the
  money, and likewise healed you. 4 Then the old man said, It is due to
  him. 5 So he called the angel, and he said to him, Take half of all
  that you have brought and go away in safety.

  6 Then he took them both apart, and said to them, Bless Yahuah (God),
  praise him, and magnify him, and praise him for the things which he
  has done to you in the sight of all that live. It is good to praise
  Yahuah (God), and exalt his name, and honourably to shew forth the
  works of Yahuah (God); therefore be not slack to praise him. 7 It is
  good to keep close the secret of a king, but it is honourable to
  reveal the works of Yahuah (God). Do that which is good, and no evil
  shall touch you. 8 Prayer is good with fasting and alms and
  righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with
  unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold: 9 For
  alms does deliver from death, and shall purge away all sin. Those that
  exercise alms and righteousness shall be filled with life: 10 But they
  that sin are enemies to their own life.

  11 Surely I will keep close nothing from you. For I said, It was good
  to keep close the secret of a king, but that it was honourable to
  reveal the works of Yahuah (God). 12 Now therefore, when you did pray,
  and Sara your daughter in law, I did bring the remembrance of your
  prayers before the Holy One: and when you did bury the dead, I was
  with you likewise. 13 And when you did not delay to rise up, and leave
  your dinner, to go and cover the dead, your good deed was not hid from
  me: but I was with you. 14 And now Yahuah (God) has sent me to heal
  you and Sara your daughter in law. 15 I am Raphael, one of the seven
  holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and which go in
  and out before the glory of the Holy One.

  16 Then they were both troubled, and fell upon their faces: for they
  feared. 17 But he said to them, Fear not, for it shall go well with
  you; praise Yahuah (God) therefore. 18 For not of any favour of mine,
  but by the will of our Elohim (God) I came; wherefore praise him for
  ever. 19 All these days I did appear to you; but I did neither eat nor
  drink, but you did see a vision. 20 Now therefore give Yahuah (God)
  thanks: for I go up to him that sent me; but write all things which
  are done in a book.

  21 And when they arose, they saw him no more. 22 Then they confessed
  the great and wonderful works of Yahuah (God), and how the angel of
  Yahuah (God) had appeared to them.

⸻

Commentary

Raphael reveals himself. Tobit and Tobias call him in to give him a
wedding-payment for his service. Raphael refuses payment and tells them
that prayer with fasting, almsgiving, and righteousness is better than
gold; that almsgiving delivers from death and purges from every sin; and
that those who do righteousness will be filled with life. He then names
himself: "I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the
prayers of the saints, and which go in and out before the glory of the
Holy One." The household falls on their faces. Raphael instructs them to
bless Yahuah (God) and to write the things they have seen in a book, and
then ascends.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, Raphael's identification of himself as one of the seven holy
angels is the second-temple development of an angelology that is not
present in the Torah and is implicit at most in the prophets. Daniel 7
names "thousand thousands" and "ten thousand times ten thousand" of
angelic ministers, and Daniel 8 and 10 name specific archangels (Gabriel
and Michael), but the Torah does not develop a hierarchy of seven
principal angels who present the prayers of the saints before the
throne. The seven-archangel structure is a second-temple Yahudi (Jewish)
development, particularly visible in 1 Enoch and in apocalyptic texts
contemporaneous with Tobit. The framework of this Series, which holds
that the Torah is the standard, does not require the awakening reader to
develop a contemporary cult around named archangels. The witness of
Tobit shows what the second-temple imagination believed. The legislation
of the Torah does not include the practice. Hold the witness as witness.
Do not legislate from it.

Second, Raphael's declaration that almsgiving delivers from death and
purges from every sin (verse 9) is one of the verses Catholic and
Orthodox traditions have used to develop a doctrine of works-based
atonement. The 1234 filter and the apostolic witness apply. The Torah's
doctrine of atonement is by sacrificial blood, ultimately fulfilled in
the Messiah's atoning death (Hebrews 9–10). Almsgiving is a Torah
commandment with profound covenant significance (Deuteronomy 15), and it
does carry weight before Yahuah (God) (Acts 10:4 names the alms of
Cornelius as having come up before Yahuah (God) for a memorial). But
almsgiving is not the basis of atonement. Salvation is by grace through
faith in the Messiah's blood, not by alms (Ephesians 2:8–9). Tobit 12:9,
taken literally as a doctrine of atonement by alms, contradicts the
apostolic witness. Read it as second-temple wisdom literature praising
the weight of almsgiving — which is true — without inflating it to a
doctrine of atonement the apostolic witness does not allow.

Third, Raphael's instruction to write the things in a book (verse 20) is
the literary frame for the book of Tobit itself. The book is presented
as the household's record of what they had seen. The genre of
memoir-as-witness is preserved across the apocryphal corpus and into the
apostolic writings (Luke names this in his preface, Luke 1:1–4). The
framework of this Series — that witness is to be heard and recorded — is
the framework Tobit's closing operates inside.

Cross-references: Daniel 7:9–10; Daniel 8:15–17; Daniel 10:13; Tobit
4:7–11; Acts 10:1–8; Hebrews 9:11–14; Hebrews 10:11–14; Ephesians 2:8–9;
1 Enoch 20:1–8; Revelation 8:3–5.

Tobit — Chapter 13

  1 Then Tobit wrote a prayer of rejoicing, and said, Blessed be Yahuah
  (God) that lives for ever, and blessed be his kingdom. 2 For he does
  scourge, and has mercy: he leadeth down to hell, and brings up again:
  neither is there any that can avoid his hand. 3 Confess him before the
  Gentiles, you children of Yashar'el (Israel): for he has scattered us
  among them. 4 There declare his greatness, and extol him before all
  the living: for he is our Elohim (God), and he is Yahuah (God) our
  Father for ever. 5 And he will scourge us for our iniquities, and will
  have mercy again, and will gather us out of all nations, among whom he
  has scattered us.

  6 If you turn to him with your whole heart, and with your whole mind,
  and deal uprightly before him, then will he turn to you, and will not
  hide his face from you. Therefore see what he will do with you, and
  confess him with your whole mouth, and praise Yahuah (God) of might,
  and extol the everlasting King. In the land of my captivity do I
  praise him, and declare his might and majesty to a sinful nation. O
  you sinners, turn and do justice before him: who can tell if he will
  accept you, and have mercy on you? 7 I will extol my Elohim (God), and
  my soul shall praise the King of heaven, and shall rejoice in his
  greatness. 8 Let all men speak, and let all praise him for his
  righteousness. 9 O Jerusalem, the holy city, he will scourge you for
  your children’s works, and will have mercy again on the sons of the
  righteous. 10 Give praise to Yahuah (God), for he is good: and praise
  the everlasting King, that his tabernacle may be builded in you again
  with joy, and let him make joyful there in you those that are
  captives, and love in you for ever those that are miserable.

  11 Many nations shall come from far to the name of Yahuah (God) with
  gifts in their hands, even gifts to the King of heaven; all
  generations shall praise you with great joy. 12 Cursed are all they
  which hate you, and blessed shall all be which love you for ever. 13
  Rejoice and be glad for the children of the just: for they shall be
  gathered together, and shall bless Yahuah (God) of the just. 14 O
  blessed are they which love you, for they shall rejoice in your peace:
  blessed are they which have been sorrowful for all your scourges; for
  they shall rejoice for you, when they have seen all your glory, and
  shall be glad for ever. 15 Let my soul bless Yahuah (God) the great
  King.

  16 For Jerusalem shall be built up with sapphires and emeralds, and
  precious stone: your walls and towers and battlements with pure gold.
  17 And the streets of Jerusalem shall be paved with beryl and
  carbuncle and stones of Ophir. 18 And all her streets shall say,
  Alleluia; and they shall praise him, saying, Blessed be Yahuah (God),
  which has extolled it for ever.

⸻

Commentary

Tobit composes a song of praise. The song is one of the great
praise-poems of the second-temple corpus. Two structural movements
matter.

First, the praise of Yahuah (God) for His chastisement and mercy (verses
1–10). The voice is the voice of one who has been disciplined, restored,
and now knows that the discipline was mercy. He has scourged us for our
iniquities, and will have mercy again, and will gather us out of all
nations, among whom he has scattered us.

The canonical anchor is Deuteronomy 30:1–5: And it shall come to pass,
when all these things are come upon you, the blessing and the curse,
which I have set before you, and you shall call them to mind among all
the nations, whither Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God) has driven you, and shall
return unto Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God), and shall obey his voice... that then
Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God) will turn your captivity, and have compassion upon
you, and will return and gather you from all the nations, whither Yahuah
(God) your Elohim (God) has scattered you. Hebrews 12:6 names the same principle
in apostolic vocabulary: For whom the Lord loves he chastens, and
scourges every son whom he receives. Lamentations 3:32–33: But though he
cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of
his mercies. For he does not afflict willingly nor grieve the children
of men. Psalm 89:30–34: If his children forsake my law, and walk not in
my judgments... Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and
their iniquity with stripes. Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not
utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant
will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.

The covenant pattern is named: scattering for sin, gathering for mercy,
the same Father working both. The framework of this Series — that the
curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell because the people walked out from under
the covenant, and that the gathering of the scattered seed is the
Father's mercy returning to His own — is the framework Tobit's song is
praying. The song is the second-temple voice that already saw the
gathering as the inevitable Word of Yahuah (God) for those scattered
among the nations.

Second, the prophetic vision of restored Jerusalem (verses 11–18). The
voice shifts to a vision of the city rebuilt with sapphires, emeralds,
and precious stones; the streets paved with beryl, carbuncle, and
ophir-stones; all nations praising Yahuah (God) in her gates. The vision
is parallel to Isaiah 60 and parallel to Revelation 21.

Read Tobit 13:16–17 with the two canonical anchors open beside it.
Isaiah 54:11–12: O you afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not
comforted, behold, I will lay your stones with fair colors, and lay your
foundations with sapphires. And I will make your windows of agates, and
your gates of carbuncles, and all your borders of pleasant stones.
Isaiah 60:14–18: The sons also of them that afflicted you shall come
bending unto you... they shall call you, The city of Yahuah (God), The
Zion of the Holy One of Yashar'el (Israel)... You shall also suck the
milk of the Gentiles, and shall suck the breast of kings... For brass I
will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver, and for wood brass,
and for stones iron... Violence shall no more be heard in your land,
wasting nor destruction within your borders; but you shall call your
walls Salvation, and your gates Praise. Revelation 21:18–21: And the
building of the wall of it was of jasper: and the city was pure gold,
like unto clear glass. And the foundations of the wall of the city were
garnished with all manner of precious stones... And the twelve gates
were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street
of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.

Three witnesses. Three centuries apart. One vision. The
eighth-century-BCE Naphtali Israelite Tobit (in the literary setting of
his book), the early sixth-century-BCE prophet Isaiah, and the late
first-century-CE seer John on Patmos all see the same restored city —
sapphires, emeralds, gates of precious stones, streets of gold, the
nations gathered in. The framework of this Series, which holds
Revelation as cyclical rather than linear and reads the restored
Jerusalem as the destination of the long arc of the prophetic
imagination, finds in Tobit 13 a second-temple witness to the same
destination. The song knows what Isaiah knew. The song hears what John
would hear. The destination has been the same since the prophets first
named it. The new Jerusalem has twelve gates with the names of the
twelve tribes (Revelation 21:12) — the bloodline-remnant claim runs
through the gates of the restored city as it runs through the entire
prophetic imagination.

Cross-references: Deuteronomy 28:64–65; Deuteronomy 30:1–10; Isaiah
60:1–22; Isaiah 62:1–12; Jeremiah 30:1–24; Jeremiah 31:1–14; Tobit
1:5–6; Ezekiel 37:21–28; Revelation 21:1–27.

Tobit — Chapter 14

  1 So Tobit made an end of praising Yahuah (God). 2 And he was eight
  and fifty years old when he lost his sight, which was restored to him
  after eight years: and he gave alms, and he increased in the fear of
  Yahuah (God), and praised him. 3 And when he was very aged he called
  his son, and the sons of his son, and said to him, My son, take your
  children; for, behold, I am aged, and am ready to depart out of this
  life. 4 Go into Media my son, for I surely believe those things which
  Jonas the prophet spoke of Nineve, that it shall be overthrown; and
  that for a time peace shall rather be in Media; and that our brothers
  shall lie scattered in the earth from that good land: and Jerusalem
  shall be desolate, and the house of Yahuah (God) in it shall be
  burned, and shall be desolate for a time; 5 And that again Yahuah
  (God) will have mercy on them, and bring them again into the land,
  where they shall build a temple, but not like to the first, until the
  time of that age be fulfilled; and afterward they shall return from
  all places of their captivity, and build up Jerusalem gloriously, and
  the house of Yahuah (God) shall be built in it for ever with a
  glorious building, as the prophets have spoken thereof.

  6 And all nations shall turn, and fear Yahuah (God) truly, and shall
  bury their idols. 7 So shall all nations praise Yahuah (God), and his
  people shall confess Yahuah (God), and Yahuah (God) shall exalt his
  people; and all those which love Yahuah (God) in truth and justice
  shall rejoice, shewing mercy to our brothers. 8 And now, my son,
  depart out of Nineve, because that those things which the prophet
  Jonas spoke shall surely come to pass. 9 But keep you the law and the
  commandments, and shew thyself merciful and just, that it may go well
  with you. 10 And bury me decently, and your mother with me; but tarry
  no longer at Nineve. Remember, my son, how Aman handled Achiacharus
  that brought him up, how out of light he brought him into darkness,
  and how he rewarded him again: yet Achiacharus was saved, but the
  other had his reward: for he went down into darkness. Manasses gave
  alms, and escaped the snares of death which they had set for him: but
  Aman fell into the snare, and perished.

  11 Wherefore now, my son, consider what alms doeth, and how
  righteousness does deliver. When he had said these things, he gave up
  the ghost in the bed, being an hundred and eight and fifty years old;
  and he buried him honourably. 12 And when Anna his mother was dead, he
  buried her with his father. But Tobias departed with his wife and
  children to Ecbatane to Raguel his father in law, 13 Where he became
  old with honour, and he buried his father and mother in law
  honourably, and he inherited their substance, and his father Tobit’s.
  14 And he died at Ecbatane in Media, being an hundred and seven and
  twenty years old. 15 But before he died he heard of the destruction of
  Nineve, which was taken by Nabuchodonosor and Assuerus: and before his
  death he rejoiced over Nineve.

⸻

Commentary

The closing of the book. Tobit, dying at the age of one hundred
fifty-eight, gives Tobias his deathbed instruction. Tobias is to leave
Nineveh because Nineveh will be destroyed (the text names the prophet
Jonah; the framework here is the second-temple memory of Jonah's
prophecy and its eventual fulfillment in 612 BCE when Nineveh fell to
the Babylonians and the Medes). Tobias is to bury his father and mother
with care. Tobias is to go to Media, where the rest of the household
awaits. Tobit recalls the prophets — that the gathering of the scattered
seed of Yashar'el (Israel) and Yahudah (Judah) will come, that the
temple will be rebuilt, that the nations will turn from idols to Yahuah
(God), that the gathering will be glorious. Tobit dies. Tobias buries
his parents at Nineveh. He moves to Ecbatane. He lives to see the
destruction of Nineveh, which he hears about before his own death, in
which he praises Yahuah (God) for the prophecy fulfilled.

Three closing notes.

First, the closing prophecy of Tobit (verses 4–7) is one of the most
explicit second-temple statements of the gathering of the scattered seed
of Yashar'el (Israel) and Yahudah (Judah) and the conversion of the
nations to Yahuah (God). The vocabulary is the vocabulary of Isaiah and
Jeremiah.

Read Tobit 14:5 alongside the prophetic chain that produced it. Jeremiah
31:8: Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them
from the coasts of the earth, and with them the blind and the lame, the
woman with child and her that travails with child together: a great
company shall return there. Jeremiah 31:31–34: Behold, the days come,
says Yahuah (God), that I will make a new covenant with the house of
Yashar'el (Israel), and with the house of Yahudah (Judah)... I will put
my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be
their Elohim (God), and they shall be my people. Ezekiel 37:21–22: Thus says the
Lord Yahuah (God); Behold, I will take the children of Yashar'el
(Israel) from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and will gather
them on every side, and bring them into their own land: and I will make
them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Yashar'el (Israel).
Hosea 1:10–11: Yet the number of the children of Yashar'el (Israel)
shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered;
and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto
them, You are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, You are
the sons of the living Elohim (God). Then shall the children of Yahudah (Judah)
and the children of Yashar'el (Israel) be gathered together, and appoint
themselves one head. Isaiah 11:11–12: And it shall come to pass in that
day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover
the remnant of his people... And he shall set up an ensign for the
nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Yashar'el (Israel), and
gather together the dispersed of Yahudah (Judah) from the four corners
of the earth.

Tobit 14 is praying in the line of these prophetic anchors. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the gathering of the
scattered seed is the long restoration the prophets named, finds in
Tobit 14 the second-temple voice naming what the prophets named. The
framework was not invented in the modern Hebrew roots movement. The
framework was alive in the second-temple Naphtali household in Nineveh,
in the eighth century BCE. The text remembers it. The awakening reader
is rejoining a memory that had never been entirely lost.

Second, the death of Tobit at 158 and the survival of Tobias to a great
age (the text names 127 in verse 14) are the second-temple genre of
patriarchal long-life. The framework of this Series does not require the
awakening reader to insist on the historical exactitude of these ages.
The genre is the genre. The text is signaling that Tobit and Tobias
lived in the long-faithful pattern of the covenant fathers, not
necessarily that the ages are calendrical. Read the genre for what it
does and let the witness stand.

Third, the closing line of the book is the framework conclusion: Tobias
praises Yahuah (God) for the destruction of Nineveh, which he had been
told about by his father, and which he has now seen. The framework of
this Series — that what the Father has named through the prophets, He
fulfills; that the awakening reader does not need to manage the timeline
but only to trust the covenant; that the destruction of every Babylonian
system that has scattered the covenant seed is in the Father's hand — is
the framework the closing of Tobit is operating inside. The household
has been restored. The covenant has been kept. The prophecy has been
fulfilled. The book closes in praise.

Cross-references: Genesis 25:7–8; Genesis 35:28–29; Tobit 1:1–2; Tobit
4:1–21; Jonah 3:1–10; Nahum 1:1–15; Nahum 3:1–19; Isaiah 11:11–12;
Isaiah 60:1–22; Jeremiah 30:1–24; Jeremiah 31:1–14; Ezekiel 37:21–28;
Hosea 1:9–11; Hosea 2:23.

Judith — Introduction

Judith is the war book the Sunday school never taught you. It is the
story of a Yahudi (Jewish) widow in the city of Bethulia who, when the
Assyrian general Holofernes lays siege to her city under the orders of
King Nebuchadnezzar, dresses herself in beauty, walks out of the city
gate, infiltrates the enemy camp, gains the trust of the general, gets
him drunk in his own tent, beheads him with his own sword, carries the
head back to her city, and breaks the siege. It is sixteen chapters of
historical-romantic narrative, with prayers, songs, genealogies,
military details, and a closing victory hymn that the early church
preserved as one of the great prayer-poems of the second-temple corpus.

Three things should be named before the reader opens chapter 1.

First, the historical setting of Judith does not match any actual moment
in history. The book opens by naming Nebuchadnezzar as king of the
Assyrians ruling from Nineveh. Nebuchadnezzar was king of the
Babylonians, ruling from Babylon, and Nineveh had already been destroyed
before he came to power. The setting is a deliberate composite. The book
is not pretending to be straight history. It is composing a narrative
whose historical references are drawn from the Babylonian and Assyrian
periods, set in a city — Bethulia — whose name does not appear on any
map and which is best understood as a literary cipher (the name means
"house of Elohim (God)"). The book is a composed witness, in the same way that a
parable is a composed witness. The truth it is telling is not the same
kind of truth that 1 Maccabees is telling. Read it as the kind of truth
it is.

Second, Judith stands inside a long tradition of widow-narratives in the
covenant scriptures. Tamar in Genesis 38, Ruth in the book of Ruth, the
widow of Zarephath in 1 Kings 17, the widow with the two mites in Mark
12 and Luke 21 — the covenant scriptures honor widows in a way that the
surrounding ancient Near Eastern cultures did not. Judith is a widow who
acts. She is not waiting passively. She prays, she fasts, she plans, she
executes, and she sings the victory afterward. The book sits in that
tradition, and the awakening reader who has been retrained by inherited
Christianity to think of women in the scriptures as primarily passive
should note where Judith fits and what she does.

Third — and this is where the awakening reader needs to be careful —
Judith is a book with a hard edge. The Assyrian general is killed by
deception. Judith lies to him about her intentions. She lies about her
people. She uses her body and her beauty as tactical assets. The book is
honest about the moral complexity of what she does, and the awakening
reader who comes from a tradition that prefers tidy moral lessons may
feel uncomfortable with what Judith does. The 1234 filter applies here.
The Torah's commandments against false witness, against bearing the
sword unnecessarily, against the misuse of beauty — the commandments do
not vanish when the Apocrypha tells a story in which a faithful daughter
of the covenant uses such things to break a siege. The Apocrypha is
showing what was done. It is not commanding the reader to do likewise.
The covenant standard is the Torah, and the Torah is the lens through
which the reader evaluates Judith's actions.

That said: the book's overall theological frame — that Yahuah (God)
delivers His people through the unlikely instrument of a faithful widow,
against the boasting of a foreign empire, in answer to prayer and
fasting — is a frame the prophets honored. Judith is a witness to a
generation that believed Yahuah (God) had not abandoned them under
foreign occupation. The book has been read in the Yahudi (Jewish)
festival of Hanukkah for centuries as a companion to the Maccabean
stories, even though Judith is not a Maccabean book proper. The festival
reading captures the spiritual logic of the book: that the deliverance
of Yahuah (God)'s people comes through unlikely instruments and against
impossible odds, in answer to the prayer of the faithful.

Read Judith as the composed narrative it is. Hold the historical
inaccuracies lightly; they are not the point. Hold Judith's deception
against the standard of the Torah; the book does not require you to
endorse what she did. Hear the closing hymn (Judith 16) as a prayer of
the second-temple imagination, and let it form your own prayer life as a
remnant believer in a foreign empire of your own.

Judith — Chapter 1

  1 In the twelfth year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor, who reigned in
  Nineve, the great city; in the days of Arphaxad, which reigned over
  the Medes in Ecbatane, 2 And built in Ecbatane walls round about of
  stones hewn three cubits broad and six cubits long, and made the
  height of the wall seventy cubits, and the breadth thereof fifty
  cubits: 3 And set the towers thereof upon the gates of it an hundred
  cubits high, and the breadth thereof in the foundation threescore
  cubits: 4 And he made the gates thereof, even gates that were raised
  to the height of seventy cubits, and the breadth of them was forty
  cubits, for the going forth of his mighty armies, and for the setting
  in array of his footmen: 5 Even in those days king Nabuchodonosor made
  war with king Arphaxad in the great plain, which is the plain in the
  borders of Ragau.

  6 And there came to him all they that dwelt in the hill country, and
  all that dwelt by Euphrates, and Tigris and Hydaspes, and the plain of
  Arioch the king of the Elymeans, and very many nations of the sons of
  Chelod, assembled themselves to the battle. 7 Then Nabuchodonosor king
  of the Assyrians sent to all that dwelt in Persia, and to all that
  dwelt westward, and to those that dwelt in Cilicia, and Damascus, and
  Libanus, and Antilibanus, and to all that dwelt upon the sea coast, 8
  And to those among the nations that were of Carmel, and Galaad, and
  the higher Galilee, and the great plain of Esdrelom, 9 And to all that
  were in Samaria and the cities thereof, and beyond Jordan to
  Jerusalem, and Betane, and Chelus, and Kades, and the river of Egypt,
  and Taphnes, and Ramesse, and all the land of Gesem, 10 Until you come
  beyond Tanis and Memphis, and to all the inhabitants of Egypt, until
  you come to the borders of Ethiopia.

  11 But all the inhabitants of the land made light of the commandment
  of Nabuchodonosor king of the Assyrians, neither went they with him to
  the battle; for they were not afraid of him: yes, he was before them
  as one man, and they sent away his ambassadors from them without
  effect, and with disgrace. 12 Therefore Nabuchodonosor was very angry
  with all this country, and sware by his throne and kingdom, that he
  would surely be avenged upon all those coasts of Cilicia, and
  Damascus, and Syria, and that he would slay with the sword all the
  inhabitants of the land of Moab, and the children of Ammon, and all
  Judea, and all that were in Egypt, till you come to the borders of the
  two seas. 13 Then he marched in battle array with his power against
  king Arphaxad in the seventeenth year, and he prevailed in his battle:
  for he overthrew all the power of Arphaxad, and all his horsemen, and
  all his chariots, 14 And became lord of his cities, and came to
  Ecbatane, and took the towers, and spoiled the streets thereof, and
  turned the beauty thereof into shame. 15 He took also Arphaxad in the
  mountains of Ragau, and struck him through with his darts, and
  destroyed him utterly that day.

  16 So he returned afterward to Nineve, both he and all his company of
  sundry nations being a very great multitude of men of war, and there
  he took his ease, and banqueted, both he and his army, an hundred and
  twenty days.

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter sets the scene with a historical conflation.
Nebuchadnezzar is named as the king of the Assyrians ruling from Nineveh
— a deliberate composite, since Nebuchadnezzar was the king of the
Babylonians ruling from Babylon, and Nineveh had already been destroyed
before he came to power. The book opens with a war between
Nebuchadnezzar and Arphaxad, king of the Medes — a war that is also
historically composite, since Arphaxad is not named in any other source.

Two things matter.

First, the opening's historical composite is a marker that the book is
not a straight chronicle. The reader who has been retrained on the
framework of this Series should mark the genre at the door. Judith is
composed witness — a narrative whose historical references are drawn
from the Babylonian and Assyrian periods, set in a city (Bethulia) whose
name does not appear on any map and which is best understood as a
literary cipher meaning "house of Elohim (God)." The truth Judith is telling is
not the same kind of truth that 1 Maccabees is telling. Read it as the
kind of truth it is.

Second, the chapter's portrait of Nebuchadnezzar is the second-temple
imagination's archetype of the imperial tyrant. He is grandiose,
militaristic, and unwilling to accept any rival. He summons the nations
to join his campaign. When they refuse, he vows revenge against them.
The framework of this Series, which holds that the imperial powers
across history have repeatedly attempted to absorb the covenant people
into their political-religious systems, finds in 2 Esdras 11's eagle and
in Judith 1's Nebuchadnezzar the second-temple archetypes of the same
imperial pattern.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 17:1–6; 2 Kings 25:1–21; Daniel 1:1–21; Daniel
2:31–45; Ezekiel 26:7–14; Jeremiah 25:8–14; Revelation 13:1–18;
Revelation 17:1–18.

Judith — Chapter 2

  1 And in the eighteenth year, the two and twentieth day of the first
  month, there was talk in the house of Nabuchodonosor king of the
  Assyrians that he should, as he said, avenge himself on all the earth.
  2 So he called to him all his officers, and all his nobles, and
  communicated with them his secret counsel, and concluded the
  afflicting of the whole earth out of his own mouth. 3 Then they
  decreed to destroy all flesh, that did not obey the commandment of his
  mouth. 4 And when he had ended his counsel, Nabuchodonosor king of the
  Assyrians called Holofernes the chief captain of his army, which was
  next to him, and said to him. 5 Thus says the great king, the lord of
  the whole earth, Behold, you shall go forth from my presence, and take
  with you men that trust in their own strength, of footmen an hundred
  and twenty thousand; and the number of horses with their riders twelve
  thousand.

  6 And you shall go against all the west country, because they
  disobeyed my commandment. 7 And you shall declare to that they prepare
  for me earth and water: for I will go forth in my wrath against them
  and will cover the whole face of the earth with the feet of my army,
  and I will give them for a spoil to them: 8 So that their slain shall
  fill their valleys and brooks and the river shall be filled with their
  dead, till it overflow: 9 And I will lead them captives to the utmost
  parts of all the earth. 10 You therefore shall go forth. and take
  beforehand for me all their coasts: and if they will yield themselves
  to you, you shall reserve them for me till the day of their
  punishment.

  11 But concerning them that rebel, let not your eye spare them; but
  put them to the slaughter, and spoil them wherever you go. 12 For as I
  live, and by the power of my kingdom, whatsoever I have spoken, that
  will I do by my hand. 13 And take you heed that you transgress none of
  the commandments of your lord, but accomplish them fully, as I have
  commanded you, and defer not to do them. 14 Then Holofernes went forth
  from the presence of his lord, and called all the governors and
  captains, and the officers of the army of Assur; 15 And he mustered
  the chosen men for the battle, as his lord had commanded him, to an
  hundred and twenty thousand, and twelve thousand archers on horseback;

  16 And he ranged them, as a great army is ordered for the war. 17 And
  he took camels and asses for their carriages, a very great number; and
  sheep and oxen and goats without number for their provision: 18 And
  plenty of victual for every man of the army, and very much gold and
  silver out of the king’s house. 19 Then he went forth and all his
  power to go before king Nabuchodonosor in the voyage, and to cover all
  the face of the earth westward with their chariots, and horsemen, and
  their chosen footmen. 20 A great number also sundry countries came
  with them like locusts, and like the sand of the earth: for the
  multitude was without number.

  21 And they went forth of Nineve three days’ journey toward the plain
  of Bectileth, and pitched from Bectileth near the mountain which is at
  the left hand of the upper Cilicia. 22 Then he took all his army, his
  footmen, and horsemen and chariots, and went from thence into the hill
  country; 23 And destroyed Phud and Lud, and spoiled all the children
  of Rasses, and the children of Yashar'el (Israel), which were toward
  the wilderness at the south of the land of the Chellians. 24 Then he
  went over Euphrates, and went through Mesopotamia, and destroyed all
  the high cities that were upon the river Arbonai, till you come to the
  sea. 25 And he took the borders of Cilicia, and killed all that
  resisted him, and came to the borders of Japheth, which were toward
  the south, over against Arabia.

  26 He compassed also all the children of Madian, and burned up their
  tabernacles, and spoiled their sheepcotes. 27 Then he went down into
  the plain of Damascus in the time of wheat harvest, and burnt up all
  their fields, and destroyed their flocks and herds, also he spoiled
  their cities, and utterly wasted their countries, and struck all their
  young men with the edge of the sword. 28 Therefore the fear and dread
  of him fell upon all the inhabitants of the sea coasts, which were in
  Sidon and Tyrus, and them that dwelt in Sur and Ocina, and all that
  dwelt in Jemnaan; and they that dwelt in Azotus and Ascalon feared him
  greatly.

⸻

Commentary

Nebuchadnezzar appoints Holofernes as the chief captain of his army,
with orders to subjugate the nations of the west — Cilicia, Damascus,
Lebanon, the Mediterranean coast, including Yahudah (Judah). The chapter
describes the great army assembled.

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's emphasis on the size and power of Holofernes' army
(verses 5–20) is the second-temple narrative setup for the impossibility
of the deliverance to come.

The canonical pattern of Yahuah (God)-delivers-against-overwhelming-odds
is repeated through scripture. 2 Kings 6:16, Elisha to his servant when
the Aramean army surrounded the city: Fear not: for they that be with us
are more than they that be with them. 2 Chronicles 32:7–8, Hezekiah to
his people against Sennacherib: Be strong and courageous, be not afraid
nor dismayed for the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude that is
with him: for there be more with us than with him: With him is an arm of
flesh; but with us is Yahuah (God) our Elohim (God) to help us, and to fight our
battles. 1 Samuel 14:6, Jonathan against the Philistine garrison: there
is no restraint to Yahuah (God) to save by many or by few.

The framework of this Series, which holds that Yahuah (God) delivers His
own through unlikely instruments against impossible odds, finds in
Judith 2 the second-temple version of the David-and-Goliath setup. The
disproportion between the army and the deliverer (a widow) is
established at the outset.

Second, the western nations' submission to Holofernes (verses 21–28) —
including the Phoenician cities and the coastal regions — sets up the
contrast with Yahudah (Judah). While the surrounding peoples submit,
Yahudah (Judah) will not. The framework of this Series, which holds that
the covenant separateness is what produces the imperial hostility, finds
in Judith 2 the second-temple foreshadowing of why the assault on
Yahudah (Judah) will be so determined.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 18:13–37; Isaiah 36:1–22; Daniel 3:1–7; Esther
1:1–3:15; Romans 12:1–2; James 4:4.

Judith — Chapter 3

  1 So they sent ambassadors to him to treat of peace, saying, 2 Behold,
  we the servants of Nabuchodonosor the great king lie before you; use
  us as shall be good in your sight. 3 Behold, our houses, and all our
  places, and all our fields of wheat, and flocks, and herds, and all
  the lodges of our tents lie before your face; use them as it pleaseth
  you. 4 Behold, even our cities and the inhabitants thereof are your
  servants; come and deal with them as seemeth good to you. 5 So the men
  came to Holofernes, and declared to him after this manner.

  6 Then came he down toward the sea coast, both he and his army, and
  set garrisons in the high cities, and took out of them chosen men for
  aid. 7 So they and all the country round about received them with
  garlands, with dances, and with timbrels. 8 Yet he did cast down their
  frontiers, and cut down their groves: for he had decreed to destroy
  all the gods of the land, that all nations should worship
  Nabuchodonosor only, and that all tongues and tribes should call upon
  him as god. 9 Also he came over against Esdraelon near to Judea, over
  against the great strait of Judea. 10 And he pitched between Geba and
  Scythopolis, and there he tarried a whole month, that he might gather
  together all the carriages of his army.

⸻

Commentary

The western nations send embassies of submission to Holofernes. They
bring tribute. They open their gates. They tear down their high places —
at Holofernes' command — and acknowledge Nebuchadnezzar as the only god.
Holofernes accepts their submission and continues his march.

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's detail that the submitting nations tear down their
own high places at Holofernes' command (verse 8) is the second-temple
commentary on the cultural assimilation that the imperial powers demand.
The empire does not merely tax the conquered nations; it requires them
to abandon their own religious systems and acknowledge the imperial god.
The framework of this Series, which holds that the contemporary cultural
pressure on the awakening reader to assimilate into the prevailing
religious-political consensus is a recurring historical pattern, finds
in Judith 3 the second-temple articulation of the pattern. The imperial
powers have always required cultic submission as the price of political
peace.

Second, the chapter's emphasis on Nebuchadnezzar's claim to be the only
god (verse 8) is the apocalyptic exaggeration of the imperial-cult
pattern. The framework of this Series, which holds that the abolition of
the worship of Yahuah (God) and the substitution of the worship of the
empire is one of the perennial temptations of the powers, finds in
Judith 3 the second-temple identification of that temptation in its
starkest form.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 18:25; 2 Kings 19:18; Isaiah 36:18–20; Daniel
3:1–7; Daniel 6:1–9; Revelation 13:11–18; Revelation 17:1–18.

Judith — Chapter 4

  1 Now the children of Yashar'el (Israel), that dwelt in Judea, heard
  all that Holofernes the chief captain of Nabuchodonosor king of the
  Assyrians had done to the nations, and after what manner he had
  spoiled all their temples, and brought them to nought. 2 Therefore
  they were exceedingly afraid of him, and were troubled for Jerusalem,
  and for the temple of Yahuah (God), their Elohim (God): 3 For they
  were newly returned from the captivity, and all the people of Judea
  were lately gathered together: and the vessels, and the altar, and the
  house, were sanctified after the profanation. 4 Therefore they sent
  into all the coasts of Samaria, and the villages and to Bethoron, and
  Belmen, and Jericho, and to Choba, and Esora, and to the valley of
  Salem: 5 And possessed themselves beforehand of all the tops of the
  high mountains, and fortified the villages that were in them, and laid
  up victuals for the provision of war: for their fields were of late
  reaped.

  6 Also Joacim the high priest, which was in those days in Jerusalem,
  wrote to them that dwelt in Bethulia, and Betomestham, which is over
  against Esdraelon toward the open country, near to Dothaim, 7 Charging
  them to keep the passages of the hill country: for by them there was
  an entrance into Judea, and it was easy to stop them that would come
  up, because the passage was straight, for two men at the most. 8 And
  the children of Yashar'el (Israel) did as Joacim the high priest had
  commanded them, with the ancients of all the people of Yashar'el
  (Israel), which dwelt at Jerusalem. 9 Then every man of Yashar'el
  (Israel) cried to Yahuah (God) with great fervency, and with great
  vehemency did they humble their souls: 10 Both they, and their wives
  and their children, and their cattle, and every stranger and hireling,
  and their servants bought with money, put sackcloth upon their loins.

  11 Thus every man and women, and the little children, and the
  inhabitants of Jerusalem, fell before the temple, and cast ashes upon
  their heads, and spread out their sackcloth before the face of Yahuah
  (God): also they put sackcloth about the altar, 12 And cried to Yahuah
  (God) of Yashar'el (Israel) all with one consent earnestly, that he
  would not give their children for a prey, and their wives for a spoil,
  and the cities of their inheritance to destruction, and the sanctuary
  to profanation and reproach, and for the nations to rejoice at. 13 So
  Yahuah (God) heard their prayers, and looked upon their afflictions:
  for the people fasted many days in all Judea and Jerusalem before the
  sanctuary of Yahuah (God) Almighty. 14 And Joacim the high priest, and
  all the priests that stood before Yahuah (God), and they which
  ministered to Yahuah (God), had their loins girt with sackcloth, and
  offered the daily burnt offerings, with the vows and free gifts of the
  people, 15 And had ashes on their mitres, and cried to Yahuah (God)
  with all their power, that he would look upon all the house of
  Yashar'el (Israel) graciously.

⸻

Commentary

The Israelites in the land hear of Holofernes' approach. Joakim the high
priest writes to the inhabitants of Bethulia and Betomesthaim,
instructing them to seize the mountain passes and prevent the Assyrian
army from reaching Jerusalem. The people fast, pray, and humble
themselves.

Three things matter.

First, the chapter's emphasis on the people's fasting and prayer (verses
9–15) is the proper covenant response to imperial threat.

The canonical anchor for the fast-and-pray-before-the-engagement pattern
is concrete. 2 Chronicles 20:3–4, Jehoshaphat: Jehoshaphat feared, and
set himself to seek Yahuah (God), and proclaimed a fast throughout all
Yahudah (Judah). And Yahudah (Judah) gathered themselves together, to
ask help of Yahuah (God): even out of all the cities of Yahudah (Judah)
they came to seek Yahuah (God). Joel 2:12–17, the prophetic call:
Therefore also now, says Yahuah (God), turn you even to me with all your
heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning... Sanctify
a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the people, sanctify the
congregation, assemble the elders, gather the children... Let the
priests, the ministers of Yahuah (God), weep between the porch and the
altar. Esther 4:16, before the queen approaches the king: Go, gather
together all the Yahudim (Jews) that are present in Shushan, and fast
for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and
my maidens will fast likewise. Ezra 8:21–23, before the journey from
Babylon: Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we
might afflict ourselves before our Elohim (God), to seek of him a right way for
us, and for our little ones... So we fasted and besought our Elohim (God) for
this: and he was entreated of us.

The framework of this Series, which honors the awakening community's
response to crisis as fasting, prayer, and humility before Yahuah (God),
finds in Judith 4 the second-temple model. Jehoshaphat, Joel's call,
Esther, Ezra, and the Bethulia community of Judith all walk the same
pattern: fast first, pray, humble the body, then act under Yahuah
(God)'s direction.

Second, the high priest's coordinating the defense — securing the
passes, sending messengers, organizing the resistance — is the
second-temple example of covenant-community leadership in time of
crisis. The framework of this Series, which honors the awakening
community's leaders organizing the protection of the household under the
covenant, finds in Judith 4 the model of such leadership.

Third, the chapter records that "even the strangers, and the hirelings,
and they that were bought with their money" (verse 10) joined in the
fasting and prayer. The household of Yashar'el (Israel) included those
who had attached themselves to the covenant community as sojourners. The
framework of this Series, on the question of the strangers and
sojourners, holds that Isaiah 56's strangers are the paternal blood
remnant living as foreigners in the lands of their scattering — not
converts from unrelated peoples. The Judith 4 sojourners and hirelings
are not necessarily the Isaiah 56 figures; they are the day-to-day mixed
company that lived in proximity to the Israelite community in any
second-temple village. They joined in the fast as a recognition of the
political-spiritual crisis. Read it as that.

Cross-references: 2 Chronicles 20:1–30; Joel 2:12–17; Esther 4:13–17;
Daniel 9:1–19; Acts 13:1–3; Isaiah 56:1–8.

Judith — Chapter 5

  1 Then was it declared to Holofernes, the chief captain of the army of
  Assur, that the children of Yashar'el (Israel) had prepared for war,
  and had shut up the passages of the hill country, and had fortified
  all the tops of the high hills and had laid impediments in the
  champaign countries: 2 With which he was very angry, and called all
  the princes of Moab, and the captains of Ammon, and all the governors
  of the sea coast, 3 And he said to them, Tell me now, you sons of
  Chanaan, who this people is, that dwells in the hill country, and what
  are the cities that they inhabit, and what is the multitude of their
  army, and in which is their power and strength, and what king is set
  over them, or captain of their army; 4 And why have they determined
  not to come and meet me, more than all the inhabitants of the west. 5
  Then said Achior, the captain of all the sons of Ammon, Let my lord
  now hear a word from the mouth of your servant, and I will declare to
  you the truth concerning this people, which dwells near you, and
  inhabiteth the hill countries: and there shall no lie come out of the
  mouth of your servant.

  6 This people are descended of the Chaldeans: 7 And they sojourned
  heretofore in Mesopotamia, because they would not follow the gods of
  their fathers, which were in the land of Chaldea. 8 For they left the
  way of their ancestors, and worshipped Yahuah (God) of heaven, the
  Yahuah (God) whom they knew: so they cast them out from the face of
  their gods, and they fled into Mesopotamia, and sojourned there many
  days. 9 Then their Elohim (God) commanded them to depart from the
  place where they sojourned, and to go into the land of Chanaan: where
  they dwelt, and were increased with gold and silver, and with very
  much cattle. 10 But when a famine covered all the land of Chanaan,
  they went down into Egypt, and sojourned there, while they were
  nourished, and became there a great multitude, so that one could not
  number their nation.

  11 Therefore the king of Egypt rose up against them, and dealt
  subtilly with them, and brought them low with labouring in brick, and
  made them slaves. 12 Then they cried to their Elohim (God), and he
  struck all the land of Egypt with incurable plagues: so the Egyptians
  cast them out of their sight. 13 And Yahuah (God) dried the Red sea
  before them, 14 And brought them to mount Sina, and Cades-Barne, and
  cast forth all that dwelt in the wilderness. 15 So they dwelt in the
  land of the Amorites, and they destroyed by their strength all them of
  Esebon, and passing over Jordan they possessed all the hill country.

  16 And they cast forth before them the Chanaanite, the Pherezite, the
  Jebusite, and the Sychemite, and all the Gergesites, and they dwelt in
  that country many days. 17 And while they sinned not before their
  Elohim (God), they prospered, because Yahuah (God) that hates
  iniquity was with them. 18 But when they departed from the way which
  he appointed them, they were destroyed in many battles very sore, and
  were led captives into a land that was not their’s, and the temple of
  their Elohim (God) was cast to the ground, and their cities were taken
  by the enemies. 19 But now are they returned to their Elohim (God),
  and are come up from the places where they were scattered, and have
  possessed Jerusalem, where their sanctuary is, and are seated in the
  hill country; for it was desolate. 20 Now therefore, my lord and
  governor, if there be any error against this people, and they sin
  against their Elohim (God), let us consider that this shall be their
  ruin, and let us go up, and we shall overcome them.

  21 But if there be no iniquity in their nation, let my lord now pass
  by, lest their Elohim (God) defend them, and their Elohim (God) be for
  them, and we become a reproach before all the world. 22 And when
  Achior had finished these sayings, all the people standing round about
  the tent murmured, and the chief men of Holofernes, and all that dwelt
  by the sea side, and in Moab, spoke that he should kill him. 23 For,
  say they, we will not be afraid of the face of the children of
  Yashar'el (Israel): for, lo, it is a people that have no strength nor
  power for a strong battle 24 Now therefore, lord Holofernes, we will
  go up, and they shall be a prey to be devoured of all your army.

⸻

Commentary

Holofernes asks his commanders about the Israelites: who are they, where
do they live, what are their gods, why are they resisting? Achior, the
captain of the Ammonites, gives a sustained speech (verses 5–21)
