awakening reader should hear the line whole. Miriam at the Red Sea
(Exodus 15:20–21): And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took
a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with
timbrels and with dances. And Miriam answered them, Sing to Yahuah
(God), for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider has he
thrown into the sea. Deborah after Sisera (Judges 5:1–3): Then sang
Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day, saying, Praise Yahuah
(God) for the avenging of Yashar'el (Israel), when the people willingly
offered themselves... I will sing praise to Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el
(Israel). Hannah after Samuel's birth (1 Samuel 2:1–5): My heart
rejoices in Yahuah (God), my horn is exalted in Yahuah (God)... He
raises up the poor out of the dust, and lifts up the beggar from the
dunghill, to set them among princes. Mary in the Magnificat (Luke
1:46–55): My soul does magnify the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in
Elohim (God) my Saviour. For he has regarded the low estate of his handmaiden...
He has put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low
degree. Judith at the close of her own hymn echoes the same
architecture: Yahuah (God) is praised, the proud have been brought down,
the low has been exalted, the deliverance has come through the unlikely
instrument.

The four women's hymns name one consistent pattern. The mighty are
brought down. The lowly are lifted up. Yahuah (God) receives the credit.
The covenant community sings. The tradition runs from Miriam to Mary,
with Judith standing inside it as one of the second-temple voices that
kept the tradition alive between the canonical witnesses. Mary's
Magnificat would not have been a strange song to her contemporaries; it
was the song the covenant women had been singing for fifteen hundred
years. Judith 16 is one of the witnesses in the line.

Second, verse 17's "fire and worms" eschatology is the second-temple
imagery the apostolic writings will pick up. Mark 9:48 cites Isaiah
66:24 ("their worm dies not, and the fire is not quenched"); the
framework of this Series, which holds that the judgment of the wicked is
eternal in its consequence and that the second-temple imagination
articulated that consequence under the imagery of fire and worms, finds
in Judith 16 the second-temple precedent.

Third, the closing notes (verses 18–25) describe Judith's later life.
She refuses remarriage. She frees her favorite maid. She gives
Holofernes' goods to the temple. She lives quietly in Bethulia until her
death at age one hundred five. She is mourned for seven days. The
framework of this Series, which honors the awakening leader's quiet
later life as much as the dramatic moments of action, finds in Judith's
closing the second-temple model of how the awakening leader returns to
ordinary covenant life after the deliverance has been accomplished.
Judith does not become a permanent celebrity. She returns to her
household. She lives faithfully. She dies in peace. The pattern is the
framework's pattern: do the work Yahuah (God) has appointed, return to
the covenant household, finish the days in faithfulness.

Cross-references: Exodus 15:1–21; Judges 5:1–31; 1 Samuel 2:1–10; Luke
1:46–55; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:43–48; Hebrews 11:32–40; Revelation
14:9–11; Revelation 15:1–4.

The Rest of Esther — Introduction

The book of Esther in the Hebrew canon is a remarkable book, and one of
its most remarked-upon features is what it does not contain: the divine
name. Yahuah (God) is never explicitly named in the Hebrew Esther. Not
once. Some of the rabbis read the absence as deliberate — a sign that
the deliverance of the Yahudim (Jews) from Haman's plot was a hidden
providence — and the book has been held up in that tradition as the
great witness to Yahuah (God)'s hidden hand in history.

The Greek translators of Esther in the Septuagint were not comfortable
with the absence. Around the second century BCE, six additional passages
— totaling 107 verses — were composed in Greek and inserted into the
book at six locations, restoring the divine name explicitly, adding
prayers from Mordecai and Esther, fleshing out Mordecai's dream and its
interpretation, providing the full text of the king's decrees, and
giving the book the explicit theological frame that the Hebrew text
leaves implicit. These additions are what the King James translators set
under the title "The Rest of the Chapters of the Book of Esther which
are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Chaldee" — a careful title
that honors the textual tradition: these passages are not in the Hebrew.
They are in the Greek. They are second-temple theological amplifications
of an originally Hebrew book.

For the awakening reader, the additions to Esther matter in three ways.

First, they show the second-temple community's discomfort with the
absence of the divine name in Esther, and they show that community's
response: explicit prayer, explicit naming, explicit theological
framing. The additions read like commentary stitched into the text. They
do not change the plot of Esther; they amplify its piety. The reader who
has been retrained on the framework of this Series will recognize what
the second-temple translators were doing — they were applying a piety
lens that they could not bear to leave off the text — and the reader can
decide for themselves whether the additions help or distract.

Second, the prayer of Mordecai (in Addition C) and the prayer of Esther
(also in Addition C) are substantive devotional pieces. They are
second-temple prayers. They reflect what a faithful Yahudi (Jew) under
Persian-era pressure prayed — for deliverance, for the preservation of
the covenant people, for the destruction of the enemies of Yahuah (God).
They are not Torah. They are not prophetic. But they are the prayer-life
of the second-temple covenant community, and they have value in showing
the awakening reader how faithful Israelites prayed when their king was
not their own and their lives were under threat.

Third, Mordecai's dream and its interpretation (in Additions A and F)
are an apocalyptic frame around the book. The dream contains images —
the two great dragons, the small fountain that becomes a great river,
the sun rising and the lowly being exalted — that have apocalyptic
resonance with later second-temple imagery. The frame turns the Esther
story from a court intrigue into a small apocalyptic episode in the
larger story of Yahuah (God)'s preservation of His people. The awakening
reader, holding the framework of scattered Yashar'el (Israel) and the
long restoration timeline, will recognize the frame as the second-temple
imagination making sense of survival under foreign powers.

A note on order. The 1611 King James translators presented the Greek
additions to Esther as a continuous text, in the order the additions
occur in the Greek manuscripts (rather than scattered through the Hebrew
text where they would be inserted). This produces a slightly
disorienting reading experience: the chapters do not flow as a story but
as a sequence of inserted passages with brief contextual headers. Read
each addition for what it is — a discrete second-temple amplification —
and let the original Hebrew Esther in your Old Testament carry the plot.
The Rest of Esther fills in the edges of a book whose center is in the
canonical Old Testament.

The Greek additions to Esther are presented in the King James tradition
as six chapters numbered 10:4 through 16:24, following the close of the
Hebrew Esther. The chapters do not flow as a continuous story; they are
six separate insertions arranged in the order they occur in the Greek
manuscript. The commentary below addresses each insertion as the
discrete amplification it is.

The Rest of Esther — Chapter 10

  4 Then Mardocheus said, Yahuah (God) has done these things. 5 For I
  remember a dream which I saw concerning these matters, and nothing
  thereof has failed. 6 A little fountain became a river, and there was
  light, and the sun, and much water: this river is Esther, whom the
  king married, and made queen: 7 And the two dragons are I and Aman. 8
  And the nations were those that were assembled to destroy the name of
  the Yahudim (Jews):

  9 And my nation is this Yashar'el (Israel), which cried to Yahuah
  (God), and were saved: for Yahuah (God) has saved his people, and
  Yahuah (God) has delivered us from all those evils, and Yahuah (God)
  has wrought signs and great wonders, which have not been done among
  the Gentiles. 10 Therefore has he made two lots, one for the people of
  Yahuah (God), and another for all the Gentiles. 11 And these two lots
  came at the hour, and time, and day of judgment, before Yahuah (God)
  among all nations. 12 So Yahuah (God) remembered his people, and
  justified his inheritance. 13 Therefore those days shall be to them in
  the month Adar, the fourteenth and fifteenth day of the same month,
  with an assembly, and joy, and with gladness before Yahuah (God),
  according to the generations for ever among his people.

⸻

Commentary

The first addition (10:4–13 in the King James numbering) is Mordecai's
interpretation of his earlier dream — a dream that is recorded in the
second addition (chapter 11 below) but is interpreted here, after the
events of the canonical Esther have already unfolded. The
narrative-frame inversion is intentional: the Greek manuscripts present
the dream-interpretation as an epilogue, naming what the events of the
book had been the fulfillment of.

The interpretation identifies the two great dragons of the dream as
Mordecai and Haman, the small fountain that became a great river as
Esther, the two nations that fought as the lot of Yahuah (God) and the
lot of all the nations, and the day of darkness and light as the Feast
of Purim. The dream is the apocalyptic frame around the Esther story.

The framework of this Series finds three things in the addition.

First, the second-temple imagination has cast the Esther story as an
apocalyptic episode in the larger covenant history. The same nation that
survived Haman's plot is the nation that the prophets had named, the
nation Yahuah (God) had committed Himself to preserve, and the
dream-frame names that the survival was not accidental but was the
working out of the long covenant promise. The framework of this Series,
which holds that the survival of the covenant people across the
dispersion is the working out of the covenant's preservation of the
seed, finds the Greek addition agreeing with what the Hebrew Esther had
implied without saying.

Second, the explicit naming of the lot of Yahuah (God) versus the lot of
all the nations places the Esther story in the framework of Deuteronomy
32:8–9, where Yahuah (God) divided the inheritance of the nations and
took Jacob for His own portion. The Greek addition is reading the Esther
story through the same covenant-portion framework the Torah established.
The reader who has been retrained on the framework of this Series will
recognize the move: the second-temple imagination understood the
covenant lot of Yahuah (God) as a specific people, and saw the
deliverance from Haman as the preservation of that lot.

Third, the dream-frame closes with Mordecai's blessing of Yahuah (God)
for what He has done. The proper response to the deliverance is praise.
The framework of this Series, which honors the covenant identification
and the praise that flows from seeing what Yahuah (God) has done, finds
the close of the addition operating in the right shape.

Cross-references: Esther 9:18–32; Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Tobit 13:1–18;
Daniel 7:1–28; 2 Esdras 11:1–46; Isaiah 41:8–10; Romans 11:1–6.

The Rest of Esther — Chapter 11

  1 In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemeus and Cleopatra,
  Dositheus, who said he was a priest and Levite, and Ptolemeus his son,
  brought this epistle of Phurim, which they said was the same, and that
  Lysimachus the son of Ptolemeus, that was in Jerusalem, had
  interpreted it. [PLACED IN THE GREEK BEFORE CHAP. 1.1 OF THE HEBREW] 2
  In the second year of the reign of Artexerxes the great, in the first
  day of the month Nisan, Mardocheus the son of Jairus, the son of
  Semei, the son of Cisai, of the tribe of Benjamin, had a dream; 3 Who
  was a Yahudi (Jew), and dwelt in the city of Susa, a great man, being
  a servitor in the king’s court. 4 He was also one of the captives,
  which Nabuchodonosor the king of Babylon carried from Jerusalem with
  Jechonias king of Judea; and this was his dream: 5 Behold a noise of a
  tumult, with thunder, and earthquakes, and uproar in the land:

  6 And, behold, two great dragons came forth ready to fight, and their
  cry was great. 7 And at their cry all nations were prepared to battle,
  that they might fight against the righteous people. 8 And lo a day of
  darkness and obscurity, tribulation and anguish, affliction and great
  uproar, upon earth. 9 And the whole righteous nation was troubled,
  fearing their own evils, and were ready to perish. 10 Then they cried
  to Yahuah (God), and upon their cry, as it were from a little
  fountain, was made a great flood, even much water.

  11 The light and the sun rose up, and the lowly were exalted, and
  devoured the glorious. 12 Now when Mardocheus, who had seen this
  dream, and what Yahuah (God) had determined to do, was awake, he bare
  this dream in mind, and until night by all means was desirous to know
  it.

⸻

Commentary

The second addition (11:2–12 in the King James numbering, but read as
the prologue) is Mordecai's dream itself — a dream he had two years
before the events of Esther. The dream contains images that have
apocalyptic resonance: noises and tumults, thunders, earthquakes, two
great dragons, a small fountain that became a great river, the sun
rising, and the lowly being exalted while the honorable were trampled.

The genre is apocalyptic. The vocabulary is the vocabulary of Daniel 7
and of the contemporaneous apocalyptic literature. The framework of this
Series, on the question of apocalyptic visions, holds that the witness
of such visions is to be heard as witness, tested by the canonical
scriptures, and not legislated into doctrine beyond what the canonical
scriptures establish. Mordecai's dream is preserved as part of the
second-temple memory of the Esther story. It is not a separate prophetic
oracle that the awakening reader is asked to integrate into the
canonical timeline. It is a literary framing that the second-temple
Greek tradition added to the Hebrew Esther.

Read the dream for what it shows. The two great dragons — Mordecai and
Haman — are the two principles fighting over the lot of Yahuah (God).
The small fountain becoming a great river — Esther — is the seemingly
small instrument Yahuah (God) uses to preserve the covenant people. The
sun rising at the end is the deliverance Yahuah (God) brings. The
pattern is the pattern the Hebrew Esther shows: Yahuah (God) preserves
the covenant people through unlikely instruments against impossible
odds.

Cross-references: Daniel 7:1–28; Daniel 8:1–27; Daniel 10:1–21; Esther
1:1–22; Joel 2:28–32; Acts 2:16–21.

The Rest of Esther — Chapter 12

  1 And Mardocheus took his rest in the court with Gabatha and Tharra,
  the two eunuchs of the king, and keepers of the palace. 2 And he heard
  their devices, and searched out their purposes, and learned that they
  were about to lay hands upon Artexerxes the king; and so he certified
  the king of them. 3 Then the king examined the two eunuchs, and after
  that they had confessed it, they were strangled. 4 And the king made a
  record of these things, and Mardocheus also wrote thereof. 5 So the
  king commanded, Mardocheus to serve in the court, and for this he
  rewarded him.

  6 Howbeit Aman the son of Amadathus the Agagite, who was in great
  honour with the king, sought to molest Mardocheus and his people
  because of the two eunuchs of the king.

⸻

Commentary

The third addition (12:1–6 in the King James numbering) elaborates
Mordecai's discovery of the plot of the two eunuchs Bigthan and Teresh,
which is briefly recorded in Esther 2:21–23. The Greek expands the
moment: Mordecai learns of the plot, reports it to the king, the eunuchs
are executed, and Mordecai is given a reward — and Haman, already
secretly plotting against Mordecai because of Mordecai's refusal to bow,
takes the reward as further provocation.

The framework finds two things.

First, the elaboration shows the second-temple desire to fill in the
political and emotional motivations the Hebrew text leaves implicit. The
Hebrew Esther is a model of compressed narrative; the Greek additions
lean toward expansion. The contemporary reader who has been trained on
inflationary commentary may find the Greek expansion familiar; the
awakening reader retraining toward the discipline of letting the Hebrew
text say what it says will note the contrast.

Second, the chapter reveals Haman's character as one whose hatred of
Mordecai precedes any specific act of provocation. Haman is identified
as a son of Belial in pattern: the corrupted seed within the
covenant-adjacent court, identifiable by his works. The framework of
this Series recognizes the type. Haman is not a Persian peculiarity. He
is the recurring figure of the corrupted within the covenant or
covenant-adjacent community. The pattern continues from Cain through
Eli's sons through Haman through Judas Iscariot, and the framework holds
the type as one of the consistent witnesses of the scriptures.

Cross-references: Esther 2:21–23; Esther 3:1–6; Genesis 3:14–15; 1
Samuel 2:12; Psalm 109:1–31; Proverbs 26:24–28; Matthew 26:14–16.

The Rest of Esther — Chapter 13

  1 The copy of the letters was this: The great king Artexerxes writeth
  these things to the princes and governours that are under him from
  India to Ethiopia in an hundred and seven and twenty provinces. 2
  After that I became lord over many nations and had dominion over the
  whole world, not lifted up with presumption of my authority, but
  carrying myself always with equity and mildness, I purposed to settle
  my subjects continually in a quiet life, and making my kingdom
  peaceable, and open for passage to the utmost coasts, to renew peace,
  which is desired of all men. 3 Now when I asked my counsellors how
  this might be brought to pass, Aman, that excelled in wisdom among us,
  and was approved for his constant good will and steadfast fidelity,
  and had the honour of the second place in the kingdom, 4 Declared to
  us, that in all nations throughout the world there was scattered a
  certain malicious people, that had laws contrary to all nations, and
  continually despised the commandments of kings, so as the uniting of
  our kingdoms, honourably intended by us cannot go forward. 5 Seeing
  then we understand that this people alone is continually in opposition
  to all men, differing in the strange manner of their laws, and evil
  affected to our state, working all the mischief they can that our
  kingdom may not be firmly established:

  6 Therefore have we commanded, that all they that are signified in
  writing to you by Aman, who is ordained over the affairs, and is next
  to us, shall all, with their wives and children, be utterly destroyed
  by the sword of their enemies, without all mercy and pity, the
  fourteenth day of the twelfth month Adar of this present year: 7 That
  they, who of old and now also are malicious, may in one day with
  violence go into the grave, and so ever hereafter cause our affairs to
  be well settled, and without trouble. [PLACED IN THE GREEK AFTER CHAP.
  4.17 OF THE HEBREW] 8 Then Mardocheus thought upon all the works of
  Yahuah (God), and made his prayer to him, 9 Saying, O Yahuah (God),
  Yahuah (God), the King Almighty: for the whole world is in your power,
  and if you have appointed to save Yashar'el (Israel), there is no man
  that can gainsay you: 10 For you have made heaven and earth, and all
  the wondrous things under the heaven.

  11 You are Yahuah (God) of all things, and there is no man that can
  resist you, which are Yahuah (God). 12 You know all things, and you
  know, Yahuah (God), that it was neither in contempt nor pride, nor for
  any desire of glory, that I did not bow down to proud Aman. 13 For I
  could have been content with good will for the salvation of Yashar'el
  (Israel) to kiss the soles of his feet. 14 But I did this, that I
  might not prefer the glory of man above the glory of Yahuah (God):
  neither will I worship any but you, O Yahuah (God), neither will I do
  it in pride. 15 And now, O Yahuah (God) and King, spare your people:
  for their eyes are upon us to bring us to nought; yes, they desire to
  destroy the inheritance, that has been yours from the beginning.

  16 Despise not the portion, which you have delivered out of Egypt for
  your own self. 17 Hear my prayer, and be merciful to your inheritance:
  turn our sorrow into joy, that we may live, O Yahuah (God), and praise
  your name: and destroy not the mouths of them that praise you, O
  Yahuah (God). 18 All Yashar'el (Israel) in like manner cried most
  earnestly to Yahuah (God), because their death was before their eyes.

⸻

Commentary

The fourth addition (13:1–7 and 13:8–18 in the King James numbering)
gives the full text of two documents. First, the decree of Haman against
the Yahudim (Jews), supposedly issued in the name of the king,
justifying the proposed extermination on the grounds that the Yahudim
(Jews) are a separate people whose laws are different from those of
every other nation and who therefore threaten the unity of the empire.
Second, Mordecai's prayer to Yahuah (God), pleading for deliverance.

The framework finds three things.

First, the decree of Haman in 13:1–7 is a remarkable document for the
awakening reader. The accusation against the Yahudim (Jews) is precisely
the accusation the framework of this Series has named: that the covenant
people, by keeping the Torah, are a separate people, whose laws differ
from the surrounding nations, and whose separateness is treated by the
political and cultural powers as a threat. The decree of Haman is the
original draft of every imperial decree against the covenant people that
has been issued in the centuries since. The empire — Persian, Roman,
Byzantine, medieval European, modern Western — has consistently accused
the covenant people of being too separate, too distinct, too unwilling
to assimilate. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
covenant people are by Torah a separate people, finds in Haman's decree
the clearest articulation of why the empires of the world have always
been hostile to that separateness. The Torah produces a separate people.
The empire wants assimilation. The hatred of Haman is the hatred of
every empire that has wanted the covenant people to be like all the
nations.

The framework's caveat: the awakening reader walking out of inherited
Christianity should not weaponize Haman's decree as a charter for Yahudi
(Jew)-hatred or Zionist-rhetoric of any direction. The framework of this
Series rejects all three common positions: Yahudi (Jew)-hatred is wrong,
theological Zionism is wrong, and "those aren't real Yahudim (Jews)" is
wrong. The decree of Haman is what it is — an empire's hatred of the
covenant separateness — and the contemporary reader's response is to
honor the covenant separateness in his or her own life, not to develop
political theories from second-temple imperial decrees.

Second, Mordecai's prayer in 13:8–18 is one of the great
covenant-recognition prayers of the second-temple corpus. Mordecai names
Yahuah (God) as the maker of all things, the one who gave Yashar'el
(Israel) as His inheritance, the one who is owed the worship that
Mordecai had refused to give to Haman. He explicitly names that he
refused to bow to Haman not out of pride or contempt but because he
would not give to a man the glory due only to Yahuah (God). The
framework of this Series, which holds that the covenant people honor
Yahuah (God) alone and bow to no man as a god, finds in Mordecai's
prayer the proper articulation of what his refusal was about.

Third, Mordecai's appeal to the covenant — that Yahuah (God) has chosen
Yashar'el (Israel) for His inheritance — is the pattern of every
covenant-based prayer in the second-temple corpus.

Deuteronomy 32:8–9 is the canonical anchor: When the most High divided
to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he
set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of
Yashar'el (Israel). For Yahuah (God)'s portion is his people; Jacob is
the lot of his inheritance. Deuteronomy 7:6 — For you are an holy people
unto Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God): Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God) has chosen you to be a
special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of
the earth. Psalm 33:12 — Blessed is the nation whose Elohim (God) is Yahuah
(God); and the people whom he has chosen for his own inheritance. Psalm
135:4 — For Yahuah (God) has chosen Jacob unto himself, and Yashar'el
(Israel) for his peculiar treasure. 1 Peter 2:9 brings the same
vocabulary into apostolic frame: But you are a chosen generation, a
royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people.

The basis is not Mordecai's worth. The basis is the covenant. The
framework of this Series, which has retrained the awakening reader to
pray on the basis of the covenant rather than on the basis of the
supplicant's worth, finds in Mordecai's prayer the right shape. The
framework's bloodline-remnant claim — that Jacob is Yahuah (God)'s named
lot of inheritance, His peculiar treasure — is articulated in Mordecai's
prayer in continuity with the canonical line.

Cross-references: Exodus 20:1–6; Deuteronomy 7:6–11; Deuteronomy 14:1–2;
Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Esther 3:1–15; Daniel 3:8–18; Psalm 33:12; Romans
9:1–5.

The Rest of Esther — Chapter 14

  1 Queen Esther also, being in fear of death, resorted to Yahuah (God):
  2 And laid away her glorious apparel, and put on the garments of
  anguish and mourning: and instead of precious ointments, she covered
  her head with ashes and dung, and she humbled her body greatly, and
  all the places of her joy she filled with her torn hair. 3 And she
  prayed to Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), saying, O my Elohim
  (God), you only art our King: help me, desolate woman, which have no
  helper but you: 4 For my danger is in my hand. 5 From my youth up I
  have heard in the tribe of my family that you, O Yahuah (God), tookest
  Yashar'el (Israel) from among all people, and our fathers from all
  their predecessors, for a perpetual inheritance, and you have
  performed whatsoever you did promise them.

  6 And now we have sinned before you: therefore have you given us into
  the hands of our enemies, 7 Because we worshipped their gods: O Yahuah
  (God), you are righteous. 8 Nevertheless it satisfies them not, that
  we are in bitter captivity: but they have stricken hands with their
  idols, 9 That they will abolish the thing that you with your mouth
  have ordained, and destroy your inheritance, and stop the mouth of
  them that praise you, and quench the glory of your house, and of your
  altar, 10 And open the mouths of the heathen to set forth the praises
  of the idols, and to magnify a fleshly king for ever.

  11 O Yahuah (God), give not your sceptre to them that be nothing, and
  let them not laugh at our fall; but turn their device upon themselves,
  and make him an example, that has begun this against us. 12 Remember,
  O Yahuah (God), make thyself known in time of our affliction, and give
  me boldness, O King of the nations, and Yahuah (God) of all power. 13
  Give me eloquent speech in my mouth before the lion: turn his heart to
  hate him that fighteth against us, that there may be an end of him,
  and of all that are likeminded to him: 14 But deliver us with yours
  hand, and help me that am desolate, and which have no other help but
  you. 15 You know all things, O Yahuah (God); you know that I hate the
  glory of the unrighteous, and abhor the bed of the uncircumcised, and
  of all the heathen.

  16 You know my necessity: for I abhor the sign of my high estate,
  which is upon my head in the days in which I shew myself, and that I
  abhor it as a menstruous rag, and that I wear it not when I am private
  by myself. 17 And that yours handmaid has not eaten at Aman’s table,
  and that I have not greatly esteemed the king’s feast, nor drunk the
  wine of the drink offerings. 18 Neither had yours handmaid any joy
  since the day that I was brought hither to this present, but in you, O
  Yahuah (God) of Abraham. 19 O you mighty Yahuah (God) above all, hear
  the voice of the forlorn and deliver us out of the hands of the
  mischievous, and deliver me out of my fear.

⸻

Commentary

The fifth addition (14:1–19 in the King James numbering) is the prayer
of Esther before she goes uninvited into the king's presence. The
narrative sets up the moment: Esther fasts three days, removes her royal
garments, puts on the garments of mourning, and prays.

Esther's prayer is one of the most spiritually concentrated prayers in
the apocryphal corpus. Three things matter.

First, Esther's prayer names the covenant by appeal to the patriarchs. O
my Lord, you only are our king: help me, desolate woman, who has no
helper but you. For my danger is in mine hand. From my youth up I have
heard in the tribe of my family that you, O Lord, took Yashar'el
(Israel) from among all people, and our fathers from among all their
predecessors, for a perpetual inheritance, and you have done for them as
you have promised. The basis is the covenant. The covenant is named by
appeal to the fathers. The covenant inheritance is named as perpetual.

Read this against the canonical-prayer line. Hezekiah in 2 Kings
19:15–19 / Isaiah 37:15–20 — the king is facing Sennacherib's siege of
Jerusalem, takes the threatening letter into the temple, spreads it
before Yahuah (God), and prays: O Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel),
which dwells between the cherubims, you are the Elohim (God), even you alone, of
all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made heaven and earth. Solomon
in 1 Kings 8:23 dedicating the temple: Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el
(Israel), there is no Elohim (God) like you, in heaven above, or on earth
beneath, who keeps covenant and mercy with your servants that walk
before you with all their heart. Daniel 9:4: O Lord, the great and
dreadful Elohim (God), keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and
to them that keep his commandments. Hannah in 1 Samuel 2:2: There is
none holy as Yahuah (God): for there is none beside you: neither is
there any rock like our Elohim (God). Five supplicants — Hezekiah, Solomon,
Daniel, Hannah, Esther — open their prayers with the same architecture:
Yahuah (God) alone is Elohim (God), covenant is the basis, the supplicant pleads
on what Yahuah (God) has already promised. The framework holds Esther's
prayer in this canonical line. The basis is not Esther's worth. The
basis is the covenant.

Esther's I have heard in the tribe of my family is also worth marking.
The covenant memory was transmitted through the family, by the fathers
and mothers, to the daughter. Esther has the prayer she now prays
because her family taught her the covenant from her youth up.
Deuteronomy 6:6–7 commanded this: And these words, which I command you
this day, shall be in your heart: and you shall teach them diligently to
your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and
when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
The teaching that Deuteronomy commanded is the teaching Esther's family
delivered. The result, decades later in the Persian court, is a queen
who can pray a covenant prayer when her life and the life of her people
depend on it. The framework reads this as the second-temple confirmation
of what the Torah commanded: teach the children, and the teaching
becomes the prayer when the day of crisis comes. Susanna in Babylon
prayed a covenant prayer. Daniel in Babylon prayed a covenant prayer.
Esther in Persia prays a covenant prayer. The covenant household
produces covenant supplicants in every generation where the teaching is
preserved.

Second, Esther's confession (verse 6–11) acknowledges that the calamity
of the present moment is not unjust. And now, we have sinned before you:
therefore have you given us into the hands of our enemies, because we
worshiped their gods. O Lord, you are righteous. The covenant frame is
intact. The exile and the present persecution are the consequence of the
covenant having been broken by the people. Yahuah (God) is righteous.
Esther is not asking for relief from a punishment she does not deserve;
she is asking for mercy on a people who deserve what they are receiving.

The architecture is identical to Daniel 9:5–7 (We have sinned, and have
committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by
departing from your precepts and from your judgments... O Lord,
righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of faces, as at this
day) and to Nehemiah 9:33 (Howbeit you are just in all that is brought
upon us; for you have done right, but we have done wickedly). The
pattern across the post-exilic prayer-tradition is consistent: the
supplicant confesses that the people sinned, names Yahuah (God) as
righteous, and pleads for mercy on the basis of Yahuah (God)'s covenant
rather than the people's deserving. The framework of this Series, which
holds that the curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell because the people walked
out from under the covenant and that the awakening reader confesses the
inheritance of lies (Jeremiah 16:19) rather than blaming the Father,
finds in Esther's prayer the same right confession Daniel and the
post-exilic community had also prayed.

Third, Esther's commitment to refuse the unclean things she has been
compelled to participate in by her position as queen (verses 15–18)
shows the Torah-observant heart. She has been forced to eat at Haman's
table; she has been forced to drink the wine of the king's libations;
she has been forced to bear the diadem of pride that her position
demands. She names that she abhors all of these and asks Yahuah (God) to
remember that she has not voluntarily desecrated her witness.

The pattern parallels Daniel 1:8 (Daniel purposed in his heart that he
would not defile himself) and Tobit 1:10–11 (I kept myself from eating)
— the covenant person under imperial-court conditions refusing the
unclean things even when the position would have made the eating easy.
The framework of this Series, which honors the awakening reader's
struggle to keep the Torah under cultural conditions that work against
keeping it, finds in Esther a witness: the heart can remain undesecrated
even when the body has been compelled into circumstances the heart did
not choose.

Cross-references: Genesis 12:1–3; Genesis 17:1–8; Exodus 19:4–6;
Deuteronomy 28:36–46; Esther 4:13–17; Daniel 1:8–17; Daniel 3:16–18;
Psalm 51:10–13; Acts 5:29.

The Rest of Esther — Chapter 15

  1 And upon the third day, when she had ended her prayers, she laid
  away her mourning garments, and put on her glorious apparel. 2 And
  being gloriously adorned, after she had called upon Yahuah (God), who
  is the beholder and saviour of all things, she took two maids with
  her: 3 And upon the one she leaned, as carrying herself daintily; 4
  And the other followed, bearing up her train. 5 And she was ruddy
  through the perfection of her beauty, and her countenance was cheerful
  and very amiable: but her heart was in anguish for fear.

  6 Then having passed through all the doors, she stood before the king,
  who sat upon his royal throne, and was clothed with all his robes of
  majesty, all glittering with gold and precious stones; and he was very
  dreadful. 7 Then lifting up his countenance that shone with majesty,
  he looked very fiercely upon her: and the queen fell down, and was
  pale, and fainted, and bowed herself upon the head of the maid that
  went before her. 8 Then Yahuah (God) changed the spirit of the king
  into mildness, who in a fear leaped from his throne, and took her in
  his arms, till she came to herself again, and comforted her with
  loving words and said to her, 9 Esther, what is the matter? I am your
  brother, be of good cheer: 10 You shall not die, though our
  commandment be general: come near.

  11 And so he held up his golden sceptre, and laid it upon her neck, 12
  And embraced her, and said, Speak to me. 13 Then said she to him, I
  saw you, my lord, as an angel of Yahuah (God), and my heart was
  troubled for fear of your majesty. 14 For wonderful art you, lord, and
  your countenance is full of grace. 15 And as she was speaking, she
  fell down for faintness.

  16 Then the king was troubled, and all his servants comforted her.

⸻

Commentary

The sixth addition begins with the dramatization of Esther's approach to
the king (15:1–16). The Hebrew Esther 5:1–2 records the approach in two
verses; the Greek expands it considerably. Esther dresses in royal
garments, takes two maids with her, leans on one for support, calls on
Yahuah (God) silently, faints in fear at the king's expression, and is
raised up by the king who has been moved by Yahuah (God) to receive her
with mercy. The king embraces her, comforts her, and assures her of the
privileges of the royal favor.

The framework finds two things.

First, the addition makes explicit what the Hebrew leaves implicit: that
Yahuah (God) was the unseen actor in the king's softening. The Hebrew
Esther famously never names Yahuah (God); the Greek addition restores
the naming. The awakening reader can hold both: that the Hebrew text
honors the hidden providence of Yahuah (God) by not naming Him, and that
the Greek addition honors the manifest providence of Yahuah (God) by
naming Him. Both are true to what happened. The framework of this Series
does not require choosing between the two.

Second, the dramatization of Esther's fear and faintness is honest
narrative. She is not a triumphant heroine striding into the king's
presence. She is a queen leaning on her maids, calling on Yahuah (God)
silently, and fainting at the king's first expression. The framework of
this Series, which honors the cost the awakening reader pays in the
moments of testing, finds in Esther's faintness the witness of someone
who walked into the testing on the strength of the covenant rather than
on the strength of her own confidence.

Cross-references: Esther 4:13–17; Esther 5:1–2; Proverbs 21:1; Hebrews
11:35; 1 Peter 3:1–6.

The Rest of Esther — Chapter 16

  1 The great king Artexerxes to the princes and governors of an hundred
  and seven and twenty provinces from India to Ethiopia, and to all our
  faithful subjects, greeting. 2 Many, the more often they are honoured
  with the great bounty of their gracious princes, the more proud they
  are waxen, 3 And endeavour to hurt not our subjects only, but not
  being able to bear abundance, do take in hand to practise also against
  those that do them good: 4 And take not only thankfulness away from
  among men, but also lifted up with the glorious words of lewd persons,
  that were never good, they think to escape the justice of Yahuah
  (God), that seeth all things and hates evil. 5 Often also fair speech
  of those, that are put in trust to manage their friends’ affairs, has
  caused many that are in authority to be partakers of innocent blood,
  and has enwrapped them in remediless calamities:

  6 Beguiling with the falsehood and deceit of their lewd disposition
  the innocency and goodness of princes. 7 Now you may see this, as we
  have declared, not so much by ancient histories, as you may, if you
  search what has been wickedly done of late through the pestilent
  behaviour of them that are unworthily placed in authority. 8 And we
  must take care for the time to come, that our kingdom may be quiet and
  peaceable for all men, 9 Both by changing our purposes, and always
  judging things that are evident with more equal proceeding. 10 For
  Aman, a Macedonian, the son of Amadatha, being indeed a stranger from
  the Persian blood, and far distant from our goodness, and as a
  stranger received of us,

  11 Had so far forth obtained the favour that we shew toward every
  nation, as that he was called our father, and was continually honoured
  of all the next person to the king. 12 But he, not bearing his great
  dignity, went about to deprive us of our kingdom and life: 13 Having
  by manifold and cunning deceits sought of us the destruction, as well
  of Mardocheus, who saved our life, and continually procured our good,
  as also of blameless Esther, partaker of our kingdom, with their whole
  nation. 14 For by these means he thought, finding us destitute of
  friends, to have translated the kingdom of the Persians to the
  Macedonians. 15 But we find that the Yahudim (Jews), whom this wicked
  wretch has delivered to utter destruction, are no evildoers, but live
  by most just laws:

  16 And that they be children of the most high and most mighty, living
  Yahuah (God), who has ordered the kingdom both to us and to our
  progenitors in the most excellent manner. 17 Wherefore you shall do
  well not to put in execution the letters sent to you by Aman the son
  of Amadatha. 18 For he that was the worker of these things, is hanged
  at the gates of Susa with all his family: Yahuah (God), who ruleth all
  things, speedily rendering vengeance to him according to his deserts.
  19 Therefore you shall publish the copy of this letter in all places,
  that the Yahudim (Jews) may freely live after their own laws. 20 And
  you shall aid them, that even the same day, being the thirteenth day
  of the twelfth month Adar, they may be avenged on them, who in the
  time of their affliction shall set upon them.

  21 For Almighty Yahuah (God) has turned to joy to them the day, in
  which the chosen people should have perished. 22 You shall therefore
  among your solemn feasts keep it an high day with all feasting: 23
  That both now and hereafter there may be safety to us and the well
  affected Persians; but to those which do conspire against us a
  memorial of destruction. 24 Therefore every city and country
  whatsoever, which shall not do according to these things, shall be
  destroyed without mercy with fire and sword, and shall be made not
  only unpassable for men, but also most hateful to wild beasts and
  fowls for ever.

⸻

Commentary

The closing addition (16:1–24 in the King James numbering) gives the
full text of the king's counter-decree, repealing Haman's plan,
reversing the orders, naming Haman as the one who had abused the king's
authority, and authorizing the Yahudim (Jews) to defend themselves on
the appointed day.

The framework finds two things.

First, the counter-decree establishes by formal imperial document what
the Hebrew narrative establishes by action. The empire that had been the
instrument of the covenant people's near-destruction has now been turned
to be the instrument of their preservation. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the powers of the world are in the Father's
hand and can be turned by Him to His purposes, finds in the
counter-decree the formal evidence of that turning.

Second, the counter-decree's language about the Yahudim (Jews) — that
they are children of the most high Yahuah (God), that their laws are
righteous, that they live according to laws which are very excellent —
represents the Greek addition's effort to repair the public reputation
of the covenant people that Haman's decree had attacked. The framework
of this Series, which acknowledges that the covenant people will at
times be vindicated publicly by the very imperial powers that had
earlier attacked them, finds in the counter-decree the second-temple
memory of one such vindication. The vindication is real. The vindication
is not the final restoration. The final restoration is the gathering of
the scattered seed under the reign of the Messiah, and no imperial
counter-decree can substitute for that. But intermediate vindications
are real, and the awakening reader can recognize them where they appear.

The closing of the addition reaffirms the establishment of the Feast of
Purim and seals the entire Esther tradition — Hebrew and Greek — under
the witness of the covenant community's preservation by Yahuah (God).

Cross-references: Esther 8:1–17; Proverbs 21:1; Daniel 2:21; Romans
13:1–7; Revelation 19:11–21.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Introduction

The Wisdom of Solomon is the most intellectually accomplished book in
the Apocrypha. Composed in Greek, almost certainly in Alexandria, Egypt,
sometime between 100 BCE and 30 CE, it is a sustained meditation on
wisdom — what wisdom is, how wisdom relates to Yahuah (God), what wisdom
does in the lives of the righteous, and what its absence does in the
lives of the wicked. The book is anonymous; it is not by Solomon. The
pseudonym was a literary convention of the period: the wisdom tradition
was associated with Solomon, and Greek-speaking diaspora Yahudim (Jews)
who wrote wisdom literature did so under his banner the way Greek
philosophical schools wrote under Plato or Aristotle. The book belongs
to the late second-temple Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish) wisdom tradition,
and it is the highest literary achievement of that tradition.

For the awakening reader, three threads in this book reach all the way
through to the New Testament and matter in particular ways.

First, the personification of Wisdom in chapters 7–9. The author writes
of Wisdom as a kind of hypostatic figure who stands beside Yahuah (God),
who orders all things, who pervades the universe, who teaches the
righteous, who guided Yashar'el (Israel) through her history. This
personification is not the Trinity. It is not Greek philosophy stitched
onto Hebrew theology. It is the second-temple recognition that there is
something about Yahuah (God)'s wisdom that has its own coherence, its
own action, its own presence in the world — and the New Testament
writers, particularly the writer of Hebrews, the writer of Colossians
(Colossians 1:15–20), and the writer of John's Gospel (John 1), pick up
this same vocabulary and apply it to Yahusha (Jesus). The Wisdom of
Solomon is not the source of New Testament Christology. The source is
the Word — the Formed One who walked with the patriarchs, who spoke from
the burning bush, who led Yashar'el (Israel) through the wilderness. But
the Wisdom of Solomon is the literary precedent for the vocabulary the
New Testament uses, and the reader who has been trained by inherited
Christianity to think of the Word as a New Testament invention will be
quietly corrected by reading this book.

Second, the meditation on death and immortality in chapters 1–6. The
book opens with a sustained argument that the souls of the righteous are
in the hand of Yahuah (God), that their hope is full of immortality, and
that the wicked have no portion in the world to come. The vocabulary is
shared with the Pharisaic tradition — the second-temple community out of
which the apostles came — and it stands behind the resurrection theology
of the New Testament. The reader who has been retrained on the framework
of this Series will note that the wisdom-of-Solomon view of death,
judgment, resurrection, and the world to come is consistent with the
Pharisaic mainstream the apostles inherited and not consistent with the
Sadducean denial of resurrection that Yahusha rebuked in Matthew 22.

Third, the historical retrospective in chapters 10–19, which retells the
Exodus and the wilderness through the lens of wisdom. The author argues
that wisdom guided Adam, preserved Noah, called Abraham, sustained
Joseph, led Moses, and brought Yashar'el (Israel) through the sea. This
is the same argument the New Testament writers make when they trace the
Word through the patriarchs. The Wisdom of Solomon does not separate
Wisdom from Yahuah (God); it presents Wisdom as the active, formed
presence of Yahuah (God) in the world. The reader who has been working
through this Series's understanding of the Formless and the Formed — the
Father as the formless source, the Word as the Formed expression who
walked with Yashar'el (Israel) in the Old Testament — will recognize
Wisdom-of-Solomon's "Wisdom" as one of the second-temple vocabularies
for the same Formed presence the New Testament names as the Word.

The Wisdom of Solomon is dense. It will reward slow reading. The first
six chapters are the sharpest meditation on death, judgment, and the
world to come anywhere in the Apocrypha. Chapters 7–9 are the
wisdom-personification material that opens up the New Testament
Christology. Chapters 10–19 are the wisdom-retelling of the Exodus that
shows what the second-temple imagination saw when it read the Torah
backward through the lens of wisdom. Take the book in pieces, and let
each piece settle.

A word about the book before the chapter-by-chapter begins. The Wisdom
of Solomon was composed in Greek by an unknown Hellenistic Yahudi
(Jewish) author in Alexandria, most likely in the first century BCE. The
author writes in the persona of Solomon — making the book one of the
great pseudepigraphic exercises in the second-temple tradition — but he
is writing for the Yahudi (Jewish) diaspora community in Egypt,
surrounded by Greek philosophy and pagan religion, addressing the
questions that community was actually wrestling with: the persecution of
the righteous, the prosperity of the wicked, the absurdity of the
surrounding idolatry, and the deeper philosophical-theological questions
about the nature of wisdom itself. The book is one of the bridges
between the second-temple wisdom tradition and the apostolic letters.
Paul had read it. The writer of Hebrews had read it. The writer of
John's prologue was operating in the same vocabulary it had already
established. The reader who has not read the Wisdom of Solomon has
missed one of the most direct second-temple precedents for the New
Testament's Christology, eschatology, and polemic against idolatry.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 1

  1 Love righteousness, you that be judges of the earth: think of Yahuah
  (God) with a good (heart,) and in simplicity of heart seek him. 2 For
  he will be found of them that tempt him not; and sheweth himself to
  such as do not distrust him. 3 For froward thoughts separate from
  Yahuah (God): and his power, when it is tried, reproveth the unwise. 4
  For into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter; nor dwell in the
  body that is subject to sin. 5 For the holy spirit of discipline will
  flee deceit, and remove from thoughts that are without understanding,
  and will not abide when unrighteousness comes in.

  6 For wisdom is a loving spirit; and will not acquit a blasphemer of
  his words: for Yahuah (God) is witness of his reins, and a true
  beholder of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue. 7 For the Spirit of
  Yahuah (God) filleth the world: and that which containeth all things
  has knowledge of the voice. 8 Therefore he that speaks unrighteous
  things cannot be hid: neither shall vengeance, when it punishes, pass
  by him. 9 For inquisition shall be made into the counsels of the
  ungodly: and the sound of his words shall come to Yahuah (God) for the
  manifestation of his wicked deeds. 10 For the ear of jealousy heareth
  all things: and the noise of murmurings is not hid.

  11 Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain
  your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that
  shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul. 12
  Seek not death in the error of your life: and pull not upon yourselves
  destruction with the works of your hands. 13 For Yahuah (God) made not
  death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living. 14
  For he created all things, that they might have their being: and the
  generations of the world were healthful; and there is no poison of
  destruction in them, nor the kingdom of death upon the earth: 15 (For
  righteousness is immortal:)

  16 But ungodly men with their works and words called it to them: for
  when they thought to have it their friend, they consumed to nought,
  and made a covenant with it, because they are worthy to take part with
  it.

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter calls the rulers of the earth — and by extension all
who would seek wisdom — to seek Yahuah (God) in singleness of heart. The
opening verse names the Father directly: Love righteousness, you that be
judges of the earth: think of the Lord with a good (heart), and in
simplicity of heart seek him.

Three things matter.

First, the chapter's argument that wisdom will not enter into a
malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sin (verse 4), is
consistent with the framework of this Series. The 1234 of Truth (1 John
2:3–4) — that he that says he knows Yahuah (God) and keeps not His
commandments is a liar — is operating in the second-temple wisdom
theology of this passage. Wisdom and the keeping of the Torah are not
separable. The body that has been given over to sin cannot host the
wisdom of Yahuah (God). The framework does not allow the inherited
Christian split between "spiritual wisdom" and "ritual obedience." The
wisdom of Yahuah (God) dwells in the body that has been brought under
the discipline of His Torah.

The verse on the body matters for the awakening reader who has been
catechized by the popular contemporary spirituality into thinking of the
body as separable from the spiritual life. The Wisdom of Solomon will
not allow the separation. The body subject to sin cannot host wisdom.
The body brought under the Torah's discipline can. This is consistent
with Romans 12:1 (the offering of the body as a living sacrifice) and 1
Corinthians 6:19–20 (the body as the temple of the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy
Spirit)). The Hebrew anthropology — and the second-temple anthropology,
and the apostolic anthropology — does not split the human into a
"spiritual self" that matters and a "physical self" that does not. The
whole person, body and soul together, is the unit of covenant
relationship. The framework holds Wisdom 1:4 plainly. What the body
does, the spirit answers for.

Second, the chapter develops the argument that envy, murmuring, secret
speech, and false witness destroy the wisdom of Yahuah (God) (verses
6–11). The point is the same as Proverbs 6:16–19 and is consistent
across the Hebrew wisdom tradition. The framework finds nothing
controversial here.

Third, the closing of the chapter (verses 12–16) addresses the question
of death. Seek not death in the error of your life: and pull not upon
yourselves destruction with the works of your hands. For Elohim (God) made not
death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living. For he
created all things, that they might have their being: and the
generations of the world were healthful; and there is no poison of
destruction in them, nor the kingdom of death upon the earth: (for
righteousness is immortal): but ungodly men with their works and words
called it to them: for when they thought to have it their friend, they
consumed to nought, and made a covenant with it, because they are worthy
to take part with it. The framework of this Series, which holds that
death entered the world through the fall and that the appointed reign of
the Messiah will undo death's hold on the covenant people, finds in
Wisdom 1 the second-temple voice already articulating that theology.

The phrase they... made a covenant with [death] (verse 16) is one of the
second-temple voices echoing Isaiah 28:15: We have made a covenant with
death, and with hell are we at agreement. The covenant with death is the
covenant of those who have rejected Yahuah (God)'s covenant and have
aligned themselves with the adversary's purposes. The framework of this
Series reads this as a second-temple anchor for what the awakening
reader sees in the contemporary cultural situation: the surrounding
culture has, in many of its major institutions and ideologies, made a
covenant with death — abortion as policy, euthanasia as compassion, war
for profit, the pharmakeia of the medical-industrial complex, the
multitude of ways the surrounding cultures kill the living and call it
good. The covenant with death is real. The framework names it without
flinching, and the awakening reader is being called out from under it.

Cross-references: Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 6:16–19; Genesis 2:16–17;
Genesis 3:1–24; Romans 5:12–21; Romans 8:18–25; 1 Corinthians 15:21–28;
Revelation 21:4; Isaiah 28:15; Romans 12:1; 1 Corinthians 6:19–20.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 2

  1 For the ungodly said, reasoning with themselves, but not aright, Our
  life is short and tedious, and in the death of a man there is no
  remedy: neither was there any man known to have returned from the
  grave. 2 For we are born at all adventure: and we shall be hereafter
  as though we had never been: for the breath in our nostrils is as
  smoke, and a little spark in the moving of our heart: 3 Which being
  extinguished, our body shall be turned into ashes, and our spirit
  shall vanish as the soft air, 4 And our name shall be forgotten in
  time, and no man shall have our works in remembrance, and our life
  shall pass away as the trace of a cloud, and shall be dispersed as a
  mist, that is driven away with the beams of the sun, and overcome with
  the heat thereof. 5 For our time is a very shadow that passeth away;
  and after our end there is no returning: for it is fast sealed, so
  that no man comes again.

  6 Come on therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present:
  and let us speedily use the creatures like as in youth. 7 Let us fill
  ourselves with costly wine and ointments: and let no flower of the
  spring pass by us: 8 Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds, before they
  be withered: 9 Let none of us go without his part of our
  voluptuousness: let us leave tokens of our joyfulness in every place:
  for this is our portion, and our lot is this. 10 Let us oppress the
  poor righteous man, let us not spare the widow, nor reverence the
  ancient gray hairs of the aged.

  11 Let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is feeble is
  found to be nothing worth. 12 Therefore let us lie in wait for the
  righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to
  our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth
  to our infamy the transgressings of our education. 13 He professeth to
  have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of
  Yahuah (God). 14 He was made to reprove our thoughts. 15 He is
  grievous to us even to behold: for his life is not like other men’s,
  his ways are of another fashion.

  16 We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways
  as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed,
  and makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father. 17 Let us see if
  his words be true: and let us prove what shall happen in the end of
  him. 18 For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help
  him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies. 19 Let us examine
  him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness,
  and prove his patience. 20 Let us condemn him with a shameful death:
  for by his own saying he shall be respected.

  21 Such things they did imagine, and were deceived: for their own
  wickedness has blinded them. 22 As for the mysteries of Yahuah (God),
  they knew them not: neither hoped they for the wages of righteousness,
  nor discerned a reward for blameless souls. 23 For Yahuah (God)
  created man to be immortal, and made him to be an image of his own
  eternity. 24 Nevertheless through envy of the devil came death into
  the world: and they that do hold of his side do find it.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter records the reasoning of the wicked (verses 1–20) and the
answer of the wise (verses 21–24). The wicked reason that life is short,
that there is nothing after death, that pleasure should be seized while
it can be, and that the righteous should be opposed because their
righteousness is a rebuke. They plot against the just man, beat him,
condemn him, expose his patience, and try whether Yahuah (God) will
deliver him.

The framework of this Series finds two things.

First, verses 12–20 contain a passage that the early church read as a
prophecy of the persecution of Yahusha (Jesus). Therefore let us lie in
wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean
contrary to our doings: he upbraids us with our offending the law, and
objects to our infamy the transgressings of our education... He
professes to have the knowledge of Elohim (God): and he calls himself the child
of the Lord... For if the just man be the son of Elohim (God), he will help him,
and deliver him from the hand of his enemies. Let us examine him with
despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness, and prove his
patience. Let us condemn him with a shameful death. The parallels to the
Gospel narratives of the trial and crucifixion are striking. The
framework of this Series does not require treating this passage as
direct prophecy in the same sense as Isaiah 53. The passage is a
second-temple meditation on what the wicked do to the righteous, and
what the wicked did to Yahusha was the same pattern brought to its full
expression. The pattern was established in the second-temple
imagination. The Messiah walked into the pattern and bore it whole.

The pattern matters for the awakening reader. The wicked say of the
righteous, He upbraids us with our offending the law. The righteous
man's faithfulness to the Torah is itself a rebuke to those who have
abandoned it. This is the second-temple voice naming what the awakening
reader experiences in the contemporary religious culture. The
Torah-faithful walk is a quiet rebuke to the antinomian church and to
the cultural Christianity that has set the commandments aside. The
rebuke is not preached at the deceived; the rebuke is the existence of
the walk itself. The deceived see the walk and feel rebuked, and the
response — historically and presently — is often hostility. He calls
himself the child of the Lord. He professes to have the knowledge of
Elohim (God). The wicked of Wisdom 2 cannot stand the existence of the righteous
because the righteous existence indicts the wicked life. The
contemporary awakening reader will find that his existence inside his
former community produces this exact reaction. He has not preached at
them. He has merely begun to walk. And the walk itself becomes
intolerable to those who refuse to walk it. Wisdom 2 names what the
awakening reader feels but may not have had words for.

Second, verse 24 is one of the explicit second-temple identifications of
the source of death: Through envy of the devil came death into the
world: and they that do hold of his side do find it. The framework of
this Series, which holds that the fall introduced death into the world
and that the corrupt seed of the adversary continues to operate against
the covenant people, finds in this verse the second-temple naming of
what the Torah's narrative shows. The serpent introduced death. Those
who side with the serpent partake of the death.

The phrase they that do hold of his side do find it deserves slow
reading. The wicked are not merely victims of the original fall. They
are active partisans. They hold of the adversary's side. They side with
him. They participate in his work. The framework of this Series, which
holds that the sons of Belial are a real persistent seed-category and
not merely a behavioral abstraction (Eli's sons, Jezebel's prophets, the
corrupt judges of Susanna's chapter, the high priestly faction that
worked with the Romans against Yahusha) finds in Wisdom 2:24 the
second-temple naming of that partisan choice. The tares are not just the
unaware. They are the actively aligned. The framework holds the verse
plainly.

Cross-references: Genesis 3:1–24; Isaiah 53:1–12; Psalm 22:1–31; John
8:44; Romans 5:12; Hebrews 2:14–15; 1 John 3:8–12; Revelation 12:9; 1
Samuel 2:12; Matthew 13:24–43.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 3

  1 But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and
  there shall no torment touch them. 2 In the sight of the unwise they
  seemed to die: and their departure is taken for misery, 3 And their
  going from us to be utter destruction: but they are in peace. 4 For
  though they be punished in the sight of men, yet is their hope full of
  immortality. 5 And having been a little chastised, they shall be
  greatly rewarded: for Yahuah (God) proved them, and found them worthy
  for himself.

  6 As gold in the furnace has he tried them, and received them as a
  burnt offering. 7 And in the time of their visitation they shall
  shine, and run to and fro like sparks among the stubble. 8 They shall
  judge the nations, and have dominion over the people, and their Elohim
  (God) shall reign for ever. 9 They that put their trust in him shall
  understand the truth: and such as be faithful in love shall abide with
  him: for grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his
  elect. 10 But the ungodly shall be punished according to their own
  imaginations, which have neglected the righteous, and forsaken Yahuah
  (God).

  11 For whoso despiseth wisdom and nurture, he is miserable, and their
  hope is vain, their labours unfruitful, and their works unprofitable:
  12 Their wives are foolish, and their children wicked: 13 Their
  offspring is cursed. Wherefore blessed is the barren that is
  undefiled, which has not known the sinful bed: she shall have fruit in
  the visitation of souls. 14 And blessed is the eunuch, which with his
  hands has wrought no iniquity, nor imagined wicked things against
  Yahuah (God): for to him shall be given the special gift of faith, and
  an inheritance in the temple of Yahuah (God) more acceptable to his
  mind. 15 For glorious is the fruit of good labours: and the root of
  wisdom shall never fall away.

  16 As for the children of adulterers, they shall not come to their
  perfection, and the seed of an unrighteous bed shall be rooted out. 17
  For though they live long, yet shall they be nothing regarded: and
  their last age shall be without honour. 18 Or, if they die quickly,
  they have no hope, neither comfort in the day of trial. 19 For
  horrible is the end of the unrighteous generation.

⸻

Commentary

The famous opening: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of
Elohim (God), and there shall no torment touch them. In the sight of the unwise
they seemed to die: and their departure is taken for misery, and their
going from us to be utter destruction: but they are in peace. The
chapter continues with the consolation that the righteous who suffered
briefly were tested as gold in the furnace, that their reward is great,
that they will judge the nations and have dominion over the peoples in
the appointed reign, that Yahuah (God) will be their king for ever.

Three things matter.

First, the chapter's articulation of the intermediate state of the
righteous dead — the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Elohim (God) — is
consistent with the second-temple Pharisaic theology that the apostles
carried into the New Testament. The dead in Yahuah (God) are with Him.
The resurrection at the end of the age will reunite them with their
bodies (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18).

The intermediate-state vocabulary is anchored across the canonical
witness. Ecclesiastes 12:7 — Then shall the dust return to the earth as
it was: and the spirit shall return to Elohim (God) who gave it. Psalm 31:5 —
Into your hand I commit my spirit: you have redeemed me, O Yahuah (God)
of truth. Yahusha cites this on the cross (Luke 23:46). Stephen says the
same at his stoning (Acts 7:59). Psalm 49:15 — But Elohim (God) will redeem my
soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me. 2 Corinthians
5:8 — Paul names the apostolic understanding: we are confident, I say,
and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with
the Lord. Philippians 1:23 — having a desire to depart, and to be with
Messiah (Christ); which is far better. Revelation 6:9–10 — the souls
under the altar of those slain for the word: I saw under the altar the
souls of them that were slain for the word of Elohim (God), and for the testimony
which they held: and they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O
Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood on them that
dwell on the earth?

Wisdom 3:1 stands in this canonical line. The souls are in Yahuah
(God)'s hand; the souls are at rest; the souls are awaiting the
resurrection. The framework of this Series, which holds that there is
one judgment of the souls of the dead at the appointed time and that the
great white throne of Revelation 20 is the same arc as the seal of
Revelation 11:18 retold from a different angle, finds in Wisdom 3 the
second-temple intermediate-state theology that informed the apostolic
writings.

The framework's reading of the intermediate state, anchored on this
verse and on 2 Esdras 7:32 and on the apostolic letters, is precise. The
dead in Yahuah (God) are at rest in the chambers — held in His hand —
but they are not at the destination. They are awaiting the resurrection.
The destination is the appointed reign on the earth, with the refined
remnant, under the rule of the Messiah, in the new heavens and new
earth. The popular Christian "heaven when you die, forever, end of
story" reading erases the resurrection of the body, the appointed reign
on the earth, and the new heavens and new earth as the actual
destination. Wisdom 3:1 does not endorse that erasure. Wisdom 3:1 says
the souls are in Yahuah (God)'s hand — at rest, safe, untormented —
until the resurrection brings them out. The framework holds the
difference between the chamber and the destination as a real
distinction. The chamber is good. The destination is greater.

Second, verses 7–8 — And in the time of their visitation they shall
shine, and run to and fro like sparks among the stubble. They shall
judge the nations, and have dominion over the people, and their Lord
shall reign for ever — articulate the reign of the saints with the
Messiah that Revelation 20 names and that the framework of this Series
holds as the appointed reign on the earth with the refined remnant. The
Wisdom of Solomon 3 is the second-temple voice articulating that reign.

The "judge the nations" language is the framework's reign-with-Messiah
language, second-temple form. The refined remnant — the awakened seed of
the covenant — reigns with the Messiah, under him, in the appointed
time. They do not reign over him; they do not replace him. They
participate in his rule, as 1 Corinthians 6:2 articulates ("do you not
know that the saints shall judge the world?") and as Revelation 20:4–6
articulates ("and they lived and reigned with Messiah (Christ) a
thousand years"). The reign is on the earth. The reign is with the
bodily-resurrected remnant. The reign is appointed. The framework holds
it whole.

Third, the chapter's treatment of those who are cursed for being barren
or childless (verses 13–19) requires care. The argument is that the
chaste woman who is barren is more blessed than the woman who has had
children with the wicked, and that the eunuch who has done no iniquity
is more blessed than the man who has had children in adultery. The point
is theological, not pronatalist: that the legacy of the wicked is
destruction even when there are physical descendants, and that the
legacy of the righteous is preserved even when there are no physical
descendants. The framework does not endorse a culture of barrenness; the
framework endorses faithfulness, regardless of household circumstances.

The verse on the eunuch is especially worth pausing over for the
awakening reader. The verse anticipates Isaiah 56:3–5, where Yahuah
(God) promises the faithful eunuch a name in His house better than of
sons and daughters — an everlasting name that shall not be cut off. The
covenant value is not biological reproduction in itself. The covenant
value is faithfulness. The eunuch who fears Yahuah (God) is honored
before Yahuah (God); the man with twenty children who has been faithless
is not. This is consistent with the framework's reading of the
bloodline-remnant in a way that is sometimes missed by the contemporary
Hebrew roots reader who has flattened bloodline into a kind of
biological credentialism. The seed is the seed; the bloodline is real;
and yet within the seed, faithfulness is the test, not mere production
of offspring. Both can be true. Wisdom 3 holds them both.

Cross-references: Psalm 31:5; Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:1–3; Matthew
27:46; Luke 23:46; Acts 7:55–60; Romans 8:18–25; 1 Corinthians 6:2–3; 1
Thessalonians 4:13–18; Revelation 20:4–6; Isaiah 56:3–5; 2 Esdras 7:32.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 4

  1 Better it is to have no children, and to have virtue: for the
  memorial thereof is immortal: because it is known with Yahuah (God),
  and with men. 2 When it is present, men take example at it; and when
  it is gone, they desire it: it wears a crown, and triumpheth for ever,
  having gotten the victory, striving for undefiled rewards. 3 But the
  multiplying brood of the ungodly shall not thrive, nor take deep
  rooting from bastard slips, nor lay any fast foundation. 4 For though
  they flourish in branches for a time; yet standing not last, they
  shall be shaken with the wind, and through the force of winds they
  shall be rooted out. 5 The imperfect branches shall be broken off,
  their fruit unprofitable, not ripe to eat, yes, meet for nothing.

  6 For children begotten of unlawful beds are witnesses of wickedness
  against their parents in their trial. 7 But though the righteous be
  prevented with death, yet shall he be in rest. 8 For honourable age is
  not that which stands in length of time, nor that is measured by
  number of years. 9 But wisdom is the gray hair to men, and an
  unspotted life is old age. 10 He pleased Yahuah (God), and was beloved
  of him: so that living among sinners he was translated.

  11 Yea speedily was he taken away, lest that wickedness should alter
  his understanding, or deceit beguile his soul. 12 For the bewitching
  of naughtiness does obscure things that are honest; and the wandering
  of concupiscence does undermine the simple mind. 13 He, being made
  perfect in a short time, fulfilled a long time: 14 For his soul
  pleased Yahuah (God): therefore hasted he to take him away from among
  the wicked. 15 This the people saw, and understood it not, neither
  laid they up this in their minds, That his grace and mercy is with his
  saints, and that he has respect to his chosen.

  16 Thus the righteous that is dead shall condemn the ungodly which are
  living; and youth that is soon perfected the many years and old age of
  the unrighteous. 17 For they shall see the end of the wise, and shall
  not understand what Yahuah (God) in his counsel has decreed of him,
  and to what end Yahuah (God) has set him in safety. 18 They shall see
  him, and despise him; but Yahuah (God) shall laugh them to scorn: and
  they shall hereafter be a vile carcase, and a reproach among the dead
  for evermore. 19 For he shall rend them, and cast them down headlong,
  that they shall be speechless; and he shall shake them from the
  foundation; and they shall be utterly laid waste, and be in sorrow;
  and their memorial shall perish. 20 And when they cast up the accounts
  of their sins, they shall come with fear: and their own iniquities
  shall convince them to their face.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the meditation on death and legacy. Verses 1–6
contrast the righteous, whose memory is immortal even if their lives are
short, with the wicked, whose multitudinous offspring shall not thrive.
Verses 7–14 contain one of the most famous passages: But though the
righteous be prevented with death, yet shall he be in rest. For
honourable age is not that which stands in length of time, nor that is
measured by number of years. But wisdom is the gray hair to men, and an
unspotted life is old age. He pleased Elohim (God), and was beloved of him: so
that living among sinners he was translated. Yea, speedily was he taken
away, lest that wickedness should alter his understanding, or deceit
beguile his soul. The "speedy taking away" of the righteous as
protection from corruption is one of the great consolations of the
second-temple wisdom tradition.

The framework finds two things.

First, the principle that honourable age is not that which stands in
length of time is consistent with the prophetic and apostolic witness.
The covenant value is faithfulness, not longevity. Methuselah lived
nearly a thousand years and produced one named heir. Yahusha (Jesus)
lived thirty-three years and changed the course of history. The
framework of this Series, which honors the awakening of the remnant as
the Father's work and not the believer's accomplishment, finds in this
passage the right valuation: the value of a life is not in its length
but in its faithfulness.

Second, the closing of the chapter (verses 16–20) describes the eventual
judgment of the wicked at the resurrection. Then shall the righteous man
stand in great boldness before the face of such as have afflicted him,
and made no account of his labours. When they see it, they shall be
troubled with terrible fear, and shall be amazed at the strangeness of
his salvation, so far beyond all that they looked for. And they
repenting and groaning for anguish of spirit shall say within
themselves, This was he, whom we had sometimes in derision, and a
proverb of reproach: we fools accounted his life madness, and his end to
be without honour: how is he numbered among the children of Elohim (God), and his
lot is among the saints! The framework of this Series, which holds that
the day of Yahuah (God) brings the vindication of the faithful before
those who afflicted them, finds in Wisdom 4 the second-temple voice
naming the same vindication.

The vindication scene is one of the most pastorally useful passages in
the Apocrypha for the awakening reader who has been mocked or
marginalized by his still-deceived family and former community for the
awakening walk. The Wisdom of Solomon names this scene plainly. The
mockery is real. The marginalization is real. We accounted his life
madness. That phrase has been said about many an awakened believer by
those who once shared his pew. The chapter does not promise present
vindication. It promises appointed vindication. In the day of their
visitation. The patience is required. The trust is required. The
vindication is appointed. The framework reads Wisdom 4 as the
second-temple anchor for what the awakened reader is being asked to walk
through, and the consolation that the present mockery is held in the
appointed vindication that is coming.

Cross-references: Genesis 5:1–32; Psalm 73:1–28; Isaiah 57:1–2; Daniel
12:1–3; Matthew 5:10–12; Hebrews 11:35; James 5:7–11; 1 Peter 4:12–19;
Revelation 7:9–17.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 5

  1 Then shall the righteous man stand in great boldness before the face
  of such as have afflicted him, and made no account of his labours. 2
  When they see it, they shall be troubled with terrible fear, and shall
  be amazed at the strangeness of his salvation, so far beyond all that
  they looked for. 3 And they repenting and groaning for anguish of
  spirit shall say within themselves, This was he, whom we had sometimes
