  in derision, and a proverb of reproach: 4 We fools accounted his life
  madness, and his end to be without honour: 5 How is he numbered among
  the children of Yahuah (God), and his lot is among the saints!

  6 Therefore have we erred from the way of truth, and the light of
  righteousness has not shined to us, and the sun of righteousness rose
  not upon us. 7 We wearied ourselves in the way of wickedness and
  destruction: yes, we have gone through deserts, where there lay no
  way: but as for the way of Yahuah (God), we have not known it. 8 What
  has pride profited us? or what good has riches with our vaunting
  brought us? 9 All those things are passed away like a shadow, and as a
  post that hasted by; 10 And as a ship that passeth over the waves of
  the water, which when it is gone by, the trace thereof cannot be
  found, neither the pathway of the keel in the waves;

  11 Or as when a bird has flown through the air, there is no token of
  her way to be found, but the light air being beaten with the stroke of
  her wings and parted with the violent noise and motion of them, is
  passed through, and in it afterwards no sign where she went is to be
  found; 12 Or like as when an arrow is shot at a mark, it parteth the
  air, which immediately comes together again, so that a man cannot know
  where it went through: 13 Even so we in like manner, as soon as we
  were born, began to draw to our end, and had no sign of virtue to
  shew; but were consumed in our own wickedness. 14 For the hope of the
  ungodly is like dust that is blown away with the wind; like a thin
  froth that is driven away with the storm; like as the smoke which is
  dispersed here and there with a tempest, and passeth away as the
  remembrance of a guest that tarrieth but a day. 15 But the righteous
  live for evermore; their reward also is with Yahuah (God), and the
  care of them is with the Most High.

  16 Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful
  crown from the hand of Yahuah (God): for with his right hand shall he
  cover them, and with his arm shall he protect them. 17 He shall take
  to him his jealousy for complete armour, and make the creature his
  weapon for the revenge of his enemies. 18 He shall put on
  righteousness as a breastplate, and true judgment instead of an
  helmet. 19 He shall take holiness for an invincible shield. 20 His
  severe wrath shall he sharpen for a sword, and the world shall fight
  with him against the unwise.

  21 Then shall the right aiming thunderbolts go abroad; and from the
  clouds, as from a well drawn bow, shall they fly to the mark. 22 And
  hailstones full of wrath shall be cast as out of a stone bow, and the
  water of the sea shall rage against them, and the floods shall cruelly
  drown them. 23 Yea, a mighty wind shall stand up against them, and
  like a storm shall blow them away: thus iniquity shall lay waste the
  whole earth, and ill dealing shall overthrow the thrones of the
  mighty.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the great vision of the day of judgment. The
wicked, when they see the righteous standing in glory, lament: What has
pride profited us? or what good has riches with our vaunting brought us?
All those things are passed away like a shadow, and as a post that
hasted by; and as a ship that passes over the waves of the water, which
when it is gone by, the trace thereof cannot be found... So we in like
manner, as soon as we were born, began to draw to our end... but the
righteous live for evermore: their reward also is with the Lord, and the
care of them is with the most High.

Verses 17–23 develop the imagery of Yahuah (God) arming Himself with His
attributes as armor for the day of judgment: righteousness as
breastplate, true judgment as helmet, holiness as shield, severe wrath
as a sword.

Read the canonical anchor first. Isaiah 59:17: For he put on
righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation upon his head;
and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with
zeal as a cloak. The image is Yahuah (God) Himself dressing for
judgment. Wisdom 5:18 echoes: He shall put on righteousness as a
breastplate, and true judgment instead of an helmet. Both texts have the
divine warrior arming Himself.

Now read the apostolic application. Ephesians 6:11–17: Put on the whole
armor of Elohim (God), that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the
devil... having on the breastplate of righteousness... taking the shield
of faith... And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the
Spirit, which is the word of Elohim (God). 1 Thessalonians 5:8: let us, who are
of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and
for an helmet, the hope of salvation. What Yahuah (God) wears in Isaiah
59 and Wisdom 5, the believer is told to put on in Ephesians 6 and 1
Thessalonians 5. The armor that Yahuah (God) wears for judgment is the
armor He shares with His own for the spiritual battle. The framework's
principle: the awakening reader's equipment is not separate from Yahuah
(God)'s; the awakening reader puts on what Yahuah (God) wears.

The framework finds three things.

First, the wicked's lament names the vanity of riches, pride, and
strength under the day of judgment. The framework of this Series, which
holds that the awakening of the remnant strips the value-systems of the
inherited culture and reveals what was always vanity, finds in Wisdom 5
the second-temple anticipation of that stripping.

Second, the imagery of Yahuah (God) armed with His attributes is the
imagery the apostolic writings will pick up and apply to the believer.
The principle is the same: the armor that Yahuah (God) wears is the
armor He shares with His own. The framework of this Series does not
separate the divine arming from the believer's arming; the apostles'
application is consistent with the prophetic and second-temple wisdom
precedent.

Third, the closing of the chapter (verses 17–23) names that creation
will fight for the righteous: Lightnings shall go abroad of true aim,
and shall fly to the mark, as from a well drawn bow of clouds, and
hailstones full of wrath shall be cast as out of a stone bow, and the
water of the sea shall rage against them, and the floods shall cruelly
drown them. Yea, a mighty wind shall stand up against them, and like a
storm shall blow them away. The framework of this Series, which holds
that the appointed day of Yahuah (God) brings creation itself into the
judgment of the wicked, finds in Wisdom 5 the second-temple
imagination's articulation of that creation-wide judgment.

This passage is in the same family as the closing chapters of Job, where
Yahuah (God) speaks out of the whirlwind and reminds Job of His ordering
of the natural order. It is also in the same family as Revelation 16,
where the bowls of the wrath of Yahuah (God) involve hail, fire, sea,
rivers, sun, and air. Creation has been groaning under the dominion of
the corrupt seed and the imperial-pattern that has scattered the
covenant people; creation will be vindicated when the powers are judged.
Romans 8:18–25 names this groaning and waiting; Wisdom 5 names this
active participation. Read them together. Creation is not a neutral
backdrop. Creation is a witness to Yahuah (God) and will be brought into
the appointed judgment of those who have desolated her.

Cross-references: Psalm 73:1–28; Isaiah 59:15–21; Joel 2:1–11; Ephesians
6:10–17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; 2 Peter 3:1–13; Revelation 6:12–17;
Revelation 19:11–21; Romans 8:18–25; Job 38:1–41:34; Revelation 16:1–21.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 6

  1 Hear therefore, O you kings, and understand; learn, you that be
  judges of the ends of the earth. 2 Give ear, you that rule the people,
  and glory in the multitude of nations. 3 For power is given you of
  Yahuah (God), and sovereignty from the Highest, who shall try your
  works, and search out your counsels. 4 Because, being ministers of his
  kingdom, you have not judged aright, nor kept the law, nor walked
  after the counsel of Yahuah (God); 5 Horribly and speedily shall he
  come upon you: for a sharp judgment shall be to them that be in high
  places.

  6 For mercy will soon pardon the meanest: but mighty men shall be
  mightily tormented. 7 For he which is Yahuah (God) over all shall fear
  no man’s person, neither shall he stand in awe of any man’s greatness:
  for he has made the small and great, and careth for all alike. 8 But a
  sore trial shall come upon the mighty. 9 To you therefore, O kings, do
  I speak, that you may learn wisdom, and not fall away. 10 For they
  that keep holiness holily shall be judged holy: and they that have
  learned such things shall find what to answer.

  11 Wherefore set your affection upon my words; desire them, and you
  shall be instructed. 12 Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away:
  yes, she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as
  seek her. 13 She preventeth them that desire her, in making herself
  first known to them. 14 Whoso seeks her early shall have no great
  travail: for he shall find her sitting at his doors. 15 To think
  therefore upon her is perfection of wisdom: and whoso watcheth for her
  shall quickly be without care.

  16 For she goes about seeking such as are worthy of her, sheweth
  herself favourably to them in the ways, and meeteth them in every
  thought. 17 For the very true beginning of her is the desire of
  discipline; and the care of discipline is love; 18 And love is the
  keeping of her laws; and the giving heed to her laws is the assurance
  of incorruption; 19 And incorruption makes us near to Yahuah (God): 20
  Therefore the desire of wisdom brings to a kingdom.

  21 If your delight be then in thrones and sceptres, O you kings of the
  people, honour wisdom, that you may reign for evermore. 22 As for
  wisdom, what she is, and how she came up, I will tell you, and will
  not hide mysteries from you: but will seek her out from the beginning
  of her nativity, and bring the knowledge of her into light, and will
  not pass over the truth. 23 Neither will I go with consuming envy; for
  such a man shall have no fellowship with wisdom. 24 But the multitude
  of the wise is the welfare of the world: and a wise king is the
  upholding of the people. 25 Receive therefore instruction through my
  words, and it shall do you good.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is addressed to the kings and judges of the earth, urging
them to seek wisdom because they will be judged most strictly for their
failures. For mercy will soon pardon the meanest: but mighty men shall
be mightily tormented. The chapter then develops a sustained meditation
on wisdom as a teacher accessible to those who seek her.

Three things matter.

First, the chapter's principle that those who hold authority will be
judged most strictly is consistent with the prophetic and apostolic
witness.

The canonical anchor is direct. James 3:1 — be not many masters, knowing
that we shall receive the greater condemnation. Luke 12:48 — For unto
whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men
have committed much, of him they will ask the more. Hebrews 13:17 — they
watch for your souls, as they that must give account. Ezekiel 34:2–10
names the prophetic indictment of the unfaithful shepherds in
concentrated form. Jeremiah 23:1–2 — Woe to the pastors that destroy and
scatter the sheep of my pasture! Malachi 2:7–9 names the priestly
judgment when the priests have departed from the way.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the corruption of
authority within the covenant community produces the sons of Belial
pattern (Eli's sons, the elders of Susanna, the corrupt priesthood of
the second temple, and the institutional leadership of every system the
awakening reader has walked out of), finds in Wisdom 6 the second-temple
articulation of why such corruption is judged severely.

The contemporary application is direct. The pastors, priests, rabbis,
teachers, and institutional leaders of the four houses occupy positions
Wisdom 6 specifically warns. Their judgment will be more severe than the
judgment of those they led. This is not a license for the awakening
reader to rejoice over the appointed judgment of his former teachers. It
is a warning to anyone — including the awakening reader, if he in turn
becomes a teacher — that the office of teaching the covenant community
is held under the strictest of standards. The framework of this Series,
which honors the watchman-corrector posture, also honors the posture of
fear-of-Yahuah (God) appropriate to the one who would presume to teach.
Be not many masters. The awakening reader who is being shown things and
who feels the call to share them with others should hold both Wisdom 6
and James 3:1 in front of him.

Second, the chapter's development of wisdom as accessible to those who
seek her (verses 12–20) is one of the great wisdom passages in the
apocryphal corpus. Wisdom is glorious, and never fades away: yea, she is
easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as seek her. She
prevents them that desire her, in making herself first known to them.
Whoso seeks her early shall have no great travel: for he shall find her
sitting at his doors. To think therefore upon her is perfection of
wisdom: and whoso watches for her shall quickly be without care. The
principle is consistent with Proverbs 8 and is the second-temple
amplification of the same theme: wisdom seeks those who seek her.

Third, the closing of the chapter (verses 21–25) connects wisdom-seeking
to the ruling of nations: If your delight be then in thrones and
sceptres, O you kings of the people, honour wisdom, that you may reign
for evermore. The principle is that the ruling that endures is the
ruling under wisdom; the ruling that does not honor wisdom does not
endure. The framework of this Series, which holds that the appointed
reign of the Messiah is the destination toward which all rule is moving,
finds in Wisdom 6 the second-temple articulation that all enduring rule
is wisdom-rule.

Cross-references: Proverbs 8:1–36; Proverbs 9:1–18; James 1:5; James
3:1–18; 1 Kings 3:5–15; Daniel 2:20–23; Ecclesiastes 12:13–14; Romans
13:1–7.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 7

  1 I myself also am a mortal man, like to all, and the offspring of him
  that was first made of the earth, 2 And in my mother’s womb was
  fashioned to be flesh in the time of ten months, being compacted in
  blood, of the seed of man, and the pleasure that came with sleep. 3
  And when I was born, I drew in the common air, and fell upon the
  earth, which is of like nature, and the first voice which I uttered
  was crying, as all others do. 4 I was nursed in swaddling clothes, and
  that with cares. 5 For there is no king that had any other beginning
  of birth.

  6 For all men have one entrance into life, and the like going out. 7
  Wherefore I prayed, and understanding was given me: I called upon
  Yahuah (God), and the spirit of wisdom came to me. 8 I preferred her
  before sceptres and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing in comparison
  of her. 9 Neither compared I to her any precious stone, because all
  gold in respect of her is as a little sand, and silver shall be
  counted as clay before her. 10 I loved her above health and beauty,
  and chose to have her instead of light: for the light that comes from
  her never goes out.

  11 All good things together came to me with her, and innumerable
  riches in her hands. 12 And I rejoiced in them all, because wisdom
  goes before them: and I knew not that she was the mother of them. 13 I
  learned diligently, and do communicate her liberally: I do not hide
  her riches. 14 For she is a treasure to men that never fails: which
  they that use become the friends of Yahuah (God), being commended for
  the gifts that come from learning. 15 Yahuah (God) has granted me to
  speak as I would, and to conceive as is meet for the things that are
  given me: because it is he that leadeth to wisdom, and directeth the
  wise.

  16 For in his hand are both we and our words; all wisdom also, and
  knowledge of workmanship. 17 For he has given me certain knowledge of
  the things that are, namely, to know how the world was made, and the
  operation of the elements: 18 The beginning, ending, and midst of the
  times: the alterations of the turning of the sun, and the change of
  seasons: 19 The circuits of years, and the positions of stars: 20 The
  natures of living creatures, and the furies of wild beasts: the
  violence of winds, and the reasonings of men: the diversities of
  plants and the virtues of roots:

  21 And all such things as are either secret or manifest, them I know.
  22 For wisdom, which is the worker of all things, taught me: for in
  her is an understanding spirit holy, one only, manifold, subtil,
  lively, clear, undefiled, plain, not subject to hurt, loving the thing
  that is good quick, which cannot be letted, ready to do good, 23 Kind
  to man, steadfast, sure, free from care, having all power, overseeing
  all things, and going through all understanding, pure, and most
  subtil, spirits. 24 For wisdom is more moving than any motion: she
  passeth and goes through all things by reason of her pureness. 25 For
  she is the breath of the power of Yahuah (God), and a pure influence
  flowing from the glory of the Almighty: therefore can no defiled thing
  fall into her.

  26 For she is the brightness of the everlasting light, the unspotted
  mirror of the power of Yahuah (God), and the image of his goodness. 27
  And being but one, she can do all things: and remaining in herself,
  she makes all things new: and in all ages entering into holy souls,
  she makes them friends of Yahuah (God), and prophets. 28 For Yahuah
  (God) loves none but him that dwells with wisdom. 29 For she is more
  beautiful than the sun, and above all the order of stars: being
  compared with the light, she is found before it. 30 For after this
  comes night: but vice shall not prevail against wisdom.

⸻

Commentary

The author speaks in the first person as Solomon. I myself also am a
mortal man, like to all, and the offspring of him that was first made of
the earth. The chapter develops a sustained autobiographical meditation:
Solomon prayed for wisdom; she came to him; she taught him every art and
every science; she is the breath of the power of Elohim (God), the brightness of
the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the power of Elohim (God), the
image of his goodness.

Three things matter, and the third is the most important.

First, Solomon's autobiographical voice (verses 1–6) is the voice of a
king who knows he is mortal. He was conceived as all are conceived. He
cried at birth. He breathed and ate and slept like every other man. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the Messiah came in the flesh
and bore the full reality of human mortality (Hebrews 2:14–18), finds in
Wisdom 7 the second-temple articulation of the principle that the
highest among men is no different in body from the lowest. The principle
does not collapse the Messiah into a mere man; the Messiah was the
Formed One in the flesh, who took on the mortal body to redeem the seed.
The principle does establish the universality of mortal experience under
which both Solomon and the Messiah operated.

Second, the prayer for wisdom (verses 7–14) is the model of the
awakening reader's prayer. Wherefore I prayed, and understanding was
given me: I called upon Elohim (God), and the spirit of wisdom came to me. I
preferred her before sceptres and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing
in comparison of her... I loved her above health and beauty, and chose
to have her instead of light: for the light that comes from her never
goes out. The framework of this Series, which honors the seeking of
Yahuah (God) above all other things, finds in this prayer the proper
shape.

Third, and most important: verses 22–30 develop the most important
Christology-precedent passage in the apocryphal corpus. For wisdom,
which is the worker of all things, taught me: for in her is an
understanding spirit, holy, one only, manifold, subtil, lively, clear,
undefiled, plain, not subject to hurt, loving the thing that is good,
quick, which cannot be letted, ready to do good, kind to man, steadfast,
sure, free from care, having all power, overseeing all things, and going
through all understanding, pure, and most subtil, spirits. For wisdom is
more moving than any motion: she passes and goes through all things by
reason of her pureness. For she is the breath of the power of Elohim (God), and a
pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty: therefore can no
defiled thing fall into her. For she is the brightness of the
everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the power of Elohim (God), and the
image of his goodness. And being but one, she can do all things: and
remaining in herself, she makes all things new: and in all ages entering
into holy souls, she makes them friends of Elohim (God), and prophets.

The vocabulary is the vocabulary the New Testament writers will pick up
and apply to Yahusha (Jesus). Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son the brightness
of [the Father's] glory, and the express image of his person. Colossians
1:15 calls the Son the image of the invisible Elohim (God). John 1:1–14 names the
Word. The framework of this Series, which holds that the Father is the
formless infinite and the Word is the Formed expression drawn from the
formless, finds in Wisdom 7 the second-temple precedent for the New
Testament's vocabulary. The Wisdom of Solomon does not invent the New
Testament Christology. The Wisdom of Solomon is the second-temple
Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish) wisdom-personification that the apostolic
writers had read, and they drew on its vocabulary because the vocabulary
already pointed at the realities the Messiah's incarnation was bringing
fully into the open. The reader who has been trained by inherited
Christianity to think of the New Testament Christology as a Christian
innovation will be quietly corrected by Wisdom 7. The Word was always
there. The vocabulary the apostles used was already in their hands when
they sat down to write.

Take this slowly. Hebrews 1:3 — Who being the brightness of his glory,
and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the
word of his power. Wisdom 7:25–26 — For she is the breath of the power
of Elohim (God), and a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty...
For she is the brightness of the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror
of the power of Elohim (God), and the image of his goodness. The same
descriptions. The same architecture. The Hebrews writer is not inventing
fresh Christology out of philosophical air. He is taking the
second-temple wisdom-personification vocabulary that his audience
already knew and applying it to the Messiah whose incarnation has now
made the vocabulary come into its full reference. Brightness of his
glory — Wisdom is the brightness of the everlasting light. Express image
of his person — Wisdom is the unspotted mirror, the image of his
goodness. Upholding all things by the word of his power — Wisdom passes
and goes through all things by reason of her pureness. The reader who
has been told that the New Testament's Christology is a strange
Christian innovation grafted onto Yahudi (Jewish) monotheism has been
kept from this passage. Read Wisdom 7 and Hebrews 1 side by side. They
are the same vocabulary applied to the same Word.

Colossians 1:15–17 closes the parallel with full force: Who is the image
of the invisible Elohim (God), the firstborn of every creature: For by him were
all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible
and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities,
or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: And he is before
all things, and by him all things consist. Compare to Wisdom 7:24 — For
wisdom is more moving than any motion: she passes and goes through all
things by reason of her pureness; and Wisdom 8:1 — Wisdom reaches from
one end to another mightily: and sweetly does she order all things.
Wisdom orders all things; the Word holds all things together. Wisdom is
the image of God's goodness; the Word is the image of the invisible Elohim (God).
Wisdom is before all things and present at the creation; the Word is
before all things and through whom all things were created. Three
witnesses — Hebrews 1, Colossians 1, Wisdom 7–8 — all naming the same
active expressed presence of Yahuah (God) in the world.

John 1:1–3 completes the Christology-precedent line: In the beginning
was the Word, and the Word was with Elohim (God), and the Word was Elohim (God). The same
was in the beginning with Elohim (God). All things were made by him; and without
him was not any thing made that was made. Wisdom in Wisdom 9:9 — And
wisdom was with you: which knows your works, and was present when you
made the world. John 1 says the Word was with Elohim (God); Wisdom 9 says Wisdom
was with Elohim (God). John 1 says all things were made by the Word; Wisdom 9
says Wisdom was present when Yahuah (God) made the world. The
architecture is identical. The reader who has been catechized to think
of John's prologue as a peculiarly Christian theological development
should be returned to Wisdom 9:9. The vocabulary was already there. The
apostle John applied it to Yahusha because Yahusha was the embodiment in
flesh of the active expressed presence of the Father that the
wisdom-tradition had been naming for centuries.

The framework's specific reading of the Father and the Formed One lands
here with full force. The Wisdom of Solomon's "wisdom" is not a separate
divine person; she is the active expressed presence of the Most High,
drawn from his glory, his breath, his power. She is the breath of the
power of Elohim (God). The Word is the breath of the power of Elohim (God). She is the
brightness of the everlasting light. The Word is the brightness of the
Father's glory. She is the unspotted mirror of the power of Elohim (God). The
Word is the express image of the Father's person. She is the image of
his goodness. The Word is the image of the invisible Elohim (God). The Wisdom of
Solomon's "wisdom" and the framework's "Formed One" and the apostolic
writings' "Word" are the same active expressed presence of the Father,
drawn from the Formless source, sent into creation, and finally come in
the flesh as Yahusha. The Trinity doctrine collapses this into "the
second person of the Godhead" — three co-equal persons, an architecture
foreign to the second-temple voice. The modalist reading collapses this
into "Jesus is the Father wearing a different hat" — also foreign to the
second-temple voice. The framework's reading of the Formless and the
Formed is the second-temple reading. Wisdom 7 is the witness.

The closing of the passage — being but one, she can do all things: and
remaining in herself, she makes all things new: and in all ages entering
into holy souls, she makes them friends of Elohim (God), and prophets — names the
work of the Word in every age. The Word entered Enoch. The Word entered
Noah. The Word entered Abraham. The Word entered Moses. The Word entered
the prophets. The Word entered Daniel. The Word entered the apostles.
The Word entered Yahusha fully — became flesh, the perfect dwelling. The
Word continues to enter the awakening remnant by the Spirit. In all ages
entering into holy souls, she makes them friends of Elohim (God), and prophets.
This is one verse. It contains the framework's whole Word-and-Spirit
theology in a single second-temple sentence. The reader of this
commentary should sit with it.

Cross-references: 1 Kings 3:5–15; Proverbs 8:22–36; John 1:1–18;
Colossians 1:15–20; Hebrews 1:1–3; 2 Corinthians 4:4; Wisdom of Solomon
9:1–18; Sirach 24:1–34; Hebrews 2:14–18.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 8

  1 Wisdom reacheth from one end to another mightily: and sweetly does
  she order all things. 2 I loved her, and sought her out from my youth,
  I desired to make her my spouse, and I was a lover of her beauty. 3 In
  that she is conversant with Yahuah (God), she magnifies her nobility:
  yes, Yahuah (God) of all things himself loved her. 4 For she is privy
  to the mysteries of the knowledge of Yahuah (God), and a lover of his
  works. 5 If riches be a possession to be desired in this life; what is
  richer than wisdom, that works all things?

  6 And if prudence work; who of all that are is a more cunning workman
  than she? 7 And if a man love righteousness her labours are virtues:
  for she teaches temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude: which
  are such things, as men can have nothing more profitable in their
  life. 8 If a man desire much experience, she knoweth things of old,
  and conjectureth aright what is to come: she knoweth the subtilties of
  speeches, and can expound dark sentences: she foreseeth signs and
  wonders, and the events of seasons and times. 9 Therefore I purposed
  to take her to me to live with me, knowing that she would be a
  counsellor of good things, and a comfort in cares and grief. 10 For
  her sake I shall have estimation among the multitude, and honour with
  the elders, though I be young.

  11 I shall be found of a quick conceit in judgment, and shall be
  admired in the sight of great men. 12 When I hold my tongue, they
  shall bide my leisure, and when I speak, they shall give good ear to
  me: if I talk much, they shall lay their hands upon their mouth. 13
  Moreover by the means of her I shall obtain immortality, and leave
  behind me an everlasting memorial to them that come after me. 14 I
  shall set the people in order, and the nations shall be subject to me.
  15 Horrible tyrants shall be afraid, when they do but hear of me; I
  shall be found good among the multitude, and valiant in war.

  16 After I am come into my house, I will repose myself with her: for
  her conversation has no bitterness; and to live with her has no
  sorrow, but mirth and joy. 17 Now when I considered these things in
  myself, and pondered them in my heart, how that to be allied to wisdom
  is immortality; 18 And great pleasure it is to have her friendship;
  and in the works of her hands are infinite riches; and in the exercise
  of conference with her, prudence; and in talking with her, a good
  report; I went about seeking how to take her to me. 19 For I was a
  witty child, and had a good spirit. 20 Yea rather, being good, I came
  into a body undefiled.

  21 Nevertheless, when I perceived that I could not otherwise obtain
  her, except Yahuah (God) gave her me; and that was a point of wisdom
  also to know whose gift she was; I prayed to Yahuah (God), and
  besought him, and with my whole heart I said,

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the autobiographical meditation. Solomon describes
how he loved wisdom and sought her as a bride from his youth, and how
she has taught him every science and every art. Three things matter.

First, the personification of wisdom as bride (verses 2–3, 9, 16)
extends the wisdom-personification of chapter 7. The framework of this
Series, on the question of the Father and the Formed One, holds that the
Word is not a hypostatic person separate from the Father in the sense
the Trinity doctrine claims. The Wisdom of Solomon's personification of
wisdom is also not a separate person; wisdom is the breath of the power
of Elohim (God) (7:25), drawn from the formless source. The framework's reading
of the Wisdom-of-Solomon Christology-precedent: the personification
language is poetic-theological; the Word is the Formed One drawn from
the Formless; the apostolic letters apply this language to Yahusha
(Jesus) because He is, in fact, the Formed One who came in the flesh.

Second, Solomon's confession that with all my prosperity, I could not
enter into wisdom unless Yahuah (God) gave her to me (verses 19–21) is
the proper covenant-confession. The wisdom is not the supplicant's
achievement. The wisdom is Yahuah (God)'s gift. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the awakening of the remnant is the work of the
Father, finds in Solomon's confession the right shape.

Third, the principle that wisdom is to be sought from Yahuah (God) alone
is the framework's principle: the awakening reader does not seek wisdom
from teachers, movements, denominations, or commentators. The awakening
reader seeks wisdom from Yahuah (God) directly, through His Word, by the
Spirit. Other voices may serve. No other voice is the source.

Cross-references: 1 Kings 3:5–15; Proverbs 8:1–36; James 1:5; 1
Corinthians 1:18–31; 1 Corinthians 2:1–16; Ephesians 1:17.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 9

  1 O Yahuah (God) of my fathers, and Yahuah (God) of mercy, who have
  made all things with your word, 2 And ordained man through your
  wisdom, that he should have dominion over the creatures which you have
  made, 3 And order the world according to equity and righteousness, and
  execute judgment with an upright heart: 4 Give me wisdom, that sits by
  your throne; and reject me not from among your children: 5 For I your
  servant and son of yours handmaid am a feeble person, and of a short
  time, and too young for the understanding of judgment and laws.

  6 For though a man be never so perfect among the children of men, yet
  if your wisdom be not with him, he shall be nothing regarded. 7 You
  have chosen me to be a king of your people, and a judge of your sons
  and daughters: 8 You have commanded me to build a temple upon your
  holy mount, and an altar in the city in which you dwellest, a
  resemblance of the holy tabernacle, which you have prepared from the
  beginning. 9 And wisdom was with you: which knoweth your works, and
  was present when you madest the world, and knew what was acceptable in
  your sight, and right in your commandments. 10 O send her out of your
  holy heavens, and from the throne of your glory, that being present
  she may labour with me, that I may know what is pleasing to you.

  11 For she knoweth and understands all things, and she shall lead me
  soberly in my doings, and preserve me in her power. 12 So shall my
  works be acceptable, and then shall I judge your people righteously,
  and be worthy to sit in my father’s seat. 13 For what man is he that
  can know the counsel of Yahuah (God)? or who can think what the will
  of Yahuah (God) is? 14 For the thoughts of mortal men are miserable,
  and our devices are but uncertain. 15 For the corruptible body
  presseth down the soul, and the earthy tabernacle weigheth down the
  mind that museth upon many things.

  16 And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth, and
  with labour do we find the things that are before us: but the things
  that are in heaven who has searched out? 17 And your counsel who has
  known, except you give wisdom, and send your Ruach HaKodesh (Holy
  Spirit) from above? 18 For so the ways of them which lived on the
  earth were reformed, and men were taught the things that are pleasing
  to you, and were saved through wisdom.

⸻

Commentary

Solomon's prayer for wisdom (verses 1–18) is one of the great prayers of
the second-temple corpus and is the climactic prayer of the Wisdom of
Solomon. The prayer asks Yahuah (God) to send wisdom from His holy
heavens, to dwell with the supplicant, to teach him what is acceptable
in Yahuah (God)'s eyes. The prayer recalls that the same wisdom guided
Adam in his creation, sustained Noah in the ark, called Abraham, led
Moses, and brought Yashar'el (Israel) through the wilderness.

Two things matter.

First, the prayer is built on the same architecture as the prayers in 1
Kings 3 (Solomon's actual prayer for wisdom at Gibeon) and as the prayer
of Daniel 9. The basis is the covenant. The supplicant asks for wisdom
on the basis of Yahuah (God)'s having promised to give wisdom to those
who ask (Proverbs 2). The prayer is not generic. It is
covenant-grounded. The framework of this Series finds in Solomon's
prayer the proper covenant-prayer shape.

Second, the prayer's identification of wisdom as the figure who has been
with Yahuah (God) from the foundation of creation, who guided the
patriarchs, who led the Exodus, who has been the active Formed presence
of Yahuah (God) in the world, is the second-temple Christology-precedent
in concentrated form. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
Formed One was the active divine presence in the Old Testament
narratives — the angel of Yahuah (God), the one who appeared to the
patriarchs, who spoke from the burning bush, who led Yashar'el (Israel)
through the wilderness — finds in Wisdom 9 the second-temple voice
articulating the same divine presence under the vocabulary of "wisdom."
The Formed One and the Wisdom of Solomon's "wisdom" are not separate
beings; they are the same Word, named under two of the second-temple's
vocabularies.

The framework's reading of the Old Testament theophanies lands hard
here. When Genesis 18 records that Yahuah (God) appeared to [Abraham] in
the plains of Mamre, the appearance was not the formless Father — the
formless Father cannot be seen by any man and live (Exodus 33:20). The
appearance was the Formed One, the Word, the same one Wisdom 9 names as
the active divine presence. When Exodus 3 records that the angel of
Yahuah (God) appeared to Moses in the burning bush and then Yahuah (God)
himself spoke to him out of the fire, the speaker was the Formed One.
When Joshua 5 records that the captain of the host of Yahuah (God)
appeared to Joshua before Jericho, the captain was the Formed One. When
Ezekiel 1 records the vision of the wheels and the throne and the
man-figure on the throne, the man-figure was the Formed One. The
framework's reading is consistent across the entire Hebrew canon, and
Wisdom 9 is the second-temple voice articulating the same recognition.
The active divine presence in the Old Testament was the Word who would
later come in the flesh as Yahusha.

Cross-references: 1 Kings 3:5–15; 1 Kings 8:22–53; Daniel 9:1–19;
Proverbs 8:22–36; Genesis 1:26; Genesis 18:1–33; Exodus 3:1–6; Exodus
33:20; Exodus 14:15–31; Joshua 5:13–15; Ezekiel 1:26–28; John 1:1–18;
Hebrews 1:1–3; Colossians 1:15–20.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 10

  1 She preserved the first formed father of the world, that was created
  alone, and brought him out of his fall, 2 And gave him power to rule
  all things. 3 But when the unrighteous went away from her in his
  anger, he perished also in the fury with which he murdered his
  brother. 4 For whose cause the earth being drowned with the flood,
  wisdom again preserved it, and directed the course of the righteous in
  a piece of wood of small value. 5 Moreover, the nations in their
  wicked conspiracy being confounded, she found out the righteous, and
  preserved him blameless to Yahuah (God), and kept him strong against
  his tender compassion toward his son.

  6 When the ungodly perished, she delivered the righteous man, who fled
  from the fire which fell down upon the five cities. 7 Of whose
  wickedness even to this day the waste land that smoketh is a
  testimony, and plants bearing fruit that never come to ripeness: and a
  standing pillar of salt is a monument of an unbelieving soul. 8 For
  regarding not wisdom, they got not only this hurt, that they knew not
  the things which were good; but also left behind them to the world a
  memorial of their foolishness: so that in the things in which they
  offended they could not so much as be hid. 9 But wisdom delivered from
  pain those that attended upon her. 10 When the righteous fled from his
  brother’s wrath she guided him in right paths, shewed him the kingdom
  of Yahuah (God), and gave him knowledge of holy things, made him rich
  in his travels, and multiplied the fruit of his labours.

  11 In the covetousness of such as oppressed him she stood by him, and
  made him rich. 12 She defended him from his enemies, and kept him safe
  from those that lay in wait, and in a sore conflict she gave him the
  victory; that he might know that goodness is stronger than all. 13
  When the righteous was sold, she forsook him not, but delivered him
  from sin: she went down with him into the pit, 14 And left him not in
  bonds, till she brought him the sceptre of the kingdom, and power
  against those that oppressed him: as for them that had accused him,
  she shewed them to be liars, and gave him perpetual glory. 15 She
  delivered the righteous people and blameless seed from the nation that
  oppressed them.

  16 She entered into the soul of the servant of Yahuah (God), and
  withstood dreadful kings in wonders and signs; 17 Rendered to the
  righteous a reward of their labours, guided them in a marvellous way,
  and was to them for a cover by day, and a light of stars in the night
  season; 18 Brought them through the Red sea, and led them through much
  water: 19 But she drowned their enemies, and cast them up out of the
  bottom of the deep. 20 Therefore the righteous spoiled the ungodly,
  and praised your holy name, O Yahuah (God), and magnified with one
  accord yours hand, that fought for them.

  21 For wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, and made the tongues of
  them that cannot speak eloquent.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter begins the long historical retrospective that runs through
chapter 19. The pattern: wisdom led each of the great covenant figures —
Adam, Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jacob, Joseph, Moses — through their trials
and brought them to their destinies. The chapter focuses on the
patriarchal period through Joseph (verses 1–14) and the Exodus
generation (verses 15–21).

Three things matter.

First, the retrospective's structure — that wisdom is the active divine
presence guiding each figure — is the same structure the framework of
this Series holds about the Formed One. Wisdom called Adam. Wisdom
preserved Noah. Wisdom called Abraham. Wisdom guided Lot out of Sodom.
Wisdom delivered Joseph from the pit. Wisdom led Yashar'el (Israel) out
of Egypt. The framework's identification of the Formed One as the active
divine presence in these narratives is the same identification the
Wisdom of Solomon is making, under the vocabulary of "wisdom." The Word
and the Wisdom of Solomon's "wisdom" are the same active Formed
presence.

Second, the historical retrospective treats the Genesis and Exodus
narratives as historically actual. Adam, Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jacob,
Joseph, Moses — these are not literary devices. They are real men whose
lives the second-temple Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish) wisdom tradition
treated as the actual history of Yahuah (God)'s working with His
covenant people. The framework of this Series, which honors the Genesis
and Exodus narratives as historically actual (with the framework's
specific Genesis 1/Genesis 2 reading on Adam, the Sons of Adam, and the
men and women of the earth), finds in Wisdom 10 the second-temple voice
operating with the same historical confidence.

Third, the chapter's treatment of the deliverance from Egypt (verses
15–21) emphasizes that it was wisdom — the Formed presence of Yahuah
(God) — who led Yashar'el (Israel) through the sea. She delivered the
righteous people and blameless seed from the nation that oppressed them.
She entered into the soul of the servant of the Lord, and withstood
dreadful kings in wonders and signs; rendered to the righteous a reward
of their labours, guided them in a marvellous way, and was to them for a
cover by day, and a light of stars in the night season; brought them
through the Red sea, and led them through much water. The framework of
this Series identifies the cloud and fire of the Exodus as the visible
presence of the Formed One, the same Word who would later come in the
flesh. Wisdom 10 is the second-temple voice articulating that
identification.

The phrase blameless seed in verse 15 is worth pausing over. The seed is
named. The seed is specific. The seed is the seed of Jacob — the twelve
tribes whom Yahuah (God) delivered out of Egypt by the hand of the
Formed One. Wisdom 10 is not abstracting the deliverance into a metaphor
for any oppressed people. The deliverance is bloodline-specific. The
Formed One delivered His own paternal blood remnant from the nation that
oppressed them. The framework reads this verse plainly. The covenant
runs through the seed. The deliverance ran through the seed. The
destination — the gathering of the seed in the appointed time — runs
through the seed.

Cross-references: Genesis 1:26–28; Genesis 6:5–9:17; Genesis 11:31–12:9;
Genesis 19:1–29; Genesis 28:10–22; Genesis 37:18–28; Exodus 3:1–6;
Exodus 13:21–22; Exodus 14:15–31; 1 Corinthians 10:1–11.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 11

  1 She prospered their works in the hand of the holy prophet. 2 They
  went through the wilderness that was not inhabited, and pitched tents
  in places where there lay no way. 3 They stood against their enemies,
  and were avenged of their adversaries. 4 When they were thirsty, they
  called upon you, and water was given them out of the flinty rock, and
  their thirst was quenched out of the hard stone. 5 For by what things
  their enemies were punished, by the same they in their need were
  benefited.

  6 For instead of a perpetual running river troubled with foul blood, 7
  For a manifest reproof of that commandment, by which the infants were
  slain, you gavest to them abundance of water by a means which they
  hoped not for: 8 Declaring by that thirst then how you had punished
  their adversaries. 9 For when they were tried albeit but in mercy
  chastised, they knew how the ungodly were judged in wrath and
  tormented, thirsting in another manner than the just. 10 For these you
  did admonish and try, as a father: but the other, as a severe king,
  you did condemn and punish.

  11 Whether they were absent or present, they were vexed alike. 12 For
  a double grief came upon them, and a groaning for the remembrance of
  things past. 13 For when they heard by their own punishments the other
  to be benefited, they had some feeling of Yahuah (God). 14 For whom
  they respected with scorn, when he was long before thrown out at the
  casting forth of the infants, him in the end, when they saw what came
  to pass, they admired. 15 But for the foolish devices of their
  wickedness, with which being deceived they worshipped serpents void of
  reason, and vile beasts, you did send a multitude of unreasonable
  beasts upon them for vengeance;

  16 That they might know, that wherewithal a man sinneth, by the same
  also shall he be punished. 17 For your Almighty hand, that made the
  world of matter without form, wanted not means to send among them a
  multitude of bears or fierce lions, 18 Or unknown wild beasts, full of
  rage, newly created, breathing out either a fiery vapour, or filthy
  scents of scattered smoke, or shooting horrible sparkles out of their
  eyes: 19 Of which not only the harm might dispatch them at once, but
  also the terrible sight utterly destroy them. 20 Yea, and without
  these might they have fallen down with one blast, being persecuted of
  vengeance, and scattered abroad through the breath of your power: but
  you have ordered all things in measure and number and weight.

  21 For you can shew your great strength at all times when you will;
  and who may withstand the power of your arm? 22 For the whole world
  before you is as a little grain of the balance, yes, as a drop of the
  morning dew that falls down upon the earth. 23 But you have mercy upon
  all; for you can do all things, and winkest at the sins of men,
  because they should amend. 24 For you lovest all the things that are,
  and abhorrest nothing which you have made: for never wouldest you have
  made any thing, if you had hated it. 25 And how could any thing have
  endured, if it had not been your will? or been preserved, if not
  called by you?

  26 But you sparest all: for they are yours, O Yahuah (God), you lover
  of souls.

⸻

Commentary

The retrospective on the Exodus continues. The chapter focuses on the
wilderness wandering, particularly on the contrast between the way
Yahuah (God) treated Yashar'el (Israel) and the way He treated Egypt.
Two themes dominate: water from the rock for Yashar'el (Israel) versus
water turned to blood for Egypt (verses 1–14), and the principle that
Yahuah (God)'s mercy to Yashar'el (Israel) and judgment to Egypt are
both expressions of His justice (verses 15–26).

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's principle that Yahuah (God)'s measured judgment of
the Egyptians proceeded by their own creatures — the frogs, the flies,
the lice, the locusts, the boils — is the second-temple articulation of
what Exodus 7–11 narrates.

The Exodus plagues are the canonical anchor. Each plague targeted a
specific Egyptian deity. The Nile turned to blood (Exodus 7:14–25)
struck at Hapi the Nile-god. The frogs (Exodus 8:1–15) struck at Heqet
the frog-headed goddess of fertility. The lice and flies struck the
Egyptian priesthood's purity-cult. The murrain on cattle (Exodus 9:1–7)
struck at Apis the bull-god and Hathor the cow-goddess. The hail (Exodus
9:13–35) struck at Nut the sky-goddess. The locusts (Exodus 10:1–20)
struck at Set the storm-god. The darkness (Exodus 10:21–29) struck at Ra
the sun-god, the supreme deity of Egypt. The death of the firstborn
(Exodus 11–12) struck at Pharaoh himself, who was worshiped as a god.
Exodus 12:12 names Yahuah (God)'s intent explicitly: I will pass through
the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the
land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I
will execute judgment: I am Yahuah (God). Numbers 33:4 confirms: upon
their gods also Yahuah (God) executed judgments.

The Egyptians worshiped the creatures. The judgment came through the
creatures. They were judged by the very things they had set up as gods.
The framework of this Series, which holds that the systems the awakening
reader has walked out of will be judged by the very mechanisms they used
to deceive (the priesthood by the offerings they consumed, the
institutions by the loyalty they demanded, the false-gospel preachers by
the texts they twisted), finds in Wisdom 11 the prototype of that
principle.

Second, the closing of the chapter (verses 23–26) names Yahuah (God)'s
mercy: But you have mercy upon all; for you can do all things, and winks
at the sins of men, because they should amend. For you love all the
things that are, and abhors nothing which you have made: for never would
you have made any thing, if you had hated it... But you spare all: for
they are yours, O Lord, you lover of souls. The framework of this
Series, which holds the victims-not-enemies posture toward those still
inside the four houses, finds in Wisdom 11:23–26 the second-temple
articulation of the same posture. Yahuah (God) is the lover of souls. He
spares. He is patient. He calls. The awakening reader's posture toward
those still inside the inherited systems is to be the same: patience,
love, the call to come home.

Cross-references: Exodus 7:14–11:10; Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:1–13;
Psalm 78:12–16; Psalm 105:23–45; Psalm 106:7–12; Romans 2:1–11; 2 Peter
3:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:1–6.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 12

  1 For your incorruptible Spirit is in all things. 2 Therefore
  chastenest you them by little and little that offend, and warnest them
  by putting them in remembrance in which they have offended, that
  leaving their wickedness they may believe on you, O Yahuah (God). 3
  For it was your will to destroy by the hands of our fathers both those
  old inhabitants of your holy land, 4 Whom you hatedst for doing most
  odious works of witchcrafts, and wicked sacrifices; 5 And also those
  merciless murderers of children, and devourers of man’s flesh, and the
  feasts of blood,

  6 With their priests out of the midst of their idolatrous crew, and
  the parents, that killed with their own hands souls destitute of help:
  7 That the land, which you esteemedst above all other, might receive a
  worthy colony of the children of Yahuah (God). 8 Nevertheless even
  those you sparedst as men, and did send wasps, forerunners of yours
  host, to destroy them by little and little. 9 Not that you were unable
  to bring the ungodly under the hand of the righteous in battle, or to
  destroy them at once with cruel beasts, or with one rough word: 10 But
  executing your judgments upon them by little and little, you gavest
  them place of repentance, not being ignorant that they were a naughty
  generation, and that their malice was bred in them, and that their
  cogitation would never be changed.

  11 For it was a cursed seed from the beginning; neither did you for
  fear of any man give them pardon for those things in which they
  sinned. 12 For who shall say, What have you done? or who shall
  withstand your judgment? or who shall accuse you for the nations that
  perish, whom you made? or who shall come to stand against you, to be
  revenged for the unrighteous men? 13 For neither is there any Yahuah
  (God) but you that careth for all, to whom you might shew that your
  judgment is not unright. 14 Neither shall king or tyrant be able to
  set his face against you for any whom you have punished. 15 Forsomuch
  then as you are righteous thyself, you orderest all things
  righteously: thinking it not agreeable with your power to condemn him
  that has not deserved to be punished.

  16 For your power is the beginning of righteousness, and because you
  are Yahuah (God) of all, it makes you to be gracious to all. 17 For
  when men will not believe that you are of a full power, you shewest
  your strength, and among them that know it you makest their boldness
  manifest. 18 But you, mastering your power, judgest with equity, and
  orderest us with great favour: for you may use power when you will. 19
  But by such works have you taught your people that the just man should
  be merciful, and have made your children to be of a good hope that you
  give repentance for sins. 20 For if you did punish the enemies of your
  children, and the condemned to death, with such deliberation, giving
  them time and place, by which they might be delivered from their
  malice:

  21 With how great circumspection did you judge your own sons, to whose
  fathers you have sworn, and made covenants of good promises? 22
  Therefore, whereas you do chasten us, you scourgest our enemies a
  thousand times more, to the intent that, when we judge, we should
  carefully think of your goodness, and when we ourselves are judged, we
  should look for mercy. 23 Wherefore, whereas men have lived
  dissolutely and unrighteously, you have tormented them with their own
  abominations. 24 For they went astray very far in the ways of error,
  and held them for gods, which even among the beasts of their enemies
  were despised, being deceived, as children of no understanding. 25
  Therefore to them, as to children without the use of reason, you did
  send a judgment to mock them.

  26 But they that would not be reformed by that correction, in which he
  dallied with them, shall feel a judgment worthy of Yahuah (God). 27
  For, look, for what things they grudged, when they were punished, that
  is, for them whom they thought to be gods; now being punished in them,
  when they saw it, they acknowledged him to be the true Yahuah (God),
  whom before they denied to know: and therefore came extreme damnation
  upon them.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the meditation on Yahuah (God)'s mercy and
judgment. The focus is on the long-suffering of Yahuah (God) toward the
Canaanites — He gave them generations to repent before the conquest, He
warned them, He sent the wasps before Yashar'el (Israel) (verse 8), and
only when they did not turn did the conquest proceed.

Two things matter.

First, the principle that the conquest of the Canaanites was a judgment
that had been delayed for generations to allow for repentance is
consistent with Genesis 15:16: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet
full. Yahuah (God) did not bring the conquest until the iniquity of the
land was complete. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
judgments of Yahuah (God) on the wicked are measured and patient, finds
in Wisdom 12 the second-temple articulation of the same principle.

Second, the chapter's argument that Yahuah (God)'s patience with sinners
is intended to lead them to repentance (verses 19–20) is consistent with
Romans 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9. The framework's posture toward those still
inside the four houses — that they are deceived victims who have been
handed inherited lies, not enemies to be condemned — is the same posture
Yahuah (God) takes toward sinners according to Wisdom 12. The patience
is purposeful. The patience is meant to lead to repentance. The
awakening reader's patience toward those still inside is the same
patience Yahuah (God) has been showing all along.

Cross-references: Genesis 15:13–16; Exodus 23:27–30; Deuteronomy 7:1–11;
Joshua 2:1–24; Joshua 9:1–27; Romans 2:1–11; 2 Peter 3:1–13.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 13

  1 Surely vain are all men by nature, who are ignorant of Yahuah (God),
  and could not out of the good things that are seen know him that is:
  neither by considering the works did they acknowledge the workmaster;
  2 But deemed either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circle of
  the stars, or the violent water, or the lights of heaven, to be the
  gods which govern the world. 3 With whose beauty if they being
  delighted took them to be gods; let them know how much better Yahuah
  (God) of them is: for the first author of beauty has created them. 4
  But if they were astonished at their power and virtue, let them
  understand by them, how much mightier he is that made them. 5 For by
  the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionably the maker of
  them is seen.

  6 But yet for this they are the less to be blamed: for they perhaps
  err, seeking Yahuah (God), and desirous to find him. 7 For being
  conversant in his works they search him diligently, and believe their
  sight: because the things are beautiful that are seen. 8 Howbeit
  neither are they to be pardoned. 9 For if they were able to know so
  much, that they could aim at the world; how did they not sooner find
  out Yahuah (God) thereof? 10 But miserable are they, and in dead
  things is their hope, who call them gods, which are the works of men’s
  hands, gold and silver, to shew art in, and resemblances of beasts, or
  a stone good for nothing, the work of an ancient hand.

  11 Now a carpenter that felleth timber, after he has sawn down a tree
  meet for the purpose, and taken off all the bark skilfully round
  about, and has wrought it handsomely, and made a vessel thereof fit
  for the service of man’s life; 12 And after spending the refuse of his
  work to dress his meat, has filled himself; 13 And taking the very
  refuse among those which served to no use, being a crooked piece of
  wood, and full of knots, has carved it diligently, when he had nothing
  else to do, and formed it by the skill of his understanding, and
  fashioned it to the image of a man; 14 Or made it like some vile
  beast, laying it over with vermilion, and with paint colouring it red,
  and covering every spot in it; 15 And when he had made a convenient
  room for it, set it in a wall, and made it fast with iron:

  16 For he provided for it that it might not fall, knowing that it was
  unable to help itself; for it is an image, and has need of help: 17
  Then makes he prayer for his goods, for his wife and children, and is
  not ashamed to speak to that which has no life. 18 For health he calls
  upon that which is weak: for life prayeth to that which is dead; for
  aid humbly beseecheth that which has least means to help: and for a
  good journey he asketh of that which cannot set a foot forward: 19 And
  for gaining and getting, and for good success of his hands, asketh
  ability to do of him, that is most unable to do any thing.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is one of the most important polemics against pagan idolatry
in the apocryphal corpus, and it stands directly behind Romans 1:18–32 —
Paul's (Paul's) argument about how the nations turned from the Creator
to the creature.

The argument runs in three movements.

First, those who worship the elements — fire, wind, water, sun, moon,
stars — are foolish but less foolish than those who worship handmade
idols. They have at least worshiped something powerful. They have failed
to reason from the beauty of created things to the Creator who made
them, but they have not descended to the absurdity of worshiping carved
wood (verses 1–9).

Second, those who worship handmade images are absurd. The carpenter who
carves a piece of wood, picking the best of his stock for use as a tool
and the leftover scraps to make into a god, has produced an idol from
material that was not even good enough for the carpenter's actual work.
The idol, made from the leftover wood, is then prayed to for life and
prosperity (verses 10–19).

Third, the chapter sets up the indictment that runs through chapter 14:
that idolatry is the source of all the social and moral disorder that
follows in human society — the corruption of marriage, of family, of
civic order, of justice. Worshiping the creature corrupts the worshiper.

The framework of this Series finds two things.

First, the parallel to Romans 1:18–32 is exact in structure. Paul's
argument that the nations failed to honor the Creator, that they
exchanged the glory of the incorruptible Elohim (God) for images of corruptible
things, that this exchange led to the moral disorder he then catalogues,
is the same argument Wisdom 13–14 makes.

Set the two passages next to each other and the dependence is
unmistakable. Wisdom 13:1: Surely vain are all men by nature, who are
ignorant of Elohim (God), and could not out of the good things that are seen know
him that is: neither by considering the works did they acknowledge the
workmaster. Romans 1:20: For the invisible things of him from the
creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things
that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are
without excuse. Wisdom 13:5: For by the greatness and beauty of the
creatures proportionately the maker of them is seen. Romans 1:19:
Because that which may be known of Elohim (God) is manifest in them; for Elohim (God) has
shown it unto them. Wisdom 13:10: But miserable are they, and in dead
things is their hope, who called them gods, which are the works of men's
hands. Romans 1:23: And changed the glory of the uncorruptible Elohim (God) into
an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted
beasts, and creeping things. Wisdom 14:12: For the devising of idols was
the beginning of spiritual fornication, and the invention of them the
corruption of life. Romans 1:24–25: Wherefore Elohim (God) also gave them up to
uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts, to dishonour their
own bodies between themselves: who changed the truth of Elohim (God) into a lie,
and worshiped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is
blessed for ever. Amen.

Paul is drawing on the second-temple Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish) wisdom
tradition. The framework of this Series, which holds that Paul wrote
within the literary world of the apocryphal corpus and drew on its
vocabulary and arguments, finds in Wisdom 13 the precise text Paul was
leaning on. The reader who has been trained by inherited Christianity to
think of Romans 1 as a Christian innovation will be quietly corrected:
the argument is in the second-temple wisdom tradition, and Paul carried
it into the apostolic writing because it was already part of the
literary world of his audience. The methodological sequence for reading
Paul lands precisely here. Step one — establish what Paul was drawing
from: Wisdom 13–14, the Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish) polemic against
pagan idolatry built on Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10. Step two — identify
what Paul was arguing against: the surrounding Greco-Roman idolatry he
was rebutting in his Romans audience, and (in Romans 2:1ff) the Yahudi
(Jewish) reader's pride that imagined the Yahudi (Jewish) community was
exempt from the same critique. The framework holds the sequence whole.

This is one of the framework's specific anchors for the methodological
sequence for reading Paul. Step one: establish what Paul was drawing
from. Romans 1 is drawing from the second-temple wisdom tradition's
polemic against idolatry, particularly Wisdom 13–14, and behind that
from the prophetic polemic of Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10. Step two:
identify what Paul was arguing against. He is arguing against the
idolatry of the surrounding Greco-Roman culture and against the way that
idolatry has produced the moral disorder he then catalogues in Romans
1:24–32. Paul is not introducing a new condemnation of "the Gentiles" as
if they were a wholly different category from his Yahudi (Jewish)
audience. He is rehearsing the second-temple wisdom polemic that his
Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish) readers already knew, and then turning the
same logic back on his Yahudi (Jewish) readers in Romans 2:1ff to show
that they are not exempt. The argument is built on Wisdom 13–14. Read
Wisdom 13–14 first, and Romans 1 reads correctly.

Second, the chapter's principle that from the greatness and beauty of
the creatures proportionably the maker of them is seen (verse 5) is the
natural-theology principle Romans 1:20 articulates. The framework of
this Series does not endorse natural theology as the basis of saving
knowledge of Yahuah (God); the basis of saving knowledge is the covenant
revelation given through the Torah, the prophets, and ultimately Yahusha
(Jesus). But the framework does affirm that the creation testifies to
the Creator (Psalm 19), and that the failure of the nations to honor the
Creator they could see in His works is an indictment Paul builds on.

Cross-references: Psalm 19:1–6; Isaiah 40:18–26; Isaiah 44:9–20;
Jeremiah 10:1–16; Romans 1:18–32; Romans 2:1–11; Acts 17:22–31; 1
Corinthians 8:4–6.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 14

  1 Again, one preparing himself to sail, and about to pass through the
  raging waves, calls upon a piece of wood more rotten than the vessel
  that carrieth him. 2 For verily desire of gain devised that, and the
  workman built it by his skill. 3 But your providence, O Father,
  governeth it: for you have made a way in the sea, and a safe path in
  the waves; 4 Shewing that you can save from all danger: yes, though a
  man went to sea without art. 5 Nevertheless you would not that the
  works of your wisdom should be idle, and therefore do men commit their
  lives to a small piece of wood, and passing the rough sea in a weak
  vessel are saved.

  6 For in the old time also, when the proud giants perished, the hope
  of the world governed by your hand escaped in a weak vessel, and left
  to all ages a seed of generation. 7 For blessed is the wood by which
  righteousness comes. 8 But that which is made with hands is cursed, as
  well it, as he that made it: he, because he made it; and it, because,
  being corruptible, it was called god. 9 For the ungodly and his
  ungodliness are both alike hateful to Yahuah (God). 10 For that which
  is made shall be punished together with him that made it.

  11 Therefore even upon the idols of the Gentiles shall there be a
  visitation: because in the creature of Yahuah (God) they are become an
  abomination, and stumblingblocks to the souls of men, and a snare to
  the feet of the unwise. 12 For the devising of idols was the beginning
  of spiritual fornication, and the invention of them the corruption of
  life. 13 For neither were they from the beginning, neither shall they
  be for ever. 14 For by the vain glory of men they entered into the
  world, and therefore shall they come shortly to an end. 15 For a
  father afflicted with untimely mourning, when he has made an image of
  his child soon taken away, now honoured him as a god, which was then a
  dead man, and delivered to those that were under him ceremonies and
  sacrifices.

  16 Thus in process of time an ungodly custom grown strong was kept as
  a law, and graven images were worshipped by the commandments of kings.
  17 Whom men could not honour in presence, because they dwelt far off,
  they took the counterfeit of his visage from far, and made an express
  image of a king whom they honoured, to the end that by this their
  forwardness they might flatter him that was absent, as if he were
  present. 18 Also the singular diligence of the artificer did help to
  set forward the ignorant to more superstition. 19 For he, perhaps
  willing to please one in authority, forced all his skill to make the
  resemblance of the best fashion. 20 And so the multitude, allured by
  the grace of the work, took him now for a god, which a little before
  was but honoured.

  21 And this was an occasion to deceive the world: for men, serving
  either calamity or tyranny, did ascribe to stones and stocks the
  incommunicable name. 22 Moreover this was not enough for them, that
  they erred in the knowledge of Yahuah (God); but whereas they lived in
  the great war of ignorance, those so great plagues called they peace.
  23 For while they slew their children in sacrifices, or used secret
  ceremonies, or made revellings of strange rites; 24 They kept neither
  lives nor marriages any longer undefiled: but either one slew another
  traiterously, or grieved him by adultery. 25 So that there reigned in
  all men without exception blood, manslaughter, theft, and
  dissimulation, corruption, unfaithfulness, tumults, perjury,

  26 Disquieting of good men, forgetfulness of good turns, defiling of
  souls, changing of kind, disorder in marriages, adultery, and
  shameless uncleanness. 27 For the worshipping of idols not to be named
  is the beginning, the cause, and the end, of all evil. 28 For either
  they are mad when they be merry, or prophesy lies, or live unjustly,
  or else lightly forswear themselves. 29 For insomuch as their trust is
  in idols, which have no life; though they swear falsely, yet they look
  not to be hurt. 30 Howbeit for both causes shall they be justly
  punished: both because they thought not well of Yahuah (God), giving
  heed to idols, and also unjustly swore in deceit, despising holiness.

  31 For it is not the power of them by whom they swear: but it is the
  just vengeance of sinners, that punishes always the offence of the
  ungodly.

⸻

Commentary

The polemic against idolatry continues. The chapter develops the
historical origins of idolatry (verses 12–21) — that it began with
parents commemorating dead children with images, with kings
commemorating their absent rulers with images, and that the practices
grew into full religious systems — and then catalogues the moral
disorders that follow from idolatry (verses 22–31).

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's account of how idolatry began is one of the few
apocryphal explanations of the historical origin of pagan religion. The
account treats idolatry as a development from grief and political
flattery, not as a primal religious instinct. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the human heart's natural movement is toward
the Creator unless it is captured by inherited systems of false worship,
finds in Wisdom 14's account a consistent articulation: the idolatry was
not original. It developed. It captured generations who inherited it
from their parents. The same pattern holds for the inherited systems the
awakening reader has walked out of: they were not original, they
developed, they have captured generations who inherited them. The
pattern of inherited deception is the pattern Wisdom 14 names in its
second-temple form.

The framework's central pastoral claim — that those still inside the
four houses are deceived victims, not enemies — finds its second-temple
anchor in Wisdom 14's account of how idolatry began. A father, afflicted
with untimely mourning, when he had made an image of his child soon
taken away, now honoured him as a god, which was then a dead man, and
delivered to those that were under him ceremonies and sacrifices. The
first father was not malicious. He was grieving. He made an image to
remember his son. Within a generation, that image was being honored as a
god. Within several generations, the practice had become a religion. By
the time the great-grandsons inherited it, they were worshiping the dead
boy without remembering why or who he had been. The deception was
inherited in good faith from a grieving father. This is exactly the
framework's reading of how the four houses came to be: not malicious
origins, not deliberate deception, but inherited frameworks that began
under specific historical pressures and grew into systems that captured
the generations who inherited them. The deceived in the contemporary
religious systems are not different in kind from the great-grandsons of
Wisdom 14's grieving father. They have inherited what they were handed.
The framework's mercy toward them is the framework's reading of Wisdom
14.

Second, the catalogue of moral disorders that follow from idolatry
(verses 22–31) is parallel to Romans 1:24–32. Both texts argue that the
worship of the creature produces the corruption of social order — the
breaking of marriages, the perversion of relations, the spread of murder
and theft and false witness. The framework of this Series, which holds
that the worship of Yahuah (God) according to the Torah is the
foundation of right social order and that the abandonment of His worship
is the foundation of social disintegration, finds in Wisdom 14 the
second-temple precedent for what Paul will articulate in Romans 1.

Cross-references: Genesis 4:1–24; Genesis 6:1–7; Romans 1:18–32; Romans
13:11–14; Galatians 5:19–21; Ephesians 5:1–14; 1 Peter 4:1–6; 2 Peter
2:1–22.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 15

  1 But you, O Yahuah (God), art gracious and true, longsuffering, and
  in mercy ordering all things, 2 For if we sin, we are yours, knowing
  your power: but we will not sin, knowing that we are counted yours. 3
  For to know you is perfect righteousness: yes, to know your power is
  the root of immortality. 4 For neither did the mischievous invention
  of men deceive us, nor an image spotted with divers colours, the
  painter’s fruitless labour; 5 The sight of which enticeth fools to
  lust after it, and so they desire the form of a dead image, that has
  no breath.

  6 Both they that make them, they that desire them, and they that
  worship them, are lovers of evil things, and are worthy to have such
  things to trust upon. 7 For the potter, tempering soft earth,
  fashioneth every vessel with much labour for our service: yes, of the
  same clay he makes both the vessels that serve for clean uses, and
  likewise also all such as serve to the contrary: but what is the use
  of either sort, the potter himself is the judge. 8 And employing his
  labours lewdly, he makes a vain god of the same clay, even he which a
  little before was made of earth himself, and within a little while
  after returns to the same, out when his life which was lent him shall
  be demanded. 9 Notwithstanding his care is, not that he shall have
  much labour, nor that his life is short: but striveth to excel
  goldsmiths and silversmiths, and endeavoureth to do like the workers
  in brass, and counteth it his glory to make counterfeit things. 10 His
  heart is ashes, his hope is more vile than earth, and his life of less
  value than clay:

  11 Forasmuch as he knew not his Maker, and him that inspired into him
  an active soul, and breathed in a living spirit. 12 But they counted
  our life a pastime, and our time here a market for gain: for, say
  they, we must be getting every way, though it be by evil means. 13 For
  this man, that of earthly matter makes brittle vessels and graven
  images, knoweth himself to offend above all others. 14 And all the
  enemies of your people, that hold them in subjection, are most
  foolish, and are more miserable than very babes. 15 For they counted
  all the idols of the heathen to be gods: which neither have the use of
  eyes to see, nor noses to draw breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers
  of hands to handle; and as for their feet, they are slow to go.

  16 For man made them, and he that borrowed his own spirit fashioned
  them: but no man can make a god like to himself. 17 For being mortal,
  he works a dead thing with wicked hands: for he himself is better than
  the things which he worshippeth: whereas he lived once, but they
  never. 18 Yea, they worshipped those beasts also that are most
  hateful: for being compared together, some are worse than others. 19
  Neither are they beautiful, so much as to be desired in respect of
  beasts: but they went without the praise of Yahuah (God) and his
  blessing.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter contains a brief but substantive theological digression.
Verses 1–3 articulate that knowing Yahuah (God) is the way of
immortality and that confessing His power is the root of righteousness.
Verses 4–6 satirize the maker of idols — the potter who shapes clay
vessels for various uses and then makes one to be his god. Verses 7–13
develop the satire and indict the deceiver. Verses 14–19 conclude with
the absurdity of idol-worship illustrated by Egypt's worship of animals.

The framework finds three things.

First, verses 1–3 are one of the great compressed statements of the
second-temple theology of salvation: But you, O Elohim (God), are gracious and
true, longsuffering, and in mercy ordering all things. For if we sin, we
are yours, knowing your power: but we will not sin, knowing that we are
counted yours. For to know you is perfect righteousness: yea, to know
your power is the root of immortality. The framework of this Series,
which holds that knowing Yahuah (God) means keeping His commandments
(the 1234 of Truth), finds in this passage the second-temple
articulation of the same principle. To know Yahuah (God) is to be in
covenant relationship with Him, which manifests in the keeping of His
commandments. The principle is consistent across the Torah, the
prophets, the wisdom literature, and the apostolic writings.

The verse — to know you is perfect righteousness — is the second-temple
voice articulating what John 17:3 will articulate in apostolic
vocabulary: And this is life eternal, that they might know you the only
true Elohim (God), and Yahusha (Jesus), whom you have sent. To know is not merely
to have intellectual information about. To know in the Hebrew sense is
relational knowing — covenant knowing, the kind a husband knows a wife,
the kind a son knows a father. The 1234 filter (1 John 2:3–4) names this
kind of knowing precisely: hereby do we know that we know him, if we
keep his commandments. The covenant knowing manifests in the covenant
walk. Wisdom 15:3 is one breath of the same theology that runs from the
Torah through the prophets through the wisdom tradition through the
apostles.

Second, the satire of the potter who makes a clay vessel and then makes
a god from the same clay (verses 7–13) is parallel to Isaiah 44:9–20 and
to Jeremiah 18:1–10. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
institutional Christian worship of statues, images, and relics is a form
of the same potter's-clay idolatry the prophets condemned, finds in
Wisdom 15's satire the second-temple voice making the same indictment.

Third, the indictment of Egypt's animal-worship (verses 14–19) is
consistent with the prophetic tradition. The Egyptians worshiped what
