crawled and what swam and what flew — and they worshiped them as gods.
The framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening of the
remnant requires the recognition that the systems of the world are full
of inherited absurdities that the believer's eyes have been opened to
see, finds in Wisdom 15 the second-temple recognition of one such
absurdity. The same posture the awakening reader takes toward the
inherited systems of contemporary religion is the posture the
second-temple Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish) tradition took toward the
Egyptians' worship of cats and crocodiles.

Cross-references: Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 18:1–10; Romans 9:19–24; 1
John 2:3–4; Hosea 4:6; John 17:3.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 16

  1 Therefore by the like were they punished worthily, and by the
  multitude of beasts tormented. 2 Instead of which punishment, dealing
  graciously with your own people, you preparedst for them meat of a
  strange taste, even quails to stir up their appetite: 3 To the end
  that they, desiring food, might for the ugly sight of the beasts sent
  among them lothe even that, which they must needs desire; but these,
  suffering penury for a short space, might be made partakers of a
  strange taste. 4 For it was requisite, that upon them exercising
  tyranny should come penury, which they could not avoid: but to these
  it should only be shewed how their enemies were tormented. 5 For when
  the horrible fierceness of beasts came upon these, and they perished
  with the stings of crooked serpents, your wrath endured not for ever:

  6 But they were troubled for a small season, that they might be
  admonished, having a sign of salvation, to put them in remembrance of
  the commandment of your law. 7 For he that turned himself toward it
  was not saved by the thing that he saw, but by you, that are the
  Saviour of all. 8 And in this you madest your enemies confess, that it
  is you who deliverest from all evil: 9 For them the bitings of
  grasshoppers and flies killed, neither was there found any remedy for
  their life: for they were worthy to be punished by such. 10 But your
  sons not the very teeth of venomous dragons overcame: for your mercy
  was ever by them, and healed them.

  11 For they were pricked, that they should remember your words; and
  were quickly saved, that not falling into deep forgetfulness, they
  might be continually mindful of your goodness. 12 For it was neither
  herb, nor mollifying plaister, that restored them to health: but your
  word, O Yahuah (God), which healeth all things. 13 For you have power
  of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up
  again. 14 A man indeed killeth through his malice: and the spirit,
  when it is gone forth, returns not; neither the soul received up comes
  again. 15 But it is not possible to escape yours hand.

  16 For the ungodly, that denied to know you, were scourged by the
  strength of your arm: with strange rains, hails, and showers, were
  they persecuted, that they could not avoid, and through fire were they
  consumed. 17 For, which is most to be wondered at, the fire had more
  force in the water, that quenches all things: for the world fighteth
  for the righteous. 18 For sometime the flame was mitigated, that it
  might not burn up the beasts that were sent against the ungodly; but
  themselves might see and perceive that they were persecuted with the
  judgment of Yahuah (God). 19 And at another time it burneth even in
  the midst of water above the power of fire, that it might destroy the
  fruits of an unjust land. 20 Instead of which you feddest your own
  people with angels’ food, and did send them from heaven bread prepared
  without their labour, able to content every man’s delight, and
  agreeing to every taste.

  21 For your sustenance declared your sweetness to your children, and
  serving to the appetite of the eater, tempered itself to every man’s
  liking. 22 But snow and ice endured the fire, and melted not, that
  they might know that fire burning in the hail, and sparkling in the
  rain, did destroy the fruits of the enemies. 23 But this again did
  even forget his own strength, that the righteous might be nourished.
  24 For the creature that serveth you, who are the Maker increaseth his
  strength against the unrighteous for their punishment, and abateth his
  strength for the benefit of such as put their trust in you. 25
  Therefore even then was it altered into all fashions, and was obedient
  to your grace, that nourishes all things, according to the desire of
  them that had need:

  26 That your children, O Yahuah (God), whom you lovest, might know,
  that it is not the growing of fruits that nourishes man: but that it
  is your word, which preserves them that put their trust in you. 27 For
  that which was not destroyed of the fire, being warmed with a little
  sunbeam, soon melted away: 28 That it might be known, that we must
  prevent the sun to give you thanks, and at the dayspring pray to you.
  29 For the hope of the unthankful shall melt away as the winter’s hoar
  frost, and shall run away as unprofitable water.

⸻

Commentary

The retrospective on Egypt and the wilderness continues. The chapter
contrasts how Yahuah (God) used the same created elements to bless
Yashar'el (Israel) and curse Egypt — locusts and flies for Egypt, manna
for Yashar'el (Israel); serpents to bite Egypt and the bronze serpent
for Yashar'el (Israel)'s healing; the elements obeying Yahuah (God)
against Egypt and serving Yashar'el (Israel).

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's pattern of contrast between Egypt and Yashar'el
(Israel) is the second-temple theology of the Exodus narrative.

The Exodus is the foundational covenant-deliverance narrative, and the
prophets repeatedly cite it as the type of the future restoration.
Isaiah 11:15–16: And Yahuah (God) shall utterly destroy the tongue of
the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over
the river... And there shall be an highway for the remnant of his
people, which shall be left, from Assyria; like as it was to Yashar'el
(Israel) in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt. Jeremiah
16:14–15: Therefore, behold, the days come, says Yahuah (God), that it
shall no more be said, Yahuah (God) lives, that brought up the children
of Yashar'el (Israel) out of the land of Egypt; but, Yahuah (God) lives,
that brought up the children of Yashar'el (Israel) from the land of the
north, and from all the lands whither he had driven them: and I will
bring them again into their land that I gave unto their fathers. Hosea
11:1: When Yashar'el (Israel) was a child, then I loved him, and called
my son out of Egypt. The Exodus pattern repeats: the covenant people
scattered, Yahuah (God) gathering, the deliverance from the imperial
power. 1 Corinthians 10:1–11 brings the typology forward into apostolic
vocabulary: the Exodus events were examples (Greek tupoi, types) for
those of later generations.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the Exodus is the
historical type of the larger redemption — the deliverance of the
covenant people from the powers that have scattered them — finds in
Wisdom 16 the second-temple articulation of that typological reading.

Second, verses 5–14 develop the bronze serpent narrative (Numbers
21:4–9) with theological reflection. The bronze serpent was not an idol;
it was a sign that the people who looked on it in faith were healed not
by the bronze but by Yahuah (God) who had appointed the sign.

Numbers 21:8–9 records the Torah account: And Yahuah (God) said unto
Moses, Make you a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall
come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looks upon it,
shall live. And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole,
and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he
beheld the serpent of brass, he lived. John 3:14–15 brings the typology
forward to Yahusha: And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the
wilderness, even so must the Son of Adam be lifted up: that whosoever
believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. John 12:32 —
Yahusha himself: And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all
men unto me.

The typology is precise. The Israelites were dying from the serpents'
bites; Adamic humanity dies under the curse of the fall. Moses set the
bronze serpent on a pole; Yahuah (God) set the Messiah on the cross. The
bitten Israelites looked at the bronze serpent and lived; the believing
reader looks to the Messiah and lives. The cross-reference also runs to
2 Kings 18:4 — Hezekiah breaking the bronze serpent (Nehushtan) when
later generations had begun to worship it as an idol. The same object
that healed under Moses became an idol under Hezekiah's predecessors.
The pattern: what Yahuah (God) appoints as sign can be turned by later
inheritance into idol when the sign is worshiped instead of the One it
points to. The framework's reading of inherited religious symbols across
the four houses applies the same principle. The cross itself, when
worshiped as a relic, becomes the Nehushtan of contemporary
Christianity. The framework holds the warning. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the apostolic theology of the Messiah's lifting
up (John 3:14–15) is built on the bronze-serpent typology, finds in
Wisdom 16 the second-temple precedent for that typological reading. The
bronze serpent saves not by its own power but as the appointed sign of
Yahuah (God). The Messiah on the cross saves not as a charm but as the
Formed One offered in the appointed atonement. Both work the same way:
faith in what Yahuah (God) has appointed.

Cross-references: Exodus 16:1–36; Numbers 11:31–35; Numbers 21:4–9;
Deuteronomy 8:2–4; John 3:14–15; John 6:30–58; 1 Corinthians 10:1–11.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 17

  1 For great are your judgments, and cannot be expressed: therefore
  unnurtured souls have erred. 2 For when unrighteous men thought to
  oppress the holy nation; they being shut up in their houses, the
  prisoners of darkness, and fettered with the bonds of a long night,
  lay there exiled from the eternal providence. 3 For while they
  supposed to lie hid in their secret sins, they were scattered under a
  dark veil of forgetfulness, being horribly astonished, and troubled
  with strange apparitions. 4 For neither might the corner that held
  them keep them from fear: but noises as of waters falling down sounded
  about them, and sad visions appeared to them with heavy countenances.
  5 No power of the fire might give them light: neither could the bright
  flames of the stars endure to lighten that horrible night.

  6 Only there appeared to them a fire kindled of itself, very dreadful:
  for being much terrified, they thought the things which they saw to be
  worse than the sight they saw not. 7 As for the illusions of art
  magick, they were put down, and their vaunting in wisdom was reproved
  with disgrace. 8 For they, that promised to drive away terrors and
  troubles from a sick soul, were sick themselves of fear, worthy to be
  laughed at. 9 For though no terrible thing did fear them; yet being
  scared with beasts that passed by, and hissing of serpents, 10 They
  died for fear, denying that they saw the air, which could of no side
  be avoided.

  11 For wickedness, condemned by her own witness, is very timorous, and
  being pressed with conscience, always forecasteth grievous things. 12
  For fear is nothing else but a betraying of the succours which reason
  offers. 13 And the expectation from within, being less, counteth the
  ignorance more than the cause which brings the torment. 14 But they
  sleeping the same sleep that night, which was indeed intolerable, and
  which came upon them out of the bottoms of inevitable hell, 15 Were
  partly vexed with monstrous apparitions, and partly fainted, their
  heart failing them: for a sudden fear, and not looked for, came upon
  them.

  16 So then whoever there fell down was straitly kept, shut up in a
  prison without iron bars, 17 For whether he were husbandman, or
  shepherd, or a labourer in the field, he was overtaken, and endured
  that necessity, which could not be avoided: for they were all bound
  with one chain of darkness. 18 Whether it were a whistling wind, or a
  melodious noise of birds among the spreading branches, or a pleasing
  fall of water running violently, 19 Or a terrible sound of stones cast
  down, or a running that could not be seen of skipping beasts, or a
  roaring voice of most savage wild beasts, or a rebounding echo from
  the hollow mountains; these things made them to swoon for fear. 20 For
  the whole world shined with clear light, and none were hindered in
  their labour:

  21 Over them only was spread an heavy night, an image of that darkness
  which should afterward receive them: but yet were they to themselves
  more grievous than the darkness.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter focuses on the plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21–29) and its
effect on the Egyptians. The argument: the darkness that fell on Egypt
was not merely physical darkness; it was the manifestation of the inner
darkness of those who had lived without the knowledge of Yahuah (God).
The Egyptians were terrified of phantoms and noises in the darkness —
terrors that came not from external threats but from the darkness inside
their own consciences.

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's psychology — that those who have lived without the
light of Yahuah (God) inhabit a deeper darkness when their familiar
daylight is removed — is one of the great second-temple meditations on
the moral consequences of unbelief. The framework of this Series, which
holds that the awakening reader who walks out of the four houses
experiences a season of disorientation as the inherited certainties
dissolve and that the disorientation is itself a form of mercy (the
false light is being removed so the true light can emerge), finds in
Wisdom 17 the second-temple voice articulating that disorientation in
its Egyptian form. The Egyptians' darkness was the manifestation of what
their hearts had been all along; the awakening reader's disorientation
is the manifestation of what the inherited systems were never able to
address.

Second, the chapter's reminder (verse 21) that the children of Yahuah
(God) had light during the plague of darkness — the same physical
environment, the same time, the same place, but the covenant people had
light while the Egyptians had darkness — is the second-temple
theological articulation of what Goshen experienced. The same external
circumstances produce different experiences depending on whether the
heart is in covenant with Yahuah (God) or in opposition to Him. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening reader walks
through the same world but sees by a different light, finds in Wisdom 17
the prototype of that double-vision.

Cross-references: Exodus 10:21–29; John 1:1–14; John 3:18–21; John 8:12;
John 12:35–36; 1 John 1:5–7.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 18

  1 Nevertheless your saints had a very great light, whose voice they
  hearing, and not seeing their shape, because they also had not
  suffered the same things, they counted them happy. 2 But for that they
  did not hurt them now, of whom they had been wronged before, they
  thanked them, and besought them pardon for that they had been enemies.
  3 Instead of which you gavest them a burning pillar of fire, both to
  be a guide of the unknown journey, and an harmless sun to entertain
  them honourably. 4 For they were worthy to be deprived of light and
  imprisoned in darkness, who had kept your sons shut up, by whom the
  uncorrupt light of the law was to be given to the world. 5 And when
  they had determined to slay the babes of the saints, one child being
  cast forth, and saved, to reprove them, you tookest away the multitude
  of their children, and destroyedst them altogether in a mighty water.

  6 Of that night were our fathers certified afore, that assuredly
  knowing to what oaths they had given credence, they might afterwards
  be of good cheer. 7 So of your people was accepted both the salvation
  of the righteous, and destruction of the enemies. 8 For with which you
  did punish our adversaries, by the same you did glorify us, whom you
  had called. 9 For the righteous children of good men did sacrifice
  secretly, and with one consent made a holy law, that the saints should
  be like partakers of the same good and evil, the fathers now singing
  out the songs of praise. 10 But on the other side there sounded an ill
  according cry of the enemies, and a lamentable noise was carried
  abroad for children that were bewailed.

  11 The master and the servant were punished after one manner; and like
  as the king, so suffered the common person. 12 So they all together
  had innumerable dead with one kind of death; neither were the living
  sufficient to bury them: for in one moment the noblest offspring of
  them was destroyed. 13 For whereas they would not believe any thing by
  reason of the enchantments; upon the destruction of the firstborn,
  they acknowledged this people to be the sons of Yahuah (God). 14 For
  while all things were in quiet silence, and that night was in the
  midst of her swift course, 15 Your Almighty word leaped down from
  heaven out of your royal throne, as a fierce man of war into the midst
  of a land of destruction,

  16 And brought your unfeigned commandment as a sharp sword, and
  standing up filled all things with death; and it touched the heaven,
  but it stood upon the earth. 17 Then suddenly visions of horrible
  dreams troubled them sore, and terrors came upon them unlooked for. 18
  And one thrown here, and another there, half dead, shewed the cause of
  his death. 19 For the dreams that troubled them did foreshew this,
  lest they should perish, and not know why they were afflicted. 20 Yea,
  the tasting of death touched the righteous also, and there was a
  destruction of the multitude in the wilderness: but the wrath endured
  not long.

  21 For then the blameless man made haste, and stood forth to defend
  them; and bringing the shield of his proper ministry, even prayer, and
  the propitiation of incense, set himself against the wrath, and so
  brought the calamity to an end, declaring that he was your servant. 22
  So he overcame the destroyer, not with strength of body, nor force of
  arms, but with a word subdued him that punished, alleging the oaths
  and covenants made with the fathers. 23 For when the dead were now
  fallen down by heaps one upon another, standing between, he stayed the
  wrath, and parted the way to the living. 24 For in the long garment
  was the whole world, and in the four rows of the stones was the glory
  of the fathers graven, and your Majesty upon the diadem of his head.
  25 To these the destroyer gave place, and was afraid of them: for it
  was enough that they only tasted of the wrath.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues with the death of the Egyptian firstborn and the
deliverance of Yashar'el (Israel) through the sea. The chapter contains
one of the most striking second-temple meditations on the Word of Yahuah
(God) as the active executor of judgment.

Verses 14–16 are the climax: For while all things were in quiet silence,
and that night was in the midst of her swift course, your Almighty word
leaped down from heaven out of your royal throne, as a fierce man of war
into the midst of a land of destruction, and brought your unfeigned
commandment as a sharp sword, and standing up filled all things with
death; and it touched the heaven, but it stood upon the earth.

The framework finds three things.

First, the personification of the Word as the active divine executor is
one of the second-temple Christology-precedent passages. The Word leaps
down from the throne. The Word stands upon the earth. The Word is
described in personal-active terms. The framework of this Series, which
holds that the Word — the Formed One — is the active divine presence in
the Old Testament narratives, finds in Wisdom 18:14–16 the second-temple
voice articulating that active presence in unmistakable terms. The
apostle John's prologue in John 1, where the Word becomes flesh and
dwells among us, is operating in the same vocabulary that Wisdom 18 had
already used. The reader who has been retrained on the framework's
understanding of the Father and the Formed One will recognize Wisdom 18
as the second-temple precedent.

The image is worth letting press. Your Almighty word leaped down from
heaven... as a fierce man of war... and standing up filled all things
with death; and it touched the heaven, but it stood upon the earth. The
Word stands upon the earth and touches the heaven simultaneously. He is
from above; he stands below. He is the bridge between heaven and earth —
drawn from the formless source, sent into the formed world, executing
the will of the Father. This is the Christology of John 1 (the Word was
made flesh, and dwelt among us) and of Hebrews 1 (who being the
brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person... when he
had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the
Majesty on high) in second-temple wisdom-vocabulary. The Word reaches
from heaven to earth. The Messiah reached from heaven to earth. Same
Word. Different mode of his coming.

Second, the chapter develops the contrast between the Egyptian firstborn
dying and the Israelite firstborn being preserved by the blood of the
Passover lamb (verses 9–13). The framework of this Series, which holds
that the Passover is the type of the Messiah's atoning death (1
Corinthians 5:7), finds in Wisdom 18 the second-temple articulation of
the same typology. The blood saves. The blood was foreshadowing the
blood that would come.

Third, the chapter records the priestly intercession of Aaron during the
plague that broke out in the wilderness when the people murmured (verses
20–25, referencing Numbers 16:46–48). The principle: the priesthood
stands between the wrath and the people. The framework of this Series,
which holds that the Messiah's priesthood is the permanent priesthood
that Hebrews articulates and that Aaron's intercession was the type of
that permanent priesthood, finds in Wisdom 18 the second-temple
recognition of the priestly principle.

Cross-references: Exodus 11:1–10; Exodus 12:1–51; Numbers 16:41–50; John
1:1–18; 1 Corinthians 5:7; Hebrews 4:14–16; Hebrews 7:23–28; Revelation
19:11–16.

The Wisdom of Solomon — Chapter 19

  1 As for the ungodly, wrath came upon them without mercy to the end:
  for he knew before what they would do; 2 How that having given them
  leave to depart, and sent them hastily away, they would repent and
  pursue them. 3 For while they were yet mourning and making lamentation
  at the graves of the dead, they added another foolish device, and
  pursued them as fugitives, whom they had intreated to be gone. 4 For
  the destiny, of which they were worthy, drew them to this end, and
  made them forget the things that had already happened, that they might
  fulfil the punishment which was wanting to their torments: 5 And that
  your people might pass a wonderful way: but they might find a strange
  death.

  6 For the whole creature in his proper kind was fashioned again anew,
  serving the peculiar commandments that were given to them, that your
  children might be kept without hurt: 7 As namely, a cloud shadowing
  the camp; and where water stood before, dry land appeared; and out of
  the Red sea a way without impediment; and out of the violent stream a
  green field: 8 Wherethrough all the people went that were defended
  with your hand, seeing your marvellous strange wonders. 9 For they
  went at large like horses, and leaped like lambs, praising you, O
  Yahuah (God), who hadst delivered them. 10 For they were yet mindful
  of the things that were done while they sojourned in the strange land,
  how the ground brought forth flies instead of cattle, and how the
  river cast up a multitude of frogs instead of fishes.

  11 But afterwards they saw a new generation of fowls, when, being led
  with their appetite, they asked delicate meats. 12 For quails came up
  to them from the sea for their contentment. 13 And punishments came
  upon the sinners not without former signs by the force of thunders:
  for they suffered justly according to their own wickedness, insomuch
  as they used a more hard and hateful behaviour toward strangers. 14
  For the Sodomites did not receive those, whom they knew not when they
  came: but these brought friends into bondage, that had well deserved
  of them. 15 And not only so, but perhaps some respect shall be had of
  those, because they used strangers not friendly:

  16 But these very grievously afflicted them, whom they had received
  with feastings, and were already made partakers of the same laws with
  them. 17 Therefore even with blindness were these stricken, as those
  were at the doors of the righteous man: when, being compassed about
  with horrible great darkness, every one sought the passage of his own
  doors. 18 For the elements were changed in themselves by a kind of
  harmony, like as in a psaltery notes change the name of the tune, and
  yet are always sounds; which may well be perceived by the sight of the
  things that have been done. 19 For earthly things were turned into
  watery, and the things, that before swam in the water, now went upon
  the ground. 20 The fire had power in the water, forgetting his own
  virtue: and the water forgat his own quenching nature.

  21 On the other side, the flames wasted not the flesh of the
  corruptible living things, though they walked in it; neither melted
  they the icy kind of heavenly meat that was of nature apt to melt. 22
  For in all things, O Yahuah (God), you did magnify your people, and
  glorify them, neither did you lightly regard them: but did assist them
  in every time and place.

⸻

Commentary

The closing chapter records the deliverance through the sea, the
destruction of the Egyptian army, and a final theological reflection on
how the elements of creation were rearranged in service of Yahuah
(God)'s purposes for both Yashar'el (Israel) and Egypt.

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's argument that the elements of creation themselves
were rearranged in service of Yahuah (God)'s redemption (the sea opened
for Yashar'el (Israel) and closed on Egypt; the cloud led Yashar'el
(Israel) by day and gave light to them by night while it was darkness to
the Egyptians; the manna fell from heaven; the rocks gave water) is the
second-temple articulation of what the prophets and apostles will both
echo: the creation is in Yahuah (God)'s hand, and the creation will be
brought into the redemption of His own. Romans 8:18–25 names the
creation groaning and waiting for the redemption of the sons of Yahuah
(God). Wisdom 19 is the second-temple precedent for that apostolic
articulation.

Second, the closing of the book (verse 22) is brief but pointed: For in
all things, O Lord, you have magnified your people, and glorified them:
neither have you lightly regarded them: but stood by them in every time
and place. The proper close. The covenant has not been forgotten. Yahuah
(God) has stood by His own. The framework of this Series, which holds
that the gathering of the scattered seed is the long restoration of the
same covenant the patriarchs received, finds in the closing of the
Wisdom of Solomon the right shape: praise to Yahuah (God) for what He
has done with His people, expectation of what He will do, and the
enduring confidence that He has not lightly regarded those He has
called.

The phrase your people in this closing verse is the closing affirmation
of the bloodline-remnant claim that runs through the Wisdom of Solomon.
The book is not addressed to "anyone who will believe." The book is the
confession of the seed of Jacob, in diaspora in Alexandria, articulating
their covenant inheritance against the surrounding paganism of Egypt.
Your people. The named seed. The covenant lineage. In every time and
place. The Father has stood by them across centuries of dispersion, in
every nation where they have been scattered, and is bringing them home.
The framework reads the closing verse as the same closing the prophets
gave. The covenant is the covenant. The seed is the seed. The gathering
is appointed.

Cross-references: Exodus 14:1–31; Exodus 15:1–21; Joshua 24:1–18; Psalm
78:1–72; Psalm 105:1–45; Psalm 106:1–48; Romans 8:18–39; Hebrews
11:1–40.

Ecclesiasticus — Introduction

Ecclesiasticus, also called the Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach or
simply Sirach, is the longest book in the Apocrypha at fifty-one
chapters. It was composed in Hebrew around 180 BCE by Jesus the son of
Sirach (a contemporary name; not Yahusha the Messiah), a teacher in
Jerusalem, and translated into Greek by his grandson around 132 BCE. The
Hebrew original was lost for most of church history but partially
recovered in the Cairo Genizah and at Qumran in the twentieth century,
confirming that the book was originally a Hebrew composition and that
the Greek translation in the Septuagint represents a faithful rendering
of the Hebrew.

The book is a long aggregation of proverbial wisdom — practical, moral,
theological — covering virtually every subject a second-temple Yahudi
(Jew) in Jerusalem would have considered worth teaching to a younger
man. Friendship, family, finance, food, women, wine, work, honor, shame,
prayer, the Torah, the priesthood, the prophets, the kings, and the long
line of fathers — all of it is present, and all of it is composed in the
proverbial cadence of the Hebrew wisdom tradition. The book reads like
Proverbs amplified to full chapter length. The reader who has read
Proverbs in their Old Testament will recognize the cadence and the shape
immediately.

For the awakening reader, three things matter about Sirach.

First, Sirach is the most explicit second-temple witness to the
integration of Torah and wisdom. In chapter 24, wisdom is personified —
and then identified explicitly as the Torah of Yahuah (God) (Sirach
24:23). This identification is not an abstract theological move; it is
the second-temple Hebrew tradition naming what the Torah, the prophets,
and the writings have always implied: that wisdom, in its highest sense,
is not a separate body of knowledge from the Torah. Wisdom is the
application of the Torah to the lived life of the covenant community.
The two are not in competition. The Hebrew roots and Torah-observant
communities of the awakening movement, who have rightly insisted on the
centrality of the Torah, will find in Sirach a second-temple witness
that integrates wisdom and Torah into a single tradition. The
institutional Christian reader, who has been trained to think of wisdom
as a generic category separate from the law, will find his or her
training corrected.

Second, Sirach 44–50 is "the praise of the fathers" — a long
retrospective hymn to the great figures of Yashar'el (Israel)'s covenant
history, from Enoch and Noah through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the
patriarchs, Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, the judges, Samuel,
Nathan, David, Solomon, Elijah, Elisha, Hezekiah, Isaiah, Jeremiah,
Ezekiel, the twelve minor prophets, Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest,
Nehemiah, and Simon the high priest (a contemporary of the author). It
is one of the great catalogues of covenant memory in any literature — a
parallel to Hebrews 11 in the New Testament. Read it for the cadence,
for the cumulative weight of remembering the long line of Yahuah (God)'s
faithfulness through specific named men. The book of Hebrews, when it
composes its own catalogue of faith in chapter 11, is writing in the
genre Sirach 44–50 had already established. The apostolic letter is
doing what the second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) wisdom teacher was already
doing.

Third, Sirach has uneven theology. It is not the prophets. It contains
passages whose treatment of women, of slaves, of the poor, and of the
dead reflects the cultural assumptions of its time more than the
prophetic correctives the prophets gave. It also contains passages whose
practical wisdom is so fine that it is quoted in the Talmud, in the
early church, and in the New Testament (the writer of James in
particular leans on Sirach so directly that the parallels are difficult
to overlook). The reader who comes to Sirach expecting prophetic-grade
material will be sometimes lifted and sometimes baffled. Take it for
what it is: the most accomplished second-temple Hebrew wisdom book, with
the full unevenness that comes with being a wisdom collection rather
than a prophetic oracle.

The 1234 filter applies. Wherever Sirach's counsel sharpens or softens
what the Torah commands, the Torah is the standard. Wherever Sirach's
portrait of the priesthood inflates the Levitical service beyond what
the prophets allowed, the prophets are the standard. Wherever Sirach's
theology of suffering, of the world to come, or of the resurrection is
silent or unclear, the apostolic witness is the standard. Sirach is a
witness — a long, rich, sometimes exhausting witness — and the reader
hears it best when the reader holds the Torah and the prophets and the
apostolic witness as the standard against which the witness is tested.

Ecclesiasticus is the longest book in the Apocrypha and the longest
sustained wisdom collection in the second-temple corpus. Its commentary
is organized chapter by chapter; for the proverbial chapters that
aggregate wisdom across many small sayings, the commentary names the
chapter's principal themes, identifies the framework-relevant moments,
and lets the proverbial cadence carry the reader. For the more
theologically substantive chapters — the great hymn to wisdom in chapter
24, the meditation on physicians and the trades in chapter 38, the
praise of the fathers in chapters 44–50, the closing prayer of the
grandson — the commentary runs heavier. Hold the rhythm of reading: the
source text speaks first, the commentary responds, and the reader
carries the cross-references forward.

A word about Ben Sira (the author) before the chapter-by-chapter begins.
The book was composed in Hebrew in Jerusalem around 180 BCE by a teacher
of Torah named Yeshua ben Eleazar ben Sira, and was translated into
Greek in Egypt around 132 BCE by his grandson, who wrote the prologue
that is preserved in the Greek manuscripts. This places Ecclesiasticus
immediately before the Hellenization crisis of 175 BCE — the events that
1 and 2 Maccabees record. The author was writing as a Torah-faithful
sage in the last generation of Jerusalem before the assault on the Torah
by Antiochus IV. His framework, his vocabulary, and his theology are
pre-crisis. He represents the second-temple wisdom tradition at its most
mature and most uncompromised. The reader who has been told that
Ecclesiasticus is "Hellenized Yahudi (Jewish) wisdom" should put that
frame down. Ben Sira was writing against the Hellenizing pressures of
his own day, not in conformity to them. He was a Torah man through and
through.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 1

  1 All wisdom comes from Yahuah (God), and is with him for ever. 2 Who
  can number the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of
  eternity? 3 Who can find out the height of heaven, and the breadth of
  the earth, and the deep, and wisdom? 4 Wisdom has been created before
  all things, and the understanding of prudence from everlasting. 5 The
  word of Yahuah (God) most high is the fountain of wisdom; and her ways
  are everlasting commandments.

  6 To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed? or who has known her
  wise counsels? 7 To whom has the knowledge of wisdom been made
  manifest? and who has understood her great experience? 8 There is one
  wise and greatly to be feared, Yahuah (God) sitting upon his throne. 9
  He created her, and saw her, and numbered her, and poured her out upon
  all his works. 10 She is with all flesh according to his gift, and he
  has given her to them that love him.

  11 The fear of Yahuah (God) is honour, and glory, and gladness, and a
  crown of rejoicing. 12 The fear of Yahuah (God) makes a merry heart,
  and gives joy, and gladness, and a long life. 13 Whoso fears Yahuah
  (God), it shall go well with him at the last, and he shall find favour
  in the day of his death. 14 To fear Yahuah (God) is the beginning of
  wisdom: and it was created with the faithful in the womb. 15 She has
  built an everlasting foundation with men, and she shall continue with
  their seed.

  16 To fear Yahuah (God) is fulness of wisdom, and filleth men with her
  fruits. 17 She filleth all their house with things desirable, and the
  garners with her increase. 18 The fear of Yahuah (God) is a crown of
  wisdom, making peace and perfect health to flourish; both which are
  the gifts of Yahuah (God): and it enlargeth their rejoicing that love
  him. 19 Wisdom raineth down skill and knowledge of understanding
  standing, and exalteth them to honour that hold her fast. 20 The root
  of wisdom is to fear Yahuah (God), and the branches thereof are long
  life.

  21 The fear of Yahuah (God) drives away sins: and where it is present,
  it turns away wrath. 22 A furious man cannot be justified; for the
  sway of his fury shall be his destruction. 23 A patient man will tear
  for a time, and afterward joy shall spring up to him. 24 He will hide
  his words for a time, and the lips of many shall declare his wisdom.
  25 The parables of knowledge are in the treasures of wisdom: but
  godliness is an abomination to a sinner.

  26 If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and Yahuah (God) shall
  give her to you. 27 For the fear of Yahuah (God) is wisdom and
  instruction: and faith and meekness are his delight. 28 Distrust not
  the fear of Yahuah (God) when you are poor: and come not to him with a
  double heart. 29 Be not an hypocrite in the sight of men, and take
  good heed what you speak. 30 Exalt not thyself, lest you fall, and
  bring dishonour upon your soul, and so Yahuah (God) discover your
  secrets, and cast you down in the midst of the congregation, because
  you camest not in truth to the fear of Yahuah (God), but your heart is
  full of deceit.

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter establishes the theology of wisdom: all wisdom comes
from Yahuah (God), and the fear of Yahuah (God) is the beginning of
wisdom. The chapter is consistent with Proverbs 1–9 in cadence and
theology. Verse 14 — "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" —
is the same principle Proverbs 1:7 articulates. The framework of this
Series finds nothing controversial here. The 1234 filter (1 John 2:3–4 —
that he that says he knows Yahuah (God) and keeps not His commandments
is a liar) is operating in the chapter's understanding that wisdom is
not separable from the keeping of the commandments (verse 26: If you
desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and Yahuah (God) shall give her to
you).

The opening verses set a frame the entire book will work within. Wisdom
is not a philosophical abstraction. Wisdom is not a Greek arete or a
Stoic detachment. Wisdom is the active ordering presence of Yahuah (God)
in the universe, given specifically to those who fear Him and walk in
His commandments.

The "fear of Yahuah (God) = beginning of wisdom" formula is one of the
most repeated formulas in the canonical wisdom literature. Proverbs 1:7:
The fear of Yahuah (God) is the beginning of knowledge: but fools
despise wisdom and instruction. Proverbs 9:10: The fear of Yahuah (God)
is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is
understanding. Job 28:28: And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the
Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding. Psalm
111:10: The fear of Yahuah (God) is the beginning of wisdom: a good
understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endures
for ever. Ecclesiastes 12:13: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole
matter: Fear Elohim (God), and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty
of man. Five canonical witnesses naming the same formula. Sirach 1:14
stands inside this canonical line: the fear of the Lord is the beginning
of wisdom. Sirach is not innovating; Sirach is repeating what Job,
Solomon, the Psalter, and Ecclesiastes had already said.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the Torah is the wisdom
of Yahuah (God) given in covenant form to Yashar'el (Israel) and that
the contemporary Christian opposition between wisdom (treated as
universal) and law (treated as Yahudi (Jewish) particular) is one of the
foundational deceptions, finds in Sirach 1 the second-temple voice
articulating exactly the framework's claim. There is no wisdom apart
from the fear of Yahuah (God). There is no fear of Yahuah (God) apart
from the keeping of His commandments. The seeker who looks elsewhere —
to philosophy, to meditation traditions, to modern self-help, to the
various inherited frameworks of the four houses — is not seeking wisdom.
He is seeking what wisdom is not.

Cross-references: Proverbs 1:1–7; Proverbs 9:10; Job 28:28; Psalm
111:10; Ecclesiastes 12:13; James 1:5; 1 John 2:3–4; Deuteronomy 4:5–8;
Psalm 19:7–11; Psalm 119:97–104.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 2

  1 My son, if you come to serve Yahuah (God), prepare your soul for
  temptation. 2 Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, and make
  not haste in time of trouble. 3 Cleave to him, and depart not away,
  that you may be increased at your last end. 4 Whatsoever is brought
  upon you take cheerfully, and be patient when you are changed to a low
  estate. 5 For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the
  furnace of adversity.

  6 Believe in him, and he will help you; order your way aright, and
  trust in him. 7 You that fear Yahuah (God), wait for his mercy; and go
  not aside, lest you fall. 8 You that fear Yahuah (God), believe him;
  and your reward shall not fail. 9 You that fear Yahuah (God), hope for
  good, and for everlasting joy and mercy. 10 Look at the generations of
  old, and see; did ever any trust in Yahuah (God), and was confounded?
  or did any abide in his fear, and was forsaken? or whom did he ever
  despise, that called upon him?

  11 For Yahuah (God) is full of compassion and mercy, longsuffering,
  and very pitiful, and forgiveth sins, and saves in time of affliction.
  12 Woe be to fearful hearts, and faint hands, and the sinner that goes
  two ways! 13 Woe to him that is fainthearted! for he believes not;
  therefore shall he not be defended. 14 Woe to you that have lost
  patience! and what will you do when Yahuah (God) shall visit you? 15
  They that fear Yahuah (God) will not disobey his Word; and they that
  love him will keep his ways.

  16 They that fear Yahuah (God) will seek that which is well, pleasing
  to him; and they that love him shall be filled with the law. 17 They
  that fear Yahuah (God) will prepare their hearts, and humble their
  souls in his sight, 18 Saying, We will fall into the hands of Yahuah
  (God), and not into the hands of men: for as his majesty is, so is his
  mercy.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses the trial and testing of those who would serve
Yahuah (God). Verses 1–6 contain one of the most quoted second-temple
wisdom passages: My son, if you come to serve Yahuah (God), prepare your
soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, and
make not haste in time of trouble. Cleave to him, and depart not away,
that you may be increased at your last end. Whatever is brought upon you
take cheerfully, and be patient when you are changed to a low estate.
For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of
adversity. The framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening
reader's walk includes seasons of trial in which the inherited
certainties are stripped away and the covenant identity is tested, finds
in Sirach 2:1–6 the second-temple voice naming what the awakening reader
is experiencing. The trial is part of the appointed walk. The endurance
is the work.

The contemporary application is direct. The reader who has begun to walk
out of one of the four houses is in the furnace. The relationships that
were built on the inherited framework strain. The certainties that were
given by the inherited teachers are exposed. The financial, social, and
emotional costs of the awakening are real. Sirach 2 is the second-temple
voice naming this exact experience and saying: prepare your soul for it;
do not haste; do not depart; cleave; the testing is the appointed
working. The gold is being tried. The acceptable man is being shown what
he is made of. The framework holds the trial as the means by which the
seed is refined for the gathering.

Cross-references: Job 23:10; Malachi 3:1–4; James 1:2–12; 1 Peter 1:6–9;
Romans 5:1–5; 2 Corinthians 4:16–18; Hebrews 12:1–11.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 3

  1 Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be
  safe. 2 For Yahuah (God) has given the father honour over the
  children, and has confirmed the authority of the mother over the sons.
  3 Whoso honoureth his father makes an atonement for his sins: 4 And he
  that honoureth his mother is as one that layeth up treasure. 5 Whoso
  honoureth his father shall have joy of his own children; and when he
  makes his prayer, he shall be heard.

  6 He that honoureth his father shall have a long life; and he that is
  obedient to Yahuah (God) shall be a comfort to his mother. 7 He that
  fears Yahuah (God) will honour his father, and will do service to his
  parents, as to his masters. 8 Honour your father and mother both in
  word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from them. 9 For the
  blessing of the father establishes the houses of children; but the
  curse of the mother rooteth out foundations. 10 Glory not in the
  dishonour of your father; for your father’s dishonour is no glory to
  you.

  11 For the glory of a man is from the honour of his father; and a
  mother in dishonour is a reproach to the children. 12 My son, help
  your father in his age, and grieve him not as long as he lives. 13 And
  if his understanding fail, have patience with him; and despise him not
  when you are in your full strength. 14 For the relieving of your
  father shall not be forgotten: and instead of sins it shall be added
  to build you up. 15 In the day of your affliction it shall be
  remembered; your sins also shall melt away, as the ice in the fair
  warm weather.

  16 He that forsaketh his father is as a blasphemer; and he that
  angereth his mother is cursed: of Yahuah (God). 17 My son, go on with
  your business in meekness; so shall you be beloved of him that is
  approved. 18 The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you
  shall find favour before Yahuah (God). 19 Many are in high place, and
  of renown: but mysteries are revealed to the meek. 20 For the power of
  Yahuah (God) is great, and he is honoured of the lowly.

  21 Seek not out things that are too hard for you, neither search the
  things that are above your strength. 22 But what is commanded you,
  think thereupon with reverence, for it is not needful for you to see
  with your eyes the things that are in secret. 23 Be not curious in
  unnecessary matters: for more things are shewed to you than men
  understand. 24 For many are deceived by their own vain opinion; and an
  evil suspicion has overthrown their judgment. 25 Without eyes you
  shall want light: profess not the knowledge therefore that you have
  not.

  26 A stubborn heart shall fare evil at the last; and he that loves
  danger shall perish in it. 27 An obstinate heart shall be laden with
  sorrows; and the wicked man shall heap sin upon sin. 28 In the
  punishment of the proud there is no remedy; for the plant of
  wickedness has taken root in him. 29 The heart of the prudent will
  understand a parable; and an attentive ear is the desire of a wise
  man. 30 Water will quench a flaming fire; and alms makes an atonement
  for sins.

  31 And he that requiteth good turns is mindful of that which may come
  hereafter; and when he falls, he shall find a stay.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter develops the commandment to honor parents. Verses 1–16 are
an extended meditation on the fifth commandment of the Decalogue — that
honoring father and mother is foundational to covenant life and that the
blessing on long life is conditional on the keeping of this commandment.
The framework of this Series, which holds that the Torah's commandments
are the standard for covenant life and that the fifth commandment
governs the covenant household across generations, finds in Sirach 3 the
second-temple amplification of what the Torah had commanded. Verses
17–20 turn to humility: the proper attitude in success is humility, not
pride. Verse 21 contains a famous saying: Seek not what is too hard for
you, neither search the things that are above your strength.

The fifth commandment is one of the framework's quiet anchors. The
covenant household is built across generations. The fathers receive what
they were given by their fathers; the sons receive it from the fathers
and pass it to the next generation; the inheritance is preserved by
honor. The contemporary cultural pattern of severing the generations —
the autonomous individual, the rejection of inherited wisdom, the
elevation of personal preference over the wisdom of the elders — is a
cultural pattern Sirach 3 would not recognize as wisdom. It is rebellion
under modern costume. The framework's reading of Jeremiah 16:19 (Our
fathers have inherited lies) is not a license to dishonor the fathers
but a recognition that the fathers themselves were under deception
inherited from their fathers. The honor remains. The lies are named. The
father is loved as the deceived victim he was, not as the enemy.

Cross-references: Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16; Ephesians 6:1–4;
Colossians 3:20; Proverbs 22:6; Matthew 15:1–9; Mark 7:9–13; Jeremiah
16:19.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 4

  1 My son, defraud not the poor of his living, and make not the needy
  eyes to wait long. 2 Make not an hungry soul sorrowful; neither
  provoke a man in his distress. 3 Add not more trouble to an heart that
  is vexed; and defer not to give to him that is in need. 4 Reject not
  the supplication of the afflicted; neither turn away your face from a
  poor man. 5 Turn not away your eye from the needy, and give him none
  occasion to curse you:

  6 For if he curse you in the bitterness of his soul, his prayer shall
  be heard of him that made him. 7 Get thyself the love of the
  congregation, and bow your head to a great man. 8 Let it not grieve
  you to bow down your ear to the poor, and give him a friendly answer
  with meekness. 9 Deliver him that suffers wrong from the hand of the
  oppressor; and be not fainthearted when you sittest in judgment. 10 Be
  as a father to the fatherless, and instead of an husband to their
  mother: so shall you be as the son of the Most High, and he shall love
  you more than your mother does.

  11 Wisdom exalteth her children, and layeth hold of them that seek
  her. 12 He that loves her loves life; and they that seek to her early
  shall be filled with joy. 13 He that holdeth her fast shall inherit
  glory; and wherever she entereth, Yahuah (God) will bless. 14 They
  that serve her shall minister to the Holy One: and them that love her
  Elohim (God) does love. 15 Whoso gives ear to her shall judge the
  nations: and he that attendeth to her shall dwell securely.

  16 If a man commit himself to her, he shall inherit her; and his
  generation shall hold her in possession. 17 For at the first she will
  walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him, and
  torment him with her discipline, until she may trust his soul, and try
  him by her laws. 18 Then will she return the straight way to him, and
  comfort him, and shew him her secrets. 19 But if he go wrong, she will
  forsake him, and give him over to his own ruin. 20 Observe the
  opportunity, and beware of evil; and be not ashamed when it concerneth
  your soul.

  21 For there is a shame that brings sin; and there is a shame which is
  glory and grace. 22 Accept no person against your soul, and let not
  the reverence of any man cause you to fall. 23 And refrain not to
  speak, when there is occasion to do good, and hide not your wisdom in
  her beauty. 24 For by speech wisdom shall be known: and learning by
  the word of the tongue. 25 In no wise speak against the truth; but be
  abashed of the error of your ignorance.

  26 Be not ashamed to confess your sins; and force not the course of
  the river. 27 Make not thyself an underling to a foolish man; neither
  accept the person of the mighty. 28 Strive for the truth to death, and
  Yahuah (God) shall fight for you. 29 Be not hasty in your tongue, and
  in your deeds slack and remiss. 30 Be not as a lion in your house, nor
  frantick among your servants.

  31 Let not yours hand be stretched out to receive, and shut when you
  should repay.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses care for the poor and the seeking of wisdom.
Verses 1–10 enumerate the obligations of the covenant member toward the
poor, the orphan, the widow, the stranger — a catalogue parallel to
Deuteronomy 24 and James 1:27. Verses 11–19 develop the seeking of
wisdom as a relationship: wisdom raises up her sons, embraces those who
hold her, leads them by paths that test them. Verses 20–28 emphasize the
importance of speaking the truth, of standing for righteousness, of not
letting fear silence the witness. The framework of this Series, which
honors the covenant community's care for the vulnerable and which holds
that the awakening reader speaks the truth even when speaking it is
costly, finds in Sirach 4 the second-temple model.

Verses 20–28 land for the awakening reader with particular force. Strive
for the truth unto death, and the Lord shall fight for you... Be not
ashamed to speak the truth concerning your soul... let your speech be
true... be as one that knows and yet holds his tongue. The
watchman/corrector posture the framework calls for is articulated here
in second-temple wisdom vocabulary. Speak when speech is required. Hold
the tongue when silence is required. Do not be ashamed of the truth. Do
not be intimidated into falsehood by the social pressure of the
deceived. The awakening reader who has been counted strange by his
former community for naming what was always there is being told, by
Sirach 4, that this striving for truth is the same striving the
second-temple sages articulated.

Cross-references: Deuteronomy 24:17–22; Proverbs 14:31; Proverbs 19:17;
Isaiah 1:17; James 1:27; James 2:1–13; Matthew 25:31–46; 1 John 3:17–18;
Proverbs 31:8–9.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 5

  1 Set your heart upon your goods; and say not, I have enough for my
  life. 2 Follow not your own mind and your strength, to walk in the
  ways of your heart: 3 And say not, Who shall controul me for my works?
  for Yahuah (God) will surely revenge your pride. 4 Say not, I have
  sinned, and what harm has happened to me? for Yahuah (God) is
  longsuffering, he will in no wise let you go. 5 Concerning
  propitiation, be not without fear to add sin to sin:

  6 And say not His mercy is great; he will be pacified for the
  multitude of my sins: for mercy and wrath come from him, and his
  indignation resteth upon sinners. 7 Make no tarrying to turn to Yahuah
  (God), and put not off from day to day: for suddenly shall the wrath
  of Yahuah (God) come forth, and in your security you shall be
  destroyed, and perish in the day of vengeance. 8 Set not yours heart
  upon goods unjustly gotten, for they shall not profit you in the day
  of calamity. 9 Winnow not with every wind, and go not into every way:
  for so does the sinner that has a double tongue. 10 Be stedfast in
  your understanding; and let your word be the same.

  11 Be swift to hear; and let your life be sincere; and with patience
  give answer. 12 If you have understanding, answer your neighbour; if
  not, lay your hand upon your mouth. 13 Honour and shame is in talk:
  and the tongue of man is his fall. 14 Be not called a whisperer, and
  lie not in wait with your tongue: for a foul shame is upon the thief,
  and an evil condemnation upon the double tongue. 15 Be not ignorant of
  any thing in a great matter or a small.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter warns against trusting in riches and against presuming on
Yahuah (God)'s mercy as license to continue in sin. Verses 1–8 warn
against complacency: Say not, I have sinned, and what harm has happened
to me? for the Lord is longsuffering, he will in no wise let you go.
Verses 9–17 develop the importance of right speech — not slandering, not
double-tonguing, not bearing false witness. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the 1234 filter applies to every reading and
that grace does not abolish the standard, finds in Sirach 5 the
second-temple voice articulating the same principle: Yahuah (God)'s
patience is real, but His patience does not erase the standard.

The contemporary Christian framework that has produced "once saved,
always saved" theology is a direct violation of the warning Sirach 5
articulates and that the apostolic letters reinforce (Romans 6:1–2,
Hebrews 10:26–31). The patience of Yahuah (God) is not a license. The
grace of Yahuah (God) does not exempt the believer from the standard.
The framework reads Sirach 5 as a second-temple voice telling the
awakening reader exactly what the contemporary Christian softening has
tried to dismiss: there is judgment for the sinner who presumes on
grace; the standard is the standard; mercy is for the repentant, not for
the rationalizing.

Cross-references: Romans 2:4; Romans 6:1–2; 2 Peter 3:9; Ecclesiastes
8:11; Proverbs 16:5; James 3:1–12; Matthew 12:33–37; Exodus 20:16;
Hebrews 10:26–31.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 6

  1 Instead of a friend become not an enemy; for thereby you shall
  inherit an ill name, shame, and reproach: even so shall a sinner that
  has a double tongue. 2 Extol not thyself in the counsel of your own
  heart; that your soul be not torn in pieces as a bull straying alone.
  3 You shall eat up your leaves, and lose your fruit, and leave thyself
  as a dry tree. 4 A wicked soul shall destroy him that has it, and
  shall make him to be laughed to scorn of his enemies. 5 Sweet language
  will multiply friends: and a fairspeaking tongue will increase kind
  greetings.

  6 Be in peace with many: nevertheless have but one counsellor of a
  thousand. 7 If you would get a friend, prove him first and be not
  hasty to credit him. 8 For some man is a friend for his own occasion,
  and will not abide in the day of your trouble. 9 And there is a
  friend, who being turned to enmity, and strife will discover your
  reproach. 10 Again, some friend is a companion at the table, and will
  not continue in the day of your affliction.

  11 But in your prosperity he will be as thyself, and will be bold over
  your servants. 12 If you be brought low, he will be against you, and
  will hide himself from your face. 13 Separate thyself from your
  enemies, and take heed of your friends. 14 A faithfull friend is a
  strong defence: and he that has found such an one has found a
  treasure. 15 Nothing does countervail a faithful friend, and his
  excellency is invaluable.

  16 A faithful friend is the medicine of life; and they that fear
  Yahuah (God) shall find him. 17 Whoso fears Yahuah (God) shall direct
  his friendship aright: for as he is, so shall his neighbour be also.
  18 My son, gather instruction from your youth up: so shall you find
  wisdom till your old age. 19 Come to her as one that ploweth and sows,
  and wait for her good fruits: for you shall not toil much in labouring
  about her, but you shall eat of her fruits right soon. 20 She is very
  unpleasant to the unlearned: he that is without understanding will not
  remain with her.

  21 She will lie upon him as a mighty stone of trial; and he will cast
  her from him ere it be long. 22 For wisdom is according to her name,
  and she is not manifest to many. 23 Give ear, my son, receive my
  advice, and refuse not my counsel, 24 And put your feet into her
  fetters, and your neck into her chain. 25 Bow down your shoulder, and
  bear her, and be not grieved with her bonds.

  26 Come to her with your whole heart, and keep her ways with all your
  power. 27 Search, and seek, and she shall be made known to you: and
  when you have got hold of her, let her not go. 28 For at the last you
  shall find her rest, and that shall be turned to your joy. 29 Then
  shall her fetters be a strong defence for you, and her chains a robe
  of glory. 30 For there is a golden ornament upon her, and her bands
  are purple lace.

  31 You shall put her on as a robe of honour, and shall put her about
  you as a crown of joy. 32 My son, if you will, you shall be taught:
  and if you will apply your mind, you shall be prudent. 33 If you love
  to hear, you shall receive understanding: and if you bow your ear, you
  shall be wise, 34 Stand in the multitude of the elders; and cleave to
  him that is wise. 35 Be willing to hear every godly discourse; and let
  not the parables of understanding escape you.

  36 And if you see a man of understanding, get you betimes to him, and
  let your foot wear the steps of his door. 37 Let your mind be upon the
  ordinances of Yahuah (God) and meditate continually in his
  commandments: he shall establish yours heart, and give you wisdom at
  your owns desire.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter develops two themes: the dangers of rash speech and the
value of true friendship. Verses 1–4 warn against being captured by
one's own lusts and being made desolate by one's own appetites. Verses
5–17 contain one of the great second-temple meditations on friendship:
that true friends are rare, that they are tested in adversity, that they
are to be honored as treasures, and that the best friend is one who
fears Yahuah (God). Verses 18–37 close with an extended exhortation to
seek wisdom by submitting to her discipline, even when the discipline is
hard. The framework of this Series, which honors the awakening reader's
relationships with those who fear Yahuah (God) and which holds that the
discipline of seeking wisdom is the foundation of long covenant
faithfulness, finds in Sirach 6 the second-temple wisdom on both
subjects.

The friendship passage matters for the awakening reader in a specific
way. The walk out of one of the four houses costs friendships. The
relationships built inside the inherited framework cannot all survive
the awakening; some will, and they will be the ones Sirach 6:14–17
describes. A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that has found
such a one has found a treasure. Nothing does countervail a faithful
friend, and his excellency is invaluable. A faithful friend is the
medicine of life; and they that fear the Lord shall find him. The
friendships that survive the awakening are the ones grounded in mutual
fear of Yahuah (God). The friendships that do not are the ones grounded
in the inherited framework that has been set down. The framework's
correction to the awakened reader's grief over lost friendships is here:
the deepest friendships are the ones the wise of the people share with
the wise of the people. They are rare. They are appointed. They are the
gift the awakening produces.

Cross-references: Proverbs 17:17; Proverbs 18:24; Proverbs 27:6; John
15:13–15; James 4:1–4; 2 Timothy 2:22; Hebrews 12:5–11; Ecclesiastes
4:9–12.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 7

  1 Do no evil, so shall no harm come to you. 2 Depart from the unjust,
  and iniquity shall turn away from you. 3 My son, sow not upon the
  furrows of unrighteousness, and you shall not reap them sevenfold. 4
  Seek not of Yahuah (God) preeminence, neither of the king the seat of
  honour. 5 justify not thyself before Yahuah (God); and boast not of
  your wisdom before the king.

  6 Seek not to be judge, being not able to take away iniquity; lest at
  any time you fear the person of the mighty, an stumblingblock in the
  way of your uprightness. 7 Offend not against the multitude of a city,
  and then you shall not cast thyself down among the people. 8 Bind not
  one sin upon another; for in one you shall not be unpunished. 9 Say
  not, Yahuah (God) will look upon the multitude of my oblations, and
  when I offer to the most high Yahuah (God), he will accept it. 10 Be
  not fainthearted when you makest your prayer, and neglect not to give
  alms.

  11 Laugh no man to scorn in the bitterness of his soul: for there is
  one which humbleth and exalteth. 12 Devise not a lie against your
  brother; neither do the like to your friend. 13 Use not to make any
  manner of lie: for the custom thereof is not good. 14 Use not many
  words in a multitude of elders, and make not much babbling when you
  prayest. 15 Hate not laborious work, neither husbandry, which the Most
  High has ordained.

  16 Number not thyself among the multitude of sinners, but remember
  that wrath will not tarry long. 17 Humble thyself greatly: for the
  vengeance of the ungodly is fire and worms. 18 Change not a friend for
  any good by no means; neither a faithful brother for the gold of
  Ophir. 19 Forego not a wise and good woman: for her grace is above
  gold. 20 Whereas your servant works truly, entreat him not evil, nor
  the hireling that bestoweth himself wholly for you.

  21 Let your soul love a good servant, and defraud him not of liberty.
  22 Have you cattle? have an eye to them: and if they be for your
  profit, keep them with you. 23 Have you children? instruct them, and
  bow down their neck from their youth. 24 Have you daughters? have a
  care of their body, and shew not thyself cheerful toward them. 25
  Marry your daughter, and so shall you have performed a weighty matter:
  but give her to a man of understanding.

  26 Have you a wife after your mind? forsake her not: but give not
  thyself over to a light woman. 27 Honour your father with your whole
  heart, and forget not the sorrows of your mother. 28 Remember that you
  were begotten of them; and how can you recompense them the things that
  they have done for you? 29 Fear Yahuah (God) with all your soul, and
  reverence his priests. 30 Love him that made you with all your
  strength, and forsake not his ministers.

  31 Fear Yahuah (God), and honor the priest; and give him his portion,
  as it is commanded you; the firstfruits, and the trespass offering,
  and the gift of the shoulders, and the sacrifice of sanctification,
  and the firstfruits of the holy things. 32 And stretch yours hand to
  the poor, that your blessing may be perfected. 33 A gift has grace in
  the sight of every man living; and for the dead detain it not. 34 Fail
  not to be with them that weep, and mourn with them that mourn. 35 Be
  not slow to visit the sick: for that shall make you to be beloved.

  36 Whatsoever you take in hand, remember the end, and you shall never
  do amiss.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is a long catalogue of practical wisdom: against ambition,
against false-swearing, against arrogance, in favor of humility, in
favor of the keeping of the commandments, in favor of honoring priests
and prophets and parents and slaves rightly. Verse 14 contains a
striking saying: Use not many words in a multitude of elders, and make
not much babbling when you pray. The principle anticipates Yahusha
(Jesus)' teaching on prayer in Matthew 6:7. Verse 36 contains the
closing wisdom: Whatever you take in hand, remember the end, and you
shall never do amiss.

The verse on prayer (Sirach 7:14) is a concrete example of why the New
Testament is not strange to the second-temple wisdom tradition. Yahusha
is not introducing a new principle when he warns against the babbling
prayers of the heathen in Matthew 6:7. He is repeating, in his own
teaching, what Ben Sira had already articulated nearly two centuries
before. The reader who has been told that Yahusha's teaching represents
a sharp break from "Old Testament religion" has been read out of
context. Yahusha's teaching is the Torah-and-wisdom tradition in its
full and matured form, addressed to the same covenant community in fresh
language. Sirach 7 is the second-temple voice that the audience of the
Sermon on the Mount had in their ears.

Cross-references: Matthew 6:7–8; James 1:19–20; Proverbs 16:32;
Ecclesiastes 7:8; Numbers 18:1–32; Deuteronomy 18:1–8; 1 Peter 5:6.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 8

  1 Strive not with a mighty man’ lest you fall into his hands. 2 Be not
  at variance with a rich man, lest he overweigh you: for gold has
  destroyed many, and perverted the hearts of kings. 3 Strive not with a
  man that is full of tongue, and heap not wood upon his fire. 4 Jest
  not with a rude man, lest your ancestors be disgraced. 5 Reproach not
  a man that turns from sin, but remember that we are all worthy of
  punishment.

  6 Dishonour not a man in his old age: for even some of us wax old. 7
  Rejoice not over your greatest enemy being dead, but remember that we
  die all. 8 Despise not the discourse of the wise, but acquaint thyself
  with their proverbs: for of them you shall learn instruction, and how
  to serve great men with ease. 9 Miss not the discourse of the elders:
  for they also learned of their fathers, and of them you shall learn
  understanding, and to give answer as need requires. 10 Kindle not the
  coals of a sinner, lest you be burnt with the flame of his fire.

  11 Rise not up in anger at the presence of an injurious person, lest
  he lie in wait to entrap you in your words 12 Lend not to him that is
  mightier than thyself; for if you lendest him, count it but lost. 13
  Be not surety above your power: for if you be surety, take care to pay
  it. 14 Go not to law with a judge; for they will judge for him
  according to his honour. 15 Travel not by the way with a bold fellow,
  lest he become grievous to you: for he will do according to his own
  will, and you shall perish with him through his folly.

  16 Strive not with an angry man, and go not with him into a solitary
  place: for blood is as nothing in his sight, and where there is no
  help, he will overthrow you. 17 Consult not with a fool; for he cannot
  keep counsel. 18 Do no secret thing before a stranger; for you know
  not what he will bring forth. 19 Open not yours heart to every man,
  lest he requite you with a shrewd turn.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter contains a series of cautions: against contention with the
powerful, against contention with the rich, against borrowing from those
above oneself, against trusting in any but the seasoned. The wisdom is
practical and second-temple culturally specific. The framework of this
Series finds nothing controversial; the wisdom is consistent with
Proverbs and serves the awakening reader who is learning how to navigate
the hierarchies of his or her culture without compromising the Torah.

Cross-references: Proverbs 22:7; Proverbs 24:21–22; Romans 13:1–7; 1
Peter 2:13–17; Ecclesiastes 8:2–4.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 9

  1 Be not jealous over the wife of your bosom, and teach her not an
  evil lesson against thyself. 2 Give not your soul to a woman to set
  her foot upon your substance. 3 Meet not with an harlot, lest you fall
  into her snares. 4 Use not much the company of a woman that is a
  singer, lest you be taken with her attempts. 5 Gaze not on a maid,
  that you fall not by those things that are precious in her.

  6 Give not your soul to harlots, that you lose not your inheritance. 7
  Look not round about you in the streets of the city, neither wander
  you in the solitary place thereof. 8 Turn away your eye from a
  beautiful woman, and look not upon another’s beauty; for many have
  been deceived by the beauty of a woman; for herewith love is kindled
  as a fire. 9 Sit not at all with another man’s wife, nor sit down with
  her in your arms, and spend not your money with her at the wine; lest
  yours heart incline to her, and so through your desire you fall into
  destruction. 10 Forsake not an old friend; for the new is not
  comparable to him: a new friend is as new wine; when it is old, you
  shall drink it with pleasure.

  11 Envy not the glory of a sinner: for you know not what shall be his
  end. 12 Delight not in the thing that the ungodly have pleasure in;
  but remember they shall not go unpunished to their grave. 13 Keep you
  far from the man that has power to kill; so shall you not doubt the
  fear of death: and if you come to him, make no fault, lest he take
  away your life presently: remember that you go in the midst of snares,
  and that you walkest upon the battlements of the city. 14 As near as
  you can, guess at your neighbour, and consult with the wise. 15 Let
  your talk be with the wise, and all your communication in the law of
  the Most High.

  16 And let just men eat and drink with you; and let your glorying be
  in the fear of Yahuah (God). 17 For the hand of the artificer the work
  shall be commended: and the wise ruler of the people for his speech.
  18 A man of an ill tongue is dangerous in his city; and he that is
  rash in his talk shall be hated.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is a long warning against improper relations with women,
against jealousy in marriage, against trusting strangers, and a closing
call to value the company of those who fear Yahuah (God). The
framework's reading: the chapter's specific second-temple cultural
assumptions about women should not be transferred uncritically into the
contemporary context (the chapter assumes a male reader and gives advice
on managing female relationships from that perspective). The principle
that the awakening reader values the company of those who fear Yahuah
(God) and avoids the company that would draw him or her away from the
covenant is consistent with the Torah and the apostolic witness, even
when the chapter's specific cultural articulations are time-conditioned.

Cross-references: Proverbs 5:1–23; Proverbs 7:1–27; 1 Corinthians 15:33;
2 Corinthians 6:14–18; Psalm 1:1–6; Hebrews 12:14.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 10

  1 A wise judge will instruct his people; and the government of a
  prudent man is well ordered. 2 As the judge of the people is himself,
  so are his officers; and what manner of man the ruler of the city is,
  such are all they that dwell in it. 3 An unwise king destroys his
  people; but through the prudence of them which are in authority the
  city shall be inhabited. 4 The power of the earth is in the hand of
  Yahuah (God), and in due time he will set over it one that is
  profitable. 5 In the hand of Yahuah (God) is the prosperity of man:
  and upon the person of the scribe shall he lay his honour.

  6 Bear not hatred to your neighbour for every wrong; and do nothing at
  all by injurious practices. 7 Pride is hateful before Yahuah (God) and
  man: and by both does one commit iniquity. 8 Because of unrighteous
  dealings, injuries, and riches got by deceit, the kingdom is
  translated from one people to another. 9 Why is earth and ashes proud?
  There is not a more wicked thing than a covetous man: for such an one
  sets his own soul to sale; because while he lives he casteth away his
  bowels. 10 The physician cutteth off a long disease; and he that is to
  day a king to morrow shall die.

  11 For when a man is dead, he shall inherit creeping things, beasts,
  and worms. 12 The beginning of pride is when one departs from Yahuah
  (God), and his heart is turned away from his Maker. 13 For pride is
  the beginning of sin, and he that has it shall pour out abomination:
  and therefore Yahuah (God) brought upon them strange calamities, and
  overthrew them utterly. 14 Yahuah (God) has cast down the thrones
  of proud princes, and set up the meek in their stead. 15 Yahuah
  (God) has plucked up the roots of the proud nations, and planted the
  lowly in their place.

  16 Yahuah (God) overthrew countries of the heathen, and destroyed
  them to the foundations of the earth. 17 He took some of them away,
  and destroyed them, and has made their memorial to cease from the
  earth. 18 Pride was not made for men, nor furious anger for them that
  are born of a woman. 19 They that fear Yahuah (God) are a sure seed,
  and they that love him an honourable plant: they that regard not the
  law are a dishonourable seed; they that transgress the commandments
  are a deceivable seed. 20 Among brothers he that is chief is
  honorable; so are they that fear Yahuah (God) in his eyes.

  21 The fear of Yahuah (God) goes before the obtaining of authority:
  but roughness and pride is the losing thereof. 22 Whether he be rich,
  noble, or poor, their glory is the fear of Yahuah (God). 23 It is not
  meet to despise the poor man that has understanding; neither is it
  convenient to magnify a sinful man. 24 Great men, and judges, and
  potentates, shall be honoured; yet is there none of them greater than
  he that fears Yahuah (God). 25 To the servant that is wise shall they
  that are free do service: and he that has knowledge will not grudge
  when he is reformed.

  26 Be not overwise in doing your business; and boast not thyself in
  the time of your distress. 27 Better is he that laboureth, and abounds
  in all things, than he that boasteth himself, and wanteth bread. 28 My
  son, glorify your soul in meekness, and give it honour according to
  the dignity thereof. 29 Who will justify him that sinneth against his
  own soul? and who will honour him that dishonoureth his own life? 30
  The poor man is honoured for his skill, and the rich man is honoured
  for his riches.

  31 He that is honoured in poverty, how much more in riches? and he
  that is dishonourable in riches, how much more in poverty?

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses leadership: the qualifications of rulers, the
dangers of pride, the dignity of the wise even when poor, the disgrace
of the proud even when rich. Verses 7–18 contain a sustained meditation
on the ruin of pride, naming the kings and empires that have fallen
because of pride. Verses 19–24 develop the principle that the fear of
Yahuah (God) is the foundation of true honor. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the corruption of authority within the covenant
community is one of the recurring sources of inherited deception, finds
in Sirach 10 the second-temple precedent for the same concerns. Honor
and authority are functions of the fear of Yahuah (God); pride and
corruption end the same way regardless of office.

The framework's principle of corrupt authority within the covenant
community lands here. Alcimus the high priest, named in 1 Maccabees 7,
was a son of Aaron in lineage; the lineage did not save the office from
corruption. Eli's sons in 1 Samuel 2 were of the Levitical priestly
line; sons of Belial within the priesthood. Sirach 10 articulates the
principle in advance: pride is the ruin of authority, and authority
severed from the fear of Yahuah (God) ends in disgrace regardless of
bloodline credentials. The framework holds this for the awakening
reader's discernment of the contemporary religious authority structures
of the four houses. Lineage is not legitimacy. Office is not
faithfulness. The fear of Yahuah (God) and the keeping of His
commandments is the only standard.

Cross-references: Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 29:23; Daniel 4:28–37; Isaiah
14:12–17; James 4:6–10; 1 Peter 5:5–6; Luke 14:7–11; 1 Samuel 2:12.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 11

  1 Wisdom lifteth up the head of him that is of low degree, and makes
