principle of covenant-faithful household life is consistent with the
Torah and the apostolic witness.

Cross-references: Proverbs 18:22; Proverbs 19:14; Ruth 4:13–17;
Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 7:1–16.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 27

  1 Many have sinned for a small matter; and he that seeks for abundance
  will turn his eyes away. 2 As a nail sticketh fast between the
  joinings of the stones; so does sin stick close between buying and
  selling. 3 Unless a man hold himself diligently in the fear of Yahuah
  (God), his house shall soon be overthrown. 4 As when one sifteth with
  a sieve, the refuse remains; so the filth of man in his talk. 5 The
  furnace proves the potter’s vessels; so the trial of man is in his
  reasoning.

  6 The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the
  utterance of a conceit in the heart of man. 7 Praise no man before you
  hear him speak; for this is the trial of men. 8 If you followest
  righteousness, you shall obtain her, and put her on, as a glorious
  long robe. 9 The birds will resort to their like; so will truth return
  to them that practise in her. 10 As the lion lieth in wait for the
  prey; so sin for them that work iniquity.

  11 The discourse of a godly man is always with wisdom; but a fool
  changeth as the moon. 12 If you be among the indiscreet, observe the
  time; but be continually among men of understanding. 13 The discourse
  of fools is irksome, and their sport is the wantonness of sin. 14 The
  talk of him that sweareth much makes the hair stand upright; and their
  brawls make one stop his ears. 15 The strife of the proud is
  bloodshedding, and their revilings are grievous to the ear.

  16 Whoso discovers secrets loses his credit; and shall never find
  friend to his mind. 17 Love your friend, and be faithful to him: but
  if you betrayest his secrets, follow no more after him. 18 For as a
  man has destroyed his enemy; so have you lost the love of your
  neighbor. 19 As one that letteth a bird go out of his hand, so have
  you let your neighbour go, and shall not get him again 20 Follow after
  him no more, for he is too far off; he is as a roe escaped out of the
  snare.

  21 As for a wound, it may be bound up; and after reviling there may be
  reconcilement: but he that betrayeth secrets is without hope. 22 He
  that winketh with the eyes works evil: and he that knoweth him will
  depart from him. 23 When you are present, he will speak sweetly, and
  will admire your words: but at the last he will writhe his mouth, and
  slander your sayings. 24 I have hated many things, but nothing like
  him; for Yahuah (God) will hate him. 25 Whoso casteth a stone on high
  casteth it on his own head; and a deceitful stroke shall make wounds.

  26 Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall in it: and he that sets a trap shall
  be taken in it. 27 He that works mischief, it shall fall upon him, and
  he shall not know whence it comes. 28 Mockery and reproach are from
  the proud; but vengeance, as a lion, shall lie in wait for them. 29
  They that rejoice at the fall of the righteous shall be taken in the
  snare; and anguish shall consume them before they die. 30 Malice and
  wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them
  both.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter contains varied wisdom about speech, about money, about
friendship. Verses 4–7 contain a striking observation: When you sift
with a sieve, the refuse remains; so the filth of man in his talk.
Verses 16–21 develop the principle that revealing a friend's secrets
ends the friendship. The framework finds in Sirach 27 the second-temple
wisdom on integrity in speech and relationships.

Cross-references: Matthew 7:1–5; James 3:1–12; Proverbs 17:9; Proverbs
25:9–10; Ephesians 4:25–32.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 28

  1 He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he
  will surely keep his sins in remembrance. 2 Forgive your neighbour the
  hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when
  you prayest. 3 One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek
  pardon from Yahuah (God)? 4 He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is
  like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins? 5 If he
  that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his
  sins?

  6 Remember your end, and let enmity cease; remember corruption and
  death, and abide in the commandments. 7 Remember the commandments, and
  bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the
  Highest, and wink at ignorance. 8 Abstain from strife, and you shall
  diminish your sins: for a furious man will kindle strife, 9 A sinful
  man disquieteth friends, and makes debate among them that be at peace.
  10 As the matter of the fire is, so it burneth: and as a man’s
  strength is, so is his wrath; and according to his riches his anger
  rises; and the stronger they are which contend, the more they will be
  inflamed.

  11 An hasty contention kindleth a fire: and an hasty fighting sheddeth
  blood. 12 If you blow the spark, it shall burn: if you spit upon it,
  it shall be quenched: and both these come out of your mouth. 13 Curse
  the whisperer and doubletongued: for such have destroyed many that
  were at peace. 14 A backbiting tongue has disquieted many, and driven
  them from nation to nation: strong cities has it pulled down, and
  overthrown the houses of great men. 15 A backbiting tongue has cast
  out virtuous women, and deprived them of their labours.

  16 Whoso hearkeneth to it shall never find rest, and never dwell
  quietly. 17 The stroke of the whip makes marks in the flesh: but the
  stroke of the tongue breaks the bones. 18 Many have fallen by the edge
  of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue. 19 Well is
  he that is defended through the venom thereof; who has not drawn the
  yoke thereof, nor has been bound in her bands. 20 For the yoke thereof
  is a yoke of iron, and the bands thereof are bands of brass.

  21 The death thereof is an evil death, the grave were better than it.
  22 It shall not have rule over them that fear Yahuah (God), neither
  shall they be burned with the flame thereof. 23 Such as forsake Yahuah
  (God) shall fall into it; and it shall burn in them, and not be
  quenched; it shall be sent upon them as a lion, and devour them as a
  leopard. 24 Look that you hedge your possession about with thorns, and
  bind up your silver and gold, 25 And weigh your words in a balance,
  and make a door and bar for your mouth.

  26 Beware you slide not by it, lest you fall before him that lieth in
  wait.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is one of the most theologically substantive in the
proverbial range. Verses 1–7 are a sustained meditation on forgiveness:
that one who would receive mercy from Yahuah (God) must extend mercy to
others. Verse 2: Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done unto
you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you pray. This is the
second-temple precedent for Yahusha's (Jesus') teaching in Matthew
6:14–15 and the parable of the unforgiving servant in Matthew 18:21–35.
The framework of this Series, which holds that the forgiveness extended
to those still in inherited deception is the proper covenant response,
finds in Sirach 28 the second-temple voice teaching exactly that
principle.

The forgiveness teaching is the framework's posture toward the
still-deceived put into second-temple wisdom vocabulary. The Christian
who handed the awakening reader the antinomian framework was acting in
good faith under what he had been handed. Forgive him. The Hebrew roots
teacher who was promoting the false-inclusion gospel was acting in good
faith under the framework his teachers handed him. Forgive him. The
Yahudi (Jewish) rabbi who layered the Talmud over the prophets was
acting under his inherited tradition. Forgive him. The awakening reader
who cannot forgive is the awakening reader who has not yet come into the
framework's full posture.

Read Sirach 28:2–4 against the canonical line. The Lord's Prayer
(Matthew 6:12, 14–15): And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our
debtors... For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father
will also forgive you: But if you forgive not men their trespasses,
neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. The parable of the
unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:23–35) closes: So likewise shall my
heavenly Father do also unto you, if you from your hearts forgive not
every one his brother their trespasses. Mark 11:25 repeats: And when you
stand praying, forgive, if you have ought against any: that your Father
also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses. Ephesians 4:32:
Be you kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even
as Elohim (God) for Messiah (Christ)'s sake has forgiven you. Colossians 3:13:
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a
quarrel against any: even as Messiah (Christ) forgave you, so also do
you.

Six witnesses across Sirach, the Sermon on the Mount, the parable, the
apostolic letters of Paul. The architecture is identical: the supplicant
who would receive Yahuah (God)'s mercy must extend mercy. The covenant
person who would be forgiven must forgive. Sirach 28 is the
second-temple voice telling that reader: forgive, that you may be
forgiven; release the offense, that you may be released; the standard is
the standard for you too. Yahusha did not introduce a new principle in
the Lord's Prayer; he locked in the principle Sirach 28 had already
named, and he gave it the full apostolic weight.

Verses 13–26 develop the dangers of slander and the bitter tongue. The
framework finds nothing controversial; the principle is consistent with
James 3.

Cross-references: Matthew 6:14–15; Matthew 18:21–35; Mark 11:25;
Ephesians 4:32; Colossians 3:13; James 3:1–12; 1 John 4:7–11.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 29

  1 He that is merciful will lend to his neighbour; and he that
  strengtheneth his hand keepeth the commandments. 2 Lend to your
  neighbour in time of his need, and pay you your neighbour again in due
  season. 3 Keep your word, and deal faithfully with him, and you shall
  always find the thing that is necessary for you. 4 Many, when a thing
  was lent them, reckoned it to be found, and put them to trouble that
  helped them. 5 Till he has received, he will kiss a man’s hand; and
  for his neighbour’s money he will speak submissly: but when he should
  repay, he will prolong the time, and return words of grief, and
  complain of the time.

  6 If he prevail, he shall hardly receive the half, and he will count
  as if he had found it: if not, he has deprived him of his money, and
  he has gotten him an enemy without cause: he payeth him with cursings
  and railings; and for honour he will pay him disgrace. 7 Many
  therefore have refused to lend for other men’s ill dealing, fearing to
  be defrauded. 8 Yet have you patience with a man in poor estate, and
  delay not to shew him mercy. 9 Help the poor for the commandment’s
  sake, and turn him not away because of his poverty. 10 Lose your money
  for your brother and your friend, and let it not rust under a stone to
  be lost.

  11 Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most
  High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold. 12 Shut up alms in
  your storehouses: and it shall deliver you from all affliction. 13 It
  shall fight for you against your enemies better than a mighty shield
  and strong spear. 14 An honest man is surety for his neighbour: but he
  that is impudent will forsake him. 15 Forget not the friendship of
  your surety, for he has given his life for you.

  16 A sinner will overthrow the good estate of his surety: 17 And he
  that is of an unthankful mind will leave him in danger that delivered
  him. 18 Suretiship has undone many of good estate, and shaken them as
  a wave of the sea: mighty men has it driven from their houses, so that
  they wandered among strange nations. 19 A wicked man transgressing the
  commandments of Yahuah (God) shall fall into suretiship: and he that
  undertaketh and followeth other men’s business for gain shall fall
  into suits. 20 Help your neighbour according to your power, and beware
  that you thyself fall not into the same.

  21 The chief thing for life is water, and bread, and clothing, and an
  house to cover shame. 22 Better is the life of a poor man in a mean
  cottage, than delicate fare in another man’s house. 23 Be it little or
  much, hold you contented, that you hear not the reproach of your
  house. 24 For it is a miserable life to go from house to house: for
  where you are a stranger, you darest not open your mouth. 25 You shall
  entertain, and feast, and have no thanks: moreover you shall hear
  bitter words:

  26 Come, you stranger, and furnish a table, and feed me of that you
  have ready. 27 Give place, you stranger, to an honourable man; my
  brother comes to be lodged, and I have need of my house. 28 These
  things are grievous to a man of understanding; the upbraiding of
  houseroom, and reproaching of the lender.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses lending and borrowing, surety, hospitality, and
the value of one's own home. Verses 1–7 develop the principle that
lending to those in need is a Torah commandment (Deuteronomy 15) and
that the lender should not despise the borrower. Verses 8–13 develop the
importance of giving alms and storing up treasure with Yahuah (God) by
giving to the poor — language that anticipates Matthew 6:19–21. Verses
14–20 warn against standing surety for strangers. Verses 21–28 develop
the value of having one's own home rather than depending on others'
hospitality. The framework finds the wisdom consistent with the Torah
and the apostolic witness; the principle of generosity to the needy is
foundational.

Cross-references: Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Proverbs 22:7; Proverbs 22:26–27;
Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 6:34–35; James 1:27; 1 John 3:17–18.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 30

  1 He that loves his son causeth him oft to feel the rod, that he may
  have joy of him in the end. 2 He that chastiseth his son shall have
  joy in him, and shall rejoice of him among his acquaintance. 3 He that
  teaches his son grieves the enemy: and before his friends he shall
  rejoice of him. 4 Though his father die, yet he is as though he were
  not dead: for he has left one behind him that is like himself. 5 While
  he lived, he saw and rejoiced in him: and when he died, he was not
  sorrowful.

  6 He left behind him an avenger against his enemies, and one that
  shall requite kindness to his friends. 7 He that makes too much of his
  son shall bind up his wounds; and his bowels will be troubled at every
  cry. 8 An horse not broken becometh headstrong: and a child left to
  himself will be wilful. 9 Cocker your child, and he shall make you
  afraid: play with him, and he will bring you to heaviness. 10 Laugh
  not with him, lest you have sorrow with him, and lest you gnash your
  teeth in the end.

  11 Give him no liberty in his youth, and wink not at his follies. 12
  Bow down his neck while he is young, and beat him on the sides while
  he is a child, lest he wax stubborn, and be disobedient to you, and so
  bring sorrow to yours heart. 13 Chastise your son, and hold him to
  labour, lest his lewd behaviour be an offence to you. 14 Better is the
  poor, being sound and strong of constitution, than a rich man that is
  afflicted in his body. 15 Health and good estate of body are above all
  gold, and a strong body above infinite wealth.

  16 There is no riches above a sound body, and no joy above the joy of
  the heart. 17 Death is better than a bitter life or continual
  sickness. 18 Delicates poured upon a mouth shut up are as messes of
  meat set upon a grave. 19 What good doeth the offering to an idol? for
  neither can it eat nor smell: so is he that is persecuted of Yahuah
  (God). 20 He seeth with his eyes and groaneth, as an eunuch that
  embraceth a virgin and sigheth.

  21 Give not over your mind to heaviness, and afflict not thyself in
  your own counsel. 22 The gladness of the heart is the life of man, and
  the joyfulness of a man prolongeth his days. 23 Love your own soul,
  and comfort your heart, remove sorrow far from you: for sorrow has
  killed many, and there is no profit in it. 24 Envy and wrath shorten
  the life, and carefulness brings age before the time. 25 A cheerful
  and good heart will have a care of his meat and diet.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses two themes: the rearing of children (verses 1–13)
and the importance of bodily and mental health (verses 14–25). The
chapter's instruction on disciplining children is severe by contemporary
standards (verse 12: bow down his neck while he is young, and beat him
on the sides while he is a child, lest he wax stubborn, and be
disobedient to you, and so bring sorrow to your heart) — the framework's
note: this is second-temple cultural practice; the framework does not
legislate it for contemporary parenting; the awakening reader should
take the principle (that children require formation in the covenant) and
apply it through the apostolic teaching that fathers should not provoke
their children to wrath (Ephesians 6:4, Colossians 3:21).

Cross-references: Proverbs 13:24; Proverbs 22:6; Proverbs 22:15;
Ephesians 6:1–4; Colossians 3:20–21; Hebrews 12:5–11.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 31

  1 Watching for riches consumeth the flesh, and the care thereof drives
  away sleep. 2 Watching care will not let a man slumber, as a sore
  disease breaks sleep, 3 The rich has great labour in gathering riches
  together; and when he resteth, he is filled with his delicates. 4 The
  poor laboureth in his poor estate; and when he leaveth off, he is
  still needy. 5 He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that
  followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.

  6 Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present. 7
  It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool
  shall be taken with it. 8 Blessed is the rich that is found without
  blemish, and has not gone after gold. 9 Who is he? and we will call
  him blessed: for wonderful things has he done among his people. 10 Who
  has been tried thereby, and found perfect? then let him glory. Who
  might offend, and has not offended? or done evil, and has not done it?

  11 His goods shall be established, and the congregation shall declare
  his alms. 12 If you sit at a bountiful table, be not greedy upon it,
  and say not, There is much meat on it. 13 Remember that a wicked eye
  is an evil thing: and what is created more wicked than an eye?
  therefore it weeps upon every occasion. 14 Stretch not yours hand
  whithersoever it looketh, and thrust it not with him into the dish. 15
  Judge not your neighbour by thyself: and be discreet in every point.

  16 Eat as it becometh a man, those things which are set before you;
  and devour not, lest you be hated. 17 Leave off first for manners’
  sake; and be not unsatiable, lest you offend. 18 When you sittest
  among many, reach not yours hand out first of all. 19 A very little is
  sufficient for a man well nurtured, and he fetcheth not his wind short
  upon his bed. 20 Sound sleep comes of moderate eating: he rises early,
  and his wits are with him: but the pain of watching, and choler, and
  pangs of the belly, are with an unsatiable man.

  21 And if you have been forced to eat, arise, go forth, vomit, and you
  shall have rest. 22 My son, hear me, and despise me not, and at the
  last you shall find as I told you: in all your works be quick, so
  shall there no sickness come to you. 23 Whoso is liberal of his meat,
  men shall speak well of him; and the report of his good housekeeping
  will be believed. 24 But against him that is a niggard of his meat the
  whole city shall murmur; and the testimonies of his niggardness shall
  not be doubted of. 25 Shew not your valiantness in wine; for wine has
  destroyed many.

  26 The furnace proves the edge by dipping: so does wine the hearts of
  the proud by drunkeness. 27 Wine is as good as life to a man, if it be
  drunk moderately: what life is then to a man that is without wine? for
  it was made to make men glad. 28 Wine measurably drunk and in season
  brings gladness of the heart, and cheerfulness of the mind: 29 But
  wine drunken with excess makes bitterness of the mind, with brawling
  and quarrelling. 30 Drunkenness increaseth the rage of a fool till he
  offend: it diminisheth strength, and makes wounds.

  31 Rebuke not your neighbour at the wine, and despise him not in his
  mirth: give him no despiteful words, and press not upon him with
  urging him to drink.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses two themes: the dangers of riches (verses 1–11)
and the proper conduct at feasts (verses 12–31). The chapter's wisdom on
wealth is consistent with the Torah and the prophets: that wealth
without righteousness is a snare, that the love of money corrupts, that
the rich who keep the covenant are rare and admirable. The chapter's
wisdom on feasts is practical: how to behave with honor at another's
table, how to drink wine without being mastered by it. Verse 27 contains
a striking observation: Wine is as good as life to a man, if it be drunk
moderately: what life is then to a man that is without wine? for it was
made to make men glad.

Cross-references: 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Proverbs 23:1–8; Ecclesiastes 9:7;
Psalm 104:14–15; John 2:1–11; Ephesians 5:18.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 32

  1 If you be made the master of a feast, lift not thyself up, but be
  among them as one of the rest; take diligent care for them, and so sit
  down. 2 And when you have done all your office, take your place, that
  you may be merry with them, and receive a crown for your well ordering
  of the feast. 3 Speak, you that are the elder, for it becometh you,
  but with sound judgment; and hinder not musick. 4 Pour not out words
  where there is a musician, and shew not forth wisdom out of time. 5 A
  concert of musick in a banquet of wine is as a signet of carbuncle set
  in gold.

  6 As a signet of an emerald set in a work of gold, so is the melody of
  musick with pleasant wine. 7 Speak, young man, if there be need of
  you: and yet scarcely when you are twice asked. 8 Let your speech be
  short, comprehending much in few words; be as one that knoweth and yet
  holdeth his tongue. 9 If you be among great men, make not thyself
  equal with them; and when ancient men are in place, use not many
  words. 10 Before the thunder goes lightning; and before a shamefaced
  man shall go favour.

  11 Rise up betimes, and be not the last; but get you home without
  delay. 12 There take your pastime, and do what you will: but sin not
  by proud speech. 13 And for these things bless him that made you, and
  has replenished you with his good things. 14 Whoso fears Yahuah (God)
  will receive his discipline; and they that seek him early shall find
  favour. 15 He that seeks the law shall be filled with it: but the
  hypocrite will be offended thereat.

  16 They that fear Yahuah (God) shall find judgment, and shall kindle
  justice as a light. 17 A sinful man will not be reproved, but finds an
  excuse according to his will. 18 A man of counsel will be considerate;
  but a strange and proud man is not daunted with fear, even when of
  himself he has done without counsel. 19 Do nothing without advice; and
  when you have once done, repent not. 20 Go not in a way in which you
  may fall, and stumble not among the stones.

  21 Be not confident in a plain way. 22 And beware of your own
  children. 23 In every good work trust your own soul; for this is the
  keeping of the commandments. 24 He that believes in Yahuah (God) takes
  heed to the commandment; and he that trusts in him shall fare never
  the worse.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses conduct at feasts continued, then turns to the
fear of Yahuah (God) and the keeping of the Torah. Verses 14–24 develop
the principle that those who fear Yahuah (God) order their lives by the
commandments and that those who do not fear Yahuah (God) walk in their
own counsel. Verse 24 closes: He that believes in Yahuah (God) takes
heed to the commandment; and he that trusts in him shall fare never the
worse. The framework of this Series, which holds the 1234 of Truth as
the master filter, finds in Sirach 32:24 the second-temple articulation
of the same principle.

Cross-references: Proverbs 3:5–8; Psalm 119:1–8; James 1:22–25; 1 John
2:3–4; Romans 4:13–25.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 33

  1 There shall no evil happen to him that fears Yahuah (God); but in
  temptation even again he will deliver him. 2 A wise man hates not the
  law; but he that is an hypocrite in it is as a ship in a storm. 3 A
  man of understanding trusts in the law; and the law is faithful to
  him, as an oracle. 4 Prepare what to say, and so you shall be heard:
  and bind up instruction, and then make answer. 5 The heart of the
  foolish is like a cartwheel; and his thoughts are like a rolling
  axletree.

  6 A stallion horse is as a mocking friend, he neigheth under every one
  that sits upon him. 7 Why does one day excel another, when as all the
  light of every day in the year is of the sun? 8 By the knowledge of
  Yahuah (God) they were distinguished: and he altered seasons and
  feasts. 9 Some of them has he made high days, and hallowed them, and
  some of them has he made ordinary days. 10 And all men are from the
  ground, and Adam was created of earth:

  11 In much knowledge Yahuah (God) has divided them, and made their
  ways diverse. 12 Some of them has he blessed and exalted and some of
  them he sanctified, and set near himself: but some of them has he
  cursed and brought low, and turned out of their places. 13 As the clay
  is in the potter’s hand, to fashion it at his pleasure: so man is in
  the hand of him that made him, to render to them as liketh him best.
  14 Good is set against evil, and life against death: so is the godly
  against the sinner, and the sinner against the godly. 15 So look upon
  all the works of the Most High; and there are two and two, one against
  another.

  16 I awaked up last of all, as one that gathers after the
  grapegatherers: by the blessing of Yahuah (God) I profited, and tred
  my winepress like a gatherer of grapes. 17 Consider that I laboured
  not for myself only, but for all them that seek learning. 18 Hear me,
  O you great men of the people, and hearken with your ears, you rulers
  of the congregation. 19 Give not your son and wife, your brother and
  friend, power over you while you livest, and give not your goods to
  another: lest it repent you, and you intreat for the same again. 20 As
  long as you livest and have breath in you, give not thyself over to
  any.

  21 For better it is that your children should seek to you, than that
  you should stand to their courtesy. 22 In all your works keep to
  thyself the preeminence; leave not a stain in yours honour. 23 At the
  time when you shall end your days, and finish your life, distribute
  your inheritance. 24 Fodder, a wand, and burdens, are for the ass; and
  bread, correction, and work, for a servant. 25 If you set your servant
  to labour, you shall find rest: but if you let him go idle, he shall
  seek liberty.

  26 A yoke and a collar do bow the neck: so are tortures and torments
  for an evil servant. 27 Send him to labour, that he be not idle; for
  idleness teaches much evil. 28 Set him to work, as is fit for him: if
  he be not obedient, put on more heavy fetters. 29 But be not excessive
  toward any; and without discretion do nothing. 30 If you have a
  servant, let him be to you as thyself, because you have bought him
  with a price.

  31 If you have a servant, entreat him as a brother: for you have need
  of him, as of your own soul: if you entreat him evil, and he run from
  you, which way will you go to seek him?

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is a meditation on the order of Yahuah (God)'s creation.
Verses 1–6 develop the principle that the wise person is steady
regardless of circumstance. Verses 7–15 reflect on why some days are
holy and others ordinary, why some people are blessed and others cursed
— and conclude that Yahuah (God) appoints the distinctions. Verses 16–18
are autobiographical: the author identifies himself as the latest in a
line of vinedressers gathering up the gleanings after others have
harvested. Verses 19–32 turn to the proper management of household and
possessions and slaves.

The framework finds in Sirach 33 the second-temple recognition of Yahuah
(God)'s sovereign appointment of distinctions and the practical wisdom
of the vinedresser. The chapter's practical wisdom on slave management
should be held in its second-temple context; the contemporary covenant
community does not have slaves, and the principle of just relations
between household members is what carries forward.

The verses on appointed distinctions (7–15) are worth a slow reading. As
the clay is in the potter's hand, to fashion it at his pleasure: so man
is in the hand of him that made him, to render to them as likes him
best. Good is set against evil, and life against death: so is the godly
against the sinner. So look upon all the works of the most High; and
there are two and two, one against another. This is the second-temple
voice articulating the framework's wheat-and-tares distinction within
the human race itself. There are two kinds; they are appointed; the
distinction is real; and the awakening reader is being asked to
recognize it without imagining that the two kinds are interchangeable.
The contemporary cultural impulse to flatten all distinctions — to treat
the wheat and the tares as a single category — is not the second-temple
wisdom. The framework holds Sirach 33's appointed distinctions as the
seed of the wheat-and-tares parable, the seed of the
broad-and-narrow-way teaching, the seed of the few-and-many warning. Two
and two, one against another.

Cross-references: Genesis 1:14; Leviticus 23:1–44; Romans 9:14–24;
Ephesians 6:5–9; Colossians 4:1; 1 Timothy 6:1–2; Philemon 1:8–22;
Matthew 13:24–43; Matthew 7:13–14.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 34

  1 The hopes of a man void of understanding are vain and false: and
  dreams lift up fools. 2 Whoso regardeth dreams is like him that
  catches at a shadow, and followeth after the wind. 3 The vision of
  dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the
  likeness of a face to a face. 4 Of an unclean thing what can be
  cleansed? and from that thing which is false what truth can come? 5
  Divinations, and soothsayings, and dreams, are vain: and the heart
  fancieth, as a woman’s heart in travail.

  6 If they be not sent from the Most High in your visitation, set not
  your heart upon them. 7 For dreams have deceived many, and they have
  failed that put their trust in them. 8 The law shall be found perfect
  without lies: and wisdom is perfection to a faithful mouth. 9 A man
  that has travelled knoweth many things; and he that has much
  experience will declare wisdom. 10 He that has no experience knoweth
  little: but he that has travelled is full of prudence.

  11 When I travelled, I saw many things; and I understand more than I
  can express. 12 I was ofttimes in danger of death: yet I was delivered
  because of these things. 13 The spirit of those that fear Yahuah (God)
  shall live; for their hope is in him that saves them. 14 Whoso fears
  Yahuah (God) shall not fear nor be afraid; for he is his hope. 15
  Blessed is the soul of him that fears Yahuah (God): to whom does he
  look? and who is his strength?

  16 For the eyes of Yahuah (God) are upon them that love him, he is
  their mighty protection and strong stay, a defence from heat, and a
  cover from the sun at noon, a preservation from stumbling, and an help
  from falling. 17 He raiseth up the soul, and lighteneth the eyes: he
  gives health, life, and blessing. 18 He that sacrificeth of a thing
  wrongfully gotten, his offering is ridiculous; and the gifts of unjust
  men are not accepted. 19 The most High is not pleased with the
  offerings of the wicked; neither is he pacified for sin by the
  multitude of sacrifices. 20 Whoso brings an offering of the goods of
  the poor doeth as one that killeth the son before his father’s eyes.

  21 The bread of the needy is their life: he that defraudeth him
  thereof is a man of blood. 22 He that takes away his neighbour’s
  living slayeth him; and he that defraudeth the labourer of his hire is
  a bloodshedder. 23 When one buildeth, and another pulleth down, what
  profit have they then but labour? 24 When one prayeth, and another
  curses, whose voice will Yahuah (God) hear? 25 He that washeth himself
  after the touching of a dead body, if he touch it again, what availeth
  his washing?

  26 So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and goes again, and
  doeth the same: who will hear his prayer? or what does his humbling
  profit him?

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses dreams (verses 1–8), the value of travel and
experience (verses 9–13), the fear of Yahuah (God) (verses 14–20), and
the importance of just dealings rather than unjust offerings (verses
21–27). Verses 21–27 are theologically substantive: He that brings an
offering of the goods of the poor does as one that kills the son before
his father's eyes. The framework of this Series, which holds that
worship without justice is offensive to Yahuah (God), finds in Sirach 34
the second-temple amplification of what Isaiah 1:10–17, Amos 5:21–24,
and Micah 6:6–8 had already established. Outward religion that is built
on injustice toward the poor is detested.

Cross-references: Isaiah 1:10–17; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8; James 1:27;
James 2:14–26; 1 John 3:17–18.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 35

  1 He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough: he that takes heed
  to the commandment offers a peace offering. 2 He that requiteth a
  goodturn offers fine flour; and he that gives alms sacrificeth praise.
  3 To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to Yahuah (God); and
  to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation. 4 You shall not appear
  empty before Yahuah (God). 5 For all these things are to be done
  because of the commandment.

  6 The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and the sweet
  savour thereof is before the Most High. 7 The sacrifice of a just man
  is acceptable. and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten. 8
  Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the
  firstfruits of yours hands. 9 In all your gifts shew a cheerful
  countenance, and dedicate your tithes with gladness. 10 Give to the
  Most High according as he has enriched you; and as you have gotten,
  give with a cheerful eye.

  11 For Yahuah (God) recompenseth, and will give you seven times as
  much. 12 Do not think to corrupt with gifts; for such he will not
  receive: and trust not to unrighteous sacrifices; for Yahuah (God) is
  judge, and with him is no respect of persons. 13 He will not accept
  any person against a poor man, but will hear the prayer of the
  oppressed. 14 He will not despise the supplication of the fatherless;
  nor the widow, when she poureth out her complaint. 15 Do not the tears
  run down the widow’s cheeks? and is not her cry against him that
  causeth them to fall?

  16 He that serveth Yahuah (God) shall be accepted with favour, and his
  prayer shall reach to the clouds. 17 The prayer of the humble pierces
  the clouds: and till it come nigh, he will not be comforted; and will
  not depart, till the Most High shall behold to judge righteously, and
  execute judgment. 18 For Yahuah (God) will not be slack, neither will
  the Mighty be patient toward them, till he have struck in sunder the
  loins of the unmerciful, and repayed vengeance to the heathen; till he
  have taken away the multitude of the proud, and broken the sceptre of
  the unrighteous; 19 Till he have rendered to every man according to
  his deeds, and to the works of men according to their devices; till he
  have judged the cause of his people, and made them to rejoice in his
  mercy. 20 Mercy is seasonable in the time of affliction, as clouds of
  rain in the time of drought.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter develops the same theme: that the offerings of the just are
received and that the offerings of the unjust are rejected. Verses 1–11
develop the principle that the keeping of the commandments is itself a
sacrifice acceptable to Yahuah (God). Verses 12–17 emphasize the
impartiality of Yahuah (God) in judgment. Verses 18–20 close with the
assurance that Yahuah (God) will not delay the vindication of the
oppressed. The framework finds in Sirach 35 the second-temple voice
articulating the same theology of acceptable worship that runs from the
prophets through the apostolic letters.

Cross-references: 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Psalm 51:16–17; Romans
12:1; Hebrews 13:15–16; James 1:27.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 36

  1 Have mercy upon us, O Yahuah (God) of all, and behold us: 2 And send
  your fear upon all the nations that seek not after you. 3 Lift up your
  hand against the strange nations, and let them see your power. 4 As
  you were sanctified in us before them: so be you magnified among them
  before us. 5 And let them know you, as we have known you, that there
  is no Yahuah (God) but only you, O Yahuah (God).

  6 Shew new signs, and make other strange wonders: glorify your hand
  and your right arm, that they may set forth your wondrous works. 7
  Raise up indignation, and pour out wrath: take away the adversary, and
  destroy the enemy. 8 Make the time short, remember the covenant, and
  let them declare your wonderful works. 9 Let him that escapeth be
  consumed by the rage of the fire; and let them perish that oppress the
  people. 10 Smite in sunder the heads of the rulers of the heathen,
  that say, There is none other but we.

  11 Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as
  from the beginning. 12 O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that
  is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have
  named your firstborn. 13 O be merciful to Jerusalem, your holy city,
  the place of your rest. 14 Fill Sion with your unspeakable oracles,
  and your people with your glory: 15 Give testimony to those that you
  have possessed from the beginning, and raise up prophets that have
  been in your name.

  16 Reward them that wait for you, and let your prophets be found
  faithful. 17 O Yahuah (God), hear the prayer of your servants,
  according to the blessing of Aaron over your people, that all they
  which dwell upon the earth may know that you are Yahuah (God), the
  eternal Yahuah (God). 18 The belly devoureth all meats, yet is one
  meat better than another. 19 As the palate tasteth divers kinds of
  venison: so does an heart of understanding false speeches. 20 A
  froward heart causeth heaviness: but a man of experience will
  recompense him.

  21 A woman will receive every man, yet is one daughter better than
  another. 22 The beauty of a woman cheereth the countenance, and a man
  loves nothing better. 23 If there be kindness, meekness, and comfort,
  in her tongue, then is not her husband like other men. 24 He that
  getteth a wife begins a possession, a help like to himself, and a
  pillar of rest. 25 Where no hedge is, there the possession is spoiled:
  and he that has no wife will wander up and down mourning.

  26 Who will trust a thief well appointed, that skippeth from city to
  city? so who will believe a man that has no house, and lodgeth
  wherever the night takes him?

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is a prayer for Yashar'el (Israel) — one of the great
second-temple prayers for the gathering of the scattered seed. Verses
1–17 plead with Yahuah (God) to gather the tribes of Jacob, to fulfill
the prophetic promises, to glorify the name of Yahuah (God) among the
nations, to bring the appointed restoration. Verse 11: Gather all the
tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the gathering of the
scattered seed of all twelve tribes is the long restoration the prophets
named, finds in Sirach 36 the second-temple voice praying for that
gathering by name. "All the tribes of Jacob" is the explicit
second-temple recognition that the gathering is of the twelve tribes,
not merely of the southern kingdom that returned from Babylon. The
framework is not a modern Hebrew roots innovation; the framework is the
second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) prayer life articulating what the prophets
had named.

This is the second of the three great anchor-prayers for the framework's
bloodline-remnant claim that the Apocrypha preserves (the others being
Tobit 13–14 and 2 Maccabees 1:24–29). Ben Sira, writing around 180 BCE,
prays for what 2 Esdras' seer two and a half centuries later will be
shown in the vision of the man from the sea — the gathering of all the
tribes of Jacob from where they have been scattered. Ben Sira does not
pray for the restoration of "anyone who walks in the Torah." He prays
for the gathering of the tribes by name. He understands the framework.
He has been taught by the prophets. The contemporary reader who has been
told that Two-House theology is a recent innovation should sit with
Sirach 36:11 and ask what Ben Sira thought he was praying for. He
thought he was praying for what the prophets had promised — and he was
right.

Cross-references: Isaiah 11:11–16; Isaiah 49:5–6; Jeremiah 31:1–14;
Ezekiel 37:15–22; Hosea 1:9–11; Hosea 2:23; Amos 9:11–15; Matthew 19:28;
James 1:1; Revelation 7:4–8; Revelation 21:12; Tobit 13:1–14:15; 2
Maccabees 1:24–29.

Verses 18–28 turn to the choosing of a wife and the value of the right
household. The transition is abrupt; the wisdom is consistent with the
chapters that surround it.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 37

  1 Every friend says, I am his friend also: but there is a friend,
  which is only a friend in name. 2 Is it not a grief to death, when a
  companion and friend is turned to an enemy? 3 O wicked imagination,
  whence camest you in to cover the earth with deceit? 4 There is a
  companion, which rejoices in the prosperity of a friend, but in the
  time of trouble will be against him. 5 There is a companion, which
  helps his friend for the belly, and takes up the buckler against the
  enemy.

  6 Forget not your friend in your mind, and be not unmindful of him in
  your riches. 7 Every counsellor extolleth counsel; but there is some
  that counselleth for himself. 8 Beware of a counsellor, and know
  before what need he has; for he will counsel for himself; lest he cast
  the lot upon you, 9 And say to you, Your way is good: and afterward he
  stand on the other side, to see what shall befall you. 10 Consult not
  with one that suspecteth you: and hide your counsel from such as envy
  you.

  11 Neither consult with a woman touching her of whom she is jealous;
  neither with a coward in matters of war; nor with a merchant
  concerning exchange; nor with a buyer of selling; nor with an envious
  man of thankfulness; nor with an unmerciful man touching kindness; nor
  with the slothful for any work; nor with an hireling for a year of
  finishing work; nor with an idle servant of much business: hearken not
  to these in any matter of counsel. 12 But be continually with a godly
  man, whom you know to keep the commandments of Yahuah (God), whose,
  mind is according to your mind, and will sorrow with you, if you shall
  miscarry. 13 And let the counsel of your own heart stand: for there is
  no man more faithful to you than it. 14 For a man’s mind is sometime
  wont to tell him more than seven watchmen, that sit above in an high
  tower. 15 And above all this pray to the Most High, that he will
  direct your way in truth.

  16 Let reason go before every enterprize, and counsel before every
  action. 17 The countenance is a sign of changing of the heart. 18 Four
  manner of things appear: good and evil, life and death: but the tongue
  ruleth over them continually. 19 There is one that is wise and teaches
  many, and yet is unprofitable to himself. 20 There is one that sheweth
  wisdom in words, and is hated: he shall be destitute of all food.

  21 For grace is not given, him from Yahuah (God), because he is
  deprived of all wisdom. 22 Another is wise to himself; and the fruits
  of understanding are commendable in his mouth. 23 A wise man instructs
  his people; and the fruits of his understanding fail not. 24 A wise
  man shall be filled with blessing; and all they that see him shall
  count him happy. 25 The days of the life of man may be numbered: but
  the days of Yashar'el (Israel) are innumerable.

  26 A wise man shall inherit glory among his people, and his name shall
  be perpetual. 27 My son, prove your soul in your life, and see what is
  evil for it, and give not that to it. 28 For all things are not
  profitable for all men, neither has every soul pleasure in every
  thing. 29 Be not unsatiable in any dainty thing, nor too greedy upon
  meats: 30 For excess of meats brings sickness, and surfeiting will
  turn into choler.

  31 By surfeiting have many perished; but he that takes heed prolongeth
  his life.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses the choosing of friends and counselors and the
importance of self-discipline in eating. Verses 1–6 develop the
difference between the true friend and the flatterer. Verses 7–15
develop the importance of seeking counsel from those who fear Yahuah
(God). Verses 27–31 contain a sharp warning against gluttony — that
intemperate eating shortens life and produces sickness.

Cross-references: Proverbs 13:20; Proverbs 18:24; Proverbs 23:1–3; James
1:5; Galatians 5:22–24; 1 Corinthians 9:24–27.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 38

  1 Honour a physician with the honour due to him for the uses which you
  may have of him: for Yahuah (God) has created him. 2 For of the Most
  High comes healing, and he shall receive honour of the king. 3 The
  skill of the physician shall lift up his head: and in the sight of
  great men he shall be in admiration. 4 Yahuah (God) has created
  medicines out of the earth; and he that is wise will not abhor them. 5
  Was not the water made sweet with wood, that the virtue thereof might
  be known?

  6 And he has given men skill, that he might be honoured in his
  marvellous works. 7 With such does he heal men, and takes away their
  pains. 8 Of such does the apothecary make a confection; and of his
  works there is no end; and from him is peace over all the earth, 9 My
  son, in your sickness be not negligent: but pray to Yahuah (God), and
  he will make you whole. 10 Leave off from sin, and order yours hands
  aright, and cleanse your heart from all wickedness.

  11 Give a sweet savour, and a memorial of fine flour; and make a fat
  offering, as not being. 12 Then give place to the physician, for
  Yahuah (God) has created him: let him not go from you, for you have
  need of him. 13 There is a time when in their hands there is good
  success. 14 For they shall also pray to Yahuah (God), that he would
  prosper that, which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life. 15
  He that sinneth before his Maker, let him fall into the hand of the
  physician.

  16 My son, let tears fall down over the dead, and begin to lament, as
  if you had suffered great harm thyself; and then cover his body
  according to the custom, and neglect not his burial. 17 Weep bitterly,
  and make great moan, and use lamentation, as he is worthy, and that a
  day or two, lest you be evil spoken of: and then comfort thyself for
  your heaviness. 18 For of heaviness comes death, and the heaviness of
  the heart breaks strength. 19 In affliction also sorrow remains: and
  the life of the poor is the curse of the heart. 20 Take no heaviness
  to heart: drive it away, and remember the last end.

  21 Forget it not, for there is no turning again: you shall not do him
  good, but hurt thyself. 22 Remember my judgment: for your also shall
  be so; yesterday for me, and to day for you. 23 When the dead is at
  rest, let his remembrance rest; and be comforted for him, when his
  Spirit is departed from him. 24 The wisdom of a learned man comes by
  opportunity of leisure: and he that has little business shall become
  wise. 25 How can he get wisdom that holdeth the plough, and that
  glorieth in the goad, that drives oxen, and is occupied in their
  labours, and whose talk is of bullocks?

  26 He gives his mind to make furrows; and is diligent to give the kine
  fodder. 27 So every carpenter and workmaster, that laboureth night and
  day: and they that cut and grave seals, and are diligent to make great
  variety, and give themselves to counterfeit imagery, and watch to
  finish a work: 28 The smith also sitting by the anvil, and considering
  the iron work, the vapour of the fire wasteth his flesh, and he
  fighteth with the heat of the furnace: the noise of the hammer and the
  anvil is ever in his ears, and his eyes look still upon the pattern of
  the thing that he makes; he sets his mind to finish his work, and
  watcheth to polish it perfectly: 29 So does the potter sitting at his
  work, and turning the wheel about with his feet, who is alway
  carefully set at his work, and makes all his work by number; 30 He
  fashioneth the clay with his arm, and boweth down his strength before
  his feet; he applieth himself to lead it over; and he is diligent to
  make clean the furnace:

  31 All these trust to their hands: and every one is wise in his work.
  32 Without these cannot a city be inhabited: and they shall not dwell
  where they will, nor go up and down: 33 They shall not be sought for
  in publick counsel, nor sit high in the congregation: they shall not
  sit on the judges’ seat, nor understand the sentence of judgment: they
  cannot declare justice and judgment; and they shall not be found where
  parables are spoken. 34 But they will maintain the state of the world,
  and all their desire is in the work of their craft.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 38 is one of the most quoted and most misread chapters in the
entire Apocrypha. The contemporary Christian and Hebrew roots community
has been catechized by the surrounding pharmaceutical-medical culture
into reading verses 1–15 as a blanket endorsement of the modern medical
industry. That reading is a misreading. Chapter 38 contains three
distinct sections — the physician (verses 1–15), the proper mourning of
the dead (verses 16–23), and the meditation on the trades and the man
set apart for the Word (verses 24–34) — and each of them lands harder
for the awakening reader than the surface reading allows. Read this
commentary slowly. There is more in this chapter than the inherited
reading has been letting through.

Verses 1–15: The Physician

The chapter opens: Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for
the uses which you may have of him: for the Lord has created him. The
verse honors the physician as a gift of Yahuah (God). The verse does not
endorse the modern pharmaceutical-medical complex. The two are not the
same thing.

What did "physician" mean in the second-temple world? The physician was
the herbalist, the bone-setter, the midwife, the wound-binder, the
oil-anointer, the man or woman of practical knowledge who knew which
plants healed which ailments and how to set a broken limb and how to
clean a wound. The pharmacology of the second-temple world was the
pharmacology of the herb garden and the apothecary's stores — plants,
oils, salts, and the natural materials Yahuah (God) had created. Verses
4–8 describe the physician's medicines: The Lord has created medicines
out of the earth; and he that is wise will not abhor them. Was not the
water made sweet with wood, that the virtue thereof might be known? And
he has given men skill, that he might be honoured in his marvellous
works. With such does he heal men, and takes away their pains. Of such
does the apothecary make a confection. The medicines are out of the
earth. The virtue is in the wood, in the herb, in what Yahuah (God) has
placed in the creation for the healing of the body.

This is what Sirach 38:1–15 honors. The man who knows the herbs and uses
them under the fear of Yahuah (God) and in submission to the prayer the
chapter explicitly commends — verse 9: My son, in your sickness be not
negligent: but pray to Yahuah (God), and he will make you whole. The
order is: sin first set right (verses 9–10 — put away wrong-dealing, and
order your hands aright, and cleanse your heart from all wickedness),
prayer to Yahuah (God) next, offering brought to the Most High next, and
only then the physician given his place. The physician is the last of
four steps. He is honored. He is not the savior.

Now turn to the New Testament's vocabulary, because this is where the
contemporary reader's catechism has obscured what Scripture itself says
about the modern equivalent of what Sirach is naming. The Greek word for
"sorcery" in the apostolic letters is pharmakeia. It appears in
Galatians 5:20, where it is listed among the works of the flesh
alongside idolatry, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife,
seditions, heresies, and murders. It appears in Revelation 9:21, where
the inhabitants of the earth refuse to repent of their pharmakeia. It
appears in Revelation 18:23, where the merchants of Babylon are named as
having deceived all nations by their sorceries — pharmakeia. It appears
in Revelation 21:8 and 22:15, where pharmakoi — sorcerers — are listed
among those excluded from the new Jerusalem.

The Greek root is the same root that gives English "pharmacy" and
"pharmaceutical." Strong's defines pharmakeia as "the use of medicine,
drugs or spells; sorcery; witchcraft." The dual meaning is not
accidental. The ancient world's drug-mixers, potion-makers, and
spell-casters were often the same people. The mixing of substances to
alter the body and the mixing of substances to alter the spirit ran in
the same trade. The apostolic Greek does not distinguish between
drug-mixing and witchcraft because the practice did not distinguish
them.

What does this mean for the contemporary reader's understanding of
Sirach 38? It means that the chapter's honoring of the physician — the
herbalist, the bone-setter, the midwife operating under the fear of
Yahuah (God) — cannot be transferred wholesale to a modern industry
whose own foundational vocabulary is the apostolic vocabulary for
sorcery. The modern pharmaceutical industry is not a continuation of
Sirach 38's physician. It is a different thing under a different name,
with different ownership structures, different production processes,
different motivations, and different spiritual histories. The reader who
has been told "Sirach 38 says take your medicine" has been read, at
best, into a category confusion; at worst, into a softening of what the
apostolic letters specifically warn against.

The framework's reading is not a blanket condemnation of every
contemporary medical intervention. Setting a broken bone is setting a
broken bone. Stitching a wound is stitching a wound. Delivering a baby
is delivering a baby. The herbalist's wisdom about which plants heal
which ailments is a wisdom Yahuah (God) gave (verse 4 — The Lord has
created medicines out of the earth). The framework's reading is that the
awakening reader cannot read Sirach 38:1–15 as a license to import the
entire modern pharmaceutical-medical-pharmacological complex into the
covenant household uncritically. The chapter does not bless the
pharmakeia of the apostolic letters. The chapter blesses the herbalist,
under prayer, in subjection to Yahuah (God)'s order, after sin has been
put away and the offering brought.

Read the chapter slowly. Verse 9 — pray to Yahuah (God), and he will
make you whole. This is not a tagline before the medicine. This is the
order of operations. Prayer first. Sin put away. Offering brought. Then
the physician. The contemporary cultural pattern of taking the
prescription and skipping the prayer — of turning the body over to a
stranger in a white coat without first turning the heart over to the
Father in the closet — is the pattern Sirach 38 is correcting in
advance. The physician who is honored in Sirach 38 is the physician who
works after the prayer, under the prayer, in submission to the prayer.
Strip the prayer away and the physician becomes something else.

The framework's specific warnings to the awakening reader on this
question:

The pharmaceutical industry's vocabulary is the apostolic vocabulary for
sorcery. Name this. Do not be embarrassed by it. The Greek says what the
Greek says.

The herbalist tradition that Yahuah (God) honors in Sirach 38 still
exists, still operates under prayer, and is still available to the
awakening reader who is willing to learn what the second-temple world
knew — that the medicines are out of the earth, that the body responds
to what was placed in the creation for it, that the herbalist's wisdom
is a wisdom Yahuah (God) gave.

Prayer remains the first step in every illness, not the last. Sin put
away remains the first response to suffering, not the last. The order of
operations in verses 9–11 is not a poetic flourish; it is a covenant
pattern.

The framework does not legislate which specific contemporary medical
interventions a particular awakening reader should accept or reject. The
framework names what Sirach 38 actually says, names what pharmakeia
actually means in the apostolic Greek, and lets the awakening reader
walk the discernment in his or her own household. Test all things. Hold
fast to that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

Verses 16–23: The Mourning of the Dead

Verses 16–23 address mourning. The instruction is balanced. Mourn — but
not excessively. Honor the dead with the appointed weeping — but do not
refuse comfort. Take no heaviness to heart: drive it away, and remember
the last end. Forget it not, for there is no turning again: you shall
not do him good, but hurt yourself. The dead are at rest in the chambers
(the framework's reading following 2 Esdras 7:32 — the holding place
where the souls of the righteous wait for the resurrection). The living
are still in the field of the present age. The proper mourning honors
the appointed grief and then returns the mourner to the work Yahuah
(God) has set before him.

The framework finds in Sirach 38:16–23 a healthy contrast to two
contemporary patterns. First, the cultural pattern of suppressing grief
— the modern productivity-culture that treats the death of the dear as
an inconvenience to be processed in three days off — is rejected. Sirach
honors weeping. Second, the cultural pattern of cultivating extended
despair — the various contemporary therapeutic frames that turn grief
into an identity rather than a passage — is also rejected. Sirach calls
the mourner forward. Both extremes are unhealthy. The covenant pattern
is to weep and then to return.

Verses 24–34: The Trades and the Man Set Apart for the Word

This is the second great section of the chapter, and it is the section
the user of the Restored Names Series will most need to hear plainly.
Sirach is laying out a theology of vocation that the contemporary reader
has rarely been taught. He surveys the trades — the farmer who plows the
field (verses 25–26), the smith who works at the anvil (verse 28), the
potter who shapes the clay (verses 29–30) — and concludes:

All these trust to their hands: and every one is wise in his work.
Without these cannot a city be inhabited: and they shall not dwell where
they will, nor go up and down: they shall not be sought for in publick
counsel, nor sit high in the congregation: they shall not sit on the
judges' seat, nor understand the sentence of judgment: they cannot
declare justice and judgment; and they shall not be found where parables
are spoken. But they will maintain the state of the world, and all their
desire is in the work of their craft (verses 31–34).

Verse 24 opened the section with the principle: The wisdom of a learned
man comes by opportunity of leisure: and he that has little business
shall become wise. The man who is set apart for the wisdom of the Torah
— the scribe, the priest, the Nazarite, the prophet — is set apart
because his hand is at leisure for the Word. The trades are necessary;
without them there is no city, no food, no tools, no vessels. The man of
leisure is also necessary; without him there is no judgment seat, no
public counsel, no parable speaking, no sentence of judgment, no
declaration of justice. Each has his appointed place. Each is honored by
Yahuah (God) in his own work.

This is where the framework's voice has to land plainly, because the
contemporary reading of this passage almost universally goes wrong in
two opposite directions and the awakening reader needs both correctives.

The first wrong reading is the egalitarian flattening: that the trades
and the wisdom-vocation are merely "different but equal" callings and
that no one is set apart in any meaningful way. This is the modern
Protestant work-ethic reading, in which "every Christian is a priest"
has been used to erase the existence of any actual set-apart vocation.
The reading is sweet on the surface and false underneath. Sirach 38
plainly says some men are set apart for leisure with the Word, and some
are not. The smith does not sit in public counsel; the scribe does not
run the forge. The vocations are not interchangeable. The set-apart man
has his place; the tradesman has his place; both are honored, but they
are not the same.

The second wrong reading is the elitist inflation: that the man of
leisure for the Word is "better than" the smith and the potter, that his
vocation is spiritually higher, that the laborer is a lesser brother.
This is the inherited religious aristocracy that has produced clergy
castes, theological superiority, and the slow accumulation of contempt
for the working hand by the religious mind. Sirach 38 explicitly rejects
this. The smith maintains the state of the world. The potter is wise in
his work. Without these cannot a city be inhabited. The set-apart man is
not above the tradesman. He is not "more spiritual." He is not "closer
to Yahuah (God)." He occupies a different appointed position in the same
body.

The framework's reading lands here. The set-apart vocation — the
Nazarite, the priest, the scribe, the prophet, the man whose hand is at
leisure for the Word — exists for the sake of the rest of the covenant
household. The set-apart man does not gather the wisdom for himself. He
gathers it for the smith, for the farmer, for the potter, for the
merchant, for the soldier, for the housewife, for the child. His leisure
with the Torah is not a private spiritual asset. It is a service
rendered to the community by appointment. The Father set him apart so
the rest of the household could work their trades under the wisdom he
brings forth from his leisure with the Word. They shall not sit on the
judges' seat — the tradesman is not asked to render the judgment that
requires long study; the set-apart man is asked, because his hand is at
leisure for the study. The arrangement is not a hierarchy of value. It
is a division of labor in a single household, with each member honored
in his place and each serving the others.

This is the framework's specific vocational theology, and Sirach 38 is
the second-temple anchor for it. The Nazarite is not "above" the smith.
The Nazarite serves the smith. The set-apart man's set-apartness is the
Father's appointment for the smith's enjoyment of life under the Word.
He gave me this position so you could enjoy life. Read the verse aloud
and let it land. The set-apart vocation is not spiritual elitism. It is
covenant service.

The contemporary application is direct and corrective for both the
awakened reader and the awakened reader's family and former pew-mates.
To the smith: the set-apart man's vocation is not a rejection of yours.
He is honoring your trade by giving his leisure to the Word so that your
work can be ordered by what Yahuah (God) has spoken. To the set-apart
man: your leisure with the Word is not your possession. It is a vocation
Yahuah (God) gave you for the enjoyment of life by the rest of the
covenant household. Do not lord it over the smith. Serve him with what
you have been shown.

The Nazarite vocation specifically — and the framework of this Series
has its own substantive teaching on the modern Nazarite walk — is one of
the appointed set-apart positions. Numbers 6 institutes it. Samson,
Samuel, John the Immerser walked under it. 1 Maccabees 3:49 records that
Nazarites whose vows had been completed were "stirred up" — gathered,
called forward, recognized — at the Mizpah assembly because they were
NZR, set apart, walking witnesses to the Torah. The Nazarite's hand is
at leisure for the Word in a particular form: the abstinence from wine
and shaved hair and corpse-uncleanness mark the body as set apart, and
the body's set-apartness frees the time, the attention, the spiritual
posture for the Father's appointment. The framework's contemporary
Nazarite walk is the modern continuation of what Sirach 38 was
describing as the man of leisure for the Word. He is not above the
smith. He serves the smith. He carries the appointment for the
household's enjoyment of life under the Torah.

The chapter closes verse 34 with the recognition that the trades-person
is not "found where parables are spoken." This is not an insult to the
trades-person. It is an observation about appointed places. The smith is
at the forge. The set-apart man is in the place where parables are
spoken. Each is in his appointed place. Both are needed. Neither is the
other. The framework holds this whole.

Cross-references: Numbers 6:1–21; Judges 13:1–5; 1 Samuel 1:11; 1
Maccabees 3:49; Luke 1:13–17; Galatians 5:20; Revelation 9:21;
Revelation 18:23; Revelation 21:8; Revelation 22:15; 2 Kings 20:1–11;
James 5:13–16; Proverbs 14:30; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; 1 Thessalonians
5:21; Genesis 23:1–20; Ephesians 6:5–9.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 39

  1 But he that gives his mind to the law of the Most High, and is
  occupied in the meditation thereof, will seek out the wisdom of all
  the ancient, and be occupied in prophecies. 2 He will keep the sayings
  of the renowned men: and where subtil parables are, he will be there
  also. 3 He will seek out the secrets of grave sentences, and be
  conversant in dark parables. 4 He shall serve among great men, and
  appear before princes: he will travel through strange countries; for
  he has tried the good and the evil among men. 5 He will give his heart
  to resort early to Yahuah (God) that made him, and will pray before
  the Most High, and will open his mouth in prayer, and make
  supplication for his sins.

  6 When the great Yahuah (God) will, he shall be filled with the spirit
  of understanding: he shall pour out wise sentences, and give thanks to
  Yahuah (God) in his prayer. 7 He shall direct his counsel and
  knowledge, and in his secrets shall he meditate. 8 He shall shew forth
  that which he has learned, and shall glory in the law of the covenant
  of Yahuah (God). 9 Many shall commend his understanding; and so long
  as the world endureth, it shall not be blotted out; his memorial shall
  not depart away, and his name shall live from generation to
  generation. 10 Nations shall shew forth his wisdom, and the
  congregation shall declare his praise.

  11 If he die, he shall leave a greater name than a thousand: and if he
  live, he shall increase it. 12 Yet have I more to say, which I have
  thought upon; for I am filled as the moon at the full. 13 Hearken to
  me, you holy children, and bud forth as a rose growing by the brook of
  the field: 14 And give you a sweet savour as frankincense, and
  flourish as a lily, send forth a smell, and sing a song of praise,
  bless Yahuah (God) in all his works. 15 Magnify his name, and shew
  forth his praise with the songs of your lips, and with harps, and in
  praising him you shall say after this manner:

  16 All the works of Yahuah (God) are exceeding good, and whatsoever he
  commands shall be accomplished in due season. 17 And none may say,
  What is this? wherefore is that? for at time convenient they shall all
  be sought out: at his commandment the waters stood as an heap, and at
  the words of his mouth the receptacles of waters. 18 At his
  commandment is done whatsoever pleaseth him; and none can hinder, when
  he will save. 19 The works of all flesh are before him, and nothing
  can be hid from his eyes. 20 He seeth from everlasting to everlasting;
  and there is nothing wonderful before him.

  21 A man need not to say, What is this? wherefore is that? for he has
  made all things for their uses. 22 His blessing covered the dry land
  as a river, and watered it as a flood. 23 As he has turned the waters
  into saltness: so shall the heathen inherit his wrath. 24 As his ways
  are plain to the holy; so are they stumblingblocks to the wicked. 25
  For the good are good things created from the beginning: so evil
  things for sinners.

  26 The principal things for the whole use of man’s life are water,
  fire, iron, and salt, flour of wheat, honey, milk, and the blood of
  the grape, and oil, and clothing. 27 All these things are for good to
  the godly: so to the sinners they are turned into evil. 28 There be
  spirits that are created for vengeance, which in their fury lay on
  sore strokes; in the time of destruction they pour out their force,
  and appease the wrath of him that made them. 29 Fire, and hail, and
  famine, and death, all these were created for vengeance; 30 Teeth of
  wild beasts, and scorpions, serpents, and the sword punishing the
  wicked to destruction.

  31 They shall rejoice in his commandment, and they shall be ready upon
  earth, when need is; and when their time is come, they shall not
  transgress his word. 32 Therefore from the beginning I was resolved,
  and thought upon these things, and have left them in writing. 33 All
  the works of Yahuah (God) are good: and he will give every needful
  thing in due season. 34 So that a man cannot say, This is worse than
  that: for in time they shall all be well approved. 35 And therefore
  praise you Yahuah (God) with the whole heart and mouth, and bless the
  name of Yahuah (God).

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is a sustained portrait of the seeker of wisdom — the
scribe, the student of the Torah, the one who gives himself to the Word.
Verses 1–11 develop the disciplines of the wisdom-seeker: he meditates
on the Torah, he meditates on the prophets, he meditates on the proverbs
of the wise, he travels to learn from foreign nations, he serves at the
courts of rulers, he is filled with the Spirit, he is honored by his
people. Verse 6: When the great Lord will, he shall be filled with the
spirit of understanding: he shall pour out wise sentences, and give
thanks to Yahuah (God) in his prayer.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening teacher's
calling is filled by the Spirit and is sustained by long meditation on
the Word, finds in Sirach 39:1–11 the second-temple model of that
calling. Verses 12–35 close with a sustained meditation on the works of
Yahuah (God) and the response of the seeker — to bless and to praise.

The canonical anchor for the seeker-of-wisdom portrait is Joshua 1:8:
This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth; but you shall
meditate therein day and night, that you may observe to do according to
all that is written therein: for then you shall make your way
prosperous, and then you shall have good success. Psalm 1:1–3 expands
the same: Blessed is the man that walks not in the counsel of the
ungodly, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of the
scornful. But his delight is in the law of Yahuah (God); and in his law
does he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by
the rivers of water, that brings forth his fruit in his season; his leaf
also shall not wither; and whatsoever he does shall prosper. Psalm
119:97–104: O how I love your law! it is my meditation all the day. You
through your commandments have made me wiser than my enemies: for they
are ever with me. I have more understanding than all my teachers: for
your testimonies are my meditation.

Sirach 39's portrait of the seeker is the second-temple amplification of
these canonical anchors. The seeker meditates on the Torah, the
prophets, the wise sayings — exactly what Joshua 1, Psalm 1, and Psalm
119 commanded the covenant person to do. The Torah-meditation produces
the wisdom-overflow the seeker pours out for the community. 2 Timothy
2:15 names the same posture in apostolic vocabulary: Study to show
yourself approved unto Elohim (God), a workman that needs not to be ashamed,
rightly dividing the word of truth. Across Joshua, the Psalter, Ben
Sira, and Paul the call is the same: meditate on the Word, walk in the
Word, be filled by the Spirit who teaches the Word, pour out the Word
for the covenant community. The set-apart vocation is not a passive
retirement from the world; it is a particular kind of active engagement,
in a particular kind of place, under a particular kind of appointment.
The framework holds Sirach 39 as the working portrait of what the
Nazarite-scribe-prophet-set-apart-man does with his leisure for the
Word.

Cross-references: Joshua 1:8; Psalm 1:1–6; Psalm 119:97–104; Acts 6:3–4;
2 Timothy 2:15; 2 Peter 1:19–21; Numbers 6:1–21.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 40

  1 Great travail is created for every man, and an heavy yoke is upon
  the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mother’s
  womb, till the day that they return to the mother of all things. 2
  Their imagination of things to come, and the day of death, trouble
  their thoughts, and cause fear of heart; 3 From him that sits on a
  throne of glory, to him that is humbled in earth and ashes; 4 From him
  that wears purple and a crown, to him that is clothed with a linen
  frock. 5 Wrath, and envy, trouble, and unquietness, fear of death, and
  anger, and strife, and in the time of rest upon his bed his night
  sleep, do change his knowledge.

  6 A little or nothing is his rest, and afterward he is in his sleep,
  as in a day of keeping watch, troubled in the vision of his heart, as
  if he were escaped out of a battle. 7 When all is safe, he awakes, and
  marvelleth that the fear was nothing. 8 Such things happen to all
  flesh, both man and beast, and that is sevenfold more upon sinners. 9
  Death, and bloodshed, strife, and sword, calamities, famine,
  tribulation, and the scourge; 10 These things are created for the
  wicked, and for their sakes came the flood.

  11 All things that are of the earth shall turn to the earth again: and
  that which is of the waters does return into the sea. 12 All bribery
  and injustice shall be blotted out: but true dealing shall endure for
  ever. 13 The goods of the unjust shall be dried up like a river, and
  shall vanish with noise, like a great thunder in rain. 14 While he
  opens his hand he shall rejoice: so shall transgressors come to
  nought. 15 The children of the ungodly shall not bring forth many
  branches: but are as unclean roots upon a hard rock.

  16 The weed growing upon every water and bank of a river shall be
  pulled up before all grass. 17 Bountifulness is as a most fruitful
  garden, and mercifulness endureth for ever. 18 To labour, and to be
  content with that a man has, is a sweet life: but he that finds a
  treasure is above them both. 19 Children and the building of a city
  continue a man’s name: but a blameless wife is counted above them
  both. 20 Wine and musick rejoice the heart: but the love of wisdom is
  above them both.

  21 The pipe and the psaltery make sweet melody: but a pleasant tongue
  is above them both. 22 Your eye desires favour and beauty: but more
  than both corn while it is green. 23 A friend and companion never meet
  amiss: but above both is a wife with her husband. 24 Brothers and help
  are against time of trouble: but alms shall deliver more than them
  both. 25 Gold and silver make the foot stand sure: but counsel is
  esteemed above them both.

  26 Riches and strength lift up the heart: but the fear of Yahuah (God)
  is above them both: there is no want in the fear of Yahuah (God), and
  it needeth not to seek help. 27 The fear of Yahuah (God) is a fruitful
  garden, and covereth him above all glory. 28 My son, lead not a
  beggar’s life; for better it is to die than to beg. 29 The life of him
  that dependeth on another man’s table is not to be counted for a life;
  for he polluteth himself with other men’s meat: but a wise man well
  nurtured will beware thereof. 30 Begging is sweet in the mouth of the
  shameless: but in his belly there shall burn a fire.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is one of the most affecting meditations on the human
condition in the apocryphal corpus. Verses 1–11 develop the long burden
of life: the labor, the anxiety, the fear of death, the sickness, the
death itself. Verses 12–17 turn to the contrast between the works of the
unrighteous (which perish) and the works of the righteous (which
endure). Verses 18–27 develop a series of "better than" sayings,
culminating in verse 26: Riches and strength lift up the heart: but the
fear of Yahuah (God) is above both.

Cross-references: Job 14:1–22; Ecclesiastes 1:1–18; Ecclesiastes 3:1–22;
Hebrews 9:27; James 4:13–17; 1 Peter 1:24–25.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 41

  1 O death, how bitter is the remembrance of you to a man that lives at
  rest in his possessions, to the man that has nothing to vex him, and
  that has prosperity in all things: yes, to him that is yet able to
  receive meat! 2 O death, acceptable is your sentence to the needy, and
  to him whose strength fails, that is now in the last age, and is vexed
  with all things, and to him that despaireth, and has lost patience! 3
  Fear not the sentence of death, remember them that have been before
  you, and that come after; for this is the sentence of Yahuah (God)
  over all flesh. 4 And why art you against the pleasure of the Most
  High? there is no inquisition in the grave, whether you have lived
  ten, or an hundred, or a thousand years. 5 The children of sinners are
  abominable children, and they that are conversant in the dwelling of
  the ungodly.

  6 The inheritance of sinners’ children shall perish, and their
  posterity shall have a perpetual reproach. 7 The children will
  complain of an ungodly father, because they shall be reproached for
  his sake. 8 Woe be to you, ungodly men, which have forsaken the law of
  the most high Yahuah (God)! for if you increase, it shall be to your
  destruction: 9 And if you be born, you shall be born to a curse: and
  if you die, a curse shall be your portion. 10 All that are of the
  earth shall turn to earth again: so the ungodly shall go from a curse
  to destruction.

  11 The mourning of men is about their bodies: but an ill name of
  sinners shall be blotted out. 12 Have regard to your name; for that
  shall continue with you above a thousand great treasures of gold. 13 A
  good life has but few days: but a good name endureth for ever. 14 My
  children, keep discipline in peace: for wisdom that is hid, and a
  treasure that is not seen, what profit is in them both? 15 A man that
  hideth his foolishness is better than a man that hideth his wisdom.

  16 Therefore be shamefaced according to my word: for it is not good to
  retain all shamefacedness; neither is it altogether approved in every
