  thing. 17 Be ashamed of whoredom before father and mother: and of a
  lie before a prince and a mighty man; 18 Of an offence before a judge
  and ruler; of iniquity before a congregation and people; of unjust
  dealing before your partner and friend; 19 And of theft in regard of
  the place where you sojournest, and in regard of the truth of Yahuah
  (God) and his covenant; and to lean with your elbow upon the meat; and
  of scorning to give and take; 20 And of silence before them that
  salute you; and to look upon an harlot;

  21 And to turn away your face from your kinsman; or to take away a
  portion or a gift; or to gaze upon another man’s wife. 22 Or to be
  overbusy with his maid, and come not near her bed; or of upbraiding
  speeches before friends; and after you have given, upbraid not; 23 Or
  of iterating and speaking again that which you have heard; and of
  revealing of secrets. 24 So shall you be truly shamefaced and find
  favour before all men.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter addresses death and shame. Verses 1–4 are a famous
meditation on death — that death is a comfort to the one who is in pain
and a terror to the one who is at ease. Verses 5–13 develop the
principle that the children of the wicked are remembered with shame and
the children of the righteous with honor. Verses 14–24 address the
various kinds of shame — true shame (which one should embrace) and false
shame (which one should reject).

The framework's note: the chapter's distinction between true and false
shame is consistent with the apostolic teaching. To be ashamed of the
gospel of the Messiah is wrong; to be ashamed of one's sin is right. The
framework finds Sirach 41 useful for distinguishing the two.

Cross-references: Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8; 2 Timothy 1:12; Hebrews
12:1–2; 1 Peter 4:16; 1 John 1:8–10.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 42

  1 Of these things be not you ashamed, and accept no person to sin
  thereby: 2 Of the law of the Most High, and his covenant; and of
  judgment to justify the ungodly; 3 Of reckoning with your partners and
  travellers; or of the gift of the heritage of friends; 4 Of exactness
  of balance and weights; or of getting much or little; 5 And of
  merchants’ indifferent selling; of much correction of children; and to
  make the side of an evil servant to bleed.

  6 Sure keeping is good, where an evil wife is; and shut up, where many
  hands are. 7 Deliver all things in number and weight; and put all in
  writing that you give out, or receivest in. 8 Be not ashamed to inform
  the unwise and foolish, and the extreme aged that contendeth with
  those that are young: thus shall you be truly learned, and approved of
  all men living. 9 The father waketh for the daughter, when no man
  knoweth; and the care for her takes away sleep: when she is young,
  lest she pass away the flower of her age; and being married, lest she
  should be hated: 10 In her virginity, lest she should be defiled and
  gotten with child in her father’s house; and having an husband, lest
  she should misbehave herself; and when she is married, lest she should
  be barren.

  11 Keep a sure watch over a shameless daughter, lest she make you a
  laughingstock to your enemies, and a byword in the city, and a
  reproach among the people, and make you ashamed before the multitude.
  12 Behold not every body’s beauty, and sit not in the midst of women.
  13 For from garments comes a moth, and from women wickedness. 14
  Better is the churlishness of a man than a courteous woman, a woman, I
  say, which brings shame and reproach. 15 I will now remember the works
  of Yahuah (God), and declare the things that I have seen: In the words
  of Yahuah (God) are his works.

  16 The sun that gives light looketh upon all things, and the work
  thereof is full of the glory of Yahuah (God). 17 Yahuah (God) has
  not given power to the saints to declare all his marvellous works,
  which the Almighty Yahuah (God) firmly settled, that whatsoever is
  might be established for his glory. 18 He seeks out the deep, and the
  heart, and considereth their crafty devices: for Yahuah (God) knoweth
  all that may be known, and he beholds the signs of the world. 19 He
  declareth the things that are past, and for to come, and revealeth the
  steps of hidden things. 20 No thought escapeth him, neither any word
  is hidden from him.

  21 He has garnished the excellent works of his wisdom, and he is from
  everlasting to everlasting: to him may nothing be added, neither can
  he be diminished, and he has no need of any counsellor. 22 Oh how
  desirable are all his works! and that a man may see even to a spark.
  23 All these things live and remain for ever for all uses, and they
  are all obedient. 24 All things are double one against another: and he
  has made nothing imperfect. 25 One thing establishes the good or
  another: and who shall be filled with beholding his glory?

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the discussion of true and false shame (verses
1–8), addresses the responsibilities of fathers regarding their
daughters (verses 9–14), and then turns to the works of Yahuah (God) in
creation (verses 15–25). The closing meditation on creation prepares for
chapters 43 and following: the works of Yahuah (God) are great, His
wisdom is unsearchable, His order is perfect.

Cross-references: Romans 1:20; Psalm 19:1–6; Psalm 104:1–35; Job
38:1–41:34; Romans 11:33–36.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 43

  1 The pride of the height, the clear firmament, the beauty of heaven,
  with his glorious shew; 2 The sun when it appears, declaring at his
  rising a marvellous instrument, the work of the Most High: 3 At noon
  it parcheth the country, and who can abide the burning heat thereof? 4
  A man blowing a furnace is in works of heat, but the sun burneth the
  mountains three times more; breathing out fiery vapours, and sending
  forth bright beams, it dimmeth the eyes. 5 Great is Yahuah (God) that
  made it; and at his commandment runs hastily.

  6 He made the moon also to serve in her season for a declaration of
  times, and a sign of the world. 7 From the moon is the sign of feasts,
  a light that decreaseth in her perfection. 8 The month is called after
  her name, increasing wonderfully in her changing, being an instrument
  of the armies above, shining in the firmament of heaven; 9 The beauty
  of heaven, the glory of the stars, an ornament giving light in the
  highest places of Yahuah (God). 10 At the commandment of the Holy One
  they will stand in their order, and never faint in their watches.

  11 Look upon the rainbow, and praise him that made it; very beautiful
  it is in the brightness thereof. 12 It compasseth the heaven about
  with a glorious circle, and the hands of the Most High have bended it.
  13 By his commandment he makes the snow to fall aplace, and sends
  swiftly the lightnings of his judgment. 14 Through this the treasures
  are opened: and clouds fly forth as fowls. 15 By his great power he
  makes the clouds firm, and the hailstones are broken small.

  16 At his sight the mountains are shaken, and at his will the south
  wind bloweth. 17 The noise of the thunder makes the earth to tremble:
  so does the northern storm and the whirlwind: as birds flying he
  scatters the snow, and the falling down thereof is as the lighting of
  grasshoppers: 18 The eye marvelleth at the beauty of the whiteness
  thereof, and the heart is astonished at the raining of it. 19 The
  hoarfrost also as salt he poureth on the earth, and being congealed,
  it lieth on the top of sharp stakes. 20 When the cold north wind
  bloweth, and the water is congealed into ice, it abideth upon every
  gathering together of water, and clothes the water as with a
  breastplate.

  21 It devoureth the mountains, and burneth the wilderness, and
  consumeth the grass as fire. 22 A present remedy of all is a mist
  coming speedily, a dew coming after heat refresheth. 23 By his counsel
  he appeaseth the deep, and planteth islands in it. 24 They that sail
  on the sea tell of the danger thereof; and when we hear it with our
  ears, we marvel thereat. 25 For in it be strange and wondrous works,
  variety of all kinds of beasts and whales created.

  26 By him the end of them has prosperous success, and by his word all
  things consist. 27 We may speak much, and yet come short: wherefore in
  sum, he is all. 28 How shall we be able to magnify him? for he is
  great above all his works. 29 Yahuah (God) is terrible and very
  great, and marvellous is his power. 30 When you glorify Yahuah (God),
  exalt him as much as you can; for even yet will he far exceed: and
  when you exalt him, put forth all your strength, and be not weary; for
  you can never go far enough.

  31 Who has seen him, that he might tell us? and who can magnify him as
  he is? 32 There are yet hid greater things than these be, for we have
  seen but a few of his works. 33 For Yahuah (God) has made all things;
  and to the godly has he given wisdom.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is a sustained hymn to the works of Yahuah (God) in the
natural world. Verses 1–10 praise the sun, moon, and stars. Verses 11–22
praise the rainbow, the snow, the storm, the cold, the heat. Verses
23–26 praise the sea. Verses 27–33 close with the recognition that the
works of Yahuah (God) are countless and that the proper response is
praise.

Verses 27–28 are the closing summary: We may speak much, and yet come
short: wherefore in sum, he is all. How shall we be able to magnify him?
for he is great above all his works. The framework of this Series, which
honors the appropriate humility before Yahuah (God)'s incomparable
greatness, finds in Sirach 43 the second-temple voice of that humility.
Praise without comprehension is the proper posture.

Cross-references: Psalm 8:1–9; Psalm 19:1–6; Psalm 104:1–35; Psalm
148:1–14; Job 38:1–41:34; Romans 1:20.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 44

  1 Let us now praise famous men, and our fathers that begat us. 2 The
  Yahuah (God) has wrought great glory by them through his great power
  from the beginning. 3 Such as did bear rule in their kingdoms, men
  renowned for their power, giving counsel by their understanding, and
  declaring prophecies: 4 Leaders of the people by their counsels, and
  by their knowledge of learning meet for the people, wise and eloquent
  are their instructions: 5 Such as found out musical tunes, and recited
  verses in writing:

  6 Rich men furnished with ability, living peaceably in their
  habitations: 7 All these were honoured in their generations, and were
  the glory of their times. 8 There be of them, that have left a name
  behind them, that their praises might be reported. 9 And some there
  be, which have no memorial; who are perished, as though they had never
  been; and are become as though they had never been born; and their
  children after them. 10 But these were merciful men, whose
  righteousness has not been forgotten.

  11 With their seed shall continually remain a good inheritance, and
  their children are within the covenant. 12 Their seed stands fast, and
  their children for their sakes. 13 Their seed shall remain for ever,
  and their glory shall not be blotted out. 14 Their bodies are buried
  in peace; but their name lives for evermore. 15 The people will tell
  of their wisdom, and the congregation will shew forth their praise.

  16 Enoch pleased Yahuah (God), and was translated, being an example of
  repentance to all generations. 17 Noah was found perfect and
  righteous; in the time of wrath he was taken in exchange for the
  world; therefore was he left as a remnant to the earth, when the flood
  came. 18 An everlasting covenant was made with him, that all flesh
  should perish no more by the flood. 19 Abraham was a great father of
  many people: in glory was there none like to him; 20 Who kept the law
  of the Most High, and was in covenant with him: he established the
  covenant in his flesh; and when he was proved, he was found faithful.

  21 Therefore he assured him by an oath, that he would bless the
  nations in his seed, and that he would multiply him as the dust of the
  earth, and exalt his seed as the stars, and cause them to inherit from
  sea to sea, and from the river to the utmost part of the land. 22 With
  Isaac did he establish likewise for Abraham his father’s sake the
  blessing of all men, and the covenant, 23 And made it rest upon the
  head of Jacob. He acknowledged him in his blessing, and gave him an
  heritage, and divided his portions; among the twelve tribes did he
  part them.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 44 begins one of the great sections of the apocryphal corpus —
the praise of the fathers, running from chapter 44 through chapter 50.
The author surveys the great covenant figures from Enoch through Simon
the high priest (a contemporary of the author), naming each, recounting
briefly what each did, and praising Yahuah (God) for the long line of
faithful through whom the covenant has been preserved.

Verses 1–15 are the introduction. Let us now praise famous men, and our
fathers that begat us. Yahuah (God) has wrought great glory by them
through his great power from the beginning. The framework of this
Series, which honors the long line of covenant fathers as the cloud of
witnesses surrounding the awakening reader, finds in Sirach 44–50 the
second-temple parallel to Hebrews 11. The two passages are operating in
the same genre — the catalogue of faith — and the writer of Hebrews drew
on the genre Sirach had already established.

This is also the section where the framework's bloodline-remnant claim
lands hardest. Read verse 1 again. Let us now praise famous men, and our
fathers that begat us. "Our fathers that begat us." The catalogue is not
a hall of admirable strangers. It is the ancestral lineage of the
covenant community — the named fathers in the named line through whom
the named covenant came down. Ben Sira is writing for the seed of Jacob,
and he is rehearsing for them their own paternal blood lineage. Our
fathers. Not "fathers in the faith" in some allegorical sense. Fathers
in the flesh. Begetters. The reader who has been told that the cloud of
witnesses in Hebrews 11 is "spiritual ancestors" of "anyone who
believes" has been read out of this verse. Hebrews 11 is doing what
Sirach 44 is doing: reciting the paternal lineage of the covenant son to
whom the letter is addressed. The recipients of Hebrews are the
scattered seed — the descendants of these fathers — and the cloud of
witnesses is the cloud of witnesses around them because the cloud is
related to them. The bloodline runs through the chapter. Hold it.

Verses 16–17 name Enoch — Enoch pleased Yahuah (God), and was
translated, being an example of repentance to all generations. The
mention is brief but theologically weighty: Enoch was translated, and
this is the second-temple recognition of what Genesis 5:24 records. The
framework of this Series, which has its own dedicated volume on the Book
of Enoch, finds in Sirach 44:16 the brief second-temple acknowledgment.

Verses 17–18 name Noah. Verses 19–21 name Abraham — including the
explicit recognition that in his flesh he made a covenant (the
circumcision, Genesis 17), that he was found faithful in temptation (the
binding of Isaac, Genesis 22), and that the covenant was sworn that the
nations would be blessed in his seed (Genesis 12, Genesis 22). The
framework of this Series, which holds that the covenant with Abraham is
the foundation of the covenant with Yashar'el (Israel) and that the seed
of Abraham is the paternal blood remnant the prophets named, finds in
Sirach 44:19–21 the second-temple confirmation.

The verse that is hardest for the contemporary inclusive-covenant reader
to receive is verse 19: in his flesh he made a covenant. The Abrahamic
covenant was cut into the flesh — circumcision, the cutting of the
foreskin, the marking of the male body of the seed of Abraham. The
framework holds the verse plainly. The covenant of Abraham was made in
the flesh of Abraham. The seed that descends from him carries that
flesh-mark. The sojourner who joins himself to the covenant takes on the
sign by his own circumcision (Genesis 17:12–13) — the sign is offered,
the sojourner is welcome, and yet the sojourner does not become a son of
Abraham by the cutting; he walks under the covenant of Abraham as a
sojourner. The flesh-covenant is the covenant of the seed. Sirach 44:19
says it plainly.

Verse 22 names Isaac. Verse 23 names Jacob, with the explicit
twelve-tribe naming: He gave him an heritage, and divided his portions;
among the twelve tribes did he part them. This is the verse that makes
the bloodline-remnant claim impossible to flatten. The heritage was
divided among the twelve tribes. By name. The inheritance is tribal. The
seed is paternal. The framework's reading is the verse's reading.

Cross-references: Genesis 5:24; Genesis 6:9; Genesis 12:1–3; Genesis
15:1–21; Genesis 17:1–27; Genesis 22:1–19; Genesis 26:1–5; Genesis
28:10–22; Hebrews 11:1–40; Romans 4:1–25; Genesis 17:12–13.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 45

  1 And he brought out of him a merciful man, which found favour in the
  sight of all flesh, even Moses, beloved of Yahuah (God) and men, whose
  memorial is blessed. 2 He made him like to the glorious saints, and
  magnified him, so that his enemies stood in fear of him. 3 By his
  words he caused the wonders to cease, and he made him glorious in the
  sight of kings, and gave him a commandment for his people, and shewed
  him part of his glory. 4 He sanctified him in his faithfuless and
  meekness, and chose him out of all men. 5 He made him to hear his
  voice, and brought him into the dark cloud, and gave him commandments
  before his face, even the law of life and knowledge, that he might
  teach Jacob his covenants, and Yashar'el (Israel) his judgments.

  6 He exalted Aaron, an holy man like to him, even his brother, of the
  tribe of Levi. 7 An everlasting covenant he made with him and gave him
  the priesthood among the people; he beautified him with comely
  ornaments, and clothed him with a robe of glory. 8 He put upon him
  perfect glory; and strengthened him with rich garments, with breeches,
  with a long robe, and the ephod. 9 And he compassed him with
  pomegranates, and with many golden bells round about, that as he went
  there might be a sound, and a noise made that might be heard in the
  temple, for a memorial to the children of his people; 10 With an holy
  garment, with gold, and blue silk, and purple, the work of the
  embroiderer, with a breastplate of judgment, and with Urim and
  Thummim;

  11 With twisted scarlet, the work of the cunning workman, with
  precious stones graven like seals, and set in gold, the work of the
  jeweller, with a writing engraved for a memorial, after the number of
  the tribes of Yashar'el (Israel). 12 He set a crown of gold upon the
  mitre, in which was engraved Holiness, an ornament of honour, a costly
  work, the desires of the eyes, goodly and beautiful. 13 Before him
  there were none such, neither did ever any stranger put them on, but
  only his children and his children’s children perpetually. 14 Their
  sacrifices shall be wholly consumed every day twice continually. 15
  Moses consecrated him, and anointed him with holy oil: this was
  appointed to him by an everlasting covenant, and to his seed, so long
  as the heavens should remain, that they should minister to him, and
  execute the office of the priesthood, and bless the people in his
  name.

  16 He chose him out of all men living to offer sacrifices to Yahuah
  (God), incense, and a sweet savour, for a memorial, to make
  reconciliation for his people. 17 He gave to him his commandments, and
  authority in the statutes of judgments, that he should teach Jacob the
  testimonies, and inform Yashar'el (Israel) in his laws. 18 Strangers
  conspired together against him, and maligned him in the wilderness,
  even the men that were of Dathan’s and Abiron’s side, and the
  congregation of Core, with fury and wrath. 19 This Yahuah (God) saw,
  and it displeased him, and in his wrathful indignation were they
  consumed: he did wonders upon them, to consume them with the fiery
  flame. 20 But he made Aaron more honourable, and gave him an heritage,
  and divided to him the firstfruits of the increase; especially he
  prepared bread in abundance:

  21 For they eat of the sacrifices of Yahuah (God), which he gave to
  him and his seed. 22 Howbeit in the land of the people he had no
  inheritance, neither had he any portion among the people: for Yahuah
  (God) himself is his portion and inheritance. 23 The third in glory is
  Phinees the son of Eleazar, because he had zeal in the fear of Yahuah
  (God), and stood up with good courage of heart: when the people were
  turned back, and made reconciliation for Yashar'el (Israel). 24
  Therefore was there a covenant of peace made with him, that he should
  be the chief of the sanctuary and of his people, and that he and his
  posterity should have the dignity of the priesthood for ever: 25
  According to the covenant made with David son of Jesse, of the tribe
  of Juda, that the inheritance of the king should be to his posterity
  alone: so the inheritance of Aaron should also be to his seed.

  26 Yahuah (God) give you wisdom in your heart to judge his people in
  righteousness, that their good things be not abolished, and that their
  glory may endure for ever.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the praise. Verses 1–5 praise Moses as the one who
saw Yahuah (God) face to face, who was given the Torah, who was
sanctified above all flesh. Verses 6–22 praise Aaron — the high priestly
office, the priestly garments, the consecrations, the offerings, the
perpetual covenant of the priesthood through Aaron. Verses 23–26 praise
Phinehas, who turned away Yahuah (God)'s wrath at Peor (Numbers 25) and
received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.

The framework of this Series, which has noted the framework's particular
concern with the corruption of the priesthood and which holds that the
Messiah's permanent priesthood (Hebrews 7) is the destination toward
which the Aaronic priesthood was always pointing, finds in Sirach 45 the
second-temple voice praising the Aaronic priesthood as it had been
instituted. The framework's reading: the praise is for the institution
as Yahuah (God) gave it; the framework's recognition that the
institution had been corrupted by the second-temple period (and that the
Messiah's priesthood would supersede it) is the framework's own; Sirach
45 does not address this. Hold the praise of the Aaronic priesthood as
Yahuah (God)'s appointed institution; hold the apostolic theology of
Hebrews on the Messiah's priesthood as the destination.

Verses 6–13 contain a detailed description of the priestly garments —
the breastplate, the ephod, the bells, the pomegranates, the gold and
blue and scarlet — that Sirach is laboring over because the priestly
garments matter to him. Why? Because the garments mark the appointed
office. The priest is set apart by what he wears. The Nazarite is set
apart by his hair. The smith is set apart by his apron and his calloused
hands. Each appointed vocation carries a visible mark. The garments are
not decoration. They are vocational identification. The framework holds
this for the contemporary reader who has been catechized into a
vocational anonymity that erases all visible marks of set-apart
appointment. Mark the appointment. Wear what was given. Live the visible
witness.

Cross-references: Exodus 19:1–20:21; Exodus 28:1–43; Exodus 29:1–46;
Numbers 25:1–13; Hebrews 7:11–28; Hebrews 8:1–13; Hebrews 9:11–28;
Numbers 6:1–21.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 46

  1 Jesus the son a Nave was valiant in the wars, and was the successor
  of Moses in prophecies, who according to his name was made great for
  the saving of the elect of Yahuah (God), and taking vengeance of the
  enemies that rose up against them, that he might set Yashar'el
  (Israel) in their inheritance. 2 How great glory got he, when he did
  lift up his hands, and stretched out his sword against the cities! 3
  Who before him so stood to it? for Yahuah (God) himself brought his
  enemies to him. 4 Did not the sun go back by his means? and was not
  one day as long as two? 5 He called upon the most high Yahuah (God),
  when the enemies pressed upon him on every side; and the great Yahuah
  (God) heard him.

  6 And with hailstones of mighty power he made the battle to fall
  violently upon the nations, and in the descent of Beth-horon he
  destroyed them that resisted, that the nations might know all their
  strength, because he fought in the sight of Yahuah (God), and he
  followed the Mighty One. 7 In the time of Moses also he did a work of
  mercy, he and Caleb the son of Jephunne, in that they withstood the
  congregation, and withheld the people from sin, and appeased the
  wicked murmuring. 8 And of six hundred thousand people on foot, they
  two were preserved to bring them in to the heritage, even to the land
  that floweth with milk and honey. 9 Yahuah (God) gave strength
  also to Caleb, which remained with him to his old age: so that he
  entered upon the high places of the land, and his seed obtained it for
  an heritage: 10 That all the children of Yashar'el (Israel) might see
  that it is good to follow Yahuah (God).

  11 And concerning the judges, every one by name, whose heart went not
  a whoring, nor departed from Yahuah (God), let their memory be
  blessed. 12 Let their bones flourish out of their place, and let the
  name of them that were honoured be continued upon their children. 13
  Samuel, the prophet of Yahuah (God), beloved of his Elohim (God),
  established a kingdom, and anointed princes over his people. 14 By the
  law of Yahuah (God) he judged the congregation, and Yahuah (God) had
  respect to Jacob. 15 By his faithfulness he was found a true prophet,
  and by his word he was known to be faithful in vision.

  16 He called upon the mighty Yahuah (God), when his enemies pressed
  upon him on every side, when he offered the sucking lamb. 17 And
  Yahuah (God) thundered from heaven, and with a great noise made his
  voice to be heard. 18 And he destroyed the rulers of the Tyrians, and
  all the princes of the Philistines. 19 And before his long sleep he
  made protestations in the sight of Yahuah (God) and his anointed, I
  have not taken any man’s goods, so much as a shoe: and no man did
  accuse him. 20 And after his death he prophesied, and shewed the king
  his end, and lifted up his voice from the earth in prophecy, to blot
  out the wickedness of the people.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the praise. Verses 1–10 praise Joshua, the son of
Nun. Verses 11–12 praise the judges. Verses 13–20 praise Samuel — his
prophetic ministry, his anointing of kings, his intercession for
Yashar'el (Israel). The framework of this Series, which honors the long
line of faithful prophets as the witnesses to Yahuah (God)'s covenant,
finds in Sirach 46 the second-temple naming of the prophetic line.

Samuel is worth pausing over. He was a Nazarite from the womb (1 Samuel
1:11). His mother Hannah dedicated him before his birth, and the razor
never came on his head. He served in the temple, anointed kings, and
walked in the prophetic office that the Father had given him. The
framework's specific Nazarite teaching finds in Samuel one of its three
great Old Testament Nazarite anchors (the others being Samson and the
appointed Nazarite at the gathering at Mizpah in 1 Maccabees 3:49). The
set-apart vocation is not a New Testament novelty. It runs from the
patriarchs through the judges through the prophets through the apostles
and into the contemporary remnant. Samuel was Nazarite. The framework
holds him.

Cross-references: Joshua 1:1–24:33; Judges 2:6–23; 1 Samuel 1:1–28:25;
Psalm 99:6; Hebrews 11:32–34; Numbers 6:1–21; Judges 13:1–25; 1
Maccabees 3:49.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 47

  1 And after him rose up Nathan to prophesy in the time of David. 2 As
  is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out
  of the children of Yashar'el (Israel). 3 He played with lions as with
  kids, and with bears as with lambs. 4 Slew he not a giant, when he was
  yet but young? and did he not take away reproach from the people, when
  he lifted up his hand with the stone in the sling, and beat down the
  boasting of Goliath? 5 For he called upon the most high Yahuah (God);
  and he gave him strength in his right hand to slay that mighty
  warrior, and set up the horn of his people.

  6 So the people honoured him with ten thousands, and praised him in
  the blessings of Yahuah (God), in that he gave him a crown of glory. 7
  For he destroyed the enemies on every side, and brought to nought the
  Philistines his adversaries, and brake their horn in sunder to this
  day. 8 In all his works he praised the Holy One most high with words
  of glory; with his whole heart he sung songs, and loved him that made
  him. 9 He set singers also before the altar, that by their voices they
  might make sweet melody, and daily sing praises in their songs. 10 He
  beautified their feasts, and set in order the solemn times until the
  end, that they might praise his holy name, and that the temple might
  sound from morning.

  11 Yahuah (God) took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever:
  he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Yashar'el
  (Israel). 12 After him rose up a wise son, and for his sake he dwelt
  at large. 13 Solomon reigned in a peaceable time, and was honoured;
  for Yahuah (God) made all quiet round about him, that he might build
  an house in his name, and prepare his sanctuary for ever. 14 How wise
  were you in your youth and, as a flood, filled with understanding! 15
  Your soul covered the whole earth, and you filledst it with dark
  parables.

  16 Your name went far to the islands; and for your peace you were
  beloved. 17 The countries marvelled at you for your songs, and
  proverbs, and parables, and interpretations. 18 By the name of Yahuah
  (God), which is called Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), you did
  gather gold as tin and did multiply silver as lead. 19 You did bow
  your loins to women, and by your body you were brought into
  subjection. 20 You did stain your honour, and pollute your seed: so
  that you broughtest wrath upon your children, and were grieved for
  your folly.

  21 So the kingdom was divided, and out of Ephraim ruled a rebellious
  kingdom. 22 But Yahuah (God) will never leave off his mercy, neither
  shall any of his works perish, neither will he abolish the posterity
  of his elect, and the seed of him that loves him he will not take
  away: wherefore he gave a remnant to Jacob, and out of him a root to
  David. 23 Thus rested Solomon with his fathers, and of his seed he
  left behind him Roboam, even the foolishness of the people, and one
  that had no understanding, who turned away the people through his
  counsel. There was also Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who caused
  Yashar'el (Israel) to sin, and shewed Ephraim the way of sin: 24 And
  their sins were multiplied exceedingly, that they were driven out of
  the land. 25 For they sought out all wickedness, till the vengeance
  came upon them.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues with David and Solomon. Verses 1–11 praise David —
the giant-slaying, the music of the psalms, the dedication of the
offerings, the appointment of the Levitical service. Verses 12–22 praise
Solomon — the wisdom, the temple, but also the failure (verses 19–21):
But you did bow your loins to women, and by your body you were brought
into subjection. You did stain your honour, and pollute your seed, so
that you brought wrath to your children, and were grieved for your
folly. Verses 23–25 transition to Rehoboam and the division of the
kingdom.

The framework of this Series, which holds that even the greatest
covenant figures were imperfect and that the framework does not idealize
any human deliverer, finds in Sirach 47:19–21 the second-temple voice
acknowledging Solomon's failure honestly. The acknowledgment matters: it
shows that the second-temple wisdom tradition did not whitewash the
kings. The framework's reading: Solomon's wisdom was real; Solomon's
failure was real; both can be true; the destination is not Solomon but
the Messiah.

Verse 21 specifies that Solomon "polluted your seed." The verse is
bloodline-language. Solomon's marriages to foreign women polluted the
covenant lineage at the highest level of the kingdom. The framework's
reading of why bloodline matters is anchored here: the seed carries the
covenant; pollution of the seed has covenant consequences. The
contemporary reading that has erased bloodline as a covenant category
cannot make sense of why Solomon's marriages were specifically called
pollution. They were called pollution because the seed was the seed and
the covenant was the covenant and the mixing dilutes what was given. The
framework's reading does not legislate a contemporary ethnic exclusivism
— sojourners join the covenant and walk in it as Isaiah 56 describes —
but the framework does hold the bloodline-specific covenant of the seed
of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as a real category. Sirach 47:21 is one of
the second-temple voices that names the category plainly.

Cross-references: 1 Samuel 17:1–58; 2 Samuel 5:1–24:25; 1 Kings
1:1–11:43; 1 Chronicles 22:1–29:30; 2 Chronicles 9:1–31; Psalm 89:1–52;
1 Kings 11:1–13.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 48

  1 Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a
  lamp. 2 He brought a sore famine upon them, and by his zeal he
  diminished their number. 3 By the word of Yahuah (God) he shut up the
  heaven, and also three times brought down fire. 4 O Elias, how were
  you honoured in your wondrous deeds! and who may glory like to you! 5
  Who did raise up a dead man from death, and his soul from the place of
  the dead, by the word of the Most High:

  6 Who broughtest kings to destruction, and honorable men from their
  bed: 7 Who heardest the rebuke of Yahuah (God) in Sinai, and in Horeb
  the judgment of vengeance: 8 Who annointedst kings to take revenge,
  and prophets to succeed after him: 9 Who was taken up in a whirlwind
  of fire, and in a chariot of fiery horses: 10 Who were ordained for
  reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah
  (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the
  father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.

  11 Blessed are they that saw you, and slept in love; for we shall
  surely live. 12 Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and
  Eliseus was filled with his spirit: while he lived, he was not moved
  with the presence of any prince, neither could any bring him into
  subjection. 13 No word could overcome him; and after his death his
  body prophesied. 14 He did wonders in his life, and at his death were
  his works marvellous. 15 For all this the people repented not, neither
  departed they from their sins, till they were spoiled and carried out
  of their land, and were scattered through all the earth: yet there
  remained a small people, and a ruler in the house of David:

  16 Of whom some did that which was pleasing to Yahuah (God), and some
  multiplied sins. 17 Ezekias fortified his city, and brought in water
  into the midst thereof: he digged the hard rock with iron, and made
  wells for waters. 18 In his time Sennacherib came up, and sent
  Rabsaces, and lifted up his hand against Sion, and boasted proudly. 19
  Then trembled their hearts and hands, and they were in pain, as women
  in travail. 20 But they called upon Yahuah (God) which is merciful,
  and stretched out their hands toward him: and immediately the Holy One
  heard them out of heaven, and delivered them by the ministry of Esay.

  21 He struck the host of the Assyrians, and his angel destroyed them.
  22 For Ezekias had done the thing that pleased Yahuah (God), and was
  strong in the ways of David his father, as Esay the prophet, who was
  great and faithful in his vision, had commanded him. 23 In his time
  the sun went backward, and he lengthened the king’s life. 24 He saw by
  an excellent spirit what should come to pass at the last, and he
  comforted them that mourned in Sion. 25 He shewed what should come to
  pass for ever, and secret things or ever they came.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter praises Elijah, Elisha, and Hezekiah. Verses 1–14 praise
Elijah — the fire from heaven, the closing of the heavens, the chariot,
the prophecy that he would return at the appointed time. Verse 10 is
significant: Who was ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the
wrath of Yahuah (God)'s judgment, before it brake forth into fury, and
to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of
Jacob.

The verse echoes Malachi 4:5–6 — Behold, I will send you Elijah the
prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of Yahuah (God):
and he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the
heart of the children to their fathers. The framework of this Series,
which holds that the appointed coming of the Messiah is preceded by the
appointed restoration through the Spirit and the witnesses, finds in
Sirach 48:10 the second-temple voice articulating the same expectation.
The phrase to restore the tribes of Jacob is also significant: the
second-temple expectation was that Elijah's appointed work included the
restoration of the twelve tribes — the framework's central concern.

Verses 15–25 praise Hezekiah and Isaiah. The framework's note: Sirach 48
names Isaiah's prophetic ministry but does not develop the substantive
content of Isaiah's prophecies. The framework's reading of Isaiah
remains the framework's reading; Sirach simply records that Isaiah was
the great prophet of his time.

Cross-references: 1 Kings 17:1–19:21; 2 Kings 2:1–13; 2 Kings
18:1–20:21; 2 Chronicles 32:1–33; Isaiah 1:1–66:24; Malachi 4:5–6;
Matthew 17:10–13; Mark 9:11–13; Luke 1:13–17.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 49

  1 The remembrance of Josias is like the composition of the perfume
  that is made by the art of the apothecary: it is sweet as honey in all
  mouths, and as musick at a banquet of wine. 2 He behaved himself
  uprightly in the conversion of the people, and took away the
  abominations of iniquity. 3 He directed his heart to Yahuah (God), and
  in the time of the ungodly he established the worship of Yahuah (God).
  4 All, except David and Ezekias and Josias, were defective: for they
  forsook the law of the Most High, even the kings of Juda failed. 5
  Therefore he gave their power to others, and their glory to a strange
  nation.

  6 They burnt the chosen city of the sanctuary, and made the streets
  desolate, according to the prophecy of Jeremias. 7 For they entreated
  him evil, who nevertheless was a prophet, sanctified in his mother’s
  womb, that he might root out, and afflict, and destroy; and that he
  might build up also, and plant. 8 It was Ezekiel who saw the glorious
  vision, which was shewed him upon the chariot of the cherubims. 9 For
  he made mention of the enemies under the figure of the rain, and
  directed them that went right. 10 And of the twelve prophets let the
  memorial be blessed, and let their bones flourish again out of their
  place: for they comforted Jacob, and delivered them by assured hope.

  11 How shall we magnify Zorobabel? even he was as a signet on the
  right hand: 12 So was Jesus the son of Josedec: who in their time
  builded the house, and set up an holy temple to Yahuah (God), which
  was prepared for everlasting glory. 13 And among the elect was
  Neemias, whose renown is great, who raised up for us the walls that
  were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our
  ruins again. 14 But upon the earth was no man created like Enoch; for
  he was taken from the earth. 15 Neither was there a young man born
  like Joseph, a governor of his brothers, a stay of the people, whose
  bones were regarded of Yahuah (God).

  16 Sem and Seth were in great honour among men, and so was Adam above
  every living thing in creation.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues with Josiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, the twelve
minor prophets, and several post-exilic figures. Verses 1–7 praise
Josiah and lament the failures of the kings who followed him. Verses 8–9
praise Ezekiel — naming him as the one who saw the chariot of cherubim.
Verses 10 names the twelve minor prophets together: And of the twelve
prophets let the memorial be blessed, and let their bones flourish again
out of their place: for they comforted Jacob, and delivered them by
assured hope.

The framework of this Series, which honors the prophets as the standard
against which all witness is measured, finds in Sirach 49:10 the
second-temple voice honoring the twelve minor prophets as a unit. The
bone-flourishing imagery is parallel to Ezekiel 37 (the valley of the
dry bones) and signals the second-temple expectation of the
resurrection.

Verses 11–13 praise Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, and Nehemiah —
the post-exilic leadership.

Verses 14–16 close with brief notices of Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth, Adam
— a curious reverse-chronological summary that ends the praise of the
fathers proper. The framework's note: the inclusion of Adam at the end
of the catalogue is the second-temple recognition that all the named
fathers were sons of Adam, in the framework's specific Genesis 1 /
Genesis 2 reading. The framework holds the Adamic lineage as the
covenant lineage; Sirach's catalogue ending at Adam is consistent with
that holding.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 22:1–23:30; Jeremiah 1:1–52:34; Ezekiel
1:1–48:35; Daniel 1:1–12:13; Hosea 1:1–14:9; Haggai 1:1–2:23; Zechariah
1:1–14:21; Genesis 5:1–32.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 50

  1 Simon the high priest, the son of Onias, who in his life repaired
  the house again, and in his days fortified the temple: 2 And by him
  was built from the foundation the double height, the high fortress of
  the wall about the temple: 3 In his days the cistern to receive water,
  being in compass as the sea, was covered with plates of brass: 4 He
  took care of the temple that it should not fall, and fortified the
  city against besieging: 5 How was he honoured in the midst of the
  people in his coming out of the sanctuary!

  6 He was as the morning star in the midst of a cloud, and as the moon
  at the full: 7 As the sun shining upon the temple of the Most High,
  and as the rainbow giving light in the bright clouds: 8 And as the
  flower of roses in the spring of the year, as lilies by the rivers of
  waters, and as the branches of the frankincense tree in the time of
  summer: 9 As fire and incense in the censer, and as a vessel of beaten
  gold set with all manner of precious stones: 10 And as a fair olive
  tree budding forth fruit, and as a cypress tree which grows up to the
  clouds.

  11 When he put on the robe of honour, and was clothed with the
  perfection of glory, when he went up to the holy altar, he made the
  garment of holiness honourable. 12 When he took the portions out of
  the priests’ hands, he himself stood by the hearth of the altar,
  compassed about, as a young cedar in Libanus; and as palm trees
  compassed they him round about. 13 So were all the sons of Aaron in
  their glory, and the oblations of Yahuah (God) in their hands, before
  all the congregation of Yashar'el (Israel). 14 And finishing the
  service at the altar, that he might adorn the offering of the most
  high Almighty, 15 He stretched out his hand to the cup, and poured of
  the blood of the grape, he poured out at the foot of the altar a
  sweetsmelling savour to the most high King of all.

  16 Then shouted the sons of Aaron, and sounded the silver trumpets,
  and made a great noise to be heard, for a remembrance before the Most
  High. 17 Then all the people together hasted, and fell down to the
  earth upon their faces to worship their Elohim (God) Almighty, the
  Most High. 18 The singers also sang praises with their voices, with
  great variety of sounds was there made sweet melody. 19 And the people
  besought Yahuah (God), the Most High, by prayer before him that is
  merciful, till the solemnity of Yahuah (God) was ended, and they had
  finished his service. 20 Then he went down, and lifted up his hands
  over the whole congregation of the children of Yashar'el (Israel), to
  give the blessing of Yahuah (God) with his lips, and to rejoice in his
  name.

  21 And they bowed themselves down to worship the second time, that
  they might receive a blessing from the Most High. 22 Now therefore
  bless you Yahuah (God) of all, which only doeth wondrous things
  every where, which exalteth our days from the womb, and dealeth with
  us according to his mercy. 23 He grant us joyfulness of heart, and
  that peace may be in our days in Yashar'el (Israel) for ever: 24 That
  he would confirm his mercy with us, and deliver us at his time! 25
  There be two manner of nations which my heart abhorreth, and the third
  is no nation:

  26 They that sit upon the mountain of Samaria, and they that dwell
  among the Philistines, and that foolish people that dwell in Sichem.
  27 Jesus the son of Sirach of Jerusalem has written in this book the
  instruction of understanding and knowledge, who out of his heart
  poured forth wisdom. 28 Blessed is he that shall be exercised in these
  things; and he that layeth them up in his heart shall become wise. 29
  For if he do them, he shall be strong to all things: for the light of
  Yahuah (God) leadeth him, who gives wisdom to the godly. Blessed be
  the name of Yahuah (God) for ever. Amen, Amen.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 50 is the climactic praise of Simon II, the high priest who
served around 200 BCE — a contemporary or near-contemporary of the
author of Ecclesiasticus. The chapter is a sustained portrait of Simon's
high priestly service: the rebuilding of the temple after damage, the
strengthening of the city walls, the leading of the temple service on
the Day of Atonement, the priestly garments, the offerings, the
Levitical music, the closing benediction.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the chapter is the second-temple high point of priestly
idealization. The framework of this Series, which has tracked the
corruption of the priesthood through the Hellenization crisis and the
Maccabean dynasty and the Hasmonean kings, notes that Simon II's high
priesthood (around 200 BCE) preceded the Hellenization crisis. He
represents the last great period of pre-Hellenization priestly
faithfulness. The framework's reading: Simon's high priesthood was, in
fact, a high point; the corruption that came afterward was real; both
can be acknowledged.

Ben Sira is writing a generation or so after Simon, and his praise of
Simon is in part an act of preservation — the kind of memorial that says
this is what was, and we are losing it. Within fifty years of Sirach's
composition, the high priesthood would be sold to Jason and then to
Menelaus, the temple would be desecrated by Antiochus, and the Maccabean
revolt would be necessary to recover even a fraction of what Simon's day
represented. The framework reads chapter 50 as a window into what the
priesthood was supposed to be, before the inherited deception of the
Hellenizing party and the imperial-puppet appointments destroyed the
office's faithfulness. The high priesthood as Simon walked it is the
standard by which every later corruption is measured.

Second, the description of the temple service (verses 5–21) is one of
the most detailed second-temple portraits of the Day of Atonement
liturgy in any literature. The framework of this Series, which honors
the appointed services of the Torah and which holds that the Messiah's
atoning work fulfilled what the Day of Atonement had foreshadowed
(Hebrews 9–10), finds in Sirach 50 the second-temple description of the
foreshadowing. Read it for what it shows; read Hebrews 9–10 for what it
pointed toward.

Third, the closing of the chapter (verses 25–29) names two peoples the
author "abhors" — the Edomites (Idumeans), the Philistines, and the
Samaritans. The framework's note: the Samaritans here are the
second-temple Samaritan community — the population that emerged after
the Assyrian deportation of the northern kingdom mixed with the foreign
peoples Assyria settled in the land — and the framework has already
addressed the second-temple Samaritan question in the introduction to 1
Esdras and elsewhere. The framework does not endorse contemporary
Samaritan-hatred from this verse; the framework reads the verse as the
second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) expression of the religious-political
tensions of its day. The contemporary awakening reader's posture toward
all peoples is the patient, victims-not-enemies posture; the apocryphal
verse's specific attitude is held in its second-temple context.

Cross-references: Leviticus 16:1–34; Numbers 6:22–27; 1 Chronicles
23:1–32; Ezra 6:13–22; Nehemiah 12:27–47; John 4:1–42; Hebrews 9:1–28;
Hebrews 10:1–18.

Ecclesiasticus — Chapter 51

  1 I will thank you, O Yahuah (God) and King, and praise you, O Yahuah
  (God) my Saviour: I do give praise to your name: 2 For you are my
  defender and helper, and has preserved my body from destruction, and
  from the snare of the slanderous tongue, and from the lips that forge
  lies, and has been my helper against my adversaries: 3 And have
  delivered me, according to the multitude of your mercies and greatness
  of your name, from the teeth of them that were ready to devour me, and
  out of the hands of such as sought after my life, and from the
  manifold afflictions which I had; 4 From the choking of fire on every
  side, and from the midst of the fire which I kindled not; 5 From the
  depth of the belly of hell, from an unclean tongue, and from lying
  words.

  6 By an accusation to the king from an unrighteous tongue my soul drew
  near even to death, my life was near to the hell beneath. 7 They
  compassed me on every side, and there was no man to help me: I looked
  for the succour of men, but there was none. 8 Then thought I upon your
  mercy, O Yahuah (God), and upon your acts of old, how you deliverest
  such as wait for you, and savest them out of the hands of the enemies.
  9 Then lifted I up my supplications from the earth, and prayed for
  deliverance from death. 10 I called upon Yahuah (God), the Father of
  my Elohim (God), that he would not leave me in the days of my trouble,
  and in the time of the proud, when there was no help.

  11 I will praise your name continually, and will sing praises with
  thanksgiving; and so my prayer was heard: 12 For you savedst me from
  destruction, and deliveredst me from the evil time: therefore will I
  give thanks, and praise you, and bless they name, O Yahuah (God). 13
  When I was yet young, or ever I went abroad, I desired wisdom openly
  in my prayer. 14 I prayed for her before the temple, and will seek her
  out even to the end. 15 Even from the flower till the grape was ripe
  has my heart delighted in her: my foot went the right way, from my
  youth up sought I after her.

  16 I bowed down my ear a little, and received her, and got much
  learning. 17 I profited in it, therefore will I ascribe glory to him
  that gives me wisdom. 18 For I purposed to do after her, and earnestly
  I followed that which is good; so shall I not be confounded. 19 My
  soul has wrestled with her, and in my doings I was exact: I stretched
  forth my hands to the heaven above, and bewailed my ignorances of her.
  20 I directed my soul to her, and I found her in pureness: I have had
  my heart joined with her from the beginning, therefore shall I not be
  foresaken.

  21 My heart was troubled in seeking her: therefore have I gotten a
  good possession. 22 Yahuah (God) has given me a tongue for my
  reward, and I will praise him with it. 23 Draw near to me, you
  unlearned, and dwell in the house of learning. 24 Wherefore are you
  slow, and what say you to these things, seeing your souls are very
  thirsty? 25 I opened my mouth, and said, Buy her for yourselves
  without money.

  26 Put your neck under the yoke, and let your soul receive
  instruction: she is hard at hand to find. 27 Behold with your eyes,
  how that I have but little labour, and have gotten to me much rest. 28
  Get learning with a great sum of money, and get much gold by her. 29
  Let your soul rejoice in his mercy, and be not ashamed of his praise.
  30 Work your work betimes, and in his time he will give you your
  reward.

⸻

Commentary

The closing chapter is a personal prayer of the author — likely a
separate composition appended to Ecclesiasticus, possibly older than the
rest of the book and possibly attached because of its character as a
wisdom-seeker's prayer. Verses 1–12 are a thanksgiving for deliverance
from various trials. Verses 13–30 are the appended autobiographical
account of how the author sought wisdom from his youth and what wisdom
has done for him. Verses 23–30 are the closing call to the reader: Draw
near unto me, you unlearned, and dwell in the house of learning.
Wherefore are you slow, and what say you to these things, seeing your
souls are very thirsty?... I opened my mouth, and said, Buy her for
yourselves without money. Put your neck under the yoke, and let your
soul receive instruction: she is hard at hand to find. Behold with your
eyes, how that I have but little labour, and have gotten unto me much
rest.

Several things matter.

First, the verses 23–26 contain language Yahusha (Jesus) closely echoes
in Matthew 11:28–30: Come unto me, all you that labour and are heavy
laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me;
for I am meek and lowly in heart: and you shall find rest unto your
souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. The vocabulary is
the vocabulary of the second-temple wisdom tradition. Yahusha was
speaking to a generation that knew Sirach. He took the wisdom-tradition
language (come to me, take my yoke, find rest for your souls) and
applied it to himself.

The "rest for your souls" phrase has a deeper canonical lineage that
locks the connection in. Jeremiah 6:16 — the canonical anchor for the
phrase: Thus says Yahuah (God), Stand in the ways, and see, and ask for
the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and you shall
find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein. The
phrase rest for your souls enters the covenant vocabulary at Jeremiah 6,
in the context of the prophet calling Yahudah (Judah) back to the old
paths — the Torah, the appointed walk, the covenant the fathers had
received. Sirach 51:27 — I have but little labour, and have gotten unto
me much rest — is the second-temple voice of one who walked in the old
paths and found the rest Jeremiah named. Matthew 11:29 — take my yoke
upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and you
shall find rest unto your souls — is Yahusha placing himself at the
center of the same call. The old paths are now embodied in the Messiah.
The rest is now found in him. The Torah — the wisdom Sirach 24 named as
Yahuah (God)'s inheritance to Jacob — is internalized through the One
who came in the flesh.

The framework of this Series, which holds that Yahusha is the Word — the
Formed One — who came in the flesh and that he is the embodied Wisdom of
Yahuah (God), finds in the parallel between Jeremiah 6:16, Sirach 51,
and Matthew 11:28–30 the prophetic-and-second-temple-and-apostolic line
that names the same rest in the same path under the same Messiah. The
wisdom-tradition called the seeker to come to wisdom for rest; the
Messiah called the seeker to come to himself for rest; Jeremiah called
Yahudah (Judah) to walk in the old paths for rest. The three calls are
the same call. The framework holds them together.

Read the parallel side by side and let it press. Sirach 51:23: Draw near
unto me. Matthew 11:28: Come unto me. Sirach 51:26: Put your neck under
the yoke. Matthew 11:29: Take my yoke upon you. Sirach 51:27: I have but
little labour, and have gotten unto me much rest. Matthew 11:29: You
shall find rest unto your souls. The vocabulary is the same vocabulary.
The audience that heard Yahusha was the audience that knew this prayer.
The reader who has not read Sirach 51 has not heard half of what the
Sermon on the Mount audience was hearing when Yahusha spoke. And the
framework's claim — that Yahusha is the Wisdom of Yahuah (God) come in
the flesh — is the claim Yahusha himself was making by deliberately
taking the wisdom-tradition's invitation language onto his own lips.
Wisdom called from the temple; the Word who is Wisdom now calls from his
own person. Come.

Second, the closing benediction (verse 30): Work your work betimes, and
in his time he will give you your reward. The framework of this Series,
which holds that the awakening reader's faithful work is rewarded by
Yahuah (God) at the appointed time, finds in Sirach 51:30 the
second-temple model of patient labor in the appointed pattern.

Third, the framework's final note on Ecclesiasticus: the book is the
largest single volume of second-temple wisdom in the Apocrypha. It is
uneven. It is sometimes culturally specific in ways that do not transfer
cleanly. It has passages of theological concentration (especially
chapter 24, the great hymn to wisdom; chapter 38, the meditation on
physicians and the trades; chapters 44–50, the praise of the fathers;
chapter 51's closing call) that are foundational for understanding the
New Testament. Read the book whole. Hold the proverbial wisdom against
the Torah. Test it by the prophets. Read the New Testament knowing that
the writers — Yahusha, the apostles, the writer of Hebrews — had this
book in their literary world. The vocabulary they used was, in part, the
vocabulary Sirach had given them. The framework's reading honors what
the book contributes without inflating it beyond what witness can
rightly bear.

Cross-references: Matthew 11:28–30; Proverbs 8:1–36; Wisdom of Solomon
7:7–14; Psalm 119:9–16; Psalm 119:33–40; James 1:5; 1 Corinthians
1:18–31; Colossians 2:3.

Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah — Introduction

Baruch is the briefest of the prophet-attributed books in the Apocrypha.
Six chapters, attributed to Baruch the son of Neriah — Jeremiah's
scribe, named throughout the canonical book of Jeremiah as the one who
wrote down the prophet's oracles — the book presents itself as written
in the years immediately following the destruction of Jerusalem in 586
BCE, and read aloud to the exiles in Babylon. The first three chapters
are a confession of sin, a prayer for restoration, and a wisdom-poem
identifying wisdom with the Torah of Yahuah (God) (closely paralleling
Sirach 24). The fourth and fifth chapters are a poetic vision of the
restoration of Jerusalem and the return of the scattered children. The
sixth chapter — sometimes counted as a separate book and titled "the
Letter of Jeremiah" or "the Epistle of Jeremy" — is a polemical letter
against the idolatry of Babylon, addressed to the exiles, instructing
them not to fear the gods of the empire because those gods are nothing.

The book is composite and is almost certainly later than the historical
Baruch. The Greek text shows knowledge of post-exilic developments, and
most scholars place its composition between the third and first
centuries BCE. The pseudonymous attribution is a literary convention of
the period: a wisdom-and-restoration text was given the name of a known
scribe to anchor its authority. The awakening reader does not need to
defend the historical Baruch's authorship to receive the book. The book
is what it is — a second-temple meditation on exile, sin, restoration,
and the foolishness of pagan idolatry, composed in the voice of one of
the great scribes of the prophetic tradition.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, Baruch 4–5 is one of the great second-temple meditations on the
gathering of the scattered seed. The voice is the personified Jerusalem
mourning over her children carried into exile, and then receiving them
back. The imagery — the gathering from the four directions, the long
highway home, the children returning carried on the shoulders of nations
— overlaps directly with Isaiah 60, Isaiah 49, and the gathering oracles
of the prophets. The reader who has been working through the framework
of scattered Yashar'el (Israel) will hear these chapters as
second-temple poetry over the same gathering the prophets named. Baruch
is not a prophet. The poetry is not new revelation. But the poetry is
faithful to the revelation, and it lifts the heart of the reader in a
way that few apocryphal passages can.

Second, the Letter of Jeremiah (Baruch 6) is a sustained polemic against
idolatry that the awakening reader walking out of institutional
Christianity will hear with particular sharpness. The argument is
simple: the idols of Babylon are pieces of carved wood overlaid with
gold, dressed up by priests, fed by people who hope for an answer they
will never receive. The idols cannot save themselves from rust, fire, or
theft. They cannot bless. They cannot judge. The Letter mocks them point
by point, and the awakening reader who has been retrained to see the
Babylonian system inside institutional Christianity (the gold-overlaid
statues, the dressed-up images, the priesthood feeding the system) will
find the Letter's polemic resonating in unexpected ways. The
first-century pagan idolatry the Letter directly addresses is not the
same as the contemporary religious systems the awakening reader has
walked out of. But the spiritual logic of idolatry — putting trust in
what cannot save, in a god dressed up by men — runs across both, and the
Letter's polemic carries into the contemporary reader's situation more
directly than the surface-level historical context might suggest.

Third, Baruch's confession of sin (Baruch 1:15–3:8) is the second-temple
liturgy of repentance for exile. It mirrors Daniel 9 in tone and
structure. The confession owns the sin that produced the exile, names
the curses of Deuteronomy 28 as the consequence the people had earned,
and turns to Yahuah (God)'s mercy as the only hope of restoration. The
awakening reader who has walked through the recognition that "our
fathers have inherited lies" (Jeremiah 16:19) will find in Baruch 1–3
the second-temple voice that already prayed that confession, in the same
shape and the same posture.

The Letter of Jeremiah is set in this volume as chapter 6 of Baruch, in
the 1611 King James convention. Some Greek manuscripts present it as a
separate document; the King James translators included it within Baruch
and gave it its own chapter heading. This volume preserves that
arrangement.

Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah — Chapter 1

  1 And these are the words of the book, which Baruch the son of Nerias,
  the son of Maasias, the son of Sedecias, the son of Asadias, the son
  of Chelcias, wrote in Babylon, 2 In the fifth year, and in the seventh
  day of the month, what time as the Chaldeans took Jerusalem, and burnt
  it with fire. 3 And Baruch did read the words of this book in the
  hearing of Jechonias the son of Joachim king of Juda, and in the ears
  of all the people that came to hear the book, 4 And in the hearing of
  the nobles, and of the king’s sons, and in the hearing of the elders,
  and of all the people, from the lowest to the highest, even of all
  them that dwelt at Babylon by the river Sud. 5 Whereupon they wept,
  fasted, and prayed before Yahuah (God).

  6 They made also a collection of money according to every man’s power:
  7 And they sent it to Jerusalem to Joachim the high priest, the son of
  Chelcias, son of Salom, and to the priests, and to all the people
  which were found with him at Jerusalem, 8 At the same time when he
  received the vessels of the house of Yahuah (God), that were carried
  out of the temple, to return them into the land of Juda, the tenth day
  of the month Sivan, namely, silver vessels, which Sedecias the son of
  Josias king of Juda had made, 9 After that Nabuchodonosor king of
  Babylon had carried away Jechonias, and the princes, and the captives,
  and the mighty men, and the people of the land, from Jerusalem, and
  brought them to Babylon. 10 And they said, Behold, we have sent you
  money to buy you burnt offerings, and sin offerings, and incense, and
  prepare you manna, and offer upon the altar of Yahuah (God), our
  Elohim (God);

  11 And pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and for
  the life of Balthasar his son, that their days may be upon earth as
  the days of heaven: 12 And Yahuah (God) will give us strength, and
  lighten our eyes, and we shall live under the shadow of Nabuchodonosor
  king of Babylon, and under the shadow of Balthasar his son, and we
  shall serve them many days, and find favour in their sight. 13 Pray
  for us also to Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God), for we have sinned
  against Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God); and to this day the fury of
  Yahuah (God) and his wrath is not turned from us. 14 And you shall
  read this book which we have sent to you, to make confession in the
  house of Yahuah (God), upon the feasts and solemn days. 15 And you
  shall say, To Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God) belongeth righteousness,
  but to us the confusion of faces, as it is come to pass this day, to
  them of Juda, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem,

  16 And to our kings, and to our princes, and to our priests, and to
  our prophets, and to our fathers: 17 For we have sinned before Yahuah
  (God), 18 And disobeyed him, and have not hearkened to the voice of
  Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God), to walk in the commandments that he
  gave us openly: 19 Since the day that Yahuah (God) brought our
  forefathers out of the land of Egypt, to this present day, we have
  been disobedient to Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God), and we have been
  negligent in not hearing his voice. 20 Wherefore the evils cleaved to
  us, and the curse, which Yahuah (God) appointed by Moses his servant
  at the time that he brought our fathers out of the land of Egypt, to
  give us a land that floweth with milk and honey, like as it is to see
  this day.

  21 Nevertheless we have not hearkened to the voice of Yahuah (God),
  our Elohim (God), according to all the words of the prophets, whom he
  sent to us: 22 But every man followed the imagination of his own
  wicked heart, to serve strange gods, and to do evil in the sight of
  Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God).

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter sets the scene. The book is presented as a writing
of Baruch, the son of Neriah, the scribe of Jeremiah, sent from Babylon
to the priests and people in Jerusalem during the reign of
Nebuchadnezzar — that is, during the period after the destruction of the
first temple in 586 BCE. The writing is to be read aloud in the courts
of the house of Yahuah (God) on solemn days. The exiles have collected
silver to send back to Jerusalem, asking that sacrifices be offered for
the king of Babylon and his son Belshazzar that they may live long in
the land.

Two things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the request that prayer be offered for the king of Babylon (verse
11) is a continuation of the prophetic instruction Jeremiah had given in
his letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29:7): "And seek the peace of the
city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray to
Yahuah (God) for it: for in the peace thereof shall you have peace." The
framework of this Series, which holds that the covenant people in
dispersion are to seek the peace of the cities where Yahuah (God) has
scattered them rather than agitating for political revolution, finds in
Baruch 1 the second-temple practice of that instruction. Pray for the
king of Babylon. Live as exiles in the city of your scattering. Wait for
the gathering Yahuah (God) has appointed.

Second, the confession of sin that opens at verse 15 and continues
through chapter 3 is one of the second-temple's great
corporate-confession liturgies. The voice is the voice of the people
gathered in Jerusalem (and the exiles in Babylon, by extension),
confessing that the calamity that has befallen them is the consequence
of their having walked out from under the covenant. "Confusion of faces,
as it is come to pass this day, to the men of Yahudah (Judah), and to
the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to our kings, and to our princes, and
to our priests, and to our prophets, and to our fathers" — the catalogue
is the catalogue of Daniel 9 and of Nehemiah 9. The covenant pattern is
acknowledged. The Father is righteous. The people have been unfaithful.
The exile is the consequence.

The framework of this Series, which holds that "our fathers have
inherited lies" (Jeremiah 16:19) is the awakening confession, finds in
Baruch 1:15–22 the second-temple voice that already prayed that
confession in the same shape. The awakening reader walking out of the
four houses can pray Baruch 1's confession as his or her own —
substituting the contemporary catalogue of inherited lies for the
ancient catalogue of covenant breach — and find that the prayer fits.

Cross-references: Jeremiah 29:1–14; Jeremiah 36:1–32; Daniel 9:1–19;
Ezra 9:1–15; Nehemiah 9:1–38; Jeremiah 16:19; Deuteronomy 28:15–68.

Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah — Chapter 2

  1 Therefore Yahuah (God) has made good his word, which he pronounced
  against us, and against our judges that judged Yashar'el (Israel), and
  against our kings, and against our princes, and against the men of
  Yashar'el (Israel) and Juda, 2 To bring upon us great plagues, such as
  never happened under the whole heaven, as it came to pass in
  Jerusalem, according to the things that were written in the law of
  Moses; 3 That a man should eat the flesh of his own son, and the flesh
  of his own daughter. 4 Moreover he has delivered them to be in
  subjection to all the kingdoms that are round about us, to be as a
  reproach and desolation among all the people round about, where Yahuah
  (God) has scattered them. 5 Thus we were cast down, and not exalted,
  because we have sinned against Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God), and
  have not been obedient to his voice.

  6 To Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God) appertaineth righteousness: but to
  us and to our fathers open shame, as appears this day. 7 For all these
  plagues are come upon us, which Yahuah (God) has pronounced against us
  8 Yet have we not prayed before Yahuah (God), that we might turn every
  one from the imaginations of his wicked heart. 9 Wherefore Yahuah
  (God) watched over us for evil, and Yahuah (God) has brought it upon
  us: for Yahuah (God) is righteous in all his works which he has
  commanded us. 10 Yet we have not hearkened to his voice, to walk in
  the commandments of Yahuah (God), that he has set before us.

  11 And now, O Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), that have brought
  your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and high arm,
  and with signs, and with wonders, and with great power, and have
  gotten thyself a name, as appears this day: 12 O Yahuah (God), our
  Elohim (God), we have sinned, we have done ungodly, we have dealt
  unrighteously in all your ordinances. 13 Let your wrath turn from us:
  for we are but a few left among the heathen, where you have scattered
  us. 14 Hear our prayers, O Yahuah (God), and our petitions, and
  deliver us for your own sake, and give us favour in the sight of them
  which have led us away: 15 That all the earth may know that you are
  Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God), because Yashar'el (Israel) and his
  posterity is called by your name.

  16 O Yahuah (God), look down from yours holy house, and consider us:
  bow down your ear, O Yahuah (God), to hear us. 17 Open your eyes, and
  behold; for the dead that are in the graves, whose souls are taken
  from their bodies, will give to Yahuah (God) neither praise nor
  righteousness: 18 But the soul that is greatly vexed, which goes
  stooping and feeble, and the eyes that fail, and the hungry soul, will
  give you praise and righteousness, O Yahuah (God). 19 Therefore we do
  not make our humble supplication before you, O Yahuah (God), our
  Elohim (God), for the righteousness of our fathers, and of our kings.
  20 For you have sent out your wrath and indignation upon us, as you
  have spoken by your servants the prophets, saying,

  21 Thus says Yahuah (God), Bow down your shoulders to serve the king
  of Babylon: so shall you remain in the land that I gave to your
  fathers. 22 But if you will not hear the voice of Yahuah (God), to
  serve the king of Babylon, 23 I will cause to cease out of the cites
  of Yahudah (Judah), and from without Jerusalem, the voice of mirth,
  and the voice of joy, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of
  the bride: and the whole land shall be desolate of inhabitants. 24 But
  we would not hearken to your voice, to serve the king of Babylon:
  therefore have you made good the words that you spakest by your
  servants the prophets, namely, that the bones of our kings, and the
  bones of our fathers, should be taken out of their place. 25 And, lo,
  they are cast out to the heat of the day, and to the frost of the
  night, and they died in great miseries by famine, by sword, and by
  pestilence.

  26 And the house which is called by your name have you laid waste, as
  it is to be seen this day, for the wickedness of the house of
  Yashar'el (Israel) and the house of Juda. 27 O Yahuah (God), our
  Elohim (God), you have dealt with us after all your goodness, and
  according to all that great mercy of yours, 28 As you spakest by your
  servant Moses in the day when you did command him to write the law
  before the children of Yashar'el (Israel), saying, 29 If you will not
  hear my voice, surely this very great multitude shall be turned into a
  small number among the nations, where I will scatter them. 30 For I
  knew that they would not hear me, because it is a stiffnecked people:
  but in the land of their captivities they shall remember themselves.

  31 And shall know that I am Yahuah (God), their Elohim (God): for I
  will give them an heart, and ears to hear: 32 And they shall praise me
  in the land of their captivity, and think upon my name, 33 And return
  from their stiff neck, and from their wicked deeds: for they shall
  remember the way of their fathers, which sinned before Yahuah (God).
  34 And I will bring them again into the land which I promised with an
  oath to their fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and they shall be
  lords of it: and I will increase them, and they shall not be
  diminished. 35 And I will make an everlasting covenant with them to be
  their Elohim (God), and they shall be my people: and I will no more
  drive my people of Yashar'el (Israel) out of the land that I have
  given them.

⸻

Commentary

The confession continues. The chapter rehearses the Torah's curses
(verses 1–10), naming explicitly that Yahuah (God) brought upon the
people the things He had warned them about through Moses — that they
would be scattered, that they would eat their own children's flesh
during the siege, that the kingdoms surrounding them would mock them,
that the corpses would be left unburied. The naming is unflinching. The
text refuses to soften what the Torah had warned.

The chapter then turns (verses 11–35) to the plea for mercy. The basis
of the plea is the covenant — that Yahuah (God) had said through
Jeremiah that He would establish an everlasting covenant with the house
of Yashar'el (Israel) and the house of Yahudah (Judah), that He would
put His fear in their hearts, that He would gather them out of the lands
where they had been scattered, that the dead among them would not return
to praise Him but the living would. The framework of this Series finds
two things.

First, the explicit naming of the gathering of "the house of Yashar'el
(Israel) and the house of Yahudah (Judah)" together, in verses 17 and
34, is one of the Two-House witnesses in the apocryphal corpus. The
second-temple prayer life remembered that the gathering would include
both houses — the southern Yahudah (Judah) and the scattered northern
Yashar'el (Israel) — under the new covenant Jeremiah had named. The
framework of this Series, which holds the Two-House framework as
foundational, finds in Baruch 2 the second-temple voice already praying
for the gathering of both houses. The framework is not a modern
theological innovation. The framework is the second-temple Yahudi
(Jewish) prayer life itself.

Second, the citation of the new-covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:31–34 is
implicit throughout Baruch 2. The fear of Yahuah (God) put in the
hearts. The gathering from the lands of dispersion. The everlasting
covenant. The vocabulary is the vocabulary of Jeremiah 31, and the
framework of this Series — which holds that the new covenant of Jeremiah
31 is the Torah written on the heart, not the Torah replaced by grace —
finds the second-temple prayer leaning on Jeremiah 31 in exactly that
way.

Cross-references: Leviticus 26:14–46; Deuteronomy 28:15–68; Jeremiah
31:31–34; Jeremiah 32:36–44; Ezekiel 36:24–28; Hosea 1:9–11; Hosea 2:23;
Romans 11:25–27.

Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah — Chapter 3

  1 O Yahuah (God) Almighty, Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), the
  soul in anguish the troubled spirit, cries to you. 2 Hear, O Yahuah
  (God), and have mercy; for you are merciful: and have pity upon us,
  because we have sinned before you. 3 For you endurest for ever, and we
  perish utterly. 4 O Yahuah (God) Almighty, you Yahuah (God) of
  Yashar'el (Israel), hear now the prayers of the dead Israelites, and
  of their children, which have sinned before you, and not hearkened to
  the voice of you their Elohim (God): for the which cause these plagues
  cleave to us. 5 Remember not the iniquities of our forefathers: but
  think upon your power and your name now at this time.

  6 For you are Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God), and you, O Yahuah (God),
  will we praise. 7 And for this cause you have put your fear in our
  hearts, to the intent that we should call upon your name, and praise
  you in our captivity: for we have called to mind all the iniquity of
  our forefathers, that sinned before you. 8 Behold, we are yet this day
  in our captivity, where you have scattered us, for a reproach and a
  curse, and to be subject to payments, according to all the iniquities
  of our fathers, which departed from Yahuah (God), our Elohim (God). 9
  Hear, Yashar'el (Israel), the commandments of life: give ear to
  understand wisdom. 10 How happeneth it Yashar'el (Israel), that you
  are in your enemies’ land, that you are waxen old in a strange
  country, that you are defiled with the dead,

  11 That you are counted with them that go down into the grave? 12 You
  have forsaken the fountain of wisdom. 13 For if you had walked in the
  way of Yahuah (God), you should have dwelled in peace for ever. 14
  Learn where is wisdom, where is strength, where is understanding; that
  you may know also where is length of days, and life, where is the
  light of the eyes, and peace. 15 Who has found out her place? or who
  has come into her treasures?

  16 Where are the princes of the heathen become, and such as ruled the
  beasts upon the earth; 17 They that had their pastime with the fowls
  of the air, and they that hoarded up silver and gold, in which men
  trust, and made no end of their getting? 18 For they that wrought in
