  silver, and were so careful, and whose works are unsearchable, 19 They
  are vanished and gone down to the grave, and others are come up in
  their steads. 20 Young men have seen light, and dwelt upon the earth:
  but the way of knowledge have they not known,

  21 Nor understood the paths thereof, nor laid hold of it: their
  children were far off from that way. 22 It has not been heard of in
  Chanaan, neither has it been seen in Theman. 23 The Agarenes that seek
  wisdom upon earth, the merchants of Meran and of Theman, the authors
  of fables, and searchers out of understanding; none of these have
  known the way of wisdom, or remember her paths. 24 O Yashar'el
  (Israel), how great is the house of Yahuah (God)! and how large is the
  place of his possession! 25 Great, and has none end; high, and
  unmeasurable.

  26 There were the giants famous from the beginning, that were of so
  great stature, and so expert in war. 27 Those did not Yahuah (God)
  choose, neither gave he the way of knowledge to them: 28 But they were
  destroyed, because they had no wisdom, and perished through their own
  foolishness. 29 Who has gone up into heaven, and taken her, and
  brought her down from the clouds? 30 Who has gone over the sea, and
  found her, and will bring her for pure gold?

  31 No man knoweth her way, nor thinketh of her path. 32 But he that
  knoweth all things knoweth her, and has found her out with his
  understanding: he that prepared the earth for evermore has filled it
  with fourfooted beasts: 33 He that sends forth light, and it goes,
  calls it again, and it obeyeth him with fear. 34 The stars shined in
  their watches, and rejoiced: when he calls them, they say, Here we be;
  and so with cheerfulness they shewed light to him that made them. 35
  This is our Elohim (God), and there shall none other be accounted of
  in comparison of him

  36 He has found out all the way of knowledge, and has given it to
  Jacob his servant, and to Yashar'el (Israel) his beloved. 37 Afterward
  did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men.

⸻

Commentary

The confession closes (verses 1–8) and the text turns to the great
wisdom hymn (verses 9–38) that is the theological climax of the book.

The wisdom hymn is one of the most important second-temple texts for the
framework of this Series. The argument runs in three movements.

First (verses 9–14), the prophet (the voice is now Jeremiah-like in
cadence) addresses Yashar'el (Israel) directly: "Hear, O Yashar'el
(Israel), the commandments of life: give ear to understand wisdom. How
happens it, O Yashar'el (Israel), that you are in your enemies' land,
that you are waxen old in a strange country, that you are defiled with
the dead, that you are counted with them that go down into the grave?"
The cause of the exile is named: "you have forsaken the fountain of
wisdom." Wisdom has been abandoned. The exile is the consequence.

Second (verses 15–28), the prophet asks who has found wisdom and entered
her treasures. The kings of the nations? They are gone. The merchants
and tradesmen? They are silent. The giants of old? They were destroyed
because they had no understanding. None of these found wisdom. None of
these knew her place.

Third, and the climax (verses 29–38), the prophet identifies wisdom: "He
that knows all things knows her, and has found her out with his
understanding... He has found out all the way of knowledge, and has
given it to Jacob his servant, and to Yashar'el (Israel) his beloved.
Afterward did he show himself upon earth, and conversed with men. This
is the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law that
endures for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as
leave it shall die. Turn yourself, O Jacob, and take hold of it: walk in
the presence of the light thereof, that you may be illuminated. Give not
your honor to another, nor the things that are profitable to you to a
strange nation."

The identification is explicit: wisdom is the Torah. "This is the book
of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law that endures for ever:
all they that keep it shall come to life." The framework of this Series
— which honors the Torah as the standard, holds 1 John 2:3–4 as the
master filter (he that says he knows Yahuah (God) and keeps not His
commandments is a liar), and refuses the antinomian readings of Paul
that have abolished the Torah in inherited Christianity — finds in
Baruch 3:36–38 the second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) prayer-life
articulating exactly that framework. Wisdom is the Torah. The Torah
endures forever. Those who keep it come to life. Those who leave it die.
The framework is not a modern theological innovation. The framework is
the second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) covenant theology in the most
concentrated form the apocryphal corpus contains.

The phrase in verse 37 — Afterward did he show himself upon earth, and
conversed with men — has been read in some Christian traditions as a
prophecy of the incarnation. The framework of this Series does not
require that reading. The text can refer to Yahuah (God)'s appearings to
the patriarchs, to His speaking through Moses on Sinai, to His
appearings as the angel of Yahuah (God) throughout the Hebrew scriptures
(which the framework of this Series identifies as the Formed One — the
Word who came in the flesh as Yahusha (Jesus)). The text is consistent
with the framework's understanding of the Formed One: the appearances of
the Word to His people across the Hebrew scriptures are real
appearances, real conversations, and the witness of Baruch 3:37 names
them as such.

The Wisdom-equals-Torah identification in Baruch 3:36–4:4 is one of the
framework's two great anchor passages in the apocryphal corpus (the
other being Sirach 24). The two passages should be read side by side.
Both identify Wisdom — the active formed presence of Yahuah (God) — with
the Torah given to Moses. Both name the Torah as the inheritance of the
seed of Jacob. Both reject any framework that would separate "wisdom"
(treated as a generic spiritual category) from "law" (treated as a
Yahudi (Jewish) particularism). The contemporary Christian split between
the two — wisdom as universal, law as ethnic — is rejected by both
texts. The framework holds Sirach 24 and Baruch 3 together as the two
second-temple voices most explicitly articulating the framework's
central claim: the Torah is the Wisdom of Yahuah (God) given as covenant
inheritance to the seed of Jacob, and apart from the Torah there is no
covenant wisdom.

The framework's specific reading of Baruch 3:36 — He has found out all
the way of knowledge, and has given it to Jacob his servant, and to
Yashar'el (Israel) his beloved — is precise. The way of knowledge is the
Torah. The recipient is Jacob, named, by lineage. The covenant is the
inheritance of the named seed. The reader who has been told that
"Yashar'el (Israel)" in this verse is a spiritual category open to
anyone who Torah-keeps has been read against the verse. The verse names
Jacob. Jacob is the patriarch by name. The inheritance is given to his
named descendants, not to a behavioral category. The bloodline-remnant
claim runs through this verse as plainly as it runs through Sirach
24:23. The framework holds it.

The closing of the chapter (3:38) — Afterward did he show himself upon
earth, and conversed with men — connects the Wisdom-Torah identification
to the appearing of the Formed One. The Wisdom that gives the Torah is
the same Word who appears, walks, and converses among men. This is the
Christology-precedent of John 1:14 (the Word was made flesh, and dwelt
among us) in Baruch's second-temple wisdom-tradition vocabulary. The
Word who is the Torah is the Word who appears in the world. The
Torah-form and the personal-form are continuous. The framework of this
Series, which holds the Father-and-Formed-One structure, finds in Baruch
3:36–38 a tightly compressed articulation of what John 1, Hebrews 1,
Colossians 1, and the framework itself articulate at length: the Word is
the Torah, the Word is the Formed One, the Word came in the flesh, and
the Word will reign in the appointed restoration.

Cross-references: Deuteronomy 4:1–8; Deuteronomy 30:11–20; Proverbs
1:20–33; Proverbs 8:1–36; Sirach 24:1–34; John 1:1–18; 1 John 2:3–4;
Hebrews 1:1–2; Colossians 1:15–20.

Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah — Chapter 4

  1 This is the book of the commandments of Yahuah (God), and the law
  that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but
  such as leave it shall die. 2 Turn you, O Jacob, and take hold of it:
  walk in the presence of the light thereof, that you may be
  illuminated. 3 Give not yours honour to another, nor the things that
  are profitable to you to a strange nation. 4 O Yashar'el (Israel),
  happy are we: for things that are pleasing to Yahuah (God) are made
  known to us. 5 Be of good cheer, my people, the memorial of Yashar'el
  (Israel).

  6 You were sold to the nations, not for your destruction: but because
  you moved Yahuah (God) to wrath, you were delivered to the enemies. 7
  For you provoked him that made you by sacrificing to devils, and not
  to Yahuah (God). 8 You have forgotten the everlasting Yahuah (God),
  that brought you up; and you have grieved Jerusalem, that nursed you.
  9 For when she saw the wrath of Yahuah (God) coming upon you, she
  said, Hearken, O you that dwell about Sion: Yahuah (God) has brought
  upon me great mourning; 10 For I saw the captivity of my sons and
  daughters, which the Everlasting brought upon them.

  11 With joy did I nourish them; but sent them away with weeping and
  mourning. 12 Let no man rejoice over me, a widow, and forsaken of
  many, who for the sins of my children am left desolate; because they
  departed from the law of Yahuah (God). 13 They knew not his statutes,
  nor walked in the ways of his commandments, nor trod in the paths of
  discipline in his righteousness. 14 Let them that dwell about Sion
  come, and remember you the captivity of my sons and daughters, which
  the Everlasting has brought upon them. 15 For he has brought a nation
  upon them from far, a shameless nation, and of a strange language, who
  neither reverenced old man, nor pitied child.

  16 These have carried away the dear beloved children of the widow, and
  left her that was alone desolate without daughters. 17 But what can I
  help you? 18 For he that brought these plagues upon you will deliver
  you from the hands of your enemies. 19 Go your way, O my children, go
  your way: for I am left desolate. 20 I have put off the clothing of
  peace, and put upon me the sackcloth of my prayer: I will cry to the
  Everlasting in my days.

  21 Be of good cheer, O my children, cry to Yahuah (God), and he will
  deliver you from the power and hand of the enemies. 22 For my hope is
  in the Everlasting, that he will save you; and joy is come to me from
  the Holy One, because of the mercy which shall soon come to you from
  the Everlasting our Saviour. 23 For I sent you out with mourning and
  weeping: but Yahuah (God) will give you to me again with joy and
  gladness for ever. 24 Like as now the neighbours of Sion have seen
  your captivity: so shall they see shortly your salvation from our
  Elohim (God) which shall come upon you with great glory, and
  brightness of the Everlasting. 25 My children, suffer patiently the
  wrath that is come upon you from Yahuah (God): for your enemy has
  persecuted you; but shortly you shall see his destruction, and shall
  tread upon his neck.

  26 My delicate ones have gone rough ways, and were taken away as a
  flock caught of the enemies. 27 Be of good comfort, O my children, and
  cry to Yahuah (God): for you shall be remembered of him that brought
  these things upon you. 28 For as it was your mind to go astray from
  Yahuah (God): so, being returned, seek him ten times more. 29 For he
  that has brought these plagues upon you shall bring you everlasting
  joy with your salvation. 30 Take a good heart, O Jerusalem: for he
  that gave you that name will comfort you.

  31 Miserable are they that afflicted you, and rejoiced at your fall.
  32 Miserable are the cities which your children served: miserable is
  she that received your sons. 33 For as she rejoiced at your ruin, and
  was glad of your fall: so shall she be grieved for her own desolation.
  34 For I will take away the rejoicing of her great multitude, and her
  pride shall be turned into mourning. 35 For fire shall come upon her
  from the Everlasting, long to endure; and she shall be inhabited of
  devils for a great time.

  36 O Jerusalem, look about you toward the east, and behold the joy
  that comes to you from Yahuah (God). 37 Lo, your sons come, whom you
  sentest away, they come gathered together from the east to the west by
  the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the glory of Yahuah (God).

⸻

Commentary

The chapter opens with the continuation of the wisdom hymn (verses 1–4),
naming the Torah explicitly: "She is the book of the commandments of
Yahuah (God), and the law that endures for ever. All they that keep her
shall come to life; but such as leave her shall die. Turn yourself, O
Jacob, and take hold of her." The framework's central claim — that the
Torah endures, that its keeping is the path of life, that its
abandonment is the path of death — is the framework Baruch 4 is praying.

The chapter then shifts (verses 5–37) to the personified voice of
Jerusalem mourning over her exiled children. The voice is the voice of
the city — the covenant people personified — speaking to her children
scattered among the nations, encouraging them to turn back, to remember
the covenant, to wait for the gathering Yahuah (God) has promised.

Two things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the personification of Jerusalem-as-mother is a recurrent figure
in the prophets (Lamentations, Isaiah 49:14–21, Isaiah 54:1–10). The
figure is not the institutional Jerusalem of the second temple; the
figure is the covenant city as Yahuah (God)'s appointed dwelling-place
and the gathering-point of His scattered people. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the gathering of the scattered seed is the long
restoration the prophets named, finds in Baruch 4 the second-temple
voice praying with the personified-Jerusalem figure that the prophets
used.

Second, the address to the children of the exile (verses 21–29) is a
remarkable second-temple call to the covenant remnant. "Be of good
cheer, O my children, cry to Yahuah (God), and he shall deliver you from
the power and hand of the enemies. For my hope is in the Everlasting,
that he will save you; and joy is come to me from the Holy One, because
of the mercy which shall soon come to you from the Everlasting our
Saviour." The voice of Jerusalem to her exiled children is the voice the
awakening reader's heart longs to hear: that the gathering is coming,
that the mercy is near, that the deliverance from the powers and hands
of the enemies is on its way. The framework of this Series, which holds
that the gathering of the scattered seed under the reign of the Messiah
is the destination, finds in Baruch 4 the second-temple voice praying
that gathering as the imminent hope.

Cross-references: Lamentations 1:1–22; Lamentations 2:1–22; Isaiah
49:14–26; Isaiah 54:1–10; Isaiah 60:1–22; Jeremiah 31:15–17; Hosea
2:14–23; Galatians 4:21–31; Revelation 21:1–4.

Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah — Chapter 5

  1 Put off, O Jerusalem, the garment of mourning and affliction, and
  put on the comeliness of the glory that comes from Yahuah (God) for
  ever. 2 Cast about you a double garment of the righteousness which
  comes from Yahuah (God); and set a diadem on yours head of the glory
  of the Everlasting. 3 For Yahuah (God) will shew your brightness to
  every country under heaven. 4 For your name shall be called of Yahuah
  (God) for ever The peace of righteousness, and The glory of the
  worship of Yahuah (God). 5 Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and
  look about toward the east, and behold your children gathered from the
  west to the east by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the
  remembrance of Yahuah (God).

  6 For they departed from you on foot, and were led away of their
  enemies: but Yahuah (God) brings them to you exalted with glory, as
  children of the kingdom. 7 For Yahuah (God) has appointed that every
  high hill, and banks of long continuance, should be cast down, and
  valleys filled up, to make even the ground, that Yashar'el (Israel)
  may go safely in the glory of Yahuah (God), 8 Moreover even the woods
  and every sweetsmelling tree shall overshadow Yashar'el (Israel) by
  the commandment of Yahuah (God). 9 For Yahuah (God) shall lead
  Yashar'el (Israel) with joy in the light of his glory with the mercy
  and righteousness that comes from him.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter is brief and is one of the most beautiful restoration
visions in the apocryphal corpus. Jerusalem is told to take off the
garment of mourning and put on the robe of righteousness, to set a
diadem on her head of the glory of the Everlasting, to stand on the
height and look toward the east and see her children gathered from the
west to the east at the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the
remembrance of Yahuah (God).

The vision is parallel to Isaiah 60. The garment-of-mourning to
robe-of-righteousness imagery is parallel to Isaiah 61:10. The
high-point looking-east-and-west gathering is parallel to Isaiah
49:18–22 and Isaiah 43:5–6. The mountains being made low and the valleys
being filled to make the way smooth is parallel to Isaiah 40:3–4 and is
cited by all four Gospels as the prophecy John the Baptist (the
immerser) was fulfilling.

The framework of this Series finds three things.

First, Baruch 5 is one of the second-temple texts that holds the
Two-House gathering imagery alive. The gathering from "the west to the
east" — and from the four directions, as the parallel prophetic texts
develop — is the gathering of the scattered seed of both houses. The
framework's claim that the gathering is of the paternal blood remnant of
all twelve tribes from every nation where they were scattered finds in
Baruch 5 the second-temple voice praying that gathering.

Second, the imagery of mountains being made low and valleys being filled
is the imagery John the Immerser would later cite as the preparation of
the way for the Messiah. The second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) imagination
understood the gathering and the appearing of the Messiah as connected
events. The framework of this Series, which holds that the gathering and
the appearing are the working out of the same long restoration, finds in
Baruch 5 the second-temple linkage.

Third, the closing of the chapter — "for Yahuah (God) shall lead
Yashar'el (Israel) with joy in the light of his glory with the mercy and
righteousness that comes from him" — is the proper close. The
destination is mercy and righteousness from Yahuah (God). The journey is
in His light. The leader is Yahuah (God) Himself. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the awakening of the remnant is the work of the
Father and not of the awakened, finds in Baruch 5's close the right
shape.

Cross-references: Isaiah 40:1–11; Isaiah 49:14–26; Isaiah 60:1–22;
Isaiah 61:1–11; Isaiah 62:1–12; Jeremiah 30:1–24; Jeremiah 31:1–14;
Ezekiel 37:21–28; Hosea 1:9–11; Matthew 3:1–12; Mark 1:1–8; Luke 3:1–17;
John 1:19–28.

Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah — Chapter 6

  1 A copy of an epistle, which Jeremy sent to them which were to be led
  captives into Babylon by the king of the Babylonians, to certify them,
  as it was commanded him of Yahuah (God). 2 Because of the sins which
  you have committed before Yahuah (God), you shall be led away captives
  into Babylon by Nabuchodonosor king of the Babylonians. 3 So when you
  be come to Babylon, you shall remain there many years, and for a long
  season, namely, seven generations: and after that I will bring you
  away peaceably from thence. 4 Now shall you see in Babylon gods of
  silver, and of gold, and of wood, borne upon shoulders, which cause
  the nations to fear. 5 Beware therefore that you in no wise be like to
  strangers, neither be you afraid of them, when you see the multitude
  before them and behind them, worshipping them.

  6 But say you in your hearts, O Yahuah (God), we must worship you. 7
  For my angel is with you, and I myself caring for your souls. 8 As for
  their tongue, it is polished by the workman, and they themselves are
  gilded and laid over with silver; yet are they but false, and cannot
  speak. 9 And taking gold, as it were for a virgin that loves to go
  gay, they make crowns for the heads of their gods. 10 Sometimes also
  the priests convey from their gods gold and silver, and bestow it upon
  themselves.

  11 Yea, they will give thereof to the common harlots, and deck them as
  men with garments, being gods of silver, and gods of gold, and wood.
  12 Yet cannot these gods save themselves from rust and moth, though
  they be covered with purple raiment. 13 They wipe their faces because
  of the dust of the temple, when there is much upon them. 14 And he
  that cannot put to death one that offendeth him holdeth a sceptre, as
  though he were a judge of the country. 15 He has also in his right
  hand a dagger and an ax: but cannot deliver himself from war and
  thieves.

  16 By which they are known not to be gods: therefore fear them not. 17
  For like as a vessel that a man useth is nothing worth when it is
  broken; even so it is with their gods: when they be set up in the
  temple, their eyes be full of dust through the feet of them that come
  in. 18 And as the doors are made sure on every side upon him that
  offendeth the king, as being committed to suffer death: even so the
  priests make fast their temples with doors, with locks, and bars, lest
  their gods be spoiled with robbers. 19 They light them candles, yes,
  more than for themselves, of which they cannot see one. 20 They are as
  one of the beams of the temple, yet they say their hearts are gnawed
  upon by things creeping out of the earth; and when they eat them and
  their clothes, they feel it not.

  21 Their faces are blacked through the smoke that comes out of the
  temple. 22 Upon their bodies and heads sit bats, swallows, and birds,
  and the cats also. 23 By this you may know that they are no gods:
  therefore fear them not. 24 Notwithstanding the gold that is about
  them to make them beautiful, except they wipe off the rust, they will
  not shine: for neither when they were molten did they feel it. 25 The
  things in which there is no breath are bought for a most high price.

  26 They are borne upon shoulders, having no feet by which they declare
  to men that they be nothing worth. 27 They also that serve them are
  ashamed: for if they fall to the ground at any time, they cannot rise
  up again of themselves: neither, if one set them upright, can they
  move of themselves: neither, if they be bowed down, can they make
  themselves straight: but they set gifts before them as to dead men. 28
  As for the things that are sacrificed to them, their priests sell and
  abuse; in like manner their wives lay up part thereof in salt; but to
  the poor and impotent they give nothing of it. 29 Menstruous women and
  women in childbed eat their sacrifices: by these things you may know
  that they are no gods: fear them not. 30 For how can they be called
  gods? because women set meat before the gods of silver, gold, and
  wood.

  31 And the priests sit in their temples, having their clothes rent,
  and their heads and beards shaven, and nothing upon their heads. 32
  They roar and cry before their gods, as men do at the feast when one
  is dead. 33 The priests also take off their garments, and clothe their
  wives and children. 34 Whether it be evil that one doeth to them, or
  good, they are not able to recompense it: they can neither set up a
  king, nor put him down. 35 In like manner, they can neither give
  riches nor money: though a man make a vow to them, and keep it not,
  they will not require it.

  36 They can save no man from death, neither deliver the weak from the
  mighty. 37 They cannot restore a blind man to his sight, nor help any
  man in his distress. 38 They can shew no mercy to the widow, nor do
  good to the fatherless. 39 Their gods of wood, and which are overlaid
  with gold and silver, are like the stones that be hewn out of the
  mountain: they that worship them shall be confounded. 40 How should a
  man then think and say that they are gods, when even the Chaldeans
  themselves dishonour them?

  41 Who if they shall see one dumb that cannot speak, they bring him,
  and intreat Bel that he may speak, as though he were able to
  understand. 42 Yet they cannot understand this themselves, and leave
  them: for they have no knowledge. 43 The women also with cords about
  them, sitting in the ways, burn bran for perfume: but if any of them,
  drawn by some that passeth by, lie with him, she reproacheth her
  fellow, that she was not thought as worthy as herself, nor her cord
  broken. 44 Whatsoever is done among them is false: how may it then be
  thought or said that they are gods? 45 They are made of carpenters and
  goldsmiths: they can be nothing else than the workmen will have them
  to be.

  46 And they themselves that made them can never continue long; how
  should then the things that are made of them be gods? 47 For they left
  lies and reproaches to them that come after. 48 For when there comes
  any war or plague upon them, the priests consult with themselves,
  where they may be hidden with them. 49 How then cannot men perceive
  that they be no gods, which can neither save themselves from war, nor
  from plague? 50 For seeing they be but of wood, and overlaid with
  silver and gold, it shall be known hereafter that they are false:

  51 And it shall manifestly appear to all nations and kings that they
  are no gods, but the works of men’s hands, and that there is no work
  of Yahuah (God) in them. 52 Who then may not know that they are no
  gods? 53 For neither can they set up a king in the land, nor give rain
  to men. 54 Neither can they judge their own cause, nor redress a
  wrong, being unable: for they are as crows between heaven and earth.
  55 Whereupon when fire falls upon the house of gods of wood, or laid
  over with gold or silver, their priests will flee away, and escape;
  but they themselves shall be burned asunder like beams.

  56 Moreover they cannot withstand any king or enemies: how can it then
  be thought or said that they be gods? 57 Neither are those gods of
  wood, and laid over with silver or gold, able to escape either from
  thieves or robbers. 58 Whose gold, and silver, and garments with which
  they are clothed, they that are strong take, and go away withal:
  neither are they able to help themselves. 59 Therefore it is better to
  be a king that sheweth his power, or else a profitable vessel in an
  house, which the owner shall have use of, than such false gods; or to
  be a door in an house, to keep such things in it, than such false
  gods. or a pillar of wood in a a palace, than such false gods. 60 For
  sun, moon, and stars, being bright and sent to do their offices, are
  obedient.

  61 In like manner the lightning when it breaks forth is easy to be
  seen; and after the same manner the wind bloweth in every country. 62
  And when Yahuah (God) commands the clouds to go over the whole world,
  they do as they are bidden. 63 And the fire sent from above to consume
  hills and woods doeth as it is commanded: but these are like to them
  neither in shew nor power. 64 Wherefore it is neither to be supposed
  nor said that they are gods, seeing, they are able neither to judge
  causes, nor to do good to men. 65 Knowing therefore that they are no
  gods, fear them not,

  66 For they can neither curse nor bless kings: 67 Neither can they
  shew signs in the heavens among the heathen, nor shine as the sun, nor
  give light as the moon. 68 The beasts are better than they: for they
  can get under a cover and help themselves. 69 It is then by no means
  manifest to us that they are gods: therefore fear them not. 70 For as
  a scarecrow in a garden of cucumbers keepeth nothing: so are their
  gods of wood, and laid over with silver and gold.

  71 And likewise their gods of wood, and laid over with silver and
  gold, are like to a white thorn in an orchard, that every bird sits
  upon; as also to a dead body, that is cast into the dark. 72 And you
  shall know them to be no gods by the bright purple that rotteth upon
  them: and they themselves afterward shall be eaten, and shall be a
  reproach in the country. 73 Better therefore is the just man that has
  none idols: for he shall be far from reproach.

⸻

Commentary

The sixth chapter — sometimes counted as a separate book and titled "The
Letter of Jeremiah" or "The Epistle of Jeremy" — is a polemic against
Babylonian idolatry, presented as a letter sent by the prophet Jeremiah
to those who were about to be carried captive into Babylon. The letter
warns the exiles that the gods of Babylon are nothing — pieces of carved
wood overlaid with gold, dressed up by priests, fed by people who hope
for an answer they will never receive — and that the exiles must not
fear them or worship them.

The polemic is sustained over seventy-three verses and proceeds by
enumeration. The idols cannot speak. They cannot hear. They cannot see.
They cannot move. They cannot save themselves from rust. They cannot
save themselves from fire. They cannot save themselves from theft. The
priests who serve them eat the offerings that are presented and use the
offerings for their own profit. The whole system is fraudulent.

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the Letter's polemic against pagan idolatry is consistent with
the prophetic polemic of Isaiah 44, Jeremiah 10, and Habakkuk 2.

Isaiah 44:9–17 names the absurdity of the idol-maker: They that make a
graven image are all of them vanity; and their delectable things shall
not profit; and they are their own witnesses; they see not, nor know;
that they may be ashamed... The smith with the tongs both works in the
coals, and fashions it with hammers, and works it with the strength of
his arms... He hews him down cedars, and takes the cypress and the oak,
which he strengthens for himself among the trees of the forest... With
part thereof he eats flesh; he roasts roast, and is satisfied: yea, he
warms himself, and says, Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire: and the
residue thereof he makes a god, even his graven image: he falls down to
it, and worships it, and prays unto it, and says, Deliver me; for you
are my god. The carpenter splits the wood. Half goes to the fire to
roast his dinner. Half is carved into the god he prays to. The same
wood. Different uses. Both useless as gods.

Jeremiah 10:3–5 names the same: For the customs of the people are vain:
for one cuts a tree out of the forest, the work of the hands of the
workman, with the axe. They deck it with silver and with gold; they
fasten it with nails and with hammers, that it move not. They are
upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne,
because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil,
neither also is it in them to do good. Habakkuk 2:18–19: What profits
the graven image that the maker thereof has graven it; the molten image,
and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusts therein, to
make dumb idols? Woe to him that says to the wood, Awake; to the dumb
stone, Arise, it shall teach! Psalm 115:4–8: Their idols are silver and
gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths, but they speak not:
eyes have they, but they see not: They have ears, but they hear not:
noses have they, but they smell not: They have hands, but they handle
not: feet have they, but they walk not: neither speak they through their
throat. They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that
trusts in them.

Five canonical witnesses naming the absurdity. The Letter of Jeremiah is
the second-temple amplification of this prophetic-and-Psalter polemic.
The framework of this Series, which holds that institutional
Christianity has carried Babylonian patterns into its own forms
(gold-overlaid statues, dressed-up images, priesthoods feeding the
system on the offerings of the deceived), finds in the Letter of
Jeremiah the original prophetic exposure that applies to those patterns.
The Letter does not specifically name the contemporary religious systems
the awakening reader has walked out of. The Letter names Babylonian
paganism. But the spiritual logic of fraudulent religion — priestly
self-enrichment dressed as worship — is consistent across all human
counterfeits, and the Letter's polemic is illuminating across the full
range of inherited religious systems.

Second, the framework of this Series rejects all forms of contemporary
iconoclastic violence. The Letter's polemic is rhetorical, not
destructive. The exiles are to refuse to worship the idols, to refuse to
fear them, to refuse to attribute power to them — but the Letter does
not call for the exiles to riot in the temples of Babylon and tear down
the images. The awakening reader walking out of inherited religious
systems is to refuse the false worship, to expose the patterns where
those patterns are being uncritically passed on, to invite the deceived
to come home — but is not to riot in the buildings or destroy the
property of the systems being walked out of. The framework of this
Series is patient, scripture-anchored, public exposure. The Letter of
Jeremiah models that posture.

Third, the Letter's repeated refrain — "whereby they are known not to be
gods: therefore fear them not" — is the right conclusion for the
awakening reader. The patterns of fraudulent religion can be recognized.
The recognition produces freedom from fear. The freedom from fear
produces the capacity to walk out and to invite others to walk out. The
Letter is, beneath its rhetorical weight, a freedom document for the
awakening exile: name what the system is, refuse to fear what cannot
save, walk in the light of the One who can save. The framework of this
Series finds in the closing of the Letter of Jeremiah the right shape
for the awakening reader's posture toward every religious system the
awakening reader is leaving behind.

Cross-references: Exodus 20:3–6; Deuteronomy 4:15–28; Deuteronomy
13:1–18; Isaiah 44:9–20; Isaiah 46:1–7; Jeremiah 10:1–16; Habakkuk
2:18–20; Acts 17:22–31; Romans 1:18–25; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6; Revelation
17:1–18; Revelation 18:1–24.

The Song of the Three Holy Children — Introduction

The Song of the Three Holy Children is the first of the three Greek
additions to the canonical book of Daniel that the King James
translators set as separate apocryphal pieces. It is a short text —
sixty-eight verses — placed in the Greek Daniel between Daniel 3:23 and
Daniel 3:24, that is, in the moment when the three Hebrews — Hananiah,
Mishael, and Azariah, called Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the
Babylonian — are inside the fiery furnace and have not yet been seen
walking with the fourth man.

The text contains three movements. First, the prayer of Azariah (called
Abednego in the Babylonian name) — a confession of sin and a plea for
deliverance, modeled on the same exilic-confession pattern that runs
through Daniel 9, Baruch 1–3, and Nehemiah 9. Second, a brief narrative
bridge that names how the angel of Yahuah (God) came down into the
furnace and made the midst of the flame as a moist whistling wind so the
fire did not touch them. And third, the song of the three — a sustained
hymn of praise that calls on every creature in heaven and earth, sea and
sky, weather and wildlife, light and darkness, to bless Yahuah (God) for
ever and ever. The song is one of the great praise-poems of the
second-temple corpus and has been sung in Christian, Yahudi (Jewish),
and ancient liturgical traditions for nearly two thousand years.

For the awakening reader, three things matter.

First, the prayer of Azariah is the second-temple confession of why the
exile happened. The voice is the voice of one of the three young men
inside the furnace — that is, inside the literal embodiment of the
Babylonian system that is trying to consume the covenant remnant — and
his prayer owns that the exile is the consequence of the people's having
broken the covenant. The prayer does not blame Babylon for the
suffering. The prayer owns the sin that brought Babylon as the rod of
Yahuah (God)'s discipline. This is the same theological frame the
awakening reader has been retrained to hold: that the four houses are
not the enemy and the curses of Deuteronomy 28 are the covenant
consequence of the people's having walked out from under the covenant.
Azariah's prayer is the second-temple voice that already prayed this
confession, in the same shape and the same posture.

Second, the song of the three is the prayer-poem of those who have been
preserved through the fire. The structure is a long invocation: bless
Yahuah (God), all you works of the Lord; bless Yahuah (God), sun and
moon; bless Yahuah (God), stars of heaven; bless Yahuah (God), every
shower and dew; bless Yahuah (God), all you winds; bless Yahuah (God),
frost and cold; bless Yahuah (God), ice and snow; bless Yahuah (God),
lightnings and clouds; bless Yahuah (God), mountains and hills; bless
Yahuah (God), every thing that grows; bless Yahuah (God), fountains;
bless Yahuah (God), seas and rivers; bless Yahuah (God), whales and all
that move in the waters; bless Yahuah (God), all you fowls of the air;
bless Yahuah (God), all beasts and cattle; bless Yahuah (God), you
children of men; bless Yahuah (God), Yashar'el (Israel). The song moves
from the highest heaven down to Yashar'el (Israel) itself, and back up
again. It is a pattern that the Christian and Yahudi (Jewish) liturgical
traditions have honored for two millennia by carrying the song into
their own services. The awakening reader can carry it into their own
prayer life as well.

Third, the placement matters. The song is placed inside the furnace,
while the three are still in the fire. They have not yet been delivered.
They do not know they will be delivered. The song is sung in the
presence of the fire. The awakening reader who has walked through their
own furnace — the long burning that comes when Yahuah (God) is breaking
the inherited lies out of His own — will recognize the posture: praise
inside the fire, before the deliverance, on the strength of what Yahuah
(God) has already shown. That is the posture this song models.

The sixty-eight verses of this addition to Daniel sit inside one of the
most dramatic moments in the Hebrew canon: the three Hebrews — Hananiah
(Shadrach), Mishael (Meshach), and Azariah (Abednego) — are bound,
thrown into the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual, and have
not yet been seen walking with the fourth man. The Greek translators of
Daniel could not let the silence inside the furnace stand. They filled
it with prayer and praise. The result is one of the great liturgical
pieces of the second-temple corpus.

Verses 1 through 22 are the prayer of Azariah. The voice is one of the
three young men inside the fire. The prayer does not begin with a plea
for deliverance. It begins with the confession of why the people are in
exile in the first place. "Blessed are you, O Yahuah Elohim (Lord God) of our fathers:
your name is worthy to be praised and glorified for evermore: for you
are righteous in all the things that you have done to us: yea, true are
all your works, your ways are right, and all your judgments truth." The
supplicant is in the furnace. The fire is real. The death is imminent.
And the first words are not why have you done this, but you are
righteous in all the things you have done to us. The covenant frame is
intact. The exile is the covenant consequence of the people's sin.
Yahuah (God) is just. The supplicant owns it.

Verses 5 through 9 itemize the confession. We have sinned and committed
iniquity, departing from you. In all things have we trespassed, and not
obeyed your commandments, nor kept them, neither done as you have
commanded us, that it might go well with us. The 1234 of Truth (1 John
2:3–4) is in the structure of the confession itself: he that says he
knows Yahuah (God) and keeps not His commandments is a liar. Azariah
does not say I know but I did not keep. He says I did not keep, and I
confess that not-keeping is the cause of what we now suffer.

Read this confession alongside three others and the pattern becomes
unmistakable. Daniel 9:5–6: We have sinned, and have committed iniquity,
and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from your
precepts and from your judgments: neither have we hearkened to your
servants the prophets, which spoke in your name to our kings, our
princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land. Nehemiah
9:33–34: Howbeit you are just in all that is brought upon us; for you
have done right, but we have done wickedly: neither have our kings, our
princes, our priests, nor our fathers, kept your law. Ezra 9:6–7: I am
ashamed and blush to lift up my face to you, my Elohim (God): for our iniquities
are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up to the
heavens. Since the days of our fathers have we been in a great trespass
to this day. Four prayers, four supplicants, one structure: the Father
is just, the people did not keep the commandments, the consequence is
the present suffering, the plea is on the covenant. Azariah's prayer in
Song of Three 5–9 stands in this prophetic-confession line. The shape is
Daniel's, Nehemiah's, Ezra's. The supplicant in the furnace prays what
the supplicant in the chamber and the supplicant at the foundation also
prayed. The covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell on the people because
they walked out from under the covenant, not because Yahuah (God) became
unfaithful — and Azariah's prayer says so explicitly.

Verse 10 turns. "Now we cannot open our mouths, we are become a shame
and reproach to your servants; and to them that worship you. Yet deliver
us not up wholly, for your name's sake, neither disannul your covenant:
and cause not your mercy to depart from us, for Abraham your beloved's
sake, for Isaac your servant's, and for Yashar'el (Israel) your holy
one's sake." The plea is on the basis of the covenant — for Abraham's
sake, for Isaac's sake, for Yashar'el (Israel)'s sake. Not on the basis
of the supplicant's worthiness. The covenant is the basis. The
patriarchs are the witnesses. The mercy is the promise. The prayer of
Azariah is, in tighter form, the same prayer the Prayer of Manasseh
prays: covenant identification, owned confession, covenant-based plea,
mercy as the only hope.

Verses 11 through 22 ask for what the Torah's sacrificial system would
normally provide — a sin offering — and acknowledge that the sacrificial
system is no longer accessible because the temple has been destroyed and
the priesthood has been scattered. And at this time there is neither
prince, nor prophet, nor leader, nor burnt offering, nor sacrifice, nor
oblation, nor incense, nor place to sacrifice before you, and to find
mercy. Nevertheless in a contrite heart and an humble spirit let us be
accepted. The principle being articulated is not that the sacrifices are
abolished. The principle is that, in their absence, the contrite heart
is offered as the sacrifice.

The cross-references chain is direct. Psalm 51:16–17, David after the
Bathsheba sin: For you do not desire sacrifice; else would I give it:
you delight not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of Elohim (God) are a broken
spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O Elohim (God), you will not despise.
Psalm 40:6–8: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; my ears have
you opened: burnt offering and sin offering have you not required. Then
said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me, I
delight to do your will, O my Elohim (God): yea, your law is within my heart. 1
Samuel 15:22, Samuel rebuking Saul: Behold, to obey is better than
sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Hosea 6:6: I desired
mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of Elohim (God) more than burnt
offerings. Micah 6:6–8: Wherewith shall I come before Yahuah (God)...
Will Yahuah (God) be pleased with thousands of rams... He has shown you,
O man, what is good; and what does Yahuah (God) require of you, but to
do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your Elohim (God)?

Five witnesses across the prophets, the psalms, and the historical books
say what Azariah is praying inside the fire: when the appointed
sacrifices cannot be brought, the contrite heart that walks in obedience
is the offering Yahuah (God) receives. The principle does not erase the
Torah's sacrificial system; it names what the system was always pointing
toward. The Messiah's permanent priesthood (Hebrews 7) and once-for-all
sacrifice (Hebrews 10:11–14) bring this prophetic principle to its
appointed close: the body offered, the heart contrite, the obedience
perfected, the sacrifice complete. Azariah, in 167 BCE in the literary
setting of Daniel 3 and the second-century-BCE composition of the Greek
addition, was praying what the prophets had named and what the Messiah
would fulfill.

Verses 23 through 27 are a brief narrative bridge. The angel of Yahuah
(God) comes down into the furnace and makes the midst of the flame as a
moist whistling wind, so the fire does not touch the three. The angel of
Yahuah (God) in the Hebrew scriptures is consistently the Formed One —
the Word, who appeared to Abraham, who wrestled with Jacob, who spoke
from the burning bush, who led Yashar'el (Israel) in the cloud and the
fire, and who came in the flesh as Yahusha (Jesus). The fourth man
Nebuchadnezzar sees in the furnace, in the underlying Daniel narrative,
is described in Daniel 3:25 as like the Son of Elohim (God). The Greek addition
here names the same figure as the angel of Yahuah (God). The figure who
delivered the three Hebrews from the fire is the same figure who
delivered Yashar'el (Israel) out of Egypt and who would later come in
the flesh to deliver the scattered seed.

Isaiah 43:1–3 names the principle the furnace narrative embodies: Fear
not: for I have redeemed you, I have called you by your name; you are
mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through
the rivers, they shall not overflow you: when you walk through the fire,
you shall not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon you. For I
am Yahuah (God) your Elohim (God), the Holy One of Yashar'el (Israel), your
Saviour. The promise is specific: the redeemed seed walks through the
fire and is not burned, because the One who called them by name is with
them. The three Hebrews in the furnace are the narrative of Isaiah 43
made literal. The flame does not kindle upon them. The Saviour is with
them in the fire.

Isaiah 63:9 names the same figure differently: In all their affliction
he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them: in his love
and in his pity he redeemed them; and he bare them, and carried them all
the days of old. The angel of His presence — the Formed One — saves the
affliction. In Egypt. In the wilderness. In the furnace. In every fire
the seed has walked through. Joshua 5:13–15 names the same figure
standing before Joshua at Jericho with sword drawn — captain of the host
of Yahuah (God) — receiving worship, telling Joshua to remove his shoes
for the ground was holy. The figure who stood before Joshua, who saved
Yashar'el (Israel) in their afflictions, who walked with the three in
the fire, is one figure under multiple titles — angel of Yahuah (God),
captain of the host, the Formed One — and is the same Word who came in
the flesh as Yahusha. The witness is consistent across the canon. The
Formed One walks with His own through the fire.

Verses 28 through 68 are the song of the three. The song is one of the
great praise-poems of the second-temple corpus. The structure is a long
catalogue of invocation: bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord;
bless the Lord, you angels of the Lord; bless the Lord, you heavens;
bless the Lord, you waters that be above the heavens; bless the Lord,
all you powers of the Lord; bless the Lord, sun and moon; bless the
Lord, stars of heaven; bless the Lord, every shower and dew; bless the
Lord, all you winds; bless the Lord, fire and heat; bless the Lord,
winter and summer; bless the Lord, dews and storms of snow; bless the
Lord, nights and days; bless the Lord, light and darkness; bless the
Lord, ice and cold; bless the Lord, frost and snow; bless the Lord,
lightnings and clouds; bless the Lord, let the earth bless the Lord;
bless the Lord, mountains and hills; bless the Lord, all things that
grow on the earth; bless the Lord, you fountains; bless the Lord, seas
and rivers; bless the Lord, whales and all that move in the waters;
bless the Lord, all you fowls of the air; bless the Lord, all beasts and
cattle; bless the Lord, you children of men; bless the Lord, O Yashar'el
(Israel); bless the Lord, you priests of the Lord; bless the Lord, you
servants of the Lord; bless the Lord, you spirits and souls of the
righteous; bless the Lord, you holy and humble men of heart; bless the
Lord, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

The song moves from the highest reaches of creation down to the
supplicants themselves and back up again. It is the entire creation
summoned to praise. Read it aloud. It does not yield to silent reading.
The song was composed to be sung, has been sung in liturgical traditions
for nearly two thousand years, and the awakening reader can carry it
into his or her own prayer life as the right shape of praise inside the
fire.

Psalm 148 is the canonical parallel. Read the two side by side. Psalm
148:1–4: Praise Yahuah (God) from the heavens: praise him in the
heights. Praise him, all his angels: praise him, all his hosts. Praise
him, sun and moon: praise him, all you stars of light. Praise him, you
heavens of heavens, and you waters that be above the heavens. Psalm
148:7–10: Praise Yahuah (God) from the earth, you dragons, and all
deeps: fire, and hail; snow, and vapours; stormy wind fulfilling his
word: mountains, and all hills; fruitful trees, and all cedars: beasts,
and all cattle; creeping things, and flying fowl. The Song of the Three
Holy Children is the second-temple amplification of Psalm 148. The same
architecture — heavens called first, then the heavens-above-the-heavens,
then the heavenly bodies, then the elements (fire, hail, snow, wind),
then the earth-features (mountains, hills, trees), then the creatures
(beasts, fowl), then man, then Yashar'el (Israel), then the priests and
servants. The supplicants in the fire are not composing a fresh song.
They are praying Psalm 148 with their lives, summoning the same creation
Psalm 148 summons, joining a praise that the Psalter had already
structured. The framework's reading: this is one of the second-temple
anchors that confirms the apocryphal hymn-tradition draws directly on
the canonical Psalter. The reader who has been told the apocryphal hymns
are alien to canonical worship is corrected by reading Psalm 148 and the
Song of the Three together. Same architecture. Same praise. Same Father.

Revelation 5:13 carries the same architecture forward into the apostolic
vision: And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and
under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them,
heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be to him
that sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb for ever and ever. Heaven,
earth, under the earth, sea, and all therein. The architecture from
Psalm 148 to Song of Three to Revelation 5 is one continuous summons of
creation to praise. The three in the furnace, the seer in Patmos, and
the Psalmist at the temple are praying the same song.

Two final notes for the awakening reader.

First, the song is sung inside the furnace. The deliverance has not
happened yet. The three are still in the fire. They do not know they
will be delivered. The song is praise on the strength of who Yahuah
(God) is, not on the strength of what He has just done. The awakening
reader who has walked through the long burning that comes when Yahuah
(God) is breaking the inherited lies out of His own — the season when
the deception is being exposed, the relationships are being tested, the
inherited identity is being burned away, and the new life has not yet
emerged — will recognize the posture. Praise inside the fire. Before the
deliverance. On the strength of what Yahuah (God) has already shown.

Second, the angel who delivered the three is the Formed One. The same
figure walks with the awakening reader through his or her own furnace.
The deliverance is not hypothetical. The witness of the second temple is
the witness of the canonical Daniel: the One who walked with the three
in the fire walks with His people in their fire. The fire does not have
the last word. The Formed One does.

Cross-references: Daniel 3:1–30; Genesis 18:1–33; Genesis 32:24–30;
Exodus 3:1–6; Exodus 13:21–22; Deuteronomy 28:15–68; Psalm 51:17; Isaiah
43:1–3; John 1:1–14; 1 John 2:3–4.

The Song of the Three Holy Children — Chapter 1

  1 And they walked in the midst of the fire, praising Yahuah (God), and
  blessing Yahuah (God). 2 Then Azarias stood up, and prayed on this
  manner; and opening his mouth in the midst of the fire said, 3 Blessed
  art you, O Yahuah (God) of our fathers: your name is worthy to be
  praised and glorified for evermore: 4 For you are righteous in all the
  things that you have done to us: yes, true are all your works, your
  ways are right, and all your judgments truth. 5 In all the things that
  you have brought upon us, and upon the holy city of our fathers, even
  Jerusalem, you have executed true judgment: for according to truth and
  judgment did you bring all these things upon us because of our sins.

  6 For we have sinned and committed iniquity, departing from you. 7 In
  all things have we trespassed, and not obeyed your commandments, nor
  kept them, neither done as you have commanded us, that it might go
  well with us. 8 Wherefore all that you have brought upon us, and every
  thing that you have done to us, you have done in true judgment. 9 And
  you did deliver us into the hands of lawless enemies, most hateful
  forsakers of Yahuah (God), and to an unjust king, and the most wicked
  in all the world. 10 And now we cannot open our mouths, we are become
  a shame and reproach to your servants; and to them that worship you.

  11 Yet deliver us not up wholly, for your name’s sake, neither
  disannul you your covenant: 12 And cause not your mercy to depart from
  us, for your beloved Abraham’s sake, for your servant Issac’s sake,
  and for your holy Yashar'el (Israel)’s sake; 13 To whom you have
  spoken and promised, that you would multiply their seed as the stars
  of heaven, and as the sand that lieth upon the seashore. 14 For we, O
  Yahuah (God), are become less than any nation, and be kept under this
  day in all the world because of our sins. 15 Neither is there at this
  time prince, or prophet, or leader, or burnt offering, or sacrifice,
  or oblation, or incense, or place to sacrifice before you, and to find
  mercy.

  16 Nevertheless in a contrite heart and an humble spirit let us be
  accepted. 17 Like as in the burnt offerings of rams and bullocks, and
  like as in ten thousands of fat lambs: so let our sacrifice be in your
  sight this day, and grant that we may wholly go after you: for they
  shall not be confounded that put their trust in you. 18 And now we
  follow you with all our heart, we fear you, and seek your face. 19 Put
  us not to shame: but deal with us after your lovingkindness, and
  according to the multitude of your mercies. 20 Deliver us also
  according to your marvellous works, and give glory to your name, O
  Yahuah (God): and let all them that do your servants hurt be ashamed;

  21 And let them be confounded in all their power and might, and let
  their strength be broken; 22 And let them know that you are Yahuah
