basis of his own merit. The prayer is the awakening prayer in compressed
form — the prayer of one who knows the depth of his deception, names it
plainly, and turns to the only one who can lift him up.

Second, the prayer models a use of the patriarchs that the awakening
reader will recognize. Manasseh appeals not to a generic mercy but to
the covenant: "the Elohim (God) of our fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of
their righteous seed." The patriarchs are named. The covenant is named.
The prayer leans on the covenant promises rather than on the
supplicant's worthiness. The awakening reader walking out of
institutional Christianity, where the covenant identity has been
replaced with a generic personal-salvation framework, will find
Manasseh's covenant-based supplication corrective. The covenant is the
basis. The covenant is what Manasseh stood on.

Third, the prayer's confession of repentance is whole. It does not
minimize. Manasseh names that he has provoked Yahuah (God)'s wrath, done
evil, set up abominations, and multiplied offences. He does not soften
the sin. He does not negotiate. He owns it whole and asks for the only
thing he can ask for: that Yahuah (God) who has appointed repentance
to sinners will receive him into the company of those who have repented.
The awakening reader who has been retrained to confess in the same shape
— owning the inheritance of lies, naming the practices the Father has
stopped, turning to the Word as the only standard — will find the Prayer
of Manasseh modeling that confession in the most concentrated form the
apocryphal corpus contains.

The prayer can be read aloud. It can be prayed personally. It is short
enough to memorize and weighty enough to carry through a long season of
repentance. The awakening reader who is walking through such a season
may find this brief book one of the most immediately useful pieces in
the entire Apocrypha.

The fifteen verses of the Prayer of Manasseh contain, in concentrated
form, the entire posture the awakening remnant is being called to take.
Read it again. Notice what Manasseh names, what he refuses to name, and
what he asks for. This prayer is a model.

Verse 1 sets the foundation. Manasseh addresses Yahuah (God) by the
covenant identification: "the El Shaddai (Almighty God) of our fathers, Abraham,
Isaac, and Jacob, and of their righteous seed." The supplicant does not
approach the Father as a generic deity. He approaches as a son of the
covenant — a son of Adam in the lineage of Abraham — and he names that
lineage at the front of his prayer. The covenant is the basis. The
patriarchs are the witnesses. The "righteous seed" — the actual paternal
blood remnant the prophets named — is named in the same breath as the
patriarchs themselves. This is not Christian individual-salvation
language. This is covenant-restoration language, and the awakening
reader walking out of institutional Christianity will recognize what has
been retrained: the covenant is the basis, not the supplicant's
sincerity.

Verses 2 through 5 establish who Yahuah (God) is. He is the maker of
heaven and earth. He bound the sea by the word of His commandment. He
shut up the deep and sealed it by His terrible and glorious name. Every
creature fears Him and trembles before His power. The majesty of His
glory cannot be borne. The angry threatening toward sinners is
unbearable.

The canonical witness for this opening of the prayer is concrete.
Genesis 1:9–10, the gathering of the seas: And Elohim (God) said, Let the waters
under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry
land appear: and it was so. Job 38:8–11: Or who shut up the sea with
doors, when it brake forth, as if it had issued out of the womb?... and
said, Hither shall you come, but no further: and here shall your proud
waves be stayed. Psalm 104:7–9: At your rebuke they fled; at the voice
of your thunder they hasted away. They go up by the mountains; they go
down by the valleys unto the place which you have founded for them. You
have set a bound that they may not pass over; that they turn not again
to cover the earth. Jeremiah 5:22: Fear you not me? says Yahuah (God):
will you not tremble at my presence, which have placed the sand for the
bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it.

The "fear of Yahuah (God) before whom Isaiah cried woe is me, for I am
undone" comes from Isaiah 6:5 at the throne-vision: Then said I, Woe is
me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in
the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King,
Yahuah (God) of hosts. Habakkuk 3:16: When I heard, my belly trembled;
my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I
trembled in myself.

The prayer does not soften the Father. It names Him whole — the One
whose holiness is consuming, whose glory is unbearable, whose
threatening toward sinners is fearful. Modern devotional language has
flattened the Father into a generic source of comfort. This prayer
refuses that flattening. The Elohim (God) before whom Manasseh bows is the same
Elohim (God) before whom Isaiah cried woe is me, for I am undone and before whom
Habakkuk's lips quivered.

Verses 6 and 7 turn from the holiness to the mercy. "But your merciful
promise is unmeasurable and unsearchable; for you are the most high
Lord, of great compassion, longsuffering, very merciful, and repentest
of the evils of men." Mercy is not soft holiness. Mercy is what the holy
Elohim (God) has chosen to extend to those He could justly destroy. "You, O Lord,
according to your great goodness have promised repentance and
forgiveness to them that have sinned against you." The promise of
repentance is a promise. It was given. It is part of the covenant.
Manasseh is not asking for something Yahuah (God) has not committed
Himself to give. He is appealing to a promise the prophets had recorded.

Verse 8 contains the first of two theological pivots in the prayer. "You
therefore, O Lord, that are the Elohim (God) of the just, have not appointed
repentance to the just, as to Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, which have
not sinned against you; but you have appointed repentance to me that am
a sinner." The line about the patriarchs not having sinned has tripped
up readers in the Christian tradition who have been trained by Romans
3:23 to say that all have sinned without exception. The line is not in
conflict with Romans. The patriarchs did sin, and Romans 3 names that
universally. What Manasseh is saying is that the patriarchs are not the
ones for whom repentance was specifically appointed in the way it was
appointed for him. Their faith was reckoned to them as righteousness in
a different mode than the deep, public, legal repentance Manasseh is now
offering. Manasseh is not denying that the patriarchs needed mercy. He
is naming his own situation: a king who set up abominations, multiplied
offences, and is now bound in iron in Babylon. The repentance appointed
to him is the repentance appointed to one who has fallen far. The
patriarchs, with all their faults, did not fall this far. Manasseh is
owning his particular weight.

Verses 9 and 10 are the confession proper. "I have sinned above the
number of the sands of the sea. My transgressions, O Lord, are
multiplied: my transgressions are multiplied, and I am not worthy to
behold and see the height of heaven for the multitude of my iniquities.
I am bowed down with many iron bands, that I cannot lift up my head,
neither have any release: for I have provoked your wrath, and done evil
before you: I did not your will, neither kept I your commandments: I
have set up abominations, and have multiplied offences." Note the
specific naming. He provoked Yahuah (God)'s wrath. He did evil before
Him. He did not do His will. He did not keep His commandments. He set up
abominations — idols, the false gods his father Hezekiah had torn down
which he had restored. He multiplied offences. This is not generic
confession. This is itemized. The 1234 of Truth (1 John 2:3–4) — the
standard that he that says he knows Yahuah (God) and keeps not His
commandments is a liar — is implicit in Manasseh's confession. He kept
not the commandments. He owns it. He is the man 1 John warns against
having become, and he is now turning back.

Verses 11 through 14 are the plea. Now therefore I bow the knee of my
heart, beseeching you of grace. I have sinned, O Lord, I have sinned,
and I acknowledge my iniquities: wherefore, I humbly beseech you,
forgive me, O Lord, forgive me, and destroy me not with my iniquities.
Be not angry with me for ever, by reserving evil for me; neither condemn
me to the lower parts of the earth. For you are the Elohim (God), even the Elohim (God) of
them that repent; and in me you will shew all your goodness: for you
will save me, that am unworthy, according to your great mercy. The plea
is for grace, not on the basis of merit but on the basis of the covenant
promise of repentance.

Manasseh's prayer stands inside the canonical confession-prayer line.
Read it with David's Psalm 51 in your other hand. Psalm 51:1–4: Have
mercy upon me, O Elohim (God), according to your lovingkindness: according to the
multitude of your tender mercies blot out my transgressions. Wash me
thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I
acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me. Against
you, you only, have I sinned, and done this evil in your sight. Psalm
51:17: The sacrifices of Elohim (God) are a broken spirit: a broken and a
contrite heart, O Elohim (God), you will not despise. Manasseh's I bow the knee
of my heart is David's broken and contrite heart in second-temple
costume. The architecture is the same.

Daniel 9:18–19 is the second canonical anchor: O my Elohim (God), incline your
ear, and hear; open your eyes, and behold our desolations, and the city
which is called by your name: for we do not present our supplications
before you for our righteousnesses, but for your great mercies. O Lord,
hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do; defer not, for your own
sake, O my Elohim (God): for your city and your people are called by your name.
Daniel pleads for the city. Manasseh pleads for himself. Both plead on
the basis of Yahuah (God)'s mercy, not on the basis of the supplicant's
merit. The covenant logic is consistent.

Nehemiah 9:17 and 9:31 also lock the pattern in: But you are a Elohim (God) ready
to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness,
and forsook them not... Nevertheless for your great mercies' sake you
did not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for you are a gracious
and merciful Elohim (God). The supplicant in Nehemiah 9, like Manasseh, names
Yahuah (God)'s mercy as the basis of the plea. The pattern is the
canonical pattern.

You will save me, that am unworthy, according to your great mercy — the
very logic that the apostle Paul will articulate in Ephesians 2:8–9: by
grace are you saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the
gift of Elohim, not of works, lest any man should boast. The Pauline
gospel of grace is not a Christian innovation. It is the consistent
witness of the covenant: that Yahuah (God) saves the unworthy who turn
to Him in repentance, not on the basis of their merit but on the basis
of His mercy. David prays it in Psalm 51. Daniel prays it in Daniel 9.
The post-exilic community prays it in Nehemiah 9. Manasseh prays it.
Paul writes it. They are the same gospel.

The historical Manasseh's case is itself a witness. He was the son of
Hezekiah — one of the most faithful kings of Yahudah (Judah). He
inherited a kingdom Hezekiah had cleansed of idolatry. He proceeded to
undo every reform his father had accomplished. 2 Kings 21:1–18 lists his
violations: rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had torn down, raised
altars to Baal, made a grove, worshiped the host of heaven, set up an
Asherah image inside the temple, made his son pass through the fire,
observed times, used enchantments, dealt with familiar spirits and
wizards, shed innocent blood until he had filled Jerusalem from one end
to another. The text is unsparing. Manasseh seduced them to do more evil
than did the nations whom Yahuah (God) destroyed before the children of
Yashar'el (Israel) (2 Kings 21:9). He was the worst king Yahudah (Judah)
ever had.

2 Chronicles 33:11–13 records the sequel that 2 Kings does not preserve:
Wherefore Yahuah (God) brought upon them the captains of the host of the
king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him
with fetters, and carried him to Babylon. And when he was in affliction,
he besought Yahuah (God) his Elohim (God), and humbled himself greatly before the
Elohim (God) of his fathers, and prayed unto him: and he was entreated of him,
and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his
kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that Yahuah (God) he was Elohim (God). The Prayer of
Manasseh, in its second-temple form, is the literary recovery of the
prayer 2 Chronicles names but does not preserve. The framework reads it
as a covenant-faithful imaginative reconstruction of what the worst king
of Yahudah (Judah) prayed when Yahuah (God) brought him into the iron
bands of Assyria — and it stands as the definitive case study that there
is no sin too great for the mercy Yahuah (God) has promised to those who
turn.

Verse 15 closes with praise. Therefore I will praise you for ever all
the days of my life: for all the powers of the heavens do praise you,
and yours is the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

The repentance-turning-to-praise pattern is canonical. Psalm 51 closes
the same way. After David's confession comes Psalm 51:15: O Lord, open
you my lips; and my mouth shall show forth your praise. Psalm 32:11
closes the second great repentance psalm: Be glad in Yahuah (God), and
rejoice, you righteous: and shout for joy, all you that are upright in
heart. Isaiah 12:1 — And in that day you shall say, O Yahuah (God), I
will praise you: though you were angry with me, your anger is turned
away, and you comforted me. Hosea 14:2, the prophet calling Yashar'el
(Israel) back: Take with you words, and turn to Yahuah (God): say unto
him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we
render the calves of our lips — that is, the offering of praise.

The prayer of repentance ends with the prayer of praise. The two are not
separable. Repentance turns toward the One whose glory is forever, and
the soul that has repented joins the praise that has been going on
without interruption in the heavens.

The Prayer of Manasseh can be prayed by the awakening reader directly.
It is the right shape. It owns the inheritance of lies. It names the
abominations. It acknowledges the consequences. It pleads for the mercy
Yahuah (God) has promised. It ends in praise. The reader who has walked
out of the four houses and into the wilderness of His Word, who has
begun to see how deep the deception ran in his or her own life, who has
named the practices the Spirit has stopped, and who is asking what to do
next — pray this prayer. The prayer is short enough to memorize and
weighty enough to carry through a long season. The covenant is the
basis. The mercy is the promise. The praise is the destination.

Cross-references: Genesis 12:1–3; Genesis 26:24; Genesis 28:13–14; 2
Kings 21:1–18; 2 Chronicles 33:1–20; Isaiah 6:5; Habakkuk 3:16; Jeremiah
16:19; Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 John 2:3–4.

The Prayer of Manasseh — Chapter 1

  1 O Yahuah (God), Almighty Yahuah (God) of our fathers, Abraham,
  Isaac, and Jacob, and of their righteous seed; 2 who have made heaven
  and earth, with all the ornament thereof; 3 who have bound the sea by
  the word of your commandment; who have shut up the deep, and sealed it
  by your terrible and glorious name; 4 whom all men fear, and tremble
  before your power; 5 for the majesty of your glory cannot be borne,
  and your angry threatening toward sinners is importable:

  6 but your merciful promise is unmeasurable and unsearchable; 7 for
  you are the most high Yahuah (God), of great compassion,
  longsuffering, very merciful, and repentest of the evils of men. You,
  O Yahuah (God), according to your great goodness have promised
  repentance and forgiveness to them that have sinned against you: and
  of your infinite mercies have appointed repentance to sinners, that
  they may be saved. 8 You therefore, O Yahuah (God), that are the
  Yahuah (God) of the just, have not appointed repentance to the just,
  as to Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, which have not sinned against
  you; but you have appointed repentance to me that am a sinner: 9 for I
  have sinned above the number of the sands of the sea. My
  transgressions, O Yahuah (God), are multiplied: my transgressions are
  multiplied, and I am not worthy to behold and see the height of heaven
  for the multitude of my iniquities. 10 I am bowed down with many iron
  bands, that I cannot lift up my head, neither have any release: for I
  have provoked your wrath, and done evil before you: I did not your
  will, neither kept I your commandments: I have set up abominations,
  and have multiplied offences.

  11 Now therefore I bow the knee of my heart, beseeching you of grace.
  12 I have sinned, O Yahuah (God), I have sinned, and I acknowledge my
  iniquities: 13 wherefore, I humbly beseech you, forgive me, O Yahuah
  (God), forgive me, and destroy me not with my iniquites. Be not angry
  with me for ever, by reserving evil for me; neither condemn me to the
  lower parts of the earth. For you are Yahuah (God), even the
  Yahuah (God) of them that repent; 14 and in me you will shew all your
  goodness: for you will save me, that am unworthy, according to your
  great mercy. 15 Therefore I will praise you for ever all the days of
  my life: for all the powers of the heavens do praise you, and yours is
  the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

⸻

Commentary

This is the shortest chapter in the book and the one that requires the
longest pause. Fifteen verses, one prayer, one voice — and a theological
density that will reward the awakening reader who reads it slowly twice.

Four things matter in this chapter.

First, the address. "O Yahuah (God), Almighty Yahuah (God) of our
fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of their righteous seed" (verse
1). The opening word names the covenant. Manasseh does not appeal to a
generic deity. He names Yahuah (God) by the covenant identity Yahuah
(God) gave himself in the Torah — the Elohim (God) of the patriarchs, the God who
promised the seed, the Elohim (God) whose covenant is in continuity through
Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and onward to their righteous seed. The
framework reads this as the right kind of prayer-address for the
awakening reader walking out of one of the four houses. The Father whose
covenant has not been revoked is the Father of the patriarchs and the
Father of the seed. The covenant identification is not optional. It is
the ground. Manasseh, the man who set up the most aggressive idolatry of
any pre-exilic king of Yahudah (Judah) — who placed a graven image
inside the temple, who passed his sons through the fire, who used
enchantments and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards (2 Chronicles
33:1–9) — addresses Yahuah (God) by the covenant identity even in his
repentance. The covenant has not been revoked even by his apostasy. The
covenant is still the framework on which his prayer rests.

Second, the confession. "I have provoked your wrath, and done evil
before you: I did not your will, neither kept I your commandments: I
have set up abominations, and have multiplied offences" (verse 10).
Manasseh names the actual transgressions. He does not generalize. He
does not pray I am a sinner like everyone else. He names that he did not
do the will of Yahuah (God), did not keep the commandments, set up
abominations, and multiplied offences. The framework reads this as the
framework's pattern for true repentance. The 1234 of Truth — 1 John
2:3–4 — is in the prayer here in negative form: he has not kept the
commandments, and he names the not-keeping as the sin. The Christian
formulation, we are saved by grace and not by works of the law, would
have nothing to confess in Manasseh's mouth. The Christian formulation
has no category for I did not your will, neither kept I your
commandments as a confession of sin, because the Christian formulation
has been retrained to treat keeping the commandments as something
Yahusha (Jesus) did so that the believer would not have to. Manasseh's
prayer is from a different theological universe. The Father wrote the
commandments. The covenant required the keeping of them. The breaking of
them was sin. The repentance from sin is the confession of the breaking.
The framework reads this as the second-temple witness to what the
prophets had already said and what 1 John 2:3–4 will repeat at the end
of the canon: knowing the Father is keeping his commandments. Manasseh's
prayer is true repentance precisely because it owns the breaking.

Third, the appeal to Yahuah (God)'s appointed mercy. "You, O Yahuah
(God), according to your great goodness have promised repentance and
forgiveness to them that have sinned against you: and of your infinite
mercies have appointed repentance to sinners, that they may be saved"
(verse 7). Manasseh appeals not to a generic mercy but to the specific
promise of repentance that Yahuah (God) has appointed for those who have
sinned. The framework reads this as the proper appeal. Repentance is not
a Christian invention. Repentance is the appointed mercy of the covenant
— promised in the Torah, demonstrated in the prophets, modeled by every
faithful Yashar'eli who fell and turned back. The reader who has been
retrained out of the institutional Christian formulation of you sinned,
Christ paid, you go free will recognize Manasseh's formulation as the
more covenant-aware one. Yahusha (Jesus) is not absent from this picture
— the framework holds that he is the promise to whom every prayer of
repentance has always been pointing — but the structure of the prayer is
the structure the Father appointed. Repentance is the appointed mercy.
The sinner returns. The Father receives him. This was true under
Manasseh; it was true at Calvary; it is true for the awakening reader
walking out of any of the four houses today.

Fourth, the closing. "Therefore I will praise you for ever all the days
of my life: for all the powers of the heavens do praise you, and yours
is the glory for ever and ever. Amen" (verse 15). Manasseh's repentance
does not end in a defensive crouch. It ends in praise. The man who set
up the abominations now closes his prayer by joining all the powers of
the heavens in the doxology that creation has been giving since the
beginning. The framework reads this as the framework's portrait of
restored covenant life. The repentance is not the end. The praise is.
The forgiven sinner does not spend the rest of his days apologizing. The
forgiven sinner joins the doxology that has never stopped. The awakening
reader walking out of one of the four houses is being invited into the
same closing line. Repentance is the door. Praise is the room.

The wider point worth naming: Manasseh's biblical narrative in 2
Chronicles 33 records that after his repentance "he took away the
strange gods, and the idol out of the house of Yahuah (God), and all the
altars that he had built in the mount of the house of Yahuah (God), and
in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city. And he repaired the altar
of Yahuah (God), and sacrificed thereon peace offerings and thank
offerings, and commanded Yahudah (Judah) to serve Yahuah (God) Elohim
(God) of Yashar'el (Israel)" (2 Chronicles 33:15–16). The repentance was
not merely emotional. The repentance produced concrete restoration: the
abominations were removed, the altar was repaired, the people were
called back to the right worship. The framework reads this as the
pattern. True repentance for the awakening reader is not merely
emotional reorientation. True repentance produces the dismantling of the
abominations one was previously serving — the inherited Christian
distortions of Paul, the Sabbath replaced by Sunday, the feasts replaced
by pagan holidays, the names of Yahuah (God) and Yahusha (Jesus)
replaced by titles, the covenant of the twelve tribes replaced by the
church-as-Israel substitute. The repentance is real when the
abominations come down. Manasseh's prayer is the inward voice. 2
Chronicles 33:15–16 is the outward result. Both are required.

Cross-references: 2 Chronicles 33:1–20; 2 Kings 21:1–18; Psalm 51:1–17;
Psalm 32:1–11; 1 John 1:9; 1 John 2:3–4; Luke 15:11–32; Jeremiah
31:18–20; Ezekiel 18:21–32; Joel 2:12–13.

1 Maccabees — Introduction

1 Maccabees is the indispensable historical companion to the New
Testament. It is the only book in the Apocrypha that is a true
historical chronicle in the sense the Old Testament 1 and 2 Kings or 1
and 2 Chronicles are historical chronicles — composed close to the
events, drawing on official records, naming the kings and battles and
treaties, and telling the political history of a specific period: the
Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid empire, from 175 BCE to roughly
134 BCE, and the rise of the Hasmonean dynasty that ruled the Yahudi
(Jewish) state from then until the Roman conquest in 63 BCE.

Without 1 Maccabees, the New Testament world appears out of nowhere. The
Pharisees, the Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy, the temple state,
the zealot factions, the Herodian client-kingship, the Roman occupation
— all of it has its political and religious roots in the period 1
Maccabees covers. The book describes the Hellenization crisis under
Antiochus Epiphanes, the desecration of the temple in 167 BCE, the
Maccabean priestly revolt under Mattathias and his five sons, the
rededication of the temple in 164 BCE (the festival of Hanukkah), the
long guerrilla war against the Seleucid dynasty, the diplomatic
negotiations with Rome, the establishment of the Hasmonean
priest-kingship under Simon, and the assassination of Simon by his
son-in-law Ptolemy in 134 BCE. It is, in sixteen chapters, the political
and religious genealogy of the world Yahusha (Jesus) walked into.

For the awakening reader, three things matter.

First, 1 Maccabees is the historical record of Hanukkah. The festival of
dedication that John 10:22 names — "And it was at Jerusalem the feast of
the dedication, and it was winter" — is the festival 1 Maccabees
institutes (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). Yahusha walked the temple courts
during Hanukkah. He did so in the temple that the Maccabees had
rededicated. The festival itself is not an appointed feast of Yahuah
(God) (it is not in the Torah's list in Leviticus 23). It is a memorial
feast established by the Hasmonean leadership to mark the rededication.
The awakening reader walking out of the four houses can take Hanukkah
for what it is: a historical memorial of a real deliverance, recognized
by Yahusha by his presence in the temple during the festival, but not an
appointed feast in the Torah's sense. The Hebrew roots community that
has made Hanukkah a major festival has done well to remember the
deliverance; but the framework of this Series asks that the appointed
feasts of Yahuah (God) be honored as Yahuah (God)'s feasts and that
Hanukkah be received as a memorial that sits beside, not in place of,
the Torah's appointed seasons.

Second, the Maccabean revolt is the historical example of a
covenant-faithful response to imperial Hellenization. The Seleucid king
Antiochus Epiphanes attempted to compel Yahudim (Jews) to abandon the
Sabbath, the food laws, circumcision, and the Torah generally. 1
Maccabees 1:41–64 records the decrees and the persecution. The book also
records the response: that the faithful chose death rather than
profanation of the covenant. Mattathias' refusal to sacrifice on the
pagan altar (1 Maccabees 2:15–28) is the moment the revolt begins. The
awakening reader who lives under contemporary cultural pressure to
abandon the Torah — pressure that is more diffuse than Antiochus' but is
no less real — will find in 1 Maccabees the historical model of what
covenant faithfulness under empire actually costs and how it actually
proceeds.

Third, the Hasmonean dynasty that the Maccabean revolt establishes is,
by the time of the New Testament, a corrupt priestly ruling class that
Yahusha will rebuke in his own ministry. 1 Maccabees ends with Simon
Maccabeus' assassination by his son-in-law in 134 BCE, but the dynasty
continues for nearly a century afterward, increasingly compromised by
political ambition, alliances with foreign powers, and intra-family
violence. By the time Herod the Great marries the last Hasmonean
princess Mariamne and eliminates the rest of the family, the
priest-kingship has become an instrument of Roman client-rule. The
reader who has been retrained on the framework of this Series — which
holds that the institutions of the covenant community can themselves
become corrupted, that the sons of Belial operate from inside, and that
even the heroes of one generation can become the systems the next
generation must walk out of — will recognize the Hasmonean trajectory.
The Maccabean revolt was a covenant-faithful rebellion. The Hasmonean
dynasty became a politically-compromised priesthood. Both can be true.
The same family produced both.

Read 1 Maccabees as the political and religious history it is. It is the
book the Spirit cited through the writer of Hebrews (Hebrews 11:35). It
is the book Yahusha's audience knew. It is the book your fathers' Bibles
preserved.

1 Maccabees — Chapter 1

  1 And it happened, after that Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian,
  who came out of the land of Chettiim, had struck Darius king of the
  Persians and Medes, that he reigned in his stead, the first over
  Greece, 2 And made many wars, and won many strong holds, and slew the
  kings of the earth, 3 And went through to the ends of the earth, and
  took spoils of many nations, insomuch that the earth was quiet before
  him; whereupon he was exalted and his heart was lifted up. 4 And he
  gathered a mighty strong host and ruled over countries, and nations,
  and kings, who became tributaries to him. 5 And after these things he
  fell sick, and perceived that he should die.

  6 Wherefore he called his servants, such as were honourable, and had
  been brought up with him from his youth, and parted his kingdom among
  them, while he was yet alive. 7 So Alexander reigned twelve years, and
  then died. 8 And his servants bare rule every one in his place. 9 And
  after his death they all put crowns upon themselves; so did their sons
  after them many years: and evils were multiplied in the earth. 10 And
  there came out of them a wicked root Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, son
  of Antiochus the king, who had been an hostage at Rome, and he reigned
  in the hundred and thirty and seventh year of the kingdom of the
  Greeks.

  11 In those days went there out of Yashar'el (Israel) wicked men, who
  persuaded many, saying, Let us go and make a covenant with the heathen
  that are round about us: for since we departed from them we have had
  much sorrow. 12 So this device pleased them well. 13 Then certain of
  the people were so forward in this, that they went to the king, who
  gave them licence to do after the ordinances of the heathen: 14
  Whereupon they built a place of exercise at Jerusalem according to the
  customs of the heathen: 15 And made themselves uncircumcised, and
  forsook the holy covenant, and joined themselves to the heathen, and
  were sold to do mischief.

  16 Now when the kingdom was established before Antiochus, he thought
  to reign over Egypt that he might have the dominion of two realms. 17
  Wherefore he entered into Egypt with a great multitude, with chariots,
  and elephants, and horsemen, and a great navy, 18 And made war against
  Ptolemee king of Egypt: but Ptolemee was afraid of him, and fled; and
  many were wounded to death. 19 Thus they got the strong cities in the
  land of Egypt and he took the spoils thereof. 20 And after that
  Antiochus had struck Egypt, he returned again in the hundred forty and
  third year, and went up against Yashar'el (Israel) and Jerusalem with
  a great multitude,

  21 And entered proudly into the sanctuary, and took away the golden
  altar, and the candlestick of light, and all the vessels thereof, 22
  And the table of the shewbread, and the pouring vessels, and the
  vials. and the censers of gold, and the veil, and the crown, and the
  golden ornaments that were before the temple, all which he pulled off.
  23 He took also the silver and the gold, and the precious vessels:
  also he took the hidden treasures which he found. 24 And when he had
  taken all away, he went into his own land, having made a great
  massacre, and spoken very proudly. 25 Therefore there was a great
  mourning in Yashar'el (Israel), in every place where they were;

  26 So that the princes and elders mourned, the virgins and young men
  were made feeble, and the beauty of women was changed. 27 Every
  bridegroom took up lamentation, and she that sat in the marriage
  chamber was in heaviness, 28 The land also was moved for the
  inhabitants thereof, and all the house of Jacob was covered with
  confusion. 29 And after two years fully expired the king sent his
  chief collector of tribute to the cities of Juda, who came to
  Jerusalem with a great multitude, 30 And spoke peaceable words to
  them, but all was deceit: for when they had given him credence, he
  fell suddenly upon the city, and struck it very sore, and destroyed
  much people of Yashar'el (Israel).

  31 And when he had taken the spoils of the city, he set it on fire,
  and pulled down the houses and walls thereof on every side. 32 But the
  women and children took they captive, and possessed the cattle. 33
  Then builded they the city of David with a great and strong wall, and
  with mighty towers, and made it a strong hold for them. 34 And they
  put in it a sinful nation, wicked men, and fortified themselves in it.
  35 They stored it also with armour and victuals, and when they had
  gathered together the spoils of Jerusalem, they laid them up there,
  and so they became a sore snare:

  36 For it was a place to lie in wait against the sanctuary, and an
  evil adversary to Yashar'el (Israel). 37 Thus they shed innocent blood
  on every side of the sanctuary, and defiled it: 38 Insomuch that the
  inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them: whereupon the city was
  made an habitation of strangers, and became strange to those that were
  born in her; and her own children left her. 39 Her sanctuary was laid
  waste like a wilderness, her feasts were turned into mourning, her
  sabbaths into reproach her honour into contempt. 40 As had been her
  glory, so was her dishonour increased, and her excellency was turned
  into mourning.

  41 Moreover king Antiochus wrote to his whole kingdom, that all should
  be one people, 42 And every one should leave his laws: so all the
  heathen agreed according to the commandment of the king. 43 Yea, many
  also of the Israelites consented to his religion, and sacrificed to
  idols, and profaned the sabbath. 44 For the king had sent letters by
  messengers to Jerusalem and the cities of Juda that they should follow
  the strange laws of the land, 45 And forbid burnt offerings, and
  sacrifice, and drink offerings, in the temple; and that they should
  profane the sabbaths and festival days:

  46 And pollute the sanctuary and holy people: 47 Set up altars, and
  groves, and chapels of idols, and sacrifice swine’s flesh, and unclean
  beasts: 48 That they should also leave their children uncircumcised,
  and make their souls abominable with all manner of uncleanness and
  profanation: 49 To the end they might forget the law, and change all
  the ordinances. 50 And whoever would not do according to the
  commandment of the king, he said, he should die.

  51 In the selfsame manner wrote he to his whole kingdom, and appointed
  overseers over all the people, commanding the cities of Juda to
  sacrifice, city by city. 52 Then many of the people were gathered to
  them, to wit every one that forsook the law; and so they committed
  evils in the land; 53 And drove the Israelites into secret places,
  even wherever they could flee for succour. 54 Now the fifteenth day of
  the month Casleu, in the hundred forty and fifth year, they set up the
  abomination of desolation upon the altar, and builded idol altars
  throughout the cities of Juda on every side; 55 And burnt incense at
  the doors of their houses, and in the streets.

  56 And when they had rent in pieces the books of the law which they
  found, they burnt them with fire. 57 And whoever was found with any
  the book of the testament, or if any committed to the law, the king’s
  commandment was, that they should put him to death. 58 Thus did they
  by their authority to the Israelites every month, to as many as were
  found in the cities. 59 Now the five and twentieth day of the month
  they did sacrifice upon the idol altar, which was upon the altar of
  Yahuah (God). 60 At which time according to the commandment they put
  to death certain women, that had caused their children to be
  circumcised.

  61 And they hanged the infants about their necks, and rifled their
  houses, and slew them that had circumcised them. 62 Howbeit many in
  Yashar'el (Israel) were fully resolved and confirmed in themselves not
  to eat any unclean thing. 63 Wherefore they chose rather to die, that
  they might not be defiled with meats, and that they might not profane
  the holy covenant: so then they died. 64 And there was very great
  wrath upon Yashar'el (Israel).

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter sets the scene. Alexander the Great's conquests
broke the Persian empire and created the Hellenistic world. After his
death, his empire was divided among his generals. The Seleucid dynasty
took the eastern portion, including Syria and Judea. The Ptolemaic
dynasty took Egypt. The Yahudi (Jewish) community in Judea passed back
and forth between the two for over a century.

The chapter then focuses on Antiochus IV Epiphanes (verses 10–64).
Antiochus, around 175 BCE, took the Seleucid throne and pursued an
aggressive program of Hellenization throughout his territories. The
chapter records the Hellenization of Jerusalem itself: a Yahudi (Jewish)
faction supported it, a gymnasium was built, the covenant circumcision
was hidden by some Yahudi (Jewish) men through a surgical procedure
(verse 15), the high priesthood was sold to the highest bidder, and the
temple was eventually desecrated by Antiochus's deliberate act of
placing an idol on the altar and sacrificing pigs to Zeus (verses
54–59). The chapter ends with the persecution: those who would not
abandon the Sabbath, the food laws, circumcision, and the Torah were
tortured and killed.

Several things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the Hellenization crisis is the second-temple historical
illustration of cultural-religious assimilation. The pressure was not
merely external. A Yahudi (Jewish) faction supported it. The high
priesthood was complicit. The temple's desecration was preceded by years
of voluntary cultural drift. The framework of this Series, which holds
that the four houses (institutional Christianity, Judaism, Hebrew roots,
and any other inherited religious system) carry inherited deception that
has been voluntarily accommodated over generations, finds in 1 Maccabees
1 the second-temple historical illustration. The covenant community had
been drifting toward Hellenization for decades before Antiochus
formalized it. The covenant community in any age has been drifting
toward whatever cultural-religious accommodation is on offer. The
pattern is consistent.

Read the chapter slowly with the framework's eye. In those days went
there out of Yashar'el (Israel) wicked men, who persuaded many, saying,
Let us go and make a covenant with the heathen that are round about us:
for since we departed from them we have had much sorrow (verses 11–12).
The Hellenizing party was internal. Their argument was that the covenant
community had become culturally backward, isolated, and disadvantaged
compared to the surrounding cosmopolitan Hellenistic world. They wanted
to make a covenant with the heathen — to enter into formal alignment
with the surrounding culture — so that the covenant community could
enjoy the prestige, the prosperity, and the social-political integration
that Hellenistic culture offered. This argument is not strange to the
awakening reader. It is the same argument every accommodating party in
every covenant community has always made: we have suffered for our
peculiarity; if we will only let go of the more inconvenient marks of
separateness, we can rejoin the surrounding world and prosper as it
does. The Hellenizers in Jerusalem in the 170s BCE made it. The Reform
movement in nineteenth-century Judaism made it. The mainline Protestant
churches in twentieth-century America made it. The contemporary
culturally-Christian celebrities and politicians make it every day. The
covenant with the heathen has been signed and re-signed across
centuries, in every generation. 1 Maccabees 1 is the second-temple
anchor for recognizing the pattern.

The specific detail of verse 15 is one of the most graphic moments in
the apocryphal corpus. They made themselves uncircumcised, and forsook
the holy covenant. The Hellenized Yahudi (Jewish) men underwent surgical
procedures to disguise the marks of circumcision so that they could
compete naked in the Greek gymnasium without being identified as Yahudim
(Jews). They literally cut away the sign of the covenant. The
framework's reading of this detail: the assimilation runs to the body.
The covenant of Abraham, made in the flesh (Sirach 44:19), is being
unmade in the flesh. The Hellenizers were not just adopting cultural
customs; they were physically removing the visible mark of paternal
covenant inheritance. This is the second-temple example of how far
accommodation can go when the covenant community begins to drift. The
contemporary equivalent is the wholesale spiritualization of the
covenant — the false-inclusion gospel that erases the bloodline-specific
covenant by redefining inclusion as a behavioral category. The mark on
the flesh is being erased by redefinition. The mark on the flesh in 1
Maccabees 1 was being erased by surgery. Both moves are the same move.
The framework names them as the same.

Second, the desecration of the temple — verses 54–59 — is one of the
most theologically weighted moments in the second-temple corpus. The
text records that Antiochus set up the abomination of desolation upon
the altar.

The phrase is the direct citation of Daniel 11:31: And arms shall stand
on his part, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and shall
take away the daily sacrifice, and they shall place the abomination that
makes desolate. Daniel 12:11 repeats: And from the time that the daily
sacrifice shall be taken away, and the abomination that makes desolate
set up, there shall be a thousand two hundred and ninety days. Daniel
8:11–13 anticipates: Yea, he magnified himself even to the prince of the
host, and by him the daily sacrifice was taken away, and the place of
his sanctuary was cast down... How long shall be the vision concerning
the daily sacrifice, and the transgression of desolation, to give both
the sanctuary and the host to be trodden under foot?

Daniel was given the prophecy in the sixth century BCE; Antiochus
fulfilled it in 167 BCE. The 1 Maccabees 1 narrative is the historical
record of the Daniel prophecy's first fulfillment. The phrase did not
stop there. Yahusha cites it in Matthew 24:15: When you therefore shall
see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet,
stand in the holy place, (whoso reads, let him understand:). Mark 13:14
repeats. The Messiah, in the first century CE, names the abomination of
desolation as something his disciples would see in the future of their
generation — and the Roman desecration of the temple in 70 CE under
Titus (and later under Hadrian in 132 CE, when a temple to Jupiter was
placed on the temple mount) is the second-fulfillment Yahusha was
naming.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the abomination of
desolation has multiple historical referents (Antiochus's desecration in
167 BCE; Roman desecrations of the temple in 70 CE and 132 CE; future
desecrations the prophets named), finds in 1 Maccabees 1 the
second-temple historical anchor for the phrase. The phrase has more than
one fulfillment, and 1 Maccabees 1 is the first.

The framework's specific reading of the abomination of desolation: this
is one of the recurring imperial-pattern moments where the appointed
dwelling-place of Yahuah (God) is desecrated by a foreign power.
Antiochus did it physically (in 167 BCE). The Romans did it physically
(in 70 CE under Titus, and again in 132 CE under Hadrian when a temple
to Jupiter was placed on the temple mount). The contemporary cultural
pattern of replacing the appointed worship with imperial worship
continues — different costumes, same pattern. The framework reads
Yahusha's reference to the abomination of desolation, spoken of by
Daniel the prophet (Matthew 24:15) as having multiple historical
fulfillments, with the appointed close still ahead.

Third, the persecution that followed the desecration (verses 60–64) is
the second-temple narrative of what covenant faithfulness costs under
imperial assimilation. Mothers who circumcised their infants were
killed, with the infants hung around their necks. Whole households who
kept the Sabbath were burned alive. Those who refused to eat unclean
food were tortured. The text is unflinching.

The canonical anchor for the cost-of-covenant-faithfulness pattern is
concrete. Daniel 3:16–18, the three Hebrews before the furnace: We are
not careful to answer you in this matter. If it be so, our Elohim (God) whom we
serve is able to deliver us... But if not, be it known to you, O king,
that we will not serve your gods. Daniel 6:10, Daniel under Darius's
decree: He kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and
gave thanks before his Elohim (God), as he did aforetime. The three Hebrews chose
the furnace; Daniel chose the lions' den; the Maccabean believers chose
the sword. The cost differed by century. The principle was the same.
Hebrews 11:36–38 catalogues the same in apostolic vocabulary: And others
had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and
imprisonment: They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted,
were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and
goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented; (Of whom the world was
not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and
caves of the earth. The framework of this Series, which holds that the
awakening reader walks under contemporary cultural pressure that is more
diffuse than Antiochus's but is no less spiritually serious, finds in 1
Maccabees 1 the second-temple historical reminder of what the cost of
covenant faithfulness can become.

The contemporary cost is rarely physical death (though in some parts of
the world it is). The contemporary cost is the
social-economic-relational cost of refusing to accommodate. The
Sabbath-keeping believer who declines the corporate weekend functions;
the Torah-faithful family who pulls children out of culturally-captured
schooling; the awakened reader who walks out of the institutional church
and is treated as having abandoned the faith — these are the
contemporary equivalents of the second-temple persecutions. The
framework holds the proportion. What the Maccabean believers paid in
blood, many awakening readers pay in relationship, in vocation, in
social standing. Both are real costs. The framework does not minimize
either.

Cross-references: Daniel 7:1–28; Daniel 8:1–27; Daniel 11:21–45; Daniel
12:1–13; Leviticus 11:1–47; Genesis 17:9–14; Exodus 31:12–17;
Deuteronomy 13:1–18; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14; 2 Maccabees 6:1–11;
Sirach 44:19.

1 Maccabees — Chapter 2

  1 In those days arose Mattathias the son of John, the son of Simeon, a
  priest of the sons of Joarib, from Jerusalem, and dwelt in Modin. 2
  And he had five sons, Joannan, called Caddis: 3 Simon; called Thassi:
  4 Judas, who was called Maccabeus: 5 Eleazar, called Avaran: and
  Jonathan, whose surname was Apphus.

  6 And when he saw the blasphemies that were committed in Juda and
  Jerusalem, 7 He said, Woe is me! wherefore was I born to see this
  misery of my people, and of the holy city, and to dwell there, when it
  was delivered into the hand of the enemy, and the sanctuary into the
  hand of strangers? 8 Her temple is become as a man without glory. 9
  Her glorious vessels are carried away into captivity, her infants are
  slain in the streets, her young men with the sword of the enemy. 10
  What nation has not had a part in her kingdom and gotten of her
  spoils?

  11 All her ornaments are taken away; of a free woman she is become a
  bondslave. 12 And, behold, our sanctuary, even our beauty and our
  glory, is laid waste, and the Gentiles have profaned it. 13 To what
  end therefore shall we live any longer? 14 Then Mattathias and his
  sons rent their clothes, and put on sackcloth, and mourned very sore.
  15 In the mean while the king’s officers, such as compelled the people
  to revolt, came into the city Modin, to make them sacrifice.

  16 And when many of Yashar'el (Israel) came to them, Mattathias also
  and his sons came together. 17 Then answered the king’s officers, and
  said to Mattathias on this wise, You are a ruler, and an honourable
  and great man in this city, and strengthened with sons and brothers:
  18 Now therefore come you first, and fulfil the king’s commandment,
  like as all the heathen have done, yes, and the men of Juda also, and
  such as remain at Jerusalem: so shall you and your house be in the
  number of the king’s friends, and you and your children shall be
  honoured with silver and gold, and many rewards. 19 Then Mattathias
  answered and spoke with a loud voice, Though all the nations that are
  under the king’s dominion obey him, and fall away every one from the
  religion of their fathers, and give consent to his commandments: 20
  Yet will I and my sons and my brothers walk in the covenant of our
  fathers.

  21 Yahuah (God) forbid that we should forsake the law and the
  ordinances. 22 We will not hearken to the king’s words, to go from our
  religion, either on the right hand, or the left. 23 Now when he had
  left speaking these words, there came one of the Yahudim (Jews) in the
  sight of all to sacrifice on the altar which was at Modin, according
  to the king’s commandment. 24 Which thing when Mattathias saw, he was
  inflamed with zeal, and his reins trembled, neither could he forbear
  to shew his anger according to judgment: wherefore he ran, and slew
  him upon the altar. 25 Also the king’s commissioner, who compelled men
  to sacrifice, he killed at that time, and the altar he pulled down.

  26 Thus dealt he zealously for the law of Yahuah (God) like as Phinees
  did to Zambri the son of Salom. 27 And Mattathias cried throughout the
  city with a loud voice, saying, Whoever is zealous of the law, and
  maintaineth the covenant, let him follow me. 28 So he and his sons
  fled into the mountains, and left all that ever they had in the city.
  29 Then many that sought after justice and judgment went down into the
  wilderness, to dwell there: 30 Both they, and their children, and
  their wives; and their cattle; because afflictions increased sore upon
  them.

  31 Now when it was told the king’s servants, and the host that was at
  Jerusalem, in the city of David, that certain men, who had broken the
  king’s commandment, were gone down into the secret places in the
  wilderness, 32 They pursued after them a great number, and having
  overtaken them, they camped against them, and made war against them on
  the sabbath day. 33 And they said to them, Let that which you have
  done hitherto suffice; come forth, and do according to the commandment
  of the king, and you shall live. 34 But they said, We will not come
  forth, neither will we do the king’s commandment, to profane the
  sabbath day. 35 So then they gave them the battle with all speed.

  36 Howbeit they answered them not, neither cast they a stone at them,
  nor stopped the places where they lay hid; 37 But said, Let us die all
  in our innocency: heaven and earth will testify for us, that you put
  us to death wrongfully. 38 So they rose up against them in battle on
  the sabbath, and they slew them, with their wives and children and
  their cattle, to the number of a thousand people. 39 Now when
  Mattathias and his friends understood of this, they mourned for them
  right sore. 40 And one of them said to another, If we all do as our
  brothers have done, and fight not for our lives and laws against the
  heathen, they will now quickly root us out of the earth.

  41 At that time therefore they decreed, saying, Whoever shall come to
  make battle with us on the sabbath day, we will fight against him;
  neither will we die all, as our brothers that were murdered in the
  secret places. 42 Then came there to him a company of Assideans who
  were mighty men of Yashar'el (Israel), even all such as were
  voluntarily devoted to the law. 43 Also all they that fled for
  persecution joined themselves to them, and were a stay to them. 44 So
  they joined their forces, and struck sinful men in their anger, and
  wicked men in their wrath: but the rest fled to the heathen for
  succour. 45 Then Mattathias and his friends went round about, and
  pulled down the altars:

  46 And what children soever they found within the coast of Yashar'el
  (Israel) uncircumcised, those they circumcised valiantly. 47 They
  pursued also after the proud men, and the work prospered in their
  hand. 48 So they recovered the law out of the hand of the Gentiles,
  and out of the hand of kings, neither suffered they the sinner to
  triumph. 49 Now when the time drew near that Mattathias should die, he
  said to his sons, Now has pride and rebuke gotten strength, and the
  time of destruction, and the wrath of indignation: 50 Now therefore,
  my sons, be you zealous for the law, and give your lives for the
  covenant of your fathers.

  51 Call to remembrance what acts our fathers did in their time; so
  shall you receive great honour and an everlasting name. 52 Was not
  Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was imputed to him for
  righteousness? 53 Joseph in the time of his distress kept the
  commandment and was made lord of Egypt. 54 Phinees our father in being
  zealous and fervent obtained the covenant of an everlasting
  priesthood. 55 Jesus for fulfilling the word was made a judge in
  Yashar'el (Israel).

  56 Caleb for bearing witness before the congregation received the
  heritage of the land. 57 David for being merciful possessed the throne
  of an everlasting kingdom. 58 Elias for being zealous and fervent for
  the law was taken up into heaven. 59 Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, by
  believing were saved out of the flame. 60 Daniel for his innocency was
  delivered from the mouth of lions.

  61 And thus consider you throughout all ages, that none that put their
  trust in him shall be overcome. 62 Fear not then the words of a sinful
  man: for his glory shall be dung and worms. 63 To day he shall be
  lifted up and to morrow he shall not be found, because he is returned
  into his dust, and his thought is come to nothing. 64 Wherefore, you
  my sons, be valiant and shew yourselves men in the behalf of the law;
  for by it shall you obtain glory. 65 And behold, I know that your
  brother Simon is a man of counsel, give ear to him alway: he shall be
  a father to you.

  66 As for Judas Maccabeus, he has been mighty and strong, even from
  his youth up: let him be your captain, and fight the battle of the
  people. 67 Take also to you all those that observe the law, and avenge
  you the wrong of your people. 68 Recompense fully the heathen, and
  take heed to the commandments of the law. 69 So he blessed them, and
  was gathered to his fathers. 70 And he died in the hundred forty and
  sixth year, and his sons buried him in the sepulchres of his fathers
  at Modin, and all Yashar'el (Israel) made great lamentation for him.

⸻

Commentary

The Maccabean revolt begins. The chapter opens with Mattathias, a priest
from the village of Modein, lamenting the desecration of the temple and
the Hellenization of the Yahudim (Jews) (verses 1–13). The Seleucid
commissioners arrive at Modein to compel the local Yahudim (Jews) to
sacrifice on the pagan altar. Mattathias refuses publicly. When a fellow
Yahudi (Jew) steps forward to comply, Mattathias kills him on the altar,
then kills the commissioner, and tears down the altar. He calls the
people to follow him into the hills if they have zeal for the Torah and
the covenant. The revolt is launched.

The chapter then records Mattathias's deathbed charge to his five sons
(verses 49–70). He blesses each of them and exhorts them to maintain the
revolt and the keeping of the Torah. He names them: Joannan (John),
Simon, Judas (Maccabeus), Eleazar, and Jonathan. He dies and is buried
at Modein.

Three things matter.

First, Mattathias's killing of the apostate Yahudi (Jew) at the altar
(verses 23–25) is one of the morally weighted moments in the apocryphal
corpus. The framework of this Series acknowledges the moral weight. The
Torah's commandment against murder applies to ordinary cases. The
Torah's specific provision in Numbers 25:6–13 (Phinehas's killing of the
apostate Israelite at Peor) provides the precedent Mattathias is
operating under: that in cases of public covenant apostasy combined with
imperial coercion, the priestly action of executing the apostate is
recognized by Yahuah (God). The framework does not legislate Phinehas's
or Mattathias's action as a contemporary practice for the awakening
reader. The contemporary equivalent is the firm refusal to participate
in apostasy, the public testimony of the Torah, and the patient
invitation to the deceived to come home — not violence. The framework
holds the second-temple narrative for what it shows in its historical
extremity, without translating the violence into contemporary practice.

The Phinehas-pattern is worth naming clearly. Phinehas in Numbers 25 saw
an Israelite man bringing a Midianite woman into the camp publicly
during the very judgment Yahuah (God) was carrying out for the seduction
at Peor. He took a spear, followed them into the tent, and killed them
both. Yahuah (God) said his action turned my wrath away from the
children of Yashar'el (Israel) (Numbers 25:11) and gave him the covenant
of an everlasting priesthood (Numbers 25:13). This is not a generic
license for vigilante action. This is a specific covenant office in a
specific moment of public covenant breach. Mattathias was a priest. He
was operating in a moment of public covenant apostasy under imperial
coercion. He acted in the Phinehas-pattern. The text records the action
as zeal for the covenant. The framework does not extend this beyond the
priestly office in the moment of public apostasy under imperial
coercion. The awakening reader is not Phinehas. The contemporary
application is patient witness, not the spear.

Second, Mattathias's deathbed charge to his sons (verses 49–70) is one
of the great patriarch-blessing speeches in the second-temple corpus. He
recounts the covenant fathers — Abraham, Joseph, Phinehas, Joshua,
Caleb, David, Elijah, the three young men in the furnace, Daniel — and
the costs they paid for covenant faithfulness. The recounting is the
second-temple version of Hebrews 11.

Compare Mattathias's catalogue with Hebrews 11 directly. Mattathias
names: Abraham (verse 52 — was not Abraham found faithful in temptation,
and it was imputed unto him for righteousness?); Joseph (verse 53 —
Joseph in the time of his distress kept the commandment, and was made
lord of Egypt); Phinehas (verse 54 — Phinees our father in being zealous
and fervent obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood); Joshua
(verse 55); Caleb (verse 56); David (verse 57); Elijah (verse 58);
Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (verse 59); Daniel (verse 60). Hebrews 11
names: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses,
Rahab, Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets;
then a closing reference to those who quenched the violence of fire (the
three Hebrews) and stopped the mouths of lions (Daniel) — the same
figures Mattathias names in 1 Maccabees 2:59–60.

The genre is the catalogue-of-faith. The architecture is consistent: the
covenant fathers named, the trials they walked through named, the
faithfulness that carried them named, and the present supplicant or
audience called to walk in the same line. Hebrews 12:1 closes the
catalogue with the conclusion: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed
about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight,
and the sin which does so easily beset us, and let us run with patience
the race that is set before us. Mattathias closes with the same
conclusion in verses 64 and following: And so consider you from
generation to generation, that none that put their trust in him shall be
overcome.

The framework of this Series, which honors the long line of covenant
faithful as the cloud of witnesses surrounding the awakening reader,
finds in Mattathias's deathbed speech the second-temple precedent for
the same cloud-of-witnesses theology. The Hebrews writer is not
innovating the genre. He is taking the second-temple
deathbed-and-confession-catalogue genre that Mattathias had already used
(and that 1 Enoch and the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs had also
used) and applying it to the apostolic audience as the proper way to
remember and walk forward.

Mattathias' catalog includes patriarchs, judges, kings, prophets, and
the heroic young men of Daniel — and yet the catalog is striking for
what it does not include. It does not include any of the post-exilic
Hellenizing accommodators. It does not include any of the high priests
who had been complicit in the assimilation. It includes only those who
were faithful at cost. The framework reads this as the second-temple
voice articulating who counts as covenant fathers: not those who held
the offices, but those who walked the walk. The contemporary application
is direct. The catalog of awakened-reader fathers does not include the
inherited-deception teachers under whom the reader was catechized; it
includes only those who walked the awakening walk at cost. Mattathias
did not name his deceased contemporaries who had accommodated. He named
only the faithful across the centuries. The framework holds that pattern
of memorial.

Third, the chapter records that the early Maccabean fighters refused to
fight on the Sabbath, and were slaughtered as a result (verses 29–38).
After this, Mattathias and his men reasoned together and decided that
defensive war on the Sabbath was permissible (verses 39–41). The
framework of this Series, on the question of Sabbath observance under
wartime threat, holds that the Torah's Sabbath commandment is the
standard but that the principle of preserving life applies (Yahusha
(Jesus) articulated this principle in the Gospels: it is lawful to do
good on the Sabbath, Mark 3:1–6). The Maccabean reasoning is consistent
with the principle. The framework does not legislate from the Maccabean
reasoning; the framework recognizes that the second-temple community had
to address the same kind of question the Messiah would later address
publicly, and reached compatible conclusions.

Cross-references: Numbers 25:6–13; Joshua 24:14–28; Psalm 106:28–31;
Mark 3:1–6; Acts 5:29; Hebrews 11:1–40; 1 Corinthians 10:14; 1 John
5:21; 2 Maccabees 5:24–27; 2 Maccabees 6:18–31.

1 Maccabees — Chapter 3

  1 Then his son Judas, called Maccabeus, rose up in his stead. 2 And
  all his brothers helped him, and so did all they that held with his
  father, and they fought with cheerfulness the battle of Yashar'el
  (Israel). 3 So he got his people great honour, and put on a
  breastplate as a giant, and girt his warlike harness about him, and he
  made battles, protecting the host with his sword. 4 In his acts he was
  like a lion, and like a lion’s whelp roaring for his prey. 5 For He
  pursued the wicked, and sought them out, and burnt up those that vexed
  his people.

  6 Wherefore the wicked shrunk for fear of him, and all the workers of
  iniquity were troubled, because salvation prospered in his hand. 7 He
  grieved also many kings, and made Jacob glad with his acts, and his
  memorial is blessed for ever. 8 Moreover he went through the cities of
  Juda, destroying the ungodly out of them, and turning away wrath from
  Yashar'el (Israel): 9 So that he was renowned to the utmost part of
  the earth, and he received to him such as were ready to perish. 10
  Then Apollonius gathered the Gentiles together, and a great host out
  of Samaria, to fight against Yashar'el (Israel).

  11 Which thing when Judas perceived, he went forth to meet him, and so
  he struck him, and slew him: many also fell down slain, but the rest
  fled. 12 Wherefore Judas took their spoils, and Apollonius’ sword
  also, and with it he fought all his life long. 13 Now when Seron, a
  prince of the army of Syria, heard say that Judas had gathered to him
  a multitude and company of the faithful to go out with him to war; 14
  He said, I will get me a name and honour in the kingdom; for I will go
  fight with Judas and them that are with him, who despise the king’s
  commandment. 15 So he made him ready to go up, and there went with him
  a mighty host of the ungodly to help him, and to be avenged of the
  children of Yashar'el (Israel).

  16 And when he came near to the going up of Bethhoron, Judas went
  forth to meet him with a small company: 17 Who, when they saw the host
  coming to meet them, said to Judas, How shall we be able, being so
  few, to fight against so great a multitude and so strong, seeing we
  are ready to faint with fasting all this day? 18 To whom Judas
  answered, It is no hard matter for many to be shut up in the hands of
  a few; and with Yahuah (God) of heaven it is all one, to deliver
  with a great multitude, or a small company: 19 For the victory of
  battle stands not in the multitude of an host; but strength comes from
  heaven. 20 They come against us in much pride and iniquity to destroy
  us, and our wives and children, and to spoil us:

  21 But we fight for our lives and our laws. 22 Wherefore Yahuah (God)
  himself will overthrow them before our face: and as for you, be you
  not afraid of them. 23 Now as soon as he had left off speaking, he
  leapt suddenly upon them, and so Seron and his host was overthrown
  before him. 24 And they pursued them from the going down of Bethhoron
  to the plain, where were slain about eight hundred men of them; and
  the residue fled into the land of the Philistines. 25 Then began the
  fear of Judas and his brothers, and an exceeding great dread, to fall
  upon the nations round about them:

  26 Insomuch as his fame came to the king, and all nations talked of
  the battles of Judas. 27 Now when king Antiochus heard these things,
  he was full of indignation: wherefore he sent and gathered together
  all the forces of his realm, even a very strong army. 28 He opened
  also his treasure, and gave his soldiers pay for a year, commanding
  them to be ready whenever he should need them. 29 Nevertheless, when
  he saw that the money of his treasures failed and that the tributes in
  the country were small, because of the dissension and plague, which he
  had brought upon the land in taking away the laws which had been of
  old time; 30 He feared that he should not be able to bear the charges
  any longer, nor to have such gifts to give so liberally as he did
  before: for he had abounded above the kings that were before him.

  31 Wherefore, being greatly perplexed in his mind, he determined to go
  into Persia, there to take the tributes of the countries, and to
  gather much money. 32 So he left Lysias, a nobleman, and one of the
  blood royal, to oversee the affairs of the king from the river
  Euphrates to the borders of Egypt: 33 And to bring up his son
  Antiochus, until he came again. 34 Moreover he delivered to him the
  half of his forces, and the elephants, and gave him charge of all
  things that he would have done, as also concerning them that dwelt in
  Juda and Jerusalem: 35 To wit, that he should send an army against
  them, to destroy and root out the strength of Yashar'el (Israel), and
  the remnant of Jerusalem, and to take away their memorial from that
  place;

  36 And that he should place strangers in all their quarters, and
  divide their land by lot. 37 So the king took the half of the forces
  that remained, and departed from Antioch, his royal city, the hundred
  forty and seventh year; and having passed the river Euphrates, he went
  through the high countries. 38 Then Lysias chose Ptolemee the son of
  Dorymenes, Nicanor, and Gorgias, mighty men of the king’s friends: 39
  And with them he sent forty thousand footmen, and seven thousand
  horsemen, to go into the land of Juda, and to destroy it, as the king
  commanded. 40 So they went forth with all their power, and came and
  pitched by Emmaus in the plain country.

  41 And the merchants of the country, hearing the fame of them, took
  silver and gold very much, with servants, and came into the camp to
  buy the children of Yashar'el (Israel) for slaves: a power also of
  Syria and of the land of the Philistines joined themselves to them. 42
  Now when Judas and his brothers saw that miseries were multiplied, and
  that the forces did encamp themselves in their borders: for they knew
  how the king had given commandment to destroy the people, and utterly
  abolish them; 43 They said one to another, Let us restore the decayed
  fortune of our people, and let us fight for our people and the
  sanctuary. 44 Then was the congregation gathered together, that they
  might be ready for battle, and that they might pray, and ask mercy and
  compassion. 45 Now Jerusalem lay void as a wilderness, there was none
  of her children that went in or out: the sanctuary also was trodden
  down, and aliens kept the strong hold; the heathen had their
  habitation in that place; and joy was taken from Jacob, and the pipe
  with the harp ceased.

  46 Wherefore the Israelites assembled themselves together, and came to
  Maspha, over against Jerusalem; for in Maspha was the place where they
  prayed aforetime in Yashar'el (Israel). 47 Then they fasted that day,
  and put on sackcloth, and cast ashes upon their heads, and rent their
  clothes, 48 And laid open the book of the law, in which the heathen
  had sought to paint the likeness of their images. 49 They brought also
  the priests’ garments, and the firstfruits, and the tithes: and the
  Nazarites they stirred up, who had accomplished their days. 50 Then
  cried they with a loud voice toward heaven, saying, What shall we do
  with these, and whither shall we carry them away?

  51 For your sanctuary is trodden down and profaned, and your priests
  are in heaviness, and brought low. 52 And lo, the heathen are
  assembled together against us to destroy us: what things they imagine
  against us, you know. 53 How shall we be able to stand against them,
  except you, O Yahuah (God), be our help? 54 Then sounded they with
  trumpets, and cried with a loud voice. 55 And after this Judas
  ordained captains over the people, even captains over thousands, and
  over hundreds, and over fifties, and over tens.

  56 But as for such as were building houses, or had betrothed wives, or
  were planting vineyards, or were fearful, those he commanded that they
  should return, every man to his own house, according to the law. 57 So
  the camp removed, and pitched upon the south side of Emmaus. 58 And
  Judas said, arm yourselves, and be valiant men, and see that you be in
  readiness against the morning, that you may fight with these nations,
  that are assembled together against us to destroy us and our
  sanctuary: 59 For it is better for us to die in battle, than to behold
  the calamities of our people and our sanctuary. 60 Nevertheless, as
  the will of Yahuah (God) is in heaven, so let him do.

⸻

Commentary

Judas Maccabeus, the son of Mattathias, takes leadership of the revolt.
The chapter records his early victories: against Apollonius (verses
10–12), against Seron (verses 13–24), against Gorgias (verse 38–40), and
the rallying of the people. The chapter ends with the gathering of the
Israelite forces at Mizpah for prayer and fasting before the next major
engagement.

Several things matter, and the gathering at Mizpah carries the weight
that the awakening reader of this Series most needs to hear.

First, the chapter contains Judas's psalm of praise after the victory
over Seron (verses 3–9). The psalm is in the cadence of the Hebrew
warrior-psalms (Psalm 18, Psalm 144) and is one of the second-temple
military poems preserved in the apocryphal corpus.

Read Psalm 18 as the canonical anchor. Psalm 18:32–35: It is Elohim (God) that
girds me with strength, and makes my way perfect. He makes my feet like
hinds' feet, and sets me upon my high places. He teaches my hands to
war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms. You have also given
me the shield of your salvation: and your right hand has held me up, and
your gentleness has made me great. Psalm 144:1–2: Blessed be Yahuah
(God) my strength, which teaches my hands to war, and my fingers to
fight: My goodness, and my fortress; my high tower, and my deliverer; my
shield, and he in whom I trust. Psalm 18:46–47: Yahuah (God) lives; and
blessed be my rock; and let the Elohim (God) of my salvation be exalted. It is
God that avenges me, and subdues the people under me.

Judas's psalm in 1 Maccabees 3 stands inside the David-warrior-psalm
tradition. The framework of this Series, which honors the awakening
community's praise of Yahuah (God) for deliverance from the powers,
finds in Judas's psalm the second-temple model. The praise is for Yahuah
(God)'s deliverance, not for the warrior's prowess. The same
architecture David used after his deliverances Judas uses after his.

Second, Judas's address to his fighters before battle (verses 17–22)
frames the fight as Yahuah (God)'s fight, not theirs: It is not on the
multitude of the host that the victory in battle stands; but strength is
from heaven... With Yahuah (God) of heaven it is all one, to save with a
great multitude, or with a small company. The framework of this Series,
which holds that Yahuah (God) delivers His own through unlikely
instruments and that the awakening reader's confidence is in Yahuah
(God) and not in the size of the awakened community, finds in Judas's
address the second-temple confirmation of the framework.

Third — and this is the load-bearing passage of the chapter for the
framework of this Series — the gathering at Mizpah (verses 44–60) is
conducted in a covenant pattern that the awakening reader needs to read
with full attention. Read the verses:

And the congregation of Jacob gathered together... And they fasted that
day, and put on sackcloth, and cast ashes upon their heads, and rent
their clothes, and laid open the book of the law... And they brought
also the priests' garments, and the firstfruits, and the tithes: and
they stirred up the Nazarites, who had accomplished their days (verses
44–49).

Take this passage slowly. The Maccabean assembly at Mizpah is not just a
war council. It is a recovery of the covenant pattern — the full
pattern, the appointed pattern, the pattern the second-temple community
knew was the proper response to crisis. They gather. They fast. They
tear their clothes. They cast ashes. They lay open the Torah. They blow
the trumpets. And then the text records that they brought, into the
gathering, four specific things in their proper order: the priests'
garments, the firstfruits, the tithes, and the Nazarites who had
accomplished their days.

This is the framework's anchor passage for the Nazarite vocation in the
second-temple period, and it has been almost universally passed over by
the institutional readings. Read what is being said. The Maccabean
leaders, in the moment of crisis, brought together at Mizpah:

The priestly garments — the visible mark of the priestly office, the
appointed clothing that signals which men carry the appointed mediation
between the Father and the people.

The firstfruits — the appointed offering of the produce of the land,
named in Deuteronomy 26 and elsewhere, the first portion given back to
Yahuah (God) in recognition that the harvest is His.

The tithes — the tenth portion appointed for the support of the
Levitical service and for the relief of the widow, orphan, and
sojourner.

The Nazarites who had accomplished their days — the men who had walked
under the vow of Numbers 6, abstaining from the fruit of the vine,
refusing the razor, avoiding the dead, marking their bodies as set apart
for Yahuah (God) for the appointed time, and who had now completed the
vow.

What is the text saying? It is saying that the proper response to
covenant crisis includes the priests in their visible appointment, the
offerings in their proper place, the tithes in their proper
distribution, AND the Nazarites stirred up. Stirred up. The Greek verb
(in the Septuagintal Greek of the apocryphal text the Latin and English
derive from) carries the sense of awakening, calling forth, gathering
with purpose, summoning to active service. The Nazarites whose vows had
been completed were not retired — they were available, they were known,
they were on the roll of the covenant community as walking witnesses to
the Torah, and in the moment of crisis they were summoned forward.

Why do this matter? Because the standard Christian and Yahudi (Jewish)
institutional reading has, for centuries, treated the Nazarite vow as a
curiosity of the Torah, a peculiar Old Testament practice attached to
figures like Samson and Samuel and (in the New Testament) John the
Immerser, but with no continuing covenant relevance. The Nazarite has
been pushed off into the historical backwater. 1 Maccabees 3:49 will not
allow this. The Nazarite was an active, recognizable, summoned-forward
category in the second-temple community. The Maccabean leaders, in the
most serious moment of their generation's covenant crisis, knew where to
find them and called them in.

The framework of this Series has its own substantive teaching on the
modern Nazarite walk, and 1 Maccabees 3:49 is one of the framework's
textual anchors. The Nazarite vocation is not a curiosity. It is a real
covenant office, instituted by Numbers 6, walked by named Old Testament
figures, preserved in the second-temple community as visible in this
passage, walked by John the Immerser at the threshold of the New
Testament, and continuing to be available as an appointed walk for those
Yahuah (God) calls into it. The Nazarite is set apart. The Nazarite's
body carries the visible mark — the long hair, the abstinence from the
fruit of the vine, the avoidance of the dead. The Nazarite's hand is at
leisure for the Word in the way Sirach 38 described the man set apart
