with Antiochus VII would within a year produce a Seleucid invasion of
Judea. The Maccabean state was never far from imperial reassertion.

Cross-references: Proverbs 21:1; Daniel 11:21–35; Acts 12:1–4; Romans
13:1–7; Revelation 17:1–18.

1 Maccabees — Chapter 16

  1 Then came up John from Gazera, and told Simon his father what
  Cendebeus had done. 2 Wherefore Simon called his two eldest sons,
  Judas and John, and said to them, I, and my brothers, and my father’s
  house, have ever from my youth to this day fought against the enemies
  of Yashar'el (Israel); and things have prospered so well in our hands,
  that we have delivered Yashar'el (Israel) often. 3 But now I am old,
  and you, by the mercy of Yahuah (God), are of a sufficient age: be you
  instead of me and my brother, and go and fight for our nation, and the
  help from heaven be with you. 4 So he chose out of the country twenty
  thousand men of war with horsemen, who went out against Cendebeus, and
  rested that night at Modin. 5 And when as they rose in the morning,
  and went into the plain, behold, a mighty great host both of footmen
  and horsemen came against them: howbeit there was a water brook
  between them.

  6 So he and his people pitched over against them: and when he saw that
  the people were afraid to go over the water brook, he went first over
  himself, and then the men seeing him passed through after him. 7 That
  done, he divided his men, and set the horsemen in the midst of the
  footmen: for the enemies’ horsemen were very many. 8 Then sounded they
  with the holy trumpets: whereupon Cendebeus and his host were put to
  flight, so that many of them were slain, and the remnant got them to
  the strong hold. 9 At that time was Judas John’s brother wounded; but
  John still followed after them, until he came to Cedron, which
  Cendebeus had built. 10 So they fled even to the towers in the fields
  of Azotus; wherefore he burned it with fire: so that there were slain
  of them about two thousand men. Afterward he returned into the land of
  Judea in peace.

  11 Moreover in the plain of Jericho was Ptolemeus the son of Abubus
  made captain, and he had abundance of silver and gold: 12 For he was
  the high priest’s son in law. 13 Wherefore his heart being lifted up,
  he thought to get the country to himself, and thereupon consulted
  deceitfully against Simon and his sons to destroy them. 14 Now Simon
  was visiting the cities that were in the country, and taking care for
  the good ordering of them; at which time he came down himself to
  Jericho with his sons, Mattathias and Judas, in the hundred threescore
  and seventeenth year, in the eleventh month, called Sabat: 15 Where
  the son of Abubus receiving them deceitfully into a little hold,
  called Docus, which he had built, made them a great banquet: howbeit
  he had hid men there.

  16 So when Simon and his sons had drunk largely, Ptolemee and his men
  rose up, and took their weapons, and came upon Simon into the
  banqueting place, and slew him, and his two sons, and certain of his
  servants. 17 In which doing he committed a great treachery, and
  recompensed evil for good. 18 Then Ptolemee wrote these things, and
  sent to the king, that he should send him an host to aid him, and he
  would deliver him the country and cities. 19 He sent others also to
  Gazera to kill John: and to the tribunes he sent letters to come to
  him, that he might give them silver, and gold, and rewards. 20 And
  others he sent to take Jerusalem, and the mountain of the temple.

  21 Now one had run afore to Gazera and told John that his father and
  brothers were slain, and, quoth he, Ptolemee has sent to slay you
  also. 22 Of this when he heard, he was sore astonished: so he laid
  hands on them that were come to destroy him, and slew them; for he
  knew that they sought to make him away. 23 As concerning the rest of
  the acts of John, and his wars, and worthy deeds which he did, and the
  building of the walls which he made, and his doings, 24 Behold, these
  are written in the chronicles of his priesthood, from the time he was
  made high priest after his father.

⸻

Commentary

The closing chapter records the campaigns of Simon's sons John
(Hyrcanus) and Judas against the Seleucid forces under Cendebeus (verses
1–10), the assassination of Simon and two of his sons by his son-in-law
Ptolemy (verses 11–22), and the assumption of leadership by John
Hyrcanus (verses 23–24).

Three things matter for the awakening reader.

First, the assassination of Simon by his own son-in-law (verses 11–22)
is the second-temple narrative end of the original Maccabean generation.
The Maccabean dynasty had begun with Mattathias's covenant zeal in 167
BCE; it ended (in its founding-generation form) with Simon's murder at a
banquet in 134 BCE. Three generations had risen and fallen. The
framework of this Series, which holds that even the most dramatic
awakening movements pass through generational transitions and that the
third generation is often where the original vision is most at risk,
finds in the assassination of Simon the second-temple example of that
risk.

The third-generation pattern is one of the framework's standing
observations. The first generation revolts in zeal — Mattathias. The
second generation consolidates and expands — Judas, Jonathan, Simon. The
third generation inherits the institutions but often loses the original
vision — John Hyrcanus and his successors, who will rule a state that
looks increasingly like the surrounding Hellenistic monarchies and
decreasingly like the priestly-revolutionary movement Mattathias began.
The contemporary application is direct. Awakening movements typically
run on this pattern. The first generation is alive in the awakening. The
second generation builds the institutions. The third generation manages
the institutions and forgets why they exist. The framework reads 1
Maccabees 16 as the second-temple anchor for that pattern and as a
warning to the contemporary awakening community: institutions must not
be allowed to ossify the awakening into another inherited deception. The
Hasmonean dynasty became, within a hundred years, the very kind of
corrupt religious-political state that the Maccabean revolt had been
launched against. The pattern can repeat. The framework is the
corrective.

Second, the assumption of leadership by John Hyrcanus (verses 23–24) is
the beginning of the Hasmonean dynasty proper. From John Hyrcanus
through Aristobulus II (the dynasty's last claimant before Roman
conquest), the Hasmoneans would rule for nearly a century. The dynasty
would become increasingly secularized, increasingly Hellenized,
increasingly entangled in dynastic succession wars, and increasingly
corrupt. The framework of this Series, which holds that the covenant
institutions are vulnerable to the same patterns of dynastic corruption
that mark all human governments, finds in 1 Maccabees 16 the
second-temple beginning of that corruption trajectory. By the time the
Romans conquered Jerusalem in 63 BCE, the Hasmonean dynasty was so
divided that two rival Hasmonean princes had invited the Romans to
arbitrate between them. The dynasty's end was the empire's beginning.

Third, the chapter's final note is brief: the rest of the acts of John,
and his wars, and his worthy deeds which he did, and the building of the
walls which he made, and his doings, behold, these are written in the
chronicles of his priesthood, from the time he was made high priest
after his father. The text closes with the matter-of-fact archival
reference. The framework of this Series, which has tracked the
trajectory of the Maccabean revolt from priestly zeal to dynastic
priesthood, marks the closing as the proper close: the founding
generation has passed, the dynasty has begun, and the historical
chronicle continues in records the text refers to but does not preserve.
The narrative the second-temple community gave the awakening reader is
the narrative of the founding generation. The dynasty's later decline is
implied by the trajectory and is filled in by the New Testament's
portrait of the world Yahusha (Jesus) walked into.

The framework's final word on 1 Maccabees: the book is the historical
companion to the New Testament. The world of Matthew is the world this
book has been preparing the reader to understand. The Pharisees, the
Sadducees, the Essenes, the Herodians, the zealots, the temple state,
the Roman occupation — all of it is the consequence of the
political-religious dynamics 1 Maccabees has documented. Read the book
to understand the world the Messiah was born into. Read 2 Maccabees for
the theological and martyrological reflection on the same period. The
two together give the awakening reader the second-temple background that
institutional Christianity has largely buried but that the Spirit cited
through the writer of Hebrews and that the Messiah walked into when he
came in the flesh.

Cross-references: 2 Samuel 13:23–29; 1 Kings 12:1–24; Hosea 5:1–7;
Matthew 22:23–33; Mark 12:18–27; Luke 20:27–40; Acts 23:6–10; Hebrews
11:35–40.

2 Maccabees — Introduction

2 Maccabees is not a sequel to 1 Maccabees. It is a parallel account,
covering roughly the same period — from the Hellenization crisis of the
late 180s BCE through the rededication of the temple in 164 BCE — but
composed in a different style by a different author for a different
purpose. Where 1 Maccabees is a sober historical chronicle, 2 Maccabees
is a dramatic theological narrative, written by an unknown author who
explicitly identifies himself as condensing a longer five-volume history
by Jason of Cyrene. It is a Greek composition, never had a Hebrew
original, and it bears the hallmarks of Hellenistic Yahudi (Jewish)
literature: rhetorical speeches, miraculous interventions, theological
reflection on the meaning of suffering, and a strong emphasis on the
temple, the priesthood, and the resurrection.

The book covers fifteen chapters and is roughly thirty percent shorter
than 1 Maccabees. It begins with two introductory letters to the
Egyptian Yahudi (Jewish) diaspora urging them to keep the festival of
the rededication of the temple. The narrative proper opens with the
corrupt high-priestly maneuvering that precedes the Hellenization
crisis, follows the persecution of the faithful under Antiochus
Epiphanes, narrates the famous martyrdoms of Eleazar (chapter 6) and the
seven brothers and their mother (chapter 7), traces the early Maccabean
victories under Judas Maccabeus, and closes with the death of the
Seleucid general Nicanor at the battle of Adasa in 161 BCE.

For the awakening reader, three things matter.

First, 2 Maccabees 7 — the martyrdom of the mother and her seven sons —
is the apocryphal text the writer of Hebrews directly cites. Hebrews
11:35 says: "Women received their dead raised to life again: and others
were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a
better resurrection." The first half of the verse is recognizable from 1
Kings and 2 Kings (the widows whose sons Elijah and Elisha raised). The
second half is 2 Maccabees 7. The mother and her seven sons are tortured
one by one for refusing to eat swine's flesh in violation of the Torah.
They explicitly testify that they hope for a better resurrection. The
fifth son tells Antiochus he will be raised again to life by Yahuah
(God), but Antiochus will not be raised at the day of judgment. The
mother encourages each son in turn. The youngest son speaks last and
longest, and then dies. This is the passage the writer of Hebrews
assumed his readers knew. The New Testament leans on 2 Maccabees here in
a way the inherited Christian reading has rarely paused over. The book
is in this volume so that the reader can hear what Hebrews was hearing.

Second, 2 Maccabees presents one of the strongest second-temple Yahudi
(Jewish) witnesses to the resurrection of the dead. The seven brothers'
explicit testimony in chapter 7 is unambiguous: Yahuah (God) will raise
the righteous to a better resurrection. The high priest Razis in chapter
14 throws himself from a tower rather than be taken alive, and as he
dies he prays that Yahuah (God) will give back to him at the
resurrection what he is now offering. This resurrection theology is the
same resurrection theology the Pharisees taught, that the apostles
preached, and that the New Testament builds on. The Sadducees denied the
resurrection (Matthew 22, Acts 23). The Pharisees affirmed it. 2
Maccabees is one of the literary witnesses to where the Pharisaic
resurrection theology came from. The awakening reader walking out of
inherited Christianity, with its often-vague treatment of the
resurrection, will find in 2 Maccabees a robust second-temple precedent
for the apostolic affirmation that Yahuah (God) raises the righteous.

Third, 2 Maccabees 12:42–46 contains a passage that has been used by the
Catholic and Orthodox traditions to argue for prayer for the dead and
the doctrine of purgatory. The passage records that Judas Maccabeus,
after a battle, found that some of the slain Yahudi (Jewish) soldiers
had been wearing pagan amulets, took up a collection from his troops,
and sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sin-offering on behalf of the slain.
The text comments approvingly on the act. The 1234 filter and the
apostolic witness apply here. The Torah does not establish a
sin-offering for the dead; the sin-offering of Leviticus is for the
living. The apostolic letters do not establish prayer for the dead as a
Christian practice; the apostles preach the resurrection and the
judgment, not the manipulation of the post-mortem state by the prayers
of the living. The 2 Maccabees passage is a witness — it shows what
Judas Maccabeus and the writer of 2 Maccabees thought was appropriate.
It is not a commandment. The framework of this Series, which holds the
Torah and the apostolic witness as the standard, does not endorse the
practice the passage records, even while it preserves the text and
acknowledges what the second-temple imagination believed. Read the
passage. Note what it shows. Hold it against the Torah and the apostolic
witness. Do not let an apocryphal narrative establish a doctrine the
Torah and the apostles did not establish.

Read 2 Maccabees for what it is: the dramatic, theological,
second-temple version of the Hellenization crisis, the martyrdoms that
fed the apostolic resurrection theology, and the historical context that
explains why the New Testament writers spoke of resurrection the way
they did. Read 1 Maccabees for the political and religious history. Read
2 Maccabees for the theological and martyrological reflection. The two
books together give the awakening reader the second-temple background
that institutional Christianity has largely buried but that the Spirit
cited through the writer of Hebrews and that Yahusha walked into when he
came in the flesh.

A word about 2 Maccabees before the chapter-by-chapter begins. Despite
its name, 2 Maccabees is not a sequel to 1 Maccabees — it is a parallel
account, written in Greek by an unknown author who is condensing a
longer five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene. The book covers a shorter
period than 1 Maccabees (roughly 175–161 BCE, ending with the death of
Nicanor) but treats that period with greater theological reflection.
Where 1 Maccabees is the political-military chronicle, 2 Maccabees is
the theological-martyrological reflection. The book preserves the most
concentrated second-temple statement of the resurrection of the body
anywhere in the Apocrypha (chapter 7), the most dramatic martyrdom
narratives (chapters 6, 7, 14), and the second-temple's own theology of
why the persecutions happened — that they were Yahuah (God)'s discipline
of His own people for their sins, not the imperial powers' victory over
Him. The reader who has read 1 Maccabees has the historical frame; the
reader who reads 2 Maccabees gets the theological frame the writer of
Hebrews and the apostles were operating within.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 1

  1 The brothers, the Yahudim (Jews) that be at Jerusalem and in the
  land of Judea, wish to the brothers, the Yahudim (Jews) that are
  throughout Egypt health and peace: 2 Yahuah (God) be gracious to you,
  and remember his covenant that he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,
  his faithful servants; 3 And give you all an heart to serve him, and
  to do his will, with a good courage and a willing mind; 4 And open
  your hearts in his law and commandments, and send you peace, 5 And
  hear your prayers, and be at one with you, and never forsake you in
  time of trouble.

  6 And now we be here praying for you. 7 What time as Demetrius
  reigned, in the hundred threescore and ninth year, we the Yahudim
  (Jews) wrote to you in the extremity of trouble that came upon us in
  those years, from the time that Jason and his company revolted from
  the holy land and kingdom, 8 And burned the porch, and shed innocent
  blood: then we prayed to Yahuah (God), and were heard; we offered also
  sacrifices and fine flour, and lighted the lamps, and set forth the
  loaves. 9 And now see that you keep the feast of tabernacles in the
  month Casleu. 10 In the hundred fourscore and eighth year, the people
  that were at Jerusalem and in Judea, and the council, and Judas, sent
  greeting and health to Aristobulus, king Ptolemeus’ master, who was of
  the stock of the anointed priests, and to the Yahudim (Jews) that were
  in Egypt:

  11 Insomuch as Yahuah (God) has delivered us from great perils, we
  thank him highly, as having been in battle against a king. 12 For he
  cast them out that fought within the holy city. 13 For when the leader
  was come into Persia, and the army with him that seemed invincible,
  they were slain in the temple of Nanea by the deceit of Nanea’s
  priests. 14 For Antiochus, as though he would marry her, came into the
  place, and his friends that were with him, to receive money in name of
  a dowry. 15 Which when the priests of Nanea had set forth, and he was
  entered with a small company into the compass of the temple, they shut
  the temple as soon as Antiochus was come in:

  16 And opening a privy door of the roof, they threw stones like
  thunderbolts, and struck down the captain, hewed them in pieces,
  struck off their heads and cast them to those that were without. 17
  Blessed be our Elohim (God) in all things, who has delivered up the
  ungodly. 18 Therefore whereas we are now purposed to keep the
  purification of the temple upon the five and twentieth day of the
  month Casleu, we thought it necessary to certify you thereof, that you
  also might keep it, as the feast of the tabernacles, and of the fire,
  which was given us when Neemias offered sacrifice, after that he had
  builded the temple and the altar. 19 For when our fathers were led
  into Persia, the priests that were then devout took the fire of the
  altar privily, and hid it in an hollow place of a pit without water,
  where they kept it sure, so that the place was unknown to all men. 20
  Now after many years, when it pleased Yahuah (God), Neemias, being
  sent from the king of Persia, did send of the posterity of those
  priests that had hid it to the fire: but when they told us they found
  no fire, but thick water;

  21 Then commanded he them to draw it up, and to bring it; and when the
  sacrifices were laid on, Neemias commanded the priests to sprinkle the
  wood and the things laid thereupon with the water. 22 When this was
  done, and the time came that the sun shone, which afore was hid in the
  cloud, there was a great fire kindled, so that every man marvelled. 23
  And the priests made a prayer while the sacrifice was consuming, I
  say, both the priests, and all the rest, Jonathan beginning, and the
  rest answering to it, as Neemias did. 24 And the prayer was after this
  manner; O Yahuah (God), Yahuah (God), Creator of all things, who are
  fearful and strong, and righteous, and merciful, and the only and
  gracious King, 25 The only giver of all things, the only just,
  almighty, and everlasting, you that deliverest Yashar'el (Israel) from
  all trouble, and did choose the fathers, and sanctify them:

  26 Receive the sacrifice for your whole people Yashar'el (Israel), and
  preserve your own portion, and sanctify it. 27 Gather those together
  that are scattered from us, deliver them that serve among the heathen,
  look upon them that are despised and abhorred, and let the heathen
  know that you are our Elohim (God). 28 Punish them that oppress us,
  and with pride do us wrong. 29 Plant your people again in your holy
  place, as Moses has spoken. 30 And the priests sung psalms of
  thanksgiving.

  31 Now when the sacrifice was consumed, Neemias commanded the water
  that was left to be poured on the great stones. 32 When this was done,
  there was kindled a flame: but it was consumed by the light that
  shined from the altar. 33 So when this matter was known, it was told
  the king of Persia, that in the place, where the priests that were led
  away had hid the fire, there appeared water, and that Neemias had
  purified the sacrifices with it. 34 Then the king, inclosing the
  place, made it holy, after he had tried the matter. 35 And the king
  took many gifts, and bestowed thereof on those whom he would gratify.

  36 And Neemias called this thing Naphthar, which is as much as to say,
  a cleansing: but many men call it Nephi.

⸻

Commentary

The opening chapter of 2 Maccabees is composed of two letters from the
Yahudi (Jewish) community in Jerusalem to the Yahudi (Jewish) community
in Egypt, urging them to keep the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah). The
first letter (verses 1–9) is brief and addresses the Egyptian community
by name. The second letter (verses 10–36) is longer and includes a
detailed account of the death of Antiochus IV and a curious narrative
about the hiding of the temple fire in a dry well during the Babylonian
exile (verses 18–36).

Three things matter.

First, the existence of the Egyptian Yahudi (Jewish) community is the
historical reality the second-temple period had created. The framework
of this Series, which holds that the covenant people had been scattered
into the nations under the judgment of Deuteronomy 28 and that the
diaspora communities were preserved across centuries, finds in 2
Maccabees 1 the second-temple example of correspondence between two
parts of that diaspora — the community in Judea and the community in
Egypt. The covenant people are larger than the geographic land of Judea.
They are scattered. They are preserved. They are in correspondence with
one another.

The Alexandrian Yahudi (Jewish) community was, by the time these letters
were written (around 124 BCE), one of the largest concentrations of the
diaspora seed anywhere in the Mediterranean. Hundreds of thousands of
Yahudim (Jews) lived in Egypt, with their own synagogues, their own
translations of the scriptures (the Septuagint had been produced in
Alexandria), and their own active intellectual-religious life. They were
part of the scattered seed. They had been preserved. The Jerusalem
community wrote to them as kindred — not as outsiders being invited in,
but as paternal blood family in a different geographic location. To our
brethren the Yahudim (Jews) that be throughout Egypt, the Yahudim (Jews)
that are in Jerusalem and in the country of Judea wish much joy and
health (verse 1). The kinship language is the bloodline-remnant
language. The framework reads the diaspora correspondence as the
second-temple voice articulating what the prophets had named — the seed
scattered into the nations remains the seed, in covenant relationship
across the geographic dispersion.

Second, the second letter's narrative about the hiding of the temple
fire (verses 18–36) is one of the apocryphal corpus's elaborations of
post-exilic legend. The story claims that the priests, before the
destruction of the first temple, hid the sacred fire of the altar in a
dry well; that after the return from exile under Nehemiah, the fire was
recovered as a thick liquid which, when poured on the altar wood,
ignited spontaneously when the sun shone on it. The framework of this
Series does not require the awakening reader to defend the legend's
historicity. The legend is the second-temple imagination's narrative of
the continuity of the temple service across the exile. Read it as
legend. Note the imaginative continuity. Do not legislate from the
legend.

Third, the urging of the Feast of Dedication on the Egyptian community
(verse 9) is the second-temple practice of the diaspora communities
reinforcing common festivals. The framework of this Series has noted
that Hanukkah is a memorial feast, not an appointed Torah feast. The
framework's reading of 2 Maccabees 1 acknowledges what the second-temple
communities were doing — building common memorial practices across the
diaspora — without endorsing the elevation of memorial practices to the
level of Torah-appointed feasts.

Cross-references: Leviticus 23:1–44; 2 Kings 25:1–21; Jeremiah 52:1–34;
Nehemiah 8:1–18; John 10:22–23; Hebrews 11:32–40.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 2

  1 It is also found in the records, that Jeremy the prophet commanded
  them that were carried away to take of the fire, as it has been
  signified: 2 And how that the prophet, having given them the law,
  charged them not to forget the commandments of Yahuah (God), and that
  they should not err in their minds, when they see images of silver and
  gold, with their ornaments. 3 And with other such speeches exhorted he
  them, that the law should not depart from their hearts. 4 It was also
  contained in the same writing, that the prophet, being warned of
  Yahuah (God), commanded the tabernacle and the ark to go with him, as
  he went forth into the mountain, where Moses climbed up, and saw the
  heritage of Yahuah (God). 5 And when Jeremy came thither, he found an
  hollow cave, in which he laid the tabernacle, and the ark, and the
  altar of incense, and so stopped the door.

  6 And some of those that followed him came to mark the way, but they
  could not find it. 7 Which when Jeremy perceived, he blamed them,
  saying, As for that place, it shall be unknown until the time that
  Yahuah (God) gather his people again together, and receive them to
  mercy. 8 Then shall Yahuah (God) shew them these things, and the glory
  of Yahuah (God) shall appear, and the cloud also, as it was shewed
  under Moses, and as when Solomon desired that the place might be
  honourably sanctified. 9 It was also declared, that he being wise
  offered the sacrifice of dedication, and of the finishing of the
  temple. 10 And as when Moses prayed to Yahuah (God), the fire came
  down from heaven, and consumed the sacrifices: even so prayed Solomon
  also, and the fire came down from heaven, and consumed the burnt
  offerings.

  11 And Moses said, Because the sin offering was not to be eaten, it
  was consumed. 12 So Solomon kept those eight days. 13 The same things
  also were reported in the writings and commentaries of Neemias; and
  how he founding a library gathered together the acts of the kings, and
  the prophets, and of David, and the epistles of the kings concerning
  the holy gifts. 14 In like manner also Judas gathered together all
  those things that were lost by reason of the war we had, and they
  remain with us, 15 Wherefore if you have need thereof, send some to
  fetch them to you.

  16 Whereas we then are about to celebrate the purification, we have
  written to you, and you shall do well, if you keep the same days. 17
  We hope also, that Yahuah (God), that delivered all his people,
  and gave them all an heritage, and the kingdom, and the priesthood,
  and the sanctuary, 18 As he promised in the law, will shortly have
  mercy upon us, and gather us together out of every land under heaven
  into the holy place: for he has delivered us out of great troubles,
  and has purified the place. 19 Now as concerning Judas Maccabeus, and
  his brothers, and the purification of the great temple, and the
  dedication of the altar, 20 And the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes,
  and Eupator his son,

  21 And the manifest signs that came from heaven to those that behaved
  themselves manfully to their honour for Judaism: so that, being but a
  few, they overcame the whole country, and chased barbarous multitudes,
  22 And recovered again the temple renowned all the world over, and
  freed the city, and upheld the laws which were going down, Yahuah
  (God) being gracious to them with all favour: 23 All these things, I
  say, being declared by Jason of Cyrene in five books, we will assay to
  abridge in one volume. 24 For considering the infinite number, and the
  difficulty which they find that desire to look into the narrations of
  the story, for the variety of the matter, 25 We have been careful,
  that they that will read may have delight, and that they that are
  desirous to commit to memory might have ease, and that all into whose
  hands it comes might have profit.

  26 Therefore to us, that have taken upon us this painful labour of
  abridging, it was not easy, but a matter of sweat and watching; 27
  Even as it is no ease to him that prepareth a banquet, and seeks the
  benefit of others: yet for the pleasuring of many we will undertake
  gladly this great pains; 28 Leaving to the author the exact handling
  of every particular, and labouring to follow the rules of an
  abridgement. 29 For as the master builder of a new house must care for
  the whole building; but he that undertaketh to set it out, and paint
  it, must seek out fit things for the adorning thereof: even so I think
  it is with us. 30 To stand upon every point, and go over things at
  large, and to be curious in particulars, belongeth to the first author
  of the story:

  31 But to use brevity, and avoid much labouring of the work, is to be
  granted to him that will make an abridgment. 32 Here then will we
  begin the story: only adding thus much to that which has been said,
  that it is a foolish thing to make a long prologue, and to be short in
  the story itself.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter continues the second letter (verses 1–18) with additional
legendary material — about Jeremiah hiding the ark of the covenant, the
tent of meeting, and the altar of incense in a cave on Mount Nebo before
the destruction of the first temple — and then transitions to the
author's preface to the work proper (verses 19–32). The author
identifies himself as condensing a longer five-volume history by Jason
of Cyrene.

Three things matter.

First, the Jeremiah-hides-the-ark narrative (verses 4–8) is one of the
most influential apocryphal legends in church history. The narrative
claims that Jeremiah, by direction from Yahuah (God), hid the ark, the
tent, and the altar of incense in a cave on Mount Nebo before the
Babylonian destruction, and that the location would remain hidden until
the people be gathered together again, and mercy come — that is, until
the messianic gathering of Yashar'el (Israel). The framework of this
Series, which honors the gathering of the scattered seed under the reign
of the Messiah as the destination of the long restoration, can read the
legend as a second-temple imagination of the recovery of the temple's
most sacred objects in connection with the gathering. The framework does
not legislate from the legend. The framework notes that the Hebrew canon
does not record this narrative; it is preserved only in 2 Maccabees 2.

The legend's connection of the hiding to the appointed gathering is
worth noting. The text explicitly says the location remains hidden until
the people be gathered together again. The second-temple imagination
understood that the ark, the tent, and the altar of incense were not
lost but stored — preserved by the Father against the appointed time of
restoration. The framework's reading: the second-temple voice was
anticipating, in concrete narrative form, what the prophets had promised
in covenant language. The gathering is appointed. The recovery of what
was hidden is appointed. Whether the literal ark is in a cave on Mount
Nebo or whether the legend is theological-symbolic, the principle the
legend names — that Yahuah (God) preserves what is appointed for the
restoration even when it is hidden during the dispersion — is the
framework's own.

Second, the author's preface (verses 19–32) is one of the most candid
second-temple authorial introductions in the apocryphal corpus. The
author confesses that condensing a five-volume history into one is hard
work, that the work is for our pains (verse 27), and that the goal is to
provide a useful summary for those who do not have time for the longer
work. The framework of this Series, which honors the awakening teacher's
labor in producing accessible work for the covenant community, finds in
2 Maccabees 2's preface the second-temple model of that labor.

Third, the preface acknowledges that the author is not the original
Jason — that the original work is by Jason of Cyrene, that Jason's five
volumes are the source, and that this volume is a condensation. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the apocryphal texts are
second-temple compositions of various authors and dates and that the
awakening reader is best served by knowing the textual situation rather
than assuming uniform inspiration, finds in 2 Maccabees 2's preface the
helpful candor.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 25:8–17; Jeremiah 3:14–17; Ezekiel 40:1–48:35;
Revelation 11:19; Hebrews 9:1–10; Luke 1:1–4.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 3

  1 Now when the holy city was inhabited with all peace, and the laws
  were kept very well, because of the godliness of Onias the high
  priest, and his hatred of wickedness, 2 It came to pass that even the
  kings themselves did honour the place, and magnify the temple with
  their best gifts; 3 Insomuch that Seleucus of Asia of his own revenues
  bare all the costs belonging to the service of the sacrifices. 4 But
  one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the
  temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city. 5
  And when he could not overcome Onias, he got him to Apollonius the son
  of Thraseas, who then was governor of Celosyria and Phenice,

  6 And told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite
  sums of money, so that the multitude of their riches, which did not
  pertain to the account of the sacrifices, was innumerable, and that it
  was possible to bring all into the king’s hand. 7 Now when Apollonius
  came to the king, and had shewed him of the money of which he was
  told, the king chose out Heliodorus his treasurer, and sent him with a
  commandment to bring him the foresaid money. 8 So forthwith Heliodorus
  took his journey; under a colour of visiting the cities of Celosyria
  and Phenice, but indeed to fulfil the king’s purpose. 9 And when he
  was come to Jerusalem, and had been courteously received of the high
  priest of the city, he told him what intelligence was given of the
  money, and declared wherefore he came, and asked if these things were
  so indeed. 10 Then the high priest told him that there was such money
  laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children:

  11 And that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of
  great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: the sum
  of which in all was four hundred talents of silver, and two hundred of
  gold: 12 And that it was altogether impossible that such wrongs should
  be done to them, that had committed it to the holiness of the place,
  and to the majesty and inviolable sanctity of the temple, honoured
  over all the world. 13 But Heliodorus, because of the king’s
  commandment given him, said, That in any wise it must be brought into
  the king’s treasury. 14 So at the day which he appointed he entered in
  to order this matter: wherefore there was no small agony throughout
  the whole city. 15 But the priests, prostrating themselves before the
  altar in their priests’ vestments, called to heaven upon him that made
  a law concerning things given to be kept, that they should safely be
  preserved for such as had committed them to be kept.

  16 Then whoso had looked the high priest in the face, it would have
  wounded his heart: for his countenance and the changing of his colour
  declared the inward agony of his mind. 17 For the man was so compassed
  with fear and horror of the body, that it was manifest to them that
  looked upon him, what sorrow he had now in his heart. 18 Others ran
  flocking out of their houses to the general supplication, because the
  place was like to come into contempt. 19 And the women, girt with
  sackcloth under their breasts, abounded in the streets, and the
  virgins that were kept in ran, some to the gates, and some to the
  walls, and others looked out of the windows. 20 And all, holding their
  hands toward heaven, made supplication.

  21 Then it would have pitied a man to see the falling down of the
  multitude of all sorts, and the fear of the high priest being in such
  an agony. 22 They then called upon the Almighty Yahuah (God) to keep
  the things committed of trust safe and sure for those that had
  committed them. 23 Nevertheless Heliodorus executed that which was
  decreed. 24 Now as he was there present himself with his guard about
  the treasury, Yahuah (God) of spirits, and the Prince of all power,
  caused a great apparition, so that all that presumed to come in with
  him were astonished at the power of Yahuah (God), and fainted, and
  were sore afraid. 25 For there appeared to them an horse with a
  terrible rider upon him, and adorned with a very fair covering, and he
  ran fiercely, and struck at Heliodorus with his forefeet, and it
  seemed that he that sat upon the horse had complete harness of gold.

  26 Moreover two other young men appeared before him, notable in
  strength, excellent in beauty, and comely in apparel, who stood by him
  on either side; and scourged him continually, and gave him many sore
  stripes. 27 And Heliodorus fell suddenly to the ground, and was
  compassed with great darkness: but they that were with him took him
  up, and put him into a litter. 28 Thus him, that lately came with a
  great train and with all his guard into the said treasury, they
  carried out, being unable to help himself with his weapons: and
  manifestly they acknowledged the power of Yahuah (God). 29 For he by
  the hand of Yahuah (God) was cast down, and lay speechless without all
  hope of life. 30 But they praised Yahuah (God), that had miraculously
  honoured his own place: for the temple; which a little afore was full
  of fear and trouble, when the Almighty Yahuah (God) appeared, was
  filled with joy and gladness.

  31 Then straightways certain of Heliodorus’ friends prayed Onias, that
  he would call upon the Most High to grant him his life, who lay ready
  to give up the ghost. 32 So the high priest, suspecting lest the king
  should misconceive that some treachery had been done to Heliodorus by
  the Yahudim (Jews), offered a sacrifice for the health of the man. 33
  Now as the high priest was making an atonement, the same young men in
  the same clothing appeared and stood beside Heliodorus, saying, Give
  Onias the high priest great thanks, insomuch as for his sake Yahuah
  (God) has granted you life: 34 And seeing that you have been scourged
  from heaven, declare to all men the mighty power of Yahuah (God). And
  when they had spoken these words, they appeared no more. 35 So
  Heliodorus, after he had offered sacrifice to Yahuah (God), and made
  great vows to him that had saved his life, and saluted Onias, returned
  with his host to the king.

  36 Then testified he to all men the works of the great Yahuah (God),
  which he had seen with his eyes. 37 And when the king asked
  Heliodorus, who might be a fit man to be sent yet once again to
  Jerusalem, he said, 38 If you have any enemy or traitor, send him
  thither, and you shall receive him well scourged, if he escape with
  his life: for in that place, no doubt, there is an especial power of
  Yahuah (God). 39 For he that dwells in heaven has his eye on that
  place, and defendeth it; and he beateth and destroys them that come to
  hurt it. 40 And the things concerning Heliodorus, and the keeping of
  the treasury, fell out on this sort.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter narrates the attempt by the Seleucid official Heliodorus to
plunder the temple treasury under orders from King Seleucus IV (verses
1–40). The high priest Onias and the people pray. As Heliodorus and his
guard enter the treasury, a horse with a fearsome rider appears, and two
young men of remarkable beauty stand on each side of him, scourging him
until he falls down speechless. The Yahudi (Jewish) people pray for him.
He recovers. He acknowledges the power of the Elohim (God) of the Yahudim (Jews)
and returns to the king with the testimony.

Three things matter.

First, the chapter's narrative of supernatural defense of the temple
(verses 24–28) is the second-temple narrative type of Yahuah (God)'s
direct intervention to protect His appointed dwelling-place.

The canonical anchors are 2 Kings 19:35 and Isaiah 37:36 — the Assyrian
army of Sennacherib annihilated overnight by the angel of Yahuah (God)
outside the walls of Jerusalem: Then the angel of Yahuah (God) went
forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore
and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold,
they were all dead corpses. 2 Chronicles 32:21 records the same. 2
Chronicles 14:11–12, Asa against the Ethiopian army: Help us, O Yahuah
(God) our Elohim (God); for we rest on you, and in your name we go against this
multitude... So Yahuah (God) smote the Ethiopians before Asa. 2
Chronicles 20:15–22, Jehoshaphat against the coalition: the battle is
not yours, but God's... Yahuah (LORD) set ambushments against the children of Ammon, Moab, and mount Seir, which were come against Yahudah (Judah);
and they were smitten.

The supernatural defense of the temple — and of the covenant community
when the temple is the target — is consistent across the canonical
witness. Heliodorus's experience in 2 Maccabees 3 stands inside this
line. The framework of this Series, which holds that Yahuah (God) is the
protector of the covenant community and intervenes when the covenant
community is attacked at its sacred center, finds in 2 Maccabees 3 the
second-temple example.

Second, Onias's intercession for the stricken Heliodorus (verses 31–33)
is the framework's posture toward those who have attacked the covenant
community: prayer for them, not vengeance.

The canonical anchor for the prayer-for-enemies posture is concrete.
Yahusha in Matthew 5:44 — But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless
them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them
which despitefully use you, and persecute you. Romans 12:14, 19–21 —
Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not... Dearly beloved,
avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is
written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord. Therefore if
your enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so
doing you shall heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil,
but overcome evil with good. Stephen in Acts 7:60, dying under stoning —
Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. Yahusha himself on the cross,
Luke 23:34 — Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.

The Onias pattern matters for the awakening reader's posture in the
contemporary religious culture. The institutional teachers, pastors,
rabbis, and movement leaders who have led the awakening reader's family
and friends into inherited deception are not the awakening reader's
enemies. They are the deceived in formal positions. The framework's
prayer for them is the same prayer Onias offered for Heliodorus: that
Yahuah (God) would have mercy, would correct, would restore. Heliodorus
came to plunder. Heliodorus left as a witness. The framework's hope is
that the same Father who turned Heliodorus's heart can turn the hearts
of contemporary deceived teachers when their walls of inherited
assumption are struck down.

Third, the high priest Onias is presented in this chapter as a faithful
priest. The narrative will eventually record Onias's deposition and
assassination by the corrupt high priestly faction (chapter 4). The
framework's note: even the most faithful priestly leadership of the
second-temple period was vulnerable to displacement by the corrupt
within the priestly community. The pattern of the corruption of
religious authority is a recurring framework concern.

Cross-references: 2 Chronicles 7:1–22; 2 Kings 19:35–37; 2 Chronicles
32:21; Daniel 11:14; Acts 12:23; Hebrews 13:17.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 4

  1 This Simon now, of whom we spoke afore, having been a betrayer of
  the money, and of his country, slandered Onias, as if he had terrified
  Heliodorus, and been the worker of these evils. 2 Thus was he bold to
  call him a traitor, that had deserved well of the city, and tendered
  his own nation, and was so zealous of the laws. 3 But when their
  hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were
  committed, 4 Onias seeing the danger of this contention, and that
  Apollonius, as being the governor of Celosyria and Phenice, did rage,
  and increase Simon’s malice, 5 He went to the king, not to be an
  accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick
  and private:

  6 For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue
  quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look to it. 7
  But after the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus, called Epiphanes,
  took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be
  high priest, 8 Promising to the king by intercession three hundred and
  threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents: 9
  Beside this, he promised to assign an hundred and fifty more, if he
  might have licence to set him up a place for exercise, and for the
  training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen, and to write them
  of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians. 10 Which when the king had
  granted, and he had gotten into his hand the rule he forthwith brought
  his own nation to Greekish fashion.

  11 And the royal privileges granted of special favour to the Yahudim
  (Jews) by the means of John the father of Eupolemus, who went
  ambassador to Rome for amity and aid, he took away; and putting down
  the governments which were according to the law, he brought up new
  customs against the law: 12 For he built gladly a place of exercise
  under the tower itself, and brought the chief young men under his
  subjection, and made them wear a hat. 13 Now such was the height of
  Greek fashions, and increase of heathenish manners, through the
  exceeding profaneness of Jason, that ungodly wretch, and no high
  priest; 14 That the priests had no courage to serve any more at the
  altar, but despising the temple, and neglecting the sacrifices,
  hastened to be partakers of the unlawful allowance in the place of
  exercise, after the game of Discus called them forth; 15 Not setting
  by the honours of their fathers, but liking the glory of the Grecians
  best of all.

  16 By reason of which sore calamity came upon them: for they had them
  to be their enemies and avengers, whose custom they followed so
  earnestly, and to whom they desired to be like in all things. 17 For
  it is not a light thing to do wickedly against the laws of Yahuah
  (God): but the time following shall declare these things. 18 Now when
  the game that was used every fifth year was kept at Tyrus, the king
  being present, 19 This ungracious Jason sent special messengers from
  Jerusalem, who were Antiochians, to carry three hundred drachms of
  silver to the sacrifice of Hercules, which even the bearers thereof
  thought fit not to bestow upon the sacrifice, because it was not
  convenient, but to be reserved for other charges. 20 This money then,
  in regard of the sender, was appointed to Hercules’ sacrifice; but
  because of the bearers thereof, it was employed to the making of
  gallies.

  21 Now when Apollonius the son of Menestheus was sent into Egypt for
  the coronation of king Ptolemeus Philometor, Antiochus, understanding
  him not to be well affected to his affairs, provided for his own
  safety: whereupon he came to Joppa, and from thence to Jerusalem: 22
  Where he was honourably received of Jason, and of the city, and was
  brought in with torch alight, and with great shoutings: and so
  afterward went with his host to Phenice. 23 Three years afterward
  Jason sent Menelaus, the aforesaid Simon’s brother, to bear the money
  to the king, and to put him in mind of certain necessary matters. 24
  But he being brought to the presence of the king, when he had
  magnified him for the glorious appearance of his power, got the
  priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred
  talents of silver. 25 So he came with the king’s mandate, bringing
  nothing worthy the high priesthood, but having the fury of a cruel
  tyrant, and the rage of a savage beast.

  26 Then Jason, who had undermined his own brother, being undermined by
  another, was compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites. 27
  So Menelaus got the principality: but as for the money that he had
  promised to the king, he took no good order for it, albeit Sostratis
  the ruler of the castle required it: 28 For to him appertained the
  gathering of the customs. Wherefore they were both called before the
  king. 29 Now Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus in his stead in the
  priesthood; and Sostratus left Crates, who was governor of the
  Cyprians. 30 While those things were in doing, they of Tarsus and
  Mallos made insurrection, because they were given to the king’s
  concubine, called Antiochus.

  31 Then came the king in all haste to appease matters, leaving
  Andronicus, a man in authority, for his deputy. 32 Now Menelaus,
  supposing that he had gotten a convenient time, stole certain vessels
  of gold out of the temple, and gave some of them to Andronicus, and
  some he sold into Tyrus and the cities round about. 33 Which when
  Onias knew of a surety, he reproved him, and withdrew himself into a
  sanctuary at Daphne, that lieth by Antiochia. 34 Wherefore Menelaus,
  taking Andronicus apart, prayed him to get Onias into his hands; who
  being persuaded to it, and coming to Onias in deceit, gave him his
  right hand with oaths; and though he were suspected by him, yet
  persuaded he him to come forth of the sanctuary: whom forthwith he
  shut up without regard of justice. 35 For the which cause not only the
  Yahudim (Jews), but many also of other nations, took great
  indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man.

  36 And when the king was come again from the places about Cilicia, the
  Yahudim (Jews) that were in the city, and certain of the Greeks that
  abhorred the fact also, complained because Onias was slain without
  cause. 37 Therefore Antiochus was heartily sorry, and moved to pity,
  and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was
  dead. 38 And being kindled with anger, forthwith he took away
  Andronicus his purple, and rent off his clothes, and leading him
  through the whole city to that very place, where he had committed
  impiety against Onias, there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus Yahuah
  (God) rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved. 39 Now when
  many sacrileges had been committed in the city by Lysimachus with the
  consent of Menelaus, and the fruit thereof was spread abroad, the
  multitude gathered themselves together against Lysimachus, many
  vessels of gold being already carried away. 40 Whereupon the common
  people rising, and being filled with rage, Lysimachus armed about
  three thousand men, and began first to offer violence; one Auranus
  being the leader, a man far gone in years, and no less in folly.

  41 They then seeing the attempt of Lysimachus, some of them caught
  stones, some clubs, others taking handfuls of dust, that was next at
  hand, cast them all together upon Lysimachus, and those that set upon
  them. 42 Thus many of them they wounded, and some they struck to the
  ground, and all of them they forced to flee: but as for the
  churchrobber himself, him they killed beside the treasury. 43 Of these
  matters therefore there was an accusation laid against Menelaus. 44
  Now when the king came to Tyrus, three men that were sent from the
  senate pleaded the cause before him: 45 But Menelaus, being now
  convicted, promised Ptolemee the son of Dorymenes to give him much
  money, if he would pacify the king toward him.

  46 Whereupon Ptolemee taking the king aside into a certain gallery, as
  it were to take the air, brought him to be of another mind: 47
  Insomuch that he discharged Menelaus from the accusations, who
  notwithstanding was cause of all the mischief: and those poor men,
  who, if they had told their cause, yes, before the Scythians, should
  have been judged innocent, them he condemned to death. 48 Thus they
  that followed the matter for the city, and for the people, and for the
  holy vessels, did soon suffer unjust punishment. 49 Wherefore even
  they of Tyrus, moved with hatred of that wicked deed, caused them to
  be honourably buried. 50 And so through the covetousness of them that
  were of power Menelaus remained still in authority, increasing in
  malice, and being a great traitor to the citizens.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter narrates the corruption of the high priesthood under the
Hellenizing factions: Jason buys the high priesthood from Antiochus IV;
Menelaus then buys it from Jason; Onias is murdered. The chapter records
the rise of Greek customs in Jerusalem — the building of a gymnasium
near the temple, the participation of the priests in athletic games (in
the nude, in keeping with Greek custom), the abandonment of priestly
duties for athletic and political pursuits.

Three things matter.

First, the corruption begins from inside (verses 7–17). Jason, who buys
the high priesthood, is the brother of the previous high priest Onias.
The Hellenization is being driven by the priestly aristocracy itself —
not imposed from outside as the first form. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the deepest corruption of religious authority
is internal and that the sons of Belial within the covenant community
are often the ones who open the doors to imperial assimilation, finds in
2 Maccabees 4 the second-temple example. The Hellenization began because
Yahudi (Jewish) priests opened the doors. The Seleucid imperial program
merely walked through the doors that had been opened.

This is the framework's anchor passage for the principle that the
deepest betrayals of the covenant come from within the covenant
community's own leadership. Jason was Onias's brother. He bought the
high priesthood by promising more tribute to Antiochus and by promising
to lead the cultural Hellenization of the Yahudi (Jewish) community. He
delivered on both promises. The temple service was neglected as the
priests participated in the gymnasium games. The traditional priestly
garments and duties were treated as backward. The covenant peculiarity
was being voluntarily eroded by the very men whose office existed to
preserve it. The pattern is the framework's pattern across covenant
history: corruption from within is more dangerous than assault from
without. The institutional pastors and teachers who have led the
awakening reader's family and friends into inherited deception are
operating in the Jason-pattern, often without recognizing it. They are
the priests in the gymnasium, neglecting the altar to participate in the
surrounding culture. The framework holds patient mercy toward them and
clear-eyed recognition of what they have been doing.

Second, the murder of Onias (verses 30–34) is one of the most dramatic
illustrations of the sons-of-Belial pattern operating within the
priesthood. Menelaus arranges Onias's murder to silence the faithful
priest who could expose the temple-treasury thefts Menelaus had
committed. The framework of this Series, which holds that the corrupt
within the religious community will silence the faithful when the
faithful threaten to expose the corruption, finds in 2 Maccabees 4 the
second-temple historical example.

Third, the chapter records the building of the gymnasium and the
participation of the priests in Greek athletic games (verses 12–15). The
text comments: they had no courage for the services of the altar. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the abandonment of the
appointed worship for cultural assimilation is a recurring pattern,
finds in 2 Maccabees 4 the second-temple version. The priests had become
more invested in Greek athletics than in the appointed altar service.
The pattern is the same pattern in every age: the religious leadership
becomes invested in the surrounding culture and lets the appointed
worship fall.

Cross-references: 1 Maccabees 1:11–15; Hosea 4:6–9; Malachi 2:1–9;
Matthew 23:1–36; 2 Peter 2:1–22; Jude 1:3–16; Revelation 2:14–16.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 5

  1 About the same time Antiochus prepared his second voyage into Egypt:
  2 And then it happened, that through all the city, for the space
  almost of forty days, there were seen horsemen running in the air, in
  cloth of gold, and armed with lances, like a band of soldiers, 3 And
  troops of horsemen in array, encountering and running one against
  another, with shaking of shields, and multitude of pikes, and drawing
  of swords, and casting of darts, and glittering of golden ornaments,
  and harness of all sorts. 4 Wherefore every man prayed that that
  apparition might turn to good. 5 Now when there was gone forth a false
  rumour, as though Antiochus had been dead, Jason took at the least a
  thousand men, and suddenly made an assault upon the city; and they
  that were upon the walls being put back, and the city at length taken,
  Menelaus fled into the castle:

  6 But Jason slew his own citizens without mercy, not considering that
  to get the day of them of his own nation would be a most unhappy day
  for him; but thinking they had been his enemies, and not his
  countrymen, whom he conquered. 7 Howbeit for all this he obtained not
  the principality, but at the last received shame for the reward of his
  treason, and fled again into the country of the Ammonites. 8 In the
  end therefore he had an unhappy return, being accused before Aretas
  the king of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued of all
  men, hated as a forsaker of the laws, and being had in abomination as
  an open enemy of his country and countrymen, he was cast out into
  Egypt. 9 Thus he that had driven many out of their country perished in
  a strange land, retiring to the Lacedemonians, and thinking there to
  find succour by reason of his kindred: 10 And he that had cast out
  many unburied had none to mourn for him, nor any solemn funerals at
  all, nor sepulchre with his fathers.

  11 Now when this that was done came to the king’s ear, he thought that
  Judea had revolted: whereupon removing out of Egypt in a furious mind,
  he took the city by force of arms, 12 And commanded his men of war not
  to spare such as they met, and to slay such as went up upon the
  houses. 13 Thus there was killing of young and old, making away of
  men, women, and children, slaying of virgins and infants. 14 And there
  were destroyed within the space of three whole days fourscore
  thousand, of which forty thousand were slain in the conflict; and no
  fewer sold than slain. 15 Yet was he not content with this, but
  presumed to go into the most holy temple of all the world; Menelaus,
  that traitor to the laws, and to his own country, being his guide:

  16 And taking the holy vessels with polluted hands, and with profane
  hands pulling down the things that were dedicated by other kings to
  the augmentation and glory and honour of the place, he gave them away.
  17 And so haughty was Antiochus in mind, that he considered not that
  Yahuah (God) was angry for a while for the sins of them that dwelt in
  the city, and therefore his eye was not upon the place. 18 For had
  they not been formerly wrapped in many sins, this man, as soon as he
  had come, had forthwith been scourged, and put back from his
  presumption, as Heliodorus was, whom Seleucus the king sent to view
  the treasury. 19 Nevertheless Yahuah (God) did not choose the people
  for the place’s sake, but the place for the people’s sake. 20 And
  therefore the place itself, that was partaker with them of the
  adversity that happened to the nation, did afterward communicate in
  the benefits sent from Yahuah (God): and as it was forsaken in the
  wrath of the Almighty, so again, the great Yahuah (God) being
  reconciled, it was set up with all glory.

  21 So when Antiochus had carried out of the temple a thousand and
  eight hundred talents, he departed in all haste to Antiochia, weening
  in his pride to make the land navigable, and the sea passable by foot:
  such was the haughtiness of his mind. 22 And he left governors to vex
  the nation: at Jerusalem, Philip, for his country a Phrygian, and for
  manners more barbarous than he that set him there; 23 And at Garizim,
  Andronicus; and besides, Menelaus, who worse than all the rest bare an
  heavy hand over the citizens, having a malicious mind against his
  countrymen the Yahudim (Jews). 24 He sent also that detestable
  ringleader Apollonius with an army of two and twenty thousand,
  commanding him to slay all those that were in their best age, and to
  sell the women and the younger sort: 25 Who coming to Jerusalem, and
  pretending peace, did forbear till the holy day of the sabbath, when
  taking the Yahudim (Jews) keeping holy day, he commanded his men to
  arm themselves.

  26 And so he slew all them that were gone to the celebrating of the
  sabbath, and running through the city with weapons slew great
  multitudes. 27 But Judas Maccabeus with nine others, or thereabout,
  withdrew himself into the wilderness, and lived in the mountains after
  the manner of beasts, with his company, who fed on herbs continually,
  lest they should be partakers of the pollution.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter records the false rumor of Antiochus's death (verses 1–10),
Jason's attempt to retake the high priesthood by force (verses 5–10),
and Antiochus's furious response — the sack of Jerusalem, the slaughter
of forty thousand inhabitants, the enslavement of forty thousand more,
and the desecration of the temple (verses 11–27).

Three things matter.

First, the chapter's narrative of the destruction is unflinching. Forty
thousand killed. Forty thousand enslaved. Antiochus enters the holy of
holies.

The canonical anchor for the covenant community under catastrophic
imperial assault is direct. 2 Kings 25:8–10, the destruction of the
first temple: Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king
of Babylon, unto Jerusalem: And he burnt the house of Yahuah (God), and
the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's
house burnt he with fire. And all the army of the Chaldees, that were
with the captain of the guard, brake down the walls of Jerusalem round
about. Lamentations 1:1–2 — How does the city sit solitary, that was
full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among
the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become
tributary! She weeps sore in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks.
Lamentations 4:11 — Yahuah (God) has accomplished his fury; he has
poured out his fierce anger, and has kindled a fire in Zion, and it has
devoured the foundations thereof.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the covenant community
has suffered catastrophic losses across history under imperial assault,
finds in 2 Maccabees 5 the second-temple historical record of one of the
worst.

Second, the chapter records the flight of Judas Maccabeus and his small
group to the wilderness (verse 27). The text says: Judas Maccabeus with
nine others or thereabout, withdrew himself into the wilderness, and
lived in the mountains after the manner of beasts, with his company, who
fed on herbs continually, lest they should be partakers of the
pollution.

The wilderness-remnant pattern is consistent across the canonical
witness. 1 Kings 19:18, the Father to Elijah on Horeb after Jezebel's
threat: Yet I have left me seven thousand in Yashar'el (Israel), all the
knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which has not
kissed him. The remnant is small. The remnant is preserved. The remnant
has not bowed. Romans 11:4–5 cites the same Elijah remnant in apostolic
vocabulary: Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant
according to the election of grace. Isaiah 10:20–22: And it shall come
to pass in that day, that the remnant of Yashar'el (Israel), and such as
are escaped of the house of Jacob, shall no more again stay upon him
that smote them; but shall stay upon Yahuah (God), the Holy One of
Yashar'el (Israel), in truth... the remnant shall return. Revelation
12:6 — the woman flees into the wilderness: And the woman fled into the
wilderness, where she has a place prepared of Elohim (God), that they should feed
her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days.

The framework of this Series, which honors the awakening remnant's
withdrawal from the corrupted institutions to keep the covenant alive in
the wilderness, finds in 2 Maccabees 5:27 the second-temple model. Ten
men in the wilderness, eating wild plants, refusing to participate in
the desecrated temple worship — this is the awakening remnant in the
second-temple form, and it stands inside the canonical
wilderness-remnant line from Elijah through Isaiah's remnant shall
return through Paul's remnant according to the election of grace through
Revelation's woman in the wilderness.

The verse — who fed on herbs continually, lest they should be partakers
of the pollution — is one of the framework's most direct second-temple
anchor for what the awakening remnant looks like in extremity. They left
the city. They left the temple (which had been desecrated and made
unfit). They went to the mountains. They lived rough. They ate what they
could gather. Why? Because they would not participate in the pollution.
The compromise was not theirs to make. The framework reads this as the
second-temple version of what the contemporary awakening reader is being
asked to do — not always physically (though sometimes), but
ecclesiastically, vocationally, relationally. Withdraw from the
desecrated worship. Eat the spiritual herbs of the Word and the Spirit.
Live in the wilderness of fresh awakening. Refuse the pollution. The
framework holds the principle, applied to the contemporary form.

Third, the chapter's framing of Antiochus's victory is clear: it was not
because Yahuah (God) had abandoned His people, but because of the
people's sins (verse 17). The text explicitly notes: Antiochus thought,
in his proud heart, that he had now conquered the highest place. But
because of the iniquities of the people Yahuah (God) was wroth, and not
for the sake of the place.

The covenant principle is anchored in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 —
the curses for breaking the covenant include scattering, foreign
occupation, and the desecration of the appointed dwelling-place. Hosea
4:6 names the principle as the prophets articulated it: My people are
destroyed for lack of knowledge: because you have rejected knowledge, I
will also reject you, that you shall be no priest to me: seeing you have
forgotten the law of your Elohim (God), I will also forget your children. 1 Peter
4:17 brings the principle into apostolic vocabulary: For the time is
come that judgment must begin at the house of Elohim (God): and if it first begin
at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of Elohim (God)?

The framework of this Series, which holds that the imperial assaults on
the covenant community proceed under Yahuah (God)'s permission as
covenant discipline rather than as Yahuah (God)'s defeat, finds in 2
Maccabees 5:17–20 the second-temple articulation.

Cross-references: 2 Kings 25:1–21; Lamentations 1:1–22; Daniel 9:1–19;
Hosea 4:6; Hebrews 11:38; 1 Peter 4:17.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 6

  1 Not long after this the king sent an old man of Athens to compel the
  Yahudim (Jews) to depart from the laws of their fathers, and not to
  live after the laws of Yahuah (God): 2 And to pollute also the temple
  in Jerusalem, and to call it the temple of Jupiter Olympius; and that
  in Garizim, of Jupiter the Defender of strangers, as they did desire
  that dwelt in the place. 3 The coming in of this mischief was sore and
  grievous to the people: 4 For the temple was filled with riot and
  revelling by the Gentiles, who dallied with harlots, and had to do
  with women within the circuit of the holy places, and besides that
  brought in things that were not lawful. 5 The altar also was filled
  with profane things, which the law forbiddeth.

  6 Neither was it lawful for a man to keep sabbath days or ancient
  fasts, or to profess himself at all to be a Yahudi (Jew). 7 And in the
  day of the king’s birth every month they were brought by bitter
  constraint to eat of the sacrifices; and when the fast of Bacchus was
  kept, the Yahudim (Jews) were compelled to go in procession to
  Bacchus, carrying ivy. 8 Moreover there went out a decree to the
  neighbour cities of the heathen, by the suggestion of Ptolemee,
  against the Yahudim (Jews), that they should observe the same
  fashions, and be partakers of their sacrifices: 9 And whoso would not
  conform themselves to the manners of the Gentiles should be put to
  death. Then might a man have seen the present misery. 10 For there
  were two women brought, who had circumcised their children; whom when
  they had openly led round about the city, the babes hanging at their
  breasts, they cast them down headlong from the wall.

  11 And others, that had run together into caves near by, to keep the
  sabbath day secretly, being discovered by Philip, were all burnt
  together, because they made a conscience to help themselves for the
  honour of the most sacred day. 12 Now I beseech those that read this
  book, that they be not discouraged for these calamities, but that they
  judge those punishments not to be for destruction, but for a
  chastening of our nation. 13 For it is a token of his great goodness,
  when wicked doers are not suffered any long time, but forthwith
  punished. 14 For not as with other nations, whom Yahuah (God)
  patiently forbeareth to punish, till they be come to the fulness of
  their sins, so dealeth he with us, 15 Lest that, being come to the
  height of sin, afterwards he should take vengeance of us.

  16 And therefore he never withdraweth his mercy from us: and though he
  punish with adversity, yet does he never forsake his people. 17 But
  let this that we have spoken be for a warning to us. And now will we
  come to the declaring of the matter in a few words. 18 Eleazar, one of
  the principal scribes, an aged man, and of a well favoured
  countenance, was constrained to open his mouth, and to eat swine’s
  flesh. 19 But he, choosing rather to die gloriously, than to live
  stained with such an abomination, spit it forth, and came of his own
  accord to the torment, 20 As it behoved them to come, that are
  resolute to stand out against such things, as are not lawful for love
  of life to be tasted.

  21 But they that had the charge of that wicked feast, for the old
  acquaintance they had with the man, taking him aside, besought him to
  bring flesh of his own provision, such as was lawful for him to use,
  and make as if he did eat of the flesh taken from the sacrifice
  commanded by the king; 22 That in so doing he might be delivered from
  death, and for the old friendship with them find favour. 23 But he
  began to consider discreetly, and as became his age, and the
  excellency of his ancient years, and the honour of his gray head, on
  which was come, and his most honest education from a child, or rather
  the holy law made and given by Yahuah (God): therefore he answered
  accordingly, and willed them straightways to send him to the grave. 24
  For it becometh not our age, said he, in any wise to dissemble, by
  which many young persons might think that Eleazar, being fourscore
  years old and ten, were now gone to a strange religion; 25 And so they
  through my hypocrisy, and desire to live a little time and a moment
  longer, should be deceived by me, and I get a stain to my old age, and
  make it abominable.

  26 For though for the present time I should be delivered from the
  punishment of men: yet should I not escape the hand of the Almighty,
  neither alive, nor dead. 27 Wherefore now, manfully changing this
  life, I will shew myself such an one as my age requires, 28 And leave
  a notable example to such as be young to die willingly and
  courageously for the honourable and holy laws. And when he had said
  these words, immediately he went to the torment: 29 They that led him
  changing the good will they bare him a little before into hatred,
  because the foresaid speeches proceeded, as they thought, from a
  desperate mind. 30 But when he was ready to die with stripes, he
  groaned, and said, It is manifest to Yahuah (God), that has the holy
  knowledge, that whereas I might have been delivered from death, I now
  endure sore pains in body by being beaten: but in soul am well content
  to suffer these things, because I fear him.

  31 And thus this man died, leaving his death for an example of a noble
  courage, and a memorial of virtue, not only to young men, but to all
  his nation.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter records the most severe stage of the persecution under
Antiochus IV (verses 1–11): the prohibition of the Sabbath, the food
laws, circumcision, and the Torah; the desecration of the temple with
the abomination of desolation; the killing of mothers who had
circumcised their infants. The chapter then narrates the martyrdom of
Eleazar (verses 18–31), an aged scribe who refused to eat swine's flesh
under torture and was killed.

Three things matter.

First, the catalogue of persecutions (verses 1–11) is one of the most
explicit second-temple historical illustrations of the cost of covenant
faithfulness under imperial assimilation. The text records that those
who kept the Sabbath were killed, that those who refused to eat swine's
flesh were killed, that the temple was named for Olympian Zeus, and that
pagan altars were set up in every Yahudi (Jewish) village. The framework
of this Series, which holds that the awakening reader walks under
cultural pressure that is more diffuse than Antiochus's but is no less
real, finds in 2 Maccabees 6 the second-temple historical reminder of
how concentrated the pressure can become.

Second, Eleazar's martyrdom (verses 18–31) is one of the great
covenant-witness narratives in the apocryphal corpus. He is offered the
option to pretend to eat swine's flesh while actually eating something
permitted — to fake the violation of the Torah for public consumption
while privately keeping the commandment. He refuses. He says explicitly
that he will not dissemble before the watching young men, lest they
think he has abandoned the Torah and follow him into apostasy. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening reader's
witness is public and that pretending to violate the Torah for political
advantage is itself a form of violation, finds in Eleazar's refusal the
second-temple model.

Read this passage slowly because it lands in the contemporary context as
forcefully as it landed in the second-temple context. Eleazar's friends,
even some of the Seleucid officials, were trying to save his life by
suggesting a compromise: bring meat of his own provision, such as was
lawful for him to use, and make as if he did eat of the flesh taken from
the sacrifice commanded by the king. They thought they were being kind.
He could appear to comply and live. The compromise would harm no one —
he would not actually eat the unclean meat — and it would preserve his
teaching life for the covenant community.

Eleazar would not do it. His reasoning is preserved in verses 24–28: It
becomes not our age, said he, in any wise to dissemble, whereby many
young persons might think that Eleazar, being fourscore years old and
ten, were now gone to a strange religion; and so they through my
hypocrisy, and desire to live a little time and a moment longer, should
be deceived by me, and I get a stain to my old age, and make it
abominable. For though for the present time I should be delivered from
the punishment of men: yet should I not escape the hand of the Almighty,
neither alive, nor dead. Wherefore now, manfully changing this life, I
will show myself such an one as my age requires, and leave a notable
example to such as be young to die willingly and courageously for the
honourable and holy laws.

The verse names the framework's standing principle on integrity in
extremity. Eleazar's concern was not for himself. His concern was for
the watching young men. If the famous old scribe was seen to compromise,
the young would conclude that the covenant could be set aside under
pressure.

Read Eleazar's witness against the canonical Daniel-witnesses pattern.
Daniel 1:8 — Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile
himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he
drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might
not defile himself. Daniel as a young man refused the king's food at the
cost of imperial favor. Daniel 3:16–18 — Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah
before the furnace: We are not careful to answer you in this matter. If
it be so, our Elohim (God) whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning
fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if
not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods, nor
worship the golden image which you have set up. Daniel 6:10 — Daniel
knowing the king's decree against prayer: he kneeled upon his knees
three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his Elohim (God), as he did
aforetime.

Four witnesses. Daniel as a young man refusing the king's meat. The
three Hebrews refusing the golden image even at the cost of the furnace.
Daniel as an old man praying openly when the law forbade it. Eleazar as
an old scribe refusing to fake compliance with swine's flesh even at the
cost of his life. The witness across the canon is consistent. The
covenant person does not dissemble. The covenant person does not pretend
to comply while privately keeping the commandment. The covenant person
does not preserve his life by appearing to break the Torah. The watching
young learn what the witnessing old will do. Daniel as a young man
learned from the elders who had taught him; Daniel as an old man taught
the next generation by his open prayer; Eleazar at ninety walked the
same line. The young would learn that the standard was negotiable. The
young would walk into apostasy because the watchman had blinked. Eleazar
refused to be the watchman who blinked. He chose death rather than the
appearance of compromise.

This is the framework's principle for the awakening reader in his or her
own community. The young are watching. The next generation is watching.
