The new awakened reader who has come into the framework recently and is
looking to see how the older walked the walk is watching. If the
watchman compromises in front of them — even in a small matter, even in
a way that "harms no one" — the next generation learns that the covenant
is negotiable. If the watchman holds, even at cost, the next generation
learns that the standard is the standard. Eleazar's "notable example to
the young" is the framework's principle of bequest. The covenant teacher
leaves the young the witness, not the pretense.

Third, Eleazar's closing words (verses 30–31) are: I will leave a
notable example to such as be young to die willingly and courageously
for the honourable and holy laws. The framework of this Series, which
honors the awakening teacher's bequest to the next generation as the
willingness to bear the cost of covenant faithfulness in front of the
young, finds in Eleazar's closing the second-temple model. The young are
watching. The teacher's faithfulness in extremity is the bequest. The
framework's principle: if the teacher's faithfulness fails under
pressure, the young learn that the covenant is negotiable; if the
teacher's faithfulness holds, the young learn that the covenant is the
standard.

Cross-references: Daniel 1:8–17; Daniel 3:16–18; Daniel 6:10; Genesis
17:9–14; Exodus 31:12–17; Leviticus 11:1–47; Hebrews 11:32–40; 1 Peter
4:12–19.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 7

  1 It came to pass also, that seven brothers with their mother were
  taken, and compelled by the king against the law to taste swine’s
  flesh, and were tormented with scourges and whips. 2 But one of them
  that spoke first said thus, What wouldest you ask or learn of us? we
  are ready to die, rather than to transgress the laws of our fathers. 3
  Then the king, being in a rage, commanded pans and caldrons to be made
  hot: 4 Which forthwith being heated, he commanded to cut out the
  tongue of him that spoke first, and to cut off the utmost parts of his
  body, the rest of his brothers and his mother looking on. 5 Now when
  he was thus maimed in all his members, he commanded him being yet
  alive to be brought to the fire, and to be fried in the pan: and as
  the vapour of the pan was for a good space dispersed, they exhorted
  one another with the mother to die manfully, saying thus,

  6 Yahuah (God) looketh upon us, and in truth has comfort in us, as
  Moses in his song, which witnessed to their faces, declared, saying,
  And he shall be comforted in his servants. 7 So when the first was
  dead after this manner, they brought the second to make him a mocking
  stock: and when they had pulled off the skin of his head with the
  hair, they asked him, Will you eat, before you be punished throughout
  every member of your body? 8 But he answered in his own language, and
  said, No. Wherefore he also received the next torment in order, as the
  former did. 9 And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You like a
  fury takest us out of this present life, but the King of the world
  shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, to everlasting life. 10
  After him was the third made a mocking stock: and when he was
  required, he put out his tongue, and that right soon, holding forth
  his hands manfully.

  11 And said courageously, These I had from heaven; and for his laws I
  despise them; and from him I hope to receive them again. 12 Insomuch
  that the king, and they that were with him, marvelled at the young
  man’s courage, for that he nothing regarded the pains. 13 Now when
  this man was dead also, they tormented and mangled the fourth in like
  manner. 14 So when he was ready to die he said thus, It is good, being
  put to death by men, to look for hope from Yahuah (God) to be raised
  up again by him: as for you, you shall have no resurrection to life.
  15 Afterward they brought the fifth also, and mangled him.

  16 Then looked he to the king, and said, You have power over men, you
  are corruptible, you do what you will; yet think not that our nation
  is forsaken of Yahuah (God); 17 But abide a while, and behold his
  great power, how he will torment you and your seed. 18 After him also
  they brought the sixth, who being ready to die said, Be not deceived
  without cause: for we suffer these things for ourselves, having sinned
  against our Elohim (God): therefore marvellous things are done to us.
  19 But think not you, that takest in hand to strive against Yahuah
  (God), that you shall escape unpunished. 20 But the mother was
  marvellous above all, and worthy of honourable memory: for when she
  saw her seven sons slain within the space of one day, she bare it with
  a good courage, because of the hope that she had in Yahuah (God).

  21 Yea, she exhorted every one of them in her own language, filled
  with courageous spirits; and stirring up her womanish thoughts with a
  manly stomach, she said to them, 22 I cannot tell how you came into my
  womb: for I neither gave you breath nor life, neither was it I that
  formed the members of every one of you; 23 But doubtless the Creator
  of the world, who formed the generation of man, and found out the
  beginning of all things, will also of his own mercy give you breath
  and life again, as you now regard not your own selves for his laws’
  sake. 24 Now Antiochus, thinking himself despised, and suspecting it
  to be a reproachful speech, while the youngest was yet alive, did not
  only exhort him by words, but also assured him with oaths, that he
  would make him both a rich and a happy man, if he would turn from the
  laws of his fathers; and that also he would take him for his friend,
  and trust him with affairs. 25 But when the young man would in no case
  hearken to him, the king called his mother, and exhorted her that she
  would counsel the young man to save his life.

  26 And when he had exhorted her with many words, she promised him that
  she would counsel her son. 27 But she bowing herself toward him,
  laughing the cruel tyrant to scorn, spoke in her country language on
  this manner; O my son, have pity upon me that bare you nine months in
  my womb, and gave you suck three years, and nourished you, and brought
  you up to this age, and endured the troubles of education. 28 I
  beseech you, my son, look upon the heaven and the earth, and all that
  is in it, and consider that Yahuah (God) made them of things that were
  not; and so was mankind made likewise. 29 Fear not this tormentor,
  but, being worthy of your brothers, take your death that I may receive
  you again in mercy with your brothers. 30 Whiles she was yet speaking
  these words, the young man said, Whom wait you for? I will not obey
  the king’s commandment: but I will obey the commandment of the law
  that was given to our fathers by Moses.

  31 And you, that have been the author of all mischief against the
  Hebrews, shall not escape the hands of Yahuah (God). 32 For we suffer
  because of our sins. 33 And though the living Yahuah (God) be angry
  with us a little while for our chastening and correction, yet shall he
  be at one again with his servants. 34 But you, O godless man, and of
  all other most wicked, be not lifted up without a cause, nor puffed up
  with uncertain hopes, lifting up your hand against the servants of
  Yahuah (God): 35 For you have not yet escaped the judgment of Almighty
  Yahuah (God), who seeth all things.

  36 For our brothers, who now have suffered a short pain, are dead
  under the covenant of Yahuah (God) of everlasting life: but you,
  through the judgment of Yahuah (God), shall receive just punishment
  for your pride. 37 But I, as my brothers, offer up my body and life
  for the laws of our fathers, beseeching Yahuah (God) that he would
  speedily be merciful to our nation; and that you by torments and
  plagues may confess, that he alone is Yahuah (God); 38 And that in me
  and my brothers the wrath of the Almighty, which is justly brought
  upon our nation, may cease. 39 Then the king being in a rage, handed
  him worse than all the rest, and took it grievously that he was
  mocked. 40 So this man died undefiled, and put his whole trust in
  Yahuah (God).

  41 Last of all after the sons the mother died. 42 Let this be enough
  now to have spoken concerning the idolatrous feasts, and the extreme
  tortures.

⸻

Commentary

Chapter 7 is the apocryphal text the writer of Hebrews directly cites in
Hebrews 11:35. A mother and her seven sons are arrested and tortured one
by one for refusing to eat swine's flesh. Each son testifies before he
dies. The mother encourages each son in turn and is killed last. The
chapter is one of the most spiritually concentrated narratives in the
entire apocryphal corpus and is the theological climax of 2 Maccabees.

Read this chapter slowly. Read the commentary that follows slowly. The
chapter is the framework's most concentrated second-temple anchor for
the bodily-resurrection theology, the bloodline-remnant theology, and
the covenant-faithfulness-unto-death witness that the apostolic writings
build on. There is no other place in the Apocrypha where these threads
converge with the force they converge here.

The first son (verses 1–6) refuses to eat. He is brought to the king.
Antiochus orders the heating of pans and cauldrons. The first son speaks
for himself and his brothers: We are ready to die, rather than to
transgress the laws of our fathers. His tongue is cut out, his scalp is
removed, his hands and feet are chopped off, he is fried in a great pan,
and he dies.

The second son (verses 7–9) is brought next. As he is being tortured, he
says to Antiochus: You like a fury take us out of this present life, but
the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, to
everlasting life. The first explicit second-temple statement of the
resurrection of the righteous in this chapter.

The third son (verses 10–12) puts forth his hands and tongue to be cut
off, saying: These I had from heaven; and for his laws I despise them;
and from him I hope to receive them again. The second
resurrection-statement: he expects his body to be raised.

The fourth son (verses 13–14) speaks just before dying: It is good,
being put to death by men, to look for hope from Elohim (God) to be raised up
again by him: as for you, you shall have no resurrection to life. The
contrast between the resurrection of the righteous and the absence of
resurrection for Antiochus is now explicit.

The fifth son (verses 15–17) prophesies the future judgment of Antiochus
and his seed. The sixth son (verses 18–19) names the persecution as a
temporary correction by Yahuah (God) of His own people, not as
Antiochus's victory. The seventh son — the youngest — is offered great
wealth and honor by the king if he will renounce the Torah. The mother
is allowed to speak privately to him in Hebrew. She encourages him to
keep the covenant. He refuses Antiochus's offer, gives a long speech
about the resurrection and the righteousness of Yahuah (God), and is
tortured to death more cruelly than the rest (verse 39). The mother is
killed last.

This chapter is the framework's most concentrated second-temple witness
to the resurrection theology that the New Testament builds on, and it is
the chapter the writer of Hebrews assumed his readers knew when he wrote
that some were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might
obtain a better resurrection (Hebrews 11:35). Several things matter for
the awakening reader.

First, the resurrection theology in 2 Maccabees 7 is unambiguous and
bodily. Read the third son's words again: These I had from heaven; and
for his laws I despise them; and from him I hope to receive them again.
He is speaking of his hands and his tongue. He had them from heaven; he
is letting them be cut off for the sake of Yahuah (God)'s laws; he
expects to receive them back at the resurrection. This is not a
spiritualized after-life. This is not a soul-going-to-heaven theology.
This is the bodily resurrection — the same hands restored to the same
arms, the same tongue restored to the same mouth — at the appointed
time. The framework of this Series, which holds the appointed reign on
the earth with the refined remnant, the bodily resurrection of the
righteous, and the new heavens and new earth as the destination of the
long restoration, finds in 2 Maccabees 7:11 the second-temple voice
articulating exactly that bodily-resurrection theology. The hands will
be raised. The tongue will be raised. The whole body will be raised. The
popular Christian "going to heaven when you die, forever, end of story"
reading erases this. The Apocrypha will not.

The fourth son's contrast is the framework's contrast between the
righteous and the wicked in eschatological terms: It is good, being put
to death by men, to look for hope from Elohim (God) to be raised up again by him:
as for you, you shall have no resurrection to life. The righteous are
raised to life. The wicked face the judgment from which there is no
resurrection to life. The framework's reading of the wheat-and-tares
burning, the appointed judgment of the tares before the wheat harvest,
the verdict of Revelation 11:18 — all of it is articulated in the fourth
son's dying words. The Apocrypha was not innovating this theology. The
apostles were not innovating it. The Pharisaic resurrection theology
that Yahusha defended against the Sadducees in Matthew 22 was the same
theology these brothers articulated under torture in 167 BCE. One stream
of revelation, one body of teaching, one expected destination: the
bodily resurrection at the appointed time, the appointed reign on the
earth, the new heavens and new earth as the closing panel.

Second, the bloodline-remnant thread runs through this chapter as
forcefully as the resurrection thread. Read what each brother and what
the mother says:

The first brother: We are ready to die, rather than to transgress the
laws of our fathers. The laws of our fathers. The covenant lineage. The
inheritance.

The second brother: You like a fury take us out of this present life,
but the King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws,
to everlasting life. The brothers know whose laws they are dying for.
They know whose people they are. They know the Father who raised up
their fathers will raise them up.

The mother to her sons (verses 21–23): I cannot tell how you came into
my womb: for I neither gave you breath nor life, neither was it I that
formed the members of every one of you; but doubtless the Creator of the
world, who formed the generation of man, and found out the beginning of
all things, will also of his own mercy give you breath and life again,
as you now regard not your own selves for his laws' sake. The Creator
who formed the generation of man — the seed in the womb, the formation
of the body, the bringing of breath into the lineage — will also raise
the body up. The mother is articulating the framework's specific
bloodline-and-resurrection theology. The seed runs through the womb. The
covenant runs through the seed. The Creator who formed the seed is the
same who will raise the seed at the appointed time. The framework reads
this as the second-temple voice articulating the bloodline-remnant claim
in its most concentrated form: the children are seed of Yahuah (God)'s
appointing, the laws are the laws of their fathers, the resurrection
will gather the seed by the same Father who formed it.

The seventh brother's speech (verses 30–38) is the chapter's theological
climax. He names that the persecution is Yahuah (God)'s correction of
His own people for their sins, that Yahuah (God) will yet have mercy on
the people, that Antiochus will face Yahuah (God)'s judgment, and that
he himself yields his body and life for the laws of our fathers,
beseeching Elohim (God) that he would speedily be merciful to our nation. The
framework reads this as the second-temple anchor for what the framework
holds: the discipline of the covenant people is real, the discipline is
for their own correction, the mercy is appointed, the gathering is
appointed, and the awakening remnant who walks in covenant faithfulness
now is participating in what the second-temple martyrs walked in then.

Third, the mother's role is unique in the apocryphal corpus. She watches
her seven sons die one by one. She encourages each. She is killed last.
The framework of this Series, which honors the second-temple women whose
witness in extremity preserved the covenant family — the mother of 2
Maccabees 7 alongside Hannah, Esther, Judith, and the women of the
Gospel narratives — finds in this mother the unnamed witness who made
the entire chapter possible. The text does not give her name. The text
gives her witness. The framework's principle: the names of the witnesses
may be lost; the witness itself is preserved.

The mother's speech (verses 22–23, 27–29) is the framework's most
concentrated second-temple voice on the covenant value of the children
of the seed. She speaks to her sons in Hebrew (the king allowed her to
address them privately, expecting she would urge them to compromise;
instead she encouraged them to die faithfully). She tells the youngest:
fear not this tormentor, but, being worthy of your brethren, take your
death, that I may receive you again in mercy with your brethren. The
mother is appealing not to political success, not to social standing,
not to the preservation of the family line in this age — she is
appealing to the appointed reunion in the resurrection. She would rather
see her sons die faithfully and be received again at the resurrection
than have them live faithlessly. The framework reads this as the
second-temple voice on the right ordering of covenant priorities: the
appointed life is greater than the present life; faithfulness in this
age is held in the appointed reunion in the next.

Fourth, the framework's principle of the cost of covenant faithfulness
is illustrated here in its most concentrated form. The brothers were not
killed for political rebellion. They were killed for refusing to eat
swine's flesh. The covenant standard — the Torah's food laws — was the
standard they refused to break. The framework of this Series, which
holds that the Torah is the standard and that the awakening reader's
faithfulness to the Torah is the basis of his or her witness, finds in 2
Maccabees 7 the second-temple historical illustration that the Torah's
commandments are worth dying for. The framework's caveat: the awakening
reader is not asked to seek martyrdom. The framework holds that the cost
of covenant faithfulness in the modern context is rarely physical death;
it is more often social isolation, financial cost, vocational
consequence, and family rupture. The principle is the same: the standard
is the standard, and the awakening reader keeps it whatever the cost.

Fifth, the chapter is about Yahudim (Jews) under persecution — and the
framework's reading of the contemporary Yahudim must be named here. The
brothers and their mother were of the southern house, the actual
paternal lineage that became the Yahudim of the modern world. They were
not a spiritual category. They were Yahudah's seed, persecuted under a
Greek tyrant, refusing to break the Torah even at the cost of their
lives. The framework holds that the contemporary Yahudim (Jews) are the
same paternal lineage — Category 1 of the Three Categories — preserved
across centuries of dispersion under Greek, Roman, Christian, and
Islamic empires. Three common positions about the Yahudim are wrong, and
2 Maccabees 7 is the right chapter at which to name them.

Yahudi (Jew) hatred is wrong. It is scripturally indefensible,
spiritually dangerous, and a tool of the enemy used to misdirect people
away from the truth. The Maccabean martyrs are the answer to anyone who
would slander the seed of Yahudah as cursed or rejected. The Father
preserved them in extremity. He preserved them at Antiochus's hand. He
has preserved them since.

Zionism as a theological program is wrong. The political construction of
the modern state is not the prophetic restoration of scattered Yashar'el
(Israel). The prophets named the gathering of all twelve tribes (Hosea
1, Ezekiel 37) under one Shepherd, the Messiah; they did not name a
political state established by Western powers and run on a secular
charter. Zionism takes the prophetic framework and bolts it to a
political program; the framework rejects the bolt without rejecting the
lineage.

Saying "those aren't real Yahudim (Jews)" is wrong. It is scripturally
ignorant. The tribal and covenant lineage of the Yahudim is real.
Denying it reveals ignorance of the scripture. The Maccabean martyrs in
this chapter are the real lineage; their seed continued; their seed
continues; the Yahudim of the modern world are the descendants of the
same tribe of Yahudah preserved through all the empires.

The harsh New Testament language toward specific groups — your father
the devil (John 8:44), wicked generation (Matthew 12:39, 16:4), brood of
vipers (Matthew 23:33) — was not a rejection of the Yahudim as a whole.
It was the identification of sons of Belial operating within the
covenant community, identifiable not by their bloodline (they had it)
but by their works. Eli's sons in 1 Samuel 2 were sons of Belial inside
the priestly line. The corrupt elders of Susanna were sons of Belial
inside the Babylonian exile community. The high priest Menelaus in 2
Maccabees 4 — who took the priesthood by the bribe of Antiochus and was
the cause of the persecution — was a son of Belial inside the
high-priestly office. The pattern is consistent across the canon: sons
of Belial operate from inside, and the harsh language identifies them,
not the whole house. Nothing in the New Testament is new. Every concept
roots in the Torah and the prophets.

The contemporary awakening reader, walking out of inherited
Christianity, must be retrained out of the inherited reflex of
conflating the Yahudim with the corrupt office-holders the Gospels
confronted. The Yahudim are kin. They are the southern house of the same
covenant the awakening remnant is being gathered back into. They will be
gathered, alongside the scattered seed of the northern house, under the
one Shepherd at the appointed time (Ezekiel 37:21–22). The framework
holds the line: Yahudi (Jew) hatred is wrong, Zionism as theological
program is wrong, denial of Yahudi (Jewish) lineage is wrong. The mother
of the seven sons is the witness. Her sons died for the laws of their
fathers. Their seed continued. Their seed continues.

Sixth, take this back to Hebrews 11:35 and read with full attention.
Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were
tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better
resurrection. The two clauses are about two different groups. The first
clause refers to women like the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17) and the
Shunammite (2 Kings 4) whose sons were resurrected by the prophets in
their lifetimes. The second clause — others were tortured, not accepting
deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection — refers
directly to 2 Maccabees 7.

Read the Greek of Hebrews 11:35 carefully. The word translated tortured
is etumpanisthēsan — they were broken on the wheel, the tympanon, an
instrument of torture. The word is rare in the New Testament. It is the
technical word for the kind of torture 2 Maccabees 7 describes — frying
in pans, scalping, dismembering. The Hebrews writer is not using generic
"they suffered" language; he is using the specific Greek vocabulary the
second-temple martyrological tradition used for what Antiochus did to
the brothers. The reference is exact.

And the phrase better resurrection — kreittonos anastaseōs — is the
apostolic articulation of what the third son of 2 Maccabees 7:11 said
when he held out his hands and tongue to be cut: from him I hope to
receive them again. The third son hoped for the resurrection of the
body. The Hebrews writer says the brothers were after the better
resurrection — better than what? Better than the temporary deliverance
Antiochus offered them, better than the deliverance the widow of
Zarephath's son received (which was a return to mortal life that would
end again in death), better than any restoration short of the appointed
bodily resurrection of the righteous at the close of the age. The
brothers refused mortal deliverance to obtain immortal resurrection. The
Hebrews writer names that exchange precisely.

Hebrews 11:36–38 continues with details that match the broader 2
Maccabees martyrology: And others had trial of cruel mockings and
scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment: they were stoned,
they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they
wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted,
tormented; (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts,
and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth. The "wandered in
deserts and mountains and caves" matches 2 Maccabees 5:27 — Judas
Maccabeus and his nine companions withdrawing into the wilderness,
eating wild plants, refusing the pollution. The "scourgings" matches
Eleazar's torture in 2 Maccabees 6. The "slain with the sword" matches
the broader Maccabean persecution. The Hebrews 11 catalogue of faith is,
in significant part, a 2 Maccabees catalogue. The writer of Hebrews has
read these books and assumes his readers have too.

The brothers were offered deliverance by Antiochus (the king explicitly
offered the youngest wealth and honor if he would renounce the Torah).
They did not accept deliverance. They wanted the better resurrection.
The Hebrews writer cites this chapter by name, in a New Testament book
that is part of the canonical scripture, and assumes his readers know
the chapter intimately. The reader who has not read 2 Maccabees 7 has
not heard half of what Hebrews 11:35 was saying. The framework's reading
of the apostolic writings as continuous with the second-temple wisdom
and martyrological tradition is not a stretch. The Hebrews writer is
doing it on the page.

Cross-references: Matthew 22:23–33; Mark 12:18–27; Luke 20:27–40; Acts
23:6–10; 1 Corinthians 15:1–58; Hebrews 11:32–40; 2 Timothy 4:6–8;
Revelation 6:9–11; Revelation 20:4–6; 1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:18–37.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 8

  1 Then Judas Maccabeus, and they that were with him, went privily into
  the towns, and called their kinsfolks together, and took to them all
  such as continued in the Yahudim (Jews)’ religion, and assembled about
  six thousand men. 2 And they called upon Yahuah (God), that he would
  look upon the people that was trodden down of all; and also pity the
  temple profaned of ungodly men; 3 And that he would have compassion
  upon the city, sore defaced, and ready to be made even with the
  ground; and hear the blood that cried to him, 4 And remember the
  wicked slaughter of harmless infants, and the blasphemies committed
  against his name; and that he would shew his hatred against the
  wicked. 5 Now when Maccabeus had his company about him, he could not
  be withstood by the heathen: for the wrath of Yahuah (God) was turned
  into mercy.

  6 Therefore he came at unawares, and burnt up towns and cities, and
  got into his hands the most commodious places, and overcame and put to
  flight no small number of his enemies. 7 But specially took he
  advantage of the night for such privy attempts, insomuch that the
  fruit of his holiness was spread every where. 8 So when Philip saw
  that this man increased by little and little, and that things
  prospered with him still more and more, he wrote to Ptolemeus, the
  governor of Celosyria and Phenice, to yield more aid to the king’s
  affairs. 9 Then forthwith choosing Nicanor the son of Patroclus, one
  of his special friends, he sent him with no fewer than twenty thousand
  of all nations under him, to root out the whole generation of the
  Yahudim (Jews); and with him he joined also Gorgias a captain, who in
  matters of war had great experience. 10 So Nicanor undertook to make
  so much money of the captive Yahudim (Jews), as should defray the
  tribute of two thousand talents, which the king was to pay to the
  Romans.

  11 Wherefore immediately he sent to the cities upon the sea coast,
  proclaiming a sale of the captive Yahudim (Jews), and promising that
  they should have fourscore and ten bodies for one talent, not
  expecting the vengeance that was to follow upon him from the Almighty
  Yahuah (God). 12 Now when word was brought to Judas of Nicanor’s
  coming, and he had imparted to those that were with him that the army
  was at hand, 13 They that were fearful, and distrusted the justice of
  Yahuah (God), fled, and conveyed themselves away. 14 Others sold all
  that they had left, and withal besought Yahuah (God) to deliver them,
  sold by the wicked Nicanor before they met together: 15 And if not for
  their own sakes, yet for the covenants he had made with their fathers,
  and for his holy and glorious name’s sake, by which they were called.

  16 So Maccabeus called his men together to the number of six thousand,
  and exhorted them not to be stricken with terror of the enemy, nor to
  fear the great multitude of the heathen, who came wrongly against
  them; but to fight manfully, 17 And to set before their eyes the
  injury that they had unjustly done to the holy place, and the cruel
  handling of the city, of which they made a mockery, and also the
  taking away of the government of their forefathers: 18 For they, said
  he, trust in their weapons and boldness; but our confidence is in the
  Almighty who at a beck can cast down both them that come against us,
  and also all the world. 19 Moreover, he recounted to them what helps
  their forefathers had found, and how they were delivered, when under
  Sennacherib an hundred fourscore and five thousand perished. 20 And he
  told them of the battle that they had in Babylon with the Galatians,
  how they came but eight thousand in all to the business, with four
  thousand Macedonians, and that the Macedonians being perplexed, the
  eight thousand destroyed an hundred and twenty thousand because of the
  help that they had from heaven, and so received a great booty.

  21 Thus when he had made them bold with these words, and ready to die
  for the law and the country, he divided his army into four parts; 22
  And joined with himself his own brothers, leaders of each band, to wit
  Simon, and Joseph, and Jonathan, giving each one fifteen hundred men.
  23 Also he appointed Eleazar to read the holy book: and when he had
  given them this watchword, The help of Yahuah (God); himself leading
  the first band, 24 And by the help of the Almighty they slew above
  nine thousand of their enemies, and wounded and maimed the most part
  of Nicanor’s host, and so put all to flight; 25 And took their money
  that came to buy them, and pursued them far: but lacking time they
  returned:

  26 For it was the day before the sabbath, and therefore they would no
  longer pursue them. 27 So when they had gathered their armour
  together, and spoiled their enemies, they occupied themselves about
  the sabbath, yielding exceeding praise and thanks to Yahuah (God), who
  had preserved them to that day, which was the beginning of mercy
  distilling upon them. 28 And after the sabbath, when they had given
  part of the spoils to the maimed, and the widows, and orphans, the
  residue they divided among themselves and their servants. 29 When this
  was done, and they had made a common supplication, they besought the
  merciful Yahuah (God) to be reconciled with his servants for ever. 30
  Moreover of those that were with Timotheus and Bacchides, who fought
  against them, they slew above twenty thousand, and very easily got
  high and strong holds, and divided among themselves many spoils more,
  and made the maimed, orphans, widows, yes, and the aged also, equal in
  spoils with themselves.

  31 And when they had gathered their armour together, they laid them up
  all carefully in convenient places, and the remnant of the spoils they
  brought to Jerusalem. 32 They slew also Philarches, that wicked
  person, who was with Timotheus, and had annoyed the Yahudim (Jews)
  many ways. 33 Furthermore at such time as they kept the feast for the
  victory in their country they burnt Callisthenes, that had set fire
  upon the holy gates, who had fled into a little house; and so he
  received a reward meet for his wickedness. 34 As for that most
  ungracious Nicanor, who had brought a thousand merchants to buy the
  Yahudim (Jews), 35 He was through the help of Yahuah (God) brought
  down by them, of whom he made least account; and putting off his
  glorious apparel, and discharging his company, he came like a fugitive
  servant through the midland to Antioch having very great dishonour,
  for that his host was destroyed.

  36 Thus he, that took upon him to make good to the Romans their
  tribute by means of captives in Jerusalem, told abroad, that the
  Yahudim (Jews) had Yahuah (God) to fight for them, and therefore they
  could not be hurt, because they followed the laws that he gave them.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter narrates the rise of Judas Maccabeus and the early military
victories of the Maccabean revolt. Judas gathers six thousand men. He
defeats Nicanor at the battle of Emmaus. He distributes the spoils,
paying particular attention to the widows and orphans of the persecuted
(verses 28–30).

Two things matter.

First, the chapter's portrait of Judas Maccabeus emphasizes his prayer
life and his trust in Yahuah (God) before each engagement. Verses 18–20
record his pre-battle exhortation: But put your trust in the Almighty
Elohim (God), who is able with a beck to cast down both them that come against
us, and also all the world.

The canonical anchor for the trust-before-battle posture is consistent.
Psalm 20:7 — Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will
remember the name of Yahuah (God) our Elohim (God). Psalm 33:16–18 already cited
under Judith 9. 2 Chronicles 20:12, Jehoshaphat: We have no might
against this great company that comes against us; neither know we what
to do: but our eyes are upon you. 1 Samuel 17:47, David: the battle is
Yahuah (God)'s, and he will give you into our hands. Proverbs 21:31: The
horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of Yahuah
(God). Hebrews 11:32–34 brings the pattern into apostolic catalogue:
Gideon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthah; of David also, and
Samuel, and of the prophets... waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight
the armies of the aliens.

The framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening reader's
preparation for any covenant struggle is rooted in trust in Yahuah (God)
rather than in calculation of resources, finds in Judas's exhortation
the second-temple model.

Second, the distribution of spoils to widows and orphans (verses 28–30)
is the second-temple application of the Torah's care for the vulnerable.

The canonical anchor for the care-of-vulnerable pattern is concrete.
Deuteronomy 24:17–22: You shall not pervert the judgment of the
stranger, nor of the fatherless; nor take a widow's raiment to pledge...
When you cut down your harvest in your field, and have forgot a sheaf in
the field, you shall not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the
stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow. Deuteronomy 26:12: When
you have made an end of tithing all the tithes of your increase the
third year... and have given it unto the Levite, the stranger, the
fatherless, and the widow, that they may eat within your gates, and be
filled. Isaiah 1:17: Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the
oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. James 1:27 in
apostolic vocabulary: Pure religion and undefiled before Elohim (God) and the
Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction,
and to keep himself unspotted from the world. Psalm 68:5: A father of
the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is Elohim (God) in his holy
habitation.

Even in the middle of military campaigns, the Maccabean leadership
remembered the Torah's commandments concerning widows and orphans. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the covenant community's care
for the vulnerable is one of the marks of its faithfulness, finds in 2
Maccabees 8 the second-temple example.

Cross-references: Deuteronomy 24:17–22; Deuteronomy 26:12–15; Psalm
68:5; James 1:27; 1 Maccabees 4:1–25; 2 Chronicles 14:9–15; Ephesians
6:10–18.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 9

  1 About that time came Antiochus with dishonour out of the country of
  Persia 2 For he had entered the city called Persepolis, and went about
  to rob the temple, and to hold the city; whereupon the multitude
  running to defend themselves with their weapons put them to flight;
  and so it happened, that Antiochus being put to flight of the
  inhabitants returned with shame. 3 Now when he came to Ecbatane, news
  was brought him what had happened to Nicanor and Timotheus. 4 Then
  swelling with anger. he thought to avenge upon the Yahudim (Jews) the
  disgrace done to him by those that made him flee. Therefore commanded
  he his chariotman to drive without ceasing, and to dispatch the
  journey, the judgment of Yahuah (God) now following him. For he had
  spoken proudly in this sort, That he would come to Jerusalem and make
  it a common burying place of the Yahudim (Jews). 5 But Yahuah (God)
  Almighty, Yahuah (God) of Yashar'el (Israel), struck him with an
  incurable and invisible plague: or as soon as he had spoken these
  words, a pain of the bowels that was remediless came upon him, and
  sore torments of the inner parts;

  6 And that most justly: for he had tormented other men’s bowels with
  many and strange torments. 7 Howbeit he nothing at all ceased from his
  bragging, but still was filled with pride, breathing out fire in his
  rage against the Yahudim (Jews), and commanding to haste the journey:
  but it came to pass that he fell down from his chariot, carried
  violently; so that having a sore fall, all the members of his body
  were much pained. 8 And thus he that a little afore thought he might
  command the waves of the sea, (so proud was he beyond the condition of
  man) and weigh the high mountains in a balance, was now cast on the
  ground, and carried in an horselitter, shewing forth to all the
  manifest power of Yahuah (God). 9 So that the worms rose up out of the
  body of this wicked man, and whiles he lived in sorrow and pain, his
  flesh fell away, and the filthiness of his smell was noisome to all
  his army. 10 And the man, that thought a little afore he could reach
  to the stars of heaven, no man could endure to carry for his
  intolerable stink.

  11 Here therefore, being plagued, he began to leave off his great
  pride, and to come to the knowledge of himself by the scourge of
  Yahuah (God), his pain increasing every moment. 12 And when he himself
  could not abide his own smell, he said these words, It is meet to be
  subject to Yahuah (God), and that a man that is mortal should not
  proudly think of himself if he were Yahuah (God). 13 This wicked
  person vowed also to Yahuah (God), who now no more would have mercy
  upon him, saying thus, 14 That the holy city (to the which he was
  going in haste to lay it even with the ground, and to make it a common
  buryingplace,) he would set at liberty: 15 And as touching the Yahudim
  (Jews), whom he had judged not worthy so much as to be buried, but to
  be cast out with their children to be devoured of the fowls and wild
  beasts, he would make them all equals to the citizens of Athens:

  16 And the holy temple, which before he had spoiled, he would garnish
  with goodly gifts, and restore all the holy vessels with many more,
  and out of his own revenue defray the charges belonging to the
  sacrifices: 17 Yea, and that also he would become a Yahudi (Jew)
  himself, and go through all the world that was inhabited, and declare
  the power of Yahuah (God). 18 But for all this his pains would not
  cease: for the just judgment of Yahuah (God) was come upon him:
  therefore despairing of his health, he wrote to the Yahudim (Jews) the
  letter underwritten, containing the form of a supplication, after this
  manner: 19 Antiochus, king and governor, to the good Yahudim (Jews)
  his citizens wisheth much joy, health, and prosperity: 20 If you and
  your children fare well, and your affairs be to your contentment, I
  give very great thanks to Yahuah (God), having my hope in heaven.

  21 As for me, I was weak, or else I would have remembered kindly your
  honour and good will returning out of Persia, and being taken with a
  grievous disease, I thought it necessary to care for the common safety
  of all: 22 Not distrusting my health, but having great hope to escape
  this sickness. 23 But considering that even my father, at what time he
  led an army into the high countries. appointed a successor, 24 To the
  end that, if any thing fell out contrary to expectation, or if any
  tidings were brought that were grievous, they of the land, knowing to
  whom the state was left, might not be troubled: 25 Again, considering
  how that the princes that are borderers and neighbours to my kingdom
  wait for opportunities, and expect what shall be the event. I have
  appointed my son Antiochus king, whom I often committed and commended
  to many of you, when I went up into the high provinces; to whom I have
  written as followeth:

  26 Therefore I pray and request you to remember the benefits that I
  have done to you generally, and in special, and that every man will be
  still faithful to me and my son. 27 For I am persuaded that he
  understanding my mind will favourably and graciously yield to your
  desires. 28 Thus the murderer and blasphemer having suffered most
  grievously, as he entreated other men, so died he a miserable death in
  a strange country in the mountains. 29 And Philip, that was brought up
  with him, carried away his body, who also fearing the son of Antiochus
  went into Egypt to Ptolemeus Philometor.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter narrates the death of Antiochus IV in Persia. Stricken with
a horrible disease — worms eating his flesh, an unbearable stench — he
confesses on his deathbed that the calamity is the consequence of his
desecration of the temple. He vows to make Jerusalem free, to make the
Yahudim (Jews) equal to the Athenians, and to adorn the temple with
gifts. He dies before any of these promises can be fulfilled.

Three things matter.

First, the chapter's portrait of Antiochus's deathbed is unflinching
about the physical horror (verses 5–10). The body that had desecrated
the temple becomes itself an object of decay. The framework of this
Series, which holds that the imperial powers that have desecrated the
appointed dwelling-place of Yahuah (God) face consequences in the body
as well as in the soul, finds in 2 Maccabees 9 the second-temple
narrative version of that judgment. The text does not gloat. The text
records.

Second, Antiochus's deathbed confession (verses 11–17) is theologically
remarkable. He acknowledges the Elohim (God) of the Yahudim (Jews). He vows
reparations. He claims he will become a Yahudi (Jew). The text comments
that the wretch... promised to do the things that he had done with
mischief (verse 8) — that is, to give to the Yahudim (Jews) the same
favors he had taken away. The framework of this Series, on the question
of deathbed confessions by those who had attacked the covenant
community, holds that Yahuah (God) alone judges the heart. The text does
not declare Antiochus saved or condemned by his deathbed words. The text
records the confession and notes that the vows were never fulfilled
because death intervened. The framework reads it the same way: the
confession is recorded; the judgment belongs to Yahuah (God).

Third, Antiochus's letter to the Yahudim (Jews) (verses 19–27), which
the chapter records as written shortly before his death, is the
second-temple example of imperial reversal under judgment. The empire
that had attempted to abolish the covenant community is, in its dying
king's words, asking for reconciliation. The framework's principle: the
imperial powers that have attacked the covenant community have shorter
time-horizons than they assume, and their attempts at reconciliation
often come too late.

Cross-references: Acts 12:20–23; Daniel 5:1–31; Isaiah 14:3–23; Ezekiel
28:1–19; 1 Maccabees 6:1–17; Proverbs 15:25; Proverbs 16:18; James 4:6.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 10

  1 Now Maccabeus and his company, Yahuah (God) guiding them, recovered
  the temple and the city: 2 But the altars which the heathen had built
  in the open street, and also the chapels, they pulled down. 3 And
  having cleansed the temple they made another altar, and striking
  stones they took fire out of them, and offered a sacrifice after two
  years, and set forth incense, and lights, and shewbread. 4 When that
  was done, they fell flat down, and besought Yahuah (God) that they
  might come no more into such troubles; but if they sinned any more
  against him, that he himself would chasten them with mercy, and that
  they might not be delivered to the blasphemous and barbarous nations.
  5 Now upon the same day that the strangers profaned the temple, on the
  very same day it was cleansed again, even the five and twentieth day
  of the same month, which is Casleu.

  6 And they kept the eight days with gladness, as in the feast of the
  tabernacles, remembering that not long afore they had held the feast
  of the tabernacles, when as they wandered in the mountains and dens
  like beasts. 7 Therefore they bare branches, and fair boughs, and
  palms also, and sang psalms to him that had given them good success in
  cleansing his place. 8 They ordained also by a common statute and
  decree, That every year those days should be kept of the whole nation
  of the Yahudim (Jews). 9 And this was the end of Antiochus, called
  Epiphanes. 10 Now will we declare the acts of Antiochus Eupator, who
  was the son of this wicked man, gathering briefly the calamities of
  the wars.

  11 So when he was come to the crown, he set one Lysias over the
  affairs of his realm, and appointed him his chief governor of
  Celosyria and Phenice. 12 For Ptolemeus, that was called Macron,
  choosing rather to do justice to the Yahudim (Jews) for the wrong that
  had been done to them, endeavoured to continue peace with them. 13
  Whereupon being accused of the king’s friends before Eupator, and
  called traitor at every word because he had left Cyprus, that
  Philometor had committed to him, and departed to Antiochus Epiphanes,
  and seeing that he was in no honourable place, he was so discouraged,
  that he poisoned himself and died. 14 But when Gorgias was governor of
  the holds, he hired soldiers, and nourished war continually with the
  Yahudim (Jews): 15 And therewithall the Idumeans, having gotten into
  their hands the most commodious holds, kept the Yahudim (Jews)
  occupied, and receiving those that were banished from Jerusalem, they
  went about to nourish war.

  16 Then they that were with Maccabeus made supplication, and besought
  Yahuah (God) that he would be their helper; and so they ran with
  violence upon the strong holds of the Idumeans, 17 And assaulting them
  strongly, they won the holds, and kept off all that fought upon the
  wall, and slew all that fell into their hands, and killed no fewer
  than twenty thousand. 18 And because certain, who were no less than
  nine thousand, were fled together into two very strong castles, having
  all manner of things convenient to sustain the siege, 19 Maccabeus
  left Simon and Joseph, and Zaccheus also, and them that were with him,
  who were enough to besiege them, and departed himself to those places
  which more needed his help. 20 Now they that were with Simon, being
  led with covetousness, were persuaded for money through certain of
  those that were in the castle, and took seventy thousand drachms, and
  let some of them escape.

  21 But when it was told Maccabeus what was done, he called the
  governors of the people together, and accused those men, that they had
  sold their brothers for money, and set their enemies free to fight
  against them. 22 So he slew those that were found traitors, and
  immediately took the two castles. 23 And having good success with his
  weapons in all things he took in hand, he slew in the two holds more
  than twenty thousand. 24 Now Timotheus, whom the Yahudim (Jews) had
  overcome before, when he had gathered a great multitude of foreign
  forces, and horses out of Asia not a few, came as though he would take
  Jewry by force of arms. 25 But when he drew near, they that were with
  Maccabeus turned themselves to pray to Yahuah (God), and sprinkled
  earth upon their heads, and girded their loins with sackcloth,

  26 And fell down at the foot of the altar, and besought him to be
  merciful to them, and to be an enemy to their enemies, and an
  adversary to their adversaries, as the law declareth. 27 So after the
  prayer they took their weapons, and went on further from the city: and
  when they drew near to their enemies, they kept by themselves. 28 Now
  the sun being newly risen, they joined both together; the one part
  having together with their virtue their refuge also to Yahuah (God)
  for a pledge of their success and victory: the other side making their
  rage leader of their battle 29 But when the battle waxed strong, there
  appeared to the enemies from heaven five comely men upon horses, with
  bridles of gold, and two of them led the Yahudim (Jews), 30 And took
  Maccabeus between them, and covered him on every side weapons, and
  kept him safe, but shot arrows and lightnings against the enemies: so
  that being confounded with blindness, and full of trouble, they were
  killed.

  31 And there were slain of footmen twenty thousand and five hundred,
  and six hundred horsemen. 32 As for Timotheus himself, he fled into a
  very strong hold, called Gawra, where Chereas was governor. 33 But
  they that were with Maccabeus laid siege against the fortress
  courageously four days. 34 And they that were within, trusting to the
  strength of the place, blasphemed exceedingly, and uttered wicked
  words. 35 Nevertheless upon the fifth day early twenty young men of
  Maccabeus’ company, inflamed with anger because of the blasphemies,
  assaulted the wall manly, and with a fierce courage killed all that
  they met withal.

  36 Others likewise ascending after them, whiles they were busied with
  them that were within, burnt the towers, and kindling fires burnt the
  blasphemers alive; and others broke open the gates, and, having
  received in the rest of the army, took the city, 37 And killed
  Timotheus, that was hid in a certain pit, and Chereas his brother,
  with Apollophanes. 38 When this was done, they praised Yahuah (God)
  with psalms and thanksgiving, who had done so great things for
  Yashar'el (Israel), and given them the victory.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter records the rededication of the temple (verses 1–8) and the
first campaigns of Judas Maccabeus against the Idumeans (verses 9–38).
The rededication is recounted briefly here (the more detailed account is
in 1 Maccabees 4); the campaigns against the Idumeans illustrate the
broader military situation.

Two things matter.

First, the rededication account (verses 1–8) emphasizes the institution
of the eight-day festival of dedication and links it explicitly to the
festival of Tabernacles. The text records that the people had been
unable to keep Tabernacles during the desecration period and that the
dedication festival was an effort to make up for the missed feast. The
framework of this Series, which holds that Tabernacles is one of the
appointed feasts of Yahuah (God) (Leviticus 23:33–43) and that Hanukkah
is a memorial feast, finds in 2 Maccabees 10:6 a small framework
illustration: the second-temple community recognized that the missed
Tabernacles needed to be honored, and they instituted a memorial feast
that honored both the rededication and the missed appointed feast. The
framework's reading: the appointed feasts of the Torah are the appointed
feasts; memorial feasts can fill in around them; but the appointed
feasts themselves should never be displaced.

Second, the chapter records the death of Timotheus the Idumean commander
(verses 28–38). The narrative emphasizes the prayer of Judas's forces
before battle and the explicit attribution of the victory to Yahuah
(God). The framework of this Series, which holds that the awakening
community's deliverance is Yahuah (God)'s work, finds in the chapter the
proper crediting.

Cross-references: Leviticus 23:33–43; Numbers 29:12–40; John 7:1–10;
John 10:22–23; 2 Chronicles 6:13–7:10; 1 Maccabees 4:36–61.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 11

  1 Not long after this, Lysias the king’s protector and cousin, who
  also managed the affairs, took sore displeasure for the things that
  were done. 2 And when he had gathered about fourscore thousand with
  all the horsemen, he came against the Yahudim (Jews), thinking to make
  the city an habitation of the Gentiles, 3 And to make a gain of the
  temple, as of the other chapels of the heathen, and to set the high
  priesthood to sale every year: 4 Not at all considering the power of
  Yahuah (God) but puffed up with his ten thousands of footmen, and his
  thousands of horsemen, and his fourscore elephants. 5 So he came to
  Judea, and drew near to Bethsura, which was a strong town, but distant
  from Jerusalem about five furlongs, and he laid sore siege to it.

  6 Now when they that were with Maccabeus heard that he besieged the
  holds, they and all the people with lamentation and tears besought
  Yahuah (God) that he would send a good angel to deliver Yashar'el
  (Israel). 7 Then Maccabeus himself first of all took weapons,
  exhorting the other that they would jeopard themselves together with
  him to help their brothers: so they went forth together with a willing
  mind. 8 And as they were at Jerusalem, there appeared before them on
  horseback one in white clothing, shaking his armour of gold. 9 Then
  they praised the merciful Yahuah (God) all together, and took heart,
  insomuch that they were ready not only to fight with men, but with
  most cruel beasts, and to pierce through walls of iron. 10 Thus they
  marched forward in their armour, having an helper from heaven: for
  Yahuah (God) was merciful to them

  11 And giving a charge upon their enemies like lions, they slew eleven
  thousand footmen, and sixteen hundred horsemen, and put all the other
  to flight. 12 Many of them also being wounded escaped naked; and
  Lysias himself fled away shamefully, and so escaped. 13 Who, as he was
  a man of understanding, casting with himself what loss he had had, and
  considering that the Hebrews could not be overcome, because the
  Almighty Yahuah (God) helped them, he sent to them, 14 And persuaded
  them to agree to all reasonable conditions, and promised that he would
  persuade the king that he must needs be a friend to them. 15 Then
  Maccabeus consented to all that Lysias desired, being careful of the
  common good; and whatsoever Maccabeus wrote to Lysias concerning the
  Yahudim (Jews), the king granted it.

  16 For there were letters written to the Yahudim (Jews) from Lysias to
  this effect: Lysias to the people of the Yahudim (Jews) sends
  greeting: 17 John and Absolom, who were sent from you, delivered me
  the petition subscribed, and made request for the performance of the
  contents thereof. 18 Therefore what things soever were meet to be
  reported to the king, I have declared them, and he has granted as much
  as might be. 19 And if then you will keep yourselves loyal to the
  state, hereafter also will I endeavour to be a means of your good. 20
  But of the particulars I have given order both to these and the other
  that came from me, to commune with you.

  21 Fare you well. The hundred and eight and fortieth year, the four
  and twentieth day of the month Dioscorinthius. 22 Now the king’s
  letter contained these words: King Antiochus to his brother Lysias
  sends greeting: 23 Since our father is translated to the gods, our
  will is, that they that are in our realm live quietly, that every one
  may attend upon his own affairs. 24 We understand also that the
  Yahudim (Jews) would not consent to our father, for to be brought to
  the custom of the Gentiles, but had rather keep their own manner of
  living: for the which cause they require of us, that we should suffer
  them to live after their own laws. 25 Wherefore our mind is, that this
  nation shall be in rest, and we have determined to restore them their
  temple, that they may live according to the customs of their
  forefathers.

  26 You shall do well therefore to send to them, and grant them peace,
  that when they are certified of our mind, they may be of good comfort,
  and ever go cheerfully about their own affairs. 27 And the letter of
  the king to the nation of the Yahudim (Jews) was after this manner:
  King Antiochus sends greeting to the council, and the rest of the
  Yahudim (Jews): 28 If you fare well, we have our desire; we are also
  in good health. 29 Menelaus declared to us, that your desire was to
  return home, and to follow your own business: 30 Wherefore they that
  will depart shall have safe conduct till the thirtieth day of
  Xanthicus with security.

  31 And the Yahudim (Jews) shall use their own kind of meats and laws,
  as before; and none of them any manner of ways shall be molested for
  things ignorantly done. 32 I have sent also Menelaus, that he may
  comfort you. 33 Fare you well. In the hundred forty and eighth year,
  and the fifteenth day of the month Xanthicus. 34 The Romans also sent
  to them a letter containing these words: Quintus Memmius and Titus
  Manlius, ambassadors of the Romans, send greeting to the people of the
  Yahudim (Jews). 35 Whatsoever Lysias the king’s cousin has granted,
  with it we also are well pleased.

  36 But touching such things as he judged to be referred to the king,
  after you have advised thereof, send one forthwith, that we may
  declare as it is convenient for you: for we are now going to Antioch.
  37 Therefore send some with speed, that we may know what is your mind.
  38 Farewell. This hundred and eight and fortieth year, the fifteenth
  day of the month Xanthicus.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter narrates the campaign of Lysias and the treaty that
followed. Lysias, the Seleucid general, marches against Jerusalem with a
large army. Judas's forces meet him near Beth-zur. The chapter records
the appearance of an angelic horseman who fights for Yashar'el (Israel)
(verse 8). The Seleucid army is defeated. Lysias proposes peace, and the
chapter records four letters that document the diplomatic settlement
(verses 16–38).

Three things matter.

First, the angelic horseman (verses 6–11) is one of the second-temple
narrative theophany elements that recur in the Maccabean campaigns. The
framework of this Series, which holds that the angel of Yahuah (God) —
the Formed One — is the active divine presence in the covenant
community's deliverances, finds in 2 Maccabees 11 the second-temple
narrative naming of that presence. The horseman is a horseman in white
clothing... shaking his armour of gold — appearing to be a man, fighting
alongside the Maccabean forces. The framework's reading: the Formed One
has been the Yashar'el (Israel)'s defender across the long covenant
history, and the second-temple narratives preserve that recognition.

Second, the treaty letters (verses 16–38) document the diplomatic
resolution of the conflict. The framework of this Series acknowledges
the political maneuvering and notes that the Maccabean leadership
operated within the imperial diplomatic system as effectively as it
operated on the battlefield. The covenant community had to learn both
languages: covenant prayer and imperial diplomacy.

Third, the chapter ends with relative peace under the terms of the
treaty. The framework of this Series, which holds that periods of
pressure are followed by periods of relative peace and that the covenant
community's task is to use both well, finds in 2 Maccabees 11 the
second-temple example of that pattern.

Cross-references: Joshua 5:13–15; 2 Kings 6:13–17; Daniel 10:5–6; Daniel
12:5–7; 2 Maccabees 3:24–28; Acts 12:7–11; Hebrews 1:14; Revelation
19:11–16.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 12

  1 When these covenants were made, Lysias went to the king, and the
  Yahudim (Jews) were about their husbandry. 2 But of the governours of
  several places, Timotheus, and Apollonius the son of Genneus, also
  Hieronymus, and Demophon, and beside them Nicanor the governor of
  Cyprus, would not suffer them to be quiet and live in peace. 3 The men
  of Joppa also did such an ungodly deed: they prayed the Yahudim (Jews)
  that dwelt among them to go with their wives and children into the
  boats which they had prepared, as though they had meant them no hurt.
  4 Who accepted of it according to the common decree of the city, as
  being desirous to live in peace, and suspecting nothing: but when they
  were gone forth into the deep, they drowned no less than two hundred
  of them. 5 When Judas heard of this cruelty done to his countrymen, he
  commanded those that were with him to make them ready.

  6 And calling upon Yahuah (God) the righteous Judge, he came against
  those murderers of his brothers, and burnt the haven by night, and set
  the boats on fire, and those that fled thither he slew. 7 And when the
  town was shut up, he went backward, as if he would return to root out
  all them of the city of Joppa. 8 But when he heard that the Jamnites
  were minded to do in like manner to the Yahudim (Jews) that dwelt
  among them, 9 He came upon the Jamnites also by night, and set fire on
  the haven and the navy, so that the light of the fire was seen at
  Jerusalem two hundred and forty furlongs off. 10 Now when they were
  gone from thence nine furlongs in their journey toward Timotheus, no
  fewer than five thousand men on foot and five hundred horsemen of the
  Arabians set upon him.

  11 Whereupon there was a very sore battle; but Judas’ side by the help
  of Yahuah (God) got the victory; so that the Nomades of Arabia, being
  overcome, besought Judas for peace, promising both to give him cattle,
  and to pleasure him otherwise. 12 Then Judas, thinking indeed that
  they would be profitable in many things, granted them peace: whereupon
  they shook hands, and so they departed to their tents. 13 He went also
  about to make a bridge to a certain strong city, which was fenced
  about with walls, and inhabited by people of divers countries; and the
  name of it was Caspis. 14 But they that were within it put such trust
  in the strength of the walls and provision of victuals, that they
  behaved themselves rudely toward them that were with Judas, railing
  and blaspheming, and uttering such words as were not to be spoken. 15
  Wherefore Judas with his company, calling upon the great Yahuah (God)
  of the world, who without rams or engines of war did cast down Jericho
  in the time of Joshua, gave a fierce assault against the walls,

  16 And took the city by the will of Yahuah (God), and made unspeakable
  slaughters, insomuch that a lake two furlongs broad near adjoining to
  it, being filled full, was seen running with blood. 17 Then departed
  they from thence seven hundred and fifty furlongs, and came to Characa
  to the Yahudim (Jews) that are called Tubieni. 18 But as for
  Timotheus, they found him not in the places: for before he had
  dispatched any thing, he departed from thence, having left a very
  strong garrison in a certain hold. 19 Howbeit Dositheus and Sosipater,
  who were of Maccabeus’ captains, went forth, and slew those that
  Timotheus had left in the fortress, above ten thousand men. 20 And
  Maccabeus ranged his army by bands, and set them over the bands, and
  went against Timotheus, who had about him an hundred and twenty
  thousand men of foot, and two thousand and five hundred horsemen.

  21 Now when Timotheus had knowledge of Judas’ coming, he sent the
  women and children and the other baggage to a fortress called Carnion:
  for the town was hard to besiege, and uneasy to come to, by reason of
  the straitness of all the places. 22 But when Judas his first band
  came in sight, the enemies, being struck with fear and terror through
  the appearing of him who seeth all things, fled amain, one running
  into this way, another that way, so as that they were often hurt of
  their own men, and wounded with the points of their own swords. 23
  Judas also was very earnest in pursuing them, killing those wicked
  wretches, of whom he slew about thirty thousand men. 24 Moreover
  Timotheus himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater, whom
  he besought with much craft to let him go with his life, because he
  had many of the Yahudim (Jews)’ parents, and the brothers of some of
  them, who, if they put him to death, should not be regarded. 25 So
  when he had assured them with many words that he would restore them
  without hurt, according to the agreement, they let him go for the
  saving of their brothers.

  26 Then Maccabeus marched forth to Carnion, and to the temple of
  Atargatis, and there he slew five and twenty thousand persons. 27 And
  after he had put to flight and destroyed them, Judas removed the host
  toward Ephron, a strong city, in which Lysias abode, and a great
  multitude of divers nations, and the strong young men kept the walls,
  and defended them mightily: in which also was great provision of
  engines and darts. 28 But when Judas and his company had called upon
  Almighty Yahuah (God), who with his power breaks the strength of his
  enemies, they won the city, and slew twenty and five thousand of them
  that were within, 29 From thence they departed to Scythopolis, which
  lieth six hundred furlongs from Jerusalem, 30 But when the Yahudim
  (Jews) that dwelt there had testified that the Scythopolitans dealt
  lovingly with them, and entreated them kindly in the time of their
  adversity;

  31 They gave them thanks, desiring them to be friendly still to them:
  and so they came to Jerusalem, the feast of the weeks approaching. 32
  And after the feast, called Pentecost, they went forth against Gorgias
  the governor of Idumea, 33 Who came out with three thousand men of
  foot and four hundred horsemen. 34 And it happened that in their
  fighting together a few of the Yahudim (Jews) were slain. 35 At which
  time Dositheus, one of Bacenor’s company, who was on horseback, and a
  strong man, was still upon Gorgias, and taking hold of his coat drew
  him by force; and when he would have taken that cursed man alive, a
  horseman of Thracia coming upon him struck off his shoulder, so that
  Gorgias fled to Marisa.

  36 Now when they that were with Gorgias had fought long, and were
  weary, Judas called upon Yahuah (God), that he would shew himself to
  be their helper and leader of the battle. 37 And with that he began in
  his own language, and sung psalms with a loud voice, and rushing
  unawares upon Gorgias’ men, he put them to flight. 38 So Judas
  gathered his host, and came into the city of Odollam, And when the
  seventh day came, they purified themselves, as the custom was, and
  kept the sabbath in the same place. 39 And upon the day following, as
  the use had been, Judas and his company came to take up the bodies of
  them that were slain, and to bury them with their kinsmen in their
  fathers’ graves. 40 Now under the coats of every one that was slain
  they found things consecrated to the idols of the Jamnites, which is
  forbidden the Yahudim (Jews) by the law. Then every man saw that this
  was the cause wherefore they were slain.

  41 All men therefore praising Yahuah (God), the righteous Judge, who
  had opened the things that were hid, 42 Betook themselves to prayer,
  and besought him that the sin committed might wholly be put out of
  remembrance. Besides, that noble Judas exhorted the people to keep
  themselves from sin, forsomuch as they saw before their eyes the
  things that came to pass for the sins of those that were slain. 43 And
  when he had made a gathering throughout the company to the sum of two
  thousand drachms of silver, he sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sin
  offering, doing in it very well and honestly, in that he was mindful
  of the resurrection: 44 For if he had not hoped that they that were
  slain should have risen again, it had been superfluous and vain to
  pray for the dead. 45 And also in that he perceived that there was
  great favour laid up for those that died godly, it was an holy and
  good thought. Whereupon he made a reconciliation for the dead, that
  they might be delivered from sin.

⸻

Commentary

The chapter narrates several smaller campaigns and contains the
controversial passage about prayer for the dead (verses 38–46). After a
battle, Judas finds that some of the slain Yahudi (Jewish) soldiers had
been wearing pagan amulets under their tunics — small idols of the gods
of Jamnia. Judas takes up a collection from his troops and sends two
thousand drachmas to Jerusalem so that a sin-offering may be offered for
the slain. The text comments approvingly on the act and articulates a
theological reflection on prayer for the dead.

Several things matter for the awakening reader, and this is one of the
most theologically weighted moments in the Apocrypha. Read this
commentary slowly, because the Catholic-Protestant cross-fire over this
passage has obscured what the framework of this Series actually holds.

First, the framework must hold the passage with care. The Catholic and
Orthodox traditions have used 2 Maccabees 12:42–46 to argue for prayer
for the dead and for the doctrine of purgatory. The Protestant tradition
has rejected the passage as evidence that the Apocrypha is not
canonical. Both responses miss what the passage actually shows.

What the passage shows: Judas Maccabeus and the writer of 2 Maccabees
thought it was appropriate to offer a sin-offering for slain soldiers
who had compromised the covenant by wearing pagan amulets. The text
records the act. The text comments approvingly. The text articulates the
theological reasoning: that the dead may be cleansed from their sins by
the offerings of the living.

What the passage does not show: it does not show that the Torah
commanded prayer for the dead; it does not show that the apostles
commanded prayer for the dead; it does not show that this practice is
the standard for the covenant community.

The 1234 filter (1 John 2:3–4 — that the standard is the keeping of the
commandments) and the apostolic witness apply. The Torah does not
establish a sin-offering for the dead; the sin-offering of Leviticus is
for the living. The apostolic letters do not establish prayer for the
dead as a Christian practice; the apostles preach the resurrection and
the judgment, not the manipulation of the post-mortem state by the
prayers of the living.

The framework of this Series, on the question of prayer for the dead,
holds the apocryphal witness for what it shows — what Judas Maccabeus
and the writer of 2 Maccabees thought was appropriate — without
inflating it to a doctrine the Torah and the apostles did not establish.
Read the passage. Note what it shows. Hold it against the Torah and the
apostolic witness. Do not let the apocryphal narrative establish a
doctrine the Torah and the apostles did not establish.

The framework's specific reading of the Catholic doctrine of purgatory
is direct. Purgatory is the doctrine that there is a third post-mortem
state — neither heaven nor hell — in which the souls of the dead who
died in grace but with venial sin remaining are purified by suffering
before being admitted to heaven. The doctrine has multiple historical
sources, but 2 Maccabees 12:42–46 is one of its primary apocryphal
anchors. The framework rejects the doctrine.

The rejection is anchored on the apostolic testimony to the once-for-all
sacrifice of the Messiah. Hebrews 9:24–28: For Messiah (Christ) is not
entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of
the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of Elohim (God)
for us: nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest
enters into the holy place every year with blood of others; for then
must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now
once in the end of the world has he appeared to put away sin by the
sacrifice of himself. And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but
after this the judgment: so Messiah (Christ) was once offered to bear
the sins of many. Hebrews 10:11–14: And every priest stands daily
ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never
take away sins: but this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for
sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of Elohim (God)... For by one offering
he has perfected for ever them that are sanctified. 1 John 1:7: the
blood of Jesus Messiah (Christ) his Son cleanses us from all sin. 1 John
2:1–2: if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus
Messiah (Christ) the righteous: and he is the propitiation for our sins.

The apostolic witness names the cleansing of sin as accomplished in the
Messiah's once-for-all sacrifice. Not annually. Not by repeated
offerings. Not by the prayers of the living for the dead. Once. Forever.
The cleansing of the dead from sin happens — when it happens — through
the Messiah's blood, not through later supplementary offerings. The
Catholic-Orthodox doctrine of purgatory inflates 2 Maccabees 12 against
the explicit apostolic witness, requiring repeated post-mortem
purification (purgatorial suffering) that the once-for-all sacrifice has
already accomplished. The framework holds the apostolic witness as the
standard and rejects the layered doctrine.

The rejection is not because the apocryphal witness is rejected; the
rejection is because the apocryphal witness has been inflated beyond
what the witness actually says. 2 Maccabees 12 records that Judas
thought the sin-offering would help the slain. It does not establish a
third post-mortem state, a graduated system of purification, the
suffering of the souls in purgatory, or the manipulation of the duration
of purgatorial suffering by the prayers and indulgences of the living.
All of those layers were added by post-apostolic tradition. The
framework holds the apocryphal text and rejects the layered doctrine.

The framework's specific reading on the proper covenant practice toward
the dead: pray to Yahuah (God) about your grief, your gratitude for the
deceased, and the comfort the Spirit gives the bereaved. Do not pray to
the dead. Do not pray for the post-mortem state of the dead. The dead
are in Yahuah (God)'s hand (Wisdom 3:1, 2 Esdras 7:32). The destination
is the resurrection at the appointed time. The atonement for sin was
accomplished in the Messiah's death and resurrection (1 John 1:7).
Nothing the living can do alters the post-mortem state of the dead. Pray
about them. Pray for the comfort of the living who grieve them. Do not
import the inherited Catholic-tradition practices that 2 Maccabees 12
has been used to support.

Second, the chapter's broader theological reflection (verses 43–45)
introduces the concept of the resurrection of the righteous and links
the offering for the dead to that hope. The text says: It had been
superfluous and vain to pray for the dead, if there had been no
resurrection. The framework's note: the writer of 2 Maccabees is
reasoning from the resurrection (which is real) to a particular practice
(offering for the dead) that is not warranted by the Torah or the
apostolic witness. The reasoning's premise (the resurrection) is right;
the conclusion (offering for the dead) does not follow from the premise.
The framework holds the right premise and rejects the unwarranted
conclusion.

Third, the closing of the chapter (verses 43–46) names that Judas's
purpose in offering for the slain was that they might be loosed from sin
in the resurrection. The framework's note: in the apostolic theology,
those who die in the Messiah are with Him (Philippians 1:23, 2
Corinthians 5:8) and are raised at His coming (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18).
The cleansing from sin happens in the Messiah's atoning work (1 John
1:7), not in the post-mortem offerings of the living. The framework,
while acknowledging what the apocryphal text shows, holds firmly to the
apostolic theology of atonement and resurrection and does not endorse
the practice the text records.

Cross-references: Leviticus 4:1–35; Leviticus 16:1–34; Hebrews 9:11–28;
Hebrews 10:11–14; 1 John 1:7; 2 Corinthians 5:6–10; Philippians 1:21–24;
1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; 1 Corinthians 15:50–58; 1 John 2:3–4; Wisdom of
Solomon 3:1; 2 Esdras 7:32.

2 Maccabees — Chapter 13

  1 In the hundred forty and ninth year it was told Judas, that
  Antiochus Eupator was coming with a great power into Judea, 2 And with
  him Lysias his protector, and ruler of his affairs, having either of
  them a Grecian power of footmen, an hundred and ten thousand, and
  horsemen five thousand and three hundred, and elephants two and
  twenty, and three hundred chariots armed with hooks. 3 Menelaus also
  joined himself with them, and with great dissimulation encouraged
  Antiochus, not for the safeguard of the country, but because he
  thought to have been made governor. 4 But the King of kings moved
  Antiochus’ mind against this wicked wretch, and Lysias informed the
  king that this man was the cause of all mischief, so that the king
  commanded to bring him to Berea, and to put him to death, as the
  manner is in that place. 5 Now there was in that place a tower of
  fifty cubits high, full of ashes, and it had a round instrument which
  on every side hanged down into the ashes.

  6 And whoever was condemned of sacrilege, or had committed any other
  grievous crime, there did all men thrust him to death. 7 Such a death
  it happened that wicked man to die, not having so much as burial in
  the earth; and that most justly: 8 For inasmuch as he had committed
  many sins about the altar, whose fire and ashes were holy, he received
  his death in ashes. 9 Now the king came with a barbarous and haughty
  mind to do far worse to the Yahudim (Jews), than had been done in his
  father’s time. 10 Which things when Judas perceived, he commanded the
  multitude to call upon Yahuah (God) night and day, that if ever at any
  other time, he would now also help them, being at the point to be put
  from their law, from their country, and from the holy temple:

  11 And that he would not suffer the people, that had even now been but
  a little refreshed, to be in subjection to the blasphemous nations. 12
  So when they had all done this together, and besought the merciful
  Yahuah (God) with weeping and fasting, and lying flat upon the ground
  three days long, Judas, having exhorted them, commanded they should be
  in a readiness. 13 And Judas, being apart with the elders, determined,
  before the king’s host should enter into Judea, and get the city, to
  go forth and try the matter in fight by the help of Yahuah (God). 14
  So when he had committed all to the Creator of the world, and exhorted
  his soldiers to fight manfully, even to death, for the laws, the
  temple, the city, the country, and the commonwealth, he camped by
