him, and the destination toward which the long restoration has been
moving is the destination at which the long restoration arrives.

The framework's last word in this volume is the framework's first word
in every awakening: come home. The fourteen books you have read were
preserved in the Bibles of your fathers for two and a half centuries;
they were stripped from the printed editions in the nineteenth century
by a decision your fathers' fathers' fathers did not make and did not
approve; they have been recovered now, in your generation, by the
providence of Yahuah (God) working through the public-domain digital
tradition of the King James Bible. They are back in your hand. The
witness is heard. The framework has been articulated. The 1234 filter
has been applied. The methodological sequence for reading Paul has been
demonstrated. The scattered seed has been named. The four houses have
been called home with the same patience.

What you do with what you have read is now between you and the Father
whose Spirit has been doing the awakening in you. The framework's task
in this volume is finished. Your task is the next step.

Test all things. Prove all things. Hold fast that which is good. Walk in
the light, as he is in the light. Keep his commandments. Pray without
ceasing. Watch and pray. Love one another. Be patient toward all men.
Wait on Yahuah (God). Wait. Wait. The destination is real. The journey
is appointed. The household is being gathered. The Messiah is coming.

In the language of Sirach 51:30: work your work betimes, and in his time
he will give you your reward.

In the language of Tobit 14:7: all those which love Yahuah (God) in
truth and justice shall rejoice, showing mercy to our brothers.

In the language of Baruch 5:9: for Yahuah (God) shall lead Yashar'el
(Israel) with joy in the light of his glory with the mercy and
righteousness that comes from him.

In the language of 2 Esdras 13:48: and now when they shall begin to
come, the Highest shall stay the springs of the stream again, that they
may go through.

In the language of the framework: come home. The seam between the houses
has been your standing-place long enough. The destination is on the
other side. The Father is calling. The Word is the way. Walk.

Appendices

Appendix A — A Glossary of Sacred Names and Key Terms

This glossary provides brief definitions of the sacred names, framework
terms, and second-temple vocabulary that recur in the volume. The
entries are alphabetical within each section.

Sacred Names

Yahuah (God) — The covenant name of the Elohim (God) of Yashar'el (Israel),
transliterated from the Tetragrammaton (the four Hebrew letters yod,
hey, vav, hey). The standard pronunciation is contested across Hebrew
roots and Restoration scholarship; the Restored Names Series uses Yahuah
(God) as the closest pronunciation supported by the manuscript and
lexical evidence available at the time of publication. The 1769 King
James text uses LORD (small caps) in place of the Tetragrammaton. This
volume restores Yahuah (God) where the underlying Hebrew or Greek text
supports the restoration.

Yahusha — The Hebrew name of the Messiah, transliterated as the standard
Hebrew form. Anglicized to "Jesus" via the Greek Iesous in the King
James tradition. The Restored Names Series uses Yahusha as the closest
form to the Hebrew Yeshua / Yehoshua, with the divine name (yah)
preserved at the front. The volume uses "Yahusha (Jesus)" at first
occurrences in each chapter and Yahusha or Jesus thereafter.

Elohim — The Hebrew word commonly translated "Elohim (God)" in the Old Testament.
The plural-majesty form is used for the singular God of Yashar'el
(Israel) and is also used in some passages for foreign gods, judges, or
angelic beings. The Restored Names Series uses Elohim where the
underlying Hebrew shows the plural-majesty form referring to the
singular God of Yashar'el (Israel); in this volume, the primarily-Greek
source text of the Apocrypha uses kurios or theos in most passages, so
Elohim restoration has been conservative.

Messiah — Hebrew "the Anointed One." Translated as "the Messiah" or "the
Messiah (Christ)" in English Bibles. The volume uses Messiah as the
Hebrew form parenthetically and "the Messiah" or "the Messiah (Christ)"
in narrative prose.

Paul — The Hebrew name of the apostle Paul. He was Paul of Tarsus, a
Pharisee of the tribe of Benjamin, before he became the apostolic
emissary to the diaspora. The Restored Names Series uses Paul at first
occurrences and Paul thereafter.

Jacob — The Hebrew name of the patriarch Jacob, transliterated. The
third patriarch, son of Isaac, father of the twelve tribes. Anglicized
to "Jacob" in the King James tradition. The volume uses Jacob at first
occurrences and Jacob thereafter where context permits.

The Most High — A formal title for Yahuah (God) (Hebrew: El Elyon). Used
frequently in the Apocrypha as a translation of the Greek hupsistos. The
volume preserves "the Most High" as the formal title.

Framework Terms

The 1234 of Truth / The 1234 Filter — Shorthand for 1 John 2:3–4 ("And
hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments. He that
says, I know him, and keeps not his commandments, is a liar, and the
truth is not in him"). The Restored Names Series uses 1 John 2:3–4 as
the master filter against which any interpretation of any scripture is
tested. If a reading requires 1 John 2:3–4 to be false, that reading is
false.

The Four Houses — The framework's term for the four major inherited
religious systems from which the awakening remnant is being called:
institutional Christianity, Judaism (Talmudic and rabbinic), Hebrew
roots / Torah observant / Messianic communities, and the Islamic
tradition. None of the four is the destination. Each has carried
inherited deception. The framework calls all four home.

The False Inclusion Gospel — The framework's term for the teaching that
anyone who believes and Torah-keeps is thereby counted as Yashar'el
(Israel) — that faith and obedience constitute covenant identity
regardless of bloodline or prophetic lineage. The framework identifies
this teaching as a Christian replacement theology in Torah clothing. The
framework distinguishes between covenant lineage (the actual paternal
blood remnant of the seed of promise) and covenant attachment (those of
the nations who have come into covenant through faith and obedience),
holding both as real categories without conflating them.

The Formed and the Formless — The framework's term for the relationship
between the Father and the Son in the framework's nature-of-Elohim (God)
theology. The Father is the Formless infinite source. The Son is the
Formed expression of the Formless, who was drawn from the Formless and
remained in relationship with the Source. The Formed One is the active
divine presence in the Old Testament narratives (the angel of Yahuah
(God), the one who appeared to the patriarchs, who spoke from the
burning bush, who led Yashar'el (Israel) through the wilderness) and is
the Word who came in the flesh as Yahusha (Jesus). The framework rejects
the Trinity doctrine (three co-equal persons) and rejects modalism
(collapsing the Father and Son into one undifferentiated being); the
framework holds the Formless-and-Formed structure as the right
articulation of what the scriptures show.

The Methodological Sequence for Reading Paul — The framework's two-step
methodology for reading the Pauline letters. Step One: establish what
Paul was drawing FROM (his Torah, prophetic, and second-temple
wisdom-tradition foundation). Step Two: identify what Paul was arguing
AGAINST (the specific external distortions he was rebutting in each
letter — the circumcision party of Galatians, the false-inclusion claim
of Romans, the temptation to retreat to the Levitical priesthood in
Hebrews). The methodology is the antidote to both the antinomian misuse
of Paul that abolishes the Torah and the Torah-observant rejection of
Paul that drops his letters entirely.

Replacement Theology — The framework's term for the teaching that one
group has replaced another in the covenant. The Christian form: the
church replaced Yashar'el (Israel). The Hebrew roots form: the
Torah-observant community has replaced the specific covenant people the
prophets addressed. The framework rejects all forms of replacement
theology. The covenant with Yashar'el (Israel) has not been transferred;
it has been preserved through the dispersion and is being restored
through the gathering of the scattered seed of all twelve tribes.

The Scattered Seed / The Two-House Framework — The framework's term for
the prophetic understanding of the gathering of the covenant people. The
northern kingdom of Yashar'el (Israel) (the house of Yashar'el (Israel),
ten tribes) was scattered by Assyria in 722 BCE. The southern kingdom
(the house of Yahudah (Judah), two tribes) was carried into Babylon in
586 BCE. Yahudah (Judah) returned in the post-exilic period under Cyrus
and Darius; the ten tribes did not return in that period and have been
scattered among the nations for nearly twenty-eight centuries. The
framework holds that the prophets named the gathering of both houses
(Hosea 1, Hosea 2, Ezekiel 37, Jeremiah 31), that the apostles preached
the gathering of the scattered seed (the diaspora communities of the
Galatians, the Thessalonians, and the others were in fact scattered seed
of Yashar'el (Israel) rather than ethnic Greeks), and that the appointed
final gathering of all twelve tribes from every nation where they have
been scattered is the destination of the long restoration.

Sons of Adam / The Adamic Lineage — The framework's term for the
specific covenant lineage of the seed of promise, beginning with Adam
(in the framework's reading, a specific covenant creation distinct from
the men and women of the earth in Genesis 1). The framework
distinguishes between Adamic seed and the other nations, while
acknowledging that the corruption of the serpent introduced the tares
within both groups. The destination of the long restoration is the
gathering of the sons of Adam — the twelve tribes — into the appointed
inheritance under the reign of the Messiah, with the surviving nations
as those over whom the sons of Adam serve as a kingdom of priests.

Sons of Belial — The framework's term for the corrupted seed within the
covenant community — those identifiable not by their bloodline (they
often are of the covenant lineage) but by their works. Eli's sons in 1
Samuel 2 are the canonical example. The two corrupt elders of Susanna
are the apocryphal example. The high priest Menelaus in 2 Maccabees 4 is
another. The framework holds that the sons of Belial operate from inside
the covenant community and that the corruption of religious authority is
one of the recurring patterns of covenant history.

The Tares — The framework's term for the corrupted seed introduced into
the world through the fall of the angels and the seduction of Eve. The
tares grow within both the sons of Adam and the other nations. They are
sifted out at the appointed harvest. The framework holds that the
parable of the wheat and the tares (Matthew 13:24–43) is the canonical
articulation of what Genesis 6, 1 Enoch, and the second-temple
imagination already understood about the corrupted seed.

Victims-Not-Enemies Posture — The framework's term for the posture
toward the four houses. The people inside the inherited religious
systems are not the enemy; they are deceived victims who inherited the
lies in good faith. The framework's response is patience,
non-condescension, the steady offering of the framework's reading, and
the call home.

Second-Temple Vocabulary

Apocrypha (the King James fourteen) — The fourteen books that appeared
between the Old and New Testaments in the original 1611 King James
Bible: 1 Esdras, 2 Esdras, Tobit, Judith, the Rest of Esther (the Greek
additions to Esther), the Wisdom of Solomon, Ecclesiasticus (Sirach),
Baruch with the Letter of Jeremiah, the Song of the Three Holy Children,
the History of Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, the Prayer of Manasseh, 1
Maccabees, 2 Maccabees. Removed from most Protestant printed editions
after the British and Foreign Bible Society's 1826 decision; restored to
printed editions in some traditions and recovered for the awakening
reader in this volume.

Apocalyptic Literature — A genre of second-temple literature
characterized by visions, angelic interpreters, eschatological frames,
and symbolic imagery. The Apocrypha contains substantial apocalyptic
material in 2 Esdras (and elements in Tobit and the Wisdom of Solomon).
The canonical Daniel and Revelation are apocalyptic literature. The
framework reads apocalyptic literature for what witness shows, applies
the canonical apocalyptic standard (the canonical Daniel and
Revelation), and does not legislate from non-canonical apocalyptic
specifics.

Diaspora — The Greek word for the dispersion of the Yahudi (Jewish) (and
broader Israelite) communities among the nations. The framework holds
that the diaspora is the same dispersion the prophets named in
Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26 — the scattering of the covenant people
under the curses of the broken covenant. The diaspora is the location
from which the gathering of the scattered seed proceeds.

The Hasmonean Dynasty — The dynasty established by the Maccabean revolt,
beginning with Mattathias and continuing through John Hyrcanus,
Aristobulus I, Alexander Jannaeus, Salome Alexandra, and the rivalry of
Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II that ended with the Roman conquest of
Jerusalem in 63 BCE. The dynasty held both the high priesthood and the
political-military leadership and is the political background of the
world the Messiah was born into.

Hellenization — The process by which Greek language, culture, and
religion spread through the territories conquered by Alexander the Great
and his successors. The Hellenization crisis of the second century BCE
under Antiochus IV Epiphanes is the historical setting of 1 Maccabees
and 2 Maccabees. The framework holds Hellenization as a recurring
pattern of imperial cultural assimilation that the covenant community
has had to navigate across centuries.

The Pharisees — The second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) school that emphasized
Torah observance, the oral tradition (which the framework holds with
care, as the rabbinic-Talmudic tradition that obscures plain reading of
the prophets), and the resurrection of the dead. The apostle Paul was a
Pharisee. Yahusha's (Jesus') ministry intersected with the Pharisaic
school at multiple points; he affirmed some of their teachings (the
resurrection, the keeping of the commandments) while rebuking others
(the elevation of oral tradition above the written Torah, the corruption
of leadership).

The Sadducees — The second-temple Yahudi (Jewish) school of the priestly
aristocracy that held to the written Torah only (rejecting the oral
tradition), denied the resurrection of the dead, and was politically
aligned with the Hasmonean and later the Roman authorities. Yahusha's
debate with the Sadducees in Matthew 22, Mark 12, and Luke 20 is over
the resurrection. The framework holds that the Sadducean denial of the
resurrection was wrong and that the apostolic affirmation of the
resurrection (drawing on the Pharisaic tradition and on second-temple
texts like 2 Maccabees 7) is the right reading.

The Septuagint (LXX) — The Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures,
made in Alexandria, Egypt, in the third and second centuries BCE. The
Septuagint includes the Hebrew canonical books and the additional
apocryphal books in Greek. The Septuagint was the Bible of the diaspora
communities and of the early Christian church; the apostles often quoted
from it in their letters. The framework holds the Septuagint as a
historically significant translation that the apostles used, while
affirming that the Hebrew text is the standard for the canonical books.

Torah — The Hebrew word for "instruction" or "law," referring most
specifically to the five books of Moses (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus,
Numbers, Deuteronomy) and more broadly to the Hebrew scriptures as a
whole. The framework holds the Torah as the standard against which all
witness is measured. The Torah is not abolished; the Torah is
internalized in the new covenant; the keeping of the Torah is the
standard of covenant faithfulness.

Appendix B — Summary of the Sacred-Name Restoration in This Volume

The 1769 King James Apocrypha source text has been examined for
sacred-name restoration. The policy in this volume is the every-mention
policy: where the underlying text supports the covenant name, the
restored name is set on every occurrence — not at the first occurrence
only, and not selectively in a curated set of prayers. The reader who
opens to any chapter, on any page, sees the sacred names in the body
text wherever the text speaks of the covenant deity, the covenant
people, the Messiah, or the Spirit. The retention mechanism is the
parenthetical equivalent in plain English. It is carried on every
mention so that a reader meeting the names for the first time is never
asked to remember a glossary entry from earlier in the book.

Where Yahuah (God) is restored:

Wherever the underlying text — Hebrew, Greek, or Latin — points to the
covenant name. In practice this means: at every occurrence of the LORD
(small caps in the original 1769) and at every occurrence of the Lord
and of God in any context where the text refers to the covenant deity
rather than to a human master or to the pagan deities of the surrounding
nations. The Apocrypha is primarily Greek, and the Greek apocryphal
books use the title kurios where the Hebrew tradition placed YHWH; the
second-temple translators were observing a vocalization taboo, not
erasing the name. Restoring the name at every mention is the editorial
decision to undo the taboo for the awakening reader.

Where Elohim (God) is used:

In the possessive title constructions — your Elohim, our Elohim, their
Elohim, his Elohim, my Elohim — where the covenant grammar attaches a
possessive to a title rather than to the personal name. The 1769 source
uses the Lord and Elohim (God) interchangeably in these constructions, and both
have been carried into Elohim (God) in this edition. The personal name
Yahuah does not naturally take a possessive in covenant grammar. The
plural-majesty title does, and it carries the right register for those
constructions.

Where the Most High is preserved as a title:

Where the underlying Greek is hupsistos. The Most High is a title in the
source text and is preserved as a title in this edition, with the
modernised capitalisation. No name restoration is performed where the
source is hupsistos, because hupsistos is not the covenant name behind a
vocalisation taboo — it is its own title in its own right.

Where Yashar'el (Israel), Yahudah (Judah), Yahudim (Jews), and Yahudi
(Jew/Jewish) are restored:

At every mention of the corresponding English names in the body text and
in the scripture quotations. The covenant people-names are restored on
the same every-mention principle as the divine name: the parenthetical
preserves the conventional English so that no reader is left to
translate, and the sacred form carries through the volume so that the
reader is steadily reoriented to the covenant identity that the King
James English flattens.

Where Messiah (Christ), Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit), and Yahusha
(Jesus) are restored:

Where the text means them. In the fourteen books, that is a small set of
named occurrences. Messiah (Christ) appears in 2 Esdras 7:29. Ruach
HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) appears in Wisdom of Solomon 9:17 and 2 Esdras
14:22. Yahusha (Jesus) appears in 2 Esdras 7:28. Every other occurrence
of "Jesus" in the Apocrypha names a different figure — Jeshua son of
Jozadak, Jesus the son of Sirach (Yeshua ben Sira), Joshua son of Nun
(Jesus the son of Nave), and others — and is preserved in the
conventional King James English form so that readers do not confuse the
high-priestly Yeshua of the second-temple period with the Messiah whose
name was given for our salvation.

What is not restored:

Patriarch names and place-names, including Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses,
Aaron, David, Solomon, Joshua, Jerusalem, Babylon, Judea, and Jewry. The
retention mechanism for the sacred names is reserved for where it is
load-bearing: the covenant name of the deity, the covenant name of the
people, and the name of the Messiah. Restoring every patriarch name to
its Hebrew form would raise the entry cost on the reader without
carrying the third-commandment weight that Yahuah (God) and Yahusha
(Jesus) carry, and without naming the covenant body the way Yashar'el
(Israel) and Yahudah (Judah) do.

The principle of every-mention restoration:

The volume's restoration policy is consistent and uniform across all
fourteen books. Where a divine name or a covenant people-name belongs,
it is restored — every time, with its parenthetical. Where the
underlying text supports nothing more than a generic title (kurios in
routine narrative, Elohim in a possessive construction, hupsistos as the
Most High), the appropriate form is used and the parenthetical is set on
every mention there as well. The reader does not need to consult an
apparatus to know what is happening on any given page. The page itself
shows the names the manuscript witness was always trying to carry.

Appendix C — A Note on the Relationship Between the Apocrypha and the Pseudepigrapha

The reader who has worked through this volume may already be familiar
with other second-temple texts that are not in the King James Apocrypha
but are in the broader corpus called the Pseudepigrapha. Books like 1
Enoch, Jubilees, the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, 2 Baruch, the
Apocalypse of Abraham, the Ascension of Isaiah, and the Sibylline
Oracles all belong to this broader category. The Restored Names Series
has dedicated volumes (or volumes in preparation) for the most
theologically significant of the pseudepigraphal texts — notably the
Book of Enoch, which is the Series's first volume.

What is the relationship between the Apocrypha (the fourteen books bound
into the original 1611 KJV) and the Pseudepigrapha (the broader corpus
of second-temple writings outside the canonical Hebrew Bible and the
King James Apocrypha)? Three distinctions matter.

First, historical-canonical reception. The fourteen King James Apocrypha
books were received by the Catholic and Orthodox traditions as
deuterocanonical or fully canonical. They were included in the original
1611 King James Bible as a distinct section between the Old and New
Testaments. They have a long printing tradition in English-speaking
Bibles. The Pseudepigrapha, by contrast, were never received into any
major Christian canon. They were preserved in various manuscript
traditions (Ethiopian Christian for 1 Enoch, Slavic Christian for 2
Enoch, Hebrew or Latin for Jubilees, etc.) but did not have the broad
canonical reception the Apocrypha had.

Second, textual-historical character. Some of the Apocrypha books (1
Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, Sirach, the Wisdom of Solomon) are the
second-temple-period historical and wisdom literature of mainstream
Yahudi (Jewish) communities. Some of the Pseudepigrapha (1 Enoch,
Jubilees) are also from mainstream Yahudi (Jewish) communities of the
second-temple period and were treated with high respect in some circles
(1 Enoch was cited as scripture by the apostle Jude in Jude 1:14–15).
The line between the two corpora is not a line of inherent quality; it
is a line of canonical reception history.

Third, the framework's reading. The Restored Names Series treats both
corpora as supplementary witness — to be heard, to be tested, to be
honored where they testify to the framework's central concerns (the
scattered seed, the appointed reign, the Torah's centrality, the
Messianic hope, the resurrection theology), and to be filtered through
the 1234 of Truth and the canonical standard where they wander into
matters the canonical scriptures address differently. The framework does
not elevate the Apocrypha above the Pseudepigrapha or vice versa. The
framework holds both as second-temple witness, with each book judged on
its own merits and its own framework-relevance.

For the reader who completes this volume and wants to continue into the
Pseudepigrapha, the framework's recommended next reads are:

- The Book of Enoch (1 Enoch) — the Series's first volume, available in
the Restored Names edition. The most important Pseudepigraphal text for
understanding the Watcher tradition, the apocalyptic literature, and the
second-temple framework of the sons of Adam, the corruption of the seed,
and the appointed judgment. - The Book of Jubilees — a second-temple
retelling of Genesis through Exodus 12, organized on the heavenly
calendar. The Series may have a dedicated volume on Jubilees in
preparation; check remnantofpromise.org for current availability. - 2
Baruch (the Apocalypse of Baruch) — a first-century-CE Yahudi (Jewish)
apocalypse with substantial overlap with 2 Esdras and significant
framework-relevance. The Series's framework reads 2 Baruch as the second
witness to the appointed reign as a symbolic measure (the framework's
note in the master framework references this). - The Testament of the
Twelve Patriarchs — second-temple deathbed-blessings of each of Jacob's
twelve sons, with significant insight into the second-temple Two-House
understanding.

The reader who has worked through the King James Apocrypha and the Book
of Enoch will have engaged with the most theologically significant
second-temple non-canonical literature available. The remaining
Pseudepigrapha is supplementary. The canonical Hebrew Bible and the
apostolic writings remain the standard. All other reading is held
against that standard.

Appendix D — Suggested Reading Sequence for the Awakening Remnant

The framework of this Series has insisted, throughout the volume, that
the awakening reader's task is the canonical scriptures first and the
supplementary witness second. As a closing aid, the framework offers a
suggested reading sequence for the awakening reader who wants to
integrate what this volume has shown into a sustained Bible-and-witness
reading practice.

Phase One — The Foundation (Six to Twelve Months)

Read through the canonical Hebrew Bible (the Tanakh / the Old Testament)
cover to cover. Read it slowly. Read it with the framework's eye for the
scattered seed, the covenant lineage, the Two-House framework, the
prophets' restoration promises, the Torah's commandments, and the
Messianic foreshadowings. Read Genesis through Deuteronomy as the
foundation. Read Joshua through 2 Chronicles as the historical
narrative. Read Ezra and Nehemiah as the post-exilic restoration. Read
Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Solomon as the wisdom
literature. Read Isaiah through Malachi as the prophets, paying
particular attention to the gathering of the scattered seed promises and
the Messianic prophecies.

Phase Two — The New Testament (Three to Six Months)

Read through the New Testament cover to cover. Read it with the
framework's eye for the world the Messiah walked into (which the
Apocrypha has now illuminated), the apostles' ministry to the diaspora
communities (which the framework reads as the gathering of the scattered
seed), the methodological sequence for reading Paul (which the framework
has demonstrated in this volume), and the apostolic theology of the
resurrection, the priesthood of the Messiah, and the appointed return.

Phase Three — The Apocrypha (this volume, three to six months)

Read through the volume you are now closing. Read it with the canonical
scriptures fresh in mind. Test every commentary moment against the
framework's master tools (the 1234 filter, the methodological sequence
for reading Paul, the victims-not-enemies posture). Carry the
cross-references forward into your personal study. Mark the framework's
sacred-name restorations and let them retrain your reading of the divine
name across all your reading.

Phase Four — The Pseudepigrapha (six to twelve months)

Read the Book of Enoch in the Restored Names edition. Read Jubilees if
the Series has produced a Restored Names edition by the time you arrive
at this phase. Read 2 Baruch and the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs
if available. Test all of these against the canonical standard.

Phase Five — The Restored Names Series (ongoing)

Read the other volumes of the Restored Names Series as they are
produced. Each volume addresses a specific framework concern — the
Galatian deception, the rapture deception, the question of who the
Yashar'el (Israel) of Yahuah (God) is, the framework's reading of the
Pauline letters, and other works in preparation.

Throughout — Daily Practice

Throughout all five phases and beyond, maintain the daily practice of
the awakening remnant: morning and evening prayer (or whatever pattern
the Spirit has given you), Sabbath observance, the keeping of the
appointed feasts of the Torah's calendar, the sustained study of the
Word, fellowship with others who are walking the same walk, and the
patient witness of the framework's victims-not-enemies posture toward
those still inside the four houses.

The framework's reading of any single text — including this volume — is
offered for your testing. The framework does not claim final authority;
the framework claims faithful witness. The standard is the Word. The
Spirit is the teacher. The framework's task is to put you back into the
Word with eyes that have been retrained by what the Word actually shows.
From that point forward, your task is the long walk in the direction the
Word has shown you.

Appendix E — A Note on the Framework's Reading of the Hasmonean Period and the World of the New Testament

The volume has named, repeatedly, that the Hasmonean period (167 BCE to
63 BCE) is the political and religious context the New Testament walks
into. A brief framework summary at the close of the volume may help the
reader carry forward what 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, and the broader
apocryphal corpus have shown.

The Hasmonean dynasty began with covenant zeal. Mattathias's refusal to
sacrifice on the pagan altar and his killing of the apostate Yahudi
(Jew) at Modein (1 Maccabees 2) was the right response to
imperial-coerced Hellenization. Judas Maccabeus's military campaigns (1
Maccabees 3–9) restored the temple, ended the official desecration, and
gave the covenant community three decades of relative peace.

But by the second generation of the dynasty — Jonathan (1 Maccabees
9–12) and Simon (1 Maccabees 13–16) — the family had moved from
priestly-revolutionary movement to dynastic priest-kingship. The
conflation of the high priesthood with the political-military leadership
in the same person was a structural problem the Torah had separated. The
Hasmoneans assumed both offices. The dynasty began to operate as a
regional power within the broader Hellenistic political system, taking
sides in the Seleucid succession wars, making treaties with Rome and
Sparta, accumulating wealth and territory.

By the third and fourth generations — John Hyrcanus, Aristobulus I,
Alexander Jannaeus, Salome Alexandra, and the rivalry of Hyrcanus II and
Aristobulus II — the Hasmonean state had become a fully-developed
Hellenistic monarchy with priestly trappings. The Pharisees emerged as
the popular opposition to the Sadducean priestly aristocracy that the
Hasmoneans embodied. Alexander Jannaeus's brutal suppression of
Pharisaic dissent (around 90 BCE) created the lasting hostility between
the priestly and Pharisaic schools that would still be visible in the
New Testament. The Essenes withdrew to Qumran, refusing to recognize
either the corrupt Hasmonean priesthood or the increasingly
Roman-aligned political compromises.

When Pompey conquered Jerusalem in 63 BCE, the Hasmonean state was so
divided that two Hasmonean princes had invited Roman arbitration.
Pompey's entry into the temple — into the Holy of Holies itself — was
the second great desecration in the second-temple period (after
Antiochus's). The Hasmonean dynasty, increasingly nominal, persisted
under Roman client status until Herod the Great married the last
Hasmonean princess (Mariamne), eliminated the rest of the family, and
established the Herodian client kingship that ruled Judea at the time of
the Messiah's birth.

This is the political-religious world Yahusha (Jesus) walked into. The
temple was the rebuilt second temple, expanded by Herod into a massive
complex but still missing the ark of the covenant and still operating
without an active prophetic ministry until the immerser (John the
Baptist) appeared. The priesthood was the Sadducean-Herodian priestly
aristocracy, deeply compromised. The Pharisees were the popular
religious authority but had developed the layered oral-tradition system
the framework critiques. The zealots were the underground military
resistance preparing for the next revolt against Rome (which would come
in 66–73 CE and would end in the destruction of the second temple). The
Essenes were withdrawn at Qumran.

Into this world the Messiah was born — in Bethlehem, of the lineage of
David, in the days of Caesar Augustus, under the local rule of Herod the
Great. His ministry intersected with all the parties: he rebuked the
Sadducean priestly aristocracy, debated with the Pharisees, addressed
the zealot impulse in some of his disciples, and (according to some
readings) was familiar with Essene practices through the immerser's
wilderness-baptism ministry. He claimed the Davidic kingship the
Hasmoneans had effectively bypassed. He claimed the priesthood of the
Messiah that Hebrews would later articulate as superseding the
Aaronic-Hasmonean line. He proclaimed the gathering of the lost sheep of
the house of Yashar'el (Israel) (Matthew 15:24) — the framework's
central concern, the gathering of the scattered seed — as the work he
had come to do.

The reader who has worked through the Apocrypha is now equipped to read
the New Testament with eyes that see the historical-political-religious
context the apostles and the Messiah were addressing. The world of the
Gospels is not a world out of nowhere. It is the world the Hasmoneans
built, the Romans inherited, and the Messiah walked into to deliver the
lost sheep from the system that had made them lost.

The framework's final framework-summary on the Hasmonean period: the
founding generation was right; the dynasty drifted; the corruption
became total; the Messiah came at the appointed time to do what no
Hasmonean ever could — to be the priest-king the Torah and the prophets
had named, and to begin the gathering of the scattered seed of all
twelve tribes that would close in the appointed final restoration.

The Apocrypha is the historical record of how the world of the Messiah
was made. The framework reads the Apocrypha for that record. The reader
who carries the record forward into the New Testament will read the
Gospels and the apostolic letters with new clarity.
